Joint statement by the members of The Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan - First anniversary of the october 26th, 2025 atrocity in El Fasher (Sudan) Sudan Conflicts Joint statement On : October 23rd 2026 One year ago, on 26 October 2025, the violence in and around El Fasher reached a devastating peak following months of siege and escalating attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Civilians were subjected to horrific atrocities including mass killings, ethnically motivated killings, summary executions, torture, disappearances, forced recruitment, arbitrary detentions, and widespread sexual and gender-based violence. Entire communities were forcibly displaced, and humanitarian access was obstructed, exacerbating hunger, insecurity, human suffering and deprivation. Today, the Coalition for Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan stands together to remember and recognise the suffering of victims and survivors, and reaffirm our shared determination to prevent further atrocities and pursue accountability. The findings of the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan have laid bare the scale and severity of violations of international humanitarian law and violations and abuses of international human rights law committed in and around El Fasher. The Coalition supports the UN Fact-Finding Mission and its work, and welcomes the recent renewal of its mandate. We also welcome the work of the African Union’s Fact-Finding Mission, and its collaboration with the UN. One year on, many civilians continue to bear the consequences of these atrocities. Across Sudan, civilians continue to be victims of violence, including systemic and widespread use of sexual violence, displacement, attacks on civilian infrastructure and restrictions on humanitarian assistance. The growing use of drones in attacks affecting civilians, and civilian infrastructure is deepening humanitarian needs and protection risks. Taken together, this demonstrates that the risk of further large-scale atrocities in Sudan remains acute. Restrictions on humanitarian access and repeated attacks on humanitarian actors, local and frontline responders are unacceptable, and are compounding the suffering of millions of Sudanese civilians. This anniversary is a reminder that we must act collectively to prevent their repetition. Justice and accountability are vital to achieving sustainable peace in Sudan. Victims and survivors deserve justice and accountability for the heinous crimes perpetrated during this conflict. Those responsible for serious violations and abuses must be investigated and held to account. The Coalition will continue working with Sudanese and international partners to support credible accountability processes, including the work of the International Criminal Court concerning Darfur, and meaningful transitional justice for the people of Sudan. Sudanese human rights defenders and civil society organisations play a crucial role in supporting victims and survivors, documenting abuses, and ensuring that Sudanese perspectives help shape future accountability and justice efforts. Often working at great personal risk, they are indispensable partners in the pursuit of peace, justice and accountability. Victims of conflict related sexual violence must have safe and confidential access to medical, psychosocial and legal support. There is no military solution to this conflict. The war must end. The Coalition calls on all parties to comply fully with international humanitarian law, including by protecting civilians and facilitating safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. We also call on all states to comply with international law, and use their influence to protect civilians, prevent further atrocities and help bring this devastating conflict to an end, including by ceasing to arm, finance and otherwise enable the war in Sudan, and by fully respecting UN sanctions including the arms embargo on Darfur. One year after El Fasher, our message is clear: the victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible. The Ministers discussed various issues of regional and international importance, namely US/Israel-Iran conflict, Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the need for a negotiated two-state solution, the appalling Houthi militia attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Government of Yemen, safety and freedom of navigation, escalated tension in Straits of Hormuz and Bab El Mandeb and the Black Sea. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has congratulated the Student List on its victory in the parliamentary elections in Serbia, calling it a new page in the country's history, and stated Ukraine's readiness to expand cooperation with Serbia.
"Changes have taken place in Serbia – the victory of the 'Student List', and this is obviously a new page in the history of the country and the people," Zelenskyy wrote on the social network X on Monday.
He wished Serbia success, real development, and warm relations with the European community.
"We in Ukraine thank Serbia for its respect for our people and state, our independence. And we are always glad of our common results – everything that strengthens our societies and gives people more opportunities. We are ready to continue increasing our cooperation, and may all the good hopes of the people in Serbia be realized," the president noted.

"We do not have final results yet, but based on the sample... it is clear that we lost these elections. The Student List won: they will have between 135 and 140 seats, and we have 105, no one else entered parliament," Vucic told reporters.
The snap elections were called by Vucic in September following nearly two years of continuous student protests against corruption and the tightening of government authoritarianism. The demonstrations erupted after the tragedy in the city of Novi Sad in 2024, where 16 people died due to the collapse of a canopy at the railway station.
The student movement gained broad public support and became the biggest political challenge to Vucic since he came to power as prime minister in 2014 and was subsequently elected president in 2017.

Liz Truss claims Brits would be on Mars by 2040 if she hadn’t been ousted

LONDON — Liz Truss claims the U.K. would have managed successful missions to Mars within years — if only her 49-day premiership hadn’t been cut short.
The assertion comes in the former British prime minister’s new book “Bank Job,” which was published Monday and claims to explain “how the Bank of England broke the bond market and brought down the government” when her mini-budget in 2022 precipitated market turmoil.
In its closing chapter, the book paints a vivid picture of what Truss believes life in 2040 would be like if her policies had been given a chance to bed in. “Several missions to Mars have now been launched from Britain’s space port,” Truss’ book imagines.
Advertisement
The ex-PM also opts for some more grounded policy dreams.
She envisages a 2040 in which “there are now no European Union laws in Britain,” a “permissive regime for artificial intelligence” is in place, and tumbling energy costs and faster planning timelines have helped make the U.K. a leader in AI.
“Bitcoin received tax treatment consistent with its status as a form of money for commercial purposes,” she imagines. “No central bank digital currency was introduced.”
Since leaving office after a revolt in her own party, Truss has dismissed claims her economic decisions — which included a huge energy bills bailout and tax cuts funded by fresh borrowing — were responsible for crashing the pound.
She has instead pointed the finger at the central bank, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility watchdog, accusing them of working against her. Her new book takes direct aim at the Bank of England, which sold £80 billion of gilts the day before the mini-budget.
Truss lost her House of Commons seat at the 2024 general election, and has since been involved in launching the Conservative Political Action Conference in Britain.

Netanyahu faces reckoning for October 7 in Israel’s first vote since attack
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:46:38 CET
20:46:38 KST

By Maayan Lubell and Michal Yaakov Itzhaki
BE’ERI, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Gal Cohen walks along a memorial wall engraved with the names of the men, women and children slain in the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on his kibbutz. For him, the idea that the man leading Israel, then and since, may be re-elected on Tuesday is painful.
One-in-ten residents of his kibbutz, Be’eri, were among the 1,200 people killed in Hamas’ surprise attack. Dozens were among the 251 taken hostage to Gaza. It was Israel’s deadliest single day.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should have taken responsibility and stepped down, said Cohen, 61, and the fact that he has fulfilled a full term in office is a slap in the face. Tuesday’s election, he said, is critical for Israel.
“If this government will stay, many hearts and minds will be broken. It will be really hard to continue,” said Cohen.
Many of Netanyahu’s opponents see the election as an opportunity at last to deliver a long-postponed reckoning for the worst security failure in generations. But even if Israel’s longest-serving prime minister loses his majority, he could well escape the decisive verdict his foes are seeking.
Netanyahu has rejected blame for the breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. He maintains that Israel’s wars against Hamas in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran will result in a more peaceful Middle East.
The task will be complete only with the downfall of Iran’s clerical rulers, Netanyahu has said on the campaign trail, and only he has the conviction and standing to deliver.
Opinion polls have for months predicted a sharp drop for Netanyahu’s Likud party. But a rival alliance of parties on the right, left and centre looking to unseat him also has no clear path to power, suggesting months of political stalemate with Netanyahu potentially at the helm of a caretaker government.
‘TWO CLICKS TO THE RIGHT’
In the days after October 7, Be’eri was crawling with Israeli soldiers patrolling through burnt and shattered homes, floors stained with blood, doors pierced with bullet holes. In some spots, the stench of dead bodies still hung in the air.
The sounds of shelling and Israeli war planes flying over Gaza were incessant.
Three years on, the kibbutz is up and running and the sounds of construction of brand-new houses are heard all around the leafy green grounds. Most members, now residing in another kibbutz, are expected to return by summer.
A collective community established in 1946, now with around 1,000 residents, Be’eri exemplifies the socialist values that dominated Israel’s politics in its early decades. Nearly all its votes went to the centre-left in the previous 2022 election, when only around 4% voted for parties in Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition.
The attack has made residents question longstanding views that there could be peace with the Palestinians in this generation.
“Everyone in Be’eri has made two clicks to the right. But I still think that most of us will stay with the opposition, the parties that want to replace this government,” he said.
Miri Gad Messika, 48, third generation in Be’eri, hasn’t yet decided how to vote. But it won’t be for Netanyahu.
“He failed as a leader so many times. And he shouldn’t be in politics anymore,” she said. “I’m looking for a leader. Unfortunately, it’s hard for me to see any leader in Israel at the moment.”
“I want to be optimistic,” she added, “and I can only hope for a better change.”
‘HOPE IS STRONGER THAN PAIN’
Through much of the past three years, opposition to the Netanyahu government gravitated around families of hostages taken to Gaza, some of whom accused the government of dodging responsibility and doing too little to secure their freedom.
A Tel Aviv open space came to be known as “Hostages Square”, site of constant rallies and vigils. Although the last of the hostages were released under a US-brokered ceasefire reached a year ago, the families are still among those most prominently calling for accountability now.
“I don’t see any legitimate reason why this government is running again for election,” said Ofri Bibas, whose young nephews, a 4-year-old and a 9-month-old, were slain in captivity in Gaza along with their mother. Their father, Ofri’s brother Yarden, was released in an early 2025 truce.
Bibas said her goal now is to make every Israeli remember October 7, “to take it with them to the day of the election and remember what happened here and who still hasn’t taken responsibility.”
On Saturday, thousands of Israelis rallied in Hostages Square. One of the speakers was Danielle Alony, who was kidnapped from Nir Oz with her 5-year-old daughter and freed from Gaza in a brief truce weeks later.
“Go vote,” Alony urged the crowd. “In three days we can start writing a new chapter for our children. One in which truth is stronger than fear, responsibility stronger than dereliction and hope is stronger than pain.”
(Writing by Maayan Lubell; Additional reporting by Rami Amichay in Tel AvivEditing by Peter Graff)

Ukrainian who fled Oleshky views US-brokered ceasefire with deep scepticism
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:46:37 CET
20:46:37 KST

KYIV, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Six weeks ago, Vitaly, his wife Iryna, their 13-year-old son Vlad and their cat left the besieged town of Oleshky in Russian-occupied Ukraine to escape what they feared was certain death by starvation.
Now back in Ukraine after a gruelling journey via Russia and Belarus, Vitaly views with deep scepticism a temporary ceasefire in his native town set to begin on Tuesday to allow evacuations and send in supplies.
Russia and Ukraine reached the agreement, announced by the White House on Friday, with the mediation of US first lady Melania Trump and after additional involvement from Pope Leo.
After more than four years living under Russian occupation in a town on the front line of fierce fighting with Ukrainian forces, Vitaly is not optimistic that the ceasefire can hold for long or the humanitarian situation significantly improve.
“Regarding the truce, I’m very sceptical about all this,” said Vitaly, 55, who declined to give his last name for security reasons because his relatives were still living in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
“I have a lot of respect for Melania Trump, but she does not influence dictator (Russian President Vladimir) Putin,” he told Reuters, sitting in a modern apartment in the Kyiv region where his family has temporarily settled.
He said many of those remaining in Oleshky are sick or elderly and it would be difficult for them to relocate.
Ukraine and Russia blame each other for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky. Drones present the greatest threat to civilian life, and the town is within easy reach of unmanned aerial vehicles belonging to both armies.
Because supplies are running out and the route north is blocked by the Dnipro river, some residents have walked 20 km (12 miles) to the next village to stock up on food and water. The journey is fraught with danger and locals call it the “road of death”.
TEMPORARY CEASEFIRE AGREED
Ukraine and Russia agreed to a temporary ceasefire around Oleshky that is expected to begin on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time (0100 GMT).
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said that Kyiv hoped it would be possible to open up Oleshky, provide access for food and medicine and allow people to leave the area.
The Kremlin has said that all civilians wishing to leave Oleshky would be allowed to do so and that the evacuation was expected to take at least several days.
Oleshky, a small town across the Dnipro from Ukraine’s regional hub of Kherson, had a prewar population of some 24,000. It is still home to around 1,700 residents, including about 35 children, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
UNDER RUSSIAN CONTROL
Russian troops have occupied Oleshky since the first days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
It has been largely cut off from running water, electricity, gas and central heating since the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023 and subsequent flooding of nearby areas.
As the war ground on, the humanitarian crisis deepened. By the middle of last year, the constant threat of drones choked off supply lines, causing food scarcity.
And from late May this year, the situation became severe, according to residents Reuters has spoken to.
Vitaly said his family survived for weeks by rationing a single cup of rice or buckwheat a day, occasionally adding a cucumber or tomato mixed with purslane, a common wild weed.
During the summer months, some residents could sell vegetables, but prices were unaffordable for most.
A kilo of tomatoes cost about 1,500 roubles ($18.50). To buy eggs, you needed to know the right people and 10 eggs would cost around 3,000 roubles, Vitaly recalled. No one was willing to sell potatoes.
After counting their meagre food stocks, and remembering last winter when the temperature in their apartment dropped to between 1 and 3 degrees Celsius (34 and 37 degrees Fahrenheit), they decided to leave.
“You look at what remained from your food supplies and realize that there is only one way for you — to go on foot or die of hunger,” Vitaly said.
Their home in Oleshky had been damaged by a drone, Iryna said, and they did not have anything left there.
ARDUOUS ESCAPE
On September 13, the family joined a small party of eight people and set out on foot. They walked for more than 20 km to the village of Radensk.
The road was heavily mined, and drones were flying overhead. Vitaly said they saw the body of a woman lying on the road as they passed by. They took with them only their autumn clothes, Vlad’s teddy bear, the cat and a handful of family photos.
They travelled from Radensk by bus deeper into Russian-occupied Ukraine, crossed into Russia after lengthy questioning by authorities at the border, and finally Belarus before returning to Ukrainian-controlled territory on September 17.
The family has spent the past several weeks settling into a new routine in the Kyiv region.
One of their first purchases was a bag of potatoes, bought to cook mashed potatoes for their son.
“The kid will be in school. We will be working. My wife needs to get her health back on track a bit,” Vitaly said.
As for his own future: “I will either join the army or will try to find a position somewhere here with weapon producers to help our country defeat its enemies.”
(Reporting by Olena Harmash; Additional reporting by Katerina Besedina, Editing by Mike Collett-White and Alexandra Hudson)

Climate damage to Philippine ports could cost US$70b a year by 2100
Rising seas and fiercer typhoons threaten to paralyse trade lines, driving up food costs and devastating coastal communities
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
The Philippines faces the highest climate-driven port damage costs in Southeast Asia, with annual losses projected to hit US$70.2 billion by 2100, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has warned.
Analysts say the damage could cripple supply chains, drive up food prices and threaten livelihoods, urging Manila to adopt a more coordinated approach to flood protection rather than simply strengthening port infrastructure.
In its latest report titled “Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the Rise – Actions for a Resilient Future”, the ADB said the Philippines could sustain US$20.6 billion in port damage under a moderate-emissions scenario, in which sea levels were projected to rise by 50cm to 80cm.

MOSCOW, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Russia’s Defence Ministry on Monday accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine with artillery and drones ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week, something it said had thwarted the delivery of food and medicine and stopped people leaving.
Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in Oleshky, that would go into effect on October 27, allowing the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said in a statement on Monday that Ukraine had struck the town 18 times with artillery fire and carried out more than 120 drone attacks on it and the main roads around it in the last week since October 19.

WARSAW, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Poland sees a lot of room to deepen cooperation with Germany in the space sector, Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said on Monday, underscoring the need to possess sovereign technology in order to bolster security in the face of external pressures.
• “We need to invest in technologies … that are not available right now in Europe, but are absolutely critical for our joint security,” Domanski said, naming the space industry, during a joint panel with Germany’s Economy Minister Katherina Reiche.
• “Together with our German partners I see lots of room for cooperation, thanks to which we’ll be more resilient from some external pressure that can appear one day,” he said, answering a question on how Poland and Germany could respond to competition from China and the U.S. in global trade.

• Domanski also said that Poland had decided to double its investment in the space sector.
• “We believe it’s not only a very efficient way of spending money – from each euro invested you get 6-7 euros back, but that’s also about our security and resilience. And we see room for further cooperation with German counterparts,” Domanski said.

French minister says Halloween protests could turn violent
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:46:14 CET
20:46:14 KST

By Crispian Balmer and Sudip Kar-Gupta
PARIS, Oct 26 (Reuters) - French authorities are bracing for more street unrest next weekend despite a huge security operation that helped contain nationwide demonstrations on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Monday.
The protests, which have rattled President Emmanuel Macron’s government for weeks, show little sign of easing after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets.
In response to the turmoil, the interior ministry deployed 70,000 police for Saturday’s demonstrations, which unions called to denounce the high cost of living and public services.
The movement has grown far beyond initial student discontent, drawing in trade unions and “yellow vest” activists, known for their high-visibility jackets and mass demonstrations against economic pressures including high fuel costs.
FAR-RIGHT GANGS CONFRONT FAR-LEFT ACTIVISTS
Nunez said the huge police presence prevented a repeat of violence seen earlier this month, but asked by BFM TV on Monday whether he expected further disturbances during demonstrations planned for October 31, he replied: “Clearly, yes.”
“Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively. We expect it to be complicated again,” he added.
Nunez said 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during Saturday’s demonstrations and said police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.
“We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses,” he said. “In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement.”
The government sought to portray Saturday’s operation as evidence it had regained the upper hand, despite sporadic violence, especially in France’s three largest cities — Paris, Marseille and Lyon.
“The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong,” government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio.
She said protesters had raised legitimate grievances that needed to be heard, but added that restoring calm was a prerequisite for meaningful negotiations.
“There are demands that must be heard and answered. To answer them, there is a prerequisite: a return to calm. We cannot have a functioning social dialogue in a climate of violence such as the one we experienced a week ago,” she said.
The government was expected later on Monday to announce measures aimed at addressing student concerns over education and university admissions, after a nationwide consultation with high school and university students.
With his presidential mandate due to expire in April and public finances under severe strain, Macron has limited scope to defuse the crisis through the costly concessions that helped quell previous waves of unrest.
On Monday he made an unannounced visit to the port city of Marseille, which saw the worst of the unrest on Saturday.
Business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage despite a calmer weekend.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding that sales had fallen by about 80%.
“We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce,” he told Radio Classique.
(Reporting by Sudip Kar-Gupta; Editing by Toby Chopra and Andrew Heavens)

Drone strikes cut power across southeast Sudan, operator says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:46:00 CET
20:46:00 KST

CAIRO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Paramilitary drone strikes hit power stations in southeast Sudan on Monday, cutting power across the region, the state electricity company said.
The operator accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces — which have been fighting a civil war with the army for around 3-1/2 years — of knocking out power in four states, which cover about half the territory currently held by the military.
The Rapid Support Forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the account from the Sudan Electricity Holding Company.
Power was cut in Sennar, Al Qadarif, White Nile and Gezira states, threatening the stability of the whole national grid, the operator said.
The attacks hit stations in the towns and areas of Sinja, El Hawata, Al Fao and Mashkour, as well as Al-Junaid in Gezira State, causing “severe damage” and “major destruction” to equipment, it added.
The United Nations has warned that attacks on power infrastructure threaten health and other services for millions of people already hit hard by the conflict.
Sudan’s army has been fighting the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when the two fell out over issues including how to integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule.
Both sides have stepped up drone strikes, with a series of attacks on Nyala, held by the RSF, and Khartoum airport, held by the army, this month.

Kremlin hails defeated Serbian ally Vucic as student election win adds to its geopolitical woes
MOSCOW, Oct 26 - The Kremlin paid tribute to its longstanding Serbian ally Aleksandar Vucic on Monday after a student-backed protest movement pulverised his party in a parliamentary election, robbing Moscow of another important partner in Europe six months after the electoral defeat of ally Viktor Orban in Hungary.
Serbia woke to a new era on Monday after Vucic, a frequent visitor to Moscow and in Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014, was humbled at the ballot box in a result that sparked nationwide celebrations, although few had an idea of how the Balkan country's new student-backed leaders would govern.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow had taken note of the result, lavished praise on Vucic, and said he hoped Serbia's new rulers realised that cooperation with Russia, traditionally a vital supplier of energy to Serbia, was in their own country's interests.
"We greatly appreciate the contribution that Mr Vucic has made to the development of our bilateral relations. We are aware that Mr Vucic will remain active in politics, and we hope that, even while in opposition, he will continue to contribute to the development of our bilateral relations," Peskov told reporters.
Serbia, although it has aspirations to join the European Union, did not sign up to EU-backed sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine and has continued to develop close economic, political and military ties to Moscow.
"As for the new political force that will come to power as a result of the elections, we wish to express our hope that its actions will also be constructively directed towards the further development of relations, and that these new political forces will understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests, because it benefits Serbia," said Peskov.
"For our part, we intend to continue to do everything we can to foster the development of our relations with Belgrade. But, as you know, it takes two to tango," added Peskov. REUTERS

Zelenskyy said the planned visit will gather Ukraine, the US, EU and NATO in high-level talks on security guarantees and diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine – but they have yet to be confirmed.
Ukrainian officials have declined to confirm President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's planned visit to Brussels this week, despite his announcement that talks with the US, EU and NATO were scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.
Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy's communications adviser, told reporters on Monday that Kyiv could not confirm the visit because of changes to the American side's plans.
Speaking to Ukrainian media on Sunday, Zelenskyy said the talks were scheduled for October 27 and 28, bringing together the leaders of Ukraine, the US and the EU, as well as NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

"The Commission continues to participate in talks and efforts with allies and partners to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine," a Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
"At this stage, we have no further information to share."
The proposed Brussels meeting follows a series of diplomatic discussions in Oslo last week, including talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff attended by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
According to Zelenskyy, wider discussions also involved security advisers to the leaders of Britain, France and Italy, alongside Björn Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The US subsequently briefed its partners following Witkoff's talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg.
"We had a briefing from the Americans, and now they want not just a briefing, but to discuss security, guarantees, the EU and its involvement more broadly," Zelenskyy said.
"They want a meeting in Brussels this week. The Americans, Ukraine, the EU at presidential level and NATO at secretary-general level. I don't know whether anyone else will be part of this group in Brussels."
The uncertainty over the Brussels visit comes ahead of another round of negotiations between Ukrainian, American and Russian teams, which Zelenskyy said was being planned for the first half of November.
Abu Dhabi has been mentioned as a possible venue, although the date and location have yet to be confirmed.

Ukrainian regulator stalling EBRD-backed capital market plan – National Bank governor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:40:21 EET
20:40:21 KST

Implementation of an integrated capital markets infrastructure model, developed jointly by the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU), the Ministry of Economy and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), is currently being held up by the position of the head of the National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC), NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.
"We are being asked what is happening with the capital markets. We explain the capital markets infrastructure model that has been developed jointly by the NBU, the Ministry of Economy and the EBRD. Unfortunately, its implementation is currently being held up by the position of the head of the NSSMC," Pyshnyy said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.
In the NBU governor's view, the proposed model takes the state's interests into account in building a vertically integrated system, and therefore confidence in it should not be undermined.
"The key idea is to bring the entire capital markets infrastructure chain together under a single holding company. The strategic investor in this infrastructure holding company should be an entity trusted by global private capital: Deutsche Börse, Euroclear, Clearstream… Naturally, it should be selected through a competitive process. But in the current circumstances, national security requirements must also be taken into account. Our model provides for all of this. So why is the process being held up?" Pyshnyy concluded.
As reported, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso expressed hope at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group that Ukraine would pay greater attention to the capital market development project.
"Despite all the short-term challenges, we have indeed managed to move this process forward, and I hope this issue will soon become a priority," she said.
In July last year, a memorandum of understanding was signed at the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Rome by the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Finance, the NBU, the NSSMC and the EBRD on supporting integrated capital markets infrastructure in Ukraine. Its signing was preceded by the Financial Stability Council's approval of a plan for the practical implementation of the target capital markets infrastructure model.
In early September 2025, the National Bank announced the launch of the memorandum's implementation. The first stage involved optimizing the ownership structure and corporate governance of the National Depository of Ukraine (NDU) by transferring management of the state-owned stake, previously managed by the NSSMC, to the NBU.
The next stage envisages the creation of a holding company involving a reputable international strategic investor selected through an open tender, an operator of trading and post-trading infrastructure, international financial institutions, local market participants, and the state and state-owned banks. The holding company, in turn, will establish a new stock exchange in Ukraine, which will become the majority owner of the Central Counterparty Clearing Institution, the Settlement Center (SC), replacing the National Bank in that role. In addition, the exchange will own a minority stake in the NDU, while the National Bank will hold a majority stake.
The final stage is to consolidate depository services under the NDU, which is to operate as a single central securities depository, by transferring to it the functions of recording and servicing the circulation of government bonds from the National Bank.
In early June this year, the Cabinet of Ministers approved a bill on establishing a capital markets infrastructure holding company with the participation of a foreign strategic investor. However, due to a change of government, the document was submitted to the Verkhovna Rada only on September 4. The NSSMC subsequently proposed substantial amendments to the government's bill, including tightening the conditions for attracting a foreign strategic investor.
In addition, an alternative bill (No. 16038-1) was registered on September 21. Its authors include 12 members of parliament, among them Serhiy Taruta, first deputy head of the Verkhovna Rada's economic committee; Andriy Nikolaienko, head of the capital markets subcommittee of the parliament's finance committee; Oleksandr Fediyenko, head of a subcommittee of the parliament's security committee; and Anton Yatsenko.

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:39:00 UTC
20:39:00 KST

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Despite growing interest in engineering, Estonia faces a shortage of more than 800 young engineers in the next decade as 40 percent retire. Changes to math teaching may help.
Interest in engineering has grown sharply, but according to OSKA, the Estonian Qualifications Authority's labor market forecasting system, the sector will still be short more than 800 young engineers over the next decade as 40 percent retire. There are no quick solutions, but efforts are being made to alleviate the shortage by changing how mathematics is taught.
Interest in studying at Tallinn University of Technology's (TalTech) School of Engineering has increased by 25 percent over the past three years. According to Fjodor Sergejev, dean of the School of Engineering, students are enrolling in a variety of programs, from energy and construction to mechanical and industrial engineering, but there will not be enough graduates to fill the gap.
"We need replacement workers because many engineers from previous generations are retiring and need to be replaced, but we also need to ensure the development of the sector, and for that we need even more engineers. Even the substantial demographic support we currently have is unfortunately unable to meet all our needs, because the replacement demand is indeed very high, in some fields even numbering in the thousands."
Cathy-Liis Põlluveer, president of the Estonian association of engineers (Eesti Inseneride Liit), also acknowledged the shortage: "We currently have a situation where it depends somewhat on the field, but when an engineer, particularly an experienced engineer, is being sought and a recruitment competition is held, there is practically no queue of applicants or diversity among candidates. Instead, engineers are being sought like needles in a haystack."
According to Anneli Leemet, an analyst at OSKA, demand will grow most for electrical and energy engineers, mechanical engineers and electronics engineers. Leemet said the issue is not only meeting the numerical demand but ensuring engineers have a diverse range of skills.
One possible solution experts see is strengthening mathematics education in basic schools (grades 1–9) — making mathematics teaching more relevant to everyday life, more integrated with other subjects, and delivered in a way that supports all children's motivation to learn. According to Tiina Kraav, a lecturer in mathematics education at the University of Tartu, there are no quick solutions, but mathematics teaching is being continuously developed.
"Making mathematics more interesting to learn, making mathematics learning more visible, making mathematical thinking more visible to students, making mathematics learning more creative, improving how problem-solving skills are taught in the classroom, getting students to talk about what they think and how they think when solving mathematics problems – all of this will certainly help in the longer term," Kraav said.
Põlluveer believes subjects that help connect natural sciences and mathematics could be beneficial.
Priit Laats, a teacher of technology education, arts and technology at Tartu Raatuse School, confirmed that schools are increasingly moving toward theme-based learning: "For example, in the first stage of basic school, there is integrated learning. It is theme-based, with Estonian, mathematics, nature studies and creative subjects all together all the time. In fact, other grades should already be structured in a similar way. But again, who is going to develop all of this? It is a huge amount of work. If I take how I, in turn, support mathematics, we introduce 3D modeling as early as fourth grade: the spatial world, shapes, symbols, symmetry, reflection, all the faces and planes – it is all mathematics all the time, and we do this right through ninth grade."
OSKA will publish a new cross-sector study of labor and skills needs in engineering in early November, which will show that competition for hybrid competencies is increasing in the labor market. This means engineers must have in-depth specialist knowledge combined with digital, data analysis, artificial intelligence, business or management skills.

Italy has made progress in several areas of equitable and sustainable well-being, including health and the environment, but continues to face challenges related to poverty, disposable income and households’ ability to make ends meet, according to the latest report by the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT).
The report, which examines 132 indicators of equitable and sustainable well-being, found that 54 indicators improved, 55 remained stable and 23 deteriorated.
Despite the overall progress, Italy’s at-risk-of-poverty rate remains 2.3 percentage points above the EU average.
Compared with the EU, Italy performs better in health and safety, while significant challenges persist in education and training, employment, work-life balance, and innovation, research and creativity.
More than 5.4 million people were living in absolute poverty in Italy in 2025, with large families and households with at least one minor child facing particularly difficult conditions.
According to the report, 8% of households were living in absolute poverty, affecting 9.3% of the country’s population.
The incidence of individual absolute poverty remained highest in southern Italy, although it declined to 11.5% in 2025 from 12.5% in 2024.
In northern Italy, the rate fell to 8.5% from 8.8% a year earlier, while central Italy continued to record the lowest incidence, at 7.4%, down from 7.6% in 2024.

As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea for sympathy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:27 UTC
20:38:27 KST

Breadcrumb
As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea for sympathy
It has become almost customary for Palestinians, whenever we speak about Palestine, to begin by telling the story of our suffering. We are expected to explain how we became refugees, how our parents and grandparents were displaced, and which members of our families were killed, imprisoned or disappeared under Israeli occupation.
We are expected to expose our deepest wounds, relive generations of trauma, and to offer our grief as evidence that our demands for justice deserve to be heard.
This is nothing but emotional labour.
And today, I refuse to audition for anyone’s sympathy.
I refuse to bare my wounds for the world to see, simply to validate the decisions and actions we take on the path towards our liberation.
Palestinian rights are not conditional upon our ability to move an audience to tears.
This is why when Green Party members voted to adopt the historic motion declaring Zionism to be racism and calling for a free Palestine from the river to the sea, it felt like a historic movement in UK solidarity efforts.
As a Palestinian and a Green Party member who co-authored and helped develop and advance this motion, I saw this as more than a political victory. It was also an affirmation that Palestinian voices could shape the policies of a major British political party without having to surrender their own understanding of their oppression or dilute their demands to be palatable.
Yet what should have been a moment of collective reflection and celebration quickly became overshadowed by opposition from several Green Party MPs and figures within the party leadership.
A democratic victory that some refuse to accept
The motion did not emerge overnight. Outsiders did not impose it, nor was it the product of some mysterious group of extremists, as some have suggested.
It was drafted and championed by ordinary Green Party members, including Palestinians and anti-Zionist Jews, who spent months organising workshops, seminars, discussions and fringe events to engage fellow members.
Even after the motion was denied a hearing following procedural delays and filibustering during the party’s spring conference, we continued organising, discussing and engaging.
We believed in the Green Party’s commitment to grassroots democracy, even when its procedures appeared to work against us.
Nevertheless, once the motion finally passed, some elected representatives responded not by acknowledging the democratic outcome, but by questioning the motivations of those who brought the motion forward, portraying our organisation and determination as something threatening.
MP Ellie Chowns called for protecting the party from extremists and entryists.
Ironically, only months earlier, party leadership was enthusiastically celebrating a remarkable surge in membership.
Apparently, welcoming new members is something to celebrate until those members organise, exercise their democratic rights and successfully influence party policy.
Even my own MP, Sian Berry, whom I personally contacted to engage with the motion and its arguments, did not respond. Yet, once the media attacks started, Berry weighed in by publicly distancing herself from the motion, describing it as seriously flawed and accusing its Palestinian proposers of being unwilling to compromise.
She has even called on the party to revisit a decision reached through its own democratic processes.
MP Adrian Ramsay, the party's former co-leader, has publicly encouraged Green council groups to distance themselves from the democratically adopted policy. In a recent public statement
Ramsay praised council groups that rejected the motion, described the conference decision as a distraction from their work, and said it did not reflect the views of most party members.
It is deeply disappointing to see a former party leader effectively encouraging a division between elected council groups and the democratic decisions of the party’s own membership.
Selective silencing
Whilst disagreement is a legitimate part of political life, actively encouraging local representatives to distance themselves from a policy adopted through the party’s highest democratic forum raises serious questions about whose voices are ultimately respected.
What message does this send to party members who invest their time, energy and conviction in the democratic process, only to see its outcome publicly undermined by those elected to represent them?
What makes this particularly painful is that these Green MPs are now among the most vocal opponents of a motion written by Palestinians, for Palestinians, and supported through the party’s democratic process.
Not long ago, Palestinians within the Green Party extended a gesture of solidarity and goodwill to those very MPs. After Israeli authorities imposed entry bans on them, we sent a letter replacing that exclusion with an invitation to visit a Free Palestine, to stand alongside us and to hear directly from Palestinians about our aspirations for freedom, dignity and self-determination.
It was an invitation to listen, to engage and to recognise that Palestinians are not merely subjects of political debate, but people with voices, histories and a right to determine their own future. Judging by some of the responses to the motion, it feels like the invitation was buried under a pile of political calculations and selective solidarity.
Palestinians are also not the only ones who’ve been silenced by opposing MPs and the subsequent media storm.
A leading accusation against the motion is that it threatens the safety of Jewish members of the Green Party. But Jewish safety is not at risk from a motion that defines and confronts Zionism as a settler colonial ideology, examining its historical and contemporary manifestations, and reaffirming the Palestinian struggle for liberation, including ending occupation and confronting the structures of displacement and dispossession.
Not only is this argument, which conflates Zionist views with Jewish identity, antisemitic in itself, but it also completely ignores anti-Zionist Jewish members. Many of those members participated in drafting the motion and organising discussions and public meetings in support of it, but opponents have shown they’re not interested in this part of the story.
No one’s safety should ever come at the expense of another people’s freedom, dignity or right to self-determination.
Amro Tabari is a British Palestinian renewable energy engineer, activist and writer. Born a refugee in Syria and raised in Jordan, his family originates from Tiberias, Palestine. He has lived in the UK since 2014 and is actively involved in grassroots campaigns for Palestinian liberation, social justice and environmental sustainability. A member of the Green Party and Greens for Palestine, he was recognised as one of The Big Issue’s 100 Changemakers in 2026 for his work in politics and activism.

Kondratov, 52, was reportedly hospitalized at the Botkin hospital last Friday for an undisclosed ailment. The cause of his death has not been made public.
Russian law enforcement authorities charged Kondratov with treason on Aug. 5, though he had been held for more than 70 days under so-called “carousel arrests,” a practice of consecutive detentions on charges of disorderly conduct.
Born and raised in Moscow, Kondratov moved to Kyiv, Ukraine, in 2012, where his family currently resides.
Russian border guards at Vnukovo International Airport detained him on May 5, when he arrived to renew his international passport.
His defense attorney Natalia Tikhonova said the treason charges, which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison for men, stemmed from “at least six” online posts Kondratov had made. The nature of those posts has not been disclosed.
Kondratov was best known for his work as an art and production designer for the 2007 post-World War II detective drama “Liquidation.” His work on the series earned him two of Russia’s highest honors in television production — the TEFI and Golden Eagle awards.
Perviy Otdel reported that Kondratov’s death marks at least the 11th known case of someone dying in Russian custody this year while standing trial on charges widely viewed as being politically motivated.

AI uses sleep to predict heart problems up to 10 years ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:37:32 UTC
20:37:32 KST

AI uses sleep to predict heart problems up to 10 years ahead
The system analyzes heart activity recorded during overnight sleep studies. Researchers found that it could identify patterns linked to future health problems, including risks that standard medical checks might not fully capture.
The study, published in the journal Sleep, used data from more than 35,000 patients at three US medical centers. Researchers trained an AI model to analyze heart signals alongside information about patients' sleep stages.
The team then tested the system on two independent groups, including 9,810 patients at Emory University Hospital and 12,576 at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.
The model predicted 5 outcomes: atrial fibrillation, a condition that causes an irregular heartbeat; stroke; heart attack; heart failure; and death from any cause. Researchers tracked health outcomes for up to 10 years in one group and 7 years in the other.
The strongest results came from predictions of irregular heartbeat, heart failure and death. Adding the AI's analysis improved the accuracy of risk assessments for these outcomes beyond estimates based on established risk factors, such as age, smoking, high blood pressure and diabetes.
For heart failure, the researchers reported an improvement of about 8% to 9% in the model's ability to distinguish between people who later developed the condition and those who did not.
However, the AI did not significantly improve predictions of stroke or heart attack beyond existing risk factors. The researchers said these conditions may be harder to predict years in advance using heart signals alone.
The approach could make better use of information already collected during sleep studies, which doctors commonly use to diagnose sleep disorders. These studies typically record an electrical signal from the heart, but clinicians do not routinely use it to assess long-term cardiovascular risk.
The researchers said the system could eventually help doctors identify patients who need closer monitoring or preventive care. It is intended as a screening tool, not a stand-alone diagnosis, and any concerning prediction would require further medical assessment.

Russia may use renewed peace talks on Ukraine to seek concessions that weaken NATO’s defenses in Europe, The Telegraph reported on Sunday, Oct. 25, citing diplomatic sources.
The sources said Moscow’s push to include European countries in the negotiations could be aimed at securing concessions on NATO expansion and the alliance’s military presence near Russia’s borders. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly described NATO’s enlargement as a “root cause” of the war.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One possible demand, according to the report, would be for NATO to return to its 1997 configuration, before former Soviet bloc countries began joining the alliance. Such a move could mean withdrawing NATO forces from Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Finland – all of which border Russia.
The report did not cite an official Russian proposal or say that a demand for a NATO rollback had been formally added to the agenda. It remains a scenario attributed to diplomatic sources, rather than an agreed negotiating position.
Moscow seeks a wider security discussion
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov has argued that European countries should be included in discussions on ending the war, saying an agreement would be difficult to reach without them. Russian officials have also said future talks should address a broader European security framework.
Putin said last week that negotiations should focus on “ensur[ing] the security of Ukraine and Russia” after a final peace agreement. He added that discussions should also cover “the architecture of European security as a whole,” according to Reuters.
It’s About Security, Stupid!
Moscow has previously sought changes to NATO’s posture in Europe. In December 2021, Russia presented the US and NATO with draft security agreements that included demands to halt further NATO enlargement and limit military activity in countries that joined the alliance after May 1997. NATO rejected the demand that it closed its doors to new members, while saying it was open to talks on arms control and other security issues.
The Telegraph’s report suggests the Kremlin could again link its demands on NATO to negotiations over Ukraine. The outlet cited sources who said Putin may argue that concessions on the alliance’s military presence are necessary to resolve the conflict.
Trilateral talks may resume in November
The report comes as Ukraine, Russia, and the US discuss restarting negotiations at the technical level. Kremlin aide Ushakov said Russia was prepared to resume trilateral talks after its Nov. 4 National Unity Day holiday, describing the next meeting as preliminary and exploratory.
Kyiv has said it is ready to take part in talks but wants concrete steps, including a ceasefire and humanitarian measures. President Volodymyr Zelensky has also said Ukraine supports proposals for an energy ceasefire and an end to the war.
As the EU is seeking a role in the next round of discussions, EU officials have proposed a broader format that would include European representatives, while the Kremlin has said the talks currently being prepared are trilateral. The exact format and participants have not been confirmed.
Earlier, Kyiv Post reported that Russian officials and analysts have used the prospect of renewed talks to raise wider demands on European security, sanctions, and territory. Moscow’s stated focus on postwar security could therefore extend beyond Ukraine’s borders, though the reported NATO rollback demand has not been confirmed as an official condition.
That said, NATO membership remains a key point of disagreement. Ukraine has said it needs strong security guarantees to prevent future Russian attacks, while Putin has rejected Ukrainian membership in the alliance. Kyiv has also rejected Russia’s demands that it surrender territory as a condition for ending the war.
The talks’ agenda, any Russian proposal on NATO, and the degree of European participation remain unsettled.

- Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.
- Share:
Exercise does more than make the heart stronger. New research suggests it also physically reshapes the nerves that control the heart, revealing an unexpected difference between the left and right sides of the body.
Scientists at the University of Bristol (UK) discovered that moderate aerobic exercise changes the structure of nerve cells involved in regulating heart activity. Even more surprisingly, the changes were dramatically different on the two sides of the body. The findings, published in Autonomic Neuroscience, could eventually help doctors develop more precise treatments for irregular heartbeats, chest pain, angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.
The discovery was made in rats, so further research is needed to determine whether the same changes occur in humans. Nevertheless, it offers a new perspective on how physical activity influences the nervous system that keeps the heart functioning.
Exercise Changes the Heart's Hidden Control System
The heart is regulated partly by the autonomic nervous system, a network of nerves that automatically manages essential functions such as heartbeat, breathing, and digestion. One branch of this system helps the heart beat faster when the body needs more oxygen, such as during exercise or stressful situations.
Small clusters of nerve cells called stellate ganglia play an important role in this process. Located on both sides of the lower neck and upper chest, these nerve hubs send signals that influence heart rate and other aspects of heart function.
The new research suggests that regular exercise changes these nerve clusters in ways scientists had not previously recognized.
Study lead author Dr. Augusto Coppi, Senior Lecturer in Veterinary Anatomy at the University of Bristol, said: "The discovery points to a previously hidden left-right pattern in the body's 'autopilot' system that helps run the heart.
"These nerve clusters act like the heart's dimmer switch and we've shown that regular, moderate exercise remodels that switch in a side-specific way. This could help explain why some treatments work better on one side than the other and, in future, help doctors target therapies more precisely and effectively."
Just 10 Weeks of Exercise Produced Striking Nerve Changes
To investigate how exercise affects these nerve clusters, the researchers examined rats that underwent 10 weeks of moderate aerobic training. Aerobic exercise is physical activity that increases heart rate and breathing, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.
The study involved researchers from University College London (UCL) in the UK, the University of São Paulo (USP), and the Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP) in Brazil.
The team used advanced three-dimensional analysis techniques known as stereology to examine the nerve cells. This approach allows scientists to estimate the number, size, and distribution of cells within tissues.
The results revealed an unusual imbalance between the two sides of the body. In the trained rats, the cardiovascular nerve cluster on the right contained roughly four times as many neurons as the cluster on the left, a striking difference from the pattern observed in untrained rats.
The nerve cells also changed in size, but in opposite directions. Neurons on the left nearly doubled in size, while those on the right became slightly smaller.
These findings suggest that exercise does not affect all the nerves controlling the heart equally. Instead, it produces distinct structural changes on each side, potentially providing clues about how the nervous system adapts to regular physical activity.
Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Treatments?
The findings may have important implications for treating conditions involving abnormal nerve activity around the heart.
Arrhythmias occur when the heart beats too quickly, too slowly, or irregularly. Angina is chest pain or discomfort typically caused by insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle. Another condition, commonly called 'broken-heart' syndrome, involves a sudden weakening of the heart muscle that is often triggered by intense emotional or physical stress.
In some patients, doctors treat these problems by reducing excessive nerve signals reaching the heart. Procedures such as stellate ganglion nerve blocks temporarily interrupt nerve activity, while denervation involves disrupting certain nerve pathways.
Understanding how the left and right nerve clusters differ could eventually help physicians determine which side should be targeted for the greatest benefit.
Dr. Coppi explained: "Irregular heart rhythms, known as arrhythmias, stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome, and certain types of chest pain are often treated by dialing down overactive stellate ganglia -- the paired small nerve hubs in the lower neck/upper chest area that send 'go faster' signals to the heart.
"By mapping how exercise changes these ganglia on each side, the study offers clues that could one day fine-tune procedures like nerve blocks or denervation to the side most likely to help. The findings are early-stage and in rats, so clinical studies would need to follow."
What's Next for Exercise and Heart Research?
Although the structural changes were substantial, scientists still need to establish exactly how they affect heart function.
The research team plans to investigate whether the differences between the left and right nerve clusters influence how the heart behaves during rest and physical activity. They also intend to look for similar patterns in other animal models and eventually in humans.
For human studies, the researchers hope to use noninvasive markers, which could provide information about nerve activity without requiring surgery or tissue removal.
If the same left-right differences are found in people, the discovery could help guide more personalized treatments for arrhythmias, difficult-to-treat angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.
Dr. Coppi added: "Understanding these left-right differences could help us personalize treatments for heart rhythm disorders and angina. Our next step is to test how these structural changes map onto function and whether similar patterns appear in larger animals and humans."

Netanyahu faces reckoning for October 7 in Israel's first vote since attack

Netanyahu faces reckoning for October 7 in Israel's first vote since attack
BE'ERI, Oct 26 - Gal Cohen walks along a memorial wall engraved with the names of the men, women and children slain in the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on his kibbutz. For him, the idea that the man leading Israel, then and since, may be re-elected on Tuesday is painful.
One-in-ten residents of his kibbutz, Be'eri, were among the 1,200 people killed in Hamas' surprise attack. Dozens were among the 251 taken hostage to Gaza. It was Israel's deadliest single day.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should have taken responsibility and stepped down, said Cohen, 61, and the fact that he has fulfilled a full term in office is a slap in the face. Tuesday's election, he said, is critical for Israel.
"If this government will stay, many hearts and minds will be broken. It will be really hard to continue," said Cohen.
Many of Netanyahu's opponents see the election as an opportunity at last to deliver a long-postponed reckoning for the worst security failure in generations. But even if Israel's longest-serving prime minister loses his majority, he could well escape the decisive verdict his foes are seeking.
Netanyahu has rejected blame for the breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. He maintains that Israel's wars against Hamas in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran will result in a more peaceful Middle East.
The task will be complete only with the downfall of Iran's clerical rulers, Netanyahu has said on the campaign trail, and only he has the conviction and standing to deliver.
Opinion polls have for months predicted a sharp drop for Netanyahu's Likud party. But a rival alliance of parties on the right, left and centre looking to unseat him also has no clear path to power, suggesting months of political stalemate with Netanyahu potentially at the helm of a caretaker government.
'TWO CLICKS TO THE RIGHT'
In the days after October 7, Be'eri was crawling with Israeli soldiers patrolling through burnt and shattered homes, floors stained with blood, doors pierced with bullet holes. In some spots, the stench of dead bodies still hung in the air.
The sounds of shelling and Israeli war planes flying over Gaza were incessant.
Three years on, the kibbutz is up and running and the sounds of construction of brand-new houses are heard all around the leafy green grounds. Most members, now residing in another kibbutz, are expected to return by summer.
A collective community established in 1946, now with around 1,000 residents, Be'eri exemplifies the socialist values that dominated Israel's politics in its early decades. Nearly all its votes went to the centre-left in the previous 2022 election, when only around 4% voted for parties in Netanyahu's nationalist-religious coalition.
The attack has made residents question longstanding views that there could be peace with the Palestinians in this generation.
"Everyone in Be'eri has made two clicks to the right. But I still think that most of us will stay with the opposition, the parties that want to replace this government," he said.
Miri Gad Messika, 48, third generation in Be'eri, hasn't yet decided how to vote. But it won't be for Netanyahu.
"He failed as a leader so many times. And he shouldn't be in politics anymore," she said. "I'm looking for a leader. Unfortunately, it's hard for me to see any leader in Israel at the moment."
"I want to be optimistic," she added, "and I can only hope for a better change."
'HOPE IS STRONGER THAN PAIN'
Through much of the past three years, opposition to the Netanyahu government gravitated around families of hostages taken to Gaza, some of whom accused the government of dodging responsibility and doing too little to secure their freedom.
A Tel Aviv open space came to be known as "Hostages Square", site of constant rallies and vigils. Although the last of the hostages were released under a US-brokered ceasefire reached a year ago, the families are still among those most prominently calling for accountability now.
"I don't see any legitimate reason why this government is running again for election," said Ofri Bibas, whose young nephews, a 4-year-old and a 9-month-old, were slain in captivity in Gaza along with their mother. Their father, Ofri's brother Yarden, was released in an early 2025 truce.
Bibas said her goal now is to make every Israeli remember October 7, "to take it with them to the day of the election and remember what happened here and who still hasn't taken responsibility."
On Saturday, thousands of Israelis rallied in Hostages Square. One of the speakers was Danielle Alony, who was kidnapped from Nir Oz with her 5-year-old daughter and freed from Gaza in a brief truce weeks later.
"Go vote," Alony urged the crowd. "In three days we can start writing a new chapter for our children. One in which truth is stronger than fear, responsibility stronger than dereliction and hope is stronger than pain." REUTERS

Dmitry Medvedev, Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council, made a string of allegations on the messaging platform MaxMessenger against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky before calling on US President Donald Trump to remove Ukraine’s president.
MaxMessenger – often referred to simply as Max – is the Russian state-sponsored social media platform, intended to supplant Western channels, that requires the user to hold a Russian or Belarusian phone number to register.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to an Oct. 25 report by The Moscow Times, the comments made on the Russian messaging platform included the statement: “American history itself offers a solution. All he [Trump] has to do is summon the secretary of war and the CIA director and tell them to take care of this ‘unfortunate little problem.’”
He then added: “The how, where, and by what means are irrelevant.”
Medvedev’s claims
Medvedev complained that while frequently demanding more money and weapons from the US, Zelensky “regularly spits in the face of the US president, ignoring his calls and turning important Americans and Europeans against him.”
He said that Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s oil refineries were in defiance of Trump’s “numerous requests” to hold off and were yet another example of Zelensky’s arrogance which he contrasted with Kyiv’s supposedly more cooperative relationship with the former US president, Joe Biden.
Zelensky: Ukraine Offered US 3 Ways to Stop Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries

He further accused Zelensky of embezzling US aid, without offering any evidence to back up such claims, and said Ukraine was intent on engineering a direct nuclear conflict between Russia, the US and NATO.
Another call for Zelensky’s elimination
Medvedev has frequently called for the “physical elimination” of Zelensky or, alternatively, a repeat of the “Venezuelan scenario” – the forcible removal of the Ukrainian head of state – on a number of social media channels, including Telegram.
On Oct. 16 he wrote in a post on Telegram:
“They [the Ukrainians] won’t make peace with Zelensky. He doesn’t want to make peace. He says he wants to make peace, but he doesn’t really want to.”
He suggested a solution to the impasse that Zelensky “should be given rat poison or consume a horse-sized dose of its favorite cocaine,” before adding he “is so cowardly that he won’t even consider such a thing.”
Medvedev, who is considered to be on of President Vladimir Putin’s closest confidantes, suggests the elimination of the Ukrainian president is the answer solving the war in Ukraine, that Russia launched, rather than a diplomatic solution.
According to the Moscow Times there have been at least ten attempts to assassinate Zelensky by Russian sabotage and reconnaissance groups in the first months of the war.
His comments, while more extreme, echo the Oct. 10 sentiments expressed by Trump that Ukraine needs to elect a new president who can “make a deal” to end the war with Russia. He said this the day after making a deal with Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel suggesting this was necessary because Zelensky had not done enough to end the war with Russia, blaming high diesel prices in the US on Kyiv’s continuing attacks on Russia’s oil infrastructure..

Health Expo Iraq to offer prime opportunity for Iranian medical sector
Unknown

Health Expo Iraq to offer prime opportunity for Iranian medical sector
TEHRAN – The sixth edition of Health Expo Iraq, the country’s annual international health exhibition and congress, will offer Iranian health-sector manufacturers a valuable opportunity to enter the Iraqi market and expand their business in the neighboring country.
The event is scheduled to take place from October 28 to 31 at the Baghdad International Fair.
The expo will feature a wide range of products and services, including medical equipment, laboratory devices, pharmaceuticals, hospital supplies, and healthcare services. Additionally, seminars, workshops, and panel discussions are organized for participants, encouraging industry professionals to share knowledge and experiences and establish new business connections.
Iranian delegation will set up their pavilions to feature the products and achievements of the Iranian knowledge-based firms, establish connections between Iranian and Iraqi experts and stakeholders, hold B2B meetings, and identify the needs of Iraq market in the field of health.
Iran’s ambassador to Iraq and embassy advisors will visit Iranian pavilions and hold meetings with companies to explore potential and capacities for the expansion of ties between the two countries.
With a population of over 46 million and the pharmaceutical market valued at 4 billion dollars, Iraq is one of the biggest health markets in West Asia. The country is planning to meet 70 percent of its pharmaceutical needs through domestic production by 2027.
Boosting academic ties to meet domestic, regional priorities
On October 19, Iran’s scientific counselor in Iraq, Mohammad-Javad Najafi, and Iraqi Deputy Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, Haider Abd Dahed, discussed ways to strengthen academic cooperation between universities in the two countries, with a focus on problem-solving approaches and addressing domestic and regional needs.
Collaboration on problem-oriented research, the provision of scholarships, the facilitation of educational issues for students, and preparation for the ‘Third Iran-Iraq Science Week’ were the key topics discussed during the meeting, IRNA reported.
The officials also discussed conducting collaborative research projects, supervising joint dissertations for postgraduate degrees, and publishing joint scientific articles in globally reputable magazines.
Addressing the challenges and educational problems faced by the students in reciprocal countries was the other issue raised by the two sides.
In September, the chancellor of Shiraz University, Alireza Afsharfar, and Najafi explored the potential to expand academic ties with Iraqi universities.
The officials met on September 26, discussing ways to develop collaborative educational courses, exchange students and professors, attract international students, and conduct joint research projects, msrt.ir reported.
Establishing dual degree programs, holding summer schools and educational courses in English and Arabic languages, and participating in Iran-Iraq Science Week were among other issues highlighted by the officials.
The officials also highlighted the need to share the scientific and educational capacities and the capabilities of Shiraz University with Iraqi students, and to implement research projects on shared challenges like dust storms and the environment. They also discussed ways to foster ties with universities and scientific centers in Lebanon and Kurdistan.
Iran regional leader in health system
In May 2025, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) director for the Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO) said Iran is a leading country in expanding its healthcare system and providing access to universal health coverage.
Lauding the country’s achievements in recent years, Hanan Balkhi said that by expanding primary health care services, increasing access to health coverage in rural areas, maintaining high vaccination rates, and reducing maternal and newborn mortality, Iran has managed to become a successful role model in the region, the health ministry’s website reported.
The official made the remarks in a meeting with Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarqandi. The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly (WHA).
The issue of medicine and medical equipment production and self-sufficiency in these areas is one of the government’s priorities, Zafarqandi said in March 2025.
Medicine and medical equipment are two important areas related to people’s health, he said, adding: “We are trying to reach self-sufficiency for the supply of medicine and medical equipment,” IRNA reported.
According to the head of Iran’s Union of Medical Equipment Manufacturers and Exporters the medical equipment is exported to more than 60 countries annually.
More than 70 percent of medical equipment and 100 percent of normal hospital beds are domestically made, IRNA quoted Abdolreza Yaqoubzadeh as saying.
Also, over 95 percent of specific ICU and CCU beds and more than 85 percent of operating room medical equipment, such as anesthesia machines and other equipment, are manufactured with cutting-edge technology in the country, he added.
Some 600 medical equipment companies are operating in the country, producing around 99 percent of the medicine supplied to the domestic market.
Medical equipment manufacturers in the country produce and supply over 10,000 types of medical equipment to domestic and foreign markets. Now, various pieces of laboratory equipment are manufactured at prices much lower than the same foreign products.

Syria says UN aviation agency withdraws 13-year-old airspace warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:34:17 UTC
20:34:17 KST

Sahin Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has withdrawn a safety warning concerning Syrian airspace that had been in place for more than 13 years, Syria’s civil aviation authority said Monday.
Omar al-Hosari, head of Syria’s General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport, said the withdrawal marked an important step toward reintegrating Syrian airspace into the international aviation network, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
He said ICAO had confirmed that its previous warning, issued in 2013, would no longer serve as a basis for operational decisions concerning Syrian airspace.
Instead, risk assessments would be based on updated international aviation safety and security standards, he added.
Al-Hosari said the development would allow countries, civil aviation authorities and international airlines to reassess their decisions regarding flights crossing Syrian airspace, as well as those arriving at and departing from Syrian airports.
The move could help increase overflight traffic and encourage additional international airlines to consider resuming operations to Syria, he said.
However, he stressed that the withdrawal would not automatically lift operational restrictions imposed by individual countries or aviation regulators.
He said the decision would support ongoing technical and diplomatic efforts to address such restrictions based on internationally recognized aviation safety and security assessments.
The Syrian aviation authority continues to coordinate with ICAO and international civil aviation authorities to strengthen confidence in the safety of flight operations and expand connectivity with regional and international markets, he added.
The original ICAO warning, dated March 22, 2013, concerned the safety of civilian aircraft operating in the Damascus Flight Information Region.
Separately, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) maintains a conflict-zone information bulletin concerning Syrian airspace, which was revised on Oct. 1 and remains valid until Nov. 30, 2026.
Syria had previously reopened its air corridors and resumed flight operations at Damascus International Airport in April following temporary closures linked to regional tensions.
Al-Hosari said restoring Syria’s role in international air navigation remains a strategic priority, citing its potential to increase air traffic and support economic activity and investment in the country’s civil aviation sector.

Over 355 earthquakes hit Iran in a month
