Pentagon Prepares US Military Bases to Operate Independently for 90 Days in Major War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:57:36 UTC
18:57:36 KST

The Pentagon is preparing US military bases to operate for at least 90 days without outside support if a major war disrupts power grids, supply chains and critical infrastructure, Fox News Digital reported, citing documents it reviewed.
The plan, known as FORTRESS, would require major military bases in the continental US to secure their own electricity, water, fuel, and communications.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We don’t want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can’t. It’s an intolerable risk,” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told Fox News Digital.
“Power is combat now. Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines, and just basic military command structures,” he said.
FORTRESS calls for portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids to keep bases running during prolonged power outages.
Preparing for a multi-front war
The Pentagon also plans to stockpile weapons, fuel, spare parts, and other essential supplies, while preparing civilian factories to switch to military production during a crisis.
“The next conflict will likely be fought on multiple fronts. Look at the geopolitics behind any major war. When that happens, global supply chains will break,” Parnell said.
The plan would require at least two qualified supply or production sources for critical military needs to reduce reliance on any single supplier or factory.
Russia Open to US-Ukraine Trilateral Talks After Nov. 4
It also includes measures to protect military communications, navigation, and satellite systems against GPS jamming and disruptions to space-based infrastructure.
Rethinking homeland defense
The initiative reflects a shift in US military planning toward the possibility that a major conflict could disrupt infrastructure supporting military operations inside the country.
“I realized that a lot of the way we think about homeland defense was built around the antiquated assumption that two oceans would protect us,” Parnell said.
“President Trump understands that world is gone, and he’s already paved the way for new thinking: Golden Dome, a renewed focus on the Western Hemisphere, Greenland, Panama,” he added.
The Pentagon has already announced plans to reduce major military installations’ dependence on civilian power grids. FORTRESS extends those efforts to water, fuel, communications, industrial production, and other essential services.
Parnell described the initiative as insurance against a major conflict disrupting the infrastructure and supply networks on which US forces rely.
“You don’t want to be making these decisions in the middle of a global multi-front conflict. We have to have a plan,” he said.

Germany plans to purchase Ukrainian Bars missiles for Bundeswehr testing – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:56:00 EET
18:56:00 KST

Germany plans to purchase Ukrainian Bars missiles for Bundeswehr testing – FT
The Financial Times reports, citing sources, that Germany is preparing its first purchase of Ukrainian-developed Bars missiles for its military. If the trials are successful, the order could be expanded to several hundred missiles.
Source: Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sources familiar with the plans indicate that the German government is expected to sign an agreement in the coming weeks to purchase an initial batch of Bars missiles for testing by the Bundeswehr.
The Bars is a jet-powered missile with a flight range of up to 1,000 km and a payload capacity of up to 105 kg, depending on the modification.
Although Ukrainians sometimes refer to it as a drone missile, Germany classifies it as a low-cost cruise missile.
The initial batch will enable the German military to conduct technical trials early next year. If the results are satisfactory, this could potentially pave the way for a larger order of several hundred units.
This initiative is part of Germany's comprehensive efforts to bolster European deterrence against Moscow by expanding its arsenal of long-range strike weapons.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described the Bars as one of the weapons used to strike military bases and energy facilities on Russian territory.
In recent months, Bars missiles have also been manufactured in Germany by a joint Ukrainian-German company whose operations remain shrouded in secrecy.
The first batch of German-made Bars missiles, funded by the German side, was delivered to Ukraine in October.
The joint venture will now also produce goods for Germany, marking the first known procurement of Ukrainian-developed offensive weaponry for the Bundeswehr's own needs.
In addition to the Bars missiles, Germany plans to acquire and test a small batch of Anthem cruise missiles produced by the US startup Covenant. The Anthem costs approximately one-tenth the price of a Tomahawk missile, which ranges from US$4 million to US$6 million.
One source familiar with the details stated that the Bars is even cheaper, but the German side is prepared to purchase both systems.
It was also noted that the potential acquisition of the Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile has been postponed for now.
Currently, the German armed forces only use the air-launched Taurus cruise missile, which has a relatively short range of about 500 km. Germany's plan to purchase the powerful BGM-109 Tomahawk missile and the Typhon ground-based launcher system from US manufacturer Raytheon could be delayed for up to five years.
Background:
- Media reports indicate that the German government expects to spend nearly €12 billion to create a new arsenal of long-range weapons designed to deter Russia.
- Recently, Denmark also announced a billion-dollar deal to purchase high-precision long-range missiles for the first time in its history, amid intentions to bolster its security.

'You hate Israel': European Parliament Left group's press officer says Israel deported him after 8-hour detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:55:02 UTC
18:55:02 KST

Melike Pala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
A press officer for The Left group in the European Parliament, Manus Carlisle, said Israeli authorities deported him after detaining him for approximately eight hours at Ben Gurion International Airport, citing political activism, previous travel to the occupied West Bank, and opposition to Israel.
Carlisle, who was traveling with his partner to participate in the olive harvest in the occupied West Bank as part of the Fa3za campaign, said the couple were denied entry into Israel upon arrival at Ben Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv.
The Fa3za campaign coordinates volunteers and solidarity efforts between Palestinian villages facing attacks, seeking to support communities, and help protect farmers during the olive harvest season.
Speaking to Anadolu, he said the couple had anticipated difficulties entering the country but were nevertheless "shocked" by the experience, describing an interrogation process during which Israeli officials allegedly demonstrated detailed knowledge of their political activities and social media presence.
"They (Israeli officials) didn’t like the Irish passport, and they didn’t like that I had spent time in Bethlehem before. Eventually, we were told that they knew every demonstration we had ever been on, and every social media post we had ever made," he said.
Carlisle said the couple had taken steps to remove social media content relating to Israel approximately one month before traveling, hoping this would make their entry into the country less difficult.
He added that they "were denied entry after about eight hours," and that Israeli officials said it is "because you hate Israel."
He said the couple were subsequently transferred to a deportation holding area after spending around eight hours in detention at the airport.
There, they encountered two other Irish men who had also been traveling to participate in the same olive harvest initiative.
"They were definitely on the lookout for us specifically," he said.

He flew a plane out of Beirut. Israel scrambled F-16s to intercept him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:52:39 UTC
18:52:39 KST

In 1982, during Israel's invasion of Lebanon, an Israeli soldier arrived at Beirut airport, climbed into a small Cessna aircraft and flew it back to Israel. His unexpected journey triggered a military alert, prompting the Israeli Air Force to scramble two F-16 fighter jets to intercept him. He landed safely in Haifa, only to find himself in military detention, accused of looting.
That soldier was Yishai Zimmerman, a decorated veteran of the IDF's legendary Unit 101, who died Monday at age 93 at Kibbutz Ein Harod Ihud in northern Israel. One of the last surviving members of the elite commando unit established in the 1950s under Ariel Sharon, Zimmerman left behind a military career marked by extraordinary bravery, repeated injuries in combat and an unmistakable rebellious streak.
He is survived by six children, 15 grandchildren and 10 great-grandchildren. His funeral will take place Tuesday at his kibbutz.
"Dad continued serving in the reserves until he was over 80, transporting tanks," his son, retired police Brig. Gen. Amal Zimmerman, a former commander of the Israel Police Air Unit, told ynet.
"He was the oldest tank transporter in the IDF, and possibly in the world. Dad was mischievous. He took the mischief of the old kibbutzniks to another level. He was also brave and didn't know the meaning of the word fear."
From military jail to Ariel Sharon's elite commando unit
Zimmerman was born in 1933 at Kibbutz Ein Harod to parents who were among the early pioneers of the Jezreel Valley and the founders of the kibbutz.
The political split that divided Israel's kibbutz movement in the early 1950s also divided his family. Zimmerman moved with his father to Ein Harod Ihud, while his mother and brother Malachi remained at Ein Harod Meuhad, the neighboring kibbutz created by the division.
As a boy, Zimmerman attended school alongside Meir Har-Zion, who would later become one of Israel's most celebrated commandos. The two eventually served together in the military.
Zimmerman initially enlisted in the Armored Corps, but his military career took an unexpected turn when Sharon began recruiting soldiers for Unit 101, the small commando force established in 1953 to conduct cross-border operations.
"When they established Unit 101, recruitment worked through friends bringing friends," his son recalled.
"Arik Sharon received glowing recommendations about Dad, so he got him out of military jail. Dad had gotten into trouble for doing foolish things and leaving for the weekend without permission."
The young soldier soon became part of some of the unit's most daring operations, serving from its establishment until its dissolution.
"He participated in the most audacious operations carried out by Unit 101," his son said.
A medal for bravery and wounds from two wars
Zimmerman later completed officer training and went on to distinguish himself during the 1956 Sinai campaign, known in Israel as Operation Kadesh.
Commanding a force tasked with capturing an Egyptian military position near Nitzana, he took part in a battle that earned him Israel's Medal of Courage.
"The mission was to take control of an artillery compound, including mortar positions," Amal Zimmerman said.
"Dad had been given command of a platoon only shortly before the operation. He didn't know the soldiers, and it turned out that he fought alone and captured the compound by himself."
Following the Sinai campaign, Zimmerman left active military service and returned to his kibbutz, where he worked in the garage for the rest of his life.
His civilian career, however, did not mean an end to his military involvement. He continued serving in the reserves and was wounded in both the 1967 Six-Day War and the 1973 Yom Kippur War, during which he served with forces fighting under Sharon.
Even decades later, long after most soldiers had retired from reserve duty, Zimmerman continued transporting tanks for the IDF.
The stolen Cessna and the F-16 interception
One of the most unusual episodes in Zimmerman's life began with a childhood ambition to fly. As a young man, he had obtained a civilian pilot's license after taking flying lessons at Megiddo airfield in northern Israel.
That qualification would eventually lead to an extraordinary incident during the 1982 Lebanon War.
Zimmerman was serving with a special intelligence unit when he arrived at Beirut airport, took a Cessna aircraft and flew it toward Israel.
"He informed the air traffic control unit over the radio that he was coming, but they scrambled two F-16s to intercept him," his son recalled.
"They were worried it was a hijacked plane carrying Israelis, so the fighter jets escorted him to a landing in Haifa."
Instead of receiving a hero's welcome, Zimmerman found himself in trouble with the military authorities.
"He spent a month in military jail before his trial and was charged with looting," his son said.
The aircraft was eventually returned to Lebanon. The report did not specify the outcome of the legal proceedings.
According to his son, even the military prosecutor appeared to recognize the extraordinary nature of the episode.
"The prosecutor told him that next time he should call him, because he also wanted to have an experience like that," Amal Zimmerman recalled.
For Zimmerman's family, the Beirut adventure captured the character of a man who had fought in several of Israel's wars, earned a decoration for bravery and continued volunteering for military service long after the age when most people retire.
He was a fearless soldier, his son said, but also a mischievous kibbutznik who never entirely outgrew his appetite for adventure.

Algeria’s military deployment to Niger: What’s behind the move?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:52:11 UTC
18:52:11 KST

Algeria’s military deployment to Niger: What’s behind the move?
This will be Algeria’s first foreign troop deployment in 50 years as the country shifts its military doctrine amid new security challenges.
Algeria’s parliament has approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger, in a major shift in the North African nation’s noninterventionist military doctrine.
Algeria’s lower house, the People’s National Assembly, ratified the deployment on Sunday after the upper house, the Council of the Nation, unanimously approved the proposal earlier in the day.
Details about the number of soldiers and when they will be deployed have yet to be made public.
It comes nearly two months after Algeria dispatched four Russian-made Sukhoi Su-30 jets, a transport aircraft and an aerial refuelling aircraft to Niamey, following what Algerian authorities described as an attempt to destabilise Niger’s military-led government.
The step comes amid a thawing of relations between Algiers and Niamey as Niger’s President Abdourahamane Tchiani visited Algeria in February and, months later, his defence minister, Salifou Mody, travelled to Algiers to discuss security cooperation.
The shooting down of a Malian drone by the Algerian army last April triggered a diplomatic crisis after Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso recalled their ambassadors from Algiers. The condemnation of the 2023 coup in Niger by Algeria had also strained ties.
The troop deployment is reportedly intended to protect oil installations belonging to Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach. Troops would be sent “to protect Algeria’s economic and strategic interests, particularly its oil facilities in Niger”, The Associated Press news agency reported, quoting Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti.
It also comes as Algiers seeks to deepen security cooperation in the Sahel, a vast belt of territory stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, including several countries along Algeria’s southern frontier.
Why does this matter?
Algeria has historically been reluctant to deploy its armed forces beyond its borders, reflecting a longstanding foreign policy built around sovereignty, noninterference and opposition to foreign military intervention.
But that does not mean it has never done so.
Algerian forces participated in the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, although overseas military deployments have remained exceptionally rare in the decades since.
A constitutional revision in 2020 formalised the conditions under which Algerian troops could be sent abroad.
Under Article 91, the president may authorise such deployments, provided they receive the backing of at least two-thirds of the members of each chamber of parliament.
The constitution also provides for Algerian participation in peacekeeping operations under the auspices of the United Nations, the African Union and the Arab League.
The move is particularly significant given Algeria’s military capabilities. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the country spent more than $25bn on its armed forces in 2025, making it Africa’s largest military spender.
But the decision also comes against a backdrop of growing diplomatic tensions and shifting regional alliances.
In September, Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, accusing Abu Dhabi of repeated “hostile” and “provocative actions” without publicly detailing the incidents behind the decision.
The two countries have long disagreed over several regional issues, including Western Sahara and the UAE’s alleged interference in North African and Sahelian affairs.
Taken together, these developments suggest that Algeria is becoming increasingly willing to assert its security interests beyond its borders, even as it continues to emphasise the principles of sovereignty and noninterference.
Why the Sahel?
For Algeria, instability in the Sahel is not a distant security concern.
The country shares thousands of kilometres of borders with Mali, Niger and Libya, making developments in its southern neighbourhood particularly consequential.
The roots of the current security crisis can be traced, in part, to the collapse of Muammar Gaddafi’s government in Libya in 2011.
At the height of the Arab Spring uprisings, Algeria took a firm stance against foreign military intervention and warned that the disintegration of the Libyan state could destabilise neighbouring countries.
Those concerns were not unfounded.
Following Gaddafi’s overthrow, weapons and armed fighters, including Tuareg who had served in Libya, spread into neighbouring countries.
Their return helped fuel a rebellion in northern Mali in 2012, contributing to a security crisis that preceded the military overthrow of President Amadou Toumani Toure that March.
Over the following decade, armed rebellion expanded across parts of the Sahel, particularly Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.
Since 2012, those three countries alone have experienced six military coups: three in Mali, two in Burkina Faso and one in Niger.
Many of the coups unfolded against a backdrop of deteriorating security, with military leaders accusing civilian governments of failing to contain increasingly powerful armed groups.
But insecurity was not the only factor. Political grievances, governance failures and rivalries within armed forces also contributed to the coups.
Who else is operating in the Sahel?
Another factor shaping Algeria’s calculations is the changing presence of foreign military forces across the region.
For more than a decade, France was a central player in counterterrorism operations in the Sahel, deploying thousands of troops to combat armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).
But that military presence has largely unravelled.
Following successive coups and deteriorating diplomatic relations, France withdrew its troops from Mali in August 2022, Burkina Faso in February 2023 and Niger in December 2023.
The withdrawals were accompanied by growing anti-French sentiment and demands from military governments for greater control over their security policies.
Niger demanded the departure of approximately 1,500 French soldiers following its July 2023 coup.
Just months later, in April 2024, approximately 100 Russian military personnel arrived in Niamey, bringing equipment and providing training to Nigerien forces.
The personnel were associated with Africa Corps, a Russian paramilitary group close to the Kremlin.
Moscow has also expanded its military cooperation with Mali and Burkina Faso, where Russian personnel have undertaken training, advisory and security roles, including combat support in Mali.
The United States has also seen its military footprint shrink.
In 2024, Washington withdrew approximately 1,000 soldiers from Niger after the military government terminated their security cooperation agreement. The withdrawal included personnel stationed at an important US drone base near Agadez.
The result has been a significant realignment of the Sahel’s security partnerships, with Western military forces departing and Russia assuming a more prominent role.
What does Algeria stand to gain?
For Algiers, the proposed deployment to Niger carries immediate security and wider strategic implications.
At the most practical level, protecting Algerian energy investments would help safeguard the country’s economic interests in a region affected by armed rebellions and political instability, including the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), which would transport Nigerian gas to Europe and traverse Niger and Algeria.
It could also deepen cooperation with Niger, whose military government has sought new security partners since taking power in 2023.
More broadly, the move would allow Algeria to establish a direct military presence in a neighbouring country at a time when the Sahel’s security architecture is being reshaped.
“We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure,” Senator Boulghiti told reporters after the vote. “It is simply an adaptation of our doctrine to evolving circumstances so we can rise to the new challenges imposed by the situation in the Sahel region.”

Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:51:15 UTC
18:51:15 KST

Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.
- Share:
A shipwreck off the coast of Turkey is the oldest shipwreck in the world, our team of archaeologists believes.
There’s little left of the ship itself but based on clues from its cargo – including pottery vessels – a research team I was part of has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700–2400 BCE.
That’s about 4,500 years ago. Prior to this discovery, the world’s oldest shipwreck was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, in Greece, thought to have been from about 4,200 years ago.
Much work remains to be done to finesse the conclusions, and a paper outlining the results is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Yet the discovery could transform our understanding of ancient Mediterranean connections during the Early Bronze Age.
Here, and perhaps even earlier, lie the foundations of extensive trade routes as we know them today.
Searching for clues
Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, Antalya, has worked along this coastline for decades excavating ancient shipwrecks.
Acting on clues from local seafarers, Öniz found a shipwreck in shallow waters off Kekova, west of Antalya in Turkey, in 2024. Earlier this year, he contacted me and asked if I would help date some of the pottery vessels found on this wreck.
As an archaeologist specializing in desert sites, this was a singular experience. New technology, water-logged methods of excavation and laborious conservation techniques were the new normal. Yet there is always room for learning new skills in life.
Of the ship itself there is now nothing to see, owing to underwater exposure. Yet the research team has now estimated the ship and its cargo dates to around 2700–2400 BCE. However, the precise dating is still under consideration. Earlier or later dates on either side of this initial determination are also possible.
A time capsule of ancient trade
This discovery promises to re-write our understanding of early trade networks from around 4,500 years ago.
The ship is a “missing piece” in the story of networks, trade and commodity exchange in the wider eastern Mediterranean. This era includes the pyramid age of Giza and its mighty pharaohs.
What remains under the sea is a time capsule of ancient trade.
Although its direction was not known, the boat was evidently traveling along the coast of southern Turkey.
Now resting on the seabed between two islands, it is apparent the ship likely sought refuge in the lee waters during a storm. One could imagine the terror of the sailors – possibly coastal people from the Levant region – as their ship crashed against the rocks.
While timbers from the ship disappeared long ago, the remains of its precious cargo were embedded in the rocky slope along the Kekova coast.
Divers worked over the past four months to extract its pottery from barnacles clinging to the rocky underwater slope.
A closer look at pottery
Pottery is like plastic: it never goes away and just breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces.
Yet humble pottery vessels hold many clues about the past.
In this case, the cargo included large ceramic storage vessels or amphorae which once contained products from regions of the eastern Mediterranean.
The pots were large ovoid, flat-based jars with two handles, many featuring a raised horizontal clay “belt” around the widest part of the jar.
Through these vessels was possible to ascertain many pieces of information. This includes the likely origin of the jars and the contents exchanged across the region.
Importantly, the shape and manufacturing technique of the pots themselves help us date the cargo. By extension, this includes also the date of other pottery, and the ship itself.
The bigger picture
Compared to later periods, trade and exchange in the eastern Mediterranean during the third millennium (3000–2000 BCE) is poorly understood.
Maritime voyages during the that period are known from Egyptian texts, pottery vessels and raw materials from ancient tombs.
Around the same time as this ship struck the rocks, the ancient Egyptians were trading in the eastern Mediterranean through the port of Byblos in Lebanon.
Commodities such as cedar, tin/lead, oils, tree resins, lapis lazuli and silver, all materials that Egypt lacked, were imported by the Egyptian state.
Recent scientific research also reveals that silver was acquired by the Egyptian state around 2600 BCE. Analyses showed this silver was acquired from the Lavrion mines east of modern Athens.
While it is unlikely Egyptian ships made this journey, boats like the Kekova ship may have used the route as part of an extended international maritime network.
And what was in the jars? Remarkably there were still residues visible to the naked eye. Again, scientific analyses are pending, but could be some of the products mentioned in the Egyptian texts, possibly olive oil, wine or tree resin.
The ship may have acquired its pottery from several ports on their journey. Our best assessment at this stage of research is that some of the “belted” jars (or clays used to make them) may have originated in the Central Jordan Valley.
The coast of southern Turkey is littered with ancient shipwrecks. While maritime archaeology is a relatively recent phenomenon, some of the world’s most famous wrecks have been discovered there. Who knows what other secrets these waters hold.
The research on which this article is based was led by Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, head of the Division of Mediterranean Underwater Cultural Heritage Research, and the Department of Restoration and Conservation of Cultural Heritage in the Faculty of Art at the Akdeniz University, Antalya, Turkey.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Karin Sowada, Senior Lecturer in Archaeology and Director of the Australian Centre for Egyptology, Macquarie University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:47:14 UTC
18:47:14 KST

Young adults in China looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks.
Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.
Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”
A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo.
Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.
One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.
Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.”
“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”
Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher.
China’s birthrate is in decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks.
The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks.
Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.

Middlesex Regiment soldier laid to rest on the Somme
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:46:28 GMT
18:46:28 KST

Middlesex Regiment soldier laid to rest on the Somme
Private (Pte) Percy Tolliday, from Camberwell, London, buried on the Somme alongside two unknown soldiers. Identification was made through DNA testing 110 years after Pte Tolliday went missing in action during the Battle of the Somme.
Pte Percy Tolliday, of 11th Battalion The Middlesex Regiment, was laid to rest on the Somme on 21 October 2026 alongside two unknown comrades, at a burial service organised by MOD’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), also known as the ‘War Detectives’. The service took place at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s (CWGC) Warlencourt British Cemetery.
Richard Tolliday, the great nephew of Pte Tolliday, had travelled from Atlanta, USA to attend the burial service with his wife and nephew. It was Richard who had provided the DNA sample that made identification of Pte Tolliday possible.
Richard Tolliday, great nephew of Pte Tolliday said:
  We are deeply grateful to the JCCC for their extraordinary dedication, expertise, and professionalism that enabled the identification of the remains of our Great Uncle, Pte Percy Tolliday, 110 years after his death in the Battle of the Somme. In 1916, Percy was a soldier but also a son and a brother. It has been an honour to be able to assist in this process and to attend his burial service that so movingly and impressively brings an appropriate recognition and closure for Percy and his family, past and present.
Pte Tolliday and the two unknown soldiers were uncovered during the installation of wind turbines near Gueudecourt. They were found lying in a shell hole, suggesting that they may have died together, possibly having been hit by the same shell. Work continues in an attempt to identify the unknown soldiers.
JCCC Caseworker, Rosie Barron said:
  It has been a privilege to have played a part in the identification and burial of Pte Percy Tolliday and to have provided answers for his family. He and these two unknown soldiers were killed in the most awful conditions in heavy rain, deep mud and under continuous shelling. The worst extremity of World War 1 conditions. JCCC will continue to do all it can to work to identify Pte Tolliday’s comrades and hopefully bring further closure to other families.
The service was supported by serving soldiers from The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, The Princess of Wales’s Royal Regiment and The Regimental Band and Corps of Drums of The Royal Welsh.
The service was conducted by the Reverend Fiona Beale CF, Chaplain to 1st Battalion The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers.
Reverend Fiona Beale CF said:
  Being the Padre to 1st Battalion The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, I find it a deeply moving and humbling privilege to conduct the burial service for Pte Percy Tolliday and two unknown soldiers, presumed to also be of The Middlesex Regiment. It is a sacred duty and profound honour to lay to rest these World War 1 heroes who endured the unimaginable horrors of the trenches.
The graves of all three men will now be cared for by the CWGC in perpetuity.
Dr Daniel Seaton, Commemorations Case Officer at the CWGC, said:
  The three casualties now laid to rest were recovered by the Commission’s specialist Recovery Unit, not far away from where today’s ceremony has taken place. I am delighted that, following research conducted by ourselves and the JCCC, Private Tolliday has been identified, and remain hopeful that it may also be possible to identify the two Unknown Soldiers in the future. All three are now remembered with honour in the Commission’s Warlencourt British Cemetery.

Bedfordshire soldiers laid to rest on the Western Front
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:46:14 GMT
18:46:14 KST

Bedfordshire soldiers laid to rest on the Western Front
Private (Pte) George McIntosh, from Ilford, Essex, buried in France on 20 October 2026 alongside an unknown soldier. Identification was made through DNA testing nearly 110 years after Pte McIntosh went missing in action during the Great War.
Pte George McIntosh, of 8th Battalion The Bedfordshire Regiment, was laid to rest in France on 20 October 2026 alongside one of his comrades, at a burial service organised by MOD’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), also known as the ‘War Detectives’. The service took place at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s (CWGC) Loos British Cemetery Extension.
JCCC Caseworker, Rosie Barron said:
  It has been an honour to have met Pte McIntosh’s family today and to have seen him laid to rest alongside his comrade. His family has travelled a long way to be here, and this shows the depth of what these men still mean to their families even 110 years on. Their sacrifice and commitment to the cause of obtaining freedom and peace must never be forgotten.
Pte McIntosh and the unknown soldier were some of around 100 sets of British and Canadian remains recovered during the construction of a hospital on the outskirts of Lens. They are the final British casualties from that site to be laid to rest. DNA testing, coordinated by JCCC, confirmed the identity of Pte McIntosh. Work continues to identify the unknown Bedfordshire Regiment soldier.
Ten members of Pte McIntosh’s family attended the burial service including his great nephew, Jeff MacIntosh, who had travelled from the North Carolina, USA to be in attendance. It was Jeff who had provided the DNA sample that made identification of Pte McIntosh possible.
Jeff MacIntosh, great nephew of Pte McIntosh said:
  The work that JCCC and CWGC do is simply remarkable. While we knew that we had a great uncle George MacIntosh we knew very little about the details of his life and death in WW1. The work of JCCC in connecting George to us via DNA has allowed us to explore his life, what his loss meant to his mother and family, as well as gain a better understanding of the horrors of WW1. Our family sincerely thanks JCCC for the work that you all do. His story has now been shared with our entire clan, and we are honoured to be in attendance at the ceremony.
Pte George McIntosh was born in 1883 in Ilford, Essex to Scottish parents. He grew up in Barnet. Before enlisting into the Army, he worked as a gardener and a florist. Having enlisted, Pte McIntosh was posted to 8th Battalion The Bedfordshire Regiment.
The Battle of Arras started on 9 April 1917. Following the successful capture of the high ground at Vimy Ridge by Canadian forces, the Douai Plain was open to the Allies. On the morning of 18 April 1917, 8th Battalion The Bedfordshire Regiment found themselves south of Loos-en-Gohelle. They moved into the frontline and spent the next two days fighting over the location where the new hospital is being built. It was during this fighting on 19 April 1917 that Pte McIntosh was killed. He was 34 years old. It is highly likely that the unknown Bedfordshire Regiment soldier was also killed during this period. As they were missing, both men would have been commemorated on the Loos Memorial.
The service was supported by serving soldiers from The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, The Princess of Wales’s Royal Regiment and The Regimental Band and Corps of Drums of The Royal Welsh and was attended by staff of The Royal Anglian Regiment Headquarters. The service was conducted by the Reverend Fiona Beale CF, Chaplain to 1st Battalion The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers.
Reverend Fiona Beale CF said:
  It is a privilege and an honour to be chosen to conduct the burial of Pte George McIntosh and this unknown soldier—known only to God—both of The Bedfordshire Regiment. The mere anticipation of standing before these World War 1 heroes’ final resting places brought an overwhelming wave of profound gratitude and solemn reverence.
The graves of both men will now be cared for by the CWGC in perpetuity.
 David Royle, Recoveries and Ceremonies Manager at the CWGC, said: 
> Nearly 110 years after they fell in action, and less than a mile from where they were recovered, it is a privilege to lay these two Bedfordshire Regiment soldiers to rest with the care and dignity they deserve. We are proud to have worked alongside the JCCC to restore Private George McIntosh’s name, and although the identity of the second soldier remains known only unto God, he is no longer lost or forgotten. Both men now rest among their comrades ensuring future generations can pay their respects and remember their stories in perpetuity.

It’s About Security, Stupid!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:46:01 UTC
18:46:01 KST

Transitioning from Ukraine to the West exposes significant shifts in perspective. My most recent reentry into Europe and the US, after a stint in Ukraine, brought to light a perceptual disconnect around one crucial issue – especially as peace talks and potential deals appear in the news. That issue is security.
Outside of Ukraine I’m often asked the question: “Would Ukrainians accept a land-for-peace deal?”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The simple answer is: “Yes, definitely. As long as they get a real security guarantee.”
In an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour aired on Thursday, Oct. 22, President Volodymyr Zelensky insisted: “The most important thing [is] security guarantees.”
Of course, the full answer to the question of “land-for-peace” is very complex.
A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology indicated that 61 percent of Ukrainians consider handing Moscow all of eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region in exchange for security guarantees completely unacceptable.
However, like all such polls, the survey needs to minimize the contingencies surrounding any given issue. In this case, giving up the so-called “fortress belt” of cities in the remainder of the Donbas region that Ukraine still controls would be “unacceptable,” as it would require Kyiv to pull troops away from what constitutes its “Maginot line” against a Russian blitz toward Kyiv. In terms of security, such a land giveaway would be tantamount to capitulation – something obvious to Ukrainians on the ground there.
Russia Won’t Negotiate Seriously While It Thinks It Can Force Ukraine to Surrender, Sybiha Says
Focusing on the issue
When I consider the question, I keep hearing the refrain of Bill Clinton during the 1992 US presidential elections, when he was running against the incumbent George H.W. Bush.
Bush had just won a quick war, liberating Kuwait and manhandling the Iraqi army, which was supposed to be the third strongest in the world. Yet, despite his undisputed foreign policy success, economic figures were beginning to hint at recession, and the young candidate Clinton jumped on them with the rally cry: “It’s the economy, stupid!”
Clinton’s success lay in his ability to simply focus on the obvious, rather than getting sidetracked by ancillary issues and spectacles.
In a sense, that’s how Ukrainians feel. Everything depends on security. And security for Ukrainians has never been easy.
3 options for security guarantees
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has sought three basic types of security guarantee.
The most desirable for Kyiv, at least initially, was NATO. But as Zelensky pleaded for some sort of NATO membership, it became clear that this would never happen as long as Ukraine was under attack. And even after a ceasefire, opposition to Ukraine’s full membership would be virtually insurmountable.
That left Ukraine with the hope of a watered-down alternative to NATO: separate bilateral security agreements with partners that could help in the event that any future peace deal were breached by Moscow. Preferably, the partner should be a NATO member with nuclear capabilities. (Only the US, the UK, and France fit that bill).
The key to any such agreement would be what’s referred to as an “Article 5-type” clause that would oblige the partner to come to Ukraine’s assistance in case of attack. But Article 5 is ambiguous enough to have even NATO members questioning what would happen if Russia attacked (ironically, the very scenario that NATO was designed to deter and/or defend against).
This second scenario is fraught with problems. What about foreign boots on the ground to monitor the ceasefire? What about foreign military bases in Ukraine? What about tripwires? It’s not surprising that most nations have diplomatically eschewed committing to Ukraine’s security beyond money and materiel.
The third scenario – at least from the perspective within Ukraine – is fast proving to be the only viable solution: Ensure that the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) become so strong and capable that any invasion of Ukrainian territory would be too costly for the aggressor. And this is exactly what’s happening.
As with any promising solution to an intractable problem, the positives tend to snowball with momentum. As the nature of warfare becomes increasingly determined by drones and artificial intelligence, all the world’s military powers are studying the tactics and technologies employed in Ukraine. Even NATO military officers understand that in order to defend against a hypothetical attack, Ukraine’s know-how – acquired and developed out of necessity – is essential.
At this stage, though, Ukraine still can’t go it alone. Kyiv is currently parlaying its battlefield experience and willingness to sacrifice blood into a flood of treasure coming from the rich countries to its west. Security autonomy will take time, so Ukrainians have little choice but to hold the line, have faith in the AFU, and hope for the best in the West.
What this means for negotiations
As Zelensky continually insists: It’s about security. All the mineral and gas deals, all the talk of Donbas lines and territorial integrity, these are sideshows – important only inasmuch as they determine Ukraine’s security.
The Donbas issue – which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio disingenuously claimed on Oct. 22 was what “the war is about” – offers a perfect example:
It’s not that Ukraine is so attached to some holy notion of land or the mineral wealth beneath it. Zelensky has publicly repeated that he would accept a ceasefire on the current line of contact. But to give away land Russia has been unable to grab in 12 years for the sake of a dubious guarantee? That would be worse than naiveté – it would be disastrously criminal negligence on the part of Ukraine’s negotiators – especially as US President Donald Trump and his cohort, most notably Elon Musk, are so quick to double-cross friends for the sake of personal (not even national) interest.
As such, any proposed peace deal, if it is to be taken seriously, must offer real security guarantees. Given the current climate of distrust, “Article 5-like” guarantees will and should be met with a politely diplomatic “Thank you very much, but…” followed by hardnosed inquiries into details of commitments and tripwires.
The view from Ukraine, now nearly five full years into Moscow’s failed full-scale invasion, is rather clear. From the front line, where Russians are dying at a 10:1 ratio in many places and being fed into a drone buzzsaw in a maniacal effort to claim ruined Donbas villages as “conquered,” to cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa, where inhabitants are bracing for a winter rife with power outages and ballistic missile attacks, no one is talking about surrendering, which is what Trump is effectively trying to coerce.
With each passing day, Ukraine’s only real security hope grows in strength, and many of its European partners have begun to realize that in terms of security they cannot do without a strong Ukraine.
Ultimately, though, Ukrainians know their security will hinge on two ineluctable facts – one biological, the other political – all dictators die, and all empires disintegrate.
This is a generational fight that can’t be framed by American or European election cycles. And the existential security problem Ukraine has with Moscow is centuries old.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Palestinians are opening their doors to the displaced of besieged Hebron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:45:25 UTC
18:45:25 KST

Palestinians are opening their doors to the displaced of besieged Hebron
Israel’s assault on the West Bank city has forced thousands of people to flee their homes.
The Farsh Al-Hawa area in the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank is unrecognisable after Israeli forces demolished a three-story building and industrial facilities there. Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds the West Bank portfolio in the Ministry of Defence, said he ordered their destruction.
It all started on Friday, when two Palestinians attacked an Israeli military checkpoint in Farsh Al-Hawa, killing two soldiers and injuring others.
Since then, Hebron, the West Bank’s economic capital, has been attacked and put under lockdown by Israeli forces.
Israel has announced a sweeping military assault in the city, targeting the neighbourhood of the gunmen, who were killed on Friday. Israeli forces have already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians. City officials say almost half of the displaced are babies and children under 18, along with 81 pregnant women and 204 elderly.
Fahd Ahmaro was forced to leave his home, along with his family. He told Al Jazeera that he planned to stay but felt compelled to seek shelter outside his neighbourhood because the women and children were terrified.
“We left with nothing but the clothes on our backs. Our savings, belongings and documents are all in the house,” he said. “I tried to go back after I got my family out safely, but I couldn’t. It’s not safe any more.”
Palestinian authorities in Hebron have declared a state of emergency and created a crisis group, bringing together government agencies, the private sector and civil society, to respond after thousands of people in the city were forced to flee their homes.
Riyadh Khamis, who serves on the committee, told Al Jazeera that philanthropists who could not bear the thought of fellow Palestinians staying in temporary shelters opened their homes to the displaced.
“Hebron is known for its social solidarity and generosity. Our city was the first to provide aid during the COVID lockdown and during the genocide,” Khamis told Al Jazeera. “Today, our neighbours needed help so we all rallied.”
Real estate developer Mohamed Al-Rujoob is one of the philanthropists who sprang to action at the start of the assault on the city.
Al-Rujoob, who owns several apartments in Dura, a town close to Hebron, announced that the properties would be made available for displaced families, prompting other owners to do the same. He now hosts three extended families in his apartments, including 30 children.
“We must preserve people’s dignity. Today, we host these good people. Tomorrow, who knows? It might be us who need shelter. We’re all under the same occupation and we’re all vulnerable,” he said.
The Israeli army says Hebron is on lockdown, which affects nearly 1 million Palestinians who live in the city and the rest of the district.
Restrictions on movement have had a severe impact on the West Bank’s largest district. Schools have moved to online classes, while Hebron’s universities have made similar arrangements for their 18,000 students until the Israeli operation ends.
The measures are essential for Palestinian students who are stuck in their homes and neighbourhoods, including the besieged Fawwar refugee camp in Hebron, home to nearly 8,000 Palestinians. Israeli soldiers closed the camp’s entrance gate on Saturday, barring residents from entering or leaving, even on foot.
Abdel Fattah Al-Ttitti, a school teacher who lives in the camp and works in a Hebron school, said “we are locked in”.
“If, God forbid, somebody needs medical attention, we may be able to get them to the clinic in Masafer Yatta, but that clinic is poorly equipped. If there’s a medical emergency, they can’t help,” Al-Ttitti told Al Jazeera.
He is glad that schools announced online classes. “Until this campaign is over, there’s no other way,” he said.
Many in Hebron believe that Israel’s military campaign in the city has a political dimension, with Israelis heading to the polls on Tuesday for a general election.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition is vying for every right-wing vote. Violence against Palestinians has proved an expedient campaign tactic for politicians such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Minister of Settlement Affairs, Orit Strook.
Both right-wing ministers have homes in illegal settlements in the Hebron area and support the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank and Gaza, which they refer to as “encouraging voluntary migration”.

spacon shapes perforated aluminum curtain and vintage shoe box carpets for adidas copenhagen
in the fitting rooms, the aluminum curtain maps the city’s running paths, while photographic carpets document local sneaker-collecting culture across the footwear department.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
SPACON designs installations for ADIDAS store in COPENHAGEN
Copenhagen-based architecture and design practice Spacon has developed two site-specific installations for the Adidas flagship store in Copenhagen. Intervening in two distinct retail zones, the fitting rooms and the Originals footwear area, the custom installations draw reference from the city’s urban running culture and the material archives of local sneaker collectors.
overview of the Adidas store in Copenhagen | all images ©Spacon
- SINE-WAVE PERFORATED ALUMINUM CURTAIN screens FITTING ROOMS
In the fitting room area, Spacon Studio installed a perforated aluminum curtain formed into a continuous sine-wave profile. The corrugated metal surface is calibrated across three viewing distances using varying perforation densities to project three nested graphic motifs: an aerial satellite view of Copenhagen centered on its central lakes with a crosshair indicating the store’s coordinates, a silhouette of a runner mid-stride, and a close-up profile of an Adidas Adizero shoe. The undulating surface of the aluminum sheet reflects ambient retail lighting while translating local running topography into a kinetic metallic partition.
detail of the custom seating installation
- PHOTOGRAPHIC CARPETS INTEGRATE ARCHIVAL VINTAGE SHOE BOXES
In the Originals footwear section, the studio placed three oversized photographic carpets across the floor. The textile prints depict an expansive field of vintage Adidas shoe boxes shown in various states—sealed, open, and empty. Embedded within the photographic field are rare archival sneakers sourced directly from the private collections of local sneaker collectors Joachim Idestrup Friis and Alexander Cummings, turning regional footwear archives into large-format floor graphics.

Can Latvia still afford Rail Baltica? Latvian Transport Minister warns current approach is no longer sustainable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:44:25 UTC
18:44:25 KST

Latvia's next government will have to assess whether and how the country can afford to continue implementing the Rail Baltica railway project when preparing the next state budget, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis of New Unity (JV) said on TV3's programme 900 Seconds.
He explained that Russia's war in Ukraine and other geopolitical developments mean the issue will require serious consideration and difficult decisions.
According to Kozlovskis, it is clear that Latvia can no longer continue implementing the project in the same way as before.
Furthermore, there is currently no clarity regarding funding from the European Union in future planning periods or financing from the European Commission.
Kozlovskis pointed out that a funding shortfall already exists within current contractual commitments, while financial obligations continue to increase.
At the same time, it is impossible to predict how much project costs may rise.
Consequently, there is also uncertainty about the financial burden on the state budget if existing contracts continue.
The minister stressed that the government must take these circumstances into account when preparing the budget and establish a clear expenditure plan for Rail Baltica.
As previously reported, the first phase of Rail Baltica's main railway line in Latvia is planned to proceed within its existing scope.
This includes establishing a cross-border Rail Baltica connection from Lithuania to the Estonian border, as well as completing construction work at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station.
These developments are intended to make it possible to connect Rail Baltica with Latvia's existing railway network.
The cost of the first phase of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 14.3 billion euros, including 5.5 billion euros in Latvia.
However, after adjusting for cost increases, Latvia's share could rise to six billion euros.
According to the project's cost-benefit analysis, the total cost of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 23.8 billion euros.
By comparison, the previous cost-benefit analysis, conducted in 2017, estimated the entire project would cost 5.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica aims to establish a European standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border, connecting the Baltic states by rail with the rest of Europe.
The project envisages constructing 870 kilometres of new European standard-gauge railway track, with a gauge of 1,435 millimetres, across the Baltic states.
Trains on the new railway are expected to be capable of reaching a maximum speed of 240 kilometres per hour.

The developments come amid continued Israeli bombardment, gunfire, and restrictions on the entry of supplies despite a ceasefire agreement in effect since October 10, 2025.
The following are four crises that have worsened in Gaza during Israel’s election campaign and their impact on Palestinians.
Food aid cuts
On October 19, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced a one-third cut in food assistance in Gaza, leaving around 500,000 Palestinians without support and reducing beneficiaries from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
It halved food rations, cut daily hot meals from 250,000 to 150,000 and reduced deliveries to hard-to-reach areas.
The WFP blamed funding shortages, saying it needed $450 million to sustain operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank from October to March 2027.
Around 1.4 million Palestinians in Gaza face high levels of food insecurity.
Meanwhile, Israeli restrictions, inspection procedures and limited crossing capacity continue to hinder aid deliveries, according to the UN.
Gaza’s government media office warned that aid cuts were worsening famine conditions, while the Palestinian government raised concerns over rising malnutrition among children and pregnant women.
Hospitals at risk of shutdown
On October 21, Gaza’s Health Ministry said stocks of fuel needed to operate hospital electricity generators had run out, warning that the remaining generators could fail and life-saving medical services could be forced to stop.
Hospitals require more than 2,500 litres of fuel each month to keep generators running for extended periods amid a lack of electricity, the ministry said.
On September 13, Mazen al-Araishi, director general of engineering and maintenance at the ministry, said the quantities of fuel allowed into Gaza were limited and insufficient to meet generator operations and maintenance needs.
The ministry did not say when the last shipment of fuel entered Gaza or how long the generators could continue operating.
Gaza hospitals have depended on generators since Israel cut electricity supplies to the enclave in October 2023 and its sole power plant stopped operating after running out of fuel, while the war destroyed large sections of electricity lines and distribution networks.
The generators power operating rooms, intensive care units, neonatal incubators, ventilators and dialysis machines, making their failure a direct threat to patients’ lives.
Expansion of Israeli-occupied areas
The Israeli army has continued expanding areas under its occupation in Gaza by moving “Yellow Line” markers westward, contrary to the ceasefire agreement’s gradual withdrawal plan. The line separates areas under Israeli military control from those where Palestinians are permitted to remain.
On October 11, Israeli forces advanced into Gaza City’s Shujaiya neighbourhood, moving concrete markers westward and forcing scores of families to flee.
The UN’s OCHA agency confirmed the changes on October 19, warning of further forced displacement.
The expansion restricts Palestinian access to homes, farmland and public facilities while complicating aid deliveries.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in June that the army occupied around 70 percent of Gaza and ruled out withdrawing from the Yellow Line.
He has linked further withdrawal to Hamas’s disarmament, while the group says the issue of its weapons can be addressed alongside a gradual Israeli withdrawal.
Palestinian deaths
Alongside the expansion of Israeli military control, the number of Palestinians killed by Israel from October 2-21 rose by around 40 percent compared with the same period in September, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry figures.
The data showed that 95 Palestinians were killed during that period in October, compared with 68 during the corresponding period in September, an increase of 27 deaths.
The number of Palestinians killed by Israel since the ceasefire agreement took effect reached 1,534 as of October 21, according to Health Ministry figures.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed 74,494 Palestinians and injured 175,604 others in Gaza, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Drive reindustrialisation from No 10 North or risk failure, MPs tell Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:42:48 UTC
18:42:48 KST

Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said.
The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode”.
John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”.
However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work.
“The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation. The state has become less knowledgable about the state of the economy and our businesses, unable to comprehensively plan and slow to make decisions,” the paper says.
The MPs are calling on Burnham to pass a new Reindustrialisation Act, to set clear targets for creating jobs by rebuilding the country’s manufacturing capacity, and to ensure ministers are held to account against them. “If we do not plan for reindustrialisation, we cannot achieve it,” the group argues.
The briefing paper urges the PM to give the job of overseeing reindustrialisation to the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and base it at No 10 North, the Manchester outpost he established in July, which has already taken on some responsibility for growth policy.
And the paper argues that the National Wealth Fund – the arm’s length body that invests in promising businesses – should be transformed into a Reindustrialisation Development Corporation, whose primary job is to provide capital for rebuilding UK industry.
Andy MacNae, the MP for Rossendale and Darwen, who chairs the group, said: “I’ve got absolutely no doubt about Andy or John’s commitment to this, but there is a kind of inertia in government, within the civil service, within economic orthodoxy, that still says that growth policy is about cities – it’s about the places that are already doing well.”
Instead, he said, reindustrialisation must be about “delivering jobs to the places that need them most.” He added: “It’s about making things again, and it’s about making the things that give us national resilience in a turbulent world.”
He cited the government’s recent decision to nationalise British Steel, adding that reindustrialisation involved policies across government, from procurement to education.
Steve Yemm, the MP for the former mining constituency of Mansfield, said: “Countries around the world are reindustrialising, yet too many in Whitehall still treat industrial policy as dangerous nostalgia. We need the prime minister’s full backing to challenge those outdated assumptions.”
A third member of the group, Lorraine Beavers, the MP for Blackpool North and Fleetwood, said she was enthusiastic about the promise of reindustrialisation for constituencies like hers, but said: “If I have learned anything since becoming an MP two years ago, it’s that Whitehall doesn’t fix a problem unless it is told to.”
In its industrial strategy, published while Keir Starmer was prime minister, Labour identified eight sectors ripe for growth, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy and defence.
In his conference speech, to which Healey had invited a young apprentice who had worked on building a new Mersey ferry, the chancellor said Labour would “get Britain growing. With hope for our young people. With good work, good jobs and a new age of industrialisation.”

Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova narrowly led the first round of presidential elections Sunday, exit polls showed, in a vote held amid security concerns following a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.

She will face Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition who came second with between 32.2 and 32.5 percent, in the November 1 runoff.
The result was closer than expected, with surveys ahead of the vote predicting a comfortable win for Iotova.
Turnout was only around 20 percent, according to the polls.
After casting her vote, Iotova said she wanted to address “the dire issue of poverty” in the EU’s poorest member state, “alongside inequalities and regional disparities”.
“I believe that there must be peace, stability, and security,” added the 62-year-old, who has made the war in Ukraine a central theme of her campaign, promising to be a “president of peace”.
Gyurov meanwhile said he wanted “a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud... and where the state works as it should”.
- Ship attacks -

Serbia’s Student Movement Ousts Longtime Leader in Parliament Poll
While Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking Moscow to them.
Iotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state, when Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections.
If successful in the runoff, she would become the first woman ever elected president in the country of 6.4 million people.
A win for Iotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Moscow.

Gyurov, 50, has sharply criticised Radev’s foreign policy and is a strong supporter of Bulgaria’s Euro-Atlantic ties.

Casting his vote earlier, Radev blamed the low turnout on the “significant lead between the first and second according to surveys, which gives reassurance in one camp and perhaps a sense of doom in the other”.
Historically close to Russia, Bulgaria remains deeply divided over its relationship with Moscow.
Twenty-seven pairs of candidates for president and vice-president were competing in the first round, nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.
Teodor Slavev, a political analyst and programme director at the Bulgarian Institute for Legal Initiatives, told AFP the results were “a resounding electoral slap in the face for Rumen Radev’s administration and their inability to address people’s problems”.
He also said voters were giving their verdict on “Iotova’s unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea”.

Israel loses two key allies in Brazil and Serbia, putting strategic ties at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:39:51 UTC
18:39:51 KST

Israel is facing two significant foreign policy setbacks following election results in Brazil and Serbia, where political figures regarded as close allies of Jerusalem suffered defeats over the weekend. While the outcome in Brazil has dashed hopes of ending a prolonged diplomatic crisis, the political upheaval in Serbia raises more immediate questions about Israel's defense cooperation with one of its most important European military partners.
In Brazil, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured another term after defeating Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. In Serbia, former President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in parliamentary elections to a student-led movement that emerged from nearly two years of anti-government protests.
For Jerusalem, the results have created the impression of a diplomatic gamble that failed. Both politicians had cultivated close relationships with Israel, but their defeats carry different consequences. Brazil represents a missed opportunity to restore diplomatic relations, while Serbia poses a potential challenge to an established strategic partnership involving weapons supplies, defense technology and military cooperation.
Neither election result automatically means that existing agreements will be canceled or diplomatic relations will deteriorate further. However, both demonstrate how quickly Israel's international relationships can become uncertain when they depend heavily on individual leaders.
Brazil: Hopes of moving the embassy to Jerusalem collapse
In Brazil, the disappointment is primarily about the diplomatic opportunity Israel has lost rather than fears of a dramatic new deterioration in relations.
Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to reverse the policies of the Lula administration, deepen Brazil's military and diplomatic cooperation with Israel and move the Brazilian Embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem.
He had also pledged to receive the credentials of a new Israeli ambassador on his first day in office, signaling his intention to restore diplomatic representation between the countries.
His defeat means those promises will not be implemented under his proposed administration, leaving Israel facing another presidential term under Lula, whose relationship with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been openly hostile.
Relations between Israel and Brazil are already at a historic low. Israel declared Lula persona non grata following his remarks comparing the war in Gaza to the Holocaust and likening the conduct of Israeli soldiers to that of the Nazis.
Neither country currently has an ambassador serving in the other's capital, reflecting the depth of the diplomatic breakdown.
Netanyahu had openly supported the possibility of a change in Brazil's leadership. Following the first round of voting, he congratulated Bolsonaro on his electoral performance and wished him success in the runoff.
The prime minister is not expected to telephone Lula to congratulate him on his victory. The two leaders remain completely estranged, and Netanyahu's public support for Bolsonaro has only deepened the divide.
Bolsonaro's defeat therefore closes off, at least for now, the possibility of a rapid diplomatic reset involving restored ambassadors, closer defense cooperation and a Brazilian Embassy in Jerusalem.
For Israel, the immediate consequence is not the loss of an existing close partnership, but the disappearance of an opportunity to rebuild one.
Serbia: The more serious challenge to Israel's defense interests
The consequences of the Serbian election could be more substantial because the relationship between Jerusalem and Belgrade has already developed into a strategic partnership.
Under Vučić, Serbia became an important defense partner for Israel, particularly during the war against Hamas and Hezbollah.
As several countries imposed restrictions or embargoes on weapons exports to Israel, Serbia continued supplying military equipment and munitions.
Serbian deliveries increased dramatically during the fighting, with an extensive airlift helping Israel replenish stocks depleted by the IDF's heavy consumption of explosives, artillery shells, missiles, bombs and interceptors.
This cooperation took on additional significance in September, when Serbia inaugurated a factory to assemble Israeli-made drones in partnership with Israeli defense company Elbit Systems.
The facility marked a further expansion of military-industrial ties between the countries, moving their relationship beyond weapons purchases and shipments toward joint defense production.
Vučić had cultivated a close relationship with Israel, making Serbia an important partner at a time when other European countries were increasingly critical of Israeli military operations.
His electoral defeat now raises questions about whether the new Serbian leadership will maintain that same level of cooperation.
The incoming student-backed political movement has not yet established a clear position toward Israel. Existing defense contracts are not automatically canceled because of a change in government, and there is no indication that the new leadership has decided to terminate them.
Nevertheless, Israel will have to assess whether the political relationship that supported those agreements can survive without Vučić.
Another consideration is Serbia's relationship with the European Union. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has already welcomed the student movement's electoral victory and expressed the EU's willingness to support democratic reforms and Serbia's accession process.
Closer integration with European institutions could potentially bring Belgrade under greater pressure to align itself with European positions on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Such a shift is not inevitable, particularly given the uncertainty surrounding the incoming government's foreign policy. But it creates a potential challenge for a bilateral relationship that has been unusually close.
For Jerusalem, the central concern is therefore not simply the departure of a friendly politician, but whether Serbia will continue serving as a dependable source of military equipment and a partner in Israeli defense manufacturing.
A wider problem for Netanyahu's foreign policy
Taken together, the election results highlight a vulnerability in the way Netanyahu has built many of Israel's international relationships.
His foreign policy has frequently relied on personal and ideological connections with individual leaders rather than broader, institutional relationships between states.
As long as those leaders remain in power, the ties can appear exceptionally strong. But when they lose elections, some of the political foundations supporting those relationships can weaken along with them.
The same challenge extends beyond Brazil and Serbia. It has implications for Israel's relationships with European countries and the United States, where changes of government can alter policies even when strategic interests remain unchanged.
The electoral defeats do not necessarily establish a broader international trend against Israel.
In Latin America, Lula's victory runs counter to the gains made by several right-wing politicians associated with U.S. President Donald Trump, including in Colombia.
The reasons for the results also appear overwhelmingly domestic.
In Serbia, the election followed nearly two years of protests against Vučić's rule. In Brazil, the presidential contest was decided by voters divided between two political camps of roughly comparable size.
Israel was not a central issue in either campaign, and the outcomes should not be interpreted as evidence of changing public attitudes toward Israel in those countries.
Nevertheless, the results underscore the strategic importance of building institutional alliances that can withstand changes in political leadership.
Lapid attacks Netanyahu, Saar responds: ‘Turning your back on friends of Israel’
The developments have also become part of Israel's domestic political debate, with Tuesday's Knesset election just hours away.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid used the defeats of Bolsonaro and Vučić to criticize Netanyahu's relationships with foreign leaders.
"Another two people close to Netanyahu lost elections last night because of high voter turnout and national pride among people who refused to accept dictates from abroad," Lapid wrote Monday morning.
"Tomorrow, the people of Israel will begin the process of putting things right, returning Israel to a path of hope and success."
Lapid subsequently clarified that he did not welcome Lula's victory.
"And let me be clear: I am very unhappy about Lula's victory. I always support the pro-Israel candidate. That is the most important criterion," he wrote.
"But today, being close to Netanyahu is a political liability everywhere in the world. In Israel too."
Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded with a sharp attack on Lapid, accusing him of belittling politicians who have supported Israel.
"For the good-for-nothing Lapid, two great friends of Israel, such as Serbian President Vučić and Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, are simply 'two Netanyahu associates,'" Saar wrote.
"Turning your back on Israel's friends and currying favor with those who act against it is contemptible and a moral low, even before considering the level of foreign policy thinking on display."
He concluded with a warning directed at voters: "Anyone with any sense should stay away from the clowns' ballot paper at the polling station."
The exchange reflects competing interpretations of the election results. Netanyahu's opponents may point to the defeats as evidence of weaknesses in his foreign policy, while his supporters can argue that the outcomes demonstrate the risks posed by the rise of governments more critical of Israel.
However, the foreign election results are unlikely to become a decisive issue for Israeli voters, who face a wide range of more immediate domestic and security concerns.
Can Israel rebuild its alliances elsewhere?
Despite the setbacks in Brazil and Serbia, Israel may still see opportunities to develop closer relationships with other governments in the coming years.
In France, Marine Le Pen has been leading in several polls ahead of the next presidential election, while in Spain, recent surveys have placed right-wing opposition parties ahead of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's governing party.
Both political environments could offer potential openings for Israel if future governments adopt more favorable diplomatic positions, although election outcomes and subsequent policies remain uncertain.
But the immediate lesson from Brazil and Serbia is not about which political camp may prevail in the next election.
In Brazil, Israel has lost the prospect of a rapid normalization of diplomatic relations and a symbolic embassy move to Jerusalem. In Serbia, a proven defense relationship now faces a period of political uncertainty.
The two setbacks differ in scale and practical consequences, but they point to the same strategic challenge: Friendly leaders can help build important partnerships, yet the durability of those partnerships ultimately depends on whether they can survive the leaders themselves.
