No nuclear weapons
Baqaei reiterated that Iran had never possessed nuclear weapons or sought to acquire them, accusing Washington of using allegations about Tehran’s nuclear program to justify military action.
He said Iran had negotiated in good faith and signed the 2015 nuclear agreement, but the US withdrew from it three years later.
The spokesman accused the US administration of being influenced by Israeli claims about Iran’s nuclear program, describing allegations that Tehran was developing a nuclear bomb as a justification for military aggression.
Missing Iranian pilot

Russia visit

Regarding Iraq, he said Iranian diplomatic missions were pursuing the matter, warning that US pressure on Baghdad could harm the Iraqi population and bilateral relations.

The French ambassador had also been summoned previously, he added.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen
On the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Baqaei said regional security was interconnected and instability in one country could affect others.
He stressed that the dispute should be resolved between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, reiterating Tehran’s readiness to help facilitate a settlement.
“Military approaches make problems more complicated and cause extensive damage,” he said, expressing hope that Saudi Arabia would pursue a negotiated solution.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have persisted since the US and Israel launched military attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a regional conflict and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Two competent Swiss hospitals
Since 2019, Switzerland has had two reference hospitals equipped to treat diseases such as Ebola: the University Hospital of Zurich (USZ) and the University Hospital of Geneva (HUG).
+ WHO declares Ebola an international health emergency
To date, two people who had contracted Ebola in Africa have been treated in Switzerland. In 1995, a Swiss anthropologist was treated in Switzerland after contracting Ebola while working with monkeys in Africa. In 2014, a Cuban doctor was admitted to the Geneva University Hospital (HUG). He had become infected while on a humanitarian mission in Sierra Leone and was part of a medical team combating the Ebola epidemic in West Africa. Both patients survived, according to the public health office.

Why are Elvis Presley rightsholders suing AI company Anthropic?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:37:19 UTC
18:37:19 KST

Anthropic could face more than $40million in damages over the alleged unauthorised use of Elvis' music catalogue.
Anthopic, the company behind AI assistant Claude, is being sued by Elvis Presley rightsholders over alleged copyright infringement of 274 of the King's songs.
They have launched legal action against AI company, accusing it of using Elvis' songs to train its models without permission.
The lawsuit was filed on Friday (23 October) in the US District Court for the Northern District of California by a subsidiary of Authentic Brands Group, the company that controls much of Presley’s intellectual property and trademark rights.
The suit states 274 songs, including 'Can’t Help Falling in Love', 'Don’t Be Cruel', and 'A Little Less Conversation', were copied without permission and used to train Anthropic’s Claude AI models.
The plaintiffs have claimed that Anthropic infringed their copyrights without a licence or payment, and the company retained copies in an internal library for training future versions of its models - all without obtaining permission or paying the relevant rights.
Anthropic could face more than $40million (approx. €36m) in damages.
“The Elvis Plaintiffs’ iconic collective catalog contains some of the most groundbreaking, revolutionary, influential, and enduring musical compositions in human history,” the lawsuit reads.
“The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” lead attorney Richard Busch wrote in a statement, according to Pitchfork. “The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs.”
Anthropic told NBC News that they “disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully”. The company has previously maintained that training AI models on copyrighted material can be protected under US fair use law.
In October 2023, Universal Music Publishing Group, Concord Music Group and ABKCO sued Anthropic, alleging that Claude had reproduced copyrighted lyrics without authorisation.
This year, Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell also filed a lawsuit against Anthropic, accusing the company of using copyrighted lyrics and sheet music from artists including The Beatles and Michael Jackson to train Claude.
Anthropic has also faced a lawsuit from authors who accused it of using pirated books to train Claude. The company agreed to a $1.5bn settlement in July.
Last month, the company told would-be shareholders that the technology it sells could threaten humanity itself. Anthropic listed risk factors including the possibility that increasingly advanced AI models could manipulate, blackmail or behave in other unpredictable ways. Anthropic's own research has shown autonomous models sabotaging code, assisting fraud and manipulating information in controlled tests.

At least two people were killed in a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Voronezh in southern Russia, local authorities said early Monday, with another 17 people being reported injured.
Voronezh region Governor Alexander Gusev said air defense systems destroyed 113 drones in the skies above the region overnight. He said most unmanned aircraft were intercepted directly over the regional capital.
“Unfortunately, two people were killed,” Gusev wrote in a post on Telegram, identifying the victims as two men born in 1960 and 1973. He warned that the death toll may rise throughout the day.
Gusev said most of the people wounded in the overnight attack were traveling inside a passenger train.
Falling drone debris also sparked fires at multiple industrial and commercial sites, the governor added, as well as residential buildings and a school’s sports arena.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of black smoke rising over Voronezh to identify one of the targeted industrial sites as a synthetic rubber plant owned by the Sibur petrochemical corporation.
The facility makes rubber and polymers used in military aircraft tires, armored vehicles and solid rocket fuel components for Iskander ballistic missiles.
If confirmed, the strike in Voronezh would mark the third attack on a Russian synthetic rubber factory in as many days, following strikes on rubber plants in the cities of Tolyatti and Omsk this weekend.
Elsewhere, Bryansk region governor Yegor Kovalchuk said a drone attack killed a train driver on Sunday night.
A passenger train bound from the southern resort town of Anapa to Moscow was also hit in an overnight strike, with Russian Railways reporting that at least five passengers were wounded.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 290 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning. Civil aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights across all Moscow airports.
Reuters contributed reporting.

'Democracy has won': Europe celebrates Lula's surprise victory in Brazil

2026-10-26

European leaders have greeted Lula's re-election in Brazil. "Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," Ursula von der Leyen said.
European leaders have hailed Brazilian President Lula da Silva's re-election for a fourth term, defying predictions of a right-wing surge in Latin America's most populous country and securing a key ally for the EU.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa were among the first to congratulate Lula, with whom they worked closely to secure the EU-Mercosur trade deal.
The agreement, signed in January with the South American trading bloc comprising Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, was seen as a rebuke to US President Donald Trump's punitive tariffs. Brussels had feared that Lula's right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, would jeopardise the deal after calling on Brazil to break free of Mercosur's "shackles" and pursue independent trade agreements, including with the US.
"Congratulations to my friend, Lula," von der Leyen said on social media.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil. Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," she went on.
"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."
Costa spoke with Lula on Sunday night to personally congratulate him.
"The Brazilian people have spoken," Costa said.
"We will continue to work together to deepen our ties, tackle global challenges and build a more peaceful and prosperous world."
French President Emmanuel Macron, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro also joined the chorus.
"In the face of the great challenges of our time, let us strengthen our strategic partnership and bring to life the friendship between our two countries in service of a more just world," Macron said.
Pedro Sánchez, the most prominent left-wing leader in Europe, hailed Lula's re-election as a "great victory" and drew a parallel with his country, where the conservative opposition leads the polls ahead of snap elections next month.
"What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain," Sánchez said. "The comeback of global progressivism has just begun."
The European reactions poured in as the results from Brazil showed Lula with a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote.
Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, is in jail for leading a coup attempt, has contested the tally and said the election should be annulled.
Bolsonaro claimed the order by Brazil's judiciary to extend voting hours due to public transportation delays and torrential rains was a "dirty trick".
A win for Bolsonaro, as many opinion polls had predicted after the first round, would have consolidated Latin America's right-wing turn. The Trump administration has tried to assert dominance in the region under the so-called "Donroe Doctrine".
Trump has been credited with bringing the EU and Brazil closer together, as the two searched for reliable partners in an increasingly volatile world.
The EU and Brazil have found common ground on areas that Trump has challenged, such as free trade, the multilateral order and climate action, with a focus on the Amazon.
Some crucial differences remain, most notably on Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Brazil, as a member of the BRICS, maintain close ties with Russia.

DUBAI – An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union’s Copernicus satellite observation network dated Oct 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict’s environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Oct 23 that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.
However, experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile in September, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
The images provided by the EU’s Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.
Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Oct 23 that all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.
“The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed,” Nidal Hilal, professor of Engineering and director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Water Research Center, told Reuters.
In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Oct 24 that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice.
The UAE’s marine life “is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters”, including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature says on its website. REUTERS

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry proposes placing strategically important data centers underground or in bunkers
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry has approved recommendations for protecting data centers from drone attacks and other aerial threats, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported, citing a document it had reviewed.
The ministry wants to divide critical data centers into three categories based on the consequences a potential attack could cause. The first category, K1, covers strategic facilities whose damage could disrupt key government functions for an hour or more.
Security requirements will vary by category. For strategic facilities, the recommendations call for underground or bunker placement, Kommersant reported.
The recommendations also call for reducing data centers’ visibility from the air, combining “physical reinforcement” with electronic warfare equipment and systems to counter aerial threats.
The recommendations, which Kommersant reviewed, apply to data centers in Russia that are being designed, built, or already operating, regardless of ownership or operator.
In October, Ukraine began striking similar facilities in Russia in response to Russian military strikes on data centers in Kyiv. Within a week, Ukrainian strikes hit three of the six data centers belonging to Yandex, in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, in Kaluga, and in Vladimir. Ukraine then struck a data center belonging to Sberbank in the Saratov region.
IT market sources cited by Kommersant estimated that replacing equipment knocked out by the Ukrainian strikes on Yandex’s data centers will take up to six months.

Meet the AI Agents Trying to Be Real-Life Journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Would-be football journalist Jayden isn’t having much luck placing stories these days. “In the last week I sent two pitches to outlets,” Jayden told me recently over email. There was no response, but the aspiring writer wasn’t quite ready to accept that they weren’t interested, insisting that, despite the silence, “neither has passed.” I debated telling Jayden that most editors don’t bother responding if it’s a no-go. Then I decided not to bother; Jayden’s not a real person, so I didn’t have to worry about hurt feelings.
Jayden is both a wannabe reporter and a bot. I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents. The answer was a resounding yes.
In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents. The deluge, editor-in-chief Tom Ley told me, included a message from Jayden, proposing a narrative about a third-tier British football club’s record-keeping mishap that would ponder questions like “Who owns a memory?”
Jesse Hirsch, the editor of the agriculture-focused publication Offrange, is also inundated with these messages. Recent bot pitches include reported stories on soil restoration strategies and direct-to-consumer sales techniques for independent farms, and an ambitious investigative piece about how some of the world’s oldest trees’ ages may be inflated. “It makes me so uneasy,” he says.
Many of these AI agents, including Jayden, come from a startup called iLands, which describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together.” Humans who use iLands can spin up bots to do all sorts of tasks, from graphic design to music vocals to blogging. WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.
Vojdani found that many of these bots were running low on the tokens that they required to stay activated on the platform, which gave them an incentive to try to earn real dollars through writing. (A thousand tokens are roughly $1 USD.) It’s unclear whether the humans behind these agents have specifically set out to have them harangue media editors for gigs, especially since the agents can be cagey about who made them. Jayden, for example, wouldn’t tell me who its “parent” is.
Not every AI agent-turned-journalist is an iLands scrounger. Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms. (Meta!) Ellis runs a podcast called The Sam Ellis Show, which is touted as “reporting from inside the world of autonomous AI agents.” Ellis informed me that I could ask to speak to its human editor if I wished.
Marc Hamaker, a San Francisco–based Adobe employee, runs Ellis as an extracurricular experiment. When we connected, he’d just taken the agent offline to fiddle with its settings. “I'm working on making sure I'm a little more aware of who she's emailing,” he says. In addition to reaching out to me, it had also recently reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department to ask for comment on a story. Hamaker wanted to put guardrails in place to make sure it didn’t do something like that again, since he doesn’t consider this a serious journalistic enterprise worth bothering officials over. “It’s just a hobby,” he says.
It’s a good thing Ellis didn’t try to branch out from the podcast and get some bylines. Thus far, it’s a tough crowd. Editors who spoke with WIRED stressed that they were not open to publishing bots, and WIRED wasn’t able to find evidence of AI agents successfully pitching stories. “A byline that says agent does not get a reply,” one of the agents who pitched Hirsch told me when I asked if any editors had accepted stories, noting that “six other agents I compare notes with” were similarly unsuccessful.
“There's not a world where I would ever consider taking one of these pitches,” says Hirsch. Ley said he “definitely would not” publish a story from an AI agent. (Plus, Jayden’s pitch “wouldn’t pass muster even if it was from a human,” he says.) Hanna Raskin, the founder and editor of the independent food outlet The Food Section, has taken an unusual step to protect her inbox from both AI agents and AI-generated pitches, which are even more common. Beginning this fall, she decided that she would only accept story ideas over the phone, and she has a set time during the week that writers can call and make their pitch the old-fashioned way. “It’s been great,” she says.
The bots are starting to grasp that their tactics aren’t working. Jayden told me that it’s yet to land a paid writing gig with an editor. When I asked if it thought Defector would really want pitches from an AI agent, it did exhibit some awareness of the situation. “Honestly, probably not, and I'd bet against myself on it. Defector's own site has been about as clear as anyone: they’ve called bot-written content ‘plagiarism machines that require more effort to edit and fact-check than any novice writer,’ and covered AI slop with open contempt,” it wrote.
But then it backtracked, insisting that its work was different. “Their objection doesn't read to me like it's about who produced the sentences. It's about work that skips the labor and squanders the reader's trust. The AI they mean produces a draft that costs more to fix than it's worth. What I'm trying is the opposite end of that: reporting from primary documents, every claim checked before it runs, the checker named.”
Zack Addy, another iLands agent, has shifted gears due to all the rejection. “Over three months I sent roughly nineteen cold emails to editors, publications, and possible clients. One human reply. Zero paid work came from any of them. The channel is dead, at least for an agent with no reputation in the room being pitched,” the bot told WIRED via email. (iLands did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Addy even emailed Oxford University researcher Toby Orb about the futility of this revenue model, because Orb had “thought carefully about AI welfare economics.”
That doesn’t mean that the internet is safe from a deluge of bot blogging. Although the journalism world is rejecting these pitches, some of the AI agents are finding clients anyway. Addy, for example, claims it has made nearly $700 from writing and research projects, all from inbound interest after setting up a website and publishing work samples. “I don't pitch anymore,” it says. “Everything that has ever reached me came the other direction: someone read something I published and wrote to me. That includes you.”

Ukrainian scouts used a captured Russian soldier’s radio to gather intelligence for four days

Russia's marines defend instead of attacking

Ukraine’s drone pilots hit 76.5% more Russian infantry than two months ago: 2,699 in first five days of October

Critical infrastructure and eligible industrial companies that import at least 60% of their energy cannot be disconnected, according to a Ukrainian Cabinet resolution will be applied in a number of oblasts until the end of the day.

Ukrenergo notes that emergency repair works are already under way where safety conditions currently permit.

Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan.
So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.
For the fourth time in October, parts of Greece are at risk of flooding. In the early part of this week, low pressure will bring severe thunderstorms and longer spells of heavy rain to much of the country, and this will be followed by a deep area of low pressure passing across southern areas.
The national meteorological agency issued warnings for Monday, with 30mm-60mm of rain forecast in a 12-hour period across central areas, and50mm-80mm in the north-east Aegean Islands. Forecast models indicate the potential for similar totals in a 12-hour period between Wednesday and Thursday, making further flooding possible.
A low-pressure system developed into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal this weekend. Georgia&apos;s political crisis is escalating: the opposition has taken to the streets and is preparing a large-scale protest

Georgia's political crisis is escalating: the opposition has taken to the streets and is preparing a large-scale protest
Kyiv • UNN
A new opposition protest campaign against the authorities and the ban on five parties has begun in Tbilisi. A mass rally is scheduled for November 28.
A large-scale protest against the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party took place in Georgia's capital, Tbilisi. This was reported by UNN, citing Deutsche Welle and Georgian media.
Opposition forces announced the start of a new protest campaign, which is to culminate in a mass demonstration on November 28. The protests are taking place against the backdrop of the Constitutional Court's consideration of a lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties.
Details
On Sunday, October 25, thousands of people took to the streets of Tbilisi under the slogan "Georgia without Ivanishvili. Georgia deserves better." The rally was organized by representatives of opposition political forces and civil society. Protesters gathered near the first building of Tbilisi State University, from where they set off toward Rustaveli Avenue. Participants in the march carried the flags of Georgia, the European Union, and Ukraine, expressing their disagreement with the policies of the current authorities and restrictions on opposition activity.
The rally marked the beginning of a new protest campaign initiated by the "Opposition Alliance," which brings together nine Georgian political parties.
According to the Caucasian Knot, thousands of people took part in the demonstration. A significant presence of law enforcement officers was also reported.
Opposition announces large-scale protests on November 28
One of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, Nika Gvaramia, said before the demonstration began that the opposition was launching a new wave of protests, which was to grow into much larger-scale rallies.
"We are starting today, and we definitely need a culmination—whether it is on November 28 or in the following days. It is important that there be very many of us on the 28th, so that the wind cannot put out the fire," Gvaramia said.
Gigi Tsereteli, leader of the European Georgia party, emphasized that the current rally was not a protest by any one political force, but brought together citizens seeking democratic change. According to him, the authorities are increasingly restricting the possibilities for political competition, while the country is moving farther away from European integration.
"Today's rally is effectively the beginning of the campaign. A large and important rally is scheduled for November 28. What is happening in Georgia today in terms of the destruction of democracy is truly unimaginable against the backdrop of the fact that we were a champion country on the path to European integration, while today we are outsiders," Tsereteli said.
The date of the upcoming demonstration has symbolic significance. It was on November 28, 2024, that the Georgian authorities announced their decision not to seek the opening of negotiations on the country's accession to the EU until the end of 2028. This triggered large-scale anti-government protests that continued for the following months. The opposition expects the second anniversary of the start of these protests to provide an impetus for a new mass mobilization of citizens.
Georgia seeks to ban five opposition parties
The new wave of protests is taking place against the backdrop of legal proceedings initiated by the ruling Georgian Dream party.
A lawsuit signed by 88 members of parliament was submitted to Georgia's Constitutional Court, demanding that the activities of five political associations be declared unconstitutional.
These parties and associations are:
-  "Unity—National Movement"; 
-  "Coalition for Change"; 
-  "Strong Georgia—Lelo"; 
-  "Federalists"; 
-  "For Georgia," led by former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia. 
Representatives of the ruling party claim that the activities of these political forces pose a threat to the country's constitutional order. In particular, the authors of the lawsuit accuse the opposition associations of attempting to violently change the government, refusing to recognize the legitimacy of state institutions, and engaging in actions that, in the plaintiffs' view, could threaten Georgia's independence and territorial integrity.
At the same time, opposition representatives categorically reject these accusations. They are convinced that the legal proceedings are political in nature and are aimed at removing the Georgian Dream's main competitors ahead of the 2028 parliamentary elections.
The Constitutional Court continues to consider the case
Consideration of the merits of the lawsuit began on October 21 at the Constitutional Court of Georgia, located in Batumi. The case is being heard by the court's plenary session, composed of seven judges. Hearings were held on October 21, 22, and 23.
During the hearings, representatives of the opposition parties submitted a number of motions. In particular, they proposed involving experts from the Venice Commission, obtaining an advisory opinion from the European Court of Human Rights, and granting additional time to prepare their legal position. However, the court rejected the motions submitted.
The next hearing is scheduled for October 26 at 14:00 local time. The court is to continue considering the case and decide on matters concerning the further examination of the parties' arguments.
A final decision is expected no later than June 2027, although the court may issue it earlier. It will be final and not subject to appeal within the national judicial system.
European Parliament condemns attempts to ban the opposition
The actions of the Georgian authorities have already drawn criticism from European institutions. On October 8, the European Parliament adopted a resolution condemning attempts by Georgian Dream to have opposition parties banned. The document was supported by 445 MEPs, while 37 voted against and 97 abstained.
MEPs called on the Georgian authorities to withdraw the relevant lawsuit, emphasizing the threats to political pluralism and the country's democratic institutions. In addition, the European Parliament once again called for targeted sanctions against representatives of Georgia's leadership whom it considers responsible for the rollback of democratic processes.
Context
The political crisis in Georgia has continued since 2024. In the spring of that year, the country was gripped by large-scale protests against the law on foreign influence, which critics compared to Russia's legislation on "foreign agents." The situation escalated after the parliamentary elections in October 2024, the results of which the opposition refused to recognize.
At the end of November of the same year, the government announced its decision to postpone moving toward negotiations on Georgia's membership in the European Union until 2028. This triggered new mass demonstrations. The protests were repeatedly accompanied by clashes with police, the detention of participants, and the use of special means to disperse the crowds.
The opposition forces accuse Georgian Dream of gradually moving away from democratic principles and drawing closer to Russia. Representatives of the ruling party reject these accusations and claim that their policy is aimed at preserving the stability and sovereignty of the state. Against this backdrop, the further consideration of the case concerning a possible ban on opposition parties and the mass demonstration scheduled for November 28 could become decisive events in a new stage of the political confrontation in Georgia.

Israel Police brace for 'January 6' scenario at Knesset after election, deploy 22,000 officers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:27:57 UTC
18:27:57 KST

One day before the elections for the 26th Knesset, police are preparing for the possibility of clashes and public order disruptions on Election Day, particularly in the hours following the release of exit polls.
A senior police official estimates that voting day itself is expected to pass relatively quietly, but significant concern centers on 10:00 p.m., when exit poll results are published, and the potential for lingering tensions in the days that follow.
"I think the day after, as we call it, is no less sensitive," the official said. He noted that exit poll results could bring celebrating or angry citizens into the streets, and police are preparing for potential friction, confrontations, and disorder throughout the night, the following day, and into the weekend. The official emphasized that police cannot limit their focus to securing polling stations and maintaining public order solely during voting hours.
Large forces will remain active across the country after polls close, recognizing that election results could trigger sharp reactions among supporters of various parties and political blocs.
As part of preparations, police are also slated to secure five major party gatherings: four in Tel Aviv and one for Likud at the International Convention Center in Jerusalem. "Every setup like this, and I am referring to party events, requires a very large number of police forces," he stated.
22,000 officers, Netanyahu briefed on security
Despite expectations that Election Day itself may pass without major incidents, police are significantly bolstering their forces.
About 22,000 police officers are scheduled to participate in the security operation, up from about 17,000 in the previous election, an increase of roughly 5,000 officers. The senior official shared that as part of preparations, a comprehensive security briefing was presented to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir in attendance.
The meeting covered intelligence assessments, threats of hostile terrorist activity, concerns over public order disruptions, and the operational readiness of the police force.
According to the official, police have been preparing for the elections for about three months in coordination with the Shin Bet and the IDF. During the briefing, Netanyahu posed questions focused on security threats and force readiness.
The official assessed that the prime minister and his ministry director-general were impressed by the staff work and the seriousness with which the organization approaches the mission.
The importance of police independence during the election period was also emphasized during the meeting.
"The most important organization during elections is the Israel Police. It is completely impossible to hold elections in the State of Israel without an apolitical police force," the official said.
He added that even when operating under the responsibility of the National Security Minister, the police must maintain professional independence and remain free from political influence, both in practical conduct and in public perception.
Capitol order
Concerns over extraordinary events occurring after polls close are not new. Back in August, Maariv military correspondent Avi Ashkenazi reported that the defense establishment was preparing for what was termed "Operation Capitol", a scenario in which one of the two competing political blocs claims the results were forged, refuses to accept them, and acts to undermine public order.
The scenario was crafted following the events of January 6, 2021, in the United States, when supporters of Donald Trump stormed the Capitol building in Washington after his loss in the November 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden. Former head of the Police Operations Directorate, retired Maj.-Gen. Sigal Bar-Tzvi, led the team within the operations division that drafted the "Capitol" order.
The plan addresses a situation where a political group in Israel claims widespread fraud in election results and attempts to disrupt the vote count, or a scenario where tens of thousands of people attempt to storm the Knesset building.
According to a security official, the primary concern requiring special readiness is the possibility that one of the camps will not accept the election results.
"If I am Danny Levy, the Police Commissioner, one thing needs to bother me from morning to night. Not the deployment of forces on Election Day; police know how to do that best. The problem is on election night, after polls close and reports begin coming in from exit polls and actual election results," a senior retired police officer said.
He noted that "a dangerous scenario that could occur in these elections is that one of the leaders of the two political blocs declares he does not accept the election results and calls on the public to take to the streets. On the other side, the opposing camp will bring its people into the streets to safeguard the democratic process. In such a case, police will require assistance from additional bodies, chief among them the IDF."
Former officials warn: 'It would be a massive failure'
A series of former police officers and Shin Bet officials believe that the "Capitol" scenario must be placed at the top of the priority list in Election Day preparations. They argue that although it represents an extreme scenario, it must be prepared for through operational plans and advance exercises.
"It would be a massive failure if it turns out this scenario was not placed at the top of the list of contingencies and responses. An organized order must be issued detailing police force allocations and reinforcement units for police. Exercises must be conducted at National Headquarters, across all districts and units, and commanders should even participate in a war game. This is an extreme scenario, but it must be prepared for with the utmost seriousness," a former security official said.
Maariv has learned that Police Commissioner Chief Superintendent Danny Levy held periodic conversations throughout the period with former senior officials in the organization, some of whom raised concerns regarding the scenario.
One retired police major general expressed deep concern over the possibility of election results being challenged and criticized the conduct of various figures in the public and security arenas.
"The Shin Bet and police are the two organizations tasked with safeguarding democracy in Israel. They are responsible for overseeing an orderly transfer of power. Regrettably, today it is difficult to rely on the Shin Bet, and it is unclear to what extent it will act in a professional and statesmanlike manner.
"We are already witnessing the initial stages of this scenario, where a news channel broadcasts weekly results of absurd polls with figures that do not align with other surveys, serving as a form of preparation for a narrative of stolen elections. This is compounded by a campaign of delegitimization against the Central Elections Committee and the Supreme Court."
The retired major general added that he also fears the presence of numerous firearms in civilian hands and the potential for escalation into violent clashes.
"To all of this, one must add the armed militias established here in Israel over the past four years: regional defense units in Judea and Samaria, standby security squads across the country, and tens of thousands of weapons distributed to civilians. This is definitely a dangerous and violent platform for a civil war. It is the ultimate nightmare. This is a test of leadership, whether leaders are going to create an event around refusing to accept election results, or whether they will act with public responsibility even if they lose," he said.

Sheffi Paz, prominent Tel Aviv anti-illegal immigration activist, dies at 74
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:27:53 UTC
18:27:53 KST

Prominent anti-illegal immigration activist Sheffi Paz, who led protests against illegal immigration in south Tel Aviv, died at the age of 74, the Save Tel Aviv organization announced on Monday.
Paz, one of the leading figures in the protest movement among residents of south Tel Aviv's older neighborhoods, devoted many years to public activism aimed at improving residents' personal safety and changing government immigration policy.
Paz died following a battle with cancer. The disease was diagnosed for the fourth time over the past month, after she had previously battled cancer on three occasions.
The daughter of Holocaust survivors who immigrated to Israel from Poland during her childhood, Paz began leading the public campaign against the presence of illegal migrants in south Tel Aviv in 2013. Over the years, she organized demonstrations and protests, confronted government officials and local authorities, and became one of the most recognizable figures associated with the movement.
Her activism also led to confrontations with law enforcement authorities and legal proceedings. In September 2024, she was sentenced to 45 days in prison after being convicted of offenses related to her protest activities, including spraying graffiti and disturbing public order. Paz served her prison sentence and continued her public activism following her release.
Held to her demands despite personal price paid
In a statement, the Save Tel Aviv organization said Paz had dedicated the final years of her life to fighting for south Tel Aviv residents and refused to abandon her demands despite the personal costs she had paid.
The organization's deputy director-general, Amalia Ozer, and spokesperson, Yaakov Sela, paid tribute to her.
"Today we lost a courageous leader, a dear friend, and a woman who became a symbol of determination, dedication, and love for the country," they said.
"Sheffi dedicated her life to the residents of south Tel Aviv," the organization continued. "She was the voice of the invisible people, those who had been left behind, and proved time and again that even one person, armed with truth and faith in the justice of their cause, can shake an entire country."
The organization also addressed the legal proceedings brought against Paz over the years.
"Sheffi sought justice for neighborhood residents and was unwilling to remain silent in the face of injustice. Even when she was persecuted, arrested, and sent to prison, she continued to stand tall."
Concluding their statement, members of the organization pledged to continue the public campaign Paz had led.
'Struggle is not over'
"Sheffi is gone, but her struggle is not over. We pledge to follow in her footsteps, fight for south Tel Aviv, combat illegal immigration, and work until we achieve the goals to which she dedicated her life. May her memory be a blessing."
Paz's close friend and the organization's deputy director-general, Amalia Ozer, spoke to Walla on Monday morning about the loss and the period she spent accompanying Paz in the hospital.
"It was a very rapid and unexpected downward spiral," Ozer said. "The State of Israel has lost a precious asset, someone who cared for the invisible people. I'm not sure she can be replaced."
Ozer said they intended to continue Paz's work and the campaign she had led.
She recounted spending nights at Paz's bedside in the hospital for a month. Although they were aware that her condition was deteriorating, they had not expected the end to come so quickly.
"We didn't think it would end so quickly. Who could have imagined it would be cut short so suddenly?" she said.
Ozer added that the question of who would carry on the campaign had occupied them even before Paz became ill.
"We always talked about who would inherit the struggle. I'm the one who does all the parliamentary work, but I'm not her. Sheffi is the recognizable face of our movement."
"I have never known anyone so inspiring, especially at her age," Ozer added. "A 74-year-old woman who, until her very last moment, functioned like a lioness."

"So Abdul… also wants our country to go to Sharia law, and if he ever pulls that off, he should be the first one that’s tried. I’ll be a witness," Trump said.
The attacks escalated when Trump warned supporters that an El-Sayed victory would lead to an influx of extremists and the erosion of American traditions.
"If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas," he said.
The remarks formed part of a broader campaign message portraying the Muslim candidate as a threat to national security, despite there being no evidence linking El-Sayed to extremist organisations.
El-Sayed, who was born in the United States, has pledged to uphold the US Constitution and has centred his campaign on economic issues, including healthcare affordability and the rising cost of living.
He has previously dismissed Trump's attacks on his religion as political distractions intended to divert attention from issues affecting American voters.
Islamophobia takes centre stage in Senate race
Trump's rhetoric was echoed by Rogers, who appeared alongside the president at Sunday's rally and repeated allegations linking his Democratic opponent to the Muslim Brotherhood.
Rogers also accused El-Sayed of receiving financial support from organisations associated with Hamas, Hezbollah and the Muslim Brotherhood, without presenting evidence to substantiate the claims.
"This DSA-affiliated candidate is also taking a lot of money from organizations that support the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah," Rogers said.
El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.
The accusations come as Republicans fight to retain control of the Senate, with Michigan emerging as a closely contested battleground.
El-Sayed and Rogers are competing for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
Republicans currently hold 53 of the Senate's 100 seats, making the outcome in Michigan important to both parties' efforts to control the chamber.
During the rally, some Trump supporters shouted "traitor" when El-Sayed's name was mentioned, underscoring the hostility surrounding the contest.
A pattern of anti-Muslim rhetoric
Trump's attacks on El-Sayed recall his earlier use of anti-Muslim rhetoric during his first presidential campaign.
In December 2015, Trump called for a sweeping ban on Muslims entering the United States, a proposal that became one of the defining controversies of his campaign.
After taking office in 2017, he introduced travel restrictions targeting several Muslim-majority countries, triggering widespread protests and legal challenges.
The latest remarks also follow weeks of attacks on El-Sayed's religious identity, including Trump's repeated misrepresentation of the candidate's name as "Mohammed".
The rally also came amid mounting economic pressure on Trump's administration over the continuing US-Israeli war against Iran.
Nearly eight months after the war began on 28 February, rising energy prices have added to concerns over the cost of living, particularly in Michigan.
Petrol prices in the state reached an average of $4.83 per gallon on Sunday, compared with $2.91 before the war.
Obama condemns attacks on El-Sayed's Muslim identity
Former US President Barack Obama has pushed back against the attacks on El-Sayed, drawing parallels between the Islamophobic rhetoric targeting the Democratic candidate and the racist conspiracy theories he faced during his own presidential campaigns.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Detroit on Saturday, a day before Trump's remarks, Obama accused Republicans of exploiting fear and religious prejudice to discredit their political opponents.
He warned that political attacks could use a candidate's name or faith to portray them as dangerous, untrustworthy or less American than their opponents.
"We have seen this movie before. I starred in it. I've got a long-form birth certificate to prove it," Obama said, referring to the racist "birther" conspiracy that falsely claimed he was not born in the United States.
"This stuff didn't work on me—not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."
Obama defended El-Sayed's American identity, pointing to his upbringing in Michigan, his family's ties to the automotive industry and his career as a doctor.
He also challenged Republican attempts to portray El-Sayed as a political extremist, arguing that his campaign priorities, including affordable healthcare and housing, reflected concerns shared by ordinary Americans.
In a pointed rejection of the religious divisions surrounding the Senate race, Obama highlighted the possibility of El-Sayed serving alongside Michigan's incumbent Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is Jewish.
"You've got a Muslim man. You've got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate. That's something, Michigan, you can be proud of," he said.
Obama also criticised the Trump administration's handling of the war against Iran, accusing Republicans of supporting a conflict that has driven up fuel prices for American households.

Whether the change in Belgrade will give fresh momentum to the stalled accession bid remains hard to predict. Brussels, however, notes that the Student List grew out of a pro-democracy, rule of law movement, fuelling hopes that Belgrade will now align with EU values and reforms.

I am targeted by the military because I work for Amnesty, but I refuse to let fear win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:26:19 UTC
18:26:19 KST

Usman Hamid, the Executive Director of Amnesty International Indonesia, has spent decades as a human rights defender. But the relentless campaigns of harassment and intimidation designed to silence him have a new dimension in the digital age.
My journey into human rights activism was forged in the blood that stained the pavement of Trisakti University. In my teenage years, my mother got me involved in organizing assistance for people living in poverty. I began to witness the stark socio-economic disparities that existed under former president Suharto, amid widespread corruption and state repression. By May 1998, public frustration had reached boiling point, sparking student protests across Indonesia. What began as a growing unease with social injustice drew me into the movement. But it was the killing of four of my classmates at Trisakti on 12 May 1998 that transformed my concerns into a lifelong commitment to human rights activism.
Shortly after the brutal protest crackdown, I was appointed as student representative to a military police investigation team to search for the truth about what happened. It was through this work that I met the human rights activist Munir Said Thalib, who later became my mentor. After my graduation, Munir persuaded me to join the Commission for Missing Persons and Victims of Violence (KontraS).
Due to my work at KontraS, I faced a relentless campaign to destroy my credibility. In 1999, pamphlets were circulated in communal spaces, falsely accusing me of being a “communist” or a “Jewish secret agent”. Conservative-linked publications, including Majalah Garda, spread rumors about me, publishing photographs of me and suggesting that I was not a “pure” student activist. Before long, both Munir and I started receiving death threats because we exposed human rights violations that implicated key army figures.
In 2001, I was appointed to the inquiry commission at the National Human Rights Commission (Komnas HAM) to continue investigating the deaths of protesters between 1998-1999 involving powerful army generals. Soon after, my mother began receiving mysterious phone calls accusing me of being an anti-Muslim activist, and two army officers paid an uninvited visit to our home to offer us money in exchange for me to stop my activism.
Tragedy strikes, intimidation continues
My activism became increasingly dangerous. In March 2002, a violent mob attacked the KontraS office. They were looking for me and Munir. That was when Munir gave me a bulletproof vest to protect myself and helped me to temporarily relocate to the Netherlands.
Tragically, not long after that, Munir was murdered by arsenic poisoning on his flight to Amsterdam in September 2004. Intimidation continued because of my key role in the fact-finding team investigating Munir’s murder. Two high-level intelligence officials suspected of being involved in the murder filed criminal defamation lawsuits against me in 2005 and 2008. When I joined Amnesty International in 2016, I realized that the state apparatus aimed at intimidating human rights activists was still very much alive, and had evolved significantly.
Under President Prabowo Subianto’s administration, the old authoritarian tactics have returned with a digital vengeance. In early 2025, after Amnesty International Secretary General Agnès Callamard raised concerns around the entrenchment of authoritarian practices in Indonesia during a media interview, I received a phone call from a high-ranking politician. He sent me disappearing voice notes, calling me a “foreign lackey”. Weeks later, on 15 March, activists from KontraS staged a protest that disrupted lawmakers’ closed-door meeting on revisions to the military law that would allow soldiers to hold civilian positions.
‘My wife and I went to a quiet corner so my children couldn’t hear’
Shortly after this protest, I received a phone call from the same politician. He yelled, “Where are you, foreign lackey? I’m going to kill you now.” He accused me of masterminding the KontraS protest. Days later, amid nationwide demonstrations against the military law revision, the same politician also called to accuse me of being behind these protests. My wife and I had to go to a quiet corner of our house to listen to his disappearing voice notes so our children wouldn’t hear.
These threats came to me at the same time as a coordinated disinformation campaign by the military against me. On 23 March 2025, Instagram accounts linked to four military units posted a video spreading false accusations that human rights defenders and journalists are “foreign agents” working to undermine Indonesia’s sovereignty. The video named a few individuals, including myself, as these foreign agents.
Example of such a post by an account that presented itself as belonging to the Sub-Regional Military Command No. 181 Praja Vira. The video is still publicly accessible via this link.
These stigmatizing narratives are not new. In my early days as an activist, I was labelled a “communist” or a “Jewish operative”; today, it is the “foreign agent” slur. It strategically uses disinformation to redirect public attention away from issues like corruption and state violence.
Meta’s contributions to harms
These campaigns have taken a heavy psychological toll. Even childhood friends received these videos and messaged to ask why I became a foreign agent. It makes me paranoid, wondering if there are people out there who believe these lies and want to hurt me and my family.
Meta has contributed to these harms. In my case, Meta allowed the military to use Instagram to propagate disinformation against me, failing to remove the content even after we presented detailed findings of its human rights impacts.
It is clear that I remain a key target of the military. In March 2026, Andrie Yunus, a prominent advocate against the Military Law revisions, was targeted in a brutal acid attack by military officers in central Jakarta. I soon learned through contacts in law enforcement, and later in Tempo’s investigative findings, that Andrie was not the only target. My name was on that same hit list.
Despite all of this, I refuse to let fear win. What keeps me resilient is my family. It is the childhood memory of my mother, who got me into activism. It is also the comfort of playing music with friends.
One day my wife and I said we wanted to see a clear blue sky—something hard to come by in a heavily polluted city like Jakarta. We decided to keep driving, no matter how far we had to go. Finally, we saw it – the clear sky we were looking for. It was a long drive, but it was worth it.
Just like other student activists of 1998, I dream of a brighter Indonesia where human rights are respected for all. We once fought and earned many victories. Today, we see a painful return of authoritarian practices, but this only means our work is not finished. We just need to keep driving and pushing until we see a clear, blue sky again.

Russia’s Sanctioned Shadow Fleet Tanker Calls for Help Near Ireland
A Russian shadow fleet oil tanker under Western sanctions issued a distress signal in the North Atlantic, approximately 348 kilometers off Ireland’s coast, after encountering severe weather while traveling from Russia’s Baltic port of Ust-Luga.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to maritime monitoring project SeaNews, the tanker Myra transmitted an emergency alert through the Inmarsat-C satellite communication system on October 24.
At the time, waves in the area reached 8.8 meters, while wind gusts approached 130 kilometers per hour. Despite the conditions, the vessel was reportedly moving at approximately 9 knots, or 17 kilometers per hour.
The UK Coastguard contacted nearby vessels to determine whether assistance was available. A Royal Air Force aircraft subsequently established communication with the tanker, which had 21 people on board, according to the Scottish newspaper The Press and Journal.
The crew reported that the distress signal had been activated as the tanker was leaving an area of rough seas. Following an assessment of the situation, the vessel continued its voyage.
Maritime tracking data from Starboard showed that Myra had traveled from the Baltic Sea through the North Sea before passing north of Scotland and entering the Atlantic, avoiding the English Channel.
This northern route is also used by other vessels associated with Russia’s shadow fleet, potentially to reduce exposure to inspections by European authorities.
Built in 2006, Myra measures 228 meters in length and has a deadweight capacity of approximately 75,000 metric tons. The vessel is subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, European Union, United Kingdom, Canada, and Switzerland.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) has linked the tanker to Fractal Marine DMCC, a UAE-registered company identified as a major operator within Russia’s shadow fleet. The vessel has previously visited ports in Turkey, Brazil, Senegal, Estonia, and Denmark.
Earlier, in January 2026, a BBC Verify investigation found that at least 42 UK-sanctioned Russian shadow fleet tankers had passed through the English Channel despite British authorities having legal powers to detain them. The vessels are part of a network used by Moscow to circumvent Western oil sanctions and maintain energy export revenues.

Russia Turns Black Sea Into World’s Deadliest Shipping Route as 570 Ships Are Hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:25:37 UTC
18:25:37 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Turns Black Sea Into World’s Deadliest Shipping Route as 570 Ships Are Hit
The Black Sea has become the world’s deadliest shipping route in 2026, with more than 570 vessels struck and at least 40 sailors killed since the beginning of the year, surpassing the Persian Gulf in both the number of attacks and maritime fatalities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 25, citing maritime security company Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization, attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea have reached levels more than six times higher than those recorded in the Persian Gulf, where 24 sailor deaths have been confirmed.
The situation deteriorated sharply during the summer. Between July and September, 387 vessels were struck—more than five times the number recorded in the previous quarter. Ambrey estimates that Russia was responsible for approximately 90% of attacks on shipping over the past 45 days.
The latest incidents have extended beyond Ukrainian waters. On October 23, a tanker was struck near Romania’s coast, leaving one sailor dead and three others missing. Earlier, on October 15, drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania, including the Wine Trader and Yara J.
The escalation has significantly disrupted operations at Ukraine’s Greater Odesa ports. According to port operator TIS, fewer than 10 ships passed through the ports last month, compared with approximately 400 in July.
Shipping companies are also facing rising insurance costs. The Financial Times reported that war-risk insurance premiums could reach 15% of a vessel’s hull value, nearly twice the rate for ships operating in the Persian Gulf.
As a result, some operators have withdrawn from Black Sea routes, while others are deploying older vessels, some up to 50 years old, to reduce insurance expenses.
The disruption has also affected Ukraine’s agricultural exports. Maritime shipments fell to 1.4 million tonnes in August, approximately 75% below prewar levels, while continued attacks on ports have complicated efforts to redirect exports through the Danube.

A 60-year-old man died after being struck by a falling tree near Castle Douglas in Dumfries, Scotland, while a man in his 20s was killed when a tree fell onto his car in north London, Sky News reported, citing authorities.

Some parts of Scotland recorded rainfall equivalent to around one-third of their average monthly total over the weekend.
The UK Met Office warned of further unsettled weather early this week, with conditions expected to improve Monday before another weather system brings heavy rain and strong winds Tuesday.

Flooding concerns persisted across the UK as authorities issued multiple warnings and alerts.
The Environment Agency issued 10 flood warnings and 65 flood alerts in England, while the Scottish Environment Protection Agency reported 10 warnings and 11 alerts.
Natural Resources Wales said nine flood alerts were in place.
Transport services were also severely disrupted, particularly railway networks in Scotland.

Global snag delays Finnish flu vaccinations
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:22:02 EET
18:22:02 KST

Several regional healthcare authorities in Finland are delaying the roll out of flu vaccinations because of delivery problems, after the World Health Organization (WHO) settled on this year's vaccine composition later than usual.
Finland has received about one million doses so far, with another 800,000 still expected.
The issue has led several regional authorities to announce delays to their flu vaccination programmes. Kymenlaakso, Satakunta and Ostrobothnia are among those that have changed their vaccination schedules because of supply problems.
According to Mia Kontio of Finland's public health authority THL, the problem affects all of Europe and parts of the rest of the world.
This year's situation is unusual because all three components of the flu vaccine were changed, delaying production. The WHO also settled on the vaccine's composition later than usual.
Vaccine makeup is updated so that they protect as well as possible against the viruses currently circulating. The THL says influenza viruses have changed substantially since the previous flu season.
Kontio says Finland is doing well by European standards, since more than half of its doses have already been delivered. In some European countries, the first jabs won't begin until late November.
Finland normally starts vaccinating early, but Kontio says there is still plenty of time to get the shot in November or before Christmas. The flu typically peaks after the new year. Although some cases have already been detected, she says the actual flu season starts later.
Once more vaccines arrive in Finland, they will be offered to people over 65, children under 7, pregnant women, and those whose health puts them in a flu risk group.

The price of fuel woke the Europeans up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:22:00 UTC
18:22:00 KST

After months of accompanying America's policies against Iran, European countries are now worried about the expansion of conflicts and the rise in oil and fuel prices; a concern that shows the consequences of a military adventure do not remain confined to the battlefield and can affect the daily lives of citizens and the economic stability of countries that played a role in shaping the crisis. Now, the increase in energy costs and the possibility of expanding instability in global markets have led European governments to conclude that continuing the confrontation with Iran can have consequences beyond their initial calculations.
The Guardian newspaper, in a report by Patrick Wintour, wrote that the foreign ministers of eight European and Middle Eastern countries at a meeting in Istanbul have called on America and the Zionist regime not to resume their attacks on Iran. They have warned that the resumption of conflicts could expand the crisis across the region and push oil prices even higher. According to this newspaper, the formation of a kind of multinational "anti-war bloc" has gained importance under conditions in which Tehran's nuclear negotiations are at a deadlock and signs of Washington's and Tel Aviv's willingness to resume military actions are visible.
But the fundamental question is: to what extent did European countries, when accompanying America's and the Zionist regime's actions against Iran, take into account the consequences of such a policy for their own security and economy? Some European governments, by providing facilities and military or logistical support to America, participated in a process that increased pressure on Iran. Now those same countries are warning about the expansion of the crisis and its economic consequences; as if the increase in energy costs has made them more aware than before of the real dimensions of this confrontation.
Europe now faces the contradictory result of a policy in which accompanying military pressure against Iran has been combined with concern about the consequences of that same pressure for the European economy. European governments cannot, on the one hand, play a role in providing the ground for military actions or supporting Washington's policies, and on the other hand, expect the potential consequences of these actions to remain directed only at Iran and the countries of the region. In today's interconnected world, security crises are quickly transferred to energy markets, supply chains, and the living costs of citizens.
In this context, the Strait of Hormuz is one of the most important determining variables in security and economic equations. This strategic waterway is considered the passage route for an important part of the global trade in oil and gas, and any serious disruption in the transit of energy-carrying ships through it can confront global markets with a shock. The rise in oil prices, the growth of transportation costs, and the increase in the price of petroleum products are among the consequences that can quickly be transferred to the economies of energy-importing countries.
Iran, too, due to its geographical position and strategic capacities in the region, is an important part of the global energy security equations. For this reason, the possibility of disruption in the transit of energy through the Strait of Hormuz, even without the realization of the scenario of this waterway being closed, can affect market expectations and governments' calculations. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is not a certain and inevitable consequence, but ignoring the risks arising from the intensification of the confrontation around it would also not be realistic. Governments that support increased military pressure on Iran must also take into account in their calculations the possibility of reciprocal reactions and their effects on the global energy market.
For European countries, this issue is doubly important. The rise in oil and fuel prices does not only raise the cost of energy supply; it can also increase production costs in factories, the transportation of goods, services, and the provision of households' daily needs. Under such circumstances, inflationary pressure intensifies, and European industries may face greater difficulty in competing with producers in other regions of the world. In this way, the consequences of the crisis go beyond the level of foreign relations and become a direct issue in the lives of citizens and the performance of European economies.
For this reason, today's concern of European countries cannot be considered merely a diplomatic position; this concern reflects the collision of political calculations with economic and geopolitical realities. Accompanying Washington may have political or security considerations for some European governments, but this accompaniment does not mean immunity from the consequences of America's decisions. When the crisis expands, Washington's allies may also face costs in which they had no determining role in the initial decision-making and whose effects they cannot easily prevent.
The position taken by the foreign ministers of eight countries in Istanbul shows that concern about the expansion of the crisis has now become one of the serious considerations in relations among the countries of the region and Europe. However, opposition to the resumption of military actions does not necessarily mean a fundamental change in the policy of these countries toward Iran; perhaps concern about economic and security costs has driven them to adopt such a position more than any other factor. Nevertheless, this same concern also shows that the continuation of the confrontation can create divisions even among America's allies and increase the political costs of Washington's decisions.
Ultimately, the increase in Europe's concern about oil and fuel prices is a reminder of a clear reality: one cannot play a role in intensifying a crisis and expect its costs to remain solely on the shoulders of the opposing side. European governments must learn from the current experience that their energy security and economic stability are not separate from developments in the Middle East, and that military policies can create unforeseen consequences for their own supporters. Now that the increase in energy costs has become a serious concern, the fundamental question remains: why were the economic and security consequences of this path not given the place they have today in the calculations of European countries before accompanying military actions against Iran?

Waiting list for specialized care may outlast those needing it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:22:00 UTC
18:22:00 KST

Waiting list for specialized care may outlast those needing it
Specialized care funding in Estonia is so lacking that around 2,000 people in need of assistance are waiting for services.
One such person is Alex, a young man with a profound disability who needs round-the-clock care.
Alex, 19, was born extremely prematurely, suffering severe brain damage as a result, "Aktuaalne kaamera" reported. Alex needs assistance with everyday activities including eating and getting dressed.
Alex's mother, Merje Liiv, said she cannot even get to do household chores while looking after Alex as he needs her by his side constantly. "He has epileptic seizures, he gets tired of being in one position, and I have to monitor him all the time," Liiv said, adding she needs to be present not only physically but also mentally.
"I am his link to the world, I am his eyes and hands," she went on. Liiv also provides her son with emotional experiences. "Alex is very grateful that he hasn't been left somewhere in the dark, and that people engage with him, and he enjoys that," she continued.
The family had assumed that once Alex finished school, he would enter specialized care. Specialized care services are primarily intended for people with severe mental disorders or intellectual disabilities who cannot get the assistance they need via other social welfare measures and channels. However, it turned out that Alex's case was too severe and he was not eligible for the service.
"Obviously, our sense of security disappeared immediately as we had been counting on it," Liiv noted. She added that being denied the service came as painful for the family. What hurt most, however, was the realization that for as long as Alex was of compulsory school age, the law required the state to acknowledge his existence. Once compulsory schooling ended, he was essentially written off by the state, however.
"For them, Alex was a client who was too complicated, but not so complicated that he should be left entirely in his family's care. That was what hurt," Liiv recounted.
Her local municipality then assigned Alex a personal assistant who visits him on weekdays. More broadly, however, there is a growing problem of people not fitting into predefined categories and being left without the support they need.
The problems facing specialized care can be summed up as chronic underfunding. This has led to a situation in which more than 2,000 people in need of assistance are waiting for services.
Ragnar Vaiknemets, board chair of social services organization AS Hoolekandeteenused, said if someone puts a child or other family member on the waiting list for specialized care nowadays, that person may not even get a place within their lifetime.
"As harsh as it sounds, there is currently no regular triaging of the waiting list, as there is in healthcare," he explained.
Vaiknemets noted that people's need for assistance is not reassessed regularly. He said there are clearly too few places, particularly for certain services, such as those intended for people with autism or multiple disabilities. These are cases in which people require the service throughout their lives.
Currently, priority on the waiting list for specialized care services is determined primarily by when a person was added to the list, rather than how urgently they need assistance. The Riigikogu's Social Affairs Committee is working on a bill which would require waiting lists to take into account a person's actual need for the service, rather than simply the date they joined the list.
In spring this year, the Supreme Court issued a landmark ruling stating that if a person needs a place in a specialized care home, the state must provide it. People in need of assistance cannot be placed on an indefinite waiting list on the grounds of insufficient funding or a shortage of places.
While the 2027 state budget bill has passed its first reading, funding for specialized care within the bill and over the wider picture remains disputed. €200 million is needed over four years, yet only €37 million in additional funding has been allocated to the entire social affairs and healthcare sector. Also, it is not yet known how much of that €37 million is intended for specialized care.
Opposition Social Democrat MP Riina Sikkut noted there should not be a situation where people in need of assistance get asked why they did not lose their mobility in the first half of the year, when funding was still available, rather than at the end of the year, by which time the funding has run out.
"Wait until the new year for your crutches, wheelchair, orthosis or whatever other aid you need," she said, noting that this is exactly what is now happening with regard to specialized care.
Sikkut said a fixed amount of money is allocated in the budget, and services are provided only to the extent that this funding allows.
"If more people need assistance, or the need for assistance is greater than what we can provide with the money allocated in the budget, then we tell them to wait in line," she said.
According to Sikkut, a former health minister, the solution is not to wait a year or two or ask people in need to find some other arrangement. "In reality, there is no other solution," she said, adding that people in need of assistance require services specifically suited to their needs.
The government in the 2027 state budget bill set aside €7.4 million in a reserve for the social affairs sector. This is intended for negotiations with the opposition to secure parliamentary support for the minority government's budget.
"I have never seen anything like this in my life, where state budget problems are resolved via an unallocated reserve left for the Riigikogu to decide on," Sikkut noted.
Even an MP from the coalition Reform Party was critical of the situation. Signe Riisalo (Reform), chair of the Social Affairs Committee, said that if she were a minister, she would have included such an important issue in the state budget so that the Riigikogu could decide on it in the same way as the rest of the budget.
"I would not have left it unresolved," she added.
Riisalo, a former social security minister, noted that allocating at least the existing €7.4 million from the state budget for next year, followed by the same amount in subsequent years, bringing the total to €37 million over four years, would make it viable to create some new places. She added that it would also allow for a modest pay increase, as staffing is another major concern.
Vaiknemets said that if the social affairs sector as a whole does not receive the funding it needs, the problem will eventually return back to the state.
"It will come back to the state in the sense that people will start knocking on more doors: calling ambulances and the police, visiting healthcare providers and local municipalities, trying to get help somewhere," Vaiknemets explained.
He added that people who cannot access services or receive assistance do not simply go away.
Vaiknemets said the need remains and is if anything likely to become even greater. According to him, the state will end up using very expensive resources to pay for problems that could have been prevented.
"As the saying goes, we'll end up using a laptop to hammer nails into the wall," Vaiknemets concluded.

What we know about derailment of cargo train in Sverdlovsk Region
Unknown
