2026-10-26
09:19:54 UTC
18:19:54 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. A cargo train derailed on a section of the railway in Russia’s Sverdlovsk Region, followed by a fire, according to a post on the Max channel of the Sverdlovsk Railway.
TASS has compiled the main facts about the incident.
Circumstances of the incident
On October 26 at 1:30 a.m. local time (11:30 p.m. Moscow time or 8:30 p.m. GMT on October 25), several cars of the cargo train derailed and subsequently caught fire along the section between the Makartsevo and Sedelnikovo stations of the double-track electrified Reshety-Aramil line on the Sverdlovsk Railway, according to a post on the Sverdlovsk Railway’s channel on Max.
There were no casualties.
The clearance gauge of the adjacent track was damaged; traffic was suspended.
Fire and recovery trains were sent to the site.
Passenger train traffic on this section is not provided for and does not take place, the Sverdlovsk Railway noted.
Twenty cars derailed on the Reshety-Sedelnikovo section in Yekaterinburg, the press service of the Sverdlovsk Region’s Main Directorate of the Emergencies Ministry said later.
Seven rail tankers are on fire; they have been uncoupled.
The remaining cars are being towed away to a safe distance.
Some 316 people and 35 pieces of equipment were deployed to respond to the incident, including 58 people and 20 pieces of equipment from the Russian Emergencies Ministry.
The fire was contained, with flames covering an area of 1,500 square meters.
The regional office of the Emergencies Ministry reported later that the open flames had been extinguished.
It also specified that 39 cars had derailed.
Recovery operations
The Sverdlovsk Railway is carrying out recovery operations and monitoring the environmental situation at the site of train cars’ derailment in the Sverdlovsk Region, the press service reported.
Recovery and fire trains, along with other specialized equipment, are operating at the scene, with 250 personnel of the Sverdlovsk Railway involved.
Investigation and response
Law enforcement officials have launched an investigation into the derailment of freight cars followed by a fire in the Sverdlovsk Region, according to information on the Max channel of the Central Interregional Investigative Department for Transport of Russia’s Investigative Committee.
Investigators and forensic experts have been dispatched to the site; the full circumstances of the incident are being established.
The Sverdlovsk Region’s transport prosecutor has traveled to the site of the train derailment, the press service of the Ural-based office told TASS.
No excessive levels of harmful substances in the air or threats to the environment have been recorded, the press service of the Sverdlovsk Railway reported.
Monitoring of air and soil conditions will continue until the aftermath of the incident is completely cleared, the report said.
No excessive levels of harmful substances have been detected in the air in populated areas near the site where the tanker cars caught fire, the press service of the regional office of the Federal Service for Surveillance on Consumer Rights Protection and Human Wellbeing (Rospotrebnadzor) said.
The Service continues to monitor air quality.

Leopard attack leaves Beekse Bergen zookeeper critically injured
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A zookeeper was mauled by a leopard at Beekse Bergen safari park on Saturday, leaving her in critical condition. Medics say she is not expected to survive.
Two Persian panthers, which had been sheltering from the weather, attacked the woman in an enclosure, according to reports. There is no CCTV footage and investigations into what happened are ongoing.
The victim was highly experienced, according to Omroep Brabant, having spent around 25 years working at the park and caring for the animals. She sustained serious wounds to her head and neck from the attack, and her conditioned worsened over Sunday night.
She managed to call for help via a walkie-talkie and was rescued by colleagues before being almost immediately operated on. A trauma helicopter and large numbers of emergency workers rushed to the sight.
It is unclear why or how she was in the enclosure with the animals – something that is never normally allowed.
Wineke Schoo, director of the Dutch Association of Zoos, described the incident as a “worst case scenario” to Omroep Brabant, and said she has only ever experienced one such incident in 25 years of Dutch zookeeping, which was a lion attack in 2001.

From metalworker to Brazil's president: Lula da Silva's rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:18:13 UTC
18:18:13 KST

Lula broke with his unfavourable record since 1989, winning the runoff after losing the first round, crowning a career that took him from metalworker to Brazil's presidency.
After losing in the first round, Lula da Silva pulled off a historic comeback to be re-elected president of Brazil in the second round. Back in the Palácio do Planalto, which he had never left, the leader of the Workers' Party (PT) defied unfavourable precedent: since 1989, the year when Brazil returned to direct presidential elections and introduced the two-round system**,** no candidate trailing after the first round had ever gone on to win the second.
"I owe this to you. I have always thought that God has been very generous to me, because there are so many people better prepared than I am, so many people with more diplomas than I have, so many people who have read more books than I have, so many people who have studied more than I have," he said in his victory speech, his fourth after a presidential election.
It was a first for Lula, too. In 1989, he finished 13.3 points behind his rival Fernando Collor de Mello in the first round and failed to close the gap in the second.
From factory worker to trade unionist, from trade unionist to politician, from politician to president of Brazil. Nothing has ever seemed impossible for Lula, who once again showed with this election that adversity is not always insurmountable.
"I want to tell you that I am enormously proud. First, because I am the only president of the Republic, a metalworker without a university degree, elected four times, democratically, to call for peace," he told the crowd.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, promised "the best term" in Brazilian history.
"The day after tomorrow, on the 27th, I will turn 81. And I want to make a pledge in front of the press and in front of you. I am going to deliver the best term any president has ever served in the history of this country," he vowed.
The seventh child of illiterate farmer parents, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was born on 27 October 1945 in the Brazilian city of Garanhuns, in the north-eastern state of Pernambuco. He was only seven when he moved with his family to São Paulo, and 14 when he was admitted to a technical course in metalworking. Before that, he had already worked as a street vendor, shoeshine boy, and dye-shop assistant. He went on to become a metalworker, a profession he later defended as a trade unionist.
"Lula" began as a nickname and was later officially incorporated into his name – he is the epitome of the worker who becomes a politician: it was as a union leader and organiser of metalworkers' strikes in the São Paulo region, during the military dictatorship, that he made his name. During his years as a metalworker, he lost a finger in a workplace accident, which later earned him the disparaging nickname “nine fingers” among opponents.
It was these strikes, which he led between 1978 and 1980, that paved the way for the founding of the Workers' Party (PT) in 1980. The party would go on to emerge as the main force on Brazil's left after the country's democratisation between 1985 and 1988, with Lula as its leading figure.
After losing the presidential elections of 1989, 1994 and 1998, he finally reached the presidency in 2002, where he remained for two terms. He was the first trade union leader and manual worker to enter the Palácio do Planalto.
Supporters of his political legacy point to the transformation of a country marked by extreme poverty and illiteracy into a more prosperous and more equal Brazil, through social policy measures such as the introduction of the "Bolsa Família" in 2003 and the creation of the "Zero Hunger" programme.
Lula ended his first term with an approval rating of 57% and was re-elected in 2006 with more than 58 million votes, the highest tally in Brazil's history.
The results would ultimately bolster Lula's narrative that the state can play a decisive role in reducing poverty and hunger. In 2014, under the government of Dilma Rousseff, Lula's political successor, Brazil left the United Nations' Hunger Map after a significant reduction in undernourishment in the country. The shift was linked to a package of social and economic policies.
Politically, he has always presented himself as a defender of multilateralism, diplomacy and an international order in which decisions are not determined solely by the power of the major powers.
"War is not the continuation of politics by other means. It is the total failure of politics. In an interdependent world, to lead is to reconcile the interests of the homeland with those of humanity. That is the reflection of someone who represents a nation that cherishes peace and freedom. Someone who fought against a military dictatorship and defended his country against an attempted coup. It is the conviction of a worker elected three times as president who took Brazil off the Hunger Map," he declared on 22 September 2026 in his speech to the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.
But the corruption scandals engulfing Lula and the PT would catch up with him, temporarily curtailing his political career.
The "Car Wash" investigation and subsequent trials led by judge Sérgio Moro (later Bolsonaro's justice minister) dominated the second half of the 2010s. It brought down numerous heavyweights and sent dozens of politicians from across the spectrum to prison. The investigation, which exposed a complex bribery and kickback scheme centred on the semi-state oil company Petrobras and the construction giant Odebrecht, was central to fuelling distrust of Brazil's political class and the rise of right-wing populism embodied by Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula was jailed in March 2018, after being sentenced to nine years in prison for allegedly receiving a flat in exchange for political favours. After 580 days in custody, Lula was released in November 2019, following a change in Supreme Federal Court case law on when a sentence may begin to be served.
In 2021, the Supreme Court went further and annulled the former president's convictions in the case, ruling that the court in Curitiba lacked jurisdiction to try him. This cleared the way for the PT founder to return to the presidential race, which he went on to win in 2022.
His victory in the 2026 election marks a new phase in a political story defined by his ability to return to power, even if the road ahead now appears somewhat steeper.
The Brazil Lula now governs is not the one he led in the 2000s: the country remains deeply polarised, Congress is dominated by the centre-right and Bolsonarism still commands significant electoral strength.

FRANKFURT – The chief executive officer of VW’s Audi unit drew heavy criticism on Oct 26 for appearing alongside US President Donald Trump at a rally to announce a US$4 billion (S$5.1 billion) plant in Georgia, with the head of Germany’s top union saying it violated the automaker’s company guidelines.
The plan, which still requires approval from the supervisory board of parent Volkswagen, comes after years of considerations over a local plant to escape painful US tariffs that have dealt a massive blow to the company.
Audi CEO Gernot Dollner appeared alongside Trump on Oct 24 at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia, to announce the plans to build its first assembly plant in the US that will produce 200,000 sport utility vehicles (SUVs) annually.
“The way in which Gernot Dollner has presented himself and Audi in the US is deeply embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company,” IG Metall president Christiane Benner said in a statement, adding that the appearance had violated Audi’s corporate rules. She is also the deputy chair of VW’s supervisory board.
German automotive expert Ferdinand Dudenhoffer referred to Dollner as a “mini Elon Musk”, comparing him to the Tesla boss who has appeared on stage with Trump.
Audi’s code of conduct stipulates that no “public engagements with political parties or politicians standing for election, nor any sponsorship of such events” are to take place in the three months leading up to an election.
The US investment also coincides with VW’s biggest corporate restructuring in history, including massive job cuts as well as potential plant closures at home.
Trump has pressured automakers to move production to the US and has raised tariffs on vehicles, steel, aluminium and parts.
In 2025, Trump’s tariffs dealt Audi a €1.2 billion (S$1.72 billion) blow as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico.
Georgia has competitive election races for the US Senate and state governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy. But critics say they have boosted vehicle prices and that the trade uncertainty has delayed some automaker investments.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Dollner said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
In Germany, meanwhile, there has been increasing tension between Volkswagen management and workers over massive job cuts in the carmaker’s home market, including possible plant closures in light of rising costs and stiff Asian competition.
“It is right and necessary to better tap into the US market via a new plant,” said Benner earlier. “However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out.”
An opportunity if German workers gain
Olaf Lies, Premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, VW’s second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit.
“Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them,” he said.
Dollner defended Audi’s planned investment. “This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations,” he told reporters on Oct 25.
“If the American President invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands.”
He declined to give full details on the investment deal with the US, including whether it involves tariff relief for the company.
The plan to set up the premium carmaker’s first US production presence was “not a decision against Germany”, Dollner added, arguing that it could protect jobs at home by strengthening Audi’s global business.
“The optics are not great, jobs are being created in the US while Audi is reducing the capacity globally,” Metzler analysts said of the US plan. “Still, we would argue the decision to produce in the US is right.” REUTERS

Lula wins Brazil election after cutting Amazon deforestation to record low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:15:46 UTC
18:15:46 KST

Lula’s victory in Brazil's presidential election brings hope for the Amazon – but far-right gains threaten progress.
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil’s election has been hailed as a win for democracy and the Amazon.
Since his return to office in 2023, deforestation in the Brazilian rainforest has hit a record low, dropping 42 per cent in the last year alone.
The left-wing President’s historic fourth-term reelection comes as a relief for environmentalists who feared a return to weakened nature and climate protections under right-wing opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
During his presidency from 2019-2023, environmental policies were dismantled and deforestation surged by around 60 per cent, with more than 45,000 square kilometres cleared.
Under Lula, deforestation has fallen 71 per cent below its 2022 level.
Greenpeace Brazil said the 2026 election result “is a win for democracy and maintains the commitment to protecting the Amazon and fighting climate change”.
This optimism has been shared by environmentalists around the world: “Hurrah for the Amazon, the Cerrado, Pantanal and all Brazil’s nature!”, posted Glenn Hurowitz, founder and CEO of global nature advocacy organisation Mighty Earth. “Lula’s reelection is a much-needed relief for the rainforest and the country’s other extraordinary ecosystems.”
Why is Brazil's Amazon important to the world?
“Brazil is home to most of the world’s largest tropical rainforest and five other biomes, harbouring around 15 per cent of global biodiversity,” says Camila Jardim, International Political Expert at Greenpeace Brazil.
“Protecting these ecosystems matters far beyond Brazil’s borders and is essential to halting biodiversity loss worldwide.”
The rainforest also stores huge amounts of planet-heating carbon dioxide and generates atmospheric moisture that helps regulate weather far beyond South America.
Under Lula’s government, deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since monitoring began in 1988.
How did Brazil cut deforestation to record lows?
The huge progress in cutting deforestation is thanks to the Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Deforestation in the Legal Amazon (PPCDAm), which had been shelved under Bolsonaro.
The plan strengthened satellite monitoring of illegal forest clearing and enforcement of sanctions. It also uses regulations and financial incentives to curb deforestation and promote sustainable actions.
“Lula’s election keeps hope alive for nature finance that can make trees worth more alive than dead,” says Hurowitz. “Under Lula, the Brazilian government launched the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, an elegant system where investors reward countries for conservation, but which needs more capital.”
“This progress must be sustained, and efforts to protect and restore ecosystems across Brazil’s biomes must intensify, respecting the rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities,” says Jardim.
Right-wing congress could dampen Lula’s power
Flávio Bolsonaro has said he does not recognise the 2026 election result and will challenge it in court, citing a last-minute Supreme Court ruling that extended voting by two hours. Lula won by about 4.4 million votes, receiving about 51.8 per cent versus Bolsonaro’s 48.2 per cent.
Despite Lula’s narrow win, his rival’s party made huge gains in the National Congress.
“These elections saw a significant surge of the far-right in the National Congress, which includes a large contingent of climate deniers and anti-environmentalists,” Greenpeace Brazil said in a statement.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party will control 121 out of 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 28 out of 81 seats in the Senate from February 2027. Lula’s Workers’ Party federation will have 88 seats in the Chamber of Deputies. Centre-right parties will be decisive in whether legislation passes.
“Over the next four years, public mobilisation will be essential to defend rights and prevent potentially irreversible environmental setbacks,” said Greenpeace Brazil.
“Although the government faces a hostile Congress, it can enforce the law and designate new parks and Indigenous reserves – locking in progress,” says Hurowitz.
Threats also remain from wildfires, logging and drought, with this year’s strong El Niño expected to bring hotter, drier conditions conducive to fires.

Beirut's $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of Lebanon divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:15:46 UTC
18:15:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Beirut's pricey $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of class divide in Lebanon
Seven years after Lebanon's devastating financial meltdown, a debate over a chicken sandwich has exposed an increasingly stark divide between those who can still spend freely and those struggling to get by.
A trendy health restaurant wanted to offer its calorie-conscious customers a healthier take on the beloved Levantine wrap known as the shish taouk. So, The Glow Paradise launched the "Chic Taouk," pricing it at around $13—nearly double what an un-chic chicken sandwich typically goes for in Beirut.
The pricy pun proved hard to swallow, with outraged critics accusing the restaurant of overcharging in a country where many households struggle to afford basic necessities.
Yet while the debate raged on social media, customers kept buying. The Glow Paradise sold more than 20,000 Chic Taouk sandwiches in just 11 days, according to managing partner Hrag Jeghalian, who described the online exchanges as "natural marketing".
The contrasting reactions touched a nerve in Lebanon, where years of financial turmoil, political dysfunction and conflict have reshaped the country's social landscape, hollowing out much of the middle class while leaving a smaller group of consumers able to sustain an affluent lifestyle.
Debate pulls focus away from urgent crises
Sami Nader, an economist at the Saint Joseph University of Beirut, said the throngs at The Glow Paradise belied another reality.
"So you see people in the restaurant, but what you don't see is that 22 restaurants closed last month," Nader told Reuters.
Lebanon's Instagram-active community was split between those accusing the restaurant of theft and others saying the sandwich was intended for those who could afford it.
Some questioned whether the dispute itself reflected misplaced priorities in a country grappling with urgent crises, from Israel’s occupation of large swaths of the country’s south to the endemic electricity and water crises.
Lebanon's 2019 financial collapse was prompted by decades of corruption and profligate spending by the ruling elite, and several rounds of conflict since then have worsened the country’s economic outlook.
GDP has declined by nearly 40% since 2019 and inflation is expected to rise to 17.5% due to rising global energy and shipping prices eating away at people’s purchasing power, according to the World Bank. The figure is more than quadruple the global headline inflation rate flagged by the International Monetary Fund in July.
Four in five households in Lebanon struggle to afford basic necessities, the UN children's agency said in September.
'People can't keep up'
The country’s middle class has "disappeared," Nader said, dismantled by a series of crises including the collapse of the financial system in 2019, the 2020 Beirut Port explosion and two wars in under two years.
Monthly bills from private generator operators, which provide electricity to many homes and businesses during outages on Lebanon's failing national grid, jumped by nearly 20% in August 2026 alone, bringing rates nearly 60% higher than they were in February of this year, according to the kilowatt-hour prices set by Lebanon's energy ministry.
For many, that means paying for 24/7 electricity now costs several hundred dollars a month, in a country where the minimum wage is set at $400.
"Everything has become expensive, and people can’t keep up," said Fouad Fakhreddine, a 53-year-old restaurant worker from nearby Hamra. "We are now getting paid, then getting in debt over that just to get by."
The years of economic instability, he said, have produced "a class that is living, and a class that is not dead and waiting to die from the unbearable situation it is in."

India-Russia trade jumps more than 20% this year – Duma chairman
Trade between India and Russia has grown by more than 20% this year, Russian State Duma Chairman Vyacheslav Volodin said during talks in New Delhi on Sunday, where he called for the removal of trade barriers and the expansion of joint business ventures.
Volodin met the speaker of the Lok Sabha, Om Birla, ahead of the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum, which New Delhi is hosting on October 26-27. The discussions covered closer cooperation on trade, industry and agriculture, along with the strengthening of parliamentary ties.
Bilateral commerce reached $47.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 24.3% from a year earlier, according to data from the Indian Commerce Ministry, cited by Russian lender Sberbank.

Excellent controllers tailored for VR or “regular” gaming. Solid performance on supported VR games. Virtual Imax-scale 2D gaming. Doesn’t pretend to be for work or productivity.
TIRED
Pricey. Blink-and-miss-it battery life. Unpredictable performance for installed games. Problematic pairing for streaming games.
Valve has had a complicated relationship with virtual reality gaming. Its Steam client—the number one distribution platform for PC games—has long supported VR titles and works with headsets from other manufacturers. But the company's flagship VR headset, 2019’s Valve Index, never quite escaped its niche. It saw a huge sales spike in the run-up to the release of headline title Half-Life: Alyx, but by February 2025, it accounted for only 13.2 percent of VR headsets used on Steam.
Enter the Steam Frame, Valve’s second attempt at snatching the VR gaming crown. More than a hardware refresh, it promises to reimagine PC VR gaming, operating as a stand-alone headset like the Meta Quest 3, the current reigning champion, while letting users seamlessly stream games from a more powerful remote machine. It mostly succeeds—but a few issues hold it back.
All in Your Head
Specs-wise, the Steam Frame is one of the better VR headsets, though far from a powerhouse. It packs a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip—a slightly dated offering, having debuted in 2023—with 16 GB of RAM, and either 256 GB (at the $1,059 price) or 1 TB ($1,299) of storage, plus a microSD slot for expansion, allowing it to install and run games locally.
It’s aesthetically pleasing, with a sleek black shell and glossy front that have given it a futuristic look. More importantly, it’s comfortable to wear, weighing 440 grams—75 grams lighter than the Quest 3. Valve smartly moved the 21.6-watt-hour Lithium-ion battery to the rear of the head strap for better balance, and thanks to cozy padding, it doesn’t feel hot against your head, even when running demanding games. The cable linking the battery to the headset makes adjusting the elastic straps a little fiddly, though.
The only real comfort drawback is if you wear glasses. While the Steam Frame comes with a spacer to add more depth (which easily clips on magnetically between the inner headset and the padded face gasket), the internal dimensions were still too narrow for me to wear with any of my spectacles. Custom Zenni prescription lenses are available if contact lenses aren’t an option, but it’s a pricey add-on.
Once it’s on your head, dual speakers push audio down the arms directly to your ears, with physical volume controls easily accessible on the left side of the headset. The audio lacks bass but has good directionality, bringing those immersive VR experiences to life. Dual microphones let you use voice controls, while outward-facing cameras enable positional tracking and provide a pass-through view—albeit monochrome with everything looking bluish. A dial at the top lets you adjust lens spacing to your required interpupillary distance, and an inner switch locks it in place.
The lenses themselves are decent, but again not spectacular. Valve uses two LCD pancake lenses (though rumors already hint at a revised OLED model), with a per-eye resolution of 2160 x 2160. That means sharp visuals and legible text—I could easily read fine details on notepads in Half-Life: Alyx, for instance—but you can discern pixels if you peer closely. The real win comes with a 110-degree field of view, enabling wide spans of virtual real estate, and refresh rates ranging from 72 to 120 Hz, with an experimental mode boosting it up to 144 Hz. As a result, games can look incredibly smooth when running on the Steam Frame.
The controllers might be the best part of the package. The dual grips mimic the Quest 3 controllers but outdo them with a full controller layout spread across the pair. They boast the same highly precise Tunneling Magnetoresistance thumbsticks as the regular Steam Controller, along with a full D-pad on the left, four ABXY face buttons on the right, two shoulder triggers and an underside button on each—squeeze that in, and the grip switches from controller mode to laser pointer to make selections in VR.
Position detection is great, with full six-degrees-of-freedom tracking, while excellent haptics deliver solid rumble and per-finger capacitive sensing for nuanced, precise interactions with virtual objects. You can also pair a regular controller to the Frame via Bluetooth, but the included ones are so good you likely won’t ever feel the need to—these are now the pinnacle of multipurpose VR controllers.
What Will Play?
After setup—a now-familiar routine for VR gamers that includes running necessary updates and drawing safe boundaries so you don't knock into furniture—you’ll sign in to your Steam account directly on the Steam Frame. It runs SteamOS 3 just like the Steam Deck or Steam Machine, the familiar home screen now floating in a VR void. Navigate to your library, and you can install whatever you like directly onto the Frame.
Unfortunately, while there’s a filter for games officially categorized as compatible, it’s unclear what rubrics Valve uses, or how many games have even been tested. Of my 1,300-plus-strong Steam library, only a meager 18 were marked “Great on Frame.” The strangest absence from that list is the totemic Half-Life: Alyx (which comes free with every Steam Frame purchase), especially odd given it runs without issue. Other dedicated VR games are hit and miss when installed directly on the Frame—I tried Obduction (opened and crashed, repeatedly), Doctor Who: The Edge of Time (ran with juddery performance and could only move by clicking in on the thumbsticks), Dungeons of Eternity (fine, bar some aiming and tracking issues), and Surgeon Simulator VR (totally fine).
You’re not limited to VR games on Frame. You can install and play anything in your library as 2D on a vast virtual cinema screen. Don’t bother with demanding AAA games—the hardware isn’t up to running them—but indies and AA-tier games can look phenomenal like this. Playing Hades II blown up to Imax-scale was a fantastic experience. Again, performance is unreliable—gorgeously animated Metroidvania MIO: Memories in Orbit launched when installed locally, but couldn’t load its assets, leaving me standing on invisible platforms and with no way to navigate the world.
The Frame also seems to default 2D games to 720p resolution. You can override this, but it may drop performance. Frame rates for all of the above games hopped all over the place, though mostly hovering around the 72 or 90 fps benchmarks. It feels like Valve has a lot of updating work to do to ensure Steam Frame can reliably function as a gaming platform for VR or non-VR titles. Right now, running anything is a gamble.
Wi-Fi Woes
The most annoying thing is that the Steam Frame isn't designed solely as a stand-alone headset—pairing it with a more powerful desktop (or laptop) should, in theory, let the PC do the grunt work and stream the output to the Frame. The package includes a dedicated 6-GHz wireless adapter—plug it into any device with a USB-A 3.0 port running Steam, and it should provide a dedicated network for the Frame. The headset connects to both the adapter and your home network, creating a mesh that reduces latency by using whichever has the least network traffic.
In practice, I could barely get it working. I tested it on a Windows 11 PC, a Windows 10 PC, and a Steam Machine—in every case, the Frame could connect to the remote device through the home network, but the adapter appeared as connected but unpaired. When it detected and created that mesh network (on rare occasions), streaming was flawless, but when connected only through the home network, performance was laggy enough to irritate.
Whether playing natively or through streaming, battery life is poor—expect two hours at the high end for locally run games, and maybe three if you’re purely streaming. Such short playing time makes the inability to physically connect Steam Frame to a PC with a cable all the worse, which would also overcome the streaming issues.
Better Days to Come
The biggest hurdle for most VR gamers is likely price. Like all of Valve’s recent tech, the Steam Frame is a casualty of RAM and storage shortages across the electronics industry. Like the Steam Machine, it feels almost compromised, especially that three-year-old processor. It doesn’t feel like $1,000-plus worth of headset, especially when its overall performance only just about beats the significantly cheaper Quest 3.
Yet despite its many early hiccups, the Steam Frame is incredible fun. The VR titles that work without issue are brilliant to play here, and the cinema mode for 2D games is the best implementation of that feature I’ve experienced on a VR headset. Streaming shows potential if Valve can work the networking kinks. If it gets that polish over the coming months as Valve pushes out inevitable updates, it could really shine.
I especially love how it’s unapologetically a gaming platform. It’s not trying to claim VR is useful for productivity, or office tasks—that ship sank along with Apple’s Vision Pro—and mercifully, there’s not even a hint of a blighted “Metaverse” here. The Steam Frame is for gaming, end of story. If Valve can iron out its software issues and make sure more games run on it properly, it’ll be a great way to play.

Iran accused the US on Monday of lacking seriousness in negotiations, saying Washington has repeatedly confused diplomacy with imposing demands on Tehran.
“The American side is not serious about negotiations,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said during his weekly news conference, as cited by the state-run IRNA news agency.
He accused Washington of repeatedly making false claims, recalling that US President Donald Trump had expressed support for negotiations shortly before the US military attacks on Iran in June 2025.
“What do you call this? Do you see any goodwill in this approach?” he asked.
Baqaei said Tehran had not received any new European proposal for negotiations beyond a political statement, criticizing Britain, France and Germany for their positions during the conflict.
He accused the three countries of following Washington’s lead on the restoration of UN sanctions and failing to condemn military attacks against Iran.
 
No nuclear weapons
Baqaei reiterated that Iran had never possessed nuclear weapons or sought to acquire them, accusing Washington of using allegations about Tehran’s nuclear program to justify military action.
He said Iran had negotiated in good faith and signed the 2015 nuclear agreement, but the US withdrew from it three years later.
The spokesman accused the US administration of being influenced by Israeli claims about Iran’s nuclear program, describing allegations that Tehran was developing a nuclear bomb as a justification for military aggression.
 
Missing Iranian pilots
Baqaei said Iran continued to hold Qatar responsible for clarifying the fate of three Iranian pilots whose aircraft were hit in the Gulf country.
“Until we have evidence of their deaths or receive precise information and documentation, we assume that the country where their aircraft were hit must be held accountable,” he said.
He added that Tehran was pursuing the matter in coordination with its military leadership and through technical delegations and legal discussions.
Baqaei also confirmed that a Qatari delegation recently visited Tehran, saying the trip involved bilateral cooperation and regional mediation efforts.
He described such visits as normal during regional conflicts, noting that Qatar had sought to convey messages and present its positions.
Commenting on Israel’s upcoming elections and threats of military action against Iran, Baqaei accused Israeli politicians of competing over who could commit more crimes.
“It makes no difference to us who takes charge of a regime with a history of violence and killings,” he said.
 
Russia visit
The spokesman confirmed that President Masoud Pezeshkian would travel to Russia on Monday night to attend a summit of gas-exporting countries.
He said the visit would provide opportunities to strengthen energy cooperation with Moscow and hold consultations with other major energy-producing countries.
Baqaei also addressed border-related difficulties with Pakistan and Iraq, saying discussions with Islamabad were progressing positively.
He said Pakistan had described the issue as technical while also raising security concerns, including reports of planned attacks.
Regarding Iraq, he said Iranian diplomatic missions were pursuing the matter, warning that US pressure on Baghdad could harm the Iraqi population and bilateral relations.
Baqaei said Iran summoned the Italian ambassador on Sunday to express concern over the authorities’ handling of protests in European countries.
He accused France, Belgium and Italy of using excessive force and restricting the right to protest, saying such measures were inconsistent with their human rights obligations.
The French ambassador had also been summoned previously, he added.
 
Saudi Arabia and Yemen
On the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Baqaei said regional security was interconnected and instability in one country could affect others.
He stressed that the dispute should be resolved between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, reiterating Tehran’s readiness to help facilitate a settlement.
“Military approaches make problems more complicated and cause extensive damage,” he said, expressing hope that Saudi Arabia would pursue a negotiated solution.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have persisted since the US and Israel launched military attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a regional conflict and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
On June 18, Trump and Pezeshkian signed a Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding, aimed at ending hostilities, reopening the strategic waterway and paving the way for a broader agreement.
However, disagreements over the implementation of the understanding, including the US naval blockade, sanctions and navigation through the strait, have continued to hinder diplomatic efforts.
Earlier this month, Iran said restoring security to the Strait of Hormuz remained central to negotiations with Washington, insisting that the US must take specific steps to resolve the standoff.

Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

18:13:17 KST

Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes
Russia's Digital Development Ministry has proposed building data centers underground, camouflaged from the air, and fitted with drone defenses, Russian state-controlled media Kommersant said on Oct. 25, following several Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers.
Guidelines for existing, planned, and under-construction facilities outline the protection standards for three tiers of data centers, including whether sites are placed above ground or underground, according to Kommersant.
The top tier includes strategic sites whose loss could disrupt key state functions for an hour or more; the second tier includes sites supporting regionally or economically important systems, where outages could last four hours or more; and the final tier covers corporate data centers whose damage would not have wider consequences for the state, Kommersant said.
Existing data centers should be protected by reducing their visibility from the air and by deploying layered defenses, including reinforced structures, electronic warfare measures, and drone defense systems.
The announcement came after Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center belonging to social media giant VK between Oct. 8 and Oct. 18.
Russia's centralized digital infrastructure leaves Moscow facing two challenges: inflicting comparable damage on Ukraine and protecting its own data centers from further strikes. Serhiy Petrenko, former head of Yandex Ukraine, estimated that around 80% of Russia's data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region — within reach of Ukrainian long-range drones.
The consequences of Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers could extend far beyond disrupted banking and online services, potentially setting back the country's AI development and affecting military technology.
On Oct. 16, Kemerovo Oblast governor Ilya Seredyuk proposed housing data centers inside depleted open-pit mines and quarries, given their natural protection from aerial bombardment.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) on Monday proposed five pillars of water governance to reconnect residents with the city’s waterways and strengthen climate resilience.
At a press conference, Shen outlined a framework focused on access, aesthetics, water quality, flood detention, and ecosystem protection, with the Tamsui and Keelung rivers at its center, per Liberty Times.

“We use water every day, but in reality, we remain far removed from the water in our city,” Shen said, adding that his proposals aim to reconnect residents with the city’s natural environment.

2026-10-26
11:12:35 EET
18:12:35 KST

The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (GUR) published data on the War&Sanctions portal regarding three dozen units of foreign-made technological equipment used by cooperation enterprises producing Russian ballistic armaments, the GUR press service reported.
"The Russian military-industrial complex retains a significant dependence on foreign technologies. In particular, despite all efforts, Russia is still unable to replace industrial equipment from global manufacturers with localized analogs. Today we are publishing 30 units of technological equipment of Chinese, German, Taiwanese, American, Turkish, Swiss, and Italian manufacture used by Russian factories producing ballistic missiles and their components – altimeters, aerodynamic rudders, gyroscopes, etc. Characteristic is the growing number of Chinese machine tools and machining centers, including five-axis ones," the message on Telegram reads.
It is noted that Chinese machine tools utilize European, Japanese, and Taiwanese components – CNC systems, servo drives, high-precision spindles and bearings, measuring and rotary systems, linear guides, thermal stabilization tools, and machining process control systems, among others.
The publication notably includes a 5-axis universal machining center GX-650 manufactured by Hyper Machine Tool (PRC), used by Votkinsk Plant – a manufacturer of 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile; Shtral (PRC) turning and milling machining centers involved in the production processes of JSC PEMZ Molot, which produces electronic equipment units for Iskander-M missiles; and measuring equipment from German manufacturer Rohde & Schwarz installed at UPKB Detal, which produces altimeters for Zircon missiles.
GUR reminded that in order to deprive the aggressor of the capability to continue the war, it is necessary, in particular: to strengthen end-user control and the actual location of product use, including introducing on-site inspections by authorized representatives at the declared equipment installation address; and to extend enhanced control procedures to spare parts, components, technical fluids, consumables, software, updates, and maintenance required for equipment operation.
GUR also noted that it is necessary to regularly conduct audits of distributors, dealers, and other intermediaries, especially those supplying to high-risk jurisdictions, as well as to identify signs of re-export or end-user changes, investigate cases where a manufacturer's products are detected in the Russian military-industrial complex, establish their supply chains, and take measures to halt further deliveries through relevant intermediaries.
In addition, it is necessary to restrict deliveries of CNCs, tools, and other components to Chinese manufacturers that supply their equipment to Russian military-industrial complex enterprises, the message states.

Poland in talks with Vietnam on defence equipment sales

Poland in talks with Vietnam on defence equipment sales
Poland is in talks with Vietnam on the sale of armoured personnel carriers, self-propelled howitzers, ammunition and coastal defence systems, Deputy State Assets Minister Konrad Golota told PAP.
Golota, who is accompanying Prime Minister Donald Tusk on his visit to Vietnam, told a briefing in Hoi An on Saturday that the talks marked the culmination of two years of close contacts between the state-owned Polish Armaments Group (PGZ) and its Vietnamese counterparts.
The discussions cover Rosomak armoured personnel carriers, Krab self-propelled howitzers, bridges, artillery ammunition and support vehicles, as well as radar and coastal defence systems. Poland is also offering communications and electronic components for combat platforms. The private WB Group is also participating in the visit.
Golota said that Vietnam had traditionally relied on Russian weapons but was now seeking to diversify its suppliers due to sanctions. Israeli, French and American companies are also strongly represented on the Vietnamese market, while Poland's advantage lies in its expertise in modernising post-Soviet equipment.
According to Golota, the two sides are discussing direct sales, the transfer of some production and technology to Vietnam, and maintenance and modernisation services, which he described as "very profitable financially".
Golota said it was too early to estimate the value of potential orders, explaining that Vietnam usually starts with small contracts that expand if the equipment proves successful. The two sides are expected to announce the main areas of cooperation on Monday, while commercial agreements could follow in December.
"We want to present specific contracts in December," he said, adding that this could happen at an arms fair scheduled to take place in Vietnam that month.
Golota also said he sees particular potential in coastal defence, which is a priority for Vietnam. Poland could offer radar and coastal surveillance solutions developed under the Digital Baltic programme. Furthermore, the Polish Naval Shipyard is exploring maritime support options, with talks covering rescue vessels and minehunters based on Poland's Kormoran-class design.
The discussions also extend to aviation maintenance services. Golota said that defence plants in Bydgoszcz could service transport aircraft, including C-130s, as well as post-Soviet aircraft from the Sukhoi (Su) family, provided that Vietnam supplies the necessary spare parts. (PAP)

Britain will not join Canada-led defence bank initiative
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:09:35 CET
18:09:35 KST

Oct 26 (Reuters) - Britain will not join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, in a setback to efforts to create the world’s first global defence bank, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The two countries instead said on Sunday that they would develop a framework for cooperation between their respective defence-funding initiatives, establishing two distinct but complementary institutions to support each other on investment opportunities and strategic challenges.
“We have been working closely to consider how the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) and Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) can best advance our shared objectives. We have agreed to develop a framework of cooperation that works in the interest of both institutions,” the statement said.
The two governments were unable to agree on key issues including the location of the headquarters of a joint institution, the level of joint procurement, lending to members, and the rules around new members joining in the future, a second person said.
The MDM will focus on accelerating defence investment, joint procurement through financing, and bringing together demand across NATO allies to reduce procurement costs, while the DSRB will complement it by supporting investment in defence industries and supply chains, focusing more on single sovereign lending, the person added.
The DSRB has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
There were hopes Britain would reconsider its position under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his team, with the two countries holding talks on the topic recently. Germany had also declined to join.
Britain and Canada said the MDM and DSRB will be designed to work in close partnership, so they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges.
AIMING TO RAISE BILLIONS
The DSRB has been aiming to raise around €100 billion ($112 billion) and use the money to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It will also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers.
So far besides Canada, where the DSRB will be based, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have pledged their support to the bank.
Reuters previously reported that potential member countries had not joined because of concerns including whether the DSRB can offer cheaper financing than highly rated national governments as well as the amount of capital countries would need to commit, the bank’s governance, and overlaps with existing initiatives.
Britain’s Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had recently described the DSRB as a “really interesting and innovative mechanism” and said that he did not see the proposed defence bank and MDM as being in competition.
Britain previously declined to join, citing concerns over value for money. Reuters previously reported that Burnham discussed the DSRB alongside the MDM initiative with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in July and with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden during an August visit to Kyiv.
($1 = 0.8925 euros)

Nigeria’s Ebola patient medically evacuated from country, Arise TV reports
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:09:30 CET
18:09:30 KST

ABUJA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Nigeria’s Ebola patient left the country on a medical evacuation flight to Switzerland on Monday morning, the health minister said, adding that her clinical condition was much improved.
The patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is Nigeria’s first Ebola case in more than a decade.
The outbreak, which started in Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
The possibility that the Nigerian patient became infected in Uganda, where officials say she spent a two-week holiday before returning to Abuja, has fuelled concerns about undetected transmission in a country where the outbreak had appeared to be under control.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said in a post on X that the woman was “stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results closing towards baseline” before her evacuation flight departed.
Her spouse has remained asymptomatic and left Nigeria on the same flight, Pate added.
The Swiss foreign ministry and Uganda’s health ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
SCIENTISTS INVESTIGATING HOW PATIENT CAUGHT RARE STRAIN
A team of leading Ebola scientists will travel to Nigeria to help investigate how the patient caught the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya told Reuters in an interview.
Switzerland said last week that she had not travelled to Congo, contradicting statements from Ugandan officials.
Her travel documents show she had not visited Congo, Kaseya said.
There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species, which has now caused almost 10,000 cases and more than 4,800 deaths in Congo, and spread to three other countries in Africa – Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
Kenya has reported nine cases and two deaths, all linked to a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda’s Entebbe airport.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June but has not recorded any since and was declared free of the virus by the World Health Organization in August.
The WHO’s Africa director congratulated Nigeria’s government and health workers for stabilising the patient’s condition, allowing her to be evacuated.
“The Nigerian medical team successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilized her condition,” Mohamed Janabi said on X.

Starvation in Gaza becomes election campaign material in Israel as crises worsen Palestinians’ lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:09:22 UTC
18:09:22 KST

Hardline Israeli rhetoric toward Palestinians has increasingly become part of campaigning ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections, while humanitarian conditions in the Gaza Strip have worsened amid tighter restrictions and continued Israeli violations.
Last week, extremist Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir released an AI-generated campaign video depicting the Gaza Strip completely destroyed by 2030 as part of his far-right Jewish Power party’s election campaign.
Four developments have emerged among the most pressing crises facing Gaza: the loss of food assistance for half a million Palestinians, the threat of vital hospital services shutting down because of depleted generator fuel, the expansion of areas under Israeli military control, and rising numbers of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces.
The developments come amid continued Israeli bombardment, gunfire, and restrictions on the entry of supplies despite a ceasefire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025.
The following are four crises that have worsened in Gaza during Israel’s election campaign and their impact on Palestinians.
On Oct. 19, the World Food Program (WFP) said that it was reducing food assistance in Gaza by around one-third, leaving about 500,000 Palestinians without support and cutting the number of beneficiaries from 1.6 million in September to 1.1 million in October.
The reductions included halving food rations, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, as well as cutting quantities of wheat flour.
The WFP also reduced the number of hot meals it provides daily from 250,000 to 150,000, while families in hard-to-reach areas, including those near the Yellow Line, now receive a meal every other day.
The UN agency attributed the measures to a funding shortage, saying financing for its operations in the Palestinian territories in 2026 had fallen to less than half the levels recorded in previous years.
It said it needs $450 million to continue operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank during the six months from October through March 2027.
Around 1.4 million Palestinians in Gaza, roughly two-thirds of the population, face high levels of food insecurity, according to the WFP.
Although the agency cited funding shortages as the reason for reducing assistance, Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and goods have further complicated efforts to meet humanitarian needs.
In a report published Oct. 19, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said aid deliveries into Gaza continued to face difficulties due to inspection procedures, limited crossing capacity and coordination requirements.
Gaza’s government media office warned the same day that aid cuts were accelerating famine conditions, accusing Israel of waging a “war of starvation.”
The Palestinian government also warned on Oct. 20 of rising malnutrition rates among children and pregnant women, calling for adequate funding for humanitarian aid and the opening of crossings.
On Oct. 21, Gaza’s Health Ministry said stocks of fuel needed to operate hospital electricity generators had run out, warning that the remaining generators could fail and life-saving medical services could be forced to stop.
Hospitals require more than 2,500 liters of fuel each month to keep generators running for extended periods amid a lack of electricity, the ministry said.
On Sept. 13, Mazen al-Araishi, director general of engineering and maintenance at the ministry, said the quantities of fuel allowed into Gaza were limited and insufficient to meet generator operations and maintenance needs.
The ministry did not say when the last shipment of fuel entered Gaza or how long the generators could continue operating.
Gaza hospitals have depended on generators since Israel cut electricity supplies to the enclave in October 2023 and its sole power plant stopped operating after running out of fuel, while the war destroyed large sections of electricity lines and distribution networks.
The generators power operating rooms, intensive care units, neonatal incubators, ventilators and dialysis machines, making their failure a direct threat to patients’ lives.
The Israeli army has continued expanding the areas under its control in Gaza by moving “Yellow Line” markers westward, contrary to the gradual withdrawal outlined in the ceasefire agreement.
The “Yellow Line” marks the area to which Israeli forces withdrew during the first phase of the ceasefire agreement and separates territory under Israeli military control from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain.
When the agreement began to be implemented, around 53% of Gaza remained under Israeli control before the area gradually expanded.
On Oct. 11, Israeli forces advanced dozens of meters into the Shujaiya neighborhood east of Gaza City and moved concrete blocks marking the Yellow Line farther west, forcing scores of families to flee.
OCHA confirmed on Oct. 19 that markers near the Shujaiya junction had been moved and warned of the risk of further displacement in the area.
The expansion of Israeli-controlled areas prevents Palestinians from reaching homes, agricultural land and public facilities while making humanitarian relief operations more difficult.
On June 24, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the army controlled around 70% of the Gaza Strip. During a visit to the enclave on Sept. 2, he said Israel would not withdraw from the Yellow Line.
Netanyahu has linked further withdrawal to the disarmament of Hamas, while the Palestinian group says it is prepared to address the issue of its weapons alongside a gradual and organized Israeli withdrawal.
Alongside the expansion of Israeli military control, the number of Palestinians killed by Israel from Oct. 2-21 rose by around 40% compared with the same period in September, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry figures.
The data showed that 95 Palestinians were killed during that period in October, compared with 68 during the corresponding period in September, an increase of 27 deaths.
The number of Palestinians killed by Israel since the ceasefire agreement took effect reached 1,534 as of Oct. 21, according to Health Ministry figures.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed 74,494 Palestinians and injured 175,604 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

MOSCOW, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Russia’s FSB security service has thwarted a planned Ukrainian drone attack from inside Russia on a key element of Moscow’s air defence system and on an electricity facility, the FSB said on Monday, saying it had arrested two men involved in the plot.
The two men, who the FSB said were from the South Caucasus region and had been acting under instructions from Ukraine’s SBU security service, had retrieved First Person View drones and explosives from two Russian regions, delivered them to the Moscow region, and configured and activated the drones, the FSB said. The drones were to be remotely controlled from Ukraine, it said.
“It has been established that one of the suspects was recruited by an SBU officer and, on that officer’s instructions and in return for a promised monetary reward, travelled to Russia to prepare and carry out a sabotage and terrorist attack. To this end, he enlisted the help of an acquaintance from his close circle,” the FSB said.
”The suspects were detained by FSB officers while preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electricity infrastructure facility and on one of the key components of Moscow’s missile defence system,” it said.
There was no immediate comment from the SBU or from Ukraine, which has intensified its attempted drone attacks on the Russian capital in recent months, as Russia has stepped up its own attacks on Ukrainian power and other infrastructure targets.

Black Sea becomes most dangerous body of water for seafarers – FT
More seafarers have died in the Black Sea in 2026 than in any other body of water, outstripping fatalities in the Gulf, which has garnered more attention worldwide.
Source: Financial Times, citing shipowners and maritime organisations
Details: Crews on oil tankers, cargo ships and grain carriers entering the Black Sea close to EU and NATO territories must run the gauntlet of drone attacks. Some estimates put the number of attacks in the Black Sea as more than six times higher than in the Gulf.
"For me, the Black Sea and calling [at] Ukrainian ports is near suicidal," said Oleh Hryhoriuk, chair of the Marine Transport Workers' Trade Union of Ukraine.
Maritime security firm Ambrey and the International Maritime Organisation report that over 570 ships have been targeted in the Black Sea this year, resulting in the deaths of at least 40 seafarers. In comparison, 24 fatalities have been confirmed in the Strait of Hormuz.
While some vessels were caught in the crossfire during port bombardments, others were intentionally targeted. Ambrey notes that the third quarter saw an average of over four attacks daily.
Driven by record-high freight rates, some shipping firms are willing to take the risk of transporting oil from the Middle East. However, shipping groups indicate that the majority are reluctant to send their fleets into the Black Sea, given the lower profit margins and significantly higher risks involved in trading there.
Background: Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu has stated that Russia is turning the Black Sea into a danger zone for civilian vessels.

Dogs and horses galore at St Hubert’s celebration in Tervuren
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:08:52 UTC
18:08:52 KST

Hundreds of animal lovers took part in the annual St Hubert’s celebration in Tervuren (Flemish Brabant) at the weekend. Visitors from Belgium and abroad came with their dogs and horses to take the traditional blessing. For many, it is a regular event. They reminisce about the past. Often several generations join up.
The lovely autumn weather drew a large crowd to Tervuren. Among those present were local residents, as well as visitors who had made the trip to Tervuren especially for the event.
Marie-Louise Selmans, a local resident, came mainly out of tradition and to spend time with her family. “I think it’s important to take part in local events, especially for the children and grandchildren, so that they realise how important it is.”
She had also brought her dog along for the blessing. “He’s part of the family, so why not?”
For many residents of Tervuren, too, the celebration remains a regular fixture. “This is an annual outing,” say a few friends from the town. “It’s a tradition in Tervuren.”
Blessing adds extra meaning
For some visitors, the blessing holds special significance. Sabine from Dendermonde drove to Tervuren with her Bernese Mountain Dog, Uta.
“I hope she’ll be with us for a very long time and doesn’t get ill,” she says. “And, in a way, I do believe that this blessing will help us.”
Visitors also emphasise the bond between humans and animals. Jolanders, who has recently moved back to Tervuren, explains that animals deserve an important place in our lives. “We must be open to animals. You get so much friendship in return.”
Memories of the past
For many visitors the St Hubert’s Festival brings back memories of their childhood. Lena has been coming to the event for 60 years.
“There used to be hundreds of horses here,” she says. “They used to gallop back then. That’s no longer allowed, and you do miss it a bit.”
Her husband Arri has also seen how tradition has changed over the years. “There are fewer horses than there used to be, but the atmosphere remains special.”
According to visitors, stricter safety regulations are the main reason why the famous horse gallop has disappeared. Nevertheless, interest remains high.
More than just a religious celebration
For many of those present, the day is not just about the blessing, but also about being together. After Mass, families and friends head into the village for a drink, a meal or a stroll.

Factbox-Battleground metros to watch in South Africa’s municipal elections
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:08:47 CET
18:08:47 KST

By Sfundo Parakozov
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 26 (Reuters) - South Africans vote in municipal elections on November 4 amid voter frustration over poor service delivery, unstable local government coalitions and rising costs.
Held every five years, the elections will be an important gauge of the political landscape ahead of the 2029 national vote, with support for the African National Congress (ANC), Nelson Mandela’s former liberation movement, continuing to erode.
Here are the key battleground metros:
JOHANNESBURG: THE PRIZE
Africa’s richest city has churned through seven mayors since the 2021 local elections as successive coalition governments have unravelled.
The pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) gained an early advantage by naming former Cape Town mayor and Western Cape premier Helen Zille as its mayoral candidate months ahead of its rivals. The 75-year-old political veteran has run an energetic campaign focused on deteriorating infrastructure and poor service delivery.
Recent polls put the DA above 30% and the ANC above 20%, raising the possibility of a coalition between the two parties, which have governed together nationally since the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024. Both parties could first seek deals with smaller parties rather than share power.
TSHWANE: ACTIONSA THE KINGMAKER
Tshwane, home to the administrative capital Pretoria, underscores the importance of smaller parties in South Africa’s fragmented municipal politics.
The ANC governed the metro until 2016, when the DA captured it in a major urban defeat for the ruling party. Coalition politics subsequently proved volatile, and the DA lost power in 2024 after its coalition partner ActionSA backed an ANC-led no-confidence motion against its mayor.
Tshwane has since been governed by a multi-party coalition led by ActionSA. The party, founded in 2020 by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, is a centre-right party that campaigns on anti-corruption and a hard line on immigration.
CAPE TOWN: DEMOCRATIC ALLIANCE BASTION
The DA is heavily favoured to retain Cape Town, which it has governed since 2006 and where it has held an outright majority since 2011.
Polls suggest the party should remain above 50%, though some analysts expect a tighter contest as voters grapple with soaring property prices and persistent gang violence.
The DA is also targeting Nelson Mandela Bay, one of South Africa’s most turbulent coalition metros and currently governed by an ANC-led coalition.
ETHEKWINI: ZUMA WILDCARD
The economic hub of KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, could deliver one of the election’s biggest blows to the ANC, with former president Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) threatening to displace it.
Zuma backed MKP after his bitter split with the ANC in 2023. Polls suggest the party could win 40% to 50% of the vote, while ANC support could fall into the low teens. MKP’s rise helped drive the ANC’s losses in the 2024 national election.
EKURHULENI: CORRUPTION TEST
Ekurhuleni, home to Johannesburg’s OR Tambo International Airport, could provide another measure of the ANC’s decline in Gauteng Province, where voters have cited concerns over corruption and crime.
Polls suggest ANC support could fall from 38% in 2021 to about 25%, leaving it neck-and-neck with the DA.
BUFFALO CITY AND MANGAUNG: LAST STRONGHOLDS OF THE ANC
Buffalo City, which includes KuGompo City in Eastern Cape province, and Mangaung, home to Bloemfontein in Free State province, remain the ANC’s strongest metropolitan bastions, making them important tests of how far the party’s urban support has eroded.
The ANC won 59% in Buffalo City and 51% in Mangaung in 2021, helped by deep-rooted loyalty to the former liberation movement.
(Reporting by Sfundo Parakozov; Editing by Bate Felix and Xevi Fontdegloria)

California’s billionaire tax faces a precarious road from rich opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:08:42 UTC
18:08:42 KST

California’s billionaire tax faces a precarious road from rich opposition
Tech billionaires have raised more than $300m to oppose the billionaire tax proposal.
San Francisco, United States – University of California at Berkeley economics professor Brian Galle recently found a flyer in his mailbox about the proposed billionaire tax he helped write. But as he read it, Galle found things he hadn’t written, including that the tax can be on anyone and even on their retirement savings.
Californians have been getting such flyers and watching similar ads as they prepare to vote in the November 3 election on whether to impose the one-time tax of 5 percent on the assets of the state’s billionaires.
Spending by the billionaires to oppose the tax has made this the most expensive ballot measure ever and among the most expensive campaigns of this midterm, says David McCuan, professor of political science at Sonoma State University, who tracks state and local elections.
California’s celebrated tech billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Doordash founder Tony Xu, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Ripple co-executive chairman Chris Larsen and venture capitalists John Doerr, Michael Moritz and Vinod Khosla, are among those who have donated more than $300m to block the additional tax on their assets.
While Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg has not donated money to oppose the tax, Meta’s SEC filings revealed that he told the company’s board, which includes Xu and Collison, that he would buy a home outside California to avoid paying the tax. This could have affected Meta stock prices and the board created a new class of shares that Zuckerberg could use to pay the tax.
The billionaire fundraising has far outstripped that of the supporters, who only raised $32m. This has led to the ubiquitous ad campaign as well as outreach to voters.
“I feel like I am in an Alice in Wonderland alternate reality,” said Ashley Craig, a volunteer for Patriotic Millionaires, a group that supports the tax.
Craig has spent months door knocking and making calls to voters to campaign for the tax and often hears misinformation about it.
“They often tell me it has secret provisions allowing everyone to be taxed, which is not entirely true,” she said.
Any change in the tax would require a two-thirds majority in the assembly and would need to stay true to the spirit of the tax. But the prevalence of the ads has meant that voters often tell Craig the tax would soon include her – and them.
Making democracy more equal
“The irony is that Prop 40 [the billionaire tax proposal] is meant to make democracy more equal, but the billionaires are using their money to avoid that,” says Galle, the proposal’s coauthor.
The US Supreme Court’s judgement in the Citizens United v FEC case gave companies and special groups the freedom to spend freely in elections, he said.
“This has led to this situation where Sergey Brin has a lot more of a political voice,” says Francesco Trebbi, the BT Rocca professor of Business and Public Policy at the University of California at Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “It’s Sergey Brin v millions of Californians. This leads people to lose trust in the system ” .
Apart from the ad buys, Craig says she has also felt alone in the campaign arena. While the state Democratic party has endorsed the tax proposal, Craig says she hasn’t had ground support from the party. “We don’t have resources like social media, door knocking, phone banking and I would place the blame at the feet of the Democratic party.”
Sonoma State’s McCuan attributes this to the Democratic party’s internal rift between the progressives and moderates, with the former in favour of such a policy and the latter resisting it.
“This is a broader proxy test between the party’s progressives and moderates. If this works, progressive candidates could try such ideas in the 2028 presidential elections,” McCuan says, which the billionaires and moderates want to avert.
So while the party has endorsed the measure, California Governor Gavin Newsom has opposed it, as has Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor in the election and Katie Porter, a former congresswoman who also ran for governor.
Newsom, who is eyeing a 2028 presidential run, has opposed the tax, saying it is “poorly written. It would harm the state if its billionaires, who have an estimated wealth of 2.3 trillion according to the measure’s authors, move, as Zuckerberg has planned,” Newsom has said.
The tax’s opponents have also backed a ballot measure that prohibits any new state taxes based on personal property or imposed retroactively. Another asks state auditors to review any proposed tax measures for their financial impact before they are voted on. If these pass and get more votes than the billionaire tax, they could negate the billionaire tax, even if it is passed.
Only a third of citizen initiatives pass
The strong campaign opposing the billionaire tax may have impacted support for it. Voters support the tax by a small margin, but also the two measures that oppose it, according to a recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC).
“Only about a third of such citizen initiatives pass. So the burden is on the yes side,” says Mark Baldassare, statewide survey director and Miller chair in public policy at PPIC. “Support can decline if people don’t feel completely sure.”
But Suzane Jiminez, chief of staff at the SEIU health workers union, which has sponsored the billionaire tax measure, said, “We are feeling confident that we will have the votes. When voters see that billionaires are funding the ads, they see through them.”
Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Congressman Ro Khanna of California rallied across the state to drum up support for the measure. Jiminez said that in the last few weeks, 3,000 volunteers have spread out to knock on doors and distributed flyers explaining the tax across the state. “The democratic figureheads do not represent the rank and file on this. They are supporting us,” Jiminez said.
It is unclear whether this will be enough, as the shortfall in funding means support for the measure remains precarious. Baldassare said he plans to do his poll again as voters read and receive the state’s voter guides explaining the ballot measures and make up their minds.
Sonoma University’s McCuan said that just the historic amount of money being spent on defeating the measure is a win in itself for the tax backers.
“Progressives can win by losing. They can say moderates sank us, use it as a morality play. They will attack big tech – as a bad bogeyman of US politics.”

Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado returns from exile, received by thousands of supporters in Caracas

Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado returns from exile
October 26, 2026
Venezuela's opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by thousands of cheering supporters in Caracas on Sunday after returning from nearly a year in exile.
Her supporters stood along highways, toll plazas and city streets waving Venezuelan flags and chanting slogans like "freedom" as Machado made her way in a convoy of cars and motorcycles to the capital, Caracas.
Wearing her trademark white T-shirt and blue jeans, she leaned out of the sunroof and shouted "this country is giving lessons to everyone" as her convoy entered the capital.
In Guacara earlier, the AFP news agency reported seeing Machado singing the national anthem in a plaza packed with supporters, waving flags and cheering her return.
Why was Machado in exile?
Machado left Venezuela last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in promoting democracy in autocratic Venezuela.
Facing arrest by the regime of former President Nicolas Maduro, she sought refuge in the Argentine embassy in Caracas and was smuggled out of the country with assistance from the United States.
At first she was unable to return for fear of detention by authorities.
After the US-led ouster and arrest of Maduro, she gave her Nobel medal to US President Donald Trump.
However, her inability to return to Venezuela for so long was partly due to the Trump administration.
Instead of backing Machado, Washington decided to support interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
Machado has said she faced travel restrictions and flight cancellations, partly due to Trump's worries that her presence in Venezuela could inflame tensions during a period of transition, and partly due to Rodriguez' interference.

New power outages caused by Russian attacks have been recorded as of the morning of October 26 in six regions of Ukraine. The schedules remain in effect. This was reported by NEC "Ukrenergo" on Monday, UNN writes.
Enemy shelling
"Over the past day, the enemy continued to attack Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure. As a result, as of this morning, there are new power outages in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Chernihiv, Kharkiv, and Sumy regions," Ukrenergo reported.

Schedules
"To prevent overloading equipment damaged by previous Russian shelling, in some regions today until the end of the day, capacity restriction schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules (up to 2.5 rounds) for all categories of consumers will be applied as a necessary measure," Ukrenergo noted.
Consumption
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has decreased. Today, October 26, as of 09:30, it was 5.8% lower than at the same time on the previous working day—Friday, October 23. The reason for the change is the necessary restrictions caused by enemy attacks.
Yesterday, October 25, the daily consumption peak was recorded in the evening. It was 4.8% higher than the maximum recorded on the previous Sunday—October 18. This was caused by a drop in air temperature, prompting consumers to use electric heaters in the evening hours.
"Given the consequences of Russian shelling and the weather conditions, the need for economical electricity consumption during the evening hours remains. Please limit the use of powerful electrical appliances from 16:00 to 22:00," Ukrenergo urged.

Nicola Lener, the ambassador to Canberra, spoke in Melbourne at the annual “Eureka Democracy” award ceremony, where this year’s prize was awarded to Antony Green, a former journalist with the public television network ABC who specializes in analyzing voter trends.
