17:30:34 KST

EU Inc, Europe’s harmonised corporate form, is stalled after Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs failed to vote. Caught between furious founders and protesting workers, could EU Inc still change how you build a startup? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
The European Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs (JURI) failed to agree on the draft report on EU Inc on 19 October, having already postponed the vote on 5 October. Disagreements among MEPs over workers' rights are driving the deadlock.
EU Inc is an EU-wide company structure that lets businesses register in one member state and operate across the bloc. It would follow a shared set of rules, the “28th corporate regime”, so founders wouldn’t have to navigate 27 different national frameworks.
Proposed by the European Commission in March 2026, EU Inc aims to make it easier and cheaper to set up a business in the EU. It tackles the fragmentation across Europe’s startup ecosystems and boosts collaboration, talent mobility, and access to funding.
Founders could set up a company fully online within 48 hours, with starting capital of €1 and no notary. Registration and documentation are handled in English, with no translation or local-language requirements when operating abroad.
While EU leaders agreed to finalise the law by year-end, pushback is coming from multiple fronts.
EU Inc founders argue that months of negotiations had weakened the proposal. On 15 October, in a public statement they accused the EU of reducing EU Inc to a fast-track registration process by stripping away its core features, including free choice of registration and a common-stock framework to attract talent.
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) warn that a proposal threatens workers’ rights. On 24 September and 20 October, trade unions from across the bloc protested in Brussels and Strasbourg, warning that it would let companies use lighter corporate rules to circumvent national labour laws and social standards.

Opinion
China may well be the next big competitor for Asian migrant labour
The country that once transformed global labour markets by exporting workers could reshape Asian migration by beginning to import them
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Juan Fernando Herrera Ramos is a Honduras-born journalist based in Taiwan covering Asia–Latin America relations, geopolitics and supply chain issues. 
For decades, China was one of the world’s largest sources of migrant labour. Its workers staffed factories at home and built infrastructure abroad. But demographic decline may eventually force China to contemplate a striking reversal: importing workers on a meaningful scale.
That change is not imminent. China still has a vast labour force and substantial youth unemployment. It is investing heavily in industrial automation, extending working lives through a gradual increase in the retirement age, and trying to move workers from regions with surplus labour to where employers struggle to recruit.
Yet the direction of travel is becoming difficult to ignore. China’s population fell for a fourth consecutive year in 2025. The number of employed people declined to 725 million from 740 million in 2023.

Russia’s Once-Feared Lancet Drones Are Turning Into a Multimillion-Dollar Failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:29:08 UTC
17:29:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Once-Feared Lancet Drones Are Turning Into a Multimillion-Dollar Failure
Russia’s Lancet attack drones, once considered among Moscow’s most effective battlefield weapons, are facing questions over their effectiveness after a Russian unit reportedly spent millions of dollars launching the drones with almost no results.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to pro-Russian militant Pavel Gubarev, Russia’s “Sparta” drone unit launched approximately 100 Lancet loitering munitions over three months, successfully striking only three targets. The operation cost between $3.7 million and $6.1 million.
The launches were conducted by a team commanded by Senior Lieutenant Kirill Ozerov, known by the call sign “Nevsky,” during a period beginning in mid-June 2026. Gubarev did not specify where the unit was operating.
Despite deploying around 100 drones, the unit reportedly managed to hit only a self-propelled artillery system, an infantry dugout, and a roadside kiosk—an estimated success rate of just 3%. Ukrainian air defenses intercepted most of the remaining Lancets, while Russian forces destroyed several of their own drones due to poor coordination between units.
Gubarev estimated the cost of each Lancet at between $37,000 and $67,000, bringing the total expenditure to as much as $6.1 million for just three successful strikes.
He also accused the unit’s commanders of deploying expensive drones without adequate preparation while submitting misleading reports about their effectiveness to senior military leadership.
The claims have not been independently verified and describe the performance of a single Russian unit rather than the entire Lancet fleet.
Manufactured by Russia’s ZALA Aero, the Lancet is a loitering munition designed to destroy artillery systems, armored vehicles, and other battlefield targets. It features optical guidance, an explosive warhead, and an estimated operational range of 40–50 kilometers.
Earlier, on March 17, Ukrainian defense adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov reported that Russia had launched up to 40 Lancet drones toward Kyiv in what he described as a largely symbolic operation.

Drones Strike Russia’s Titanium Giant Supplying Su-34 Fighters and Iskander Missiles

- Category

Drones Strike Russia’s Titanium Giant Supplying Su-34 Fighters and Iskander Missiles
Drones struck the AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant in Russia’s Perm region overnight on October 25, targeting a major titanium production facility supplying materials used in Russian military aircraft and missile systems.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The attack took place in Berezniki, where AVISMA operates as part of VSMPO-AVISMA, Russia’s largest titanium producer. The facility manufactures titanium sponge, a key raw material used in aircraft engines, fighter jets, and missile components. Footage of the reported strike was published by the OSINT community Exilenova+.
Perm region Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed the drone attack on October 25, claiming Russian air defenses intercepted 11 drones. He acknowledged minor damage to an industrial facility and reported that five employees had been injured. According to Makhonin, the facility continued operating.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), VSMPO-AVISMA produced approximately 33,500 metric tons of titanium sponge in 2024, accounting for roughly 96% of Russia’s total production.
The corporation supplies titanium alloys to Russian aircraft manufacturers Sukhoi and Irkut, which produce Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35 fighter jets. Its products are also used in Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has identified VSMPO-AVISMA as a supplier involved in the production chains of Su-34 fighter-bombers and Su-35S fighter jets.
The company also supplies Russia’s missile industry, including the Votkinsk Machine Building Plant, which manufactures Iskander ballistic missiles and Yars and Topol-M intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The reported strike follows Ukrainian attacks on two Russian defense-related facilities on October 24. Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed strikes on the Proton-Electrotex electronics plant in Orel and the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant in the Samara region, both linked to Russia’s cruise and ballistic missile production.

Army drone deal widened to cover heavier aircraft
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:27:37 GMT
17:27:37 KST

The Ministry of Defence intends to raise the maximum take-off weight allowed under the British Army’s mini drone contract from twenty kilograms to fifty, and to confirm that the contract covers flights beyond visual line of sight, without running a new competition, according to a transparency notice published by the department.
The TIQUILA contract was awarded to Lockheed Martin UK on 7 December 2022 and is worth £129,350,000 excluding VAT. It runs for one hundred and twenty months, with options to extend by up to a further twenty four months and to vary the volume of goods and services delivered.
The notice says the department proposes “to broaden the contractual technical envelope so that TIQUILA can continue to procure and integrate relevant UAS capability as technology and operational demands evolve”, and that the change will “confirm the inclusion of VLOS and BVLOS Packable MUAS capability” and “increase the platform take-off weight from a maximum of 20kg to 50kg”.
Arguing that it can make the change without a fresh procurement, the department says: “The modification does not change the contract into a requirement for a different category of capability. The requirement remains focused on UAS capability supporting field operations through the existing SI-led model, while accommodating unanticipated technological advancement beyond the parameters originally defined.”
It goes on: “It preserves the commercial model, of engagement with the wider UAS market and new entrants through flexible supply-chain arrangements; supports the same field-operational purposes and retains the same SI-led integration, modular architecture and through-life delivery model, while responding to technological advancement and developing operational demands in the manner contemplated by the original procurement, and is therefore considered a vertical evolution of the existing UAS capability, rather than horizontal expansion.”
The department says all pricing mechanisms stay the same, that it considers the change a permissible non-material modification under the principles established in the Pressetext case and the Defence and Security Public Contracts Regulations 2011, and that it published the notice voluntarily to provide transparency.
TIQUILA delivers mini uncrewed air systems for intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition and reconnaissance in packable and portable loads, with Lockheed Martin UK acting as systems integrator and bringing in other suppliers through enabling arrangements intended to reach new entrants, industry and academia. The original scope required a modular technical and digital architecture built on open-standard interfaces so that new capabilities could be integrated as they emerged.
The aircraft bought under the programme so far are the Stalker VXE 30, a near-silent long-endurance machine weighing under twenty kilograms, and the Indago, a backpack-sized aircraft under eight kilograms that can be put in the air in around two minutes. Ninety nine Stalkers and fifteen Indagos were ordered, deliveries began in March 2023, and full operational capability for four Future Soldier batteries was expected this year, as this publication reported when the contract was signed.
Brigadier Pete Drew, the Army’s senior responsible owner for the programme, said at the time that “TIQUILA will bring the next generation of remotely piloted air systems into service in the Army”, and that it would speed up decision making and make the force more lethal, responsive and resilient.
Raising the ceiling to fifty kilograms takes the contract past the weight of anything currently flying under it and into a class of aircraft carrying heavier sensors and flying longer. Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, told Parliament this week that military flights beyond visual line of sight use temporary segregated airspace notified through the warning system pilots check before flying, or permanent segregated airspace such as danger areas, with the Civil Aviation Authority responsible for United Kingdom airspace throughout.

Plane parts for Russia’s air force, rubber for its industry—Voronezh’s factories came under drone attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:25:38 UTC
17:25:38 KST

Drones attacked the VASO aircraft plant in Russia's Voronezh overnight on 26 October, Ukrainian Telegram channel Supernova+ reported. The plant builds Il-96 airliners and parts for Russia's military transport planes. A synthetic-rubber plant was also reportedly hit and fires broke out across Voronezh, while another rubber plant in Tolyatti, farther east, reportedly came under attack again.
Ukraine keeps hitting the plants behind Russia's weapons, from Voronezh's missile chips to Urals titanium for warplanes. Each supplier knocked out of rhythm slows how fast Russia replaces the hardware it loses and keeps using against Ukraine.
What the Voronezh plant builds
Supernova+ described VASO as part of Ilyushin, which belongs to Russia's state-owned United Aircraft Corporation (UAC). The channel published a photo of fire and smoke at the site. The plant lies about 190 km from the Ukrainian border.
VASO makes pylons, engine nacelles, and flap rails for the Il-76MD-90A, a modernized military transport plane, and sends them to Ulyanovsk, UAC's press service said in 2024. "We have reached the production pace of Il-76MD-90A aircraft kits that our Ulyanovsk colleagues need," Igor Butyrin, who runs the plant's Il-76 program, stated at the time. In 2016, the plant built an Il-96-300 that UAC handed over to the Rossiya special flight detachment of Russia's presidential property office.
A rubber plant and a bridge on the list too
Supernova+ also named Voronezhsintezkauchuk, a plant of Russian petrochemical group Sibur that makes synthetic rubbers. The channel later reported a hit on the plant's industrial zone and claimed an attack on the city's Northern Bridge. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ published footage of a drone arriving, reportedly at the rubber plant.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev declared a missile alert at 04:47 Kyiv time, but no source has named a missile type. Kyiv has not commented. Ukraine's Air Force, which launches Storm Shadow cruise missiles, and its Navy, which fires Neptunes, have posted nothing on Voronezh.
Earlier this month, Ukraine's Navy said it hit six Su-34 bombers in Voronezh Oblast with Neptunes. Storm Shadows reportedly struck an electronics plant in Oryol on 23 October and a battery plant in Yelets two days later.
Fires across the city
Gusev claimed air defenses downed 113 drones over the region, more than 70 of them over the city. He listed fires at several industrial enterprises, which he said caused no serious consequences, plus a business center, an apartment block, and a school stadium. Russian Telegram channel Astra published video of a drone hitting the Galereya Chizhova business center. Exilenova+ footage showed cars burning below apartment blocks.
Damage in residential districts may have come from downed drones or from Russian air-defense missiles falling back on the city. During a 23 October attack on Gorodets, in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Exilenova+ claimed a Pantsir air-defense missile hit a house.
Russia still parks its best bombers in the open. Ukraine has spent a year knocking out the air defenses that were supposed to protect them
Gusev also claimed two men were killed and 17 people injured, many of them on a train struck by drone debris. Russian Railways said five passengers were hurt at Somovo station and traffic on the line stopped. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses downed 290 drones over 15 regions and the Moscow area.
Tolyatti's rubber plant reportedly attacked again
Locals reported an attack on the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant in Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, Exilenova+ said. The city lies about 890 km from the front line. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a strike on the same plant on 24 October. Its synthetic rubbers go into solid fuel for Russia's tactical and ballistic missiles, among other uses.
Until Kyiv comments or satellite imagery shows the site, the damage at VASO stays unconfirmed, and so does any delay to Russia's Il-76 parts line.

Russia says it caught Ukrainian agents preparing close range drone attack on Moscow's air defences
MOSCOW, Oct 26 - Russia's FSB security service has thwarted a planned Ukrainian drone attack from inside Russia on a key element of Moscow's air defence system and on an electricity facility, the FSB said on Monday, saying it had arrested two men involved in the plot.
The two men, who the FSB said were from the South Caucasus region and had been acting under instructions from Ukraine's SBU security service, had retrieved First Person View drones and explosives from two Russian regions, delivered them to the Moscow region, and configured and activated the drones, the FSB said. The drones were to be remotely controlled from Ukraine, it said.
"It has been established that one of the suspects was recruited by an SBU officer and, on that officer’s instructions and in return for a promised monetary reward, travelled to Russia to prepare and carry out a sabotage and terrorist attack. To this end, he enlisted the help of an acquaintance from his close circle," the FSB said.
"The suspects were detained by FSB officers while preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electricity infrastructure facility and on one of the key components of Moscow's missile defence system," it said.
There was no immediate comment from the SBU or from Ukraine, which has intensified its attempted drone attacks on the Russian capital in recent months, as Russia has stepped up its own attacks on Ukrainian power and other infrastructure targets. REUTERS

Zelensky Says Ukraine Wants to Keep 800,000-Troop Army, Rules Out Neutrality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:25:03 UTC
17:25:03 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine should maintain an army of 800,000 personnel to ensure its security, adding that the size of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) is an internal matter that will not be negotiated with Russia or the US.
In an interview with Alla Mazur, host of TSN.Tyzhden (TSN.The Week), Zelensky said the key question was how Ukraine’s military would be funded and what security guarantees the country would receive as part of any peace settlement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If I have sufficient funding, I want to maintain an army of 800,000 people. If we are in NATO, the number could be 800,000 or less,” he said.
According to Zelensky, the central issue is who is prepared to finance Ukraine’s armed forces.
“And that is my question for NATO,” he added.
Starlink and intelligence sharing resume
Zelensky also said Starlink had resumed operating in Ukraine and that the country was once again receiving uninterrupted intelligence on ballistic missiles following what he described as productive talks in Oslo.
He said Ukrainian intelligence on ballistic missile strikes was now functioning at 100% capacity.
“The dialogue between Ukraine and the US – which had become quite emotional – has returned to a functional state. Starlink is back up and running (as of Saturday, Oct. 24, at 5:20 a.m.). We achieved the right outcome; we secured what we needed. This was one component of our discussions in Oslo,” Zelensky said.
Why Are Laws Vital to Ukraine’s EU Integration Stuck in Parliament as the Country Loses Money?
He revealed that tensions in the dialogue with Washington had centered on three main issues: shortages of air defense systems, operational restrictions on Starlink, and limitations on the intelligence provided by the US.
Two of those issues have now been resolved, Zelensky said, although the provision of additional air defense systems remains unresolved.
Zelensky rejects neutrality and restrictions on Ukraine’s army
Zelensky also discussed a document containing US proposals for ending Russia’s war against Ukraine that US special envoy Steve Witkoff delivered to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
According to Zelensky, the document contains various proposals from Washington, but Ukraine has made clear that two issues are non-negotiable: the country’s neutrality and restrictions on its armed forces.
“The document contains various proposals from the American side. We maintain that key aspects of this are that there can be no discussion of our state adopting neutrality, nor can there be any talk of placing restrictions on the Ukrainian army,” Zelensky said.
He did not disclose whether Ukraine’s red lines were explicitly spelled out in the document, saying that agreements with the US prevented him from sharing all the details.
However, Zelensky reiterated that Russia cannot dictate the terms of Ukraine’s security guarantees.
“Therefore, restrictions on our army and the neutrality of Ukraine are not up for discussion. The issue of territory is a ‘red line’ that can only be addressed at the level of the leaders themselves. For us, this has always been a non-negotiable constant,” he said.
“Yet, the Americans frequently raise the question of territory – asking what we might be willing to trade in exchange for certain fundamental principles,” Zelensky added.
Zelensky stressed that Ukraine does not intend to give up territory but remains open to discussions.
He said territorial questions must be addressed directly by the leaders, while other issues could be handled by technical groups.
“If the discussion concerns the territorial issue, it must take place at the level of leaders. Other matters should be handled by technical groups. What constitutes ‘other matters’? Security guarantees. For instance, the issue of NATO – which, naturally, appears in relevant documents and new proposals – is one such matter,” Zelensky said.
“We are discussing security guarantees; someone must provide assurances that Russia will not launch a new act of aggression,” he added.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine expects such guarantees from the US and Europe.
He also stressed that the document delivered by Witkoff was not a plan simply presented to Putin for approval.
“It is not Russia that makes the decision; all parties involved do. There are proposals for discussion – including those from the American side – which are being discussed with us,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky proposes energy truce as first step toward peace
Asked by Mazur what Putin would need to do to demonstrate that he genuinely intended to end the war, Zelensky pointed to an energy truce as a possible first step.
“This would be a signal. If that doesn’t happen, then we look to a trilateral meeting at the level of leaders,” he said.
Zelensky believes such a meeting involving Ukraine, the US, and Russia is possible. However, he cautioned that Putin’s apparent willingness to resume negotiations does not guarantee that the Kremlin will follow through.
However, he suggested that Moscow could be feigning readiness for dialogue to avoid further confrontation with US President Donald Trump.
Zelensky said it was too early to judge the outcome of a potential leaders’ meeting before it took place.
“One should discuss the outcome ‘after’ the meeting in question, not ‘before’ it. What will unfold there? What escalatory developments might arise in the Middle East? Will this meeting take place in Abu Dhabi, or perhaps in Europe? We shall see,” he said.
Zelensky added that he did not know what had prompted Putin’s sudden shift in position on peace negotiations.
“What influenced this? I cannot say. Perhaps there are some agreements between America and Russia of which I am unaware,” he said.
Ukraine is prepared to participate in trilateral negotiations involving technical groups, Zelensky added, but he stressed that the talks must produce concrete results.
He recalled that the American side had asked what specific outcomes Ukraine wanted to see.
“The Americans asked me, ‘What kind of specifics are you looking for?’ I replied, ‘Look, could the war end in November during a meeting of the technical group?’ Without the leaders present, it won’t be a complete resolution,” Zelensky said.
He then outlined several alternatives that could produce tangible progress even without a comprehensive peace agreement.
“Fine – if that’s not on the table, then let’s have an ‘energy truce,’ address the maritime situation and grain exports, carry out an ‘all-for-all’ prisoner exchange, or hold a meeting of the leaders. That, undoubtedly, constitutes a result. A result creates opportunity,” he added.
Zelensky added that these were proposals put forward to the American side, not demands.
He said it should become clear in November whether Putin was genuinely prepared to negotiate or was merely making political gestures to avoid escalating tensions with Washington ahead of the elections.
“And if this is merely a political stunt – if Putin is simply saying ‘Yes, I’m ready’ because he wants to avoid escalation with America ahead of the elections – we will find out very quickly in November whether it was a ruse or not,” Zelensky said.
US proposes temporary ceasefire in Oleshky
Zelensky also said the US had proposed a ceasefire in the Oleshky area starting Tuesday, Oct. 27 and lasting several days to facilitate a humanitarian mission.
Under the proposal, representatives of Ukraine, the US, and Russia would travel to the area. Russian forces would be expected to clear roads of mines, while Ukraine would verify the work and carry out the necessary measures.
Zelensky said he had issued specific instructions to Ukraine’s ombudsman and that the government had also consulted the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the military.
He cautioned, however, that Russia could clear the roads in a way that directs people toward Russian-controlled territory, rather than allowing them to leave freely.
Zelensky said some people would nevertheless be evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
“The main thing is to unblock these people so that they can live. Ideally, they will be able to reach their goal and be evacuated here – to us, to Ukraine,” he said.

Hungarian Tycoon’s Firm Funded Pro-Orbán Advertising Agency, Records Show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

A firm owned by Hungarian construction mogul László Szíjj — who amassed a fortune under previous Prime Minister Viktor Orbán — donated about $863,000 to Megafon, a political advertising agency that promoted the former ruling party.
The donations are detailed in two years of annual financial statements from Szíjj’s firm, Vakond Via Kft., which were examined by OCCRP and Direkt36. The company made “cash grants” that totaled 300 million Hungarian forints to Megafon Digital Incubator Center, adding up to about $252,000 in 2024, and $611,000 the following year.
Launched in 2020, Megafon became one of Hungary’s most influential political advertising agencies, mainly running social media campaigns in support of Orbán’s Fidesz party.
But since Orbán’s stunning electoral defeat in April, after 16-years in power, Megafon has kept a low profile. The company’s website was taken offline in August, and its employees have fallen from 72 to three, according to information from a firm that provides commercial registry data.
Neither Megafon nor Szíjj responded to requests for comment.
Megafon’s situation mirrors the condition of other media organizations that backed Fidesz, and received generous state advertising contracts or donations from government-friendly entrepreneurs.
Since coming to power, Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has taken steps to halt state advertising being funneled into pro-Fidesz media. Some outlets have stopped publishing, while others have downsized as their budgets dried up.
OCCRP and Direkt36 recently reported that Megafon had received about $12 million between 2022 and 2024 from a firm owned by Lőrinc Mészáros, another wealthy pro-Orbán businessman. Mészáros, who is also a business partner of Szíjj, did not respond to questions at the time.
Magyar cited those findings in a Facebook post following publication, saying the reporting confirmed that Mészáros’ firm, while “funded by public money,” had supported Megafon’s “propaganda.” Magyar asked in the post how long the State Audit Office would “remain silent” about the funding.
The State Audit Office has confirmed to Direkt36 it is investigating finances around this year’s election.
“The audit naturally includes an evaluation of news reports and conclusions published in the press, including an examination of Megafon’s activities,” the office said in an emailed response to questions.
It is unknown if Szíjj’s firm, Vakond Via, made donations to Megafon this year. Vakond Via’s 2026 annual financial reports are not yet available, and the company did not respond to a request for comment.
Vakond Via is part of Szíjj’s sprawling Duna Group of companies. The conglomerate’s flagship firm, the road-building company Duna Aszfalt Út és Mélyépítő Ltd., “won the highest value of public contracts” in a ranking compiled by Transparency International.
The anti-corruption group’s Hungarian chapter calculated that Duna Aszfalt received around $2 billion worth of public contracts between 2018 and 2020.

Hong Kong looks to profit from Halloween ghosts and zombies during longer festivities
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:22:35 CET
17:22:35 KST

By Joyce Zhou
HONG KONG, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Tens of thousands of revellers in costumes ranging from evil bartenders to Donald Trump impersonators, zombies and Taoist priests, packed an entertainment zone as Hong Kong lit up for Halloween celebrations set to stretch over three weekends.
The colourful crowds thronged the narrow streets of Lan Kwai Fong as onlookers scrambled to take pictures during month-long festivities to ring in Halloween, which falls on Oct. 31, as part of an effort to boost tourism.
“Being here gives me this real carnival vibe — it’s a great way to completely let loose and release ourselves after work,” said 34-year-old Huang Wei, outfitted as the beloved Monkey King of Chinese mythology.
“I feel like the main reason for coming here is to free ourselves,” added the visitor from the southern technology hub of Shenzhen, who rode the metro with nine friends.
The carnival atmosphere lingered well into the night, as Western horror characters mixed with figures from Chinese folklore, and others inspired by the pandemic era.
Mock enforcers of COVID-19 curbs, dressed in white protective suits, roamed the streets carrying thermometers and swab kits, as loudspeakers blared orders to report for testing, in scenes once familiar across China.
A signature attraction is a giant eyeball installation in Central’s Statue Square Gardens, drawing large crowds, while similar Halloween-themed displays have sprung up elsewhere.
MAINLAND CURBS OFFER OPPORTUNITY FOR HONG KONG
Growing curbs have hemmed in Halloween festivities in mainland China since 2023, when authorities in the commercial hub of Shanghai detained some revellers over costumes that satirised social and economic issues.
In Hong Kong, authorities and businesses hope the longer Halloween celebrations will boost tourism, nightlife and consumer spending in the Asian financial hub while luring more visitors across the border.
The effort aims to pull more visitors to the city’s bars, restaurants and retailers, said Allan Zeman, chairman of the Lan Kwai Fong Group, who helped introduce Halloween celebrations to the district more than four decades ago.
“Halloween, which was a Western holiday, was able to suddenly be accepted by the East now,” added Zeman, who estimated that the festivities led to a bump of 20% to 25% in food and beverage sales each year.
“So that’s really what Hong Kong is all about, ‘One country, two systems’. And so we can celebrate all together.”
Organisers said about 80,000 people celebrated in Lan Kwai Fong on October 31, 2025, but this year’s festivities spread over three consecutive weekends in Hong Kong’s effort to position itself as a regional Halloween destination.
“Every year it gets stronger and people spend, and every year the costumes get more and more outrageous,” Zeman added. “So that brings a lot of income here and it really helps the GDP of the area.”
(Reporting by Joyce Zhou; Editing by Anne Marie Roantree and Clarence Fernandez)

Ebola scientists to probe Nigeria case origin, Africa CDC says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:22:30 CET
17:22:30 KST

By Jennifer Rigby
LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - A team of leading Ebola scientists will travel to Nigeria to help investigate how the country’s first patient in more than a decade got infected, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said.
Their task will involve trying to work out how the female patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, caught the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. Her travel documents show she had not visited the outbreak epicentre in Democratic Republic of Congo, Kaseya said in an interview with Reuters in London.
Finding out how she became ill matters to ensure that the deadly Bundibugyo outbreak, already the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, is not spreading silently in as-yet undiscovered locations, and to help trace and isolate all contacts.
‘MANY UNKNOWNS’
“We have so many unknowns,” said Kaseya. “I’m bringing a group of scientists in Abuja because… we need to be led by science.”
One of the theories the scientists will investigate is a potential link between the patient in Nigeria and the first case in Kenya, reported earlier this month in a man who had travelled from Congo. On Friday, genomic sequencing showed that the viruses that infected the two patients were closely related.
The patient in Nigeria had been on holiday in Uganda and travelled through Entebbe Airport on October 3. The patient in Kenya, who has since died, was likely in the airport at the same time, as their flights were around 40 minutes apart, although they did not depart from the same gate and it is not clear whether they had any contact, Kaseya said.
Kaseya said while genomic sequencing had shown that the viruses were similar, it did not mean that one of the patients had directly infected the other and the patient in Abuja, whose condition is improving, has said she does not remember meeting the Kenya patient.
However, he said they were not excluding any options, including that there may have been indirect contact through another person, for example. Ebola spreads through close contact with the infected bodily fluids of a person with symptoms, according to the World Health Organization.
INVESTIGATION ONGOING
Kaseya said all countries involved were now willing to collaborate in the investigation, after what he described as tension last week when Uganda’s government insisted the patient in Abuja had been to Congo, while Nigerian authorities suggested she had not and was infected in Uganda, which has been Ebola-free since August.
Kaseya said the team, which will be led by the co-discoverer of Ebola, Congolese expert Jean-Jacques Muyembe, would also look at more sequencing data to work out where the Kenyan patient was infected.
The Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in Congo has now caused almost 10,000 cases and more than 4,600 deaths in Congo, and spread to three other countries in Africa – Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. There is currently no approved vaccine or treatment for Ebola Bundibugyo.
(Reporting by Jennifer Rigby; Editing by Toby Chopra)

Bulgaria heads to presidential runoff after close vote

SOFIA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Bulgaria will head to a runoff vote on November 1 after a tight race between the two leading presidential candidates failed to produce an outright winner in Sunday’s elections, which garnered record-low participation, official results showed.
With 95% of the votes counted, incumbent Iliana Iotova, 61, attracted 34.6% against 32% for ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, falling short of the 50% threshold for the largely ceremonial role in a race of 27 candidates.
Sunday’s vote took on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast that likely killed some two dozen international seafarers. However, only about 22% of the eligible voters showed up to cast their ballot, according to polling agencies.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
BOTH CANDIDATES CONDEMN DRONE STRIKES
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
“I want to share a certain worry and tell Bulgarians that it is an illusion if they think we can change something in this country without (them) voting,” Iotova said after polls closed at 8 p.m.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
(Reporting by Alex Lefkowitz; Writing by Angeliki Koutantou; Editing by David Holmes)

INTERVIEW – Over 2,200 Palestinians displaced in Hebron amid Israeli offensive: Mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:20:53 UTC
17:20:53 KST

Layan Bsharat and Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The Israeli army has forced more than 2,200 Palestinians from their homes and demolished five commercial and industrial facilities and a three-story residential building amid a large-scale military offensive in Hebron in the southern West Bank, the city’s mayor said.
Speaking in an interview with Anadolu, Yousef al-Jabari said the forced evacuations affected Deir Bahha and parts of Al-Jilda in western Hebron, an area that covers approximately 330 dunams (330,000 square meters), and contains more than 495 housing units.
He said Israeli forces surrounded Deir Bahha and Al-Jilda and used loudspeakers to order residents out of their homes.
“Those displaced include children, women, young men and older people,” he said. Some residents initially refused to leave before troops stormed their homes and forced them out.
On Saturday, Hebron municipality said that around 1,500 Palestinians from 250 families had been displaced, before the mayor updated the figure to over 2,200 people.
Al-Jabari did not specify where the displaced residents had gone, while witnesses said some families sought refuge in other West Bank towns and villages.
In a separate count covering three neighborhoods, Riyad Khamis, a media official with a local committee supporting affected families, told Anadolu that more than 380 Palestinian families had been forced from their homes in Deir Bahha, Al-Jilda and Khirbet al-Maghariba.
The Israeli army launched its offensive on Friday following a shooting that killed two Israeli soldiers in the Farsh al-Hawa area at the city’s northwestern entrance.
Khamis said the affected neighborhoods form a contiguous residential area within Area A, where the Palestinian Authority is supposed to exercise civil and security control under the Oslo Accords.
The neighborhoods are “located far from settlements, outposts or settler roads,” he said.
 
Collective punishment
Al-Jabari said the Israeli army closed Hebron’s entrances, preventing Palestinians from entering or leaving.
Israeli forces also closed the Ibrahimi Mosque and prevented prayers, as troops and military vehicles deployed across the city, he said.
Streets have become largely deserted because of the siege and movement restrictions, the mayor said, describing the measures as a “policy of collective punishment.”
Al-Jabari accused Israeli authorities of using Friday’s attack to intensify measures against Hebron’s residents ahead of Tuesday’s Israeli elections.
He said the escalation aimed to bolster occupiers’ support for the far right.
Following Friday’s attack, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened a wider military operation in the occupied West Bank that he described as unprecedented since the 1967 war, including evacuating Palestinian neighborhoods and raiding homes.
The Israeli siege has forced hundreds of businesses in Hebron and neighboring villages to close because workers cannot reach their workplaces and goods cannot move in or out, al-Jabari said.
“Israeli forces have continued demolishing commercial and industrial facilities and residential buildings since Friday,” he added.
Al-Jabari said the municipality declared a state of emergency in the area and deployed teams to assist displaced residents.
“Municipal teams are working to secure shelter for displaced families, assess residents’ needs and address damage to roads, water networks and sewage infrastructure,” he said.
The offensive comes amid escalating Israeli army and occupier attacks across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
The attacks have included killings, arrests, demolitions of homes and other structures, destruction of agricultural land and displacement of Palestinian communities, alongside settlement expansion.

Switzerland suspends MSF funding after reports of sexual exploitation

Switzerland suspends MSF funding after reports of sexual exploitation
The humanitarian organisation Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is accused of failing to adequately inform the Swiss authorities of the scale of reports of sexual misconduct by MSF staff in Chad. The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) has now suspended funding of CHF1.25 million ($1.52 million) to MSF.
The frozen amount represents one tranche of the CHF6.25 million pledged to MSF for the current year.
According to the newspaper NZZ Am Sonntag, an internal investigation by MSF revealed 59 reports of sexual violence and exploitation, particularly involving women and young girls who are refugees from neighbouring Sudan. Eighteen staff members have been dismissed, including six employees from the NGO’s Swiss branch.
The NZZ explains that this constitutes “widespread sexual exploitation”, adding: “Money, jobs or humanitarian aid in exchange for sex: staff members are alleged to have taken advantage of the distress of refugee women and girls”.
The German-language newspaper notes that “the Confederation’s aid workers were effectively operating in the dark”. Although the SDC received the first indications as early as November 2024, it only became aware of the true scale of the problem following articles published in the press in June 2026 by the AP news agency.
More
MSF in Sudan: ‘It’s very hard to reach people in need’
“Internal emails now reveal just how reluctant the Swiss Confederation was to act, even though it was already aware of the facts,” reports the NZZ.
Whilst fighting rages in Central Africa, which has been experiencing a major humanitarian crisis since 2023, hundreds of thousands of people are fleeing the civil war in Sudan to seek refuge in neighbouring Chad.
The first alert from MSF staff at the Geneva headquarters reached the SDC by email on a Friday in November 2024, “shortly before the end of the working day”. Three female refugees “are reported to have described cases of sexual exploitation in Chad; the allegations are reportedly already under investigation”, the NGO stated.
A very slow response
In mid-December 2024, it was agreed at the Swiss foreign ministry “that a meeting with MSF would take place in January”. But it was not until June and July 2025 that the department resumed discussions on how to handle the case.
+ Switzerland pledges CHF23 million more aid to war-torn Sudan
Meanwhile, dozens of allegations of abuse were brought to MSF’s attention and disciplinary measures were taken; however, the SDC was kept in the dark (see box).
It was not until February 2026 that representatives of the SDC and MSF “met to discuss protection against sexual exploitation; once again, the Confederation received no new information”.
Breach of contractual obligation to report
When the scandal broke in June 2026 following revelations by the AP news agency, the SDC “demanded documents” from MSF.
More
What is the cost for killing humanitarians?
According to the foreign ministry, MSF breached its contractual reporting obligation; mistrust of the NGO is “now immense within the Confederation”, the NZZ writes. MSF eventually acknowledged its mistakes.
The Confederation is considering the possibility of further sanctions and an external investigation. From 2027, reporting obligations will be tightened for all Swiss partner NGOs.

The movement grew into some of Serbia’s largest protests since the 2000 overthrow of strongman Slobodan Milosevic.
At the Student List headquarters, supporters hugged, cried and chanted, “Victory, victory!” Candidate Radomir Saicic, a university professor, declared: “Serbia has won as we promised. Never again a tyrant in this country,” while he urged peaceful, dignified celebrations and “serious, responsible hard work” from Monday.
Elsewhere, pro-government encampments near parliament were dismantled as riot police trucks withdrew to the sound of cheering crowds.

RFE/RL: 16 more air defense towers spotted near Putin’s Valdai residence, bringing total to about 50 — nearly half the number in Moscow and its outskirts
At least 15 new towers appeared in October within a 50-kilometer radius (31 miles) of Vladimir Putin’s residence in Valdai, likely intended to carry Pantsir or Tor surface-to-air missile systems, RFE/RL’s Russian service reported, citing satellite images it examined.
A ring of towers appeared south of the residence, facing Ukraine, according to the journalists. One tower in the “outer ring” was built as early as March 2026 on the grounds of the Khotilovo military base, which is connected to the residence by a dedicated railway line that allows travel by train.
According to an OSINT analyst who posts on X under the handle @jembobineuse, Russia now has about 177 towers equipped with short-range air defense systems. About 98 are in and around Moscow, and about 50 are near the residence in Valdai.
Russian authorities claimed that more than 90 Ukrainian drones attempted to attack Putin’s residence in Valdai in late December 2025. Ukraine denies attempting such an attack. The CIA concluded that the target of the Ukrainian drone attack in the Novgorod region was an unspecified “military facility” not located near Putin’s residence.
The first air defense system near Putin’s residence in Valdai appeared in January 2023, and a second arrived in July 2024. By April 2026, satellite images examined by RFE/RL’s Russian service showed that at least 27 air defense units already ringed the residence.

China’s H-6 bomber spotted with a new large jamming pod
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:16:59 UTC
17:16:59 KST

- A Chinese H-6KG bomber has been seen carrying a new large jamming pod resembling the RKZ930 pods used on the J-16D electronic warfare jet.
- Analyst Andreas Rupprecht reported the configuration, and China has not commented on the pod or whether it is operational.
A Chinese H-6KG bomber has been seen carrying what appears to be a new large electronic jamming pod that closely resembles the pods carried by the J-16D, the People’s Liberation Army Air Force’s dedicated electronic warfare jet, military aviation analyst Andreas Rupprecht reported on Oct. 25.
Rupprecht, who closely tracks Chinese military aircraft, said the pod looks almost identical to the RKZ930-22 or RKZ930-32 jamming pods used on the J-16D, but has a differently shaped nose section, and he did not say where or when the aircraft was photographed. China has not commented on the new configuration, and it is not known whether the pod is in operational use or still being tested.
“Apparently the H-6KG is now using a new large jammer pod … looks almost like one the J-16D pods, namely the RKZ-930-22 or -32 albeit with a different front,” wrote Andreas Rupprecht.
The H-6KG belongs to the H-6K family, the most modern version of China’s H-6 bomber, a much-modernized descendant of the Soviet Tu-16 that entered service in 2011 with new Russian D-30KP2 turbofan engines, upgraded electronics and the ability to carry long-range cruise missiles under its wings. Fitting a powerful jamming pod would let the bomber blind or confuse enemy radars on its own while it approaches a target, instead of relying entirely on escorting electronic warfare aircraft.
The RKZ930 series is a family of jamming pods developed for the J-16D, a two-seat Flanker-derived jet that China first showed publicly at the Zhuhai Airshow in September 2021 and that is often compared to the U.S. Navy’s EA-18G Growler. The J-16D has been seen carrying several versions of the pods, marked RKZ930-10, -22, -31 and -32, each with a distinct shape, which analysts believe allows them to cover different radar frequency bands, an approach similar to the U.S. Navy’s Next Generation Jammer.
This would not be the first time China has hung jamming pods on its H-6 fleet. In late 2017, Chinese state television showed PLA Navy H-6G bombers, an older variant of the aircraft, converted to carry electronic countermeasure pods under their wings after nearly a decade of modifications, and the PLA has also flown JH-7 fighter-bombers with similar pods.

Nigeria’s Ebola patient on medical evacuation flight to Switzerland, condition stable
- Nigeria’s first Ebola case in over a decade was evacuated to Switzerland. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said she was “stable, conscious, communicating”.
- Scientists will investigate how she caught the rare Bundibugyo strain. Africa CDC said there are “so many unknowns” and all countries will work together.
- The outbreak has spread to four African countries and caused nearly 10,000 cases in Congo. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for Ebola Bundibugyo.
AI generated
ABUJA – Nigeria’s Ebola patient left the country on a medical evacuation flight to Switzerland on the morning of Oct 26, the health minister said, adding that her clinical condition was much improved.
The patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is Nigeria’s first Ebola case in more than a decade.
The outbreak, which started in the Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
The possibility that the Nigerian patient became infected in Uganda, where officials say she spent a two-week holiday before returning to Abuja, has fuelled concerns about undetected transmission in a country where the outbreak had appeared to be under control.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said in a post on X that the woman was “stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results closing towards baseline” before her evacuation flight departed.
Her spouse has remained asymptomatic and left Nigeria on the same flight, he added.
The Swiss foreign ministry and Uganda’s health ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Scientists probing how patient caught rare strain
A team of leading Ebola scientists will travel to Nigeria to help investigate how the patient caught the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, Africa CDC director-general Jean Kaseya told Reuters in an interview earlier.
Switzerland said last week that she had not travelled to Congo, contradicting statements from Ugandan officials.
Her travel documents show she had not visited Congo, Kaseya said.
Finding out how she became ill matters to ensure that the outbreak, already the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, is not spreading silently in as-yet undiscovered locations, and to help trace and isolate all contacts.
‘Many unknowns’
“We have so many unknowns,” said Kaseya. “I’m bringing a group of scientists in Abuja because… we need to be led by science.”
One of the theories the scientists will investigate is a potential link between the patient in Nigeria and the first case in Kenya, reported earlier in October in a man who had travelled from Congo. On Oct 23, genomic sequencing showed that the viruses that infected the two patients were closely related.
The patient in Nigeria had been on holiday in Uganda and travelled through Entebbe Airport on Oct 3.
The patient in Kenya, who has since died, was likely in the airport at the same time, as their flights were around 40 minutes apart, although they did not depart from the same gate and it is not clear whether they had any contact, Kaseya said.
Kaseya said while genomic sequencing had shown that the viruses were similar, it did not mean that one of the patients had directly infected the other and the patient in Abuja, whose condition is improving, has said she does not remember meeting the Kenya patient.
However, he said they were not excluding any options, including that there may have been indirect contact through another person, for example.
Ebola spreads through close contact with the infected bodily fluids of a person with symptoms, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Investigation ongoing
Kaseya said all countries involved were now willing to collaborate in the investigation, after what he described as tension last week when Uganda’s government insisted the patient in Abuja had been to Congo, while the Nigerian authorities suggested she had not and was infected in Uganda, which has been Ebola-free since August.
Kaseya said the team, which will be led by the co-discoverer of Ebola, Congolese expert Jean-Jacques Muyembe, would also look at more sequencing data to work out where the Kenyan patient was infected.
The Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in Congo has now caused almost 10,000 cases and more than 4,600 deaths in Congo, and spread to three other countries – Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.
There is currently no approved vaccine or treatment for Ebola Bundibugyo.
Kenya has reported nine cases and two deaths, all linked to a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda’s Entebbe airport.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June but has not recorded any since and was declared free of the virus by the WHO in August.
The WHO’s Africa director congratulated Nigeria’s government and health workers for stabilising the patient’s condition, allowing her to be evacuated.
“The Nigerian medical team successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilized her condition,” Mohamed Janabi said on X. REUTERS

From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs — and why the connection is complicated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:13:00 UTC
17:13:00 KST

Rotten food, sex and politics: What connects them?
October 26, 2026
Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?
The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.
Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.
One explanation begins with evolution.
"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.
What are the three types of disgust?
But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:
- Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.
- Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.
- Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.
One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.
Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.
"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.
Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."
Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.
"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.
Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?
Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.
A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.
Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.
However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.
Can our bodies reveal our politics?
Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.
But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.
Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.
"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.
How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?
Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.
Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.
"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."
The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."
They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.
But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.
What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.
"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.
Can disgust actually be measured?
Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.
He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.
Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.
"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.
The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.
Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."
How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?
Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.
"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.
Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.
"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.
Does disgust influence how people vote?
The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.
"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.
Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.
"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."
Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.
He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.
"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said.

Brazil's Lula reelected president, beats former president's son
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:12:51 UTC
17:12:51 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO (AP) -- Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening U.S. influence in Latin America.
With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon-to-be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes -- 51.8% of the total vote -- over opponent Flavio Bolsonaro. The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.
Late Sunday, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, calling the move to extend voting hours unprecedented -- though both he and Lula made the request -- and asked for the election results to be annulled, saying they were impossible to accept.
Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Trump have been winning. Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-center leaders. It also positions Latin America's largest economy, with a gross domestic product (GDP) of $2.6 trillion, to remain independent of the U.S., despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.
A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with first lady Rosangela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on Sao Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.
In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red -- the color of Lula supporters -- shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.
Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.
"I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing."
Lula is set to begin his fourth non-consecutive term as president on Jan. 5, 2027.
The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favored.
In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.
The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.
Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Zanin, who made the decision, is Lula's former lawyer.
Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday night's apparent victory by Lula marked the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency.
Lula faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs while Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives.
Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.
This will likely be the last victory of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.
Rousseff was impeached for accounting maneuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.
Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.
Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.
He joins Trump and Nicaragua's President Daniel Ortega -- all aged 80 -- as the oldest presidents in the Americas.

Eric Bauza, the modern voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:08:14 UTC
17:08:14 KST

Prolific voice actor Eric Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Road Runner and Porky Pig, along with hundreds of other characters.
Emmy-award winning voice actor Eric Bauza, best known as the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, has died aged 46.
The voice actor’s death was announced by his family, who shared a statement to the actor’s Instagram account. The cause of death, hypertensive cardiovascular disease, was released by the Los Angeles county medical examiner.
“Eric Bauza, Emmy award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly. More details to come,” his family wrote.
Born in Scarborough, Toronto, in 1979, Bauza worked for Warner Bros Animation for 15 years, succeeding the legendary Mel Blanc as the voice behind some of the studio’s best-known cartoon characters.
In addition to Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, his roles included Porky Pig, Road Runner, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Marvin the Martian, and countless other classic characters.
He also had roles in The Adventures of Puss in Boots, Rise of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and his film credits included Space Jam: A New Legacy (2021) and The Super Mario Bros Movie (2023). This year, he voiced characters in Rick and Morty, Minions & Monsters, Avatar: Seven Havens, and appeared in Coyote vs Acme.
Channing Dungey, chairman of Warner Bros Television Group and US Networks, paid tribute to Bauza, saying in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter: “Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world. He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honours of his life.”
She added: “In addition to his incredible talent, Eric was a treasured part of our animation family. Our hearts go out to his loved ones.”

EU-Inc: is the EU’s startup booster losing steam? Take our poll.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:07:54 UTC
17:07:54 KST

With EU-Inc, the EU wanted to help European businesses and startups scale across the entire single market. But loopholes and concerns over worker’s rights keep stalling the initiative.
EU-Inc wants to create one single, fully digital framework that lets startups bypass the red tape of 27 different legal systems and operate seamlessly across the entire single market. By introducing this unified "28th regime," the EU wanted to stop the flight of top tech talent and venture capital to more integrated markets like the US.
But the initiative has run into some roadblocks. Member states are protecting their sovereign tax laws and corporate registration systems, while trade unions are protesting to warn that a unified corporate framework could allow companies to bypass national labour protections and weaken collective bargaining rights.
Because of these issues, the initiative is losing steam and facing a severe backlash from the very tech founders and investors it was designed to help.
In October 2026, the grassroots EU-INC campaign (backed by over 26.000 startup leaders from companies like Stripe and Klarna) warned that months of closed-door negotiations have heavily watered down the proposal. The tech community cautions that crucial features, such as a unified employee stock option framework and a single tax regime, are being stripped away. They warn that Europe risks creating a hollow, "useless" compromise that offers fast online setup but still leaves businesses fragmented.
To break the deadlock and prevent the law from being permanently diluted, European Council President António Costa announced a special EU leaders' summit for February 2027 dedicated specifically to European competitiveness and driving the legislation forward.
Can EU-Inc solve its loopholes? Would this fix the fragmented EU startup ecosystem? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across XL's EU-wide coverage, including videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

The fire has been contained to an area of 1,500 square meters (about 16,000 square feet), the regional branch of the Emergency Situations Ministry said, without specifying what was inside the tank cars.
Residents of nearby homes were advised to stay indoors and, if that was not possible, to wear masks and respirators. The Yekaterinburg-based news outlet E1 reports that residents were also asked not to open their windows, to do wet cleaning more often, drink more fluids, and rinse their eyes, nose, and throat.
The regional office of Rospotrebnadzor said it would conduct an air quality inspection for “pollutants characteristic of this type of fire.”
The cause of the derailment remains under investigation. No official explanation for what happened had been offered as of publication.

Unknown

Israeli opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman on Monday demanded a criminal investigation into Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on suspicion of treason, accusing him of attempting to drag Israel into a war with Iran to avoid defeat in Tuesday’s general elections.
Lieberman, leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, submitted a formal request to Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported.
In his letter, Lieberman said that Netanyahu had been pressuring senior security officials over the past month to take steps that could trigger a military confrontation with Iran.
“Over the past month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pressuring the heads of the security establishment to take steps that could lead to a miscalculation with Iran,” Lieberman wrote.
He accused Netanyahu of attempting to involve Israel in another war because of concerns about losing the elections.
“Attempting to drag the State of Israel into war on the eve of elections, along with the willingness to sacrifice IDF (Israeli army) soldiers solely out of fear of electoral defeat, constitutes treason against the state, its security and IDF soldiers,” he said.
“I demand the immediate opening of a criminal investigation against Benjamin Netanyahu on suspicion of treason,” he added.
Earlier Monday, Lieberman made similar accusations during an interview with Israeli radio station 103FM, according to Israeli newspaper Maariv.
“Netanyahu is clearly betraying the state when he wants to drag us into war,” Lieberman said, accusing the premier of being willing to sacrifice soldiers’ lives because of fears of electoral defeat.
Political-military tensions
The opposition leader also alleged unprecedented tensions between Israel’s political and military leadership.
“Never has there been such a strained relationship between the military and political leadership as there is today,” he said, attributing the situation to Netanyahu’s efforts to provoke a miscalculation with Iran.
Lieberman stressed that any military action potentially leading to war or a large-scale confrontation required government deliberation and approval under Israeli law.
He also accused Netanyahu of attempting to undermine the legitimacy of the Central Elections Committee and the election results, warning that such efforts could trigger serious internal confrontation.
“We are simultaneously seeing an intensified effort by Netanyahu to delegitimise the Central Elections Committee and the election results, even at the cost of a severe internal confrontation, civil war and the disintegration of the state,” he said.
Lieberman further claimed that Netanyahu was aware of the possibility of losing the elections and was therefore seeking to escalate tensions with Iran.
“Even Netanyahu knows he is going to lose. That is why all his hysteria and his attempt to drag us into war,” he said.
There was no immediate response from Netanyahu to Lieberman’s accusations.
Election tensions
The accusations come ahead of Israel’s general elections on Tuesday, amid heightened tensions with Iran.
Netanyahu claimed Sunday that Israeli intelligence indicated Iran and its regional allies could launch attacks aimed at disrupting the elections.
He warned Tehran against such actions, threatening a severe military response.
On October 13, Lieberman accused Netanyahu of preparing possible military offensive against Iran, Hamas or Hezbollah to remain in power, claiming that the prime minister was motivated by political survival rather than security considerations.
Netanyahu also unveiled a new national security doctrine on October 18, identifying the overthrow of Iran’s government as a strategic objective and emphasising preemptive military operations.
The latest accusations come amid continuing tensions between Israel and Iran following their military confrontation earlier this year.
