Simulated North Korean attack pierces South’s lines without nukes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:04:23 UTC
17:04:23 KST

- A computer simulation during this summer’s South Korea-U.S. exercise reportedly ended with North Korean troops breaking through and advancing to Seoul’s outskirts.
- North Korea has since deployed a self-propelled howitzer in plain view near the border, while South Korea’s opposition accuses the government of weakness.
A computer simulation run by South Korean and U.S. forces during this summer’s Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise ended with North Korean troops breaking through allied defensive lines and advancing to the outskirts of Seoul, South Korea’s Chosun Ilbo newspaper said, a result that has deepened a dispute over when Seoul should take wartime command of its own forces from the United States.
The breakthrough came in a conventional scenario that did not assume North Korean use of nuclear weapons, the newspaper said in its original Oct. 15 report.
The newspaper said it was not clear why the simulation turned out that way, but cited views inside the South Korean military that the problem lay either in how the combined forces were commanded or in recent changes to North Korea’s military capabilities. The exercise was overseen by the commander of the Combined Forces Command, while the South Korean Army’s four-star Ground Operations Commander played a leading role as commander of the combined ground forces, a setup widely seen as rehearsal for the day South Korea commands U.S. troops in wartime after the transfer of operational control.
This year’s exercise was already shorter than planned, as the allies cut Ulchi Freedom Shield to Aug. 17-21, six days ahead of schedule, after President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back the drills, and the second phase, a simulated counteroffensive against North Korea, was canceled outright even though the exercise was meant to help verify Seoul’s readiness to lead the combined command.
On Oct. 14, U.S. Forces Korea commander Gen. Xavier Brunson told a seminar in Washington that the conditions for the transfer had changed, citing North Korea’s recent missile launches, and that the allies now had new standards to meet because they had revised their plans, The Korea Times reported. South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul responded that the three core conditions remained unchanged, though assessments of whether they had been met could differ, and the government of President Lee Jae-myung has repeatedly said it intends to complete the transfer within his term. The Chosun Ilbo noted that South Korea still lacks the ability to track North Korea’s mobile missile launchers in real time without U.S. satellites and reconnaissance aircraft, a gap that would undermine its “Kill Chain” plan to strike missiles before launch.
Tensions along the border have risen as well. On Oct. 25, photos taken from the Aegibong observatory in Gimpo, about 1.5 km (0.9 mile) from North Korean territory, showed what appeared to be a North Korean 122 mm self-propelled howitzer deployed in the open on the coast of Kaepung County in North Hwanghae Province with its barrel facing south, South Korean outlet Aju News reported, citing Yonhap News Agency. The armor carried a propaganda slogan calling for the destruction of the “U.S. imperialist aggressors,” and several North Korean soldiers were seen raising and lowering red flags in what looked like training. The 122 mm guns, deployed in large numbers along the front, have a range of 15 to 24 km (9 to 15 miles), and analysts called the exposed position unusual because artillery is normally hidden behind terrain to avoid detection and counterfire. The deployment followed warnings by Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, that Pyongyang would reinforce “tactical strike means” along the border.
The border standoff began with a landmine blast on Sept. 21, when three South Korean Army officers from the 25th Infantry Division were wounded while clearing a patrol route inside the Demilitarized Zone, and a battalion commander lost his foot in a second explosion as he tried to rescue an injured sergeant. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff concluded on Oct. 5 that the explosions were caused by North Korean plastic anti-personnel mines buried about 10 meters (33 feet) south of the Military Demarcation Line, and the United Nations Command found that the mines had been placed deliberately within the past year, in violation of the armistice. Kim Yo Jong dismissed the findings as staged, and the Chosun Ilbo criticized the military for what it described as a slow and confused response to the mine-laying.
The two Koreas are now also locked in a dispute over propaganda loudspeakers. Kim Yo Jong warned on Oct. 19, 21 and 22 that North Korea would switch on loudspeakers aimed at the South along the entire border within days, and the South Korean Defense Ministry said it would not rule anything out, with spokesperson Jeong Bit-na saying Seoul should naturally take proportionate measures if the North acts but that no decision had been made, Money Today reported. The issue is politically sensitive because the Lee government halted its own broadcasts in June 2025 and removed the speakers, and both Kang and Joint Chiefs Chairman Jin Yeong-seung have publicly questioned how effective the broadcasts are.
The conservative opposition People Power Party has seized on the mine blast and the loudspeaker dispute to accuse the government of weakness toward Pyongyang. Floor leader Jung Jeom-sik said the military was still keeping a “low posture” toward North Korea and demanded that the government immediately reinstall the speakers and resume broadcasts, as Seoul did after the 2015 wooden-box mine attack, South Korean outlet Dailian reported. Party officials have described the government’s North Korea policy as appeasement and “submission” to Pyongyang and stayed away from the Oct. 1 Armed Forces Day ceremony in protest, while the ruling Democratic Party has joined in condemning the North but has backed a more measured response.

At Ipswich, where he was a rare bright spot with 12 goals in the relegation season of 2024-25, Delap was booed on every touch. The jeers got louder when each of his four attempts on goal missed their target. Only three of 18 Premier League shots in a Forest shirt have been on target. The raw materials that Chelsea moved for in summer 2025 remain present, the physical prowess and ability to find promising positions. The finishing touches are, at present, lacking, when Forest need someone to start scoring. Failing to take their chances at Portman Road left Forest in the relegation zone, endangering Oliver Glasner, when the ownership is trigger-happy with managers. Chris Wood, previously Forest’s talisman, came on in the 89th minute for Delap, but has been no super-sub so far, without a goal or assist from seven cameo league appearances. JB

Exploitation and misinformation hinder DRC Ebola response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Exploitation and misinformation hinder DRC Ebola response
Ebola is spreading through the rainforests and mining camps in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), fuelling one of the country’s most devastating epidemics. A doctor with the Swiss NGO Medair explains why the fight to contain the epidemic has so far failed.
It’s been five months since authorities in the DRC officially confirmed the latest Ebola epidemic, the seventeenth in the country’s history and one of the deadliest to date.
“You have to grasp the sheer scale of the affected area,” says Pierre-Oliver Ngadjole, a doctor and nutritionist with the Swiss aid organisation Medair. “The epidemic has spread across an area larger than Switzerland.”
The National Institute of Public Health has recorded more than 9,000 confirmed cases and over 4,300 deaths. In the eastern provinces of Ituri – the epicentre – as well as North Kivu and Haut-Uélé, the virus continues to spread unchecked among the population.
Seven river-crossings to the nearest hospital
At the Ebola treatment centre of Katwa in Butembo, the figures are just as grim. “Over 70 of the 252 patients admitted have died so far,” says Ngadjole.
For Ngadjole, the main reason for the high death toll is not the aggressiveness of the virus, but delays in treatment. Patients simply arrive at hospitals too late.
The profile of those infected also reflects the region’s social structure: the 15- to 49-year-old age group is the hardest hit, which can be put down to work in the mining camps. Young children are also quickly infected within their families.
Getting to a treatment centre is often an odyssey. “The roads are in a terrible state. During the rainy season, not even motorbikes can get through,” says Ngadjole. Some patients have to travel for days and cross several rivers to reach a hospital. With little transport, families often resort to home remedies, which means they lose precious time. The delays can be fatal.
The devastating effect of myths
At the start of the epidemic, geographical isolation was compounded by a fatal communication failure that delayed treatment. Rumours spread that there was neither a vaccine nor a cure for the current strain of the virus.
“This message seriously undermined the population’s willingness to seek treatment,” Ngadjole explains.
It is true that currently no approved vaccine is available for the Bundibugyo strain that caused this epidemic. However, early intensive care, including intravenous fluids containing electrolytes, can dramatically improve a patient’s chances of survival. Isolation in hospital also helps to break the chain of transmission.
Another compounding factor is the dire security situation in the country. People infected with Ebola fear being attacked by armed militias on their way to hospital. Religious communities also urge patients to pray rather than seek medical help. Aid organisations such as Medair are therefore increasingly involving survivors to help build trust. “We let survivors tell their stories,” says Ngadjole.
About the organisation: MedairExternal link is an international emergency relief organisation based in the Swiss canton of Vaud. It provides medical and infrastructure support in crisis zones. Founded in 1989 by two medical doctors and other volunteers, the organisation now has an annual operating income of around $91.6 million (CHF75.6 million) and employs more than 1,500 people worldwide. In Switzerland, it receives financial support from the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), among others. According to its 2025 annual report, other donors include the EU’s humanitarian aid office (ECHO) and USAID. Congolese doctor Pierre-Olivier Ngadjole works for Medair on the ground.
The challenge of contact tracing
Paris-based infectious disease specialist Xavier Lescure believes that contact tracing is another obstacle to containing the epidemic.
“We have to trace every link in the chain of transmission,” says Lescure, who heads France’s coordination mission for epidemic risks and co-coordinates international research networks of the World Health Organization (WHO). Currently, contact tracing in the DRC reaches about 75% of all contacts.
“Given the circumstances, this is remarkable, but it is simply not enough to put out the fire – we would need more than 95%,” Lescure tells Swissinfo. He also blames the information crisis for the dire situation in the DRC. He calls it an “epidemic of post-truth” in which unfounded myths and mistrust undermine public health measures.
Hence, hope lies in medical research. According to Lescure, two approaches are being pursued. One involves testing vaccines specifically developed against the Bundibugyo strain, while the other involves using the existing rVSV vaccine developed against the Zaire strain.
“Early scientific evidence points to possible cross-immunity. If this vaccine proved even partially effective and prevented severe cases, we would have an immediate weapon to fight the epidemic,” Lescure says.
>>For the health authorities, containing the outbreak of Ebola is a regional priority:
More
Ebola vaccine: ‘In an outbreak situation we’re racing against time’
Raw materials, uprooting and the trauma of war
It’s no surprise that the epidemic is hitting the mining camps in Ituri particularly hard. Hundreds of thousands of people work in informal mines in appalling hygienic conditions. Many of these sites lie deep in the rainforest, where workers have little choice but to rely on wild animals for food – known as bush meat, the primary source of virus transmission. The crammed conditions in the mines and camps for internally displaced persons provide ideal conditions for the virus to spread.
And then there are the psychological scars. The virus is hitting people who have endured three decades of war. “We deal with families who are deeply traumatised because their relatives were murdered while fleeing,” Ngadjole tells Swissinfo from Bunia.
An Ebola death is doubly devastating for families already struggling to survive. Traditional funeral rites are banned because of the risk of infection. The deceased must be buried immediately under strict safety precautions, while all their belongings, including clothes, mattresses and rubbish, must also be burnt. For families already living in extreme poverty, this means losing the last of their possessions. For this reason, Medair also provides material assistance to support them.
The price of digital consumption
For Ngadjole, the fight against Ebola must not end with emergency medical aid. “We need structural change across the entire production chain,” he says, pointing to the dismal hygienic conditions in the mining camps.
The outbreak, says Lescure, is also a reflection of our global consumption culture. “The minerals mined in the DRC are used in our smartphones, computers and numerous other everyday devices. Their extraction comes at a heavy cost: the overexploitation of natural resources, the destruction of ecosystems, geopolitical tensions and the suffering of local communities.”
Epidemics, he says, are never merely a natural phenomenon but also a reflection of economic and social choices: “Our consumption habits have global consequences.”
>>An analysis of the conflict minerals situation in DRC:
More
UN experts warn Congo’s conflict minerals slipping into global market
Switzerland’s response to Ebola in the DRC
In 2026, Switzerland increasedExternal link its support for the fight against Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to an annual amount of CHF4.6 million ($5.6 million). The funding is going primarily to the World Health Organization (WHO), the coordination of emergency medical teams, expanded laboratory capacity and epidemiological surveillance.
According to the foreign ministry, Switzerland also works closely with the DRC’s health authorities as well as with international partner organisations.
Switzerland support projects run by aid organisations such as Medair in the hardest hit provinces of Ituri and North Kivu.
Swiss institutions also cooperate with Congolese partners to monitor the virus’ genome. Basel-based pharmaceutical company Roche is providing lab equipment and testing methods to detect the Bundibugyo Ebola virus in collaboration with the Congolese National Institute of Public Health (INSP).
Donations from Switzerland also help to fund the fight against Ebola. In May 2026, Swiss SolidarityExternal link allocated CHF 1.2 million ($1.45 million) from its emergency relief fund.

Israelis put voting first as overseas travel declines ahead of election, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:56:52 UTC
16:56:52 KST

Israelis are postponing vacations and business trips, while others are returning from abroad to vote in Tuesday's Knesset elections, Channel 13 reported Sunday, citing Ben-Gurion Airport data that shows a significant shift in passenger traffic.
The figures indicate that far fewer Israelis are leaving the country ahead of the October 27 election than in corresponding periods in previous years, while incoming passengers increasingly outnumber those departing.
A comparison of airport traffic between October 17 and 27 in 2022, 2025, and 2026 points to a decline in outbound travel, suggesting that many Israelis consider the upcoming election important enough to change their travel plans.
According to the Channel 13 report, approximately 245,000 passengers were recorded as departing Israel during the period under examination in 2026, compared with 270,000 in 2025, following the end of the war, and 323,000 in 2022, when Israel last held a general election.
The decline is particularly notable because travelers now have access to more aircraft and flights than in previous years.
Incoming passenger traffic presents a different picture. Although no large-scale airlift of special flights was organized to bring voters back to Israel, and arrivals have largely relied on existing aviation infrastructure, the number of passengers entering the country has significantly exceeded departures.
According to the figures cited by Channel 13, the difference between incoming and outgoing passengers has surpassed 90,000 in 2026, compared with a gap of approximately 77,000 during the corresponding period in 2025.
Entering passengers could be equivalent to two Knesset seats in election
The growing difference could carry political significance in an election where relatively small changes in voter turnout may affect the distribution of Knesset seats.
Channel 13 estimated that 90,000 people would be equivalent to approximately two Knesset seats if they were eligible voters who cast valid ballots.
However, the passenger figures do not establish how many people returned specifically to vote. They also include children and foreign nationals ineligible to participate in Israeli elections.
Israel's electoral threshold is 3.25% of valid votes, so small shifts in turnout could affect whether parties close to the threshold secure representation in the next Knesset.
The increased interest in returning to Israel the vote aligns with a recent Fly&Vote survey, which estimated that about 67,000 Israelis living abroad intended to travel to Israel to vote. The estimate drew on registration data and a voluntary survey, not confirmed arrivals.
Unlike in many other countries, most Israeli citizens living abroad cannot vote remotely and must return to Israel to cast their ballots. The Fly&Vote initiative, run by the AID Coalition, has tried to help overseas Israelis with the process, but its activities were restricted after legal proceedings initiated by Likud.
Ben-Gurion's grandson returns from US to cast ballot
Among those traveling to Israel specifically to vote is Alon Ben-Gurion, grandson of Israel's first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion.
Ben-Gurion arrived in Israel from the United States with his family and traveled to Tiberias to vote, according to Channel 13.
His arrival illustrates the efforts some Israelis living overseas are making to participate in the election.
Interest in traveling to Israel for the vote had already been evident in August, when organizers arranged dedicated flights from New York and Lisbon to accommodate demand among overseas Israelis.
Under Israel's electoral system, the 120 Knesset seats are distributed proportionally among parties that cross the electoral threshold. Consequently, additional votes from returning Israelis could influence the final seat distribution, though the impact will depend on how those votes are divided among parties.

Yemen’s foreign minister sets out five conditions for peace, calls for Houthi disarmament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:56:18 UTC
16:56:18 KST

Yemen’s Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba outlined five conditions for peace, saying the Houthi militia must surrender their weapons and join the political process.
Speaking to Anadolu during an official visit to Türkiye, al-Zouba said a settlement also requires rebuilding state institutions, ensuring the group can no longer carry out what she described as terrorism in Yemen or the region, and implementing agreed frameworks for peace.
Those frameworks include UN Security Council Resolution 2216, the outcomes of Yemen’s National Dialogue Conference and the Gulf Cooperation Council initiative, she said.
Resolution 2216 calls on the Houthis to withdraw from areas they seized, including Sanaa, hand over weapons taken from military and security institutions, and facilitate humanitarian access.
Peace talks used to rearm
Al-Zouba accused the Houthi militia of exploiting successive rounds of peace talks to build up their arsenal. “We went through the peace process repeatedly, moving from one round of negotiations to another,” she said.
She argued that the government and international community had long pursued negotiations in the belief that a peaceful settlement was possible, but the Houthis had used those efforts to acquire weapons and expand their military capabilities.
She said she believed neighbouring countries and international partners increasingly recognised that the group “was not a genuine partner for peace.”
The top diplomat said Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” launched by Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi on Oct. 5, aimed to end Houthi control, restore state authority and return Yemen’s sovereign decisions to the government.
Fighting has intensified in Yemen since July in the sharpest escalation since the relative calm brought by a UN-brokered truce in April 2022.
Iranian support
Al-Zouba accused the Houthis of seeking to turn Yemen into a base for attacks on neighbouring countries, citing their strikes on Saudi Arabia and threats to shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab Strait.
She described the group as a threat to regional and international security and accused it of cooperating with armed groups in the Horn of Africa.
Iranian expertise had helped the Houthis develop their arsenal since seizing Sanaa in 2014, including the ability to manufacture some weapons components and assemble weapons inside Yemen, she said.
Al-Zouba also said she believed the group was beginning to develop the ability to train others, including Somalia’s Al Shabab, to use certain equipment.
“The Houthis are using the power they have acquired through Yemen’s resources against Yemenis, neighbouring countries and the world,” she said.
Siege restricts supplies to Taiz
Al-Zouba said continued Houthi shelling and a partial siege were restricting access to essential supplies in southwestern Taiz province, home to roughly 4 million people.
Taiz has resisted years of Houthi attempts to bring it under their control, she said, but residents continued to face barriers to obtaining water, food, medicine and fuel.
The province has been a major front in the latest fighting. Government forces and their allies have announced gains near the strategic Bab al Mandab Strait and in Dhubab district, while Houthi advances in rural areas have tightened pressure on the city.
Taiz connects northern and southern Yemen and includes a strategically important stretch of Red Sea coastline, making it vital to transport and supply routes.
Türkiye’s regional role
Al-Zouba praised Türkiye’s political and diplomatic initiatives, describing Ankara’s role in regional security as “pivotal and strategic.”
She said the two countries shared longstanding historic ties and welcomed Türkiye’s efforts to promote stability.
“We believe Türkiye has a pivotal and strategic role in maintaining the region’s security and stability,” she said.

Bulgaria heads to presidential runoff after close vote
SOFIA, Oct 26 - Bulgaria will head to a runoff vote on November 1 after a tight race between the two leading presidential candidates failed to produce an outright winner in Sunday's elections, which garnered record-low participation, official results showed.
With 95% of the votes counted, incumbent Iliana Iotova, 61, attracted 34.6% against 32% for ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, falling short of the 50% threshold for the largely ceremonial role in a race of 27 candidates.
Sunday's vote took on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast that likely killed some two dozen international seafarers. However, only about 22% of the eligible voters showed up to cast their ballot, according to polling agencies.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
BOTH CANDIDATES CONDEMN DRONE STRIKES
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president.
"I want to share a certain worry and tell Bulgarians that it is an illusion if they think we can change something in this country without (them) voting," Iotova said after polls closed at 8 p.m.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier. REUTERS

[FEATURED]
A NEW GREEN DISTRICT FOR TBILISI
Italian architecture studio Stefano Boeri Architetti has won an international competition to transform a former Soviet-era locomotive factory in Tbilisi, Georgia, into a new residential neighborhood. Named Loco Park, the masterplan reimagines a 73,600-square-meter industrial site as a network of residential buildings, public parks, pedestrian routes, and community facilities. Developed for LOCO Alliance, the proposal seeks to reconnect the former factory grounds with the surrounding city while preserving elements of their industrial identity.
The project introduces nine buildings arranged across a continuous landscape of public and semi-public spaces. Rather than creating an enclosed residential development, the masterplan establishes pedestrian connections with neighboring districts through a series of green areas, shared gardens, and a linear boulevard. A dedicated sports forest adds recreational facilities to the landscape, while the buildings are conceived as individual architectural volumes connected by a common network of open spaces.
NINE RESIDENTIAL BUILDINGS REINTERPRET TBILISI’S INDUSTRIAL HERITAGE
The architectural approach developed by Stefano Boeri Architetti draws on the history of the former locomotive factory, translating its industrial character into contemporary residential structures. Each of the nine buildings features a distinct form, with ground floors accommodating shops, cafés, workshops, and shared services that encourage activity at street level. Above, apartments of different sizes are designed to accommodate varying residential needs, combining private living spaces with communal areas accessible to residents.
The buildings’ rooflines take inspiration from the silhouettes of the factories and workshops that once occupied the site. Their varied geometries introduce a new skyline while accommodating greenhouses, terraces, loft apartments, photovoltaic systems, and shared outdoor spaces. According to the architects, these configurations are also intended to optimize natural lighting, ventilation, and solar exposure. Stefano Boeri describes the buildings as ‘islands in an urban archipelago,’ connected by tree-lined pedestrian spaces open to the wider city.
BRICK FACADES DRAW FROM TBILISI’S ARCHITECTURAL COLOR PALETTE
Materiality plays a central role in connecting the development to its urban context. Stefano Boeri Architetti carried out a photographic color study of Tbilisi’s built environment, identifying a palette of blue-grey, terracotta, green, taupe, and mineral white. These tones inform the brick facades, which combine different colors, textures, and laying patterns to give each building an individual identity. The choice of brick also references both the factory’s industrial past and the city’s local construction traditions.
With a planned gross floor area of 120,000 square meters, Loco Park brings together residential, recreational, and public functions within a single urban redevelopment. The proposal places particular emphasis on the relationship between architecture and landscape, using interconnected green spaces to integrate the former industrial grounds into Tbilisi’s everyday life. Currently in development following the competition win, the project outlines a new use for a site previously dedicated to locomotive production, replacing its industrial function with housing and shared urban infrastructure.
project info:
name: Loco Park
architect: Stefano Boeri Architetti | @stefanoboeriarchitetti
location: Tbilisi, Georgia

Shale oil to replace gas for winter heating, but bills still may not fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:54:00 UTC
16:54:00 KST

Shale oil to replace gas for winter heating, but bills still may not fall
Heat producers may turn to shale oil in severe winter cold if gas is scarce or too expensive, but the cheaper fuel may not mean major savings for household consumers.
The Environmental Board has granted temporary exemptions to two heat producers — Enefit Power in Narva and Utilitas in Tallinn — allowing them to replace natural gas with shale oil from November 1 this year to April 30, 2027. Shale oil is cheaper, but consumers will also bear the costs of procurement, transportation and handling.
Winter district heating prices are forecast to stay high, with natural gas prices elevated on the global market and other fuels such as wood chips also having risen in price.
Estonia wants to keep its oil-shale sector alive, but the EU's emissions trading rules are set to cut free allowances and hike the cost of polluting.
Narva was last heated with shale oil four years ago, when gas prices were extremely high. Enefit Power was then allowed to use it for the whole heating season. Producers want to ensure continuity of district heating and reduce the risk of gas supply disruption. Shale oil is cheaper than gas but causes more air pollution, and the permit does not necessarily mean it will be burned. The board is attaching conditions because the exemptions must be precisely regulated.
Enefit may burn 23,000 tons of shale oil over the winter; Utilitas 20,000 tons. Erik Kosenkranius, the board's deputy director general for environmental use, said the board assesses the technology while the Ministry of Climate assesses the gas market. Producers must monitor quantities and operating hours, notify the board when they start and stop, and carry out additional checks and sampling. "We want to know very precisely how emissions change," he said. "They must comply with existing limit values for air quality outside the production site."
In October the Competition Authority approved maximum district heating prices of €84/MWh in Tallinn and €137.69/MWh in Narva. Shale oil could reduce prices, but compliance costs, production, procurement, transport, handling and environmental charges could cancel the savings. Enefit board chairman Raine Pajo said the cogeneration plant offers cheaper heat — "€74/MWh plus VAT" — and would be used when prices are higher, reducing oil volumes. "When prices are low, the unit cannot be started, cogeneration is not possible and we cannot use oil shale and wood chips. In that case, there must be a backup plan that provides consumers with heat at a reasonable price."
Utilitas board chairman Robert Kitt said gas prices have doubled in a year, creating both price risk and supply risk. "The permit is very recent, and we are still clarifying the details with the Environmental Board, including what quantities must be nominated in advance," he said. "We will use it as little as possible, but as much as necessary." Shale oil and gas cannot be burned together, and three of Utilitas's four Mustamäe boilers are covered by the permit, two of which may not run simultaneously.
VKG has proposed a permanent right to switch to shale oil when gas is expensive. Technical director Raivo Attikas said it is strange that domestic fuel is available but producers must apply for a permit each time prices rise. "Currently, we sell five percent of our oil on the domestic market, while 95 percent is exported, where it is used mainly as marine fuel," he said. "Because our shale oil has a low sulfur content, it is a highly valued product."
Prices of almost all heating types are rising this winter. Natural gas has more than doubled in a year, wood chips are dearer, and costs at the Iru power station just outside Tallinn are up. Utilitas is pinning hopes on a Paljassaare heat pump plant and shale oil to curb further increases.
District heating involves hot water piped in to apartment blocks in larger settlements, for heating purposes only. Heating season is taken to run October to March inclusive.

Bulgaria failed to elect a president - a second round is expected
Kyiv • UNN
Incumbent President Iliana Iotova received 34.6% of the vote, while Andrey Gyurov received 32%. The second round of the election is likely to take place on November 1.
Bulgaria failed to elect a president in the first round. The second round is expected on November 1. UNN reports this, citing DW.
Details
In Bulgaria's presidential election on October 25, none of the candidates secured the required absolute majority of votes in the first round. According to the country's Central Election Commission, after 95.3% of the ballots had been processed, the incumbent head of state, Illyana Yotova, had 34.6% of the vote, while the pro-Western former prime minister Andriy Gyurov came second with 32%.
Voter turnout was significantly below the required level of over 50% — only 22.2%. The second round will likely take place on November 1.
Despite the president's formally limited powers in Bulgaria, the politician holding this office represents the country on the international stage (with some exceptions), serves as supreme commander-in-chief, signs decrees appointing the prosecutor general and the heads of the higher courts, appoints an acting prime minister (from a constitutionally defined closed circle of individuals), and has the right to approve laws.

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign-made equipment used by Russian ballistic missile manufacturers
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 30 items of foreign-made technological equipment used by Russian firms involved in the production of ballistic missiles and their components.
Source: War&Sanctions portal
Quote from the DIU: "Today we are publishing [details of] 30 items of technological equipment manufactured in China, Germany, Taiwan, the US, Türkiye, Switzerland and Italy which are used by Russian factories producing ballistic missiles and their components, including altimeters, aerodynamic rudders, gyroscopes, and so on."
DIU noted an increase in the number of Chinese machine tools and machining centres, particularly five-axis ones.
Quote: "It is important to note that Chinese machine tools use European, Japanese and Taiwanese components – CNC systems, servo drives, high-precision spindles and bearings, measuring and rotary systems, linear guides, thermal stabilisation and machining process control devices, etc."
Details: The list includes the GX-650 five-axis universal machining centre made by the Chinese manufacturer Hyper Machine Tool, which is used by the Votkinsk Plant, a manufacturer of 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and the missile body of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile.
The list also includes turning and milling machining centres by the Chinese manufacturer Shtral, which are used in the production processes at PEMZ Molot JSC. The company manufactures electronic equipment units for Iskander-M missiles.
In addition, measuring equipment from the German firm Rohde & Schwarz has been installed at UPKB Detal, a company that manufactures altimeters for Zircon missiles.
DIU stressed the need to tighten control over the end users of the equipment, in particular by conducting on-site inspections at the locations where it is installed. The intelligence agency also urged that the supply of spare parts, software, consumables and maintenance be monitored.
In particular, they propose checking distributors and intermediaries, investigating cases of equipment that ends up in the Russian defence industry, and restricting the supply of CNC systems and other components to Chinese manufacturers whose products are used by Russian defence firms.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that DIU had released data on 13 items of foreign technological equipment used to produce Kometa navigation modules for Russian missiles and drones.
- DIU has also revealed details of the components of the Russian Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile and the companies involved in its production.

Sexy wicker and an Agatha Christie exhibition: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:51:34 UTC
16:51:34 KST

Olivia Coleman gets freaky with a wicker husband on the big screen, while London's British Library celebrates the life and works of legendary crime novelist Agatha Christie. Here's what to look out for this week.
Animatronic gorillas, an author's mysterious disappearance, and husbands made out of wicker? No, these aren't fragments from a fever dream, but indeed a taster of what's coming up this week.
The British Library is about to open a major exhibition on the life and works of crime novelist Agatha Christie, while Turin Art Week is launching an exhibition all about the visual manifestations ofQuantum theory (think infinity rooms and Kubrick).
Then there's Wicker, a strange, surreal and saucy movies about a woman that marries a man made from, well, wicker. Call her a basket case all you want, but it surely beats those terrifying humanoid robot partners.
And speaking of terrifying, we can't forget Halloween. If you're not too busy dressing up, watching one of these movies, or just hiding in bed waiting for it to be over, Apple TV+'s new serial killer thriller Nocturne perfectly fits the mood.
And if you think all of that sounds perfect, wait until you hear the title of Queens of the Stone Age's new album...
Exhibitions
Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery
When: 30 October 2026 - 20 June 2027
Where: The British Library (London, United Kingdom)
It's 50 years since the Queen of Crime passed away, and to mark the occasion, London's British Library is hosting a new major exhibition. Featuring everything from early manuscripts to private letters and personal objects, it's every wannabe Poirot's dream — filled with puzzle pieces from Christie's singular life and career. Highlights include the original 1937 Remington typewriter that Christie reportedly used to write her best-selling novel, And Then There Were None, along with life-sized replicas of an Orient Express carriage. Not only is it educational, it's also a lot of fun, with easter eggs scattered among the displays. Find out more here.
Turin Art Week: 'The Quantum Effect’
When: 31 October 2026 - 25 February 2027
Where: OGR Torino (Turin, Italy)
Quantum theory refers to the atomic and subatomic foundations of matter and energy. It's a head-spinning concept that has not only aided our understanding of the universe, but also permeated the stories we tell about it — through art, pop culture and cinema. A new group exhibition explores this visual impact as part of Turin Art Week, using the black monolith from Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey as a central reference point. Curated by art critic Daniel Birnbaum and filmmaker Jacqui Davies, it investigates concepts such as parallel universes, teleportation and dark matter through the works including one of Yayoi Kusama's infinity rooms and an animatronic gorilla by British artist Ryan Gander.
Bonus highlight: A fascinating exploration of cosmic imagination, 'Night Maps' is a new exhibition at London's Warburg Institute that charts humanity's historical depictions of the night skies. Entry is free and it's open now until 17 April.
Movies
Wicker
Where: Cinemas
When: 30 October
Between all the dating app apathy and existential dread, times are tough for romantics. It makes you wonder: wouldn't it just be easier to make a partner out of wicker?
This is the strangely alluring plot of Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson's new film, which sees a frustrated medieval fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) commission a basket weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make the man of her dreams (Alexander Skarsgård — who is fast becoming this generation's James Spader). Based on a short story by Ursula Wills, it's a darkly comic folk tale that explores female desire while critiquing gender norms and the transactional nature of marriage.
Bonus highlights: Robert Pattinson stars in Lance Oppenheim's Primetime, which is released at UK cinemas on 30 October. For Friends fans, new documentary The One About Matthew Perry is released on Netflix on the 27 October.
TV series
Nocturne
Where: Prime Video
When: 30 October
Stephen Graham plays as serial killer Jurek Walter in Apple TV+'s new crime thriller series, Nocturne. Based on Lars Kepler's novels The Sandman and Lazarus, it follows a former homicide detective (Liev Schreiber) and FBI agent (Zazie Beetz) as they attempt to track down a missing child and decipher clues from Walter, who, despite being locked away in a high-security prison, appears to still be puppeteering outside horrors. It's a compelling procedural drama that perfectly fits the mood of the darkened evenings, but the biggest sell is always Graham — anything he's in is usually guaranteed to be gritty and good.
Bonus highlight: Michael C. Hall returns for Dexter: Resurrection season 2, alongside Brian Cox as the New York Ripper. Out on Paramount+ on 30 October.
Music
Queens of the Stone Age: Perfecth
When: 30 October
Where the Goth Girls At? California rockers Queens of the Stone Age want to know in their 2000s-tinged upcoming 9th studio album, 'Perfecth'. According to frontman Josh Homme, the title was coined as a more honest spelling of "perfect" — a concept he does not believe exists. While we can't see it catching on, it does give a sense of the album's overall mood: a raw, vulnerable and fragmented sound that reflects on human connection, health and emotional set-backs. It's Homme's way of coming to terms with the past and assembling new perspectives. As he told Pitchfork: "Nothing in this world is perfect, but everything seems to be 'perfecth'".
Bonus highlight: American industrial metal band Ministry are releasing their 17th (and final ever) studio album 'Hate to Go' on 30 October.

Pomors boat museum opens on island in Northern Dvina River delta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:50:47 UTC
16:50:47 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 26. /TASS/. The museum of the karbas, a traditional vessel of the Pomors (or coast-dwellers), was opened on an island in the delta of the Northern Dvina River in the village of Kalkino near Arkhangelsk, a TASS correspondent reported. The Karbas is a sailing and rowing fishing and transport wooden vessel, common at least from the 15th century in the White and Barents Seas. Karbases are so common in the Arkhangelsk Region, that the world is practically a synonym of "boat".
The first syllable is stressed in the word "karbas." Karbases were mentioned in the Solovki Monastery notes in 1531. Apparently, by then, the White Sea coast inhabitants - the Pomors - had been actively using them.
"We have been building it for two years, quite a long time. The winters were so severe that it was impossible to work, and no roads to use. Now, we have here a museum that tells about the ancient history of karbases, and a club where everyone can learn how to sail karbases," Evgeny Shkaruba, leader of the Pomors' Shipbuilding Association, the project's author, told TASS.
The Karbas Museum's architecture is based on the Pomor wooden port structures of the 19th century: boat sheds, warehouses and fish warehouses that used to be built along coasts in berthing areas of the northern rivers and seas. The museum's building is divided into three zones. The first part is a museum, where a karbas is presented - it was built under the old technology without using nails. This part also hosts an exhibition about traditional Pomor boats.
The second part is a workshop where karbases are stored and repaired. Since 2017, the project participants have built 15 karbases using old technologies. The first one was built in the Arkhangelsk Region's Leshukonsky District back in 2017.
"We built the first karbas in 2017 together with Viktor Kuznetsov in Leshukonye," the project's author said. "It was a revelation. The main revelation was that the tradition, which is more than 500 years old, is still alive. This preserved karbas-building language is unique precisely due to its very long background. Over the time of the kind any structure develops to perfection."
The building's third part is the Karbas Club: a hall and a classroom for the theory of maritime affairs, a meeting place for members of the community that has formed around the Pomors' Shipbuilding Association's initiatives. The museum is located by the water, and four karbases are berthed by the pier there.
Houses made of ships
The island, where the museum was opened, is called the Krivaya Koshka (Crooked Cat). This is the territory of pilots, who used to settle there for several centuries. The Northern Dvina delta is very complicated for navigation, and thus the pilotage service was established in the area back in the 17th century.
Karbases were used for a variety of purposes. Some karbases were for hay delivery. Arkhangelsk is located in swamps, and hay used to be a problem there. Hay was delivered from the islands and from the Dvina's other side. People needed to have a lot of hay, as hay was practically gasoline of that time, said Evgeny Tenetov, the Northern Maritime Museum's director said. Other variations of karbases were built for herring, for sea hunting, and special pilotage karbases, which pilots used to approach vessels and board them.
"A karbas was in every yard, in every family. Sometimes even more than one - for different purposes," the Northern Maritime Museum's director said.
Interestingly, even houses in Calchino were built of ships. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Russian grain supplies to Norway ran through Arkhangelsk. From Vologda, grain was transported along the river on rough-hewn barges. Further on, the grain was re-loaded onto sea schooners, and the barges were dismantled. The locals used their parts to build pavements, warehouses, and parts of houses.
"If you walk along the streets of Calchino and take a closer look at the houses, you will see holes of the same diameter on the log cabins, and those holes are located more or less synchronously. These are the holes for the nails used to hold the logs together when they were not houses, but ships," the historian explained.
Ship houses and a historic island
Elena Kudryashova, Vice President of the Lomonosov Foundation, Chair of the Arkhangelsk Regional Branch and Vice President of the Association of Polar Explorers, told TASS that Calchino had been one of the biggest pilot villages in the Arkhangelsk Region. Nowadays, it is a very picturesque village, where has been erected a memorial cross in honor of the 400th anniversary of the pilotage service, and a museum of Pomors.
"Nikolay Portyanko, a well-known lawyer, lived here for many years and created a completely unique museum of everyday Pomor culture. He has completely renovated a traditional pilot house, and all rooms there have been turned into museum spaces. He was collecting furniture, utensils, paintings, carpets, and statuettes," she said. "The villagers are very sensitive to shipbuilding and to the development of marine spaces. Even on the playground there are two boats that were once used, but now the kids are playing on them."
The Karbas Museum project won the Museum 4.0 competition of the Vladimir Potanin Charitable Foundation's Museum Without Borders charity program. The Karbas Club project's implementation was supported by the Arkhangelsk Region Governor's Center.

Australia expands biometric requirements for visa applicants in India from October 26
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:50:06 UTC
16:50:06 KST

Australia introduces fingerprint and facial image requirements for certain new visa applications from India, effective Oct 26
NEW DELHI: The Australian government on Monday expanded biometric collection requirements for visa applicants in India from October 26, introducing fingerprint and facial image collection for certain new visa applications.The change covers applications filed on or after that date, while those submitted earlier and visas already issued remain unaffected, the Australian high commission said. The department of home affairs will inform applicants who need to complete the additional step and explain how to do so.
Applicants may be directed to one of 16 biometric collection centres operated by VFS Global across India. Those who meet the eligibility criteria may instead be able to submit their biometrics through the Australian Immi App.The government said the move is intended to make identity checks more reliable, curb fraud and protect applicants from identity misuse. Australia already collects biometric data from visa applicants in nearly 60 countries, and the extension brings India into the programme.
Visa processing times are not expected to be adversely affected if applicants provide their biometrics promptly after being notified.Applicants have been advised not to book an appointment or use the app until they receive an official notification from the department of home affairs.
The Australian government said applicants’ personal information would be handled under relevant laws and transferred through encrypted channels.

The “Cobalt-2026” special exercise involving special-purpose formations of the CSTO Collective Operational Reaction Forces has concluded in Tajikistan
23.10.2026
From October 18 to 23 this year, in accordance with the 2026 Plan for the Joint Training of Command and Control Bodies and Formations of Forces and Assets of the Collective Security System of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the “Cobalt-2026” special exercise was held at the Magob training range of the Special Purpose Units Training Center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Tajikistan.
The exercise involved special units of internal affairs and national security agencies, internal troops (national guards), special services and anti-drug agencies, as well as emergency rescue and firefighting services incorporated into the special-purpose formations of the CSTO Collective Operational Reaction Forces (CORF). The Ministry of Defense and Border Troops of the State Committee for National Security of the Republic of Tajikistan also participated.
Under conditions approximating combat situations and taking into account the experience gained during the special military operation, special forces personnel from CSTO member states improved their skills in conducting independent special operations to combat illegal armed formations and paramilitary drug-trafficking groups, as well as to rescue hostages.
The Operational Headquarters, composed of representatives of CSTO member states, gained practical experience in planning a special operation in the Central Asian Collective Security Region, making decisions on its conduct, and organizing command and control of the actions of diverse forces and assets. A field command post was deployed to direct the special operation.
As part of the exercise, combined special operations groups practiced operational tasks in mountainous terrain, including comprehensive support for the force grouping and coordination with aviation. A mountain field training march was conducted, and tactical shooting competitions using various types of small arms were held. An exhibition of weapons and special equipment used by the competent authorities was also organized. An international research team analyzed the participants’ actions.
The exercise involved armored vehicles, special-purpose vehicles, army aviation, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and search dogs.
Overall command of the exercise was exercised by Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Tajikistan Major General of Internal Service Nozim Ibrohimzoda.
The active phase of the exercise was observed by heads of the relevant ministries and agencies of the Republic of Tajikistan, as well as representatives of the Executive Committee of the SCO Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure.
CSTO Deputy Secretary General Valery Semerikov and an operational team from the relevant department of the CSTO Secretariat took part in the exercise.
Speaking at the closing ceremony, the CSTO Deputy Secretary General emphasized the importance of special exercises in preparing special-purpose units to carry out their assigned missions in the event of a crisis in the CSTO area of responsibility.
He also highly commended the field skills and coordinated actions of the personnel who took part in the “Cobalt-2026” exercise.
In conclusion, Valery Semerikov noted that the successful conduct of the exercise was largely attributable to the extensive organizational work undertaken by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Tajikistan in preparation for the event, including the development of the Magob training range and the provision of good living conditions for the participants.
Following the exercise, a detailed debriefing was held. Personnel and service members who had distinguished themselves were commended.

Address by CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov at the conference “Greater Eurasia: Institutions for the Development of Cooperation”

07:49:06 UTC

From October 18 to 23 this year, in accordance with the 2026 Plan for the Joint Training of Command and Control Bodies and Formations of Forces and Assets of the Collective Security System of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the “Cobalt-2026” special exercise was held at the Magob training range of the Special Purpose Units Training Center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Tajikistan.
	 An international scientific and practical conference entitled “Greater Eurasia: Institutions, Development, Cooperation” was held at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, jointly organized with the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences (ICCA RAS). CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov took part in the conference.

	 Today, a conference entitled “The Role and Place of Media in CSTO Member States in Efforts to Contain Crisis (Emergency) Situations in Collective Security Regions” was held in Minsk.
Address by CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov at the conference “Greater Eurasia: Institutions for the Development of Cooperation”
23.10.2026
An international scientific and practical conference entitled “Greater Eurasia: Institutions, Development, Cooperation” was held at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, jointly organized with the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences (ICCA RAS). CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov took part in the conference.
Address by CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov:
Dear colleagues,
The world is experiencing a transformation of the international relations system. In the 2025 Declaration of the Collective Security Council, the heads of CSTO member states noted the growing importance of collective efforts at the regional and global levels to prevent and resolve crises and conflicts. These efforts must be based on the guiding principles of the UN Charter.
Regional conflicts are intensifying, and new security threats are emerging, particularly near the borders of CSTO member states. External actors are attempting to influence developments in our region.
The leaders expressed concern over attempts to turn Eurasia into an arena of geopolitical confrontation and undermine established ties and processes of Eurasian integration. They also rejected unilateral coercive measures that run counter to the UN Charter and are used as instruments of political, economic and financial pressure.
This is a matter of fundamental importance for development institutions: sustainable cooperation cannot be built on pressure. It is essential to establish clear parameters.
The CSTO area of responsibility is clearly defined: it encompasses the territories of its member states. However, it is not isolated. It borders the Far East, the Middle East and the Near East, and is adjacent to the Caspian and Black Sea regions, Eastern Europe and the Baltic region. Developments in all these regions inevitably have repercussions within our area of responsibility.
The response of CSTO member states is to build a sustainable security architecture across Eurasia based on the principles of equality and indivisibility of security.
Our states have also supported the negotiation process on the Eurasian Charter of Diversity and Multipolarity in the 21st Century. We proceed from the premise that security and development are inseparable.
Central Asia provides a clear example. Just a few years ago, the situation in the region was difficult, with border disputes frequently escalating into armed clashes. Today, the situation has changed dramatically. This is the result of the political will of the leaders of the countries in the region, their personal commitment and their readiness to seek compromises at the negotiating table.
On March 13, 2025, the Treaty on the State Border between the Kyrgyz Republic and the Republic of Tajikistan was signed. On March 31, 2025, the presidents of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan signed the Treaty on the Junction Point of the State Borders of the Three Countries and adopted a Declaration of Eternal Friendship.
The heads of CSTO member states welcomed these historic developments, as they contribute to greater stability in the Organization’s area of responsibility. The experience of the region shows that even complex differences can be resolved when there is a willingness to engage in dialogue and respect one another’s interests.
Dear colleagues,
I would like to emphasize the importance of expert assessments. Decisions on security and development are made in an environment of uncertainty, and the cost of error is high. Sound expert assessments are no less important than political will. Threats can be prevented only if emerging trends are identified in advance. Analysis and forecasting are becoming integral components of the security system itself.
Expert platforms make it possible to compare assessments before decisions are made, identify common approaches and resolve misunderstandings. This work helps states make more balanced decisions and thereby strengthens trust.
The CSTO Secretariat consistently develops cooperation with research and expert communities, both in member states and in third countries. Analytical reports are prepared annually at our initiative.
This year, the report prepared by the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia focuses on CSTO cooperation with other organizations and institutions across Greater Eurasia.
At the Collective Security Council session in Bishkek, a proposal was made to establish an association of CSTO member states’ analytical centers specializing in international relations and security. We are ready to support its implementation. Similar ideas are also being discussed in Central Asia, where the inclusion of an expert forum in the regional cooperation framework is under consideration.
A broad community of experts from around the world is already taking shape around the CSTO. They share a common vision of the principles underpinning a new Eurasian security architecture: equality, indivisibility and consideration of the interests of all participants. We will continue to develop contacts with analytical institutions in different parts of Eurasia and strengthen the CSTO’s role as an open platform for substantive international discussions.
Expert work delivers results when it is matched by coordinated action among organizations. The heads of state have declared their readiness to expand CSTO cooperation with the CIS and the SCO, which share the common task of ensuring stability and security across Eurasia. The basis for this cooperation is the Road Map for Developing Cooperation between the CSTO, CIS and SCO for 2026–2028, signed by the secretaries general of the three organizations in Beijing on September 3, 2025.
Dear colleagues,
A new security architecture for Greater Eurasia cannot be built by any one country or organization acting alone. It requires the political will of leaders, coordinated efforts by institutions, and precise and impartial expert assessments. I am confident that we will achieve this through our joint efforts.
Thank you for your attention!

Fireworks, blaring car horns and chants of “Lula, Lula” filled São Paulo's iconic Paulista Avenue as thousands celebrated President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory in Sunday's presidential runoff.
Supporters waved Brazilian flags, danced, sang and embraced one another, some overcome with emotion. The celebrations stretched into Monday, while similar scenes unfolded in other cities across Brazil.
The left-wing president won 51.8% of valid votes, compared with 48.2% for Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, securing a fourth term with a margin of roughly 4.4 million votes, according to the Superior Electoral Court.
Lula's victory came after he overturned a first-round deficit against his right-wing challenger. Bolsonaro, however, has refused to accept the outcome and said he would seek to have the result annulled.

Zelensky: Ukraine Offered US 3 Ways to Stop Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries

Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries at the request of US President Donald Trump’s team, but only if one of three conditions was met, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with journalist Alla Mazur.
Speaking on the TSN.Tyzhden (TSN.The Week) program, Zelensky said that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries could not have a significant impact on global prices, noting that Russia accounts for only 2% of global diesel exports, while the remaining 98% comes from other exporters.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“How can one reach an ‘energy truce’ with the Russians? You might be hated, but you should at least be respected as an adversary. They must respect Ukraine – and our strength. He [Putin] inflicts great pain upon us, and we respond. It is a matter of justice,” Zelensky said.
According to him, Ukraine had proposed three possible ways to resolve the dispute to the American side. However, none of the proposals had been implemented, which is why Ukraine continues to strike Russian oil refineries, he said.
“I said: if you want us to stop hitting diesel facilities and refineries, then they [the Russians] must stop striking our power infrastructure. That is fair – an ‘energy truce.’ A second option: you enable Starlink coverage over Russia, and we show you the locations of their ballistic missile launchers. We want to destroy them.
Trump’s Big Lie About Ukraine
“The third option is this: if you won’t enable Starlink for us – which is entirely up to you – and you’ve said that Musk doesn’t want to, then give us something that doesn’t depend on Musk or Putin: missiles for the Patriot systems,” Zelensky said.
He added that Ukraine had received none of the three proposed forms of support.
“That is why the reaction is what it is – we are fighting for our lives,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky warns against lifting sanctions before negotiations
Zelensky also said that lifting sanctions against Russia should be considered only as part of the process of ending the war, rather than as a precondition for negotiations.
“I would not want us to approach the meeting of the three leaders – Ukraine, the United States, and Russia – having already lifted all sanctions against the Russian Federation. This is a crucial point. Sanctions were imposed in response to aggression, not as a price for the mere opportunity to talk.”
He said he had conveyed this position to the American delegation, cautioning that Russia could benefit from sanctions relief before any agreement on ending the war had been reached.
He warned that once sanctions were lifted, restoring them could prove difficult, requiring Ukraine and its partners to rebuild international support for a new round of restrictions.
“Without sanctions, we could reach a point in the trilateral dialogue where the future remains uncertain, yet the sanctions have already been removed,” Zelensky added.
He said that the international community had adopted more than 20 separate sanctions packages against Russia and questioned whether the same political resolve could be mobilized again if Moscow failed to follow through on its commitments.
“I do not want us to find ourselves without any leverage – lacking sanctions, funds, or frozen assets – when we sit down with Putin. Because then, as Mr. Trump put it, we would truly have very few cards left in our deck,” Zelensky added.
Ukraine, US, EU and NATO plan security talks in Brussels
Zelensky also said Ukraine, the United States, the European Union and NATO planned to hold a broad meeting in Brussels this week to discuss security issues, guarantees and European integration.
According to the president, the format of the discussions had expanded following a visit by the American delegation to St. Petersburg and a preliminary briefing to Ukraine.
The talks had initially been limited in scope, but the Americans were now seeking a broader discussion, Zelensky said.
“The Americans [after Oslo] went to St. Petersburg; we received a ‘brief’ from them, but now they want more than just a ‘brief’ – they want a broad discussion regarding security, guarantees, the EU, and involvement,” he added.
The meeting was expected to take place this week, tentatively on Tuesday or Wednesday. Zelensky said the participants would include representatives of Ukraine, the US and the EU at the presidential level, as well as NATO, represented by the alliance’s secretary-general.

MPs urged 'let light win' as cockatoo sits in for Helen Haines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:47:12 UTC
16:47:12 KST

A cardboard cockatoo sits in tribute for Helen Haines as MPs are urged to 'let light win over darkness'
Far from the gum trees of north-east Victoria where cockatoos gather in noisy flocks, an orange cardboard bird perched in the parliament on Monday, saving a seat for Helen Haines.
"How lonely it looks," Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said.
But cockatoos are not normally lonely birds, and Ms Haines has built her life in much the same way.
The Independent Member for Indi could be loud for those she cared about. She made sure her people were impossible to ignore, and was surrounded by her community, building her political career from a grassroots campaign run by locals.
And unlike the rest of parliament, loud and raucous, Ms Haines was calm.
A week ago, she was standing by the boot of her car outside her Wangaratta office when a man hit her with his own car in what police say was a targeted attack.
The injuries were so severe both of her legs were later amputated.
"This should not just shock us," Wentworth MP Allegra Spender said.
"It should change us."
As the parliament suspended normal business to make time for messages of support for Ms Haines and her family, it was hard to escape the feeling that something had shifted.
One after another, for hours, MPs stood up to speak in the House about Ms Haines's uncommon kindness, wisdom and respect for civility as a politician.
"These are the type of politicians we wish we had more of," friend and crossbench colleague Kate Chaney said.
Like a "trick the heart plays on the mind", Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described finding himself looking across to where Ms Haines would normally sit, expecting to see her there.
"It is hard to think of anyone in this place with a more irrepressible twinkle in the eye," he said.
But the tributes were also threaded with another message: that the tenor of Australian politics must change, and that the country needed to find a better way to argue.
"And this is a moment for all of us to rise to the challenge," Speaker of the House Milton Dick said.
What Would Helen Do?
Members of the crossbench cried as they listened to messages of support for the woman they regard as the "matriarch" of Australia's independent movement.
Ms Haines was among the first wave of community-backed independents to reshape Australian politics, winning Indi after the retirement of fellow independent Cathy McGowan.
Community Strong MP Zali Steggall spoke of the role Ms Haines had played in helping shape the modern crossbench, guiding newly elected independents through the workings of parliament and teaching them how to advocate for their communities without the backing of a major party.
"There will be much discussion ahead about the need for better health and mental health services in the regions, our increasingly polarised political environment, harmful online debate and the need for greater civility in disagreement in parliament, in our media, online and in our communities," she said.
"So, Helen, I look forward to seeing you back here and getting on with the job. Let light win over darkness."
Independent MP Allegra Spender shared the first words Ms Haines spoke after the attack, as relayed by her husband, Phil Haines, who had met with parliamentarians earlier on Monday.
"Your first concerns were for your staff and gratitude to the first responders, nurses and bystanders," she said.
"And that exactly speaks to the character of who you are."
But for all her decency, Ms Spender said, Ms Haines was not a "benign force wandering through the parliament".
"People have spoken about your empathy and grace, and they deserve recognition," she said.
"What I will say is that you are also a force for change."
After winning Indi, voters have rewarded Ms Haines with two further terms, entrusting her with an electorate of mountains, rivers and fertile farmland, which was also acutely exposed to the effects of a warming climate.
After years of advocacy by Ms Haines, the federal government adopted temporary disaster roaming, an emergency system that allows mobile phones to switch to another carrier's network when their own service fails during a major disaster.
But few issues, her friends and colleagues said, animated her more than integrity in government.
Independent MP Andrew Gee was emotional speaking about the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), which she is credited for establishing.
Several politicians chose to commit to a Civility Pledge, inspired by the family of British MP Jo Cox, who was murdered in 2016. Ms Haines was the first MP to sign the pledge earlier this year.
MP Kate Chaney spoke about t-shirts printed for a Christmas party in her first year in parliament with the slogan: What Would Helen Do?
"I ask myself that question all the time," she said.
"Helen, please come back to us. We need you here more than ever".
The rage is getting worse, but we can get better
Mr Albanese said Australia had a proud tradition of disagreement but warned against confusing the vigour of democracy with "this rising tide of rage".
"We cannot allow disagreement to become a full stop. We keep talking. We keep working towards something better," he said.
There was a shared disbelief in the chamber that someone like Helen Haines, among parliament's most respected and unassuming figures, had become a target.
She had been "so, so far down" his list of potential security concerns, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
Mr Burke said Phil Haines had earlier urged the parliament to think not only about the words they choose, but about who might hear them.
"It goes to not simply would I be capable of doing something horrific, but would my words, if heard by someone on the edge, potentially have an impact that I wouldn't want them to have,"
Mr Burke said.
A number of people also called for an honest conversation about mental health, including Liberal MP Dan Tehan.
Ms Haines is a former nurse and maternal health expert, and has long campaigned for additional support for regional services.
"We have to look at mental health services in and around regional and rural Victoria and across this nation," Mr Tehan said.
"We have to see whether we can do better."
As one man hurt Haines, others ran to help
Many MPs said they had spent the week hearing from Australians worried about a country growing more angry and more divided.
But in the same breath, they pointed to people like Ricky Jefferies, the local barber who ran towards danger when Haines needed help.
"One man drove at Helen, but others ran to her instinctively and courageously, and they saved her life," Independent MP Monique Ryan said.
"Our basic decency and our selflessness are there still, and we have to use those muscles, not the others."
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said Mr Jefferies knew most of the first responders because he cut their hair, "not because of social media networks".
"And there's something in that," he said.
"We thrive as a nation when we are in a community with our neighbours, when we are known by them and they are known by us."
He encouraged all politicians to behave better in parliament and online.
"We can all go better and we should strive to do better," he said.
"Lets play the ball, not the person and leave nasty personal politics of MAGA in the US."
Labor MP Ged Kearney broke down as she spoke about Ms Haines but said she had tried to honour her example by making herself as "visible as possible" over the weekend.
"I walked the streets amongst kids in Halloween costumes. I went to listen to music. I had lunch in a cafe, and visited a scouts party," she said.
"We all have fears and we do things differently now to assess risks … but at the end of the day, if I can't walk down High Street or Edward Street or Station Street and be with the people I represent, then well, what is this for?"
Parliament looks to the day it is made whole again
At a vigil held in Wangaratta to honour Ms Haines in the days after her attack, cockatoos wheeled overhead.
"They make a lot of noise, but they're very supportive of each other as a flock," former politician and friend Cathy McGowan told the ABC.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said when Ms Haines resumed her seat, it would be a "resounding moment for democracy".
"In those horrific moments last Monday, and in the critical hours and days afterwards, one man's cruelty stood in stark contrast to the courage and decency of so many Australians," he said.
In her maiden speech, Ms Haines had reflected on the erosion of trust affecting democracies around the world.
Indi, she argued, offered a different lesson.
"Division and polarisation are not the inevitable outcome," she said then.

Singapore, Saudi Aramco agree to store crude oil in rock caverns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:47:01 UTC
16:47:01 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Singapore and Saudi Aramco plan to store Saudi crude oil in the underground Jurong Rock Caverns starting in 2027 to boost energy security amid global supply disruptions.  
Tan See Leng, Singapore's minister for energy, trade and industry, announced the joint intention during the Singapore Energy Lecture 2026 on Monday.  
Tan said the arrangement would enhance the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain across Southeast Asia.
The minister noted that the initiative would also contribute to the city-state's energy security during supply emergencies.  
"Today, Saudi Arabia and Singapore are announcing our joint intent to establish an arrangement for Saudi crude oil to be stored at the Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027," the minister said.
Saudi Aramco, the Energy Market Authority and JTC signed a memorandum of understanding to finalize the storage agreement.
Officials aim to conclude negotiations within a few months.  
The global energy landscape has faced significant challenges this year following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabian airports and energy infrastructure have further escalated the international energy situation.
Tan emphasized that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would not be the last supply disruption.
Singapore has established multiple lines of defense to mitigate the economic impact of sudden supply chain crunches.
The government requires electricity-generating turbines to run on either gas or diesel to draw on reserve fuels.
The country also plans to expand its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity by 50% with a second terminal by 2030.
