'Tyranny of distance' weighs against big cycling call
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:10:10 UTC
16:10:10 KST

Cadel Evans says an Australian Grand Tour start is possible but he wouldn't want to ride it
In short:
Cadel Evans has said one of cycling's three great stage races could start here, but the tyranny of distance would make it unlikely.
Australia's only Tour de France winner, Evans said some Grand Tour races were considering starts in America, and that he would be open to them coming to the Southern Hemisphere.
Evans's Great Ocean Road Race will take place in late January.
Cadel Evans is intrigued by the revolutionary idea of Australia hosting a Tour de France stage, especially given he's long retired as a pro cyclist.
The 2011 Tour champion, the only Australian to win cycling's most famous event, remains heavily involved in his sport as a race promoter and commentator.
Cycling's three-week Grand Tours, the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España, regularly start with stages outside their own borders.
Next year, the Tour's "Grand Depart" will be three stages through Scotland, England and Wales.
But it would be something else entirely to bring a Grand Tour start to the other side of the world.
The San Francisco 49ers and LA Rams faced massive logistical challenges last month to stage their NFL game at the MCG and they didn't have to play again until several days later.
"It would be possible — I wouldn't want to be the one telling the riders," Evans said on Monday.
"But it's never out of the question. There's been talk before … some Grand Tours are maybe considering stages in America.
"I'd be totally open to it, but I wouldn't want to ride it myself. Australia — as we all know, the tyranny of distance — it's pretty far."
There was speculation last summer that the WA government was sounding out Giro organisers.
While a Grand Tour start remains at long odds, the likelihood of cycling superstar Tadej Pogačar returning to race in Australia may well be firming.
Pogacar crashed out of the Vuelta in late August, ending his season early.
Tour Down Under race director Stuart O'Grady has been trying to lure Pogačar to Adelaide for several years. The project took a step forward this year when Pogačar's manager visited and spoke highly of the race.
If Pogačar returned to Adelaide, he would most likely also race at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race in Geelong the following weekend.
Pogacar competed at the two events in 2019 and last raced in Australia at the 2022 Wollongong world road championships.
"He wants to start his season early, apparently. If he would like to come back to our race, that would be amazing," Evans said.
"When you have the opportunity to see the greatest of all time in any sport, it's pretty unique for any sporting fan."
The Slovenian's stunning run of sustained success has invited comparisons with Belgian Eddy Merckx — until now, cycling's all-time greatest rider.
Evans gives the nod to Pogačar.
"It's unfair to compare periods, but it's a far more competitive environment that we race in now," he said.
"There are so many more specialists in our sport now and he's been an all-rounder, winning everywhere, It's just remarkable, and at such a young age as well [28].
"One thing that's so great about Pogačar, other than that he's just an amazing rider, is he wants to win everything."
Evans, at 174 centimetres, was standing alongside Max Gawn, at 209cm, to announce the Melbourne captain as an ambassador for the People's Ride, held on January 30 before the women's road race at Geelong.
"Particularly someone like Pogačar, he goes beyond our sport — and of course, that's having Max part of it [as well]," Evans said.

Jordan says 3 arrested in deadly attack on Greek Orthodox church
Amman, Jordan — Jordanian security forces arrested three men Monday for an attack on a Greek Orthodox church that killed nine people and wounded more than two dozen.
The Public Security Directorate said the three suspects were arrested following a dawn shootout and that all three were wounded. No members of the security forces were injured in the dawn operation in Karak governorate, south of Jordan's capital, Amman. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.
The attack on the Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak took place Friday during a funeral. Three men were reported to have taken part in the attack.
There was still no claim of responsibility, and no armed group has been accused of the attack.
Jordan's Interior Minister, Mazen Al-Faraya, identified the three men as those responsible for the attack.
"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," he said in a phone interview with state TV Al-Mamlaka. "They put up fierce resistance against the security forces, but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."
He added that there "are three individuals involved; they were identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident, and the security services employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
The directorate said, "Terrorism has no place among us," and that the three had met their "just fate," according to the Reuters news agency. The directorate didn't name the suspects or point to any possible links to any Islamist militant groups, Reuters added.
King Abdullah II directed authorities to respond with "an iron fist" against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

According to the outlet, a residential complex at 4K Arkhitektora Troitskogo Street was struck, while the newly built Uritsky residential complex at 135 Uritskogo Street also sustained damage. The latter building was completed last year, Astra reported.
At least 10 cars were reportedly on fire in a parking area at 275/1 45-y Strelkovoy Divizii Street. The outlet also reported fires in residential areas and smoke spreading across the city.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ claimed that some of the impacts resulted from Russian electronic warfare systems operating inside the city, alleging that Russian air defenses caused damage while attempting to counter the drones. The claim has not been independently verified.
Missiles Strike Energiya Defense Battery Plant in Yelets
Another monitoring channel, Supernova+, reported that the Severny Bridge in Voronezh may also have been targeted, citing reports that the bridge was closed and smoke was visible nearby.
Industrial and aviation facilities possibly targeted
Supernova+, citing their own open-source intelligence analysis, suggested that the Voronezhsintezkauchuk synthetic rubber plant and the Voronezh Aircraft Joint-Stock Company (VASO) may also have been targeted.
Voronezhsintezkauchuk, part of Russian petrochemical group SIBUR, produces synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. VASO is part of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation and participates in the production of Il-96 long-haul aircraft and components for other aircraft.
Killed and injured in Voronezh drone attack, governor says
A drone attack reportedly killed two people and injured 17 others in Voronezh.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev said the two people killed were men born in 1960 and 1973. One child was among the injured, and two of the wounded were in serious condition.
A significant number of those injured were traveling on a train passing through Voronezh’s left-bank suburbs when drone debris fell onto it, Gusev said. Emergency services were working at the scene.
The attack also sparked fires at several industrial facilities, a business center, an apartment building, two dacha settlements, a school stadium, and a garage cooperative, according to the governor. He said the industrial fires had no major consequences.
Building facades and windows were damaged in nearly every district of the city, Gusev added.
According to the governor, air defense forces shot down more than 70 drones over Voronezh, while 113 were intercepted across the metropolitan area and several districts of the region. These figures have not been independently verified.
Neither the Russian defense ministry nor Ukrainian officials have commented on the reported attack.
Freight train derails in Sverdlovsk Region
Separately, 20 freight train cars derailed in Russia’s Sverdlovsk Region, with seven fuel tankers catching fire, according to reports cited by Astra. The cause of the incident has not been disclosed, and no casualties have been reported.
The Sverdlovsk Railway said traffic on the Reshety-Aramil section had been suspended after the derailment compromised clearance of an adjacent track. Firefighting and recovery trains were dispatched to the scene.
Local residents reported seeing flames and thick black smoke, with one witness telling media that an explosion had illuminated the area near the Chusovsky Tract.
Russia’s consumer rights watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it would test air quality in nearby residential areas.
The derailment comes amid a series of reported disruptions to Russian railway infrastructure in recent months.
The Moscow Times reported that Ukrainian drone attacks on railway infrastructure in the Bryansk Region on Sept. 28 caused 10 railcars to derail after a railway bridge section collapsed, while a separate incident derailed 18 empty freight cars.
Other reported railway incidents in September and July caused train delays and damage, although the causes differed.
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian officials have publicly attributed the Sverdlovsk derailment to an attack.

Discovering Almaty: Mountain mornings, street art and market flavours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:08:20 UTC
16:08:20 KST

Kazakhstan’s former capital marked its birthday with music, markets and apple fairs. Beyond the celebrations, mountain breakfasts, colourful architecture and art hiding in plain sight offer reasons to linger.
The first thing many newcomers notice about Almaty is the skyline. Snow-capped peaks of the Trans-Ili Alatau rise beyond the rooftops, close enough to shape everyday life. They even influence the way people give directions. In a city laid out largely on a grid, locals may tell you to head “up”, meaning towards the mountains, or “down” - away from them.
You can start with coffee in the city centre and head towards the foothills for a walk or a late breakfast. The mountains are close enough to be part of an ordinary morning, and not just a weekend escape.
To explore the mountains, head to the Medeu base station and take the cable car up to Shymbulak Mountain Resort. In winter, skiers and snowboarders come for the slopes, but you can also visit simply for the views or a meal in the mountains. There are opportunities for walking and hiking all year round.
Art on the walls, and a city shaped by history
Almaty was Kazakhstan’s capital until 1997, and its cultural reputation runs deep. Look closely at older buildings and you’ll find layers of the city’s artistic history: brightly coloured mosaics embedded in facades.
Many date from the 1960s to the 1980s, when monumental artists from across the Soviet Union worked in the city. Some have since been damaged or lost, making the surviving works worth seeking out.
Almaty’s buildings tell other stories too. The colourful wooden Ascension Cathedral, completed in 1907, survived a major earthquake just four years later.
For a contemporary contrast, visit the Almaty Museum of Arts, which opened last year. Designed by the British architectural firm Chapman Taylor, its two interlocking forms represent the mountains and the city, one clad in limestone and the other in aluminium. Inside, the collection brings together modern and contemporary art from Kazakhstan, Central Asia and beyond.
Come hungry
The Green Bazaar is a good place to discover another side of Almaty. Apples share space with dried fruit, nuts and local produce, while the surrounding food scene moves easily between Kazakh staples and dishes familiar across Central Asia.
Try beshbarmak, a dish of meat served over flat pieces of pasta, or kazy, a traditional horsemeat sausage. Dairy specialties are worth sampling too: kurt (salty dried curd balls) and kumys (fermented mare’s milk with a tangy flavour).
Make room for plov, a rice pilaf, lagman noodles or steamed manty dumplings. The range of flavours offers a glimpse of the different communities and traditions that have shaped the city.
Almaty’s appeal changes with the seasons: winter brings skiing, warmer months invite mountain walks, and the city’s museums, markets and varied food scene offer plenty to explore throughout the year.
It can also be the starting point for a longer journey. With flight connections to Europe and East Asia, as well its location next to neighbouring Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan and Tashkent in Uzbekistan, Almaty lends itself to a stopover for a wider Central Asian itinerary. Before moving on, though, leave a few days for the city itself.

Discovery of baby orangutans in India exposes booming illegal pet trade
India is emerging as an important market in the global illegal wildlife trade, estimated to be worth US$34 billion annually
The three males and two females, aged six to eight months – were left on a plantation in eastern India’s Odisha, over 2,700km (1,700 miles) from their native rainforests in Borneo and Sumatra, evidence of a growing illicit trade of apes being trafficked into India. They are now at an Indian zoo, where keepers reportedly have been playing classical music to soothe them.
Wild orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, where they sustain rainforests by spreading seeds across vast areas, allowing trees to regenerate and store carbon that would otherwise contribute to global warming. The species is critically endangered, threatened by severe habitat loss. There are about 119,500 orangutans left in the wild, according to conservation organisation WWF.

North Korea has told the UN Security Council that a mine explosion in the Demilitarized Zone was a "fabrication" by South Korea, state media reported Monday.
North Korea's permanent representative to the UN sent a letter to the Security Council president Sunday, according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency, or KCNA.
The letter came amid tensions on the Korean Peninsula after three South Korean soldiers were wounded in a mine explosion on Sept. 21.
Seoul blamed Pyongyang for the incident and called for the restoration of military talks. North Korea rejected the accusations and has yet to respond to the South Korean Defense Ministry's offer to resume communication.
Pyongyang's letter followed a similar communication from South Korea to the Security Council, demanding an apology from the North over the incident, the Korea Herald newspaper reported.
The exchange came as South Korea and the US began joint air drills Monday, a day after Yonhap News reported that North Korean troops were seen conducting drills with a self-propelled howitzer in coastal border areas of Hwanghae province.
North Korea's letter described the mine explosion as a "sinister obstructive move" by South Korea aimed at portraying Pyongyang's border fortifications as a military invasion.
It also accused Seoul of attempting to delay the fortification work and evade responsibility for escalating tensions on the Korean Peninsula.
The letter said the fortification of North Korea's southern border was a "legitimate and just exercise of its sovereignty" in accordance with the UN Charter and international law.
Pyongyang described the work as a defensive measure against external threats of aggression.
"If the RoK violates the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DPRK despite our warnings, the former will be held wholly accountable for all the ensuing consequences," the letter said.
The Democratic People's Republic of Korea is North Korea's official name, while the Republic of Korea is the official name of South Korea.
 
South Korea, US launch joint air drills
South Korea's Air Force said Monday that joint air drills with the US were focused on "counter-air and air interdiction missions aimed at enhancing wartime joint operations."
The two-week Freedom Flag exercise is being held at Kunsan Air Base in Gunsan, about 180 kilometers (112 miles) southwest of Seoul.
The 1950s Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.
Some 39,000 US military personnel are stationed in South Korea under a mutual defense pact.

Israel’s election: The main issues in the words of the leading candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:03:43 UTC
16:03:43 KST

Israel’s election: The main issues in the words of the leading candidates
From judicial reform to conscription and the Palestinians, here’s where candidates stand on the key issues dominating the campaign.
For an election often billed as the most consequential in Israel’s history, many issues that outsiders might expect to divide the candidates are, in fact, points of consensus among the frontrunners.
None of the leading contenders in Tuesday’s election has questioned the case for unleashing a genocide on Gaza in response to the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, or the wars that have followed, including the one on Iran. Nor have most candidates for the premiership offered a clear path towards implementing a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict that was envisaged in the 1990s, or towards an equitable settlement with the Palestinians whose territory Israel occupies.
Instead, the points of division centre almost exclusively on Israel’s internal politics and how voters see the future character of their country. The choice is between the hard-right government of incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, unconstrained by the judicial oversight he has railed against, and the future outlined by the disparate coalition of his opponents, which promises a broadly similar policy agenda but within the confines of the law and without the more extreme elements of the current governing coalition.
So, what have the leading candidates said about the main issues?
The two-state solution
Despite having committed to working towards a two-state solution in the 1990s’ Oslo Accords, with many of their allies adjusting their policies towards Israel to reflect that commitment, few of the contenders in Tuesday’s election appear ready to honour it. Instead, their government stands widely accused of abetting the settler pogroms now raging across the West Bank, while supporting continued construction in the occupied territory in defiance of international law. This includes the E1 settlement plan, which ministers openly boast will bury the two-state solution.
Here’s what some of the contenders have said:
- Likud party leader, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu: “We are going to fulfill our promise that there will be no Palestinian state; this place belongs to us.”
- Yashar party Gadi Eisenkot: “My position on the Palestinian issue has remained consistent: The principle of two states for two peoples is a mistake.”
- Religious Zionist party leader, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich: The next government should “destroy the idea of an Arab terror state; finally, formally and practically cancel the cursed Oslo Accords and get on the path of sovereignty, while encouraging migration both from Gaza and from Judea and Samaria [occupied West Bank]. There is no other long-term solution.”
- The Democrats leader Yair Golan: “We need to understand that Israeli society is still in trauma from October 7. To make the galactic leap from the current situation to a two-state solution is impossible. It’s not enough to return to old formulas, we need to adjust our plans, our ideas, our perceptions. My concept is about civil separation and security responsibility.”
Haredi draft
The conscription of Israel’s growing ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, population into the army is an issue largely unique to Israel, and one whose prominence has grown as the human and economic costs of the wars in which many refuse to take part have mounted.
Netanyahu has continued to rely on the two main Haredi parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), for support in the Knesset. They have in turn insisted that he pass legislation overturning the Supreme Court ruling of June 25, 2024 and offering ultra-Orthodox youth a legislative shield against conscription.
Here is what leaders have said:
- Netanyahu after the arrest this month of about 40 Haredim – plural for Haredi – for avoiding the draft: “We must preserve the world of Torah because it preserved us. These arrests are a deliberate attempt to harm the process of drafting Haredim without coercion.”
- Shas leader Aryeh Deri: “There will be no government in Israel with Shas’s support or participation unless the status of yeshiva [seminary] students is regulated.”
- Eisenkot: “That is what the upcoming election is about: Netanyahu’s draft-dodging government, or a government of conscription led by me.”
- Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor Liberman: “Netanyahu is issuing an impassioned call against the arrest of draft evaders, once again proving that he is a hostage to the draft evaders – without them, he has no government.”
Judicial overhaul
Days after taking office in 2022, Netanyahu’s government unveiled a plan to curb the powers of Israel’s courts, which triggered months of mass protests in 2023 before the war on Gaza paused the fight.
The coalition has passed measures reshaping how judges are appointed, while in July a law stripped Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara of many of her powers, allowing the government to reject her legal advice and choose its own lawyers in court. Both are due to take effect after the election and most of the opposition has promised to reverse them.
The government has also boycotted Chief Justice Isaac Amit. Critics call it a deliberate assault on democracy by a prime minister embroiled in a long-running corruption trial of his own, while Justice Minister Yariv Levin says the election is a historic chance to finish the job.
Here are some of the contenders’ statements:
- Netanyahu: “Democracy is the rule of the people. It’s ‘we the people,’ not ‘we the judges … In Israel, [judicial reform] was completely derailed, and we have to bring it back. We don’t have to crush the judiciary, but we have to make sure it doesn’t crush the legislative branch, the Knesset or the executive branch of government.”
- Together alliance co-leader, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett: “I want to be clear. We will cancel all the legal revolution laws immediately upon the convening of the Knesset.”		
October 7 inquiry
While the killing of more than 74,000 people in Gaza has been entirely absent during the campaign of the two main alliances, questions over political accountability for security failures ahead of and during the Hamas-led attack in 2023 have dominated this election cycle.
Inquiries into failings by the security services ahead of and during the Hamas-led attack led to the resignation of Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi, announced in January 2025. They also fed a long, drawn-out and bitter fight with the prime minister that ended with the departure of Shin Bet head Ronen Bar in June last year.
However, despite recent news reports suggesting that Netanyahu was warned by both the UAE and Egypt ahead of the attack, and longstanding criticism of his policy of keeping Hamas in power in Gaza as a bulwark against the Palestinian Authority, no similar inquiry into his own alleged failings before October 7 has happened.
Here are some of the leaders’ statements:
- Eisenkot: “Netanyahu was warned and did not act. A State Commission of Inquiry that we will establish will investigate the disaster. The heads of the systems took responsibility and resigned long ago. We will not allow the master of evaders to escape the truth.”
- Netanyahu: The prime minister told the Knesset that his government “wants to establish a commission of inquiry with as broad public support as possible” and not one dismissed by what he claimed is “at least half the country”. The proposed government-led inquiry never reached its final reading and has been deferred to the next session.

“Said to be a brand-new Il-78 mid-air refueling tanker, spotted rolling out of the factory floor sometime in early October,” wrote ACuriousPLAFan.
Neither Russia nor China has commented on the photo, and the aircraft’s customer has not been confirmed. The tail element is only partly visible, and observers have pointed to its resemblance to the People’s Liberation Army Air Force insignia rather than to a full, readable marking.
“So maybe indeed that rumoured contract was real and was not cancelled?” wrote military aviation analyst Andreas Rupprecht on X.
Other forum users suggested the aircraft could be the result of an older order that is only now being delivered. One wrote that, given the Chinese air force’s need for tankers even as it receives new Y-20B aircraft, it was plausible Beijing chose to take the jets instead of canceling the deal.
The contract Rupprecht referred to surfaced in October 2025, when aviation analyst Piotr Butowski cited a leaked document indicating that China was negotiating the purchase of 20 Il-78MK-90A tankers, the export version of Russia’s newest tanker, with deliveries discussed for 2027 and 2028. Neither government confirmed the deal.
The Il-78MK-90A is built by Aviastar-SP in Ulyanovsk on the airframe of the modernized Il-76MD-90A transport. It can refuel one heavy aircraft or two fighters at a time in flight. In August, footage emerged of a new Il-78MK-90A rolling out in export configuration, and reports at the time pointed to Algeria, which has reportedly signed for three tankers with an option for three more, as the likely customer.
China already flies a small number of Il-78s. Beijing ordered four Il-78s along with 34 Il-76 transports from Russia in 2005, but that deal stalled because Russia could not build the aircraft. China instead bought three refurbished Il-78s from Ukraine in 2011, which were delivered between 2014 and 2016.
Since then, the Chinese air force has built up its own tanker fleet based on the Y-20 heavy transport. The IISS Military Balance 2026 lists about 30 YY-20A tankers and 10 of the re-engined YY-20B.
The photo does not show a serial number or clear national markings, and it remains unclear whether the aircraft is the first of a Chinese order, an export tanker for another customer, or a jet for the Russian Aerospace Forces.

‘It’s improved my life’: Solar kits provide essential power in refugee camps and war zones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:02:37 UTC
16:02:37 KST

Portable solar kits in disaster zones fuel everything from communication and cooking to cooling and education.
Portable solar kits handed out as humanitarian aid are helping people in disaster zones and refugee camps stay cool and connected.
Every day, Mohammed Saber places a single rectangular solar panel on the roof of the bamboo-and-tarpaulin shack that he and his family have called home for years. It was the last stop on their journey after fleeing the Myanmar military’s brutal crackdown on the Rohingya in 2017.
Since they were given it six years ago, the portable panel has been the family's primary source of electricity, making daily life much easier in the camp for displaced people in Teknaf, Bangladesh.
"We can now charge our phones, cook with light, children can study at night and use fans during the hot season,” says Saber, 35.
From the flood zones of Nepal to refugee camps in Africa, experts say that solar energy is increasingly becoming part of disaster relief as technology improves, costs fall and humanitarian organisations recognise that having access to electricity is a fundamental need.
Renewable energy solutions are needed more than ever, they say, as climate change drives and intensifies extreme weather while wars, sanctions and political upheavals keep fossil fuel prices volatile.
Solar energy kits are portable, rechargeable and grid-independent
When disasters strike and humanitarian needs surge, solar kits can become an invaluable resource, says Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen, a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute, an independent research and policy institute specialising in sustainable development.
These solar kits – all-in-one, compact units that use solar panels and are not reliant on utility companies – are easy to move and recharge, according to Rosenberg-Jansen.
“In emergency situations, solar kits can be deployed immediately,” she says, adding that they are particularly useful in situations with rapidly rising floodwaters, changing front lines in a conflict, or for moving around in areas where damaged roads make it difficult to travel.
In terms of function, the kits can be "anything from solar lanterns to solar home systems, solar torches, solar heating pads, to electric cook stoves that use solar as their energy source,” she says.
Lower costs of solar energy helped its role in disaster relief
Rosenberg-Jansen also points out that solar panels are not prone to price shocks like fossil fuels, which can be difficult and costly to transport to a disaster zone.
Only a few decades ago, solar energy was a luxury, she adds, but as technology evolved, mindsets and the price tag changed. Now it's more affordable, thanks to the scaling up of mass manufacturing and technology advancement.
It's also so much easier to use, says Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a nonprofit based in the United States that provides solar kits to families living in war-torn Ukraine.
“We have grandmas and grandpas who are around 75-80 years old... receiving kits,” says Boyechko. “It’s just a matter of plug and play.”
Solar panels are becoming more common now.
On the outskirts of Karachi, Pakistan's economic hub, a tuberculosis clinic run by Doctors Without Borders uses solar energy. In South Sudan's Renk county, the UN migration agency installed solar-powered water filtration systems for families displaced by the war in neighbouring Sudan.
And after Nepal's massive floods in August that killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing – including hundreds of foreign nationals – solar kits were distributed by local and international organisations, including Australia-based charity SolarBuddy.
Funding issues and bureaucracy are still obstacles in disaster relief
Mark Gibson from Global Platform for Action, or GPA, which promotes affordable, reliable and clean energy access, says that integrating solar energy hasn't come without difficulties.
Aid agencies have had time-tested systems in place, which often include diesel generators as part of long-term leases and agreements. Switching to solar means having to trust new systems and setting up new distribution chains, sometimes in risky environments.
Recent slashes in international donor funding have also undermined – or completely erased – new practices that were starting to take root, says Aimee Jenks, a programme leader at GPA.
“Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut,” she says. “That’s now retracting a lot of progress.”
And while the cost of solar energy has decreased, it's still prohibitive for many.
Boyechko, of Hope For Ukraine, says that by the end of 2026, his nonprofit will have distributed over 3,200 kits.
“But it took us two years to get to that number, because of funding needs,” he says. ”We have a waiting list of about 20,000 families. We just cannot keep up with demand.”
While no energy source is perfect, the move towards renewable energies is likely to decrease reliance on polluting fossil fuels.
For Saber, whose family is among more than one million refugees from Myanmar’s Rohingya ethnic and religious minority now living in Bangladesh, the kit means keeping the lights on.
“It’s improved my family’s life,” he says.

North Korea deployed a howitzer on the border with South Korea amid escalating tensions
Kyiv • UNN
Pyongyang accused Seoul of fabricating the landmine incident and threatened self-defense. A howitzer and North Korean troops were spotted near the border.
Tensions between North and South Korea escalated this week after Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council reiterating its accusations that Seoul fabricated the September landmine incident, and after a North Korean howitzer was spotted near the border. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
On Monday, October 26, a Reuters witness at an observation post in South Korea, located along the heavily fortified border, confirmed the presence of a North Korean artillery gun positioned in plain view near the border.
South Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday, October 25, identified the weapon as a self-propelled 122-mm howitzer, saying its deployment near the border was a rare public display of such artillery.
Reuters also observed three North Korean armored vehicles with their gun barrels pointed south, as well as approximately 20–30 North Korean soldiers carrying out fencing work inside the demilitarized zone (DMZ).
"It is highly unusual for North Korea to put its self-propelled artillery on such prominent display," said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.
"By deliberately displaying it, North Korea is signaling through actions rather than words that it intends to enforce its border policy by force, not through dialogue or negotiations," he added.
He also cautioned South Korea to be careful about escalating friction along the border in order to prevent an accidental clash, he added.
North Korean state media KCNA reported that in a letter sent on Sunday, October 25, the country's representative to the United Nations said Seoul was using the landmine incident to portray Pyongyang's construction of a border strip as a military invasion.
In the letter, North Korea warned that violations of its sovereignty could lead to self-defense measures, and that South Korea would be "fully responsible for all consequences."
The letter was a response to South Korea's letter to the UN Security Council last week, which said that the September 21 explosion in the demilitarized zone had been planted by North Korean troops and constituted a violation of the Korean War Armistice Agreement.
The United Nations Command, which oversees the demilitarized zone, said that a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Pyongyang denies responsibility.
A spokesperson for South Korea's Ministry of Unification said on Monday that North Korea's letter appeared to repeat its existing position and was an attempt to justify its so-called work marking the border line.
The ministry had no separate comment on the deployment of the howitzer. Seoul has proposed dialogue with North Korea to ease tensions along the border.
North Korea's letter also repeated accusations that South Korea had opened fire on North Korean personnel, calling this a violation of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity of another state.
Seoul said its military issues warnings and fires warning shots to force North Korean soldiers to return behind the line when they cross the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), which divides the DMZ.
A Yonhap report carries photographs taken at an observation post in the South Korean border city of Gimpo that appear to show the howitzer, as well as North Korean troops conducting drills along the coast of Kaepung County, approximately 1.5 km from the observation post.
A similar incident occurred in 2015, when South Korean troops were wounded by North Korean mines. Seoul then resumed broadcasting anti-North Korean slogans across the demilitarized zone, leading to a military standoff. After North Korea expressed regret, the standoff ended with a high-level inter-Korean agreement.

What will a pedestrianised Oxford Street mean for transport?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

Much of Britain’s most famous shopping street will be closed to traffic from Monday as the long-awaited pedestrianisation of London’s Oxford Street begins.
About half of the 1.2 mile street will initially be vehicle-free, after decades of planning and dispute over how to best use the street, an important transport thoroughfare and the home for flagship stores for big shopping chains.
Private cars have been barred for years but now all motorised traffic, including buses and black cabs, as well as bicycles, will be kept away.
For the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, who has targeted the switch as part of clean air plans throughout his tenure, it is a political victory, aided by the backing of central government to override local council objections.
While towns and cities around the UK have long pedestrianised their centres, the location, scale and notoriety of Oxford Street, attracting millions of foreign visitors each year, will make the £150m scheme’s outcome of interest to city planners around the world.
London has studied the pedestrianisation of central Sydney, and discussed the scheme with Barcelona, whose La Rambla is similarly viewed as shabbier than its renown deserves.
The big retailers, Transport for London and those who just want a pleasanter, green city centre will be hoping the changes live up to their promise. Here we unpack what is changing:
Where will be pedestrianised?
From 7am on 26 October, a stretch of nearly 0.6 miles (almost 1km) of Oxford Street, containing the most famous department stores including John Lewis and Selfridges, will be vehicle-free.
The junction with Orchard Street, near Marble Arch, to Great Portland Street, east of Oxford Circus Ikea, will be closed to all traffic between 7am and midnight on every day of the week.
Businesses will be able to make deliveries outside those hours via certain access routes, but vehicles will not be able to travel the length of Oxford Street.
What does this mean for transport?
Private vehicles, such as cars, are already forbidden to drive on the street between 7am and 7pm and this ban will now extended to 24 hours a day seven days a week and cover buses, black cabs and bikes too.
Vehicles will still be able to cross the pedestrianised stretch of street at several points including the major junction of Regent Street and Oxford Circus, and others including New Bond Street.
Bus routes including the numbers 7, 98 and 390 will now run along Wigmore Street, which runs parallel to Oxford Street.
There will be taxi ranks within 100m of the traffic-free area on Oxford Street and surrounding roads.
In contrast to some other traffic-free areas of London, cycles, e-bikes and e-scooters will not be allowed on the pedestrianised strip at any time.
What about disabled people and essential services?
Mobility scooters will still be allowed. Access for disabled people may prove easier than many other parts of London, with Bond Street and Tottenham Court Road stations, on the Underground and Elizabeth line, both step-free.
Emergency services will be able to access the entire area whenever required via the cross streets. Cargo e-bikes will be introduced to collect litter and enable street cleaning during pedestrianised hours.
What other plans are there for the street?
Khan has talked about making Oxford Street a public plaza with outdoor dining, and improved street furniture and lighting is coming.
Early next year, more trees and seating are due to be installed, while the road surface will be raised level with the pavements in places to create public squares and event spaces.
Will the rest of Oxford Street follow?
The pedestrianisation of this stretch of the landmark shopping street has repeatedly been described as the “first phase”, although plans for the rest of the thoroughfare are likely to depend on the success – or otherwise – of the scheme.

====================================================================================================

Stung with a parking fine for an 18-second airport stop to tackle a wasp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

I had to stop my car for 18 seconds in a red zone at Leeds Bradford airport to deal with a wasp. It was buzzing in front of my face and making safe-driving impossible.
The result was a £100 parking charge notice (PCN) sent to my wife (the registered keeper) by Vehicle Control Services (VCS).
I’ve explained the circumstances to VCS, whose CCTV footage shows I only stopped for seconds and never left the car, but it won’t listen. 
 
AW, Hebden Bridge
Its hearing improved when I contacted the airport, which ordered VCS to refund the charge as “goodwill”. The airport tells me that if you had contacted it directly, it would have intervened. However, it is evidently worried that its actions in this case will open the floodgates to wasp-ridden drivers.
“Stopping in this area remains enforceable,” it says sternly. “And due to the safety-critical nature of the road, we would not be able to consider cancellation of any future penalty notices for stopping in this area.” VCS did not respond to a request for a comment.
Parking operators are infamously ruthless when enforcing airport no-stopping zones. Drivers have been charged for stopping at temporary lights, or waiting in traffic queues.
By remarkable coincidence, SM of Pontyclun in Wales also stopped for 18 seconds in an airport red zone. She was billed £100 by VCS, via her husband, who is the vehicle’s registered keeper.
In her case, the airport was Bristol, and she stopped to read the terms and conditions on a sign planted in the no-stopping area.
“I had prepaid £103.60 for three days in the short-stay car park,” she writes. “At the entrance was a prominent sign stating that payment was on exit, and including several lines of information. Confused, I wanted to make sure I was at the right place.”
Her appeal was rejected by VCS, which argued that it is “the motorist’s responsibility to ensure they are familiar with the terms and conditions displayed on the signage” – which is ironic given that SM was doing just that.
It was also rejected by the Independent Appeals Service, which concluded that red-route restrictions prohibit stopping under any circumstances.
“Is it reasonable to expect a motorist to read a substantial amount of car park information while their vehicle is moving, particularly when that information is relevant to determining whether they are entering the correct car park?” asks SM.
There are 24 lines of information, in varying sizes of font, on the sign SM was studying.
Drivers enter a contract when using a car park and are assumed to have agreed the terms and conditions, or else risk a PCN. It was therefore imperative SM read the notice, and not unreasonable she stopped to do so safely.
Bristol airport says: “The customer did not contact us to make us aware of the situation and that she had pre-booked parking. After the circumstances were reviewed, the penalty charge was refunded by the enforcement company.” VCS was contacted for a comment.
In fact, neither AW nor SM were obliged to pay the charge because of a loophole in the law. Airports are “statutory land” governed by bylaws, and are not subject to the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012, which governs private parking enforcement in England and Wales.
The act allows private parking operators to pursue the registered keeper of a vehicle for charges. There is no such keeper liability on statutory land, so if the keeper declines to confirm who was driving, the parking operator is powerless. Operators don’t, of course, want you to know this.
The clue is in the small print of PCNs sent to the spouses of AW and SM which “invite” them to pay up or name the driver. Anyone else in this situation should reply stating that as an airport is statutory land, they are not liable as the vehicle keeper and not obliged to name the driver.
Motorists penalised for reasonable stops on land that does fall under the act, may have a future get-out clause.
The government’s newly announced crackdown on private parking charges means that when the new official code of practice takes effect (we don’t have a date yet), charges will be cancelled on appeal for things such as stopping briefly because of a medical emergency (potential wasp stings, hopefully, included).

‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.
A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.
Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.
As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.
The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.
Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.
“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”
At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.
The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.
“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”
By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.
“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.
By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.
“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

The UAE has so much blood on its hands in Sudan. For its nominee to lead the UN would be an outrage | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Over the past few years, you can plot the plunge into global instability not only through the unchecked assaults on international law and civilian life, but through the decline and undermining of the authority and credibility of international institutions. The latest level in this spiral is the proposed appointment of Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as the UN secretary general. Her bid has been rapidly gaining momentum and endorsements. And it has been met with outrage among the Sudanese.
Nusseibeh is the minister of state at the UAE and a former UAE ambassador to the UN. For the past three years, the country has been connected to – bear with me, this will be a long sentence – supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia in Sudan, facilitating mercenaries to fight alongside the militia (which is accused of ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity and sexual violence), and appropriating international aid infrastructure to smuggle weapons into the country.
The war between the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) is an ongoing calamity of historic proportions. It is grinding and brutal, and has already resulted in hunger, displacement and a humanitarian crisis. Although it has drawn in external actors, multiple investigations and reports point to the UAE as the country that has in essence fuelled the conflict by aggressively sponsoring one side from the start. The result has been intractable conflict, unfathomable losses and relentless momentum fed by external supply lines.
The UAE’s role in Sudan’s war has been the target of years of media investigations, human rights activism and political condemnation. There were calls from two US congressmen to American media and sports organisations to end all associations with the UAE in response to its “abetting genocide” by “arming one faction”. In the UK, a complaint was submitted to the government demanding an investigation into the Manchester City owner and deputy prime minister of the UAE, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, due to the “abundance of evidence” of UAE involvement. Attention has been called to the well-established violations associated with the vastly wealthy and hitherto immune power, which has used that wealth to try to secure a toehold in territories in Africa with geopolitical significance. Sudan’s Red Sea coastline, its bountiful gold reserves and strategic location within the continent seemingly drew the Gulf power’s predatory eye.
In the face of all efforts to highlight the gravity and high stakes of the situation, the UAE has behaved with arrogance, dissimulation and, according to reports, the use ofmisinformation and digital propaganda. Wherever such prevarications were made, there was Nusseibeh, affirming the denial of “baseless allegations”, undermining the work of the international media and, in one instance that should surely be disqualifying, disputing the findings of a UN panel of experts.
In one instance, Nusseibeh was confronted by an indignant Sudanese man in Chad who rejected her whitewashing visit to his refugee camp, imploring her delegation to keep their aid and insisting that if the UAE wants to help, it should stop interfering and stoking the war. Another enraged refugee refused aid, saying the UAE killed her brothers. Against this backdrop, the appointment of Nusseibeh, who has been the face of the UAE’s Sudan strategy, would be a slap in the face to the millions of people suffering the horrors of war, a dereliction of duty towards those thousands who have already been killed, and a green light to the prolonging of conflict.
It has been a lesson, or I should say another lesson, about the extent to which so many of the pleas from those who purport to care about Sudan are performative. How so much of the rhetoric about Sudan or even cursory interest in it is a sort of box-ticking, name-checking exercise. Something to be put on the record – here is the official statement of concern for civilians, here is the pundit with their once-and-that’s-enough treatment, here is the post on X. Going beyond that, making the necessary links that render the conflict not just a sad clash of armed groups but a war in which powerful external parties have been allowed to play abjectly immoral and accelerating roles, is a step too far.
It has also been a lesson in how much a certain kind of Arab politics and mien goes a long, long way to securing consent and licence. Nusseibeh is an operator, that’s for sure, but she is also a beneficiary of a branding exercise that the UAE has been working on for a long time to ingratiate itself with western establishments. One pillar of that strategy has been presenting itself as a “moderate” Muslim country that is alive to the dangers of radical Islam (up to and including being allegedly linked to the funding and support of hard-right groups in Europe). The other is in the cultivation of close financial ties with the UK and the US, particularly with the Trump family, conjoining itself with political and business elites.
And it has understood that between the allied, the gullible and the ignorant, Nusseibeh can easily be presented as the obvious choice for the position as a Muslim woman with liberal credentials and a western education, regardless of the dark politics she advances and represents. It is hard for some to see beyond the facts of her CV – Wycombe Abbey, Cambridge University and, on top of that, of Palestinian origin, serving a country that has normalised relations with Israel. A high identity-politics jackpot.
All which makes Nusseibeh and the country she represents far more relatable and knowable to the world than the vastly weaker, poorer and underrepresented Sudanese people who have been victimised. The UAE, to put it simply, is seen as one of the club, its offences the private business of a country that is too wealthy to antagonise and too solicitous to spurn. Its rise speaks to this moment. At a time of big regional wars, multipolarity, energy crises and fraying norms, who better to become a global anchor than a country that is offering value-free transactional politics, is backed with sovereign wealth, and is expert in the opulent backroom gangsterism of the new world order.
Appointing a representative widely seen as one of the authors of Sudan’s tragedy to such a prestigious and influential post, one that only entrenches the UAE’s position and secures it even more wriggle room vis-a-vis its actions in Sudan, is not just another small way in which the business of international affairs is changing. It is a new chapter, one in which a perpetrator and its tribunes are not just not held to account, but crowned. The contempt is exceptionally bewildering even in an era of outrages. Nusseibeh’s appointment can only be secured by stepping over the dead, and turning backs on the living.
- Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

‘Meet my new après buddies!’: a joyous group skiing trip in Les Deux Alpes, France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Everyone had their reasons for joining the trip. Louisa from south London was putting her life back together after a split from her partner; first-timer Tim was strapping on ski boots following years of hesitation; and Lexi from Bristol had a classic case of the non-skiing boyfriend.
I was there because I needed a ski gang. None of my friends ski, and my brother was out of action with an injury. Not only that, I needed a good night’s sleep. I love my two-year-old son dearly, but I have somehow spawned an insomniac – still waking four times a night. Weary from bedtime battles, Holly, my partner, bluntly pointed out we could both benefit from “a temporary break from family life”. In other words: separate holidays.
Holly arranged a walking trip with friends; I opted for a week’s skiing in the French ski resort of Les Deux Alpes with Friendship Travel, a specialist operator in solo travel for more than 20 years. They find a chalet, fill it with solo skiers, provide travel, most meals and group ski lessons – that’s the basic service.
We were staying in a comfortable, largeish chalet just back from the resort’s mile-long drag. Entering a group holiday with strangers is a leap into the unknown. I was greeted by Sam and Mike, our (thankfully) low-key hosts, shown to my private room (you can save by bunking up with a same sex stranger), then introduced to my fellow holidaymakers. It turned out that there were 17 of us – nine women, eight men – and we were whisked into the lounge for a briefing and welcome drink. The atmosphere was upbeat and easy, and we gathered round one large table for an excellent three-course dinner.
Most Friendship Travel guests are aged between 35 and 65, and our group was at the top end of that range. There was Vivienne, a retired nurse from Cumbria who had just lost her partner, and Adriana, a “silver splitter” relishing retirement. For a few – myself included – it was the first such holiday, but many were inveterate solo travellers, with Ivyon, a former production operator from Bridgend, clocking up more than 90 trips.
The first morning, we set off to our ski lockers at the bottom of the slopes (tip: I booked my equipment hire in advance, saving €40). The group naturally fragmented, allowing small cliques to form – people relaxed as they started to identify potential après buddies.
I skied with Elaine, Clemmie, James and our guide, Luke, in the “level 4 advanced” group (we were asked to rate our ability beforehand). The backbone of Les Deux Alpes, the new Jandri 3S cable car, whisked us up to an altitude of 3,200 metres in 17 minutes – instead of the previous 40. Above broken clouds, we paused to admire the astonishing jagged peaks of the Écrins national park.
We blasted down a mixture of broad blue and red runs, plus some not overly challenging blacks. Although none of us had met before, we quickly settled into a rhythm, looking out for one another as the snow fell softly. There’s safety in numbers, especially on the off-piste sections. “I’d never have tried that alone,” said Clemmie.
Afternoons brought more skiing, followed by hands-in-the-air après at Skandal – reopened in 2025 following an extension – with a DJ on a packed terrace. Around sundown, the chalet WhatsApp group would start to ping. “Polar Bear Pub, anyone?” would be a typical message, often sent by Mícheál from Armagh, a dependable partner for a pint.
Solo travel has undergone a perception shift in recent decades, according to Colum McLornan, who founded Friendship Travel in 1999. “Travelling alone was often seen as unconventional, and for many it carried a stigma. But travellers are increasingly seeking independence, flexibility and personal growth. What was once viewed with hesitation is now celebrated, and solo holidays have become one of the fastest-growing segments in the industry,” he said.
At times, group etiquette could be a minefield: nobody likes waiting for latecomers (me); is it rude to always sit in the same seat at breakfast? (probably); is it OK to peel away from the group and ski by oneself? (up to a point); will I look like a skinflint if I buy my own wine? (absolutely, but life’s too short for plonk).
Honourable mention to Steve, a jolly retired doctor from north London. I enjoyed his vivid stories of cruising the Yangtze River, and skiing with his father in Austria during the late 1950s. Despite our age gap, we struck up a bond that lasted all week. Naturally, not all guests are interesting and fun. One seemingly endless dinner conversation about printer cartridges had me dreaming of Netflix in my room.
Then, suddenly, I found myself hugging my ski gang goodbye, bound for the train. Would I go solo again? Yes. Our hosts were helpful without being intrusive, the skiing superb (especially the high-altitude stuff on Glacier de Mont-de-Lans) and I met people I will stay in touch with. Best of all, I finally got some sleep.
The trip was provided by Friendship Travel. A seven-night package with a private room in a shared chalet, daily breakfast and afternoon tea, dinner with wine on five evenings, and six days of group ski lessons in Les Deux Alpes, costs from £1,820pp. Return rail travel from London to Grenoble was provided by Eurostar

Young people's household income in Europe: How does France compare?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:06 UTC
16:00:06 KST

Households with young people aged 18 to 24 generally have lower equivalised disposable income, but experts note that this may not show the full picture.
Protests have spread across several European countries over rising living costs, unaffordable housing, low wages and pressure on public services in recent weeks. In France, students and young people have been at the forefront of the protests.
That has turned attention to Europe’s Gen Z.
Alberto Alemanno, EU law expert, believes framing protest as “teenage revolution” deeply misleading, and he emphasises that youth protests around Europe are multifaceted.
So, how does the household income of young people compare across Europe? What is the financial situation of their households? And how does France compare with other European countries?
While it does not show all the picture, the equivalised disposable income is one useful indicator. It is “the total income of a household, after tax and other deductions, that is available for spending or saving, divided by the number of household members converted into equalised adults,” according to Eurostat. This also includes social benefits.
Eurostat data are available for young people aged 18 to 24. The figures show the income of the households they live in, rather than what young people themselves earn.
Young people in France live in households with a median equivalised income of €23,850 in 2025, according to Eurostat. The EU average is €21,482.
Among 34 European countries, including EU members, EU candidate countries and EFTA members, France ranks 11th.
“In France, the indicator does not capture students living on their own or in collective housing such as university halls of residence (excluded from the sample),” Anne Brunner, director of studies at Observatoire des inégalités, told Euronews Business.
She also pointed out that the 18–24 age group is heterogeneous: it includes both students living with their parents and young workers, many of whom have few or no qualifications and are in precarious employment and at risk of poverty.
Switzerland has the highest median equivalised household income for young people at €52,206. Luxembourg (€43,028) and Austria (€37,299) follow it.
Among the EU’s ‘Big Four’ economies, Germany has the highest income at €26,330. Italy (€20,315) and Spain (€19,338) are below the EU average.
North Macedonia (€4,640), followed by Albania (€5,736) and Turkey (€5,987), has the lowest median equivalised income for people aged 18 to 24.
This figure is also less than half the EU average in Bulgaria (€8,680), Hungary (€8,576), Serbia (€7,754) and Romania (€7,237).
Data vs reality
The European Youth Forum secretariat noted that income is only part of the equation. In some countries, young people may look better off on paper because they stay in the parental home for longer. But behind those figures is a generation that cannot afford to move out, rent or buy a home, and build a life on their own.
“The paradox is that young people can look better off when they depend on their families for longer, and poorer when they go out on their own,” the secretariat told Euronews Business.
Young people fall behind in most countries
Comparing young people with the whole population in their own country shows whether they are falling behind. Combination of several factors has a role in this.
“Overall, less work experience and a lower level of education (often young people are still studying) than older adults. Additionally, being a student is often associated with a lower level of income. Also, housing arrangements can matter [as the Nordic countries],” Ilari Ilmakunnas, senior researcher at the Finnish Centre for Pensions (ETK), told Euronews Business.
In 28 of the 34 countries, young people live in households with a lower median income than the overall population.
Across the EU, young people have 93.6% of the median income of the whole population: €21,482 compared with €22,939.
In France, the figure is 90.1%. Young people live in households with a median income €2,609 lower than the national median: €23,850 compared with €26,459.
Where is the gap widest?
Finland has the widest gap. Young people there live in households with a median income of €22,277, compared with €29,740 for the whole population. That is 74.9% of the national median.
Denmark (78.3%), Norway (82.7%), Luxembourg (86.0%) and Sweden (88.2%) follow Finland.
Anne Brunner noted that public policy in the Nordic countries actively promotes the autonomy of young people, who consequently leave the parental home earlier and are far more likely to live independently.
“Their household income is then measured on their own, often modest, resources rather than pooled with that of their parents, which mechanically widens the gap with the overall population. A low ratio in these countries should therefore not be read as a sign of greater hardship,” she said.
In six countries, young people live in households with higher income than the whole population. In Croatia, young people’s households have a median of €15,921, compared with €15,057 for the whole population
Croatia leads at 105.7%, followed by Malta (105.5%) and Slovenia (105.4%). Lithuania and Austria are both at 102.1%. Switzerland is at 100.5%.
Austria leads in purchasing power
Price levels differ across Europe. Measured in purchasing power standards (PPS), the median equivalised household income of young people aged 18 to 24 is highest in Austria at 33,052 PPS. Luxembourg (32,391) and Switzerland (29,989) follow.
In PPS terms, France (21,446) ranks 13th, slightly above the EU average.
Germany (24,237) ranks higher, while Spain (21,272) and Italy (20,883) are below France, although the gaps are relatively small.
Albania (8,175), North Macedonia (8,994) and Montenegro (9,955) have the lowest figures.
Call for looking beyond income
The European Youth Forum calls for looking beyond just income and considering the idea of the social wage: the affordable housing, public services, education, healthcare and social protection that determine how far our incomes actually go.
“A decent life should not depend on a good salary alone, or on having family wealth to fall back on. It requires decent wages alongside strong public services that make the essentials affordable,” the secretariat said.

Kweichow Moutai Becomes Premier Partner of the Hong Kong Open 2026, Deepening Its Global Presence
In golf, you must hit one good shot after another while waiting for a rare hole-in-one. Moutai demands a parallel patience: perfecting every step of its craft and letting time do its work. From October 22 to 25, 2026, Moutai served as a Premier Partner of the Link Hong Kong Open, staged at Hong Kong Golf Club at Fanling, where it witnessed outstanding international players in action. One depends on probability, the other on time, yet both point to the same philosophy: bring every part of the process to its highest standard, and then wait for the result to come.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
In golf, you must hitFrom the Chishui River to the Golf Course
Reframing Moutai’s Brand Narrative
For Moutai, waiting is not a metaphor, but part of the craft itself. Its production takes one year and eight months, followed by three years of storage, then blending and stabilization; from the start of production to release takes at least five years. Through years of maturation, its initial sharpness gradually gives way to greater mellowness, richness and complexity. The idea that Moutai “grows more fragrant with age” is more than a simple description; it is the physical trace that time leaves within the spirit.
When Moutai ventures overseas, it brings with it more than a product. It carries a philosophy of time and a set of values steeped in Eastern thought. These values happen to resonate with the spirit of golf: discipline, etiquette, patience and the pursuit of excellence.
For years, brand narratives around Chinese baijiu in its home market have been closely tied to banquet and dining occasions. Golf offers a distinctly different context for communication. It naturally brings together high-net-worth audiences who value quality living and social affinity. Through its partnership with the Asian Tour, Moutai is reaching this audience. During the Hong Kong Open, golf clinics and spectator engagement activities turned the brand from something simply seen into something that could be experienced and participated in. The sophistication of Moutai’s association with golf lies in the new associations the brand gains between each swing: “healthy social interaction” and “elegant living.”
From the Hong Kong Fairways to a Way of Life
A Shared Journey in Step with Time
There is a quiet composure within Hong Kong’s sporting culture that resonates deeply with golf. The Hong Kong Jockey Club and the Hong Kong Golf Club jointly launched the Jockey Club Community Golf Programme, supported by a HK$32 million grant from The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust, helping golf move from an “elite sport” towards one with broader public participation. The city is working to make golf a way of life that more people can experience for themselves.
This time, as Moutai and the Asian Tour join hands again in Hong Kong, Moutai is moving from a “participant” in the tournament experience to a “companion” to the city’s sporting culture.
From On-Course Experience to Podium Glory
Anchoring Moutai’s Place on the Global Stage
The credibility of the Link Hong Kong Open, a tournament regarded as a “gold standard”, further elevates this moment of honour within the global professional golf landscape. The event has been voted The International Series Tournament of the Year by Asian Tour players for the third consecutive year. At a deeper level, golf allows Moutai to communicate more than the baijiu itself; it conveys a lifestyle that resonates with enthusiasts worldwide: precision, discipline, respect for tradition and the courage to challenge.
From the banks of the Chishui River to the fairways of Fanling, from taking products global to taking culture global, Moutai is quietly deepening its international presence - one swing and one raised glass at a time.

TOKYO, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda died of heart failure at a hospital in Tokyo on Oct. 22 at the age of 90, local media reported Monday.
Born on July 16, 1936, in Takasaki, Gunma Prefecture, Fukuda was the eldest son of former Prime Minister Takeo Fukuda and graduated from Waseda University.
He was elected to the House of Representatives in 1990 and served as chief cabinet secretary in the cabinets of Yoshiro Mori and Junichiro Koizumi.
Fukuda became prime minister in September 2007 and resigned in September 2008.
During his tenure as prime minister, Fukuda worked to improve and develop China-Japan relations. In 2008, the two countries issued the China-Japan Joint Statement on All-round Promotion of Strategic Relationship of Mutual Benefit.
After retiring from politics in 2012, Fukuda remained a committed advocate of China-Japan friendship and visited China many times. ■

Antonelli dominates U.S. Grand Prix but must wait to clinch F1 title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:52:00 CST
15:52:00 KST

Race winner Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli of Italy celebrates on the podium after the Formula One United States Grand Prix, in Austin, Texas, the United States, Oct. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Xiaoling)
by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli took another major step toward becoming Formula 1's youngest world champion with a commanding victory at the United States Grand Prix on Sunday, although the Italian must wait at least another week to secure the title.
Starting from pole position, Antonelli controlled the 56-lap race at the Circuit of the Americas, making a one-stop strategy work to claim his ninth victory of the season, finishing 13 seconds ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.
Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the podium in third, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and McLaren's Lando Norris.
The result extended Antonelli's championship lead over Mercedes teammate George Russell to 123 points with five races remaining. However, Russell's eighth-place finish and Hamilton's fourth place prevented the 20-year-old from securing the title in Austin.
Antonelli, who is in only his second F1 season, could now clinch the championship at next weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, potentially surpassing Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 when he became the sport's youngest world champion in 2010.
The Italian made a clean getaway from pole, while Leclerc and Verstappen battled behind him on the opening lap. Leclerc initially moved ahead of the Dutchman, only for Verstappen to reclaim second place before the end of the lap.
Their battle allowed Antonelli to establish an advantage of more than two seconds almost immediately, and the Mercedes driver steadily extended his lead as the opening stint progressed.
While most of his rivals opted for two pit stops, Antonelli made his medium tyres last before switching to the hard compound, allowing him to maintain track position and control the race without needing a second stop.
The strategy proved decisive as Ferrari and Red Bull were unable to mount a sustained challenge, with Antonelli managing his tyres effectively through the closing stages.
Behind him, Leclerc and Verstappen fought over second place, with the Ferrari driver eventually emerging ahead to claim his second consecutive runner-up finish.
Verstappen struggled with his Red Bull's performance during the race but held on to third, while Hamilton finished fourth to help Ferrari secure a strong points haul.
Russell endured a difficult afternoon in the other Mercedes, finishing eighth after struggling for pace and receiving a five-second penalty. His result effectively ended any realistic prospect of challenging Antonelli for the championship, although he remains mathematically in contention.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri finished seventh, behind Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, while Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson and Alpine's Pierre Gasly completed the top 10.
The race saw three retirements, with Haas driver Oliver Bearman, Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas all failing to finish.
Antonelli's victory also provided encouragement for Mercedes following an uncertain introduction to its latest upgrade package, which had initially struggled to deliver the expected performance gains at the previous two rounds in Malaysia and Singapore.
With 125 points still available over the final five races, Antonelli now needs only to avoid a substantial loss of ground to his closest rivals in Mexico to secure a historic first world championship. ■
