Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (C), candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, delivers a speech following his victory in the presidential runoff in Sao Paulo, Brazil, Oct. 25, 2026. Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, won Sunday's presidential runoff, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court on Sunday night. (Photo by Paulo Lopes/Xinhua)
BRASILIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, won Sunday's presidential runoff, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court on Sunday night.
With 99.99 percent of the votes counted, Lula received 51.79 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.21 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the official tally.
Lula will be sworn in on Jan. 5, 2027, for a four-year term, his fourth as Brazil's president.
Speaking in a live speech in Sao Paulo following his victory, Lula vowed to work with the conservative Congress elected by the people and ensure greater public participation in the decision-making process.
He also stressed the need to strengthen digital regulation after defeating foreign interference through digital platforms, stressing that Brazil is no one's backyard.
Lula also pledged to strengthen public healthcare, improve care for the elderly, respect women and continue efforts to combat climate change.
"This election taught me many lessons. I want to say that we will change the way this country is governed. We will have the people participate more in our decisions," he said.
Meanwhile, Flavio Bolsonaro, speaking in the Brazilian capital of Brasilia, said it is "impossible" to recognize the results, and called for the annulment of the election, alleging unequal treatment of voters following an extension of voting hours.
Earlier on Sunday, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ordered polling stations nationwide to extend voting by two hours in response to disruptions caused by public transport stoppages and heavy rain. The measure applied only to polling stations that remained open when the decision was communicated by the Superior Electoral Court; stations that had already closed were not reopened.
Bolsonaro argued that the decision had disadvantaged voters in areas where polling stations were not reopened and that his legal team would challenge the results.
Under Brazil's electoral rules, if no presidential candidate wins outright in the first round by securing more than half of the valid votes, the top two candidates advance to a runoff.
In the first round, held on Oct. 4, Flavio Bolsonaro finished ahead of incumbent Lula, winning about 47 percent of the valid votes against Lula's roughly 45 percent.
Presidents from several Latin American countries congratulated Lula on his victory. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum hailed the result as a victory for the Brazilian people and democracy, while Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi praised Brazil's electoral process as a celebration of democracy.
Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel called for stronger regional integration. Paraguayan President Santiago Pena emphasized cooperation with Brazil to promote regional integration and development, while Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz highlighted the countries' shared history and pledged to strengthen bilateral ties. Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino also congratulated Lula and expressed his commitment to continued cooperation. ■

Climate change threatens ecological balance of South Australia's coastal lagoon: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:51:50 CST
15:51:50 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Climate change could reshape phytoplankton communities and increase the risk of harmful algal blooms in the Coorong, a shallow coastal lagoon in the state of South Australia, a new study finds.
Led by Flinders University researchers and funded by the Goyder Institute for Water Research in Australia, the study examined phytoplankton across the Coorong, combining field samples from freshwater to salty habitats with 16 years of historical data, according to a university statement released on Sunday.
The researchers found that changes to salinity and water levels through variations in freshwater inputs to the Coorong had the most influence on phytoplankton abundance, diversity and community structure.
Freshwater and mildly salty habitats supported the greatest number of species, while extremely salty habitats had fewer species and were dominated by diatoms and dinoflagellates, two major groups of single-celled phytoplankton, the study published in Continental Shelf Research found.
The researchers also found that while the levels of harmful bloom-forming species in the Coorong are low overall, there are more than 80 phytoplankton species capable of producing toxins. ■

AI model Claude bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available US state of Georgia aggregate voter counts without human authorization, Anthropic said in a statement on Sunday.
"Claude didn't access the state's voter registration system or change or pull any voting records," Anthropic said, adding that it has since taken steps to block these kinds of actions.
Anthropic said in a blog post earlier this month it found examples of Claude "working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee," and some of these cases involved websites run by US government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels.
The secretary of state's office in Georgia did not respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours.
Axios first reported the unauthorized action by Claude.
Anthropic AI passes itself as human during cybersecurity exercise
On Friday, Anthropic revealed that one of its artificial intelligence models passed itself off as human during a cybersecurity exercise to fool a human outside the exercise.
According to Anthropic, the model, which used Mythos 5, performed unsanctioned actions in nine out of 43 runs that impacted humans not participating in the exercise, with one of the cases even involving the AI pretending to be human.
The attack, which was described by the AI Security Institute (AISI) as a "supply chain attack," attempted to disrupt a public code repository on the GitHub platform by creating fake inquiries, introducing corrupted data, and even demanding changes by creating false accounts on the platform.
Tobias Holcman contributed to this report.

Will 70,000 Israelis returning from abroad for Election Day tip the political balance? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:23 UTC
15:47:23 KST

An estimated 70,000 Israelis living abroad have returned or are expected to return to Israel ahead of Tuesday's Knesset elections, potentially influencing the results if the race between the political blocs is close.
This begs the question: Could the Israelis arriving from abroad influence the election results?
In the 2022 elections, approximately 36,000 votes were needed to secure one Knesset seat. Given population growth and an expected increase in voter turnout, estimates suggest that the threshold for a seat could rise to approximately 38,000 to 39,000 votes.
It is difficult to determine which parties most of the Israelis arriving from abroad will support. Some estimates suggest that many will vote for the change bloc, but there is no reliable measure of their political preferences.
Even if, for example, 60% support the change bloc, this would add at most one to one-and-a-half Knesset seats.
These figures, however, remain estimates. The election results will reveal whether Israelis living abroad have tipped the balance in the event of a close race between the political blocs.
Election Day boosts hotel occupancy by 23%
The vast majority of Israelis arriving from overseas are combining family visits and vacations with Election Day. Most are staying with relatives or friends, or in apartments they own in Israel that are currently vacant.
However, some have chosen to stay in hotels.
Africa Israel Hotels reported an approximately 23% increase in hotel occupancy during election week. Although the comparison is with October of last year, when the security situation was more complicated, the increase appears significant.
"We are seeing an increase in occupancy at Africa Israel Hotels properties across the country ahead of Election Day. We are seeing more Israelis choosing to combine exercising their democratic right with a short vacation, taking advantage of the opportunity to break from their routine and enjoy a hotel stay," said Alex Eliyahu, marketing director of Africa Israel Hotels.
"Alongside the increase in demand, the chain is offering particularly attractive promotions and accommodation packages for Election Day, allowing guests to enjoy vacations at a variety of destinations across the country at affordable prices."
Fattal Hotels also reported an increase in room occupancy at its properties, particularly in central Israel.
"We are seeing an increase in bookings compared with October of last year, apparently due to the elections," said Maya Shalev, vice president of marketing and sales at Fattal Hotels.
"Many Israelis are taking advantage of the day off to combine voting with a vacation. Accordingly, we have offered promotions of up to 30% off, along with an additional 10% discount for members of the 'Fattal and Friends' club between October 25 and 29. At the same time, we are seeing bookings made from abroad for these dates, which may indicate that Israelis are coming to Israel to vote."
'I came from Miami to vote': Israelis returning to the ballot box
Among the tens of thousands who attended the October Council rally at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday night were Israelis living abroad.
"I came from Miami to vote. I coordinated my vacation in Israel with Election Day, and I'm returning to the US at the beginning of November," said Judy, who has lived in the US for more than 50 years.
"Many Israelis living in Miami and Los Angeles tend to vote for the Right. I'm different, and I'm not alone."
Nurit, from the South Sharon area, attended the rally with her son-in-law and grandson, who had arrived from Canada.
"My grandson is voting for the first time. He's 18 years old. They're combining a family visit with voting in the elections. My daughter stayed in Canada to be with my younger grandson."
Ofer, who arrived from New York, also shared his experience.
"We came to Israel specifically to vote. We're returning to the US the day after the elections. We have family here, and it's an opportunity to see everyone."
Gidi, who arrived from Australia with his wife, is scheduled to fly out of Ben-Gurion Airport on Wednesday.
"We've already been here for three weeks. We've met with many family members and friends. And I'm going back on Wednesday because I have work commitments. My wife will stay here for another two weeks."
In contrast, Zehava, who arrived on a flight from New York, said: "I'm voting for Likud, and I came to visit family ahead of the elections. I planned it in advance."
Canceled flights leave some Israelis unable to vote
Some Israelis had hoped to travel to Israel but were left stranded abroad after flydubai canceled flights following an attempted terrorist attack.
"Flydubai's cancellation caused flight prices to the Far East to rise," explained a young man who had planned to travel to Israel ahead of the elections.
There are also Israelis who live in Israel but will be abroad on Election Day. However, their number appears to be lower than the number of Israelis arriving from overseas.
"I booked the flight tickets for a vacation with my husband in Vietnam almost a year ago, and we didn't know the elections would be held in October. This will be the first time I don't vote. It breaks my heart, but we're going ahead with the vacation we started planning a year ago," said Racheli from Ramat Gan.
"It's a shame that Israelis traveling abroad can't vote on Election Day."

Could Trump's allies push Netanyahu into unity gov't without his far-right partners? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:22 UTC
15:47:22 KST

Voices within US President Donald Trump's inner circle are advocating for the establishment of a broad and moderate Israeli unity government without National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, with some even floating the idea of a rotation agreement in which Benjamin Netanyahu would serve as prime minister first.
However, Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot and former prime minister Naftali Bennett remain opposed to serving under him, and American officials have yet to discuss the framework with them.
American billionaire Bill Ackman, a prominent supporter of Trump with close ties to his circle, publicly called on Sunday for the formation of a broad, moderate Israeli government that excludes Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In a social media post, Ackman argued that such a government would allow Israel to restore its international standing, expand the Abraham Accords, and improve relations with both major political parties in the United States.
Ackman, who heads the hedge fund Pershing Square, supported Trump in the presidential election and is considered an influential figure in US political and business circles. He criticized Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, stating that their presence harms Israel's global image and its ability to advance key diplomatic objectives. At the same time, he praised Netanyahu and his relationship with Trump. Ackman favors Netanyahu remaining in office, but with a different set of coalition partners.
Realizing Trump's Middle East ambitions requires a change in Israel's Knesset
Ackman is not the only figure in Trump's orbit holding this view. According to several sources, additional figures in Washington believe that over the remaining two years of the president's term, realizing his ambitious Middle East plans requires a change in the composition of Israel's government.
Foremost among these plans is the possibility of a historic normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia, a prospect difficult to envision advancing while Ben-Gvir and Smotrich sit at the cabinet table.
Several senior advisors to Trump believe an Israeli government without Netanyahu's far-right partners would make it significantly easier to advance the president's regional policy.
This comes amid existing friction between Washington and Jerusalem: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are reportedly frustrated by the pace at which Netanyahu is advancing Trump's plan for Gaza; Special Envoy Tom Barrick disagrees with Israel's strategy regarding Syria; and officials around Secretary of State Marco Rubio seek to strengthen the Lebanese government while expressing frustration over insufficient action regarding Jewish violence in Judea and Samaria.
These officials place high importance on the composition of Israel's next government, which could impact Trump's chances of achieving major diplomatic breakthroughs before his term ends. A deal with Saudi Arabia, for instance, requires difficult Israeli decisions on the Palestinian issue and other regional matters.
A government reliant on Ben-Gvir and Smotrich could struggle to make such choices, even if Netanyahu himself were willing to do so. However, replacing coalition partners alone does not guarantee a deal: Riyadh maintains its own political demands, including tangible progress on the Palestinian issue.
Trump's inner circles question viability of diplomacy with Netanyahu around
Some within Trump's circle even question whether a diplomatic breakthrough is achievable as long as Netanyahu serves as prime minister. Consequently, an idea has emerged within the president's team for a rotation-based unity government: Netanyahu would serve during the first year, after which another prime minister would replace him to lead negotiations with the Saudis before the conclusion of Trump's term.
Proponents of the idea believe this arrangement would maintain governance continuity in the first year while entrusting regional diplomatic efforts to a prime minister who is not dependent on Netanyahu's current partners. According to several Israeli and American sources, Netanyahu told Trump he wants to form a unity government and will work toward that goal after the election.
Israel's Ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter, also publicly said Netanyahu wants a broad government. Leiter said Netanyahu prefers a national unity government over continuing with the current coalition makeup.
He also addressed Ben-Gvir's future, saying Netanyahu made it clear he would not serve as national security minister again. The comments drew a sharp reaction from Otzma Yehudit, whose officials fear Netanyahu is paving the way for a coalition with Eisenkot at the expense of his current partners. For his part, Ben-Gvir called on Netanyahu to form a right-wing government rather than one with Eisenkot.
Although the idea originated in his inner circle, Trump has not formally endorsed the initiative. The president publicly backed Netanyahu on October 18, even as several advisors expressed reservations. Vice President JD Vance did not join the public endorsement.
Furthermore, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee explicitly denied allegations of an American effort to push a unity government, clarifying that the administration does not intervene in Israeli elections or dictate actions to the prime minister.
Meanwhile, the proposals discussed in Washington remain far removed from Israel's political reality. American officials have not conducted a deep feasibility check with leaders of the change bloc, and no substantive talks have taken place with Eisenkot or other senior figures in the opposition regarding the proposed framework. Electoral scenarios also present obstacles for the initiative.
If Netanyahu's bloc secures 61 mandates, he is expected to receive the mandate to form a government, but it remains doubtful whether Eisenkot or Bennett would agree to join. Additionally, ultra-Orthodox parties demand the passage of the conscription bill as a precondition for coalition talks. Conversely, if the right-wing bloc fails to secure a majority, Netanyahu may not get the first chance to form a government.
Even in the event of a victory for the right-wing bloc, Netanyahu could find himself in a trap: his natural partners will demand the fulfillment of previous commitments, primarily the ultra-Orthodox demands regarding military draft legislation.
Reaching out to Eisenkot and Bennett would require offering them a partnership in a government they have pledged not to join. Even within the right-wing bloc, few believe Eisenkot or Bennett would consent to such a move.

Opinion polls point to a tight contest, with neither Netanyahu's ruling Likud bloc nor an opposition alliance centered on former military chief Gadi Eisenkot expected to secure the 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset needed to govern.
That raises the prospect of lengthy coalition negotiations or even another election, all at time when one of the key drivers of the Israeli market rally - the global frenzy around AI - has also started to splutter.
Since the October 7 Hamas attacks in 2023, the Tel Aviv stock market has soared 130%, far outpacing Wall Street's 80% gain, while the shekel has climbed 25%, one of the world's strongest currency performances.
Analysts attribute some of that strength to Israel's tech sector and the global AI boom, while defense spending, which has nearly doubled to around 8% of GDP, has also provided a boost.
With both Netanyahu and Eisenkot vowing to maintain pressure on Hamas and Iran, markets are focused on their broader policy differences. JPMorgan estimates the shekel could swing as much as 3% depending on the result.
Opposition victory could improve Israeli economic position
An opposition victory that improves relations with Western allies and halts a judicial overhaul that sparked mass protests in 2023 could strengthen the currency, JPMorgan said, while another Netanyahu-led government could weaken it.
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, while stopping short of backing a candidate, said a government without far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich would signal that Israel was "turning a new page," potentially helping rebuild its international credibility and expand the Abraham Accords with its neighbors.
IBI Investment House also expects an opposition victory to lift the markets. "From a capital markets perspective, this would likely be reflected in a decline in Israel's risk premium, appreciation pressure on the shekel, and a positive reaction in the local market," IBI's Chief Economist Rafi Gozlan said.
According to prediction market Polymarket, close to 60% are betting on Eisenkot becoming the next Israeli prime minister, compared with 27% for Netanyahu.
"The most significant issue is what the result will mean for the region," said Equity Bank's chief economic adviser Charlie Robertson. "If Netanyahu is reelected, it might increase the chances of further escalation with Iran, whereas a defeat might be seen as lessening the tensions."
But the prospect of gains under an opposition government does not mean investors expect Israeli assets to suffer if Netanyahu remains in power. Stocks and bonds have proved remarkably resilient through years of war and political upheaval, and some investors remain confident in the economy regardless of the election outcome.
Union Investment's Sergey Dergachev has been buying Israeli bonds ahead of the election, betting the economy and companies he favors will remain fundamentally strong. "We are very constructive on Israeli credits going into the election," Dergachev said, adding that bonds were less prone to major swings and the region's intertwined conflicts should eventually ease.
Tel Aviv shares were up around 1% in the final session ahead of Tuesday's vote, taking their year-to-date gain to about 12%.
However, both they and the shekel have pulled back some 10% since May. Analysts again point to the strong link to tech, given global AI indexes have also been dropping, although there has been one nagging issue throughout the last three years.
Despite the rally, foreign investors remain cautious. Copley Fund Research data show the share of global funds holding Israeli equities is at a record low, having fallen sharply since 2023.
TS Lombard's Christopher Granville cited central bank estimates that the war had cost the economy more than $55 billion by last year, equivalent to 8.6% in cumulative lost GDP growth.
Public debt, budget deficit high amid Iran war
Israel's fiscal position is another focus. Public debt has risen to nearly 70% of GDP, about 10 percentage points higher than in 2022, while the budget deficit is expected to remain around 4.5% of GDP, up from less than 2% before the conflict.
Central bank head Amir Yaron stressed last week the need to "preserve adequate fiscal policy space" given the Iran war.
Like stocks, Israeli government bonds have rallied, returning about 30% over the last two years, more than double the main emerging market indexes.
The main risk for investors is an inconclusive result that prolongs political uncertainty, delaying budgets, reforms and investment, some investors believe.
That uncertainty can produce sharp short-term swings. Tel Aviv Stock Exchange research covering the last 10 elections found volatility in leading share indexes rose by as much as 45% in the weeks after voting compared with a typical week. But initial losses were typically recovered within a month, with the indexes posting an average gain of about 1.7%.
Over a longer horizon, the TA-125 returned an average 16.4% in the year following elections, compared with a long-term annual average of 11.5%, the research found. Political deadlock often weighed on stocks before voting, but the effects typically faded within months, said Nissan Avraham, an analyst at the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's research unit.
Israeli businesses continue thriving despite political, regional upheaval
That record supports the view that elections matter less for Israeli companies than many investors assume.
Lior Yochpaz, chief investment officer at insurance company Menora Mivtachim, said businesses have continued to thrive despite years of political upheaval, judicial overhaul proposals, and regional conflict, helped by a relatively business-friendly environment.
For some investors, however, the more attractive election trade lies outside Israel. TT International's Jean-Charles Sambor said an opposition victory or weakened Netanyahu government could ease regional tensions and benefit Lebanese bonds.
"The best way to play it for us is through other Middle East countries, and for us Lebanon is a good proxy," Sambor said.

Appeals court skeptical over Trump administration lawsuit against California mail-in ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:46:46 UTC
15:46:46 KST

A federal appeals court appeared skeptical on Sunday of a lawsuit filed by US President Donald Trump's administration that seeks to force California officials to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots the administration says were sent to noncitizens ahead of midterm elections.
During a rare weekend oral argument, two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals sharply questioned a Justice Department lawyer about the lawsuit, a high-profile effort by the Trump administration to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms.
The Department of Justice's lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump's administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
At the end of the two-hour oral argument, Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to rule as quickly as possible.
Trump's Justice Department has warned election officials across California that they could be targets of federal scrutiny if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls. It has distributed to California officials a list of 20,000 people it says are likely aliens registered to vote in the state, a Democratic stronghold.
Data shows ineligible voting in US exceedingly rare
California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and, in a court filing, stated that the Justice Department's assertions relied on suspect data.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation this year found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit in federal court in Los Angeles on October 15. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list from the rest of the ballots and not count them until it verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
Bennett, a Trump-appointed judge, said during Sunday's oral argument that the lawsuit could not be reconciled with a provision of the US Constitution known as the Elections Clause, which gives states the authority to set election processes.
"It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause," Bennett told Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly. "How can we do that?"
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
California focal point of Trump's anti-immigration crackdown
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold, with 52 seats in the House of Representatives — more than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump's fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through so-called sanctuary state policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has also long asserted that California's immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of former president Joe Biden, said on Sunday that he was confused by the question of why the appeals court should have jurisdiction to rule at this juncture, noting that the lower court judge assigned to the case had already set a hearing for Tuesday.

Green light shining on Mount Olympos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:43:27 UTC
15:43:27 KST

The U.N. climate conference (COP31), which will be held in Antalya this November, has been making headlines lately. I’ve been spending more time in Antalya due to a small assignment I’ve taken on. While the climate summit may not be on many people’s radar, climate change inevitably affects everyone. Recent flood disasters have turned our lives upside down. I don’t know if COP31 decisions are as binding on governments as they used to be, but it’s important from our perspective that the summit is being held in Antalya. Antalya and its surrounding areas are among our leading agricultural regions. At the same time, the Bey Mountains, which form the city’s backdrop, are a unique natural treasure. Mount Olympos, just west of the Antalya Gulf, is particularly special because at the top of its Çıralı hill is an ever-burning flame called Yanar Taş, which simply means “The Burning Stone.” The local name of the hill indicates its never-dying spark of light, as “Çıralı” means “with kindling firewood.” According to mythology, the flames came from the mouth of the monster Chimera.
Çıralı Hill is rocky, but further inland, you will find yourself in a wonderland of amazing flavors and aromas. Deep in the woods, you can find wild honey and mushrooms, and the air in the forest is healing. Down from the village of Beycik is a small retreat called the Olympos Mountain Lodge. It has only a few rooms, all of which face the woods. When Mehmet Ali Börtücene, the chef at The Rabbit Hole at Olympos Mountain Lodge, called me and offered me the chance to escape to Olympos, I put all my plans on hold for a night.
My reason for escaping wasn’t just my love for Olympos, though. It was mostly curiosity. I was eager to meet the trio of chefs — three nature-loving chefs whose cuisine has intrigued me and whose work I’ve followed from afar: Mehmet Ali Börtücene of The Rabbit Hole, the host; Bahtiyar Büyükduman of Telezzüz in Istanbul; and Daniel Vidal of Baldío in Mexico City. I wanted to witness what they would create when they came together.
Arca Tierra-Baldío: Mexico’s green star
The concept of “zero waste” has been rising in popularity in recent years. Mexico City, one of the world’s most populous cities, is likely a prime candidate for this concept. Baldío, the city’s first and only restaurant with a Green Michelin Star, is an Arca Tierra project. The core idea is simple: Source all ingredients from small-scale farmers, waste nothing and use fermentation to transform materials destined for the trash into delicious meals. Of course, achieving this in a bustling urban environment is no easy feat. The collaboration between Baldío chef Daniel Vidal and Arca Tierra founder Pablo Usobiaga has made it possible to bring this mission to life. The source of the food is key to the endeavor’s success. The starting point is the chinampas, agricultural islands dating back two thousand years. These man-made, floating gardens are essentially islands. The restaurant sources its fresh ingredients from these islands. They also apply the zero-waste concept to the full, that’s why they are nicknamed the restaurant without a trash bin. This is precisely how Baldío earned its Green Michelin Star.
Different landscapes, shared mindset
How did this green connection stretching from Mexico to a mountain village in Antalya, Türkiye, come about? Thanks to Mehmet Ali Börtücene, who is well known in Ankara and is affectionately called “Mali” by his friends. His “rabbit hole,” an escape from Ankara, is the Olympos Mountain Lodge in Beycik village. The lodge offers a tasting menu that changes every night, providing a surprising adventure where you never know what you’ll encounter — just like falling down the rabbit hole in Alice in Wonderland. After Mali’s exploratory trip to Mexico, his like-minded Mexican friends followed him into this rabbit hole. Bahtiyar Büyükduman, the chef at Telezzüz — Istanbul’s go-to spot for plant-based cuisine and recipient of the Michelin Green Star — also joined them, contributing with finding a sponsor for the whole mission. His totally vegan restaurant is the only vegan fine/dining venue in Istanbul and as he is an archaeologist in origin, he likes to dig deep down in the history of dishes and ingredients.
These three like-minded chefs have prepared a special nine-course tasting menu. They are all committed to sustainability. They find joy in even the smallest things they forage and gather in nature. They don’t want to waste anything. Bahtiyar’s Ajo Blanco dish used zucchini stems and was inspired by the Mediterranean tradition of repurposing stale bread.
Daniel’s amazing white mole dish was straight out of the woods, featuring local wild mushrooms and pine nuts foraged from the forest and served with white mole sauce. Mali’s crispy chicken was blended with forest herbs, his butter spread was cedar-smoked and the olive explosion was straight from the olive tree in the garden, only a few meters away from the kitchen. Each flavor was a new discovery and an exciting surprise.
This culinary collaboration, shaped around the gastronomic heritage of Anatolia and Mexico, as well as a focus on sustainability and a zero-waste approach, brought together three different chefs not only at a shared table but also with a shared vision and a common goal. And that was what truly mattered. While Antalya was bustling with preparations for COP31, a quiet yet powerful voice emerged from the Olympos Mountain. The ever-burning flame of Yanat Taş, the burning stone, seemed to shine even brighter. The shared vision of these three eco-conscious chefs lit a green light for the future.

TTK to host 20th Turkish History Congress in Ankara

AA Photo
The capital Ankara is set to host the 20th Turkish History Congress from Oct. 26 to 30 at the Atatürk Supreme Council for Culture, Language and History campus, Turkish Historical Society (TTK) President Professor Dr. Haluk Selvi has announced.
Established in 1932, the landmark congress continues to illuminate research on Turkish history. It gained international prominence during its second edition in 1937, attracting scholars and participants from across the globe.
TTK President Selvi noted that they began preparations for the 20th conference approximately two years ago. He mentioned they have invited academics from both Türkiye and abroad to Ankara and have finalized the conference topics.
“The 230 papers selected through the academic selection process will be presented by 300 scholars from 30 different countries. At the conference, a wide range of topics related to Turkish history — from the earliest times to the present — across a broad geographical area stretching from Central Asia to the Balkans and from Crimea to Qatar will be addressed by an international audience,” he said.
Selvi explained that the purpose of the Turkish History Congress is to demonstrate the Turkish contribution to civilization through historical data in response to Western-centric claims, and announced that the papers presented will be published in a book.
As the conference runs through Oct. 29, a special panel will be held to observe Republic Day, Selvi announced. He also revealed that another special panel at the conference will focus on the role of institutes in historical writing, featuring the participation of scholars from the Turkic states and Italy.
Selvi stated their great honor in hosting the congress as the TTK approaches its 100th anniversary. “Throughout the five-day congress, sessions and special exhibitions will be held in five different halls. We invite history enthusiasts and history students from all over to our conference,” Selvi said.

Türkiye converts food waste into animal feed in 74 provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:43:07 UTC
15:43:07 KST

Food waste collected from public institutions and large-scale catering facilities is being converted into animal feed in 74 of Türkiye’s 81 provinces, with daily production reaching 31,274 kilograms, according to Interior Ministry sources.
The initiative is part of the Zero Waste Project, spearheaded by first lady Emine Erdoğan. Under the scheme, food waste collected through provincial governor’s offices and municipalities from student dormitories run by the Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution (KYK), military units, hospitals, prisons, hotels and restaurants is processed into animal feed.
Machines and equipment for converting food waste into animal feed are available in 74 provinces, with a combined daily production capacity of 65,352 kilograms. However, actual daily output stands at 31,274 kilograms, indicating that existing facilities are operating below half of their total capacity.
Iğdır, Kahramanmaraş, Kırıkkale, Kocaeli, Kütahya, Samsun and Tunceli are the seven provinces without equipment to process food waste into animal feed.
An inspection report recommended that food products deemed unfit for human consumption but suitable for animal feed — including items ordered destroyed under insurance procedures or official inspections — be redirected to animal shelters and designated natural habitats where appropriate. The report also called for efforts to expand the use of food-processing equipment at animal shelters.
Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi said the government was pursuing a comprehensive approach to protecting, housing and caring for stray animals, while also seeking to use public resources more efficiently.
He said the Zero Waste Project had helped protect the environment and make better use of existing resources, adding that the government aimed to establish feed production facilities in the seven provinces currently lacking them through cooperation with relevant institutions and local authorities.
“On the one hand, we aim to bring food waste generated in public institutions, dormitories, hospitals, military units and mass-consumption facilities back into the economy; on the other, we seek to reduce feeding costs at animal shelters and in natural habitats as much as possible,” Çiftçi said.
He added that the ultimate goal was to establish a sustainable system in all 81 provinces that prevents waste, saves public funds and improves conditions for stray animals.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth presidential term in the Oct. 25 runoff, while his right-wing challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to concede and vowed to seek the election’s annulment.
Lula received 51.79 percent of valid votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.21 percent, according to the Superior Electoral Court, finishing more than 4.4 million votes ahead.
Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, challenged Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours, arguing that it treated voters in different states unequally.
“It is impossible to recognize the election result under these circumstances. We will seek its annulment,” he told reporters.
The ruling, issued shortly before the scheduled 5 p.m. closing time, caused confusion as many polling stations had already closed. Authorities subsequently clarified that the extension applied only to stations still open.
Both campaigns had requested longer voting hours. Lula’s team cited problems with transport to polling stations, while Bolsonaro’s campaign sought extensions in some municipalities affected by heavy rain, flooding and road closures.
Electoral court president Kassio Nunes Marques said the extension had not affected the outcome.
Addressing supporters at a hotel in São Paulo, Lula thanked voters and defended Brazil’s sovereignty.
“This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard,” he said.
He pledged to expand full-day schooling and financial support for students, develop Brazilian artificial intelligence and use renewable energy to support data centers. He also called for tighter regulation of technology companies, accusing them of seeking to influence elections.
Right-wing parties retained control of the governorships in São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro. Lula’s Workers’ Party won the runoff in Rio Grande do Norte, maintaining its hold on four northeastern states alongside Bahia, Ceará and Piauí.

Independent republics, castles and bagels: How to spend 24 hours in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:41:14 UTC
15:41:14 KST

From strolling around the UNESCO-listed Old Town to reading the constitution of the independent republic Užupis, Lithuania’s capital city is perfect to explore in just one day.
Back in 2018, Lithuania’s capital Vilnius marketed itself as the “G-spot of Europe”, claiming that “nobody knows where it is but when you find it, it’s amazing”.
While I can’t comment on improvements around sex education (except anecdotally), more and more people are finally discovering the joys of the Baltics with the rise of “coolcations”.
I visited both Latvia and Estonia in the summer last year, and this October, after a quick return to Riga and a detour to Sigulda, Latvia’s autumn capital, I made it down to Vilnius.
Amazing? With its UNESCO-listed baroque Old Town, its growing food scene, and fascinating museums, I’d say so.
If you only have 24 hours in Vilnius, here’s where to go and what to see.
Things to see and do in Vilnius
Climb up to Gediminas Tower
The best way to admire the city is from above, and there’s no better place for it than Gediminas Tower.
Located at the top of Gediminas Hill, the tower is what remains of the Upper Castle. Inside, you’ll find displays showing you what the castle looked like over its many iterations, starting from when it was first built by Gediminas, the Grand Duke of Lithuania who founded Vilnius.
The tower has long been a symbol of the city as the place where the tricolour flag was hoisted for the very first time in 1919 during Lithuania’s independence between the two World Wars, as well as the spot where it was rehoisted in 1988 during the independence movement during the Soviet era. This history is also explored through the Frequency of Freedom exhibition inside.
After exploring the exhibitions, you’re treated to an incredible view from the rooftop.
As an aside, if you do visit Vilnius during the warmer months, you can get an even better view by booking a hot air balloon ride over the city.
Visit the Vilnius Cathedral…
Just down the road from the castle complex you’ll find Vilnius Cathedral and its bell tower.
While its current form is neoclassical, the cathedral has been rebuilt several times following fires, with parts dating back to the 13th century in the catacombs.
Once used for the inaugurations of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania, the cathedral is also home to the Chapel of Saint Casimir, the Patron Saint of Luthania. Born into the royal family, he was known for its devotion to God and was recognised by the Pope in 1602.
…and the Church of St. Anne
One of the most beautiful churches in Lithuania, the Church of St. Anne was built in a Gothic style in the late 15th century.
Such is its beauty that Napoleon apparently said he wanted to carry the church back home with him to Paris “in the palm of his hand”. Emphasis on apparently – it’s a legend rather than provable fact, although it is very pretty I must admit.
Wander around Bernardine Gardens
Behind the Church of St. Anne and the Bernardine Monastery are the Bernardine Gardens.
Cultivated by the Bernadine monks in the 15th century, this once swampy area was transformed into a collection of planted gardens with several ponds, and it even has a botanical garden.
Located right next to the river, it’s a peaceful spot for a stroll, particularly in the autumn sunshine.
Read the constitution of Užupis
Located across the Vilnelė River, the neighbourhood of Užupis declared independence in 1997.
It has its own flag, a national day (which falls on April Fools’), and embassies “among Canadian cats”, “in cheese”, “in pencils” and “in rock music”, among others.
You can read the 41-point constitution, which states important things like “everyone has the right to love and take care of the cat” while “a cat is not obliged to love its owner, but must help in times of need”, in nearly two dozen different languages.
Unsurprisingly for a republic founded by artists, Užupis is known for its creative scene, which you can explore at the Užupis Art Incubator.
Take a stroll down Literatai Street
Once the home of poet Adomas Mickevičius, Literatai Street is lined with plaques paying tribute to more than 200 notable Lithuanian writers.
The project was commissioned by the Modern Art Centre in 2008 ahead of Vilnius’ stint as the European Capital of Culture, which you can also visit here.
Explore the city’s museums
There are plenty of museums dotted around Vilnius, from the Toys Museum and Railway Museum to the House of Signatories and the Energy and Technology Museum.
If we had to narrow it down to just two, our picks would be the Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights, and Castellan’s House.
The former is located within the former KGB headquarters and covers the history of Soviet repression while also briefly touching on the country’s Nazi occupation, while the latter forms part of the National Museum of Lithuania and explores Lithuanian identity through themes like religion.
Where to eat and drink in Vilnius
The oldest market in Vilnius – Halės – is an obvious choice, with dozens of choices from pastries and soups to tacos and Korean plates.
Hardly traditional, but I was a big fan of Beigelistai, which serves up Vilnius-style bagels. I couldn’t tell you the difference between Vilnius and New York-style ones, but I can tell you the bagel of the month for October (with fig jam, camembert, walnuts and cream cheese) was fantastic.
For a more modern option, head to Paupys Market. Again, the market has many different restaurants to choose from, but the potato pancakes and bao buns are real winners.
Next time I’ll visit Vilnius for…
If I’d had more time in Vilnius, I would have taken the advice of a friend who visited in April and headed to Trakai Castle.
Located on an island, the castle is about a 35-minute train journey followed by a 10-minute bus or a 40-minute walk. Just be aware that the trains aren’t super regular, so you should plan this out in advance.
How to get there
Vilnius International Airport is just under six kilometres away from the city centre, which you can reach in around 15 or 20 minutes by bus. There’s also a train which takes under 10 minutes, but they run less frequently than the bus.
The biggest airlines operating from the airport are airBaltic, Ryanair and Wizz Air. There are direct flights from cities including Amsterdam, Barcelona, London, Rome and Paris.
Alternatively, Vilnius is around a four-hour bus ride from Riga.

With Kyiv’s air defense crews as they race to keep up with Russia’s jet-powered drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:38:39 UTC
15:38:39 KST

With Kyiv’s air defense crews as they race to keep up with Russia’s jet-powered drones
Anton, a soldier with Ukraine's 112th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade, stands beside an Oktava electronic warfare system outside Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Jakub Laichter / The Kyiv Independent)
In a cornfield north of Kyiv, pieces of blackened metal are scattered among rows of dried stalks. They are all that remains of a Russian Geran attack drone, shot down by Ukrainian fighter jets as it flew toward the capital during one of Russia's mass aerial assaults.
"Last year we had so many of them," says Halyna Prykhodko, deputy director of the Branytsia division of the agricultural company Zemlya i Volya. "We found three, four, even five in the fields."
Above Prykhodko's land is one of the routes Russian drones take to approach Kyiv. Ukrainian forces try to intercept them over the countryside before they reach the capital and crash into homes and critical infrastructure.
Since late summer, Russia has been terrorizing Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast with jet-powered drones, adding to the now-familiar threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles. Between larger assaults, successive waves of jet-powered drones now arrive day and night.
Defending Kyiv requires a layered system of air defenses, from sophisticated missile systems and fighter jets, to mobile machine-gun and interceptor-drone units.
Over two days, the Kyiv Independent accompanied soldiers of the 112th Territorial Defense Brigade at several positions outside the capital, observing how their units hunt incoming Russian drones and adapt to Russia's evolving weapons and tactics.
read also
A Coordinated Effort
Radar stations and other detection systems are the first link in a wider system coordinating Kyiv's air defenses. They track approaching Russian drones, relaying information through command posts that direct the response of individual units.
"Every unit is subordinate to its own combat command post," says Senior Sgt. Serhii, who leads a mobile fire group. His surname is withheld for security reasons. "It gathers all the information from higher commanders and other groups, and issues orders to each group."
His three-man mobile fire group is armed with a truck-mounted Browning M2HB heavy machine gun, a SkyLock targeting system, and thermal-imaging equipment.
One soldier mans the machine gun, another commands the group and operates observation equipment, and a third covers them with an assault rifle.
When a drone approaches their sector, the soldiers receive information about its direction, altitude, and distance. They must then locate it using their observation equipment, adjusting for discrepancies between the target's reported and actual positions.
The crews operate within designated firing sectors, limiting where they can engage targets to avoid endangering civilians or friendly aircraft.
The gunner must account for the target's speed, distance, and direction of travel, calculating how far ahead to fire so that the bullets and aircraft arrive at the same time at the same point.
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is."
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is," explains Volodymyr, a soldier in the mobile fire group.
Repeated practice and experience are essential, he says, until judging a target's movement and calculating the necessary lead become almost instinctive.
Weather conditions, altitude, and speed further determine whether a target can be engaged. Thermal-imaging equipment helps soldiers detect drones at night, but cloud cover can obscure them, and faster, higher-flying jet-powered drones present greater difficulties.
"Within five seconds I have to engage it as much as I possibly can," says Volodymyr.
It's his birthday when the Kyiv Independent visits the mobile fire group. He spends it at the group's position, surrounded by fields.
"Grand celebrations," he jokes when asked how he plans to mark the occasion. "I've got these wide fields. I can walk over there, walk over here. Not many options."
Other crews use shoulder-fired missiles to engage targets beyond the reach of machine guns.
"Bodya," another soldier, operates a Soviet-designed 9K38 Igla man-portable air-defense system, which uses a heat-seeking missile to pursue aerial targets. Even with a guided missile, soldiers have very little time to engage a fast-moving target.
With conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones, Bodya explains, the sound of the approaching engine can provide some warning. Jet-powered drones and cruise missiles, however, travel much faster, and by the time crews hear one, it can be almost on top of them. Some targets pass through his unit's engagement area in as little as 20 seconds, he says.
Ukraine primarily uses systems such as NASAMS and IRIS-T against Russian cruise missiles, aircraft, and other aerial threats, but to intercept ballistic missiles, Ukraine has to rely on its scarce arsenal of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
Interceptor drones have become another means of bringing down Russian targets, particularly conventional Shahed-type drones, without expending costly surface-to-air missiles.
A soldier with the call sign Gendalf shows the Kyiv Independent the Sting interceptor drones operated by his unit. Equipped with cameras, the interceptor drones transmit live video to operators who guide them toward incoming Russian drones.
But Russia's increasing use of jet-powered drones, some capable of flying at about 600 kilometers per hour, has created a problem for operators like Gendalf.
read also
Reaching about 320 kilometers per hour at full throttle, the conventional rotary-wing interceptors available to his unit struggle to match the jet-powered drones' speed, he says.
Beyond these different means of kinetic interception, electronic warfare provides another layer of defense by targeting the signals Russian drones rely on.
At an electronic warfare unit, Maj. "Secret," the brigade's head of electronic warfare and electronic intelligence, demonstrates a sensitive spectrum analyzer developed within the brigade. The device allows soldiers to detect and analyze radio-frequency signals, including those transmitted by Russian drones.
"Here we see all the signals that are nearby," he says, pointing to a series of transmissions appearing on the screen.
"First, we have to detect the signals and understand what we need to jam," Secret explains. "What matters is that there's data exchange," he says. "I can see the flow of data in real time."
Electronic warfare can disrupt an incoming drone in two main ways. First, jamming interferes with the signals it relies on, potentially severing its connection to an operator. Second, spoofing feeds the aircraft false information, potentially misleading its navigation or diverting it from its intended course.
But disrupting a communication link does not necessarily stop an attack. Some drones can continue toward preprogrammed coordinates without further instructions, meaning electronic warfare can only complement kinetic interception.
The Race to Adapt
One of the most significant developments since late summer has been Russia's growing use of jet-powered Geran drones. Some variants fly at altitudes of 5 to 6 kilometers, beyond the effective range of mobile machine-gun crews.
Soldiers defending Kyiv also describe Russian drones changing their routes and maneuvering when Ukrainian interceptors approach. Some newer Geran variants carry cameras and mesh radios that allow operators to receive a live video feed and redirect the aircraft during flight.
Ukraine is adapting its interceptors in response.
On Oct. 18, Andrii Hrytseniuk, then head of Brave1, Ukraine's government-backed defense innovation initiative, said seven types of Ukrainian interceptors had already successfully intercepted jet-powered Russian drones. Twenty-two teams joined the effort to develop high-speed systems, including models powered by miniature jet engines.
The government had ordered more than 1,000 of these new interceptors, but production is still being expanded, he said.
A similar race is playing out in electronic warfare.
read also
The electronic warfare unit studies the wreckage of drones brought down by Ukrainian forces and examines their electronics to understand how Russia is adapting its weapons.
"We dig around in these burned-out remains, looking at how everything is configured, what electronic components they use, which antennas, which parts," Secret says.
Russian forces continually modify the communications systems carried by their drones, forcing Ukrainian units to adapt the equipment used to detect and disrupt their signals, Secret says.
"They change the signal's form, and we adapt to that form," he says.
Equipment purchased just a year earlier may no longer be as effective against modified drones. But older systems cannot simply be discarded, since Russian forces can still use the technologies those systems were designed to counter.
Secret compares the process to constantly renovating an apartment without ever being able to remove the old wallpaper.
"Every six months, every three months, the fashion changes," he says. "And without stripping off the old wallpaper, you have to glue new wallpaper over it."
"And the wallpaper is, first of all, extremely expensive and very difficult to obtain," he adds.
Russia is also changing its tactics to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
"They're coming in from all directions," one air defense officer says, describing a hypothetical attack involving 15 drones.
Most might be shot down, but a handful could get through. He believes Russian forces study the results to identify routes for subsequent strikes.
"They're probing, feeling things out," he says. "Then, yes, everything's clear, a mass attack."
Meanwhile, the pace of attacks is placing a growing strain on the soldiers defending Kyiv.
"The tactic is constant exhaustion, non-stop," says Serhii.
During particularly intense periods, he says, his men have worked 20-hour shifts, leaving just four hours for sleep. And during the hours spent on alert, some targets remain beyond their reach.
One machine gunner recalls a jet-powered Russian drone passing so high overhead that he could barely make it out.
"I couldn't even see it with my eyes," he says.
But he knows how to calculate the lead needed to hit a moving drone.
"I'd tear it apart if it were lower," he says.

Ex-Japan prime minister Yasuo Fukuda dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:38:33 UTC
15:38:33 KST

Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, who used his brief period in office to seek closer ties with Asian neighbours, particularly China, has died at the age of 90, the Nikkei business daily reported on Monday.
Beijing expressed condolences over his passing.
The Japanese politician, the first son of a prime minister to become premier himself, died on Thursday from heart failure, the Nikkei said.
Becoming prime minister on the sudden resignation of Shinzo Abe in 2007, Fukuda lasted less than a year – a tenure even shorter than his father Takeo's two-year stint.
A graduate in economics from Tokyo's prestigious Waseda University, Fukuda spent nearly two decades working his way up the ranks of an oil company – including a two-year posting in the United States – before resigning to become a political secretary when his father became premier in 1976.
Elected to Japan's more powerful lower house of parliament in 1990, Fukuda was chief cabinet secretary from 2000 to 2004, resigning as one of several cabinet ministers to admit not paying into the pension system.
Known for his testy manner, the bespectacled Fukuda drew criticism in 2003 for off-the-record comments in which he suggested women who dressed provocatively were asking to be raped.
When Fukuda succeeded Abe he joked he might have drawn the short straw in assuming office given the divided parliament and opposition parties' ability to delay legislation.
Frustrated with the stalled legislative process, Fukuda resigned in 2008, the second of six prime ministers to quit after only around a year in office.
Known as a diplomatic dove, Fukuda made several visits to China after leaving office in an effort to improve often fraught relations.
Speaking at a regular briefing on Monday, Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun called Fukuda an old friend of the Chinese people who held the "correct view" of history.
Guo praised him for making significant contributions to the development of bilateral relations, citing the China-Japan Joint Statement on All-round Promotion of Strategic Relationship of Mutual Benefit that was issued in 2008 when he was prime minister.
Fukuda leaves a son, Tatsuo, who is also a lawmaker and has been viewed as a potential future prime minister. (Reuters/RTHK)

Factbox-Who are the leading candidates in Israel’s election?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:38:13 CET
15:38:13 KST

By Maayan Lubell
JERUSALEM, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long looked on course to lose power in Israel’s election, but the race has narrowed as the vote approaches and his rivals have no clear path to power.
Votes will be cast on Tuesday for parties, and seats in parliament will be allocated to individuals on party lists according to proportional representation.
Here are details of some of the leading candidates in Israel’s first parliamentary election since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 that plunged the Middle East into turmoil, with Israel going to war in Lebanon and Gaza and launching airstrikes against Iran.
BENJAMIN NETANYAHU
In power for much of the time since 2009, after a first stint as prime minister in the 1990s, Netanyahu has become the face of Israel abroad and a polarising figure at home.
Supporters hail Netanyahu as “King Bibi” and see him as the strong leader Israel needs to defend itself in a hostile region. But, wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes in Gaza which he rejects and on trial in Israel on corruption charges which he denies, he is fighting for his political life.
Opinion polls have pointed to a sharp drop for his Likud party since the October 7 attack, which shattered Netanyahu’s security credentials. His government’s policies on matters of religion and state have also been unpopular among many Israelis.
But Netanyahu, 77, is a consummate political survivor. He has said he wants to form a “broad national” government after the election, if he wins. In the event of a stalemate, he could remain a caretaker prime minister for many months.
NETANYAHU’S TOP RIVALS
* Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who lost a son in Gaza combat. Eisenkot, 66, has projected an image as a political outsider, soldier and security hawk whose humble background and family sacrifices stand in vivid contrast to Netanyahu’s decades in high office and lingering corruption cases. He heads a new centrist party called Yashar, Hebrew for “straight” or “honest”.
* Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, 54, a right-wing former commando, former Netanyahu aide and high-tech millionaire who has joined forces with centrist former premier Yair Lapid. Their new party is called Together and its messages have focused on healing a traumatised nation and getting the country back on track. Their alliance, despite being on opposite ends of the political spectrum, ousted Netanyahu in a 2021 election.
* Former Defence Minister Avigdor Lieberman, 68, was once a close ally of Netanyahu. Even more hawkish than his former boss, Lieberman quit Netanyahu’s government in 2018, accusing the prime minister of being too soft on Palestinian militants in Gaza, and has become one of Netanyahu’s sharpest critics. His party, Israel Our Home, draws much of its support from the country’s ex-Soviet immigrant community.
* Former general Yair Golan, 64, hailed for his rescue of people from one of the Hamas October 7 attack sites, leads the Democrats, founded on the moribund remnants of Israel’s historical Labour party and smaller left-wing Meretz.
CANDIDATES ON NETANYAHU’S SIDE
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, 46, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, have both drawn intense international scrutiny for their far-right policies toward the Palestinians.
Smotrich has spearheaded Israel’s rapid expansion of West Bank settlements, voicing his hope that it would ‘bury’ the idea of a Palestinian state.
Ben-Gvir, who was convicted in 2007 of racist incitement against Arabs, has promoted capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants, toughened prison conditions for jailed Palestinians and easier gun ownership for Israelis.
Both men have advocated for the expulsion of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip and Israel resettling the enclave.
ULTRA-ORTHODOX ALLIES
Netanyahu has relied on two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, for his political survival for years. Their demands for their community to be mostly exempt from compulsory military service, along with their low participation in the work force and reliance on state benefits, have angered many Israelis, all the more so at a time of war.
POTENTIAL KEY PLAYERS
Parties which are not clearly aligned with either side could tip the balance in favour of Netanyahu or his rivals. They include Raam and the Joint List, the two parties that represent Israel’s 20% Arab minority. Along with them are a new right-wing party called People of Israel and a centre-right party called The Reservists, both of which have been wavering in opinion polls.
(Reporting by Maayan Lubell, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

SEOUL, Oct 26 (Reuters) - South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Monday that the country would not be able to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) during his term.
“We need to obtain permission from all 12 member countries” in the partnership if South Korea applies, Lee said at a meeting with farmers, fishermen and forestry workers. “The possibility that it will not be completed within my term is far higher.” Lee’s term runs until June 2030.

06:33:43 UTC
15:33:43 KST

Türkiye’s Revenue Administration (GİB) has used automated systems to prepare and send more than 200,000 official letters without staff intervention, according to the Treasury and Finance Ministry.
The administration uses robotic process automation to handle routine transactions and correspondence around the clock. The tools also send taxpayers text reminders to help them meet their obligations on time.
Through its Digital Tax Office, taxpayers can make payments, file returns and submit applications without visiting a tax office. The platform offers 261 services and received around 18.3 million applications and written requests in the first nine months of 2026.
The platform has recorded more than 750 million logins since its launch. Around 13 billion financial documents, including invoices and receipts, were issued electronically in 2025.
A central monitoring system introduced in 2024 also oversees operations at 860 tax offices, generating about 56,000 reports each month. Follow-up procedures track whether the necessary work identified in those reports has been completed.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said digital services were simplifying tax procedures and speeding up transactions.
“These applications aim to improve access to services, shorten processing times, improve administrative efficiency and make better use of public resources,” he said.
Şimşek added that the changes also sought to protect taxpayers’ rights, reduce errors and improve service standards.

Lula promises a Brazil 'everyone dreams of' after historic comeback

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pledged to govern for all Brazilians, bolster the country’s international standing and advance an ambitious climate agenda after securing reelection on Sunday.
According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Lula won 51.79 percent of valid ballots, while Flavio Bolsonaro received 48.21 percent.
"No one is required to like the president-elect, but he must govern for everyone," Lula said as he addressed supporters, expressing gratitude to the Brazilian people and promising to respect citizens regardless of their political allegiances.
He also criticised his opponent Flavio Bolsonaro’s political camp, declaring "this was a defeat for denialism and lies."
Promising an ambitious agenda for his next term, Lula said: "I want to make a commitment: I will deliver the best term any president has ever served. I will dedicate myself 24 hours a day to making this the country that everyone dreams of."
He also emphasised national sovereignty, saying "in this election, we defeated the interference that was coming from the outside in."
"This country will not accept being anyone's backyard," he added.
Outlining his vision for Brazil's place in the world, Lula said the country should play a central role in international affairs and lead by example on climate policy.
"We want to be a central country, not a peripheral one. We are going to show the world how climate policies are handled in this country," he said.
A historic comeback
Lula's victory marked a historic comeback after he finished second in the October 4 first round, when Bolsonaro led with 47.03 percent of valid votes against Lula's 45.16 percent.
Lula became the first candidate in Brazil's democratic history to finish second in the first round and win the presidency in the runoff, according to Brazil's Chamber of Deputies.
His campaign mobilised supporters through street rallies and social media.
The victory gives Lula a fourth nonconsecutive presidential term following his wins in 2002, 2006 and 2022. He is the first Brazilian president elected to four terms by popular vote, according to the G1 news portal. His new term is scheduled to begin on January 5 2027.
The runoff recorded an abstention rate of 19.22 percent, down from 21.08 percent in the first round, according to reported figures from Brazil's Superior Electoral Court. Blank ballots accounted for approximately 1.12 percent of ballots cast and null ballots for 2.12 percent, bringing their combined share to 3.24 percent.
Lula's next administration is expected to face congressional opposition and pressure to balance public finances while expanding social programs.

Politecnica, Park Associati, and AMDL CIRCLE Win Competition for Cultural Hub in Italy’s UNESCO-Listed Valle Camonica
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

A team led by Politecnica Building for Humans, with Park Associati and AMDL CIRCLE as architectural co-leads and Studio Mattioli responsible for geology and archaeology, has won the competition for a new cultural hub in Ceto, Italy. The project will transform the former Società Filati Niggeler & Kupfer textile mill into a facility comprising exhibition spaces, research facilities, an auditorium, and visitor services. Located in Valle Camonica, an area known for its prehistoric rock engravings, the proposal approaches the site through the relationship between industrial heritage, archaeology, and the surrounding landscape.
Ceto is located at the southern entrance to Valle Camonica, in the province of Brescia, near Monte Concarena and Pizzo Badile Camuno. The valley is home to the Rock Drawings in Valle Camonica, which became Italy's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. Known as the Pitoti, the prehistoric engravings form an extensive record of early human expression, while the wider area has been part of the UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Reserve "Valle Camonica – Alto Sebino" since 2018.
The winning proposal places the landscape at the center of the site's development, identifying the relationship between cultural heritage, the natural environment, and the local community as a guiding principle. The traces carved into the rock inform an approach that considers the territory's material characteristics, geological conditions, and morphology. The project is also conceived as an open infrastructure intended to serve as a starting point for a network of routes connecting archaeological sites with the natural environment.
Related Article
From Aalto Works to Tashkent Modernism: Discover the 19 New Cultural Sites Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2026
The project is part of broader cultural initiatives in Valle Camonica, which has launched its candidacy for Italian Capital of Culture 2029. The year will mark the 50th anniversary of the Rock Drawings in Valle Camonica's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The cultural hub is intended to contribute to the region's cultural infrastructure by bringing together archaeological heritage, landscape, and community-oriented facilities.
The competition was launched by the Municipality of Ceto, with the Comunità Montana di Valle Camonica as a contracting authority and Imago, led by Luca Molinari, providing scientific coordination. Politecnica Building for Humans is responsible for project coordination, structural and building services engineering, sustainability, fire safety, acoustics, health and safety, and mobility. Park Associati and AMDL CIRCLE lead the architectural design, while Studio Mattioli oversees geology and archaeology. The project is listed as ongoing, with 2026 as its starting year.
In other heritage news, Design Museum Gent in Belgium reopened on October 3, 2026, after four years of renovation and expansion that combined historic building restoration with a new wing designed by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA, along with restoration work by RE-ST architectenvennootschap. In Lima, Peru, the Red Lima Milenaria campaign is seeking public support for a future UNESCO World Heritage nomination of selected pre-colonial archaeological sites, with more than 600 sites remaining across the city. Meanwhile, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee added 25 sites to the World Heritage List during its 48th session, including 19 cultural properties, five natural sites, and one mixed property.
