France's debt woes in focus as ECB meets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:05:02 UTC
15:05:02 KST

European Central Bank (ECB) headquarters is pictured behind a construction site in Frankfurt am Main, western Germany, on October 23, 2026. (AFP Photo)
France's deteriorating public finances will take center stage when the European Central Bank meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone's second-biggest economy just yet.
The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.
But the focus of Oct. 29’s meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis," said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.
French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year's budget, which aims to reduce the country's vast debts.
Concerns have also been fueled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combatting sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields.
However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France's problems do not meet the threshold.
The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted" moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading — but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB President Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France's finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea.
Asked about France's rising yields earlier this month, she responded, "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
France's central bank chief, who sits on the ECB's governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met" for the central bank to step in.
Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France" at the Oct. 29 meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5 percent.
The ECB's rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the U.S. central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September.
Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8 percent in September, although closely watched core inflation — excluding volatile energy and food prices — hardly changed.
There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices," ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France's crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike," he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB's task."
Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year.
She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos.
But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB's last meeting in September there was "nothing to report" on the matter.

Insurance company adds 'war risk' protection without customers' consent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:03:00 UTC
15:03:00 KST

Insurance company adds 'war risk' protection without customers' consent
Insurance companies have begun offering coverage for war-related risks, such as damage caused by drones or missiles, but in some cases, fees have increased without customers' consent.
Seesam Insurance customers recently received an unpleasant surprise when their home insurance premiums increased overnight.
For example, a customer insuring a 200-square-meter property received an offer requiring them to pay €245 a year instead of the previous €190 – an increase of nearly 30 percent.
The reason was a new charge for coverage against war-related risks.
Indrek Petter, head of the insurance department at Seesam Insurance, said coverage against war-related risks primarily protects people's homes against explosions caused by stray military drones, missiles, shells and mines.
He explained that the monthly premium is around €1 for smaller apartments and around €3 for an average detached house. "It depends on the size of the house," Petter noted.
Customers must opt out themselves
The change was introduced by default, without asking for consent. Customers must now notify the company themselves if they wish to opt out.
"We add it to the insurance offer. Generally, the customer reviews it and consults their account manager or salesperson," Petter said. He added that this should then lead to a discussion about whether the customer wishes to opt out of coverage against war-related risks.
The company began offering war insurance following events in the spring, when Ukrainian drones started appearing in Estonian airspace after being knocked off course.
But several other insurance companies are moving in the same direction.
Swedbank and Elama Insurance also offer compensation for war-related damage, but their customers do not have to pay an additional fee. The new terms will take effect this week.
Hardi Saarniit, head of home insurance products at insurance company If, said that average insurance premiums may eventually change, but the company does not charge extra for compensation for war-related damage.
Coverage does not apply during a state of war
He explained that their coverage is intended for the current situation, in which Russia and Ukraine are at war and drones also stray into Estonian airspace.
"If the situation were to change, for example, if a state of war were declared in Estonia, then this coverage would no longer apply," Saarniit noted.
The Estonian Insurance Association hopes prices will not rise with the new terms.
Lauri Potsepp, a board member of the Estonian Insurance Association, said that insurance is moving toward packages tailored as precisely as possible to customers' interests and needs.
"In other words, individual customers are offered coverage for the risks they are interested in, and this makes it possible to keep insurance prices under control so that insurers remain competitive," he said.
Insurance providers are not the only sector using war risks to push up prices. Last week, ERR reported that utility providers are also raising prices due to increased security risks.

Passengers board an Air New Zealand aircraft operating the first international departure from the newly-opened Western Sydney International Airport in Sydney on October 26, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The first international flight took off on Oct. 26 from a new, multi-billion-dollar airport in the fast-growing western suburbs of Sydney.
After more than four decades of planning, Western Sydney International Airport offers the first alternative to the city's main airport, which has been operating for more than a century.
An Air New Zealand plane from Auckland landed and soon afterwards flew out of the airport in the morning, launching a three-flights-a-week service to Sydney's largely working-class western suburbs.
The new single-runway airport, Australia's first new major aviation hub in more than five decades, began domestic flights on Oct. 25, and freight operations in July.
Sydney's main airport, Kingsford Smith, is Australia's busiest, its three runways handling more than 42 million passengers last year.
Lying in Botany Bay just nine kilometres (six miles) from the city center, planes using the airport roar over many city homes, and a curfew bars passenger aircraft from operating during the night.
The new airport in western Sydney has no such restrictions.
Qantas' budget carrier Jetstar is now the main domestic carrier, flying to the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane.
The airport says other international carriers are coming, including Qatar Airways from December 2027, Fiji Airways from March 2027, and Vietjet Air from January 2027.
Built at a cost of AUS$5.3 billion ($3.7 billion), excluding surrounding transport works, the airport is reachable by road but is not expected to have a direct rail link until at least December 2027.

We have therefore decided to continue the service until early January, providing a convenient connection between cities in Latvia and Lithuania throughout the autumn and winter months,” says Aldis Ķibēns, Management Board Member of Lux Express Latvia.
Riga increasingly serves as a starting point for travel across the Baltics
While Latvian and Lithuanian residents continue to make up the largest passenger groups on the route, Lux Express is also seeing growing interest from international tourists. Travellers from Germany stand out in particular, with their number increasing by 8% this year compared with 2025.
“Our data show that Riga is increasingly becoming a starting point for international tourists who want to explore more of the Baltics. People arrive in the Latvian capital and then travel on to other cities, including Liepaja and Klaipeda. This change in travel patterns is a positive sign not only for transport operators but also for regional tourism, as it helps attract visitors beyond the traditional summer season,” says Ķibēns.
For now, Lux Express continues to operate the route as a seasonal service but, depending on passenger demand, does not rule out running it year-round in the future.
Services will continue on the existing timetable
The Riga–Liepaja–Palanga–Klaipeda route will continue to operate once a day in each direction, with the current timetable remaining unchanged.
From Monday to Saturday, buses depart Riga Bus Station at 7.00 and Liepaja Bus Station at 10.30. On Sundays, departures are scheduled for 11.30 from Riga and 15.00 from Liepaja. From Klaipeda Bus Station, buses depart at 12.55 from Monday to Saturday and at 17.10 on Sundays.
The journey from Riga to Klaipeda takes approximately 5 hours and 10 minutes, while the journey from Liepaja to Klaipeda takes around 1 hour and 40 minutes.
Tickets for travel until 3 January 2027 are already on sale, with ticket prices remaining unchanged. Tickets are available at luxexpress.lv and via the Lux Express mobile app.
About Lux Express
Lux Express Group is an international coach operator providing long-distance services to major cities across the Baltics and to Warsaw, as well as domestic passenger services in Latvia and Estonia. The company operates a fleet of 105 high-comfort coaches. Last year, Lux Express Group marked 30 years of operations in Latvia and is the international coach operator with the longest track record in the Latvian market.

'Having money is not enough': Why a job no longer guarantees access to housing in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:41 UTC
15:00:41 KST

House prices rose 84.6% between 2015 and 2025, against 27.85% for average wages. Lack of affordable housing, rent burdens and saving difficulties deepen the crisis as experts call for structural reform.
In Spain, having a job no longer guarantees being able to access housing. The increase in property and rental prices in recent years, far outpacing wage growth, makes it difficult both to pay a mortgage and to save up enough for a deposit.
This is a gap that particularly – though not exclusively – affects young people and low- and middle-income households and that, in recent weeks, has placed access to housing at the centre of social and political debate, to the point that Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez opted to bring forward the general election after failing to secure approval in Congress for a set of urgent measures aimed at addressing the discontent felt on the streets.
"The problem is essentially structural," says Rafael Pampillón, professor of Applied Economics at San Pablo-CEU University in Madrid, who acknowledges that the current gap between wages and the high cost of rents and mortgages "makes it harder to access housing" and emphasises that "having money for the deposit is not enough".
According to data from the National Statistics Institute (INE), housing prices rose by 84.6% between 2015 and 2025, while average annual gross wages increased by 27.85% between 2015 and 2024, reaching 29,540 euros. Wages agreed in collective bargaining went up by around 27% over the same period.
The gap persists today. Housing prices climbed 12.2% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, compared with average wage increases of between 3% and 4%, according to figures cited by the Ministry of Labour. Housing is becoming more expensive at a pace that earnings from work cannot keep up with.
A recent study by Oxfam Intermón, presented last week, warns that housing costs have pushed the in-work poverty rate up to 15.49%, affecting around 770,000 people across the country. According to the report, one in three working people who rent at market prices falls into poverty after paying the rent. The rate stands at 34.08%, compared with 10.22% among those paying a mortgage and 7.95% among those who own their home outright.
"Evictions are the most extreme face of the housing crisis, but not the only one," argues Oxfam Intermón's head of housing, employment and social policies, Alejandro García-Gil. "There is another, less visible reality: people who are working and just about manage to pay for their home every month, but who, once they have done so, do not have enough income left to sustain a decent standard of living."
Rent, a cost that makes buying harder
The problem is not limited to purchase prices. According to the latest annual report from the Bank of Spain, four in ten households living in rented accommodation face an excessive financial burden, spending more than 40% of their income on rent. In major cities and areas most exposed to tourism, pressure on prices further aggravates these difficulties.
"These access problems are compounded by the fact that housing prices have risen more than household income, which has increased the effort required and tightened the conditions for buying a home in Spain to a greater extent than in the large European economies," the document notes.
Rent also creates a barrier for those hoping to buy a home. Although in some cases a mortgage instalment could be more affordable than a monthly rent payment, putting together the money needed to qualify for a loan becomes increasingly difficult when a substantial share of wages goes on rent, explains Pampillón, who reiterates that "having money for the deposit is not enough".
"A pay packet allows you to meet monthly payments, but buying a home requires a large upfront payment to purchase a flat, for which you need to have built up considerable savings," says the economist, who also holds a doctorate in Economic and Business Sciences from the University of Barcelona and an MBA from IESE. "The longer it takes to save up the deposit, the more years you continue paying rent."
With an average home price of around 200,000 euros, a buyer needs approximately 60,000 euros to cover the deposit and the costs associated with the purchase. Without the ability to save, Pampillón adds, family support is often the only way to "break that circle". "Those who do not have it have to travel a much longer road. In this way, family wealth – together with generous pensions – is playing an ever bigger role in shaping children's opportunities," he laments.
In this respect, the difficulty of leaving the parental home reflects a growing inequality between those who can draw on family resources and those who depend solely on their wages. Since 2008, the share of households that do not own their home has risen by 45%, according to the National Statistics Institute's Survey of Living Conditions.
A structural problem that goes beyond wages
The fall in pay during the financial crisis, slower wage recovery and the arrival of investment funds in the property market have all helped widen this gap. On top of that comes a shortage of supply: between 2021 and 2025 an estimated deficit of around 750,000 homes built up, according to the Bank of Spain. In 2025, around 225,000 households were formed, while some 92,000 new homes were completed.
Despite the impact of this divide, many experts warn that the mismatch between incomes and housing will not be solved by wage rises alone. "Employment has always been seen as the best tool against poverty, and this analysis shows that having a job is not enough," notes García-Gil, referring to the Oxfam Intermón study.
The European Commission is blunt in its assessment of the sector's situation: "The housing sector in Spain faces deeply rooted structural challenges. The Spanish property market shows a severe mismatch between supply and demand, coupled with a lack of a substantial stock of affordable and social housing, including social rental options."
Faced with the current situation, the trade unions CC.OO. and UGT have called a 24-hour general strike on 11 November, under the slogan "wages, housing, prices", with which they hope to channel the social discontent generated by this crisis in Spain, especially in the wake of the eviction – and subsequent death – of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who died in early October after being forced out of her home days earlier.
"Under the current conditions there is no wage or collective agreement that can allow us to access housing," recently said the UGT general secretary, Pepe Álvarez, speaking to the media. "We cannot continue for much longer with a situation in which it is practically impossible for the vast majority of workers in our country – with the wages we have – to access housing, whether to rent or to buy."
Both unions are demanding at least a 7% increase in the statutory minimum wage in 2027, taking it above 1,300 euros in 14 instalments. However, Unai Sordo, the CC.OO. general secretary, acknowledges the limits of wage policies in the face of surging property prices.
"There is no wage policy in any country in the world capable of dealing with the outrageous situation of increasing housing prices by 12% year-on-year," the union leader stated in a statement dated 13 October.
The organisation proposes allocating at least 1% of annual gross domestic product (GDP) to public housing for a decade and is calling for measures to curb speculation and rein in rising property prices.
In this regard, Pampillón also calls for reforms that go far beyond a simple pay rise, which in the end would itself require "more productive companies, investment and jobs that generate greater added value", and he stresses that one of the main problems is that "housing demand is rising much faster than the time it takes to build".
"Economic policy must address wages, but above all the supply of housing," the professor argues. "We need to make it easier to build where there is demand: ensure land is available for development, speed up permits, coordinate infrastructure and cut procedures that add costs without providing effective protection."
In any case, if there is one point on which all those involved agree – the political class, unions, experts and, more broadly, most of the population – it is that Spain's housing crisis is a structural problem, with few short-term solutions and one that requires much broader long-term planning.

Higher training costs for older workers risks plan to tackle youth jobs crisis, employers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis.
The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead.
Drawn up before Wednesday’s budget, the proposal, which was first reported last week, is expected to form part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are unemployed.
The chancellor, John Healey, is widely tipped to announce measures to bolster opportunities for young people to help the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the country.
However, business leaders urged the government to reconsider the plan to make training older workers more expensive.
“It will just mean opportunities are shifted around instead of creating new ones,” said Robert Halfon, a former Conservative skills minister who is now the executive director of policy at the manufacturing lobby group Make UK.
“We agree that getting young people back into employment and training is a moral and economic imperative. But making it more expensive for employers to train older workers isn’t the answer,” he added.
Calling on Healey to “break the cycle” of cutting and reallocating the apprenticeship budget in England, Halfon said the system was already struggling to deliver what businesses and young people need.
“If the government is serious about getting young people into good jobs and giving industry the skills it needs, it should use that opportunity to grow the number of apprenticeships available rather than restrict training elsewhere.”
Andy Burnham has placed youth jobs at the heart of his agenda, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and plans to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.
With over-25s accounting for more than half of new apprenticeship enrolments, ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the system towards supporting more younger people.
Under the latest proposal, which is yet to be finalised, employers would be able to fund the full cost of an apprentice under the age of 25 using the money they contribute to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn-a-year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system.
However, for an older worker, they would face a “co-investment rule” whereby levy funds would cover 75% of the costs. The rest would need to be covered separately.
Employers have for years been told they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.
John Foster, the chief policy and campaigns officer at the CBI lobby group, said: “We can’t make skills a zero-sum game.
“While it is right to focus on supporting young people who are Neet into work, adult training also has a vital role to play in opening up entry-level opportunities and helping people adapt and update their skills mid-career, particularly as AI reshapes the workplace.”
Ben Rowland, the chief executive of the Association of Employment and Learning Providers, said: “The key to any further changes to the apprenticeship system is to bring employers on the journey. Anything that is too abrupt or too quick significantly endangers that.”
Business leaders have been pressing Healey to use Wednesday’s budget to provide support with soaring costs amid the war in the Middle East, and have urged the chancellor not to add to the pressure on firms after Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions.
Kate Shoesmith, the director of policy and insights at the British Chambers of Commerce, said: “At a time when businesses are under pressure to improve productivity and drive growth, employers need greater flexibility and support to invest in skills at every stage of a person’s career.
“The best way to encourage more youth apprenticeships is to make it easier and more affordable for firms to take on young people by reducing the wider costs of doing business, rather than creating new barriers to training.”
Labour has been told its youth skills strategy risks failure without reform, after just 160 young people were enrolled into its foundation apprenticeship scheme in the first eight months. Ministers have an ambition for 30,000 starts over the current parliament.
Joe Dromey, the general secretary of the Fabian Society, said that while flexibility was important for business, the current system was skewed too heavily towards funding older, often already highly qualified workers.
“These will not be easy decisions, and some will be unpopular with businesses. But tackling youth unemployment means making difficult choices about where public funding is spent.”
A government spokesperson said: “It’s right that we focus on reversing the 40% decline in the number of young people starting an apprenticeship and give them the skills they need to succeed.
“That’s why we have reformed the system backed by £3.3bn to deliver 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people and support employers with a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16- to 24-year-old apprentice.
“The Milburn Review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report.
The findings, based on a survey of almost 7,200 captains and first officers by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), include pilots reporting insufficient rest, pressure to extend working hours and fears of being penalised for declaring themselves unfit to fly.
Almost a quarter (24%) of pilots admitted they usually continue flying rather than report themselves unfit due to fatigue, while another 16.8% said they call in sick instead.
In aviation, fatigue can result from long duty hours, insufficient rest, irregular schedules and flying across time zones, which disrupt the body’s natural sleep cycle. It is a significant safety concern because it can impair pilots’ judgment, slow their reactions, reduce alertness and impair responses to unexpected situations.
Under European aviation safety regulations, airlines are required to have systems in place to identify, monitor and manage crew fatigue.
The survey, conducted in August, found that three-quarters of respondents had experienced at least one microsleep – a brief, involuntary episode of sleep – while operating an aircraft in the previous four weeks.
Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta reported the highest levels of microsleeps. More than a third said they were not getting enough rest to prevent fatigue from building up over time.
Despite the prevalence of exhaustion, only one in three pilots said they usually reported themselves unfit for duty when fatigued. Half admitted they had operated a flight in the three months before the survey when they should have declared themselves too fatigued to fly.
Almost half of the respondents said they feared negative consequences from management if they reported themselves unfit because of fatigue, while just 11.9% trusted their airline’s fatigue reporting system.
Ian Holder, the managing director of the aviation safety consultancy Baines Simmons, said the results showed persistent differences in how airlines and national authorities manage fatigue. “This survey captures how European pilots experience fatigue risk management in practice,” he said.
He stressed that the findings represented pilots’ first-hand experiences rather than a direct measurement of aviation safety outcomes, but said the consistency of the results over three years highlighted areas requiring attention.
Holder pointed to Finland and the Netherlands as evidence that stronger fatigue reporting cultures were achievable.
Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta were among the most likely to fear management reprisals and the least likely to trust the reporting systems.
The proportion of pilots who said they would fly when fatigued was higher in Spain, Ireland and France. Two in five of the pilots working for airlines based in Spain and a third of those working for Ireland- and France-based airlines said they usually fly when fatigued. That compares with only one in 10 of the pilots flying for an airline based in the UK.
Only 15.6% of pilots at low-cost carriers believed their airline managed fatigue risks well, compared with 18.6% at ACMI or wet-lease operators – companies that supply aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance to other airlines.
Almost two in five pilots said they had used commander’s discretion – allowing captains to extend crew working hours or reduce rest periods in exceptional circumstances – at least once in the month before the survey.
But nearly 70% expressed concern about refusing to extend their duty, suggesting that a measure intended for exceptional situations may be accompanied by significant pressure on flight crews.
Pilots at low-cost and wet-lease operators, as well as those working for airlines registered in Ireland and Malta, reported the greatest concerns.
Capt Tanja Harter, the president of the ECA, said airlines and regulators should take responsibility rather than leaving pilots to manage the risks themselves.
“This cannot be simply left to us – the pilots – to manage, while we are on the flight deck and expected to bring our passengers safely to their destination,” she said.
She urged the European Union Aviation Safety Agency to strengthen fatigue management rules and ensure airlines comply with requirements for non-punitive reporting and the proper use of commander’s discretion.
“Waiting for another three years to discover that nothing has changed is simply not an option,” Harter said.
“The problems are identified, solutions are there, and we as the European pilot community are ready to contribute. What is needed now is the political will to act.”

We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too | Sadiq Khan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

At around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare.
Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience. He filled his store with dazzling window displays, world-class entertainment, restaurants and lounges. He even installed women’s toilets – a rarity in Edwardian England – giving women a newfound freedom to make the most of the city. As he opened the doors to his first customers, he told them “everyone is welcome”.
That spirit has been at the heart of Oxford Street’s success ever since. We love it because it feels as if it belongs to all of us. It’s where teenagers come for their first shopping trip with friends. Where families marvel at the magic of festive lights and decorations. And where generations of Londoners and visitors have come to discover the latest music, fashion and trends. It’s also the beating heart of British retail – pumping billions into our national economy, with the surrounding area accounting for an incredible 1% of the UK’s total economic output in 2022.
But in recent years this iconic street has started to lose some of its sparkle. Changing consumer habits and the legacy of the pandemic have taken their toll. Footfall has fallen. Some of our best-loved stores have closed their doors, only to be replaced by vape shops and candy stores. And, too often, the experience of visiting a chaotic, congested Oxford Street has felt more like an ordeal to survive than a day out to enjoy.
If we’re to restore this beloved street to its former glory, we must rediscover the pioneering spirit of Harry Gordon Selfridge and create a space for everyone to enjoy, breathing new life into the high street and bringing back big brands. And that’s what our bold plans – backed by the overwhelming majority of Londoners and businesses – are all about. And with household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks investing in new stores, there’s already excitement for what Oxford Street can become.
People need a reason beyond simply buying something to visit their high street. And in an age when almost anything can be delivered right to our door, that principle matters more than ever. Coming to Oxford Street should feel like a positive experience. Somewhere you want to spend time, as well as your hard-earned money. A place where you’re not choked by tailpipe fumes or deafened by the noise of passing motorists. And that starts with reclaiming it for pedestrians, not traffic – rebalancing the relationship between cars and people in the centre of our city.
That’s why I’m so delighted that, thanks to our efforts, the road stretching between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is now officially traffic-free. But removing cars is just the beginning. Imagine an Oxford Street where you can stroll at your own pace, take a break from shopping with a coffee under the trees, or stumble across some live music, a fashion show, a sports exhibition or a cultural event. We’re determined to put Oxford Street not just on par with top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla, but make it even better.
And while it’s a process – we’re deliberately keeping disruption to a minimum over the busy Christmas period – by next spring, visitors can expect to see new trees, new seats and new public plazas, alongside improved lighting and signage. This ambitious project has been far from straightforward or easy. As usual, we’ve had to overcome opposition from a vocal minority, and 14 years of a previous government that didn’t back the plans. But with seven in 10 Londoners expressing support for our vision, after extensive consultation, I knew we owed it to our city and to our businesses to deliver these improvements, which will help to boost jobs, growth and investment as we build a fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.
Of course, we’ll continue to listen to Londoners. Many of the initial changes are temporary, and we’ll use real-time feedback to help refine the final designs in a test and review period throughout 2027. But for centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way. And now it’s in need of its next great transformation. One that honours its extraordinary past while creating new possibilities for the future. A future where new memories are made, new businesses flourish and new chapters of British history are written.
Today marks the beginning of that journey – and I encourage everyone to come to explore this newly transformed street, as we work together to ensure its best days are still to come. In the words of Harry Gordon Selfridge – everyone is welcome.
- Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

Think Architecture's fragmented House on a Slope overlooks Lake Zurich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Think Architecture’s fragmented House on a Slope overlooks Lake Zurich
A cluster of interconnected volumes in dark limestone and cedar gradually descend down a narrow and steeply sloping site overlooking Lake Zurich at House on a Slope by Swiss studio Think Architecture.
Designed to sit harmoniously within the surrounding terrain, the 1,000-square-metre private home is split into two distinct blocks connected by a “subterranean art corridor”.
“The brief was to bring a very large programme into a narrow, steeply sloping site with as much sensitivity as possible,” Think Architecture creative director Marco Zbinden told Dezeen.
“We were interested in the quiet rhythm of the neighbouring houses, their individual scale, and the way they sit within the landscape. Breaking the residence into smaller volumes allowed us to respond to that context without losing the generosity of the interior,” he continued.
“From the outside, the house feels less like a single monumental object and more like a group of familiar structures that have always belonged to the hillside.”
Intended to emulate the surrounding landscape, the lakeside home was divided into two blocks, a “family house above, and a more grounded, protective house for children and guests below”.
“They are intimately connected through a corridor – filled with art – and the central garden level, which becomes the social heart of the home,” said Zbinden. “There, the architecture opens up, materials continue from outside to inside, and the different parts of the family’s life naturally meet.”
The larger, upper block, which is entered at street level, contains all the main living spaces including the kitchen, living room and dining room. These spaces are arrange over the first and lower floors, with large cedar-clad-timber windows giving views down the hillside. Several bedrooms are located on the top floor.
The lower level of the home opens up to a garden and large pool with a planted roof terrace sitting on the roof of the lower block. Clad in dark-limestone, this lower block is more enclosed with additional bedrooms for the family.
Carefully positioned openings within both structures allowed for the planting of native trees, ensuring a seamless transition into the mature foliage of the hillside.
Think Architecture designed the upper interior spaces to be open and airy, while the spaces in the lower block were more enclosed and calm.
“The interiors were conceived as a direct continuation of the architecture, extending its material language into the most private and lived-in spaces,” said Zbinden.
“We worked with a limited palette of bog oak, cedar, oak, Belgian bluestone, terrazzo, and patinated brass. Materials that are tactile, honest, and become more beautiful as they age,” he continued.
“The aim was to create spaces that felt warm and enveloping rather than decorated: quiet rooms shaped by light, texture, and proportion, where one can truly slow down and feel at home.”
House with a Slope is the most recent addition to a number of homes overlooking Lake Zurich completed by Think Architecture in recent months, including a minimal hilltop home and a home next to a vineyard.

Lithuanian defence companies seek more state help amid suspected sabotage and threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Lithuanian defence industry companies are calling for more government support to protect against suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and intimidation, after an attempted arson attack on a facility storing Starlink communications equipment in Vilnius.
Businesses producing defence and dual-use technologies say they face growing security concerns, including cars with Russian license plates parked outside their offices, employees being photographed and psychological pressure. They want the authorities to provide more training and practical advice on how to respond to potential threats.
The attempted arson took place overnight Sunday at a Vilnius facility storing Starlink equipment used to provide satellite connectivity, including to Ukraine.
“Incendiary liquids and Molotov cocktails were used in an attempt to start a fire,” Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said.
A security guard spotted the fire and extinguished it. Only a control unit was damaged, and surveillance cameras recorded the incident.
Police Commissioner General Arūnas Paulauskas said the investigation was progressing intensively but no suspects had been detained.
“We treat this as sabotage,” Sinkevičius said, adding that the company had received a general warning about potential threats on Friday but that authorities had no advance information about the specific incident.
The attack follows other incidents targeting Starlink infrastructure. Antennas were set on fire in Bulgaria last week, while a Starlink station was targeted in Poland a month ago. Four suspects in the Polish case were detained in Germany.
Lithuanian authorities also suspect that Russian intelligence services may have been behind an earlier incident involving a drone manufacturer. Wreaths were left outside the company’s premises, and a photograph of its chief executive was marked with a black ribbon.
Tomas Milašauskas, head of RSI Europe, said cyberattacks and other attempts to harm his company had become routine several years ago. The company receives security advice from Lithuanian authorities and has implemented the recommendations, he said.
The National Crisis Management Centre has sent security guidelines to more than 40 companies, including advice on camera placement, perimeter surveillance, access controls and monitoring deliveries, its head, Vilmantas Vitkauskas, said.
But not all companies in the defence sector say they have received sufficient guidance.
Edvinas Kerza, head of ScaleWolf, called for more events and training focused on physical security, including affordable measures to prevent unauthorised access to company premises.
“We need more help from intelligence services and law enforcement structures,” said Vidmantas Janulevičius, president of the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists.
Smaller businesses face particular challenges because young companies tend to prioritise product development over cybersecurity and physical protection, Kerza said. He called for free or subsidised assistance to help them improve their defences.
Vitkauskas said authorities assess companies according to how likely they are to become potential targets. Following last Sunday’s incident, agencies were instructed to strengthen the protection of strategic facilities, and the list of companies considered at risk is expected to expand.
Public Security Service chief Gen. Viktoras Grabauskas said the alert level had been raised, although authorities had detected no specific indications of an imminent threat.
The government is also considering asking companies to respond more actively to security recommendations. However, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the state could not provide physical protection to every business because it must also safeguard critical infrastructure.
“The state cannot physically contribute everywhere. We have our own critical infrastructure that we must protect. Our contribution is to provide information,” Katelynas said.
Vitkauskas likewise warned that businesses should not expect police officers to be stationed outside every company.
“Security starts with yourself,” he said.
Janulevičius warned that companies could reconsider investments in dual-use technologies if they felt abandoned by the government.
“If businesses are left alone and incidents like these continue, no one will be willing to undertake the production of dual-use products,” he said.
Kerza urged companies not to be intimidated into silence.
“The worst thing we can do is become frightened and keep quiet, even if we are blackmailed or otherwise pressured,” he said.
Estonia has determined that a fire at a defence industry company during the summer was a deliberate arson attack commissioned by Russian intelligence services. Lithuanian law enforcement also thwarted an attempted arson attack several years ago.
Dozens of incidents and intimidation cases targeting European defence industry companies were recorded in seven countries during the first half of this year.

Lula da Silva wins 51.79% of vote after 100% of ballots counted — electoral court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, which performs the functions of the Central Election Commission, has completed the vote count for the second round of the presidential election. According to the final results, with 100% of ballots counted, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has officially been reelected.
According to the election authority’s final statistics, Lula da Silva, the candidate of the left-wing Workers’ Party, won with 51.79% of the vote, receiving 64,256,232 votes. His rival, right-wing opposition Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, received 48.21%, with 59,826,041 people voting for him. The total number of valid votes was 124,082,273.
Lula da Silva is now the first politician in the present-day Brazilian history to win the presidential election after trailing in the first round of voting. The elected head of state will assume the office on January 1, 2027.
Earlier, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who represents the right-wing opposition and lost in the second round of the Brazilian presidential election, refused to recognize the election results and stated that they should be annulled.

Investors brace for tech earnings, central bank decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:59:19 UTC
14:59:19 KST

A person walks past an electronic stock board displaying Japan’s Nikkei index at a securities firm in Tokyo, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (AP Photo)
Investors are gearing up for a crucial run of central bank decisions and tech earnings this week.
A drop in oil prices provided limited support after both main contracts soared on Oct. 23 to a six-month high, though sentiment remains fragile owing to fears of a resumption of U.S. attacks on Iran after next week's midterm elections.
AI-linked firms continued to struggle amid worries about the sustainability of the colossal investment boom that pushed stock markets to multiple record highs in the first half of the year.
Traders are growing increasingly worried about when the vast sums pumped into the sector will see returns, if any, while rising interest rates and bond yields are now calling companies' finances into question.
This week sees the release of earnings from U.S. titans and Magnificent Seven members Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet as well as South Korean chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung.
Results from Tesla and Meta last week further stoked spending worries and helped drag stocks lower.
"The AI complex remains under a microscope ahead of what may be the most important stretch of earnings season so far," said SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.
"Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are about to walk on stage, and this is not one of those quarters where a company can simply beat the number, raise the guidance by a whisker and expect applause. Investors want proof now.
"They want to know whether the billions going into the compute buildout are building a durable earnings machine or just a shinier version of the same old capex furnace."
Also in view this week are policy decisions by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.
While the Fed is expected to hold borrowing costs, traders will be keen to get an insight into its thinking following last month's hike and as inflation remains well above its two percent target.

Albania PM proposes tougher protest laws amid student demonstrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:57:09 UTC
14:57:09 KST

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has announced plans for tougher legislation on demonstrations as student-led protests demanding improved education conditions continued in the capital, Tirana.
The protests, which began on October 13, entered their 13th day on Sunday, drawing support from high school students, university faculty members, citizens and trade unions. Some demonstrations have turned violent.
Protesters marched through streets and squares across the capital, gathering first outside the Education Ministry, where they threw stones at the building, before moving to the prime minister’s office.
Tensions escalated as demonstrators threw stones at police and public institutions, while security forces responded with tear gas. Some protesters were injured during clashes in which molotov cocktails were occasionally used.
Rama renewed his calls for dialogue, but protesters rejected the appeals and said they would continue their demonstrations.
Proposed measures target protest conduct
Rama said the current law governing demonstrations dates back to 2001 and does not address digital tools that have become a key part of organising and conducting protests.
The proposed legislative package would introduce fines for organising unauthorised demonstrations, failing to comply with orders to disperse, wearing masks during protests and obstructing traffic.
It would also provide compensation for businesses affected by demonstrations, impose penalties on participants in violent protests and amend the Criminal Code.
The measures would further require the removal of social media posts calling for violence and allow legal proceedings against those responsible.
The proposals come as student demonstrators continue to press for better education conditions despite the government’s calls for dialogue.
Protests in Albania since June
Earlier in June, thousands of protesters gathered in Tirana under the slogan “Albania is not for sale,” over a planned tourism project linked to US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner.
The project aims to transform Sazan Island and parts of the nearby Narta-Zvernec wetland and lagoon area into a luxury tourism destination, claiming 250 hectares within the protected coastal ecosystem.
The resort project is being pursued by Kushner's investment firm and has received support from the Albanian government.
Demonstrators raised environmental concerns and accused authorities of opening protected areas to large-scale construction projects.

US says helped Gulf nations export 1.5 bln barrels of oil through Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:56:52 UTC
14:56:52 KST

A man looks out over the water as a small boat passes cargo ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, early Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. (ISNA via AP)
U.S. Central Command has said it helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via the Strait of Hormuz since summer, bypassing an Iranian blockade.
"U.S. forces reach the milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer," CENTCOM said in a statement posted on X on Oct. 25.
"More than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz with support from CENTCOM forces over the last six months," it added, stating that "over 95 percent of ships navigating the Strait of Hormuz have sailed through safely."
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," said CENTCOM chief admiral Brad Cooper, who was visiting U.S. troops in Hormuz.
Iran has seized control over the vital waterway since the Middle East war erupted with U.S.-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic on Feb. 28.
It has demanded permission for ships to transit the strait, through which a fifth of global oil exports normally pass.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this month that Iran has "lost complete control" of the Strait of Hormuz, claiming that Tehran's economy was "in total and complete freefall."
"The Straits of Hormuz are open. There's almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began. So they've lost complete control of the Straits," he said.
According to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler, crude oil exports reached pre-war levels in September, with at least 16.5 million barrels leaving the region excluding Iran.

The French government is hiding behind a ‘riots’ narrative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:56:04 UTC
14:56:04 KST

The French government is hiding behind a ‘riots’ narrative
It is much easier to fearmonger and try to delegitimise the protests than to address students’ demands.
Images from the violent unrest in France have travelled around the world. Smashed shop windows, destroyed property, acts of looting and raging fires have rightly caused outrage and condemnation.
There is no single explanation of the motives of the perpetrators. There are certainly opportunistic “criminal elements” who take advantage of such situations. But there is also a lot of public anger that has boiled over after it had simmered for years as living conditions have deteriorated and demands for changes have been left unanswered.
The French government has taken full advantage of these violent acts, using them to justify the overly securitised response to the protests and to avoid public scrutiny for the failure to address its own failures. The images of chaos allow those in power to pose as the defenders of a public order they have actively helped undermine.
These acts of violence, however, cannot delegitimise the reasons behind the mass mobilisation of students across France. They also must not distract from the brutal police violence that has unfolded.
Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out by a tear gas grenade fired from a police launcher. Sixteen-year-old Mael lost the sight in one eye after a suspected hit from a police rubber bullet. Fifteen-year-old Evan had a hand blown off by a police stun grenade.
By October 14, 7,950 people had been placed in police custody since the protests began in September, 85 percent of them minors. A further 2,700 were taken into custody following the October 17 protests. Yesterday, police made another 1,000 arrests.
The staggering scale of detention and the mobilisation of tens of thousands of police officers make this one of the most heavily repressed protest movements of this century.
But there is also the quieter violence of social deprivation that the students are protesting and that has largely been ignored in the public narrative.
Across France, the sense of growing impoverishment deepens year after year. Poverty rates are the highest they have been since the 1990s, with 9.8 million people living under the official poverty line. Meanwhile, 53 French billionaires own as much wealth as nearly half of the French population, according to Oxfam.
Deteriorating socioeconomic conditions have hit the French educational system hard.
In Acoua, on the island of Mayotte, the Cite du Nord secondary school was blockaded as early as August 31. Long before protests in the Paris region attracted attention, parents and staff came out in protest to demand better learning and teaching conditions.
Built for 900 pupils, this school accommodates 2,300 in cramped, poorly ventilated classrooms. Alongside staff shortages, the school also struggles with water supply failures and unsanitary conditions in toilets.
In Sevran, a suburb of Paris, pupils and teachers at Blaise-Cendrars secondary school have complained since 2024 about water leaks, mould, unusable toilets, and shortages of tables and chairs.
At Marcelin-Berthelot secondary school in Pantin, another Parisian suburb, windows no longer open at a time when heatwaves can bring temperatures as high as 40C.
At Politzer secondary school in Bagnolet, also a Parisian suburb, staff, pupils and parents learnt in late September that the water was unsafe to drink, although it had been tested in June.
These are just a few examples of a countrywide trend of an educational infrastructure that is fast deteriorating, especially in impoverished areas.
This is compounded by the erosion of the level of education pupils actually receive. According to the education ministry’s own figures, 20.2 million teaching hours were not delivered in state secondary schools in 2024–25, excluding Mayotte: almost one in 10 scheduled hours. Of these, 15 million were lost because absent teachers were not replaced.
According to French economist Lucas Chancel, since 2017, when Emmanuel Macron came to power, government spending per student has declined by 20 percent.
This is the structural violence French students are asking those in power to end. Instead of listening, the government has responded with repressive tactics and narrative spin.
In his address to the public, Macron said he understood the students, but he did not express support for them the way he did for police officers. A meeting with 20 students on Friday resulted in a promise to reform the university entrance platform – not to address the students’ key demands.
Macron has doubled down on the security “solution”, deploying 70,000 police officers and pledging to ban protests. He has accused the “far left” of seeking to “bring down the republic”.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has called on the left to “choose a side”: the Republic equated with the police, or the rioters and their “violent agenda”. As if taking part in a protest amounted to an attack on the state.
Unsurprisingly, the far right is revelling in the chaos that appears to be engulfing the country, obscuring these needs by focusing on the presumed origins of people filmed committing acts of violence. Some far-right politicians have denounced the “hordes of thugs of foreign origin”, others have called for broader powers to strip people of their citizenship.
This rhetoric serves Macron’s political camp well as it allows it to present itself once again as the last defence against the far right, asking the general population to rally behind out of fear rather than because of its governance record. Voters are offered an increasingly bleak choice between those who have fuelled their anger and those seeking to turn it into racial hatred.
At this point, it is clear the government does not seem interested in genuinely addressing the demands of the students is in the cards. Doing so would mean confronting the priorities of Macron’s presidency: protecting the wealth of the few and abandoning the many.
Instead, the government will wait for the movement to exhaust itself, be weakened by fear or be discredited by unrest, until it dies out on its own.
This strategy, however, is a failed one. Even if this protest movement fizzles out, a new one will soon replace it. The French people cannot be scared into complacency forever while their living conditions continue to deteriorate.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Coalition says cuts to climate, housing and more would save $31 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:55:16 UTC
14:55:16 KST

Coalition says cuts to climate, housing and more would save $31 billion
In short:
The Coalition has released costings for a handful of its proposed spending cuts, including cuts to climate and housing initiatives and a plan to strip permanent residents of welfare and NDIS access.
The opposition has accused the government of fuelling inflation with its spending, which Treasurer Jim Chalmers denies.
The Reserve Bank's monetary policy board meets to consider the interest rate next Tuesday.
The spending cuts proposed by the opposition to date would save $31 billion over four years, according to a partial costings update.
Launched at a press conference held while MPs were paying tribute to Helen Haines in the lower house, the document puts dollar figures on pledges to slash Labor climate and housing initiatives and strip welfare from permanent residents.
The fiscal update is unusual at this point of the political cycle, with opposition costings typically finalised close to elections. It is also incomplete, focusing mostly on spending and ignoring the cost of its migration cuts and its pledge to scrap Labor's tax cuts.
But the emphasis on proposals to rein in spending is intended to sharpen attacks on Labor's own spending and counter perceptions that the Coalition's policy offering is underdone, according to a Liberal source involved in the process.
"It is absolutely critical at this time to control spending," Opposition Leader Angus Taylor told reporters, framing the savings as a "down payment" to pay for tax cuts.
Cuts to housing schemes and climate initiatives
The $31.3 billion savings package, which has been costed by the independent Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), comfortably offsets the $9.7 billion cost of the Coalition's income tax policy to index brackets and scrap the $250 workers' tax offset.
It is unlikely to offset the rest of the Coalition's policy commitments, including its plans to scrap Labor's tax hikes on capital gains, negative gearing, trusts, and high-balance super accounts, slash net migration to 100,000 for two years, and lift defence spending.
More than half of the $31 billion in cuts comes from slashing climate-related policies. Those costs have only been broken down into two large bundles, rather than itemised.
Taken together, $9.4 billion would be saved by ditching the new vehicle efficiency standard; the electric vehicle (EV) discount; home battery subsidies; the net zero advisory body; some functions of renewables agency ARENA; and Scope 3 emissions reporting for business.
Another $7.3 billion would be saved by ending subsidies for green aluminium and hydrogen, critical minerals, and other industrial subsidies through Labor's National Reconstruction Fund.
Abandoning Labor's first homebuyer scheme Help to Buy, its social housing fund, its tax incentives for build-to-rent developers and its payments to states that meet housing supply targets would save a combined $4.7 billion.
Stripping eligibility for welfare payments and the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) to permanent residents and other non-citizens would save $2 billion over four years.
As previously announced, the PBO estimates that slashing the tobacco excise and legalising vapes would save $7.9 billion over four years, in part because of an assumption that smokers would switch back to the legal cigarette market.
Emphasis on inflation ahead of RBA meeting
The opposition blames government spending, which is at historically high levels, for persistent inflation.
"The government is absolutely addicted to spending and [that is why] Australian household mortgage rates are going up," Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said today.
In an interview with Nine newspapers, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was budgeting "responsibly" and would outline fresh savings measures in December.
"That will be the ninth consecutive budget update from this government that will have savings in it … That's one of the reasons why the budget is in better condition now than it was expected to be a few years ago," he said.
Mr Chalmers denied government spending was to blame for inflation, noting private demand was growing faster than public demand.
"I think that tells us there are other factors at play … Of course, there'll be commentators who say that we should cut harder and faster … They should nominate, I think, those areas that should be cut more substantially."
The Reserve Bank's monetary policy board meets next Tuesday to consider whether to further increase the cash rate.
The bank's deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, said last week inflation was "materially worse" than expected.
