Israel election enters final 24 hours: Netanyahu's digital blitz, Eisenkot's knockout bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:52:14 UTC
14:52:14 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is preparing a massive social media blitz, Gadi Eisenkot is pushing for a decisive victory over Likud, and Naftali Bennett is racing between cities and WhatsApp conversations in a final effort to win over undecided voters. Across Israel, political parties are entering the final 24 hours of an election campaign that could determine the country's direction for years to come.
Polling stations will open at 7 a.m. Tuesday, October 27, and party leaders are sharpening their messages, mobilizing volunteers and preparing extensive operations to bring supporters to the polls. From parties competing to lead the next government to smaller factions hovering around the electoral threshold, each has its own strategy for the final stretch.
Here is how Israel's major parties and their leaders are planning to spend the hours before voting begins and Election Day itself.
Yashar!: Eisenkot seeks a decisive lead over Likud
Former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot has made finishing as Israel's largest party the central objective of his final campaign push. The leader of Yashar! believes a clear lead over Netanyahu's Likud would strengthen his chances of securing enough recommendations from newly elected lawmakers to be tasked with forming the next government.
"Netanyahu wants a tie, but Israel needs a knockout," Eisenkot said. "Why does Yashar! have to be Israel's largest party? The race is close. The election is between Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Netanyahu is aiming for a tie, a deadlock and another election."
Eisenkot argued that the leader of the largest party receives the mandate to form a government in 90% of cases, warning that unless Yashar! finishes significantly ahead of Likud, Netanyahu could be given the first opportunity to assemble a coalition.
"Change is in danger," Eisenkot said. "We cannot gamble with the country. We need a decisive victory."
He presented Yashar! as a party capable of bringing together Israelis from across the political spectrum and promised a stable four-year government without a rotating premiership or what he described as political extortion. He said all parties seeking political change would be included.
Eisenkot has also intensified his personal confrontation with Netanyahu, framing the vote as a direct choice between the two leaders.
"It's either Netanyahu or me," he said.
Yashar!'s campaign advertising accuses Netanyahu of maintaining a coalition that enables exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox men, funding educational institutions that do not teach core subjects and providing financial benefits to people who do not serve, at the expense of those who work and serve in the military.
Eisenkot is promoting an alternative platform centered on broader military service, compulsory core education, a balanced free-market economy, employment incentives and reduced benefits for those who avoid service.
On Sunday night, thousands of supporters attended a major Yashar! election rally at Hangar 11 in Tel Aviv Port. Eisenkot again stressed that his party needed to finish well ahead of Likud.
Addressing Likud supporters and voters who had backed Netanyahu's coalition, he said he understood how difficult it could be to change political allegiance but argued that Likud itself had departed from its traditional path.
"Deep down, you know Israel cannot go on like this," he said. "Israel needs change. Look me in the eye. You can trust me."
Likud: Netanyahu prepares a digital blitz and an urgent final message
Netanyahu's final-day campaign will concentrate heavily on delivering messages directly to potential voters through their mobile phones and social media accounts.
Likud is preparing to shift from its regular campaign activity into a more urgent operation, a strategy the party has frequently employed in the final hours before polls close.
In recent days, Netanyahu has intensified warnings that a Palestinian state could be established if Likud does not form the next government. His official social media accounts have also published an alarming image depicting an atomic bomb striking Tel Aviv.
The prime minister's final day before voting includes diplomatic and security engagements at his office, alongside interviews with media outlets regarded as sympathetic to him.
But the central campaign effort will take place online. Likud plans to distribute hundreds of videos to supporters identified and targeted throughout the campaign, including footage featuring Netanyahu himself and other material in which he does not appear.
A substantial portion of the party's campaign budget has been reserved for the final stretch. Likud officials believe that, alongside the party's voter-mobilization operation, social media will be the decisive arena until polling stations close.
On Election Day, Netanyahu is expected to vote in Jerusalem before visiting major cities. Toward the evening, he plans to call mayors, local campaign headquarters and party branches to encourage efforts to bring supporters to polling stations.
Likud strategists consider turnout in traditional party strongholds especially important. They are not expecting large numbers of voters to switch political camps at the last minute, making the mobilization of existing supporters and the prevention of complacency central priorities.
Together: Bennett courts undecided voters in person and online
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett is continuing his intensive campaign of public appearances and personal conversations until the last possible moment.
Bennett, who leads the Together alliance, known in Hebrew as Beyachad, has been visiting city centers and residential neighborhoods, organizing informal public discussions he calls "parliaments." The meetings are livestreamed on social media, allowing viewers to follow the debates and discussions.
Between appearances, Bennett has been joining family and friends' WhatsApp groups to speak directly with potential supporters and encourage them to participate in the election.
On Sunday, he visited a neighborhood in Rishon Lezion, where he held a discussion with undecided voters and attempted to persuade them to withdraw their support from Netanyahu.
Bennett has also been reinforcing his pledge that he will not cooperate with Netanyahu under any circumstances, insisting that the prime minister must leave office.
His Monday schedule begins with a workout alongside young people in Tel Aviv, followed by a visit to Beersheba, a city identified by his campaign as having roughly 40% support for Likud.
There, he plans to hold a large public discussion and meet students from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. He will then travel to Herzliya for a discussion with women before visiting the Western Wall in Jerusalem in the evening.
On Tuesday, Bennett is expected to vote early near his home in Ra'anana before beginning a prearranged tour of major cities.
Hundreds of Israelis have recently received personalized recorded messages from Bennett. People close to him say that even during his limited free time, while traveling or late at night, he continues recording messages and speaking directly with undecided voters.
The Democrats: Golan targets Netanyahu over cryptocurrency and the economy
Yair Golan's Democrats are combining a large-scale ground operation with a final round of political messaging.
Thousands of volunteers are expected to operate across Israel, emphasizing the party's pledge not to join a Netanyahu government and its claim that none of its lawmakers will defect to Netanyahu's political camp.
"Only we can be trusted" is the party's central message to voters seeking to replace the current government.
The final campaign is built around the slogan "From despair to hope," with Golan expected to repeat the choice he says faces the country: "An underdeveloped Bibistan or a strong, democratic Israel."
Golan is also seeking to capitalize on a controversy surrounding Netanyahu's comments about cryptocurrency, using the issue to attack the prime minister's economic record.
New billboards ask: "What's happened, Bibi? Did Qatar start paying in crypto?" The slogan is a campaign attack, rather than an established claim about payments.
The Democrats are also highlighting Israel's deteriorating international standing and promising to repair relations with other countries, restore foreign investment and pursue normalization with Saudi Arabia.
Their campaign platform calls for shifting government spending away from West Bank settlements toward development in northern and southern Israel, combating violence by Jewish extremists, evacuating unauthorized outposts and investing in education, vocational training and the technology sector.
According to the party, it has held 1,300 campaign events, while 1,500 volunteer phone operators have made approximately 40,000 calls to voters.
The Democrats say they are also preparing for possible disinformation campaigns and have expressed concerns about potential voting irregularities, violence and provocations, including accusations directed at figures associated with the government and Ben-Gvir. Those concerns and accusations are the party's claims.
Joint List: Personal outreach in Arab communities and beyond
The Arab-led Joint List is focusing its final campaign efforts on direct contact with voters through neighborhood meetings, house gatherings and conversations with residents.
Candidates are visiting communities across the Galilee, the Triangle region in central Israel and the Negev, seeking to persuade undecided voters and encourage those who have shown little interest in the election to participate.
At the same time, the Joint List is continuing to reach out to Jewish voters. Billboards in Tel Aviv and central Israel feature the message "Arab, Jewish and democratic," promoting Jewish-Arab partnership and equality.
The party hopes the campaign will broaden its support beyond its traditional electorate and strengthen its position in the next Knesset.
A large election rally was also held in Iksal in northern Israel in support of Joint List candidate and lawyer Ahmad Darawshe.
In the final hours, the party's emphasis will remain on personal conversations and converting public expressions of support into actual votes.
Otzma Yehudit: Ben-Gvir competes with his right-wing allies
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is dedicating his final campaign day to visits across southern Israel and cities outside the country's main metropolitan centers.
The leader of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party plans to meet residents and broadcast live appearances on social media, promoting the message that "Israel needs a strong Ben-Gvir, and Bibi needs a strong Ben-Gvir."
Ben-Gvir's campaign argues that without a powerful Otzma Yehudit faction, Netanyahu could eventually form a government with Eisenkot. Netanyahu has rejected that suggestion and said Ben-Gvir would serve as a senior minister in his next government, but Otzma Yehudit is continuing to promote the claim.
Ben-Gvir is also targeting voters who might otherwise support the Religious Zionist Party, led by Bezalel Smotrich.
He argues that voting for Religious Zionism will not help bring Moshe Feiglin into the Knesset, because Feiglin's place is already secure, but will instead help elect additional candidates associated with Smotrich.
On Election Day, Ben-Gvir is expected to vote in the West Bank settlement of Kiryat Arba before beginning an extensive tour that includes Jerusalem, Netanya, Petah Tikva, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Sderot, Beersheba, Netivot, Ofakim, Modi'in and Bat Yam.
Much of that route overlaps with areas where Religious Zionism is concentrating its own campaign efforts.
The difference is organizational. Likud and Smotrich's party are operating a joint voter-mobilization headquarters, while Ben-Gvir is running an independent operation focused on increasing Otzma Yehudit's representation rather than necessarily expanding the entire right-wing bloc.
Otzma Yehudit officials say they were never invited to participate in the joint operation.
The result is an increasingly direct competition between two parties that would ordinarily be considered natural coalition partners, with Ben-Gvir presenting himself as a guarantee that Netanyahu will not form a more centrist government.
Yisrael Beytenu: Liberman calls for the end of Netanyahu's era
Avigdor Liberman is entering the final 24 hours with a central campaign message: "The end of the Netanyahu era and ultra-Orthodox rule."
His Yisrael Beytenu party is also stressing Liberman's political experience and presenting him as a leader who will not reverse his commitments after the election.
The campaign portrays him as someone whose word can be trusted, contrasting that image with its criticism of other political leaders.
Yisrael Beytenu's immediate goal is to increase turnout in liberal and secular areas, particularly major cities where supporters of parties seeking to replace Netanyahu have a significant presence.
Party officials say the remaining hours should be devoted to personal phone calls, direct contact with undecided voters, coordinating transportation and ensuring that supporters know where and when to vote.
Field teams will operate nationwide, updating voter lists, assigning responsibilities and maintaining contact with campaign volunteers.
Telephone operations are expected to continue throughout Election Day, with staff contacting potential supporters and helping those who need reminders, directions or transportation to polling stations.
United Torah Judaism: Rabbis frame voting as a religious duty
United Torah Judaism is relying heavily on its rabbinical leadership and tightly organized ultra-Orthodox communities to maximize turnout.
On Sunday night, Degel HaTorah, the party's Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox component, gathered tens of thousands of yeshiva students at a major event in Bnei Brak. Senior rabbis, leading yeshiva heads and lawmakers attended.
Rabbis Landau and Hirsch led the gathering, alongside other prominent religious figures who described voting as a religious obligation and warned that a decline in the party's strength could constitute a desecration of God's name.
Speakers repeated the slogan "Do not shirk voting," a play on the Hebrew language surrounding military-service exemptions, and described the election as a "vote for the Torah."
They also warned supporters against backing newly established ultra-Orthodox parties competing in the election.
Within Agudat Yisrael, the party's Hasidic component, preparations are continuing for an extensive Election Day operation designed to ensure that eligible voters in each Hasidic community reach polling stations.
Because polling officials are prohibited from sharing voter-participation information with party representatives, United Torah Judaism plans to station activists outside polling stations to record which known supporters arrive to vote, rather than relying on official turnout records.
Shas: Warnings over Jewish identity and a push for Sephardic support
Shas is concentrating on its traditional Sephardic and religious electorate, framing the election around the preservation of Jewish identity.
The party's spiritual leader, Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, addressed a rally in Netivot on Sunday and urged supporters to continue the political and religious legacy of his late father, former Sephardic chief rabbi Ovadia Yosef.
Shas is establishing a telephone operation to monitor turnout among its supporters throughout Election Day.
Where participation appears low, party rabbis are expected to contact local religious leaders and encourage them to mobilize their communities.
The party is also seeking support from additional Sephardic ultra-Orthodox communities and is approaching religious figures in the hope that they will publicly endorse its election campaign.
Campaign videos warn of threats to "Jewish identity." Another video uses footage of the late Rabbi Ovadia Yosef entering a polling station and blessing people voting for Shas.
Religious Zionism and Zehut: Mobilizing their traditional base
The joint Religious Zionism-Zehut list, led by Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin, is preparing an extensive field operation concentrated on its traditional electorate.
According to the party, thousands of activists have registered to participate in its final campaign activities, with operations planned in approximately 25 major cities and 65 buses assigned to transport supporters.
The effort is divided into three geographic areas: religious Zionist strongholds such as Jerusalem, Petah Tikva, Givat Shmuel, Ra'anana and Modi'in; peripheral cities including Ashkelon, Sderot, Beit She'an, Tiberias and Dimona, as well as communities in the Galilee and Negev; and Jewish settlements across the West Bank, including smaller communities.
One of the campaign's more unusual features is a branded roulette wheel intended to encourage conversations with passersby.
The wheel features issues the party wants to highlight, including governance, construction in the disputed E1 area east of Jerusalem, the evacuation of farms and communities in the West Bank and opposition to what the party calls the "exclusion of Judaism." Security, settlement policy and legal issues also appear on the wheel.
These messages are aimed at the party's core electorate, particularly voters who may be considering a switch to Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit.
On Election Day, the party will also operate a telephone headquarters led by candidate Yossi Bachar, a retired major general from Kibbutz Be'eri.
Ra'am: Abbas seeks higher turnout in the Negev
Mansour Abbas and his Ra'am party, also known as the United Arab List, are concentrating on increasing participation among Arab voters, particularly Bedouin communities in the Negev.
Thousands attended election rallies on Sunday in Hura and the nearby al-Sayyid area, according to the party.
Abbas appeared alongside lawmakers Walid al-Hawashla and Yasser Hujirat, local government leaders, religious figures and political activists.
Speakers emphasized the importance of participation and argued that every vote could strengthen Ra'am's representation in the next Knesset.
During the events, party officials highlighted what they described as achievements from Ra'am's participation in a previous governing coalition, including the recognition of four Negev villages, measures intended to permit construction in previously unrecognized communities and an economic and social development program.
Ra'am also emphasized the issue of home demolitions and its demand for changes to government policy affecting Arab communities.
The party's final message is centered on higher turnout as a means of increasing its parliamentary strength and contributing to its stated goal of replacing the government.
Reservists-Economic Party: Hendel and Zelekha appeal to the middle class
Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, whose joint Reservists-Economic Party is battling to cross the electoral threshold, are trying to present a vote for their list as a protest against Israel's established political parties.
Their central message targets Israelis frustrated by the burden of military reserve service and the rising cost of living.
The party is appealing to working and middle-class voters who believe traditional political parties have failed to address the financial and social pressures they face.
Hendel and Zelekha are also promoting themselves as a potential source of political stability, arguing that their entry into the Knesset could help prevent another election.
In doing so, they are attempting to turn their precarious position near the electoral threshold into a reason for voters to support them.
The party is also seeking to generate momentum through public declarations of support from military reservists, an effort associated with Idan Amedi, while continuing visits to locations popular with younger voters.
Amcha Yisrael: Winter targets former Netanyahu supporters
Just six weeks after announcing its formation, Amcha Yisrael, led by retired general Ofer Winter, held a major final campaign rally in Jerusalem on Sunday night.
The event was used to distribute responsibilities among activists and volunteers ahead of Election Day.
According to the party, its campaign has included more than 250 house meetings, over 12 major rallies and more than 100 field visits across Israel.
The party's final-day strategy is based on an analysis of polling stations that it commissioned to identify areas where it believes support could be increased.
Amcha Yisrael says it plans to target former Netanyahu voters, as well as people who previously supported Bennett and Liberman, on the assumption that these groups contain voters who may still be open to persuasion.
Campaign volunteers will be dispatched to those locations, alongside a major billboard operation in areas the party has identified as strategically important.
The emphasis will be on younger neighborhoods with concentrations of soldiers and military reservists, as well as cities with religious Zionist populations outside the West Bank settlements, where Smotrich's party is considered stronger.
On Tuesday, Winter is expected to vote in Mitzpe Netofa before touring polling stations identified by his campaign as having significant potential. He will meet activists and volunteers throughout the day.
Winter plans to end the evening at Hangar 11 in Tel Aviv Port, where he will watch the exit polls alongside party supporters.

The Port of Riga to become a testbed for resilient maritime connectivity, as LVR Flote and HARDMODE sign MoU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:50:39 UTC
14:50:39 KST

LVR Flote, a provider of technical port services, and connectivity technology company HARDMODE have partnered to develop and test secure communications technologies for ports and the wider maritime sector as a crucial part of critical infrastructure. The goal is to deploy resilient and secure communication from routine operations to crisis situations. The parties signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during the Techritory Forum in Riga.
The Port of Riga will serve as a real-world testing environment for new connectivity solutions designed to remain reliable in challenging conditions, where connectivity is a must for
mission-critical operations. The partners will pilot technologies in real port operations, jointly pursue research and development projects, and explore how successful solutions could be commercialised and deployed in other European ports.
Ports and the maritime sector rely on real-time data exchange. A port fleet is more than vessels: it also includes infrastructure that has to keep working at all times. HARDMODE develops multi-technology communication solutions that keep sensors, people, vehicles, drones and other infrastructure elements connected even when no commercial network is available, but high stability is critical.
Artūrs Lindenbergs, Founder & CEO at HARDMODE: “Critical infrastructure is getting more demanding every year. As more sensors, vehicles and systems are connected, more of a port’s daily work stops when connectivity drops. Our approach has two parts. The first is layering: resilience cannot depend on a single technology, so we combine several, and when one is degraded, the others carry the traffic. The second is decentralisation: each node carries both the network and the software the use case needs, and the nodes connect directly to each other. The result is one solution rather than a set of systems someone has to integrate on site, and the Port of Riga is the right place to prove that in real operations.”
The Baltic Sea region has experienced repeated GNSS interference affecting shipping and port operations in recent years. Such incidents highlight the need for communications systems that do not depend on a single technology or infrastructure layer.
As a developer of dual-use connectivity solutions for defence, critical infrastructure, first responders and maritime environments, HARDMODE, together with LVR Flote, will research how different communication technologies, such as mobile, non-terrestrial, tactical and narrowband, can support port operations in a single joint ecosystem.
For LVR Flote, which provides technical port services and supports the maintenance and operation of infrastructure at the Port of Riga, the partnership allows testing technologies against real operational requirements. Potential applications include infrastructure monitoring, data management, navigation safety, maintenance, and other port services that will increasingly depend on reliable and resilient communication.
Kaspars Ozoliņš, Member of the Board of LVR Flote: “Port technical services have to keep running in everyday operations and in a crisis alike. Together with HARDMODE, we want to explore how hydrographic surveys, infrastructure maintenance and coordination with other port stakeholders could continue even when conventional networks are disrupted. For us, this is what innovation, cooperation and development mean in practice: developing solutions based on real operational needs and growing stronger together.”
The cooperation will extend beyond connectivity alone. The partners intend to create an open testing framework that can involve other technology companies whose products rely on secure communications. Those include developers of sensors, monitoring systems, automation technologies, and digital port services.
LVR Flote brings direct operational expertise and real service requirements, helping technology companies pilot new solutions for ports and the wider maritime sector in a real port environment and see how different systems work together. In return, LVR Flote gains access to solutions that could improve the efficiency, resilience and quality of port technical services.
This cooperation also opens a new chapter between the Netherlands and Latvia in the maritime sector. HARDMODE has roots in both Latvia and the Netherlands, which gives the partnership an international dimension. The partners intend to use the pilots in Riga as a basis for joint international R&D initiatives and potential pathways to scale successful pilots into wider European markets.
H.E. Carl Peersman, Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to Latvia: “Resilient critical infrastructure and secure digital connectivity are vital for both the security and economic stability of Europe’s maritime gateways. As a proud country partner of the Techritory Forum, the Embassy of the Netherlands is pleased to see this collaboration take shape between Dutch-Latvian innovators like HARDMODE (Sentyiv B.V.) and Latvia’s LVR Flote. Using the Port of Riga as a real-world testbed underscores the strength of our bilateral innovation ties and our shared commitment to building robust, future-proof solutions for the entire European maritime sector.”
About LVR Flote
LVR Flote, a provider of comprehensive technical port services, plays an integral role in maintaining and supporting port infrastructure at the Port of Riga. Through public-private cooperation, LVR Flote drives innovation in port operations, digitalisation, and navigation safety, contributing to the efficiency and competitiveness of Latvia’s ports.
About HARDMODE
HARDMODE provides dual-use communication solutions and products for defence, critical infrastructure, first responders and maritime environments, where communication has to work even when existing networks are unavailable. Drawing on deep expertise in telecom engineering, software development and cybersecurity innovations, the company delivers reliable and secure multi-technology solutions.

Yasuo Fukuda, Japan’s first second-generation prime minister, dies at 90, Nikkei reports
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:49:24 CET
14:49:24 KST

TOKYO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who used his brief period in office to seek closer ties with Asian neighbours, particularly China, has died at the age of 90, the Nikkei business daily reported on Monday.
The Japanese politician, the first son of a prime minister to become premier himself, died on Thursday from heart failure, the Nikkei said.
Becoming prime minister on the sudden resignation of Shinzo Abe in 2007, Fukuda lasted less than a year — a tenure even shorter than his father Takeo’s two-year stint.
A graduate in economics from Tokyo’s prestigious Waseda University, Fukuda spent nearly two decades working his way up the ranks of an oil company — including a two-year posting in the United States — before resigning to become a political secretary when his father became premier in 1976.
Elected to Japan’s more powerful lower house of parliament in 1990, Fukuda was chief cabinet secretary from 2000 to 2004, resigning as one of several cabinet ministers to admit not paying into the pension system.
Known for his testy manner, the bespectacled Fukuda drew criticism in 2003 for off-the-record comments in which he suggested women who dressed provocatively were asking to be raped.
When Fukuda succeeded Abe he joked he might have drawn the short straw in assuming office given the divided parliament and opposition parties’ ability to delay legislation.
Frustrated with the stalled legislative process, Fukuda resigned in 2008, the second of six prime ministers to quit after only around a year in office.
Known as a diplomatic dove, Fukuda made several visits to China after leaving office in an effort to improve often fraught relations.
Fukuda leaves a son, Tatsuo, who is also a lawmaker and has been viewed as a potential future prime minister.
(Reporting by Tokyo Newsroom; Editing by Christopher Cushing and Kate Mayberry)

‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:45:22 UTC
14:45:22 KST

Standing on the streets of Belgrade, as passing cars honked excitedly and revellers high-fived police officers, Sara, 24, gestures to the streets around her to explain just how much things had changed for Serbia’s student-led movement.
Moments earlier, the country’s longstanding leader, Aleksandar Vučić, had conceded defeat to the student movement, ushering in a seismic political shift in the Balkan country.
It was a surreal reversal of fortunes for the hundreds of thousands of people who had spent nearly two years peacefully protesting against a ruling power that had become increasingly authoritarian. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” says Sara.
The realisation saw people pour into streets across Serbia to mark the incredible trajectory. In Novi Sad – where the protests had begun in November 2024 following the deadly collapse of a train station roof – thousands gathered in celebration after Vučić conceded that the Students’ List movement had likely won between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament, while his rightwing SNS party had 105, citing preliminary results.
In Belgrade, tens of thousands of people flooded the city’s main boulevards, chanting euphorically, waving flags and setting off flares against an unrelenting backdrop of honking car horns. “Oh my gosh, I don’t know how to explain it,” says Tamara, 35. “I’m so happy and excited.”
Sunday’s results would ultimately set Serbia on a path towards “freedom and hope for a better tomorrow,” she says. But she was under no illusions that it would come easily.
“I know we have a tough period ahead of us, I do,” she says. “But even so, it’s a huge relief and gives us energy to keep going.”
The tremendous task of reversing the country’s drift towards authoritarianism and deeply entrenched corruption now falls to the list of 250 candidates, which includes more than 160 doctorates as well as a sprinkling of farmers, athletes and others.
Adding to the challenge is the fact that the students’ policy platform downplayed some of the country’s more divisive issues: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum, and Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia.
On Sunday, however, many were simply thrilled to celebrate the end of a government that had become known for routinely threatening its critics and chipping away at press freedoms.
“The people have won! The people defeated a dictator! The people will lead Serbia!” Nebojsa Cosic told Reuters as people in the street linked arms to dance the traditional Serbian folk dance, Kolo.
The crowds were also swift to descend on the central park in Belgrade where Vučić’s loyalists had camped out for more than a year, joyfully tearing down the fences and tents that had blocked off access to the park.
Duško Suvajac, 52, points to the broader implications as the elections kicked off 10 pivotal days of ballots across the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces. “This is a symbol for Europe and the world,” he says. “It’s a demonstration of how freedom can defeat evil.”
As he spoke, those around him hugged, kissed, cried and screamed with joy. For many, it was a singular moment to reclaim the same streets where the student-led call for change had been met by police wielding batons and teargas and even a suspected sound cannon.
“It’s simply the realisation of our dream,” says Sara. “We will remember this moment for the rest of our lives.”

14:43:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Railway Corp. generated a record NT$876 million (US$26.89 million) in bento sales revenue in 2025, up 9.07% from a year earlier.
TR sold an average of about 25,800 bentos a day last year, although total sales volume remained below the record of 10.54 million set in 2019, per CNA.
Pork chop bentos, a longtime staple dating back to the railway’s early meal offerings, remained the clear favorite. They accounted for 7.18 million sales, far ahead of chicken leg bentos at 560,000 and the “Kaohsiung Double Happiness Bento” at 260,000.
Taipei Main Station led sales with 2.65 million bentos sold in 2025, followed by Xinzuoying Station with 800,000 and Banqiao Station with 680,000.
TR’s bento production is handled by six catering units in Taipei, Qidu, Taichung, Kaohsiung, Hualien, and Taitung. The Taipei unit is the largest, producing 3.5 million bentos last year.
TR said it was cautiously optimistic about sales this year and plans to maintain food quality while introducing special bentos featuring holiday themes and local ingredients. Its bento business began in 1949 and has since expanded to include options such as braised pork and fish.

Brazil pauses presidential vote count after Supreme Court extends hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:39:00 UTC
14:39:00 KST

BRASILIA, Brazil (Reuters) -- Brazil's Supreme Court allowed some polling stations to extend voting in the country's presidential election by two hours on Sunday, leading the electoral authority to pause a vote count that had already started publishing early-stage results.
The Supreme Court's decision and the subsequent pause of the vote count add confusion to a tense contest between two opposing political forces: leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva versus right-wing Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro.
A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to U.S. President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a bulwark against Washington's influence in the region as his government has pushed back on U.S. trade and security policies.
Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin accepted a request by Lula's campaign to extend voting, pointing to public transportation issues in three cities in the state of Bahia.
Zanin's decision landed right around the election's 5 p.m. Brasilia time (2000 GMT) cutoff, creating confusion as some polling stations had already closed.
In a subsequent ruling, Zanin said those stations would remain shut, allowing authorities to begin tallying those votes, but that polling stations that had not closed after the official cutoff could keep receiving voters for an additional two hours.
The electoral court, or TSE, had already started publishing results that showed Lula leading Bolsonaro with 0.25% of ballots counted. Lula had 57.66% of votes, compared with 42.34% for Bolsonaro, the early count showed.
After the Zanin ruling, the TSE said it would pause the vote count to allow for the extended voting window to close.
The pause in the vote count injects uncertainty into a Brazilian electoral process still grappling with the fallout from 2022, when Jair Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat to Lula. His supporters later invaded government buildings in protest against the result, and Bolsonaro received a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup.
The candidate's brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, speaking on a livestream on his YouTube channel, questioned why the Supreme Court had ruled in a process overseen by the country's federal electoral court: "Strange, isn't it?" he said. "It's hard to imagine what the legal basis for this could possibly be. It doesn't inspire credibility."
Two legal experts told Reuters the extension of voting hours and allegations around disrupted public transportation could draw legal challenges.
"Depending on the election result, there is a possibility that the losing side might attempt to contest the outcome, arguing that many people were unable to vote even with the extended deadline," said Vera Chemim, a constitutional lawyer in Sao Paulo.
Lula had asked electoral authorities to extend voting in at least nine states after his campaign alleged some officials reduced election day public transportation, impacting voters' ability to get to the polls.
Earlier on Sunday, a court in Bahia, a Lula stronghold in the Northeast, ordered the arrest of a top transportation official in the city of Salvador over allegations that he directed a reduction in the city's bus fleet.
In comments before Zanin's decision, Lula said "something abominable is happening" in this election.
Flavio Bolsonaro had also asked for voting to be extended in at least three states, citing bad weather.
Lula and his allies see Sunday's runoff as a chance to stem Latin America's conservative drift.
Reuters on Saturday revealed a campaign within Trump's State Department to help get the Bolsonaros back in power.
Trump has so far declined to endorse a candidate. Asked on Sunday who he hoped would win, Trump declined to say.
"I don't want to get into that, but we are watching," he told reporters in Washington.

China’s political elite gather for talks on Communist Party discipline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:38:41 UTC
14:38:41 KST

China’s political elite gather for talks on Communist Party discipline
The four-day meeting is being watched closely for clues as to the country’s direction and future leadership
China’s political leaders and elites have begun a four-day meeting to discuss ways to strengthen discipline within the ruling Communist Party, as President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty from officials and deepens his anticorruption campaign.
The fifth plenum, which started on Monday, is also being watched closely for clues to the country’s direction and future leadership.
The closed-door gathering comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as party leader and ahead of expected personnel changes to key leadership bodies.
Roughly 300 members of the Communist Party’s Central Committee are attending.
While Xi has consolidated his grip on power, analysts say the plenum will give him another chance to align what Chinese officials do with what Beijing wants.
“The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising [through] the ranks share Xi’s assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces,” Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London’s Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, told The Associated Press news agency.
“The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising through the ranks share Xi’s assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces,” Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London’s Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, told The Associated Press news agency.
Previous plenums have helped Xi to cement his authority.
The Chinese leader has waged a 14-year campaign against corruption that has purged thousands of officials, including dozens of committee members.
Yet Xi remains frustrated with cadres he says are still not implementing his orders.
In a January speech, published by state media in advance of this week’s plenum, he railed against “two-faced” officials who appear to comply with directives but “inwardly resist”, are “politically opportunistic” and pursue “individualism”.
During the plenum, the committee will discuss a draft policy decision on advancing “full and rigorous party self-governance,” China’s official Xinhua news agency reported.
The push is meant to make cadres more disciplined, effective and less corrupt.
Analysts say Xi is trying to maximise efficiency and loyalty among cadres by imposing more supervision and rules.
Neil Thomas, senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said he expects demands for tighter scrutiny of public spending and major projects, more use of technology to uncover corruption and tougher consequences for officials who fail to deliver on Xi’s priorities.
Because of Xi’s extensive purges, this year’s plenum is expected to have the lowest turnout since former leader Mao Zedong died in 1976.
Eight of the Central Committee’s seats are vacant, with another 15 members under investigation and at risk of being replaced.
Xi’s anticorruption drive has also targeted the military, toppling five of the seven members of the Central Military Commission (CMC), the party’s top armed forces body.
The plenum could see new members appointed to the CMC, and Xi might even restructure the party’s control over the military.
The talks come as the world’s second-largest economy is struggling to address persistently sluggish domestic spending and a protracted crisis in the crucial property sector.
Turbulent political and economic ties with the United States are weighing on China’s leaders as well.

Saint Demetrius protects Bulgaria in times of trouble and hardship

Saint Demetrius protects Bulgaria in times of trouble and hardship
The church bearing the name of the saint in Pancharevo is a symbol of the desire for freedom and unity
Monday 26 October 2026 06:25
Monday, 26 October 2026, 06:25
PHOTO facebook.com/hramsvetidimitarpancharevo
Font size
St. Demetrius of Thessalonica is one of the most revered saints in Bulgaria. There are many churches in this country, built in honor of the saint who died a martyr's death in the 4th century, because of his refusal to persecute and punish the Christian believers. During the Second Bulgarian State (1185-1396), the Bulgarians regarded Saint Demetrius as the heavenly protector of the capital city of Tarnovo.
According to historical records, in 1185 an icon of St. Demetrius miraculously arrived in Tarnovo. The icon came from a basilica that was looted during the Norman invasion in Thessaloniki where the relics of the saint were kept. The icon's arrival was a sign for the Bulgarian rulers that the saint will protect the recently restored Bulgarian state. In honor of the saint, a magnificent church was built at the foot of the Trapezitsa fortress. Until the third decade of the 13th century, it served as the leading church of the Bulgarian state. It was there that Archbishop Basil I became the head of the restored independent Bulgarian Church following Byzantine rule. All Bulgarian rulers who reigned between 1186 and 1241 received the insignia of their royal dignity in the Church of St. Demetrius.
The Church of St. Demetrius the Great Martyr of Thessaloniki in Pancharevo district
PHOTO bg-patriarshia.bg
The tradition of building churches dedicated to St. Demetrius continues to this day, reinforcing the saint’s enduring role as a protector of Bulgaria. The beautiful white church of St. Demetrius in the Pancharevo district of Sofia is one such example. The local residents did not have their own church for many years, but even before Bulgaria became a free state, large-scale construction of a church began in the then village of Pancharevo, situated near Sofia. The building was finally completed in 1882 and solemnly consecrated on October 26, St. Demetrius Day. The church is located in the historical center of Pancharevo and is designated a cultural monument of local significance.
Archpriest Krastin Apostolov
PHOTO facebook.com/HramRojdestvoHristovoMladost
"The church was built through the efforts of the entire Pancharevo community, embodying the dream of a free and united Bulgaria", Archpriest Krastin Apostolov says. In the 17th-19th centuries, at the end of the Ottoman Empire, Pancharevo was a remarkably diverse place, inhabited by refugees from Macedonia and Thrace, as well as Circassians. The settlers gave the name of the settlement, which is believed to derive from the old Bulgarian word "panitsa”, meaning a bowl and the Turkish word “çare”, meaning "resort", in reference to the healing mineral springs in the area, which have been known since antiquity.
"Many of the Bulgarians who fled from Macedonia had ties to Thessaloniki, the center of the geographical region of Macedonia, so choosing St. Demetrius as the patron saint was a natural decision. In a way, this church heralded the emergence of a free Bulgaria, not only because of its beautiful appearance but also because it became a gathering place for the people who would go on to build modern Bulgaria. One of the first hydroelectric power plants, not only in this country, but in the entire Balkan Peninsula, was built here. This happened a few decades after the church was built, but the people who constructed the power plant came from France and Italy and some of them settled in the small village of Pancharevo. In the beginning of the 20th century the population rapidly increased and the church became the gathering place for both newcomers and long-time residents."
"Today, the situation in Pancharevo is not much different from what it was 140 years ago, when the temple was built", Archpriest Krastin Apostolov adds.
"The church was built in a multicultural environment. That is why, I personally feel responsible for continuing the work of those who managed to build such a majestic and iconic temple before the Liberation and within the framework of the Ottoman Empire - a true symbol of a new and free Bulgaria."

Houthi militia targets Riyadh airport, Saudi-led coalition strikes Sanaa missile launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:31:49 UTC
14:31:49 KST

Yemen’s Houthi militia said they targeted Riyadh airport and pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, while the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two Houthi militia ballistic missile launchers in Sanaa.
Houthi militia spokesman Yahya Saree said on X that the group targeted the airport with a ballistic missile. Saree also said the Houthi militia carried out drone attacks on crude oil pumping stations along the East-West Pipeline.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence Directorate earlier announced that its early warning system had issued a danger alert for Riyadh. Major General Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said a Houthi militia ballistic missile targeting the capital had been intercepted.
The East-West Pipeline is one of Saudi Arabia’s most important crude oil transportation routes. Operated by state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco, it stretches approximately 1,200 kilometres (745 miles) from the Abqaiq area in eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
The pipeline transports crude oil from production and processing facilities in the east to refineries and export terminals along the Red Sea, providing an overland alternative to maritime shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen’s internationally recognised government since March 2015. Clashes between government forces and the Houthi militia have intensified in recent months. The group has targeted Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones, accusing the kingdom of responsibility for attacks against it.
Striking missile launchers
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen launched strikes on the capital, Sanaa, early on Monday, claiming to have destroyed two Houthi militia ballistic missile launchers.
Al-Maliki said one of the launchers had been used in a Houthi militia attack on Riyadh in recent hours. In a post on X, he said the coalition was continuing operations to dismantle the group’s ballistic missile network.
The Yemeni army said on Sunday that its forces had “neutralised” around 218 Houthi militias and field commanders in 753 operations over the previous 24 hours, destroying or damaging 78 military vehicles and weapons.
The army said the operations, part of Operation ‘Dawn of Yemen’, targeted forward command centres, fortifications, firing positions, troop concentrations, reinforcements and supply vehicles. It added that the attacks disrupted Houthi militia reinforcements heading to front lines and supported raids and ground assaults by government forces.
The army did not specify how many of those it said had been “neutralised” were killed or wounded. The Houthi militias did not immediately comment.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthi militias seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, including Sanaa, while the government and allied forces retain Aden and substantial areas of southern and eastern Yemen. Renewed fighting has shifted front lines, particularly along the Red Sea coast, and control of some areas remains contested.

Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:30:27 UTC
14:30:27 KST

Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
There has long been talk of “hunter” satellites and an intensifying confrontation in space between Russia and the United States. But this week brought an unprecedented escalation in the new “star wars.” On October 18, a Russian inspector satellite came closer than ever to a spacecraft operated by the Finnish-American company ICEYE. The company openly helps Ukraine, giving its armed forces access to satellite images of Russian military facilities, including airfields, naval ports, and oil refineries. Here’s what we know about the exceptionally close encounter, how Moscow is describing it, and why independent experts are alarmed.
Russian Kosmos satellites have pursued this spacecraft before, but never like this
Overnight into October 18, the Russian satellite Kosmos-2612 approached the radar imaging satellite ICEYE-X36 after a series of maneuvers that began four days earlier. The Ukrainian military uses data from the ICEYE satellite.
This was not their first close encounter. In the spring, four Russian spacecraft were “hunting” this same satellite: Kosmos-2612, 2610, 2611, and 2613 all approached it. Earlier, in February, news outlets reported on maneuvers by Luch spacecraft pursuing telecommunications satellites operated by Intelsat and Eutelsat.
This time, Kosmos-2612 came exceptionally close to its target: hundreds or even tens of meters away, rather than tens of kilometers as before. Observational astronomer Marco Langbroek estimates that at their closest approach, at 1:35 a.m. GMT on October 18, the spacecraft were between 26 and 470 meters apart. Measurement errors make a more precise estimate impossible. Bart Hendrickx, an independent researcher of Russia’s space program, told Meduza that he knew of no previous encounter at such close range in low Earth orbit. In earlier encounters, he said, satellites had remained at least several dozen kilometers apart.
He said the complexity and methodical persistence of the maneuvers by Kosmos-2612 and its fellow satellites, numbered 2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614, were also surprising. All these spacecraft, along with satellite 2609, were launched aboard a single rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on April 16.
“The satellites used a considerable amount of fuel on these maneuvers. By May, it was already clear that these weren’t ordinary Earth-observation and communications satellites, which generally conserve their fuel. Perhaps [through this latest escalation] Russia is demonstrating its ability to change orbits quickly and unpredictably to threaten enemy satellites,” Hendrickx said.
Moscow calls these maneuvers “a tool of strategic deterrence” and a warning to commercial companies
The Russian military previously acknowledged launching inspector satellites but said their sole purpose was “monitoring the condition of Russian satellites” — and said they had carried out such monitoring. Now, following Kosmos-2612’s dangerous maneuvers, the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta has published an article by Yuri Knutov, a military expert, retired colonel, and director of the Air Defense Forces Museum in Balashikha, outside Moscow. The article says Russia’s actions “do not violate international law” and that the inspector satellites themselves are “a tool of strategic deterrence.”
“Russia is demonstrating its ability to ‘blind’ or at least identify sources of threats. The approach to ICEYE-X36 sends a clear signal: Any commercial company making its capabilities available for intelligence gathering against Russia must recognize that its spacecraft may be subjected to forced inspection in orbit,” Knutov wrote. He said both ICEYE satellites and the Starlink constellation, which is critical to Ukrainian military command and communications, had effectively become part of NATO’s intelligence apparatus.
Like analyst Georgy Trishkin, whose views we quoted here, Knutov believes the Kosmos maneuvers were intended to force the ICEYE satellite to take evasive action to avoid a collision and quickly use up its fuel, turning it into “a useless piece of metal that will eventually burn up in the upper atmosphere.”
Knutov said the Russian satellites were less vulnerable to such a tactic because modern inspector spacecraft have much larger fuel reserves than their predecessors. Earlier models could perform only two or three orbital maneuvers before running out of fuel, he said, whereas newer satellites can remain in orbit for extended periods, carry out complex close approaches, and track other spacecraft over long stretches.
This latest episode in the space cold war was clearly visible from Earth. On Monday, Spaceweather.com asked whether the close encounter between Kosmos and ICEYE would be visible through binoculars or a backyard telescope. By Tuesday, it had its answer: yes.
This image, taken by the Swiss company s2a systems, shows the encounter. The bright object in front is the ICEYE-X36 radar satellite. Its apparent magnitude is about 7, making it invisible to the naked eye but easy to see through binoculars or an amateur telescope. The fainter object behind it is Kosmos-2612.
Russia isn’t the only country with space programs like these
Other countries, particularly the United States and China, have their own programs to develop inspector satellites. These spacecraft are designed to approach other objects in space that aren’t built for such encounters — those without docking ports, for example. These approaches can have various purposes: intercepting radio transmissions, inspecting another spacecraft, diagnosing problems, or even destroying it.
Militaries initiated and funded nearly all of these programs, so the public first learned they existed from amateur astronomers tracking the strange behavior of uncataloged satellites. Since 2011, when these observers identified an American satellite nicknamed Prowler this way, dozens more inspector satellites and many cases of pursuit have been detected, most involving Russian spacecraft.
Russian satellite maneuvers are easier to track because of censorship in the Pentagon’s main space catalog
Unequal access to information partly explains this pattern of observations. The U.S. military maintains Space-Track, the main publicly accessible catalog of artificial objects in space. It withholds the full orbital parameters of some U.S. military and intelligence satellites or publishes them with a delay. Until 2018, the Pentagon even classified data on civilian spacecraft launched as secondary payloads alongside military ones.
The U.S. military does not conceal Russian satellites’ orbital data, so anyone with the relevant skills can use the available data to plot their movements rather than track them through a telescope.
In 2018, the State Department protested the “very abnormal behavior” of Russian satellites. The U.S. military has protested their “threatening” maneuvers and anti-satellite weapons tests (we wrote about these nesting-doll satellites). Then, in 2024, Washington accused Moscow of preparing to deploy nuclear weapons in space.
Yet the United States has operated GSSAP satellites since 2014. These are essentially the same kind of inspector satellites, used to monitor satellites in geostationary orbit. And in June 2026, the U.S. military launched Jackal, built by True Anomaly, and Puma, made by Rocket Lab, as part of the Victus Haze exercise to practice space “hunting” scenarios.
In September of this year, the Pentagon acknowledged for the first time that it had deployed weapons in space — both kinetic and nonkinetic. The next few years in Earth orbit will clearly be tense.
Inspector satellites are also being developed for entirely civilian purposes. One example is LINK, a spacecraft meant to attempt a rescue of the Swift space telescope, but its mission ended in failure.
It’s hard to predict what the Kosmos satellites will do next
What happens next depends largely on how much fuel the Russian satellites have left. They may continue maneuvering around ICEYE spacecraft. According to Langbroek, as of midday on October 21, Kosmos-2612 had stopped moving away from its target and was holding at a distance of 480 kilometers. Hendrickx cautioned that the pursuit might not be over: Kosmos-2612 could return if it had enough fuel. He also pointed to four other Russian satellites launched alongside it — Kosmos-2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614 — that operate in similar orbits and probably have the same mission. Both ICEYE-X36 and ICEYE-X37 could be targets, he said.

Stefano Boeri Architetti Selected to Transform Former Locomotive Factory into Green Neighbourhood in Tbilisi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The LOCO Alliance architectural competition in Tbilisi, Georgia, was organized to transform a 73,600 m² brownfield site, the former Soviet-era Tbilisi Electric Locomotive Manufacturing Plant in the "Temka" residential area, into a new green neighborhood and cultural destination called Loco Park. On October 18, 2026, LOCO Alliance officially announced Stefano Boeri Architetti's design as the selected project for the site's transformation, with the official masterplan images unveiled on October 23. The selected masterplan is designed to integrate the industrial heritage of the factory with contemporary architecture, dense green public spaces and community recreation hubs. The site is already hosting large-scale cultural events, organized in parallel with the formal masterplan competition.
Stefano Boeri Architetti's Loco Park masterplan transforms the 73,600 m² site in the Georgian capital, the grounds of a large Soviet-era locomotive factory, into an integrated network of homes, green spaces, services and community facilities, open to the city. The gross floor area is 120,000 m² across nine buildings, with different home typologies on the upper floors and services such as local shops, cafés and workshops at ground level. The buildings are surrounded by a sequence of open spaces, including a sports forest, parks, shared gardens and a linear boulevard. Shared spaces are continuous and walkable, and extend pedestrian connections to the surrounding neighborhoods.
To incorporate the site's industrial heritage into the new neighborhood's identity, the project uses brick to establish material continuity. Brick is also rooted in local building traditions and can take on the characteristic colors of Tbilisi's architectural legacy. Through photographic color mapping of the urban landscape, Stefano Boeri Architetti identified the dominant color families (blue-gray, terracotta, green, taupe and mineral white) and translated these shades into a brick palette for the facades. The buildings' roofs are shaped after the silhouettes of the factories and workshops historically located in the area. In a more contemporary approach, the roofs also accommodate greenhouses, terraces, photovoltaic systems, loft apartments and communal spaces for residents.
 The new Loco Park neighbourhood will combine the memory of the large Soviet-era locomotive factory with a vision of a contemporary, vibrant space that is green and open to everyone. The buildings of Loco Park will be islands in an urban archipelago, distinct yet connected by a network of tree-lined pedestrian public spaces for the whole city to enjoy ― Architect Stefano Boeri
Other projects announced this year by Stefano Boeri Architetti include a new affordable housing development in Ibiza, which proposes approximately 190 affordable rental apartments distributed across four timber volumes. Earlier this year, the Rome City Council approved a memorandum for the urban regeneration of the Depositi delle Vittorie in Piazza Bainsizza, a former ATAC depot in Rome dating back to the early 1900s. The firm will be in charge of envisioning the adaptive reuse of the former transportation infrastructure by introducing cultural, educational, commercial, co-working and leisure functions. Also in Italy, the office revealed a design for the new Ambrosian Monastery in Milan's MIND district, a project conceived as a space integrating worship, interreligious dialogue and educational activities.

Cooperation with Russia helps to bolster energy security — Iran’s top diplomat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:27:27 UTC
14:27:27 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The development of the Iranian energy cooperation with Russia and other members of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum provides for stronger energy security, expansion of investment possibilities and diversification of supply routes, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was quoted as saying in an article published by Russia’s Vedomosti daily.
"Enhanced cooperation among members of the Forum of Gas Exporting Countries and the further development of strategic relations between Iran and Russia paves ways for important opportunities to up joint investments, transfer technologies, develop infrastructure and increase natural gas supply capacity, which, in turn, will enhance energy security in the region and across the world," he noted.
Among the most important areas of cooperation between Moscow and Tehran, Araghchi named possible investments by Russian companies in the development of Iran’s oil and gas fields, the transfer of technology, the supply of equipment and the use of joint technical and engineering capabilities.
According to him, such cooperation might help to increase the production output volumes and reduce the consequences caused by unilateral coercive measures.

Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:24:59 UTC
14:24:59 KST

Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
Serbia’s longtime leader concedes defeat to a student-led protest movement in parliamentary elections.
Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap parliamentary elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years.
After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List.
The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.
The youth-led protests grew into a broader wave of social unrest and evolved into the Student List political platform, which promised to tackle corruption, depoliticise public institutions and restore citizens’ rights.
During the election campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad.
Vucic referred to the demonstrators, who included university professors, doctors and workers, as “blockaders” and accused them of seeking to destabilise Serbia.
A former ultranationalist, Vucic cultivated an image of a pragmatic leader who maintained ties with the European Union, Russia and China as well as, increasingly, with Israel in recent years.
Born in Belgrade in 1970, the nearly 2-metre-tall (6.5ft-tall) Vucic graduated from the University of Belgrade’s faculty of law. He entered politics in 1993, joining the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party led by Vojislav Seselj.
His political record during the 1990s was marked by nationalist rhetoric. One of his most remembered statements came in Serbia’s parliament in July 1995, nine days after the Srebrenica genocide: “Kill one Serb, and we will kill 100 Muslims.” Vucic made the comments during a debate on possible NATO strikes against positions held by the Army of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Vucic’s political mentor at the time, Seselj, was sentenced in 2018 to 10 years in prison by the Appeals Chamber of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals for persecution, deportation and forcible transfer of non-Serbs during the wars in the Balkans in the 1990s.
Aleksandar Seselj, the son of Vojislav Seselj, was on Vucic’s electoral list in Sunday’s elections.
After a split within the Serbian Radical Party, Vucic and Tomislav Nikolic founded the SNS in 2008. The new party sought to move closer to mainstream European politics.
Safeta Bisevac, a Serbian journalist who has long followed Vucic’s political career, believes he was initially less popular than Nikolic, who appeared closer to common citizens.
“Vucic lagged far behind in popularity at the time and was essentially the organiser of the newly formed party,” Bisevac told Al Jazeera.
In 2012, the SNS came to power promising to fight corruption, organised crime and abuses committed under previous governments.
One of the most prominent cases was the December 2012 arrest of businessman Miroslav Miskovic and his son Marko on suspicion of financial irregularities and tax evasion. After years of legal proceedings, both were acquitted and the state paid them compensation.
Bisevac said the results of the fight against corruption remained modest while the authorities expanded their control over institutions, the media and political life.
Vucic served as first deputy prime minister from 2012 to 2014 before ascending to the post of prime minister in 2014. Three years later, he became president of Serbia and won re-election in 2022. His term was due to run until 2027.
Under pressure from the student-led protests, he resigned in September and called early elections. Although the Serbian presidency is constitutionally limited, Vucic has retained a dominant influence over his party and state policy.
“He made many promises and fulfilled few of them, but in the meantime, he established almost complete control over the state apparatus,” Bisevac said.
Economic growth and the debate over living standards
The Serbian economy has expanded significantly since Vucic took Serbia’s political centre stage in 2012. Unemployment dropped from 26 percent to 8 to 9 percent while nominal gross domestic product nearly tripled, reaching about 90 billion euros ($101bn), according to official data cited by the Reuters news agency.
Annual foreign direct investment inflows rose from about 800 million euros ($896m) in 2012 to a record 5.2 billion euros ($5.8bn) in 2024.
A network of modern motorways has also been built.
However, rising wages have not necessarily translated into a proportional improvement in living standards. The rising cost of living and public debt remain important elements of the debate over the government’s economic record.
Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said “the students simply gave a voice to the justified anger of citizens.”
Speaking to Al Jazeera about Vucic’s policies, Radosavljevic said the past decade was characterised by “systematic pressure and the destruction of social institutions”.
“State intelligence services have spent less time on their actual duties and more time monitoring political opponents while critical thinking has been pushed out of the public media,” Radosavljevic said.
