The Trump administration has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban to consider running for UN secretary-general, with Russia and China said to be receptive to the idea, The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday.
According to the newspaper, officials from three countries confirmed that Washington had raised Orban's potential candidacy, which could make him a joint candidate backed by the US, Russia and China. The proposal is awaiting a final decision.
A US State Department official acknowledged that the idea might initially sound far-fetched but argued that the three powers could secure sufficient support in the UN Security Council.
The official estimated that eight of the council's 15 members would "comfortably" support Orban, with 10 votes potentially within reach. Britain and France, both permanent members with veto power, could oppose the proposal, although the editorial noted that they have generally been cautious about using their vetoes.
The newspaper reported that Orban's name repeatedly surfaced in discussions among US, Chinese and Russian officials about potential candidates. According to the editorial, American officials eventually began asking "Why not Mr. Orban?"
The proposal reflects the Trump administration's ideological alignment with Orban, whom the editorial described as "the dream MAGA-conservative candidate." It cited his opposition to mass migration, liberal nongovernmental organizations and Hungary's left-leaning courts and media, as well as his frequent clashes with the European Union.
Despite his close alignment with China, Orban has maintained an image as a defender of Western civilization, the editorial said.
US President Donald Trump endorsed Orban in Hungary's April 2026 election, while Vice President JD Vance campaigned for him. A third source familiar with the process told the newspaper that both were expected to support Orban again if he entered the UN race, although an announcement was being held back until after the US midterm elections.
US officials initially contacted Orban to gauge his interest in the position. He was reportedly receptive but remained cautious, with the nationalist politician unwilling to run unless he believed he had a strong chance of winning. Orban declined to comment.
The editorial contrasted Orban with other potential candidates, describing the field as dominated by figures with international bureaucratic or diplomatic experience.
One official from another country characterized Orban as a "general" rather than a "secretary," a view shared by the US official, who argued that Orban possessed the ideological convictions and political resolve to challenge the UN establishment.
Lana Nusseibeh, a diplomat from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), entered the race the previous week.
The editorial said the UAE's alleged support for a paramilitary force involved in Sudan's civil war could weigh against her candidacy, although it described her as qualified and gaining momentum. Nusseibeh was scheduled to answer questions Tuesday, followed by a new Security Council straw poll Wednesday.
Additional candidates could still enter the contest.
Current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term ends on Dec. 31, 2026. The editorial criticized his leadership and argued that Orban's potential candidacy would expose the extent of the institution's decline.

Brazil's President Lula da Silva wins historic 4th term after defeating Flavio Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:53:11 UTC
09:53:11 KST

Laura Gamba
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva was declared the winner of Sunday's presidential runoff by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), securing a fourth nonconsecutive term after defeating Flavio Bolsonaro in a closely contested race.
With nearly all polling stations tallied, the TSE reported that Lula had secured 51.76% of valid votes against Bolsonaro's 48.24%, a margin of more than 4 million votes.
The result marks an unprecedented development in modern Brazilian political history. Since the introduction of the two-round presidential election system in 1989, Lula has become the first candidate to win a runoff after finishing second in the first round.
In the initial vote on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro finished ahead with 47.03% of valid votes, compared with Lula's 45.16%, setting the stage for three weeks of intense campaigning across Latin America's largest country.
The runoff outcome represents a setback for the Bolsonaro family. Flavio, a 45-year-old senator and the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, had sought to return his family to the presidency.
The lead changed hands multiple during the early stages of vote counting before Lula pulled ahead as more ballots were tallied, including returns from urban centers and the heavily populated Northeast.
Lula, who previously governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010 before winning another term in 2022, will begin his fourth term on Jan. 5, 2027.

What challenges await Brazil's Lula in his fourth term as president?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:52:54 UTC
09:52:54 KST

What challenges await Brazil's Lula in his fourth term as president?
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will have to wrestle with a divided Brazil, an unfriendly Congress, feeble public finances and a Donald Trump-shaped menace during his unprecedented fourth term.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Days before his 81st birthday, the former union leader won Sunday's runoff with 51.7 percent of the vote over 48.2 percent for his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro.
The narrow result confirms the political divide that has split Brazil for a decade and shows that Bolsonarism remains strong, despite its far-right leader's 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.
Here are the main challenges awaiting Lula in his next mandate.
Governability
As in his current term, Lula will not have a majority in Congress.
Legislative elections earlier this month bolstered the right, making Bolsonaro's Liberal Party the leading force with 121 out of 513 deputies and 28 out of 81 senators.
To get his proposals through, Lula will depend heavily on the so‑called "Centrao", a bloc of centre-right parties that usually backs whoever is in power in exchange for benefits.
But negotiating with them is becoming increasingly difficult, according to political scientist Mayra Goulart of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.
Lawmakers now decide the fate of an ever larger share of the federal budget, she told AFP, giving them "more independence from the executive".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Money
Economically, "Brazil's three big problems are the fiscal problem, the fiscal problem, and the fiscal problem," economist Mauro Rochlin of the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) told AFP.
The state spends more than it collects, public debt exceeds 80 percent of GDP, and Brazil's central bank maintains one of the world's highest interest rates to contain inflation.
The situation "could very quickly turn into an economic crisis", said Rochlin.
Adjustment is inevitable but difficult since it involves "unpopular measures" and confronting "very powerful lobbies within Congress", he said.
The challenge is likely going to clash with Lula's flagship welfare programs, which have lifted millions out of poverty, and which he expanded during the campaign to win voters – drawing fierce criticism from the opposition.
Insecurity
The election campaign was dominated by security concerns, with violence a huge worry for many Brazilians.
Accused by the opposition of having a soft touch, Lula will be under pressure to show results, particularly by tackling criminal groups and militias that control territory in several cities.
On the campaign trail, he said he would support lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 for heinous crimes, while the political right wants to reduce it to 14 years.
Trump
Lula campaigned on a pledge to protect Brazilian sovereignty as concerns grow about the broadening interventions of the United States across Latin America.
Trump slapped tariffs on Brazil last year in retaliation for legal proceedings against his ally Jair Bolsonaro, followed by another 25 percent tariff on some products this year.
Brazil's president will have to manage relations with Washington without relaxing his anti-imperialist tone, all while the Trump administration increasingly asserts itself in the region.
Right-wing leaders across Latin America have meanwhile aligned with Trump in a trend dubbed the "Orange Wave", in reference to the US leader's complexion.
Although ideology "matters for symbolic encounters", it is "not that relevant" in practice, according to Oliver Stuenkel, an international relations professor at the FGV.
He points to Brazil-Argentina relations as an example.
"Deep down, the substance of the relationship hasn't changed that much" despite Argentine leader Javier Milei's insults toward Lula, Stuenkel told AFP.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

====================================================================================================

Brazil election drama: anti-Israel Lula takes lead over Bolsonaro's son in vote count
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:38:48 UTC
09:38:48 KST

Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva scored a dramatic and unexpected victory overnight Sunday into Monday in the country's fiercely contested presidential election, defeating far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro. With 99.9% of the votes counted, Lula secured 51.77%, compared with 48.23% for Bolsonaro. Although relatively narrow, the margin was clear and decisive, defying polls that had predicted a razor-thin victory for Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro's defeat is a blow to U.S. President Donald Trump, who did not explicitly endorse him but would have seen his growing influence in Latin America expand further with a right-wing victory. Lula, by contrast, has frequently clashed with Trump. His victory is also unwelcome news for Israel. The incumbent president, who at 80 will begin his fourth nonconsecutive term, is one of Israel's fiercest critics worldwide and has repeatedly accused it of "genocide."
Brazil uses electronic voting machines, allowing results to be counted rapidly overnight. Polling stations were originally scheduled to close Sunday at 5 p.m. local time (10 p.m. in Israel), but Lula's campaign petitioned to extend voting following reports of public transportation disruptions in several areas, including São Paulo. Brazil's Supreme Court subsequently extended voting nationwide by two hours. Bolsonaro's campaign also requested an extension, citing rainy weather in the country's south.
Bolsonaro's defeat came as a surprise after he entered the decisive runoff as the favorite. In the first round earlier this month, when several other candidates were also competing, he finished first with 47% of the vote, compared with 45% for the incumbent. That result had surprised pollsters, who predicted Lula would finish first by a relatively comfortable margin. In the 2022 election, when Lula defeated his current rival's father, Jair Bolsonaro, his margin of victory was also much narrower than polls had forecast, prompting speculation that surveys were once again underestimating the younger Bolsonaro's support. Historical precedent had also favored Bolsonaro: Never before had a candidate who finished second in the first round of a Brazilian presidential election gone on to win the decisive runoff. That changed overnight with Lula's victory.
The ideological divide between the two candidates could hardly have been greater. Bolsonaro, 45, and Lula, 80, hold sharply opposing views on a range of issues, from Brazil's relations with the United States to climate change and welfare policy. Lula's victory also dashed hopes among Latin America's right-wing movements that the conservative wave sweeping the region over the past year, with election victories in Chile, Peru and Colombia, would reach its most populous country and largest economy. Instead, Lula's reelection leaves Brazil and Mexico, Latin America's second-most populous country, led by President Claudia Sheinbaum, under center-left leadership.
A victory visit to the Western Wall?
As noted, incumbent President Lula secured his fourth nonconsecutive term overnight. He previously served as Brazil's president from 2003 to 2010 and won the presidency again in 2022. He was released from prison in 2019 after spending more than 500 days behind bars, and his corruption convictions were annulled in 2021. In recent months, he faced an increasingly difficult election campaign amid public dissatisfaction over the cost of living and concerns about personal security. His rival, Bolsonaro, made a tough stance on crime the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to lower food prices. Bolsonaro, who has served as a senator since 2019, also promised judicial reform, which he planned to pursue in part through the next president's power to appoint at least three of the Supreme Court's 11 justices, with several retirements expected in the coming years.
Bolsonaro and Lula also differ sharply in their attitudes toward Israel. Flávio Bolsonaro, like his father Jair, is a staunch supporter of Israel, and their political movement is known in Brazil for its support for Israel and the Jewish people. Israeli flags are traditionally displayed at rallies held by both father and son. At his final campaign rally Saturday in Barra da Tijuca, in Rio de Janeiro state, Flávio himself was filmed waving an Israeli flag.
Earlier this year, the younger Bolsonaro made his fourth visit to Israel alongside his brother Eduardo. He toured Samaria in the northern West Bank, prayed at the Western Wall and pledged to move Brazil's embassy to Jerusalem. "We appreciate and love Israel," he said at the time. "We support Israel's right to defend itself in every way."
Estevam Hernandes, Bolsonaro's personal pastor and one of his closest associates, who has accompanied him throughout the campaign, told ynet's Itamar Eichner in an interview Sunday that if Bolsonaro wins, he could make a victory visit to Israel as early as next month.
"Flávio Bolsonaro is a man who loves Israel with all his heart. We agreed that we would celebrate his victory in Jerusalem. We will visit Israel in November and bring Brazil's future economy minister with us, and Flávio may join us as well. In any case, the plan is to bring Flávio to the Western Wall to celebrate the victory," Hernandes said.
Lula, by contrast, has become one of Israel's fiercest critics worldwide during his current term, particularly since the October 7 massacre and the war in Gaza. In February 2024, he accused Israel of committing genocide, comparing its actions to those of Hitler. Two months later, he incorrectly claimed that more than 12 million children had been killed in the Gaza war. That same year, he recalled Brazil's ambassador from Israel, and in 2025 refused to approve the appointment of a new Israeli ambassador to Brasília. In his address to the UN General Assembly this past September, although he condemned Hamas, he also accused Netanyahu's government of "the genocide of women and children in Gaza."
$12 million for a movie and a promise to pardon his father
Both candidates have faced allegations of corruption involving family members and political allies. Bolsonaro himself is currently embroiled in a sprawling investigation into corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. As part of the affair, he acknowledged seeking approximately $12 million from Daniel Vorcaro, a former banker, to finance a film about his father's life.
His father, Jair Bolsonaro, is still serving the 27-year prison sentence imposed after he was convicted of attempting a coup following his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election, although he is currently under house arrest for medical reasons. In the run-up to the vote, Lula repeatedly portrayed the younger Bolsonaro as a threat to democracy, while Bolsonaro pledged to pursue a pardon for his father if elected.
Since his defeat in the first round, Lula has attempted to woo undecided voters with costly economic incentives. His government approved a debt-relief program for small businesses, among other measures, and promised free public transportation on weekends. But those efforts appeared to have fallen short. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, Elba Marques, a 75-year-old retiree, said her vote for Bolsonaro was a vote against Lula's Workers' Party rather than an endorsement of Bolsonaro himself.
"I can't stand hearing the same man say for 40 years that he's going to fix Brazil. It's the same promise over and over again," she said.
Bolsonaro, speaking after casting his ballot at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro earlier Sunday, said the time had come for change. "Brazil can’t take another four years the way things are ... Everyone’s life has got worse," he warned, as supporters nearby chanted, "Lula, thief, you belong in jail!"
Lula: It's either our flag or the US flag
Lula, meanwhile, once again sought to frame the election as a referendum on Brazil's independence, portraying his opponent as a proxy for U.S. President Donald Trump. Speaking to reporters after casting his ballot in his political stronghold of São Bernardo do Campo, near São Paulo, he accused Bolsonaro of wanting to "govern under the U.S. flag." Lula said Brazilians had to choose between someone who would defend their national flag and someone who would defend the American flag. Perhaps to reinforce that message, Lula also posed for photographs holding up the Brazilian flag inside the polling station.
The remarks came against the backdrop of Lula's sharp criticism of Trump throughout the campaign and his warnings about attempted U.S. interference in Brazil's election. The Trump administration imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian exports, announced sanctions against the Supreme Court justice who oversaw the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro's conviction, and designated drug trafficking organizations as foreign terrorist organizations. Some experts suggested the latter move may have been intended to portray Lula as soft on crime.
Flávio Bolsonaro, for his part, has boasted of his close ties to White House officials and insisted that Brazil must negotiate better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare-earth minerals sector. Brazil's reserves are estimated at up to 21 million metric tons, second only to China's. Politically, however, Bolsonaro denies receiving assistance from the U.S. administration.

Brazil election: Lula, iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback

Brazil election: Lula wins historic fourth term, Bolsonaro refuses to concede
- Lula won an unprecedented fourth term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro in a shock comeback that defied polls and slowed a right-wing shift in Latin America.
- The 80-year-old campaigned on lower poverty, less inequality and welfare gains, while warning Bolsonaro would cut social spending and weaken Brazil’s sovereignty.
- He now faces a hard term with a more conservative Congress, weak growth, high debt and pressure for spending cuts, which could limit his power and spark unrest.
AI generated
SAO PAULO – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Oct 25, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.
However, his opponent Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept defeat and said he would ask for the result to be annulled due to an Oct 25 ruling from a Supreme Court justice that extended voting for two hours.
Bolsonaro led the election’s first round but lost in the runoff by over four million votes, rattling Brazilian financial markets which had bet on his victory.
Futures of Brazil’s benchmark stock index Bovespa sank nearly 15% in early trading on Oct 26, while interest rate futures rose sharply, with January 2031 contracts soaring 182 basis points.
In the currency market, the Brazilian real weakened 12.2% against the US dollar in spot trading.
Flavio Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father’s reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later sentenced by the Supreme Court to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup to remain in power.
The scale of Flavio’s loss to Lula – by more than twice his father’s losing margin – and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension due to rains in the conservative-leaning south, make any annulment unlikely, analysts said.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but “it’s very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result”.
Comeback king
The victory marks another comeback in a career full of them for Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century.
The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
“He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.
At times, Lula’s re-election looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices.
Sweeping societal changes also left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Bolsonaro’s novelty.
“People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.
He warned that Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.
Lula’s win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration.
Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance”.
As Bolsonaro challenged the result at home, foreign leaders were quick to recognise Lula’s victory.
French President Emmanuel Macron said France and Brazil had “much to build together”, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil”.
The Kremlin welcomed Lula’s re-election and praised him for his contribution to bilateral ties and to BRICS. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy congratulated the leftist leader on “remarkable election results” and said he looked forward to expanding cooperation.
Notable absences were the White House and the US State Department, which did not immediately comment, and Argentine President Javier Milei.
Late-campaign boost
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.
His campaign this year mixed the kind of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.
These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare programme that is already being implemented.
He also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labour reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.
Challenges ahead
Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the Lower House and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers.
That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations.
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meagre 2.3% in 2027, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash. REUTERS

How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:31:51 GMT
09:31:51 KST

How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić
- Published
Theirs is a movement born from tragedy that began with students blockading streets and turned into almost daily protests and a national movement against corruption and government negligence.
In just under two years the students have succeeded in tearing up 14 years of political dominance under Aleksandar Vučić, who has seen support for his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) ebb away and ultimately fail in what became a referendum on the future of Serbia.
From Belgrade to Novi Sad and Niš, the mood was euphoric as supporters gathered in town centres or in front of Student List headquarters. In a post on social media, the students declared "Serbia is free".
Most symbolic of all was the demise of so-called Ćaciland, a pro-Vučić tent camp set up 18 months ago at Pioneers Park in central Belgrade in front of the Serbian parliament. Metal fences were torn down amid shouts of "Vučić is leaving".
How the students changed Serbia
They have no obvious leaders and have no grounding in politics, and yet the "Student List-Students Win" movement attracted anti-government voters across Serbian society.
They fielded candidates for all 250 parliamentary seats, and yet no students were among them.
As he joined the students marching towards Belgrade last week, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."
"We offer our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time," he told the BBC.
It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.
The tragedy was seen as emblematic of widespread corruption. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.
"When the canopy collapsed that served as the last straw," says Helena Ivanov of the think tank the Henry Jackson Society.
It was an emotional moment that triggered a spark and a national campaign of marches and events, she said, that captured the hearts and minds of Serbians in a way no opposition party had been able to do.
From protests to direct challenge to Vučić
What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.
Vučić's SNS was clearly shaken and by January 2025 his prime minister had resigned "to defuse tensions". In March 2025 Belgrade saw Serbia's biggest ever anti-government protest and as the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.
By the time Vučić had announced snap elections last month, they were ready. "They have been able to take that emotional momentum into a proper organisation and have people learn how to protect fairness at polling stations," Helena Ivanov explained.
"The message was clear: the rule of law and not ruled by the law," said Gordana Delić, head of the Balkans programme at the German Marshall Fund of the US, who said Sunday's vote was in effect a referendum.
Initially Vučić sought to praise the protesters as "well-intentioned", but ahead of the elections he accused them of trying to "bring down" Serbia. Even after conceding victory on Sunday night he made the unfounded allegation that they had the support of unnamed "European countries and the American deep state".
Who will run Serbia now?
One thing is clear, it will not be the students, as they were not standing for election. That was a calculated decision as the electorate would probably not voted for a list of candidates with little life experience.
Although their top candidate was Ilija Srdanović, a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, he is not really seen as a likely prime minister.
Few candidates stand out as potential leaders.
According to a projection by independent polling groups CeSID and Ipsos, 140 people on the list have won seats in parliament. They include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga (24th on the list), renowned actor Tihomir Stanić (8th), opera singer Nikola Mikić (46th), former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić (27th), and a rather large number of professors.
Šoškić's name has been mentioned in connection with the top post. He has spoken out about reforms he would make to the economy, and he has been widely criticised in pro-government media.
What is their programme?
The elected MPs will have the task of fulfilling what is in effect a manifesto.
In the words of the students themselves, they were looking for people who could enter institutions "do their jobs responsibly and not forget why they are there".
Under an 11-point programme, , externalthe student movement wants to:
- Eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it
- Purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime
- Reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control
- Stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises.
Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
Will it still be a student movement, without students?
Although they have not been elected, it is the students who have made the promises to the Serbian people and they will come under pressure to follow through on their manifesto.
The ordinary Serbian citizens they chose to represent their movement have "been entrusted with transferring part of the struggle we have been waging on the streets for the past year into the institutions", the students say.
In his speech on Sunday evening, Vučić told party supporters that the students had destroyed two years of life in Serbia and they would be defeated "faster than they think".

Brazil elections: Lula wins another term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro

Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory
Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."
French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."
"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.
"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.
Big challenges face Lula's fourth term
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is likely to face several difficulties in enacting his agenda in a fourth-term.
Among other things, Brazil has elected its most conservative congress since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.
Flavio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allies could control more than 280 seats in the 513-seat lower house and up to 50 seats in the 81-seat Senate following parliamentary elections three weeks ago.
This could lead to Lula's being forced to cede to congress on decisions about the budget, important legislation and key nominations.
Economic woes
Brazil is also in a period of weak economic growth, with his government forecasting just a 2.3% rise in GDP next year.
This is combined with public debt that surpasses 82% of GDP, the highest rate since the coronavirus pandemic.
Security concerns
Public security also remains a major concern in Brazil, with criminal organizations holding considerable influence in parts of the country.
Lula has said he plans to establish a Ministry of Public Security to combat the problem.
Environmental problems
There are also environmental challenges ahead.
Although deforestation in the Amazon — a major carbon sink and thus vital for the stability of the world climate — fell significantly during Lula's third term, Brazil is still a long way from its goal of ending deforestation by 2030.
EU's von der Leyen hails Lula's win
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has posted an online message of congratulation to "my friend" Lula on his win in Brazil's election runoff.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," she wrote.
"Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," her post continued.
"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."
Could Bolsonaro succeed in annulling the vote?
Some uncertainty still surrounds the final result of Brazil's election, as Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to challenge the outcome over the two-hour extension of polling hours ordered by a Supreme Court judge at the request of Lula da Silva's campaign.
However, legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether such a complaint would meet the legal threshold for the election to be annulled.
Bolsonaro's case would be weakened by at least two factors, analysts said. Firstly, the scale of his loss to Lula and second, the fact that his campaign had also requested an extension in some states.
The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said that the extension of voting hours had not influenced the vote.
The Associated Press cited Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at Brazil's Fluminense Federal University, as saying that Bolsonaro could ask for the elections to be declared null and void by filing a complaint with electoral authorities or the Supreme Court.
"But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said.
"The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact," he said.
Shortly before scheduled voting ended, Supreme Court Judge Christiano had ordered polling stations to remain open for longer after problems with public transport were reported to be affecting voters.
The decision followed a request from Lula's campaign.
Bolsonaro's campaign had also called for an extension of voting hours but only in some conservative-leaning southern states hit by heavy rainfall, flooding and power outages that were said to be disrupting voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."

The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazil's leftist president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, according to the country's electoral court.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Sunday's second round vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula's claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
The campaign season was also marred by scandals and mudslinging.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. US President Donald Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."

Lula wins fourth term as Brazil president after historic upset over far-right Flávio Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:19:05 UTC
09:19:05 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.
With 100% of votes counted the 80-year-old leftist received 4.4m votes more than Bolsonaro, with a 51.79% share to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.21%. However, soon after Brazil’s electoral authority confirmed Lula’s victory, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat and asked for the results to be annulled.
Lula narrowly lost the first round of the election to Bolsonaro in early October, casting his political future into doubt and plunging progressive Brazilians into three weeks of despair. Never, since the return of democracy in the 1980s, has the first round runner-up won the second vote.
But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following events, and at the hotel where he was watching the count.
Addressing a packed crowd of ecstatic supporters in a São Paulo conference hall, Lula said: “We are going to change the way that this country is governed … This election was a defeat for denialism … I want to thank God and to thank you, Brazilian men and women of this country … it was democracy that made this happen.”
After the result was confirmed, Alexandre Padilha, Lula’s health minister, said: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defense of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed.”
“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha added.
The 8o-year-old appears to have made up much of the difference through what his allies had identified as his main opportunity: persuading his voters to turn out. After a record abstention rate of 21.08% in the first round, which disproportionately affected Lula voters because they tend to live further from polling stations, the rate fell to 19.21%.
Speaking during Lula’s victory speech, Bolsonaro said it was “impossible to concede the election result” and that his legal team would seek to have the election annulled.
Following in the footsteps of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat to Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – the senator cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason.
His speech made no mention of the fact that his campaign had also asked the electoral court to extend voting hours, but he nevertheless said Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours to 7pm “was not normal, it was unacceptable” and amounted to “changing the rules of the game while the game was being played”.
For Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, the victory represents a sensational final chapter in a storied political career that began when he emerged as a union leader in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs in the late 1970s.
After entering politics, the former factory worker who was born in rural poverty made three unsuccessful presidential bids, in 1989, 1994 and 1998, before finally becoming Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002.
Lula stepped down after the maximum two consecutive terms allowed by the constitution but returned to power after winning the 2022 election against Bolsonaro’s father, then the incumbent president Jair Bolsonaro, who was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup.
Lula’s win is bad news for Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for that botched power grab and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son prevailed.
It is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally. The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina.
Confirmation of Lula’s victory was greeted with anger and bewilderment in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is living under house arrest and where his son watched the count.
On Sunday night, political leaders applauded Lula. Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum said: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!”, while Paraguayan president Santiago Peña said “I salute the Brazilian people for this great democratic journey.”
Lula’s victory came after his supporters staged two massive shows of support on Saturday, with more than a million people flocking to Rio’s Copacabana beach and an even larger number marching on Paulista Avenue.
Many people on the streets of São Paulo were angry at an apparent attempt by pro-Bolsonaro politicians to derail the election by sabotaging public transport in Lula-leaning voting areas across the country.
“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.
But that alleged attempt to scupper a Lula victory failed.
“I’ll be sincere: in the first round the left failed. But in the second round they woke up,” said Caio Marques, a 40-year-old photographer from Franca, a city in the interior of São Paulo state. “And there is no coup that will take this away from us.”
“I feel so, so happy … There’s not enough room in my chest for all this joy. Lula’s victory represents so much. It means life for those who believe in love and in life,” said Maicon Douglas Bento, a 34-year-old photographer, as he joined tens of thousands of jubilant Brazilians on Paulista Avenue at the heart of São Paulo.

S. Korea to expand international flights in winter season
South Korea will increase international passenger flights for the winter season, with more services to Japan and China amid strong travel demand, the transport ministry said Sunday, Yonhap reports.
5,353 weekly international flights are scheduled on 264 routes connecting 44 countries during the winter season from Oct. 25 to March 27, 2027, according to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport.
The flights will be operated by 84 airlines, including 11 South Korean carriers and 73 foreign airlines.
The weekly total marks a 7.6 percent increase from 4,973 flights during last year's winter season, surpassing the pre-pandemic level of 4,980 in the winter of 2019.
The expansion will be driven mainly by additional services to Japan and China, with weekly flights increasing by 314 and 232, respectively, amid robust inbound and outbound travel demand.

Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:16:29 UTC
09:16:29 KST

Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election
Leftist president mounts stunning comeback after unexpected first-round loss galvanised supporters of Flavio Bolsonaro.
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s contentious presidential race, pulling off a remarkable comeback after a first-round loss that galvanised the country’s political right.
Shortly after 9pm Brasilia time on Sunday (00:00 GMT), Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court called the race for Lula, who had earned more than 51 percent of the vote. More than 64 million ballots were cast for the incumbent.
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, netted 48 percent, or north of 59 million ballots. More than 4 million votes separated the two candidates, with the final votes still being counted.
Coughing and audibly hoarse, Lula took to a flag-draped podium shortly after to give his victory speech. He acknowledged clashes ahead, including with his legislative agenda.
“I do not choose the Congress,” he said, citing the legislature’s rightward tilt. “It was the people who chose it, and it is with them that I will vote, work and get things approved.”
He also thanked the voters who cast their ballots “to secure democracy in the country”.
With his victory, Lula has made history. No other politician in modern Brazilian history has lost the first round of a presidential election only to win the second.
“A historic turning point for democracy,” Edinho Silva, the head of Lula’s Workers’ Party, posted on social media, along with a video of supporters chanting, “Ole, ole, ole, ole, ola! Lula, Lula!”
But Bolsonaro has so far refused to concede, teeing up a likely court battle over the legality of a Supreme Court decision to extend the voting time by two hours.
“It is impossible to acknowledge the result,” Bolsonaro said in a short speech, accusing the Supreme Court of having “changed the rules of the game mid-game”. He added that he would seek an annulment of the results.
Tumult in the voting process
Leaders across the Western Hemisphere, particularly on the left, applauded the result. “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil have won,” Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote in the wake of the results. “Congratulations, President Lula!”
United States Senator Bernie Sanders likewise offered his felicitations, calling Lula’s re-election “extraordinary”.
“Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers & democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years,” Sanders said in a statement.
Still, the vote process was marred by allegations of voter suppression after reports emerged that public transport in some areas had been suspended.
Lula’s allies accused Bolsonaro’s supporters of reducing bus availability in an attempt to dampen the president’s working-class base.
Heavy rains, meanwhile, affected southern areas considered to be Bolsonaro strongholds.
The campaigns of both Lula and Bolsonaro ultimately petitioned the Supreme Court for a voting extension. Polls across the country were kept open two hours later than expected, until 7pm Brasilia time (22:00 GMT), following a ruling from Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin.
Bolsonaro, however, has argued that some polling stations were not able to reopen in time, harming any additional votes he may have earned.
A left-wing victory
Sunday’s victory means Lula will retain the presidency of Latin America’s largest country, denying a crucial victory to the region’s right wing.
In recent years, right-wing leaders have swept presidential races in nearby countries like Peru, Colombia, Argentina, Bolivia and Ecuador. Many have ridden a wave of anti-incumbent energy and enjoyed support from US President Donald Trump, who returned to office in January 2025.
A former union leader for metalworkers, Lula – at age 80 – will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, when he will beat his own record as the oldest Brazilian president to take the oath of office since the country’s return to democracy.
His victory has earned him an unprecedented fourth non-consecutive term.
Lula came into Sunday’s run-off as an underdog. While he narrowly led pre-election, the first round of voting on October 4 showed him trailing Bolsonaro.
He earned 45 percent of the first-round vote, compared with the right-wing senator’s 47 percent, both tallies short of the 50 percent needed to avoid a run-off.
But in the weeks since, Lula has rallied supporters around cost-of-living issues. He championed a constitutional amendment passed this month that shortened the Brazilian workweek, and floated the possibility of providing free public transport on weekends.
Having entered politics in the 1980s, during the twilight of the country’s military dictatorship, Lula has run for president seven times.
He won two consecutive terms from 2002 through 2010, as well as a third term in 2022, in what was the tightest race in modern Brazilian history up to that point.
His rival in that election, former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, is the father of Senator Bolsonaro, Lula’s adversary in this race.
Jair Bolsonaro has since been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in plotting a coup following his loss to Lula.
Despite overseeing a decline in poverty and low unemployment during his third term, Lula has faced questions about his advanced age, his ability to combat crime, and the country’s polarised political landscape.
An explosion of household debt has also left many Brazilians feeling their economic circumstances have worsened.
In September, Lula banned online gambling and sport betting apps to address the issue.
Uncertainty ahead
While the victory over Bolsonaro cements Lula’s status as one of the most significant and influential figures in Brazil’s modern history, efforts to advance legislative priorities during his fourth term could be stymied by the most right-wing Congress in recent memory.
There are also questions about how Bolsonaro’s right-wing base and the Trump administration might react to Lula’s re-election.
Already, Bolsonaro has suggested he would seek to nullify the election, citing the prolonged voting hours.
“What happened today was not normal. It was, in fact, unacceptable,” Bolsonaro told his supporters.
Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, also suggested there had been judicial malpractice as a result of the extension.
“If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” Trump Jr wrote on social media.
The Trump White House has been openly supportive of the Bolsonaro family, issuing 50-percent tariffs last year on certain Brazilian products in a push to end the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro.
Judges involved in the case were also subjected to US sanctions, most notably Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.
Lula has framed such manoeuvres as an attack on the sovereignty of Brazil’s judicial system.
One of Trump’s critics, US Representative Ro Khanna, suggested the US president could take further actions against Brazil in response to Sunday’s vote.
“People all across the world are fighting back against extremism. With Lula in Brazil, they just won,” Khanna wrote.
“Trump must respect the results and not undermine Brazil’s elections.”

Brazil's Lula thanks voters for his victory, Bolsonaro does not recognise the results
It is the first time in Brazil's history since the return of democracy in the country that a candidate who lost in the first round managed to come back and win in the runoff. The left-wing president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva obtained 51.7% of the votes, compared with 48.2% won by right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Veteran pro-union President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva suddenly found himself the underdog after right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro took 47% compared to 45% for the incumbent in the October 4 first round.
A combative, three-week run-off campaign turned the political atmosphere electric. The left threw all its energy into securing a comeback, taking to the streets and mobilising on social media – notably with a WhatsApp channel dubbed "Lula’s Army" that now boasts 8.5 million subscribers. Finally, Lula, a former labour leader, sought and won a fourth (non-consecutive) term in what he has framed as his final battle.
Thank you to all our readers who followed our live coverage of Brazil’s presidential election. This live blog was coordinated first by our team in Paris and then by María Clara Calle and Léa Hurel from our Spanish-speaking newsroom in Bogotá.
Lula’s victory reverses the trend of the right’s rise in Latin America
For more than a year, right-wing candidates had won every election held in the region, as happened in Chile with Jose Antonio Kast, in Peru with Keiko Fujimori, in Ecuador with Daniel Noboa, and in Colombia with Abelardo de la Espriella. Once in office, these countries also joined the U.S. military cooperation initiative known as the Shield of the Americas.
In this way, Washington has been consolidating a bloc favorable to Donald Trump’s policies. Nevertheless, Brazil’s elections represent a setback for the U.S. president, after the Republican supported the Bolsonaro family and the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva breaks this streak.
In his speech, he defended his country’s sovereignty and stressed that Brazil needs to develop its own artificial intelligence so as not to depend on the United States. “We had to overcome the external interference of digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate,” he said.
Thus, he continues as one of the few left-wing leaders in the region, alongside Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico.
Even so, Brazil remains split in two: those who support Lula’s progressive ideas and those who want change with the Bolsonaros.

Former Colombian president also congratulated Lula.
Abstention decreased in Brazil’s second round
Lula’s campaign focused over the last three weeks on winning new votes in order to come back from Flavio Bolsonaro’s first-round victory.
In that effort, securing votes from those who had abstained was essential. In the end, abstention was three million votes lower than in the first round. Although not all of those can be attributed directly to Lula, the difference between the president and Flavio Bolsonaro was just over four million votes in the runoff.
According to the Superior Electoral Court, 33.4 million people abstained from voting on October 4, compared with 30.4 million abstentions in the runoff.

It is the first time in Brazil’s history since the return of democracy that a candidate who lost in the first round manages to win the runoff and become president.

Brazil's Lula overtakes Bolsonaro in runoff, with half of votes counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:12:06 UTC
09:12:06 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country's electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.
Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election's first round and hoped to revive his father's far-right movement.
At times, Lula's reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
Lula's victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
"He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.
Unlikely path to victory
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula's familiar embrace over Bolsonaro's novelty.
"People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights," he said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.
He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil's sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.
Lula's win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington's agenda on security and migration.
Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist "would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance."
Comeback King
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.
Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.
These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented.
Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil's biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.
Challenging legislative reality
Still, Lula's fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers.
"He is likely to be a lame duck from the start," said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo.
The incoming legislature will likely deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress, Stuenkel said, predicting Lula will face waning influence over Supreme Court nominations, unwieldy party coalitions, and even the threat of impeachment.
Economic headwinds
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meager 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.
The president's critics blame spending, though interest costs have driven most of the increase in debt.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could fuel social upheaval.

Will Israel's election bring Netanyahu a reckoning or vindication?
By Tuesday evening, we will know whether Israelis have delivered Netanyahu a reckoning or vindication. This time, things feel different from his usual last-ditch panic campaign.
Friday's final polls still point to the deadlock we've seen for months – unless Gadi Eisenkot agrees to rely on one of Israel's Arab parties. Netanyahu is now doing everything he can to persuade voters to abandon small parties in his bloc hovering around the electoral threshold, hoping to pick up their votes. The more liberal Haredi Public party is polling below 2 percent, while former general Ofer Winter's far-right Amcha Yisrael hovers around 3 percent, just below the threshold. The race is that tight – a fight over fractions of a seat.
Last night, Netanyahu took his message to Channel 14's The Patriots, where he is cheered as "King Bibi," urging voters to abandon these small parties and vote Likud. He even acknowledged that the election could come down to half a seat, with the other side holding a razor-thin lead. That, of course, is also part of his last-minute spin.
Likud has twice been defeated by former IDF chiefs: Yitzhak Rabin in 1992 and Ehud Barak in 1999. Netanyahu now warns that a government without him will bring no less than a second Holocaust. Pundits close to Netanyahu during the 1999 campaign describe hysteria within the family, "just like then."
When I covered Viktor Orbán's defeat in Hungary this year, the day before the election was filled with anxiety, then hope – and finally ecstasy. I asked Hungarians leaving polling stations whether they had voted for change. Some quietly nodded yes. In the end, a landslide sent a strongman home. Last night, we saw similar scenes in Serbia, while another Netanyahu ally lost in Brazil. All eyes are now on Israel.

Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up
- Published
Jose Mourinho has done it again.
The Real Madrid manager celebrated Kylian Mbappe's late winner at Barcelona on Sunday with a trademark knee slide, as he maintained his midas touch over their bitter rivals.
Mourinho has become just the third Real boss to go six El Clasicos in a row without defeat - 13 years after he last led Los Blancos in this fixture.
Four wins and two draws in his past six matches in charge of Real Madrid against Barcelona puts him up there with Miguel Munoz (1962 to 1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001 to 2003).
It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions
And more importantly for Mourinho, Mbappe's double in Real's 2-1 win ended Barcelona's nine-game unbeaten domestic run with a crucial Clasico victory at the Camp Nou.
A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho's side to within three points of their rivals.
"In my view, Real Madrid do not play to win at the Camp Nou, Real Madrid play to win La Liga," Mourinho said.
"We could win with luck, but we won with calmness and with all merit," he said. "It's a very strong group. Everyone works very hard. Everyone was ready to win.
"The credit goes to the players. When you win, the credit goes to the players. But when you lose, the blame falls on you. And that's why we see coaches being sacked from their positions every week."
The Portuguese has now won six and lost six El Clasicos across his two stints as manager.
He said: "I've learned that I have an extraordinary group, with the quality and mindset to play.
"In midfield, having a mix of talents gives us more than just having two players with similar characteristics. This mix of talents gives us balance when defending and quality when we go on the attack.
"We've beaten several teams by four or more goals, but this is Barca, and the players put on a great performance. We need to continue like this and don't go over the moon after this win."
Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he did not want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team lacked fresh legs after a demanding few weeks.
"We missed the freshness," he said. "It's not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat.
"In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn't on our side.
"I can see that today we were not fresh and this is what we have to change."

Bulgaria's presidential election heads to Nov. 1 runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:02:53 UTC
09:02:53 KST

Dzhanan Mehmed Ismail and Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Bulgaria’s presidential election will proceed to a runoff, as no candidate ticket secured more than 50% of the vote.
According to unofficial results from polling agency Alpha Research released by Bulgarian National Television (BNT), incumbent President Iliana Yotova and her vice presidential running mate Kiril Valchev received 34.6% of the vote, while former Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov and his running mate Georgi Kandev secured 32.7%.
Voter turnout stood at 22.5%.
Unofficial results from polling agency Myara put Yotova at 35% and Gyurov at 31.9%, with turnout reported at 22.2%.
Yotova and Gyurov will face each other in the runoff scheduled for Nov. 1.
Speaking to the media after polls closed, Yotova expressed concern over the low voter turnout, thanking Bulgarian citizens who voted and those who supported her.
"Thinking that we can change anything in the country without voting is an illusion," she said.
Yotova said her campaign would continue with a renewed effort to engage more decisively with all Bulgarian citizens. She also stressed that Bulgaria needed stable governance rather than alliances formed between political parties.
Gyurov challenged Yotova to take part in a public debate ahead of the runoff, saying Bulgaria needed an active president who united citizens rather than divided them.
"I invite Yotova to an open, honest and civilized debate to present our views on how we would exercise our powers and how we would act when Bulgaria faces difficult choices," he said.

Interpol’s Hong Kong meeting to consider ‘silver notice’ targeting criminal assets
Global police body aims to adopt resolution on new system for tracing and seizing criminals’ assets at first Hong Kong assembly
Interpol will seek approval at its general assembly in Hong Kong next month for a new “silver notice” system to target criminals’ assets and speed up financial investigations into transnational crime.
Hong Kong’s police chief also pledged to make financial investigations and scams a top priority in discussions with overseas counterparts during Interpol’s annual meeting, which the city is hosting for the first time.
Interpol secretary general Valdecy Urquiza said in an interview in Hong Kong that the global law enforcement organisation would strive to keep technical channels for data exchange open among member states despite growing geopolitical tensions worldwide.
