Brazil elections: Lula wins another term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro
Published October 25, 2026last updated October 26, 2026
What you need to know
- Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro
- It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed
- In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race
- Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win
- Bolsonaro refused to concede, calls for election results to be annulled
Keep reading for the latest updates from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25, with continued coverage into Monday, October 26.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.
Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close

France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory
Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."
French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."
"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.
"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.
Big challenges face Lula's fourth term
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is likely to face several difficulties in enacting his agenda in a fourth-term.
Among other things, Brazil has elected its most conservative congress since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.
Flavio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allies could control more than 280 seats in the 513-seat lower house and up to 50 seats in the 81-seat Senate following parliamentary elections three weeks ago.
This could lead to Lula's being forced to cede to congress on decisions about the budget, important legislation and key nominations.
Economic woes
Brazil is also in a period of weak economic growth, with his government forecasting just a 2.3% rise in GDP next year.
This is combined with public debt that surpasses 82% of GDP, the highest rate since the coronavirus pandemic.
Security concerns
Public security also remains a major concern in Brazil, with criminal organizations holding considerable influence in parts of the country.
Lula has said he plans to establish a Ministry of Public Security to combat the problem.
Environmental problems
There are also environmental challenges ahead.
Although deforestation in the Amazon — a major carbon sink and thus vital for the stability of the world climate — fell significantly during Lula's third term, Brazil is still a long way from its goal of ending deforestation by 2030.
EU's von der Leyen hails Lula's win
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has posted an online message of congratulation to "my friend" Lula on his win in Brazil's election runoff.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," she wrote.
"Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," her post continued.
"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."
Could Bolsonaro succeed in annulling the vote?
Some uncertainty still surrounds the final result of Brazil's election, as Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to challenge the outcome over the two-hour extension of polling hours ordered by a Supreme Court judge at the request of Lula da Silva's campaign.
However, legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether such a complaint would meet the legal threshold for the election to be annulled.
Bolsonaro's case would be weakened by at least two factors, analysts said. Firstly, the scale of his loss to Lula and second, the fact that his campaign had also requested an extension in some states.
The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said that the extension of voting hours had not influenced the vote.
The Associated Press cited Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at Brazil's Fluminense Federal University, as saying that Bolsonaro could ask for the elections to be declared null and void by filing a complaint with electoral authorities or the Supreme Court.
"But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said.
"The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact," he said.
Shortly before scheduled voting ended, Supreme Court Judge Christiano had ordered polling stations to remain open for longer after problems with public transport were reported to be affecting voters.
The decision followed a request from Lula's campaign.
Bolsonaro's campaign had also called for an extension of voting hours but only in some conservative-leaning southern states hit by heavy rainfall, flooding and power outages that were said to be disrupting voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazil's leftist president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, according to the country's electoral court.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Sunday's second round vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula's claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
The campaign season was also marred by scandals and mudslinging.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. US President Donald Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."

Aleksandar Vucic: Serbia’s veteran ruler felled by student-led movement

Aleksandar Vucic: Serbia’s veteran ruler felled by student-led movement
- Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s dominant leader for 14 years, conceded defeat in the Oct 25 snap poll after a student-led protest movement won support.
- He rose from Milosevic’s camp to found the pro-European SNS, but critics saw him as increasingly authoritarian and tied to corruption and nationalist politics.
- Anger grew after a station canopy collapse killed 16 in 2024, and mass protests forced snap elections after demands for transparent investigations and political change.
AI generated
Belgrade - The dominant force in Serbian politics for over 14 years, Aleksandar Vucic, who conceded defeat in a snap parliamentary poll on Oct 25, rose from the wreckage of strongman Slobodan Milosevic’s cabinet to the centre of power using his brand of populist nationalism.
For supporters, the 56-year-old represented stability, development and patriotism in a country scarred by the bloody wars of the 1990s and ensuing international isolation.
But opponents saw him as an increasingly authoritarian figure, twisting between the Kremlin and Brussels and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.
Vucic conceded his party had lost after voters cast ballots in record numbers in the vote on Oct 25, defeated by a new political force that emerged from a years-long protest movement.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vucic told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.
Political turnaround
Vucic rose to prominence in the 1990s as an ultra-nationalist ally of Milosevic, serving as his information minister in 1998.
After protests ousted the Yugoslav strongman in 2000, Vucic became a senior figure in the far-right Serbian Radical Party.
He was then a vocal supporter of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, both later sentenced to life for genocide and other crimes committed during the Bosnian war.
But Vucic underwent a dramatic rebrand in 2008, co-founding the conservative, pro-European Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics since.
He served as deputy prime minister, defence minister and prime minister before becoming president in 2017.
Even after polishing his image, Vucic has been reluctant to distance himself from nationalist leanings and far-right associates.
He has stopped short of condemning Serbs convicted of atrocities during the 1990s conflicts and looked the other way as pro-government media and political allies openly praised war criminals.
Despite trying to deny state involvement in a large funeral gathering for Mladic in the Serbian capital in September, several of his ministers attended, drawing sharp criticism from Brussels.
‘Land of cranes’
A relentless campaigner, he maintained a near-constant presence on pro-government television channels, embracing locals in tiny rural villages and chastising critics during lengthy news conferences.
He has cultivated the image of a tireless leader criss-crossing Serbia, attracting investment and creating jobs.
At the same time, he has juggled the competing interests of European Union aspirations and Serbia’s close ties to Russia.
Supporters praised him as a brave defender of Serbian sovereignty, spending billions of euros on defence – as he warned of foreign influence and pressure from NATO-member neighbours.
He often cited Serbia’s infrastructure and improved living standards as proof of his success, once pledging to make the country a “land of cranes”.
From the gleaming waterfront district to the numerous projects unfolding in preparation for Expo 2027, his party’s slogan “United Serbia” is plastered on billboards across the capital.
Rail station tragedy
But when a concrete canopy collapsed at a newly renovated train station in 2024 killing 16 people, the accusations of corruption which had dogged many of his signature projects caused an outpouring of anger.
Student-led demonstrations calling for transparent investigations drew hundreds of thousands to the streets in the largest protests since the Milosevic era.
As demands grew into calls for snap elections, Vucic and his supporters pushed back.
Students manning university blockades were labelled tools of foreign powers.
In September, nearly two years into the protests, Vucic finally called snap elections for October, citing “major turbulence on the domestic political scene”, thus meeting a key student demand.
“All of this will end on Oct 25,” Vucic said, referring to the protests, at a major pre-election rally in Novi Sad, the city where the canopy had collapsed. AFP

Brazil Re-Elects Lula for Historic Fourth Term, Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been re-elected to a historic fourth term as Brazil’s President after a tight race with far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President and Donald Trump ally Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula won with 51.8% of the vote to Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court announced. Sunday’s vote was a rematch after neither reached an outright majority in the first round on Oct. 4. Lula had trailed then, becoming now the first presidential candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985 to finish second in the initial vote and win the run-off.
The election also marks a remarkable win for the global left, as it bucks a trend of right-wing electoral victories across Latin America. Lula will serve for another four-year term beginning on Jan. 5, 2027.
“I want to thank the generosity of the Brazilian youth who took to the streets, who went to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night. “I want to thank the elderly. I saw scenes today of people being carried by their grandchildren to vote, people unable to move around, people with cancer and other illnesses. And people went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important to ensure democracy in the country.”
“This election was a defeat for denialism, a defeat for lies,” he continued.
Bolsonaro, however, said late on Sunday that he would not concede defeat to Lula and would seek an annulment of the result. The senator for Rio de Janeiro said a ruling by the Supreme Court to extend voting for two hours, citing public transport issues, was “unacceptable.”
Nevertheless, several liberal leaders around the world have already lauded the result.
“Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney posted, “The relationship between Canada and Brazil has flourished under our partnership. Let’s seize this opportunity to make it even stronger, together — to create major new trade opportunities, protect the environment, and build greater prosperity for both our peoples.”
Several U.S. lawmakers have also congratulated Lula on the result, including Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, Rep. Ro Khanna (D, Calif.), California Gov. Gavin Newsom, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
A former metalworker and union leader, Lula co-founded the Workers’ Party in 1980 and continues to serve as its honorary president. He served as Brazil’s President between 2003 to 2011, before he was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption convictions that were later annulled. He went on to defeat incumbent President Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, winning his third presidential term.
Lula’s campaign focused on labor reform, welfare benefits, and affordability. At a time when public debt as a share of GDP has risen to its highest level since the pandemic, Lula cited his achievements in lowering poverty rates, as well as reducing unemployment, illiteracy, and deforestation to record lows. He pledged to make public transit free on the weekends, a program that would need congressional approval. He also increased benefits under his signature Bolsa Família program and championed a landmark constitutional amendment shortening the working week, which Congress approved.
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, campaigned on harsher criminal penalties, tougher policing, lower taxes, and cuts to government spending. His campaign highlighted a corruption investigation involving Lula’s son and a pension fraud scandal that spanned both Lula’s and Jair Bolsonaro’s administrations.
Bolsonaro also called for amnesty for his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest after being found guilty of plotting a coup to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election.
In his election night speech, Lula pledged to strengthen federal involvement in public security, expand education and healthcare, and develop Brazil’s technological and artificial intelligence industries.
“This country will not be built by me,” he said. “But by you.”
A blow to the right
Lula’s win pumps the brakes on the broader political shift towards the right in Latin America. Colombia, Peru, Costa Rica, and Chile elected right-wing presidents in recent election cycles, reversing an earlier “pink tide” of left-wing governments.
Lula’s victory also denies Trump another political ally in Latin America, which include Argentinian President Javier Milei and Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele.
Bolsonaro had portrayed himself as an ally of Trump, courting closer ties with Washington and backing U.S. terrorist designations for Brazil’s major criminal gangs. Reuters reported on Saturday, citing current and former U.S. officials, that two U.S. State Department officials had pushed sanctions and other measures intended to weaken Lula and help return the Bolsonaros to power. The State Department did not comment specifically on the reported efforts but told Reuters that “all actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections.”
Trump previously expressed support for Jair Bolsonaro and labelled Lula a “radical left lunatic” during Brazil’s 2022 presidential election. He also criticized the criminal prosecution of Bolsonaro, calling it a “witch hunt” and demanding it end.
Trump has not reacted to the election results as of early Monday. After Bolsonaro led in the first round on Oct. 4, Trump called the result “close, but a very, very big victory.” His son, Donald Trump Jr., posted earlier criticizing the Supreme Court’s decision to extend voting hours and what he described as the lack of American mainstream media coverage of it.
Lula had warned that Bolsonaro would surrender Brazil’s sovereignty to Trump.
Lula has publicly sparred with Trump on multiple occasions. He accused the Trump Administration of interfering in Brazil’s election and imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil under alleged pressure from the Bolsonaros. The Bolsonaro family and the U.S. State Department denied the allegations.
At the same time, Lula has pursued closer ties with China, Brazil’s largest trading partner and the U.S.’s geopolitical rival, although he rejected subordination and said Brazil was not choosing between the two countries.
“This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard,” Lula said on Sunday night.
Analysts, however, warned that Lula’s political influence could wane despite his re-election. Earlier this month, Brazil elected its most conservative National Congress since the 1980s. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control majorities in both chambers, with more than 280 of 513 seats in the lower house and up to 50 of 81 seats in the Senate.
That could make it difficult for Lula to pass his legislative agenda, analysts said.
But Lula shrugged off those concerns and promised to work with the more conservative Congress to govern for all Brazilians.
“The day after tomorrow, the 27th, I turn 81 years old, and I want to make a commitment in front of the press and in front of you,” Lula said. “I will have the best term a President has ever had in the history of this country”

IDF veteran completes Hawaii Ironman race three years after losing leg in Gaza combat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:55:17 UTC
08:55:17 KST

Three years after being injured and losing his right leg while in Gaza, IDF veteran Boris Baruch Shtonda completed the Ironman World Championship in Hawaii on October 10.
Shtonda competed in the long-distance triathlon consisting of a 3.8-kilometer swim, a 180-kilometer bike ride, and a full marathon in a division for athletes with disabilities while wearing a custom-fitted specialized running prosthetic.
Shtonda lost his right leg while serving in the IDF’s Duvdevan as a reservist after Hamas’s October 7 massacre. A month after being deployed, he was severely wounded by an explosive device in the northern Gaza city of Beit Hanoun.
He underwent multiple surgeries before his leg was amputated above the knee and made athletic challenges a central goal for his recovery.
Since starting his recovery, Shtonda climbed Mount Kilimanjaro twice, swam across the Sea of Galilee, and finished a half Ironman race in Spain before deciding to train for the Hawaii Ironman.
Shtonda completed the race after a year and a half of training and support from Friends of the Israel Defense Forces (FIDF).
Shtonda dedicates Ironman achievement to wounded soldiers in rehabilitation
Shtonda dedicated his race to wounded soldiers and others undergoing rehabilitation, encouraging them to draw on their inner strength, believe in themselves, and become their own heroes.
“I want to share a message with all wounded soldiers and anyone going through a rehabilitation process: you are your own compass,” Shtonda said. “Sometimes, we have to be our own heroes and pull ourselves out of the predicaments we find ourselves in. Keep the faith, and always–always–believe in yourselves.”
Shtonda also received support from FIDF supporter Mike Hochstein of Dallas, who was moved by his aspirations, determination, and mental resilience after meeting him during a visit to Israel.
“I first met Boris during an FIDF bike ride through Israel last year, and from that first meeting, Boris’s determination and spirit made a lasting impression,” Hochstein said. “His dedication, perseverance, and commitment to pushing his limits are truly inspiring. I'm so proud to support Boris on this extraordinary journey.”
FIDF helps wounded IDF soldiers rebuild their lives through sports and rehabilitation
FIDF's support for Shtonda is part of the organization's broader efforts to assist wounded IDF soldiers and their families through rehabilitation programs, sports, and adventure activities designed to build physical and mental resilience. These initiatives aim to help wounded veterans regain their independence, return to everyday life, and pursue new goals beyond their initial medical treatment.
“Boris’s achievement reflects the determination wounded soldiers bring to the long process of rehabilitation,” said FIDF CEO Maj. Gen. (Res.) Nadav Padan. “Recovery does not end when medical treatment is over. It takes continued support, opportunities to rebuild strength and confidence, and the chance to set new goals. Through the commitment of FIDF supporters in the United States, we help wounded soldiers and their families navigate that process and continue moving forward.”
Shtonda's journey highlights the inner strength and resilience of wounded IDF soldiers, demonstrating how rehabilitation extends beyond medical treatment and how sports, personal determination, and community support can help wounded soldiers regain confidence, overcome challenges, and rebuild their lives after injury.

Voting ends in Brazil's presidential runoff after 2-hour extension
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:55:17 CST
08:55:17 KST

BRASILIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Voting in Brazil's presidential runoff ended at 7 p.m. Brasilia time (2200 GMT) on Sunday, two hours later than originally scheduled, following a Supreme Federal Court (STF) ruling extending voting hours amid disruptions caused by public transportation problems and heavy rains in several parts of the country.
Results of the closely contested runoff were expected within hours of the close of voting.
STF Justice Cristiano Zanin issued the ruling earlier Sunday, with the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) responsible for its implementation.
TSE President Kassio Nunes Marques notified regional electoral courts of the decision at 5:49 p.m. Brasilia time, instructing polling stations that were still open to continue operating until 7 p.m.
As some polling stations had already closed when the decision was communicated, Zanin later clarified that the extension would apply only to those that remained open, while stations that had already closed would not reopen.
Earlier Sunday, the campaign of incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party requested an extension of voting hours until 7 p.m., citing difficulties faced by voters in reaching polling stations due to reduced bus services and other public transportation problems in at least nine states, including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Pernambuco.
The campaign of his rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, candidate of the Liberal Party and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, also sought extended voting hours in Belo Horizonte, capital of Minas Gerais state, and other areas affected by power outages, as well as parts of Rio Grande do Sul state affected by heavy rains.
In the first round of voting on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro secured 47.03 percent of valid votes, ahead of Lula's 45.16 percent. Neither secured more than 50 percent of valid votes, the threshold required to win outright, sending the two candidates into Sunday's decisive runoff. ■

Brazil’s Lula overtakes Bolsonaro in runoff, with half of votes counted
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:55:13 CET
08:55:13 KST

By Lisandra Paraguassu, Brendan O’Boyle and Luciana Magalhaes
SAO PAULO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Sunday, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.
However, his opponent Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept defeat and said he would ask for the result to be annulled due to a Sunday ruling from a Supreme Court justice that extended voting for two hours.
Bolsonaro led the election’s first round but lost in the runoff by over 4 million votes, rattling Brazilian financial markets which had bet on his victory. His refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father’s reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later sentenced by the Supreme Court to 27-years in prison for plotting a coup to remain in power.
The scale of Flavio Bolsonaro’s loss to Lula — by more than twice his father’s losing margin — and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension due to rains in the conservative-leaning south make any annulment unlikely, analysts said.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but “it’s very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result.”
COMEBACK KING
Investors expect recent bets on a change of government to unwind in a volatile week ahead on financial markets. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil’s Bovespa index dived nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula’s victory, while the Brazilian real was set to fall sharply against the US dollar.
The victory marks another comeback in a career full of them for Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
“He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.
At times, Lula’s reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping social changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Bolsonaro’s novelty.
“People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.
He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.
Lula’s win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration.
There was no immediate comment from Trump or the US State Department, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Latin American leaders were quick to offer their congratulations.
Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance.”
LATE-CAMPAIGN BOOST
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.
His campaign this year mixed the kind of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.
These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented.
Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.
CHALLENGES AHEAD
Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers.
That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations.
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow just 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash.
(Reporting by Oliver Griffin, Luciana Magalhaes and Lisandra Paraguassu in Sao Paulo; Ricardo Brito, Bernardo Caram and Brendan O’Boyle in Brasilia; Marta Nogueira in Rio de Janeiro, Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Writing by Brendan O’Boyle and Oliver Griffin; Editing by Brad Haynes, Gabriel Stargardter, Alistair Bell, Christina Fincher, Andrew Heavens, Nick Zieminski, Aurora Ellis and Lincoln Feast.)

Israel fuel prices could top NIS 9 per liter as tax cut expires after elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:55:12 UTC
08:55:12 KST

Fuel prices in Israel are expected to rise sharply immediately after the elections, as a temporary NIS 1 per liter fuel tax reduction introduced by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is set to expire on November 3.
Combined with rising global oil prices amid expectations of renewed fighting involving Israel, the US and Iran, the expiration of the tax cut could push the price of 95-octane gasoline above NIS 9 per liter, up from its current price of NIS 7.77.
Smotrich introduced the temporary reduction in the state's excise tax on gasoline last month to prevent fuel prices from soaring ahead of the elections.
The original order, signed a month earlier, reduced the tax by half a shekel per liter. However, rising oil prices prompted Smotrich to double the reduction.
Under normal circumstances, taxes account for more than 60% of the price of gasoline in Israel, generating approximately NIS 20 billion in annual state revenue.
According to the Finance Ministry's Budget Department, the tax cuts introduced over the past two months are expected to reduce state revenue by approximately NIS 467 million, at a time when the ongoing war has driven defense spending to record levels.
Election outcome could determine fate of fuel tax relief as fuel prices could top NIS 8
Following the elections, Smotrich will have to decide whether to extend the tax reduction. However, if it becomes clear the current government will not remain in office, he could let fuel prices surge, leaving the next government to deal with the economic consequences.
Regardless of whether the tax cut is extended, the first fuel price increase is expected as early as Saturday night.
Expectations of a third round of fighting involving Israel, Iran and the US have already pushed oil prices up by approximately 10% compared with late September, when the Energy Ministry's Fuel Administration set gasoline prices for October.
As a result, even if the tax reduction remains in effect, gasoline prices are currently expected to rise by approximately 30 agorot per liter, bringing the price to just over NIS 8.
The final price will be determined toward the end of the week, based on oil prices in the Mediterranean basin at that time. However, the new price could remain in effect for only a few days.

Zelenskiy says US fully resumes warnings on ballistic strikes
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:55:04 CET
08:55:04 KST

KYIV, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said US warnings about imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes, critical to Ukraine’s air defences, had been fully restored after recent issues.
Speaking to Ukraine’s TSN television channel, he said SpaceX’s Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420 kilometres per hour since early on Saturday morning, after it had been throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington.
Zelenskiy said he discussed both issues in a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, casting the changes as results of that meeting.
The US has pressed Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, which it argues added to high energy prices, a sensitive issue for the Trump administration amid its war on Iran and US midterm elections next month.
Zelenskiy said that in order for Kyiv to halt the strikes, Moscow must stop hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or the US should allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles.
Speaking about the upcoming technical talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in November, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced post-war neutrality. Kyiv has long sought entry into NATO despite the reticence of some members.
Zelenskiy also renewed his push for a trilateral US-brokered meeting between him and Vladimir Putin.
The Ukrainian leader has long argued Putin is the only person in Russia who can make major decisions to end the war or meaningfully discuss core issues, such as the fate of the nearly 20% of Ukraine that Russia occupies.
“The issue of territories is a red line that can be discussed exclusively at the level of leaders,” Zelenskiy said.
(Reporting by Max Hunder, Bogdan Kochubey and Jekaterīna Golubkova; Editing by Chris Reese)

Antonelli misses out on clinching F1 title despite dominant US Grand Prix win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:54:57 UTC
08:54:57 KST

Efe Ozkan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli moved closer to his maiden Formula One world title with a dominant victory at the United States Grand Prix on Sunday.
The 20-year-old Italian finished ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc but narrowly missed the opportunity to clinch the championship in Austin, Texas.
Antonelli now leads Mercedes teammate George Russell by 123 points with the championship set to continue in Mexico City next weekend.
He will be crowned world champion if he does not lose more than 23 points to Russell or 24 points to Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in Mexico.
A ninth-place finish would therefore be enough for Antonelli to secure the title even if Russell wins the race, while 10th place would be sufficient if Hamilton takes victory.
If neither Russell nor Hamilton wins in Mexico City, Antonelli will become world champion regardless of where he finishes.
Antonelli dominated Sunday's race in the same fashion as he has controlled much of the 2026 season, pulling clear of the field from the opening corner as his rivals battled behind him.
The victory was Antonelli's first since the Spanish Grand Prix last month and his ninth of the season.
The main battle of the race was for second place, with Verstappen and Leclerc engaged in a race-long contest.
Despite missing the chance to seal the championship in the US, Antonelli now has a clear opportunity to complete his title-winning campaign in Mexico City next weekend.

'MAGA conservatives' dream candidate': Trump administration eyes Orban as next UN chief - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:54:41 UTC
08:54:41 KST

US President Donald Trump is pushing former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban as a candidate for UN secretary-general, according to a report citing sources from three countries.
US officials reportedly approached Orban with the proposal and encouraged him to enter the race. Although he expressed interest, he has not yet made a final decision on whether to run.
According to the report, Washington believes, based on previous discussions, that Russia and China would also back Orban, potentially making him a joint candidate supported by all three powers.
Officials from the US and another country said that when Washington, Moscow, and Beijing agree on an outcome at the Security Council, they can generally secure it.
A US State Department official acknowledged that the proposal initially seemed far-fetched but maintained that Orban could garner substantial support on the council.
The official estimated that eight of the Security Council's 15 members would "easily" back his candidacy, with the possibility of securing as many as 10 votes.
However, the report did not cite any public commitments from countries to support Orban.
A key question is how the UK and France, both permanent Security Council members with veto power, would respond.
The report suggested that the two countries might refrain from blocking a candidate backed by a majority of the council and the other three permanent members. However, neither London nor Paris was cited as having taken an official position.
From 'someone like Orban' to direct outreach
According to the report, Orban's name repeatedly surfaced during discussions among US officials about their preferred candidate for the next UN secretary-general.
American officials reportedly said they were looking for "someone like Orban," a suggestion their Chinese and Russian counterparts agreed with. Washington subsequently began considering whether to approach Orban directly.
US officials then contacted Orban to gauge his interest in the position. According to the report, he was receptive to the proposal but expressed reservations related to his identity as a nationalist politician.
Orban was also reportedly reluctant to announce his candidacy unless he was confident he could win. He declined to comment on the report.
A State Department official described Orban as the "dream candidate for MAGA conservatives," citing his opposition to large-scale immigration, liberal nongovernmental organizations, and established centers of power within Hungary's judiciary and media.
During his time in office, Orban repeatedly clashed with the European Union while cultivating closer ties with China.
Trump endorsed Orban during Hungary's April elections, while Vice President JD Vance also took part in campaigning on his behalf.
According to another source familiar with the initiative, Trump and Vance are expected to back Orban in the race for UN secretary-general if he decides to run.
The source said any potential announcement would be delayed until after the US midterm elections.
Orban's potential candidacy could spark controversy
An official from another country said the current field of candidates consists largely of figures with backgrounds in international bureaucracy or behind-the-scenes diplomacy.
Orban, by contrast, would bring the approach of a political leader accustomed to exercising power, the official said.
The US official echoed that assessment, arguing that Orban has the right ideological outlook, knows how to navigate opposition, and would not be intimidated by the UN establishment.
However, the report also raised concerns that Orban's appointment could turn the UN secretary-general into a defender of Russian President Vladimir Putin and other authoritarian leaders.
His ties to Moscow and Beijing, along with controversies surrounding his policies in Hungary, are expected to come under scrutiny if he enters the race.
Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh gains momentum in UN leadership race
Among the other candidates is Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh, who entered the race last week and whose candidacy is reportedly gaining momentum.
Nusseibeh is expected to answer questions on Tuesday, ahead of another Security Council "straw poll" scheduled for Wednesday, which will also gauge support for her candidacy.
The informal vote is intended to assess support for the various candidates as Security Council members work toward reaching a consensus on a nominee.
It remains unclear whether Orban's name will be included in Wednesday's vote, and additional candidates could still enter the race.
The term of current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres ends on December 31.
For now, efforts to advance Orban's candidacy remain based on discussions and assessments provided by sources cited in the report. There has been no official announcement of his candidacy or public confirmation that the three powers would support him.

Trump invokes 9/11 in urging Michigan voters to oppose Muslim Senate candidate El-Sayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:54:39 UTC
08:54:39 KST

President Donald Trump at a Sunday campaign rally ratcheted up his push to link US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim extremists, comparing him to the 9/11 attackers while saying Democrats would let violent anti-American terrorists into the United States.
"I'm here to keep a jihadist, Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator," Trump told a receptive audience in Port Huron, Michigan.
If he wins, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint him as an anti-American Muslim radical, and on Sunday he took the rhetoric to a new level, likening El-Sayed to the attackers who took over United Flight 93 during the September 11, 2001 attacks.
Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive US Senate contests going into the November 3 midterm elections, with former US Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, and El-Sayed vying for an open seat that will help to decide control of the chamber.
The president on Sunday compared voting against El-Sayed to the actions of Michigan native Todd Beamer and others who fought back against the Flight 93 hijackers.
"Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said.
If El-Sayed wins, "he would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go in the Senate," Trump said.
El-Sayed says questioning his loyalty is 'shameful'
El-Sayed has dismissed the accusations against him and, in a recent advertisement, defended his religion, saying, "Faith is a thing there's just too little of in Washington."
Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.
El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the group, saying it is "shameful" for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States.
Rogers said in an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, before the Port Huron rally, that El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about the allegations.
"He's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America," he said.
Trump's speech in eastern Michigan on Sunday came a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's elections.
At Saturday's rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks by El-Sayed's opponents as an attempt to make him look "less patriotic and less American than they are."
The former president compared them to his experience as the target of false claims that he was born in Kenya.
"We have seen this movie before," Obama said. "I starred in it ... This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."
Manufacturing investments
Port Huron is part of an area of Michigan that Trump won in the 2024 presidential election with more than 66% of the vote.
One issue in focus during the campaign in the state has been the US-Canada tariff standoff, which has affected the Detroit-based US auto industry and prompted Rogers to distance himself from the president's policy.
Rogers on Sunday hailed Trump's tariffs for securing manufacturing investments for Michigan by Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel, but said "the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit."
"There's some good and there's some things we have to work on," he told "Meet the Press."
In a Fox News interview ahead of Sunday's rally, Trump praised Rogers as someone who shares Michigan voters' beliefs.
"He's going to be an amazing senator," Trump told the "Sunday Briefing" program. "Solid as a rock. Apple pie."
Democrats need to gain just a handful of seats each in the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

Serbia’s Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:54:34 CET
08:54:34 KST

By Ivana Sekularac, Edward McAllister and Aleksandar Vasovic
BELGRADE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country.
Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014.
But he called snap elections in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won,” Vucic said in a televised speech.
Within moments of his announcement, the streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration. Tens of thousands of people thronged along the city’s main boulevards, with cars honking, people dancing and students shouting “victory” and “he’s done”.
The students’ win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April. It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
Vucic said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would have 105, based on preliminary results.
“Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters.
“Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”
European leaders and officials congratulated the Student List on its victory, among them President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.
“We stand ready to…work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” von der Leyen wrote on X.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar assured the students of his country’s support.
RECORD TURNOUT SPURS STUDENTS TO VICTORY
Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout close to 70%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.
“(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years,” said voter Katarina Petrovic.
Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent and few in the student protest movement dared believe he would concede so fast.
Supporters credit him with modernising Serbia’s economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.
“Some businessmen, some people will leave us but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition,” Vucic said.
UNCERTAINTY OVER THE STUDENTS’ CANDIDATES
Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare.
Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who was in tears after Vucic’s announcement.
However, it is unclear who will be prime minister and enact the students’ domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions.
As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor, Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, and the European Union, Serbia’s largest trading partner.
“The biggest uncertainty is…who is going to lead the government, who will be the key ministers, and how they will operate based on the promises they made to fight corruption, to reintroduce the rule of law, but also to re-establish Serbia’s position in foreign policy,” said Radivoje Grujic, a Warsaw-based election consultant.
PROTEST MOVEMENT INCREASED PRESSURE
The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression worsened in the period since.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He has said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.
Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a “students are champions” jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students’ list of candidates.
“We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much,” said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends.
Dejan Soskic, a former central bank governor and a candidate of the Student List, called on people to maintain order and peace, and thanked voters for their civilised conduct during the electoral process.
(Reporting by Ivana Sekularac, Aleksander Vasovic and Edward McAllister; Editing by Kirsten Donovan )

Belgrade in rapture as Serbian students topple Vucic in historic election
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:54:31 CET
08:54:31 KST

By Edward McAllister, Kirsten Donovan and Aleksandar Vasovic
BELGRADE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Trams and traffic halted by crowds. Tens of thousands of people choking the city’s main boulevards; the air thick with smoke; a man on a car waving a flare.
Familiar-sounding scenes after a month of sometimes violent protests across European cities as students take to the streets calling for better education standards and better prospects.
Except, on Sunday night in Serbia’s capital Belgrade, students were not protesting but celebrating an election victory after long-time ruler Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-backed list of candidates in parliamentary elections.
It was the culmination of a two-year, peaceful protest movement that called for Vucic to step down and an end to what they said is rampant corruption in the Balkan country - a charge Vucic denies.
The students’ win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and shows what power younger generation have when they are able to harness widespread discontent.
“That is the best thing that happened in my life. We will now breathe freely,” said Milica, a law student.
Vucic had ruled as prime minister or president since 2014, and oversaw a period of strong economic growth, but he faced growing opposition from student-led protests after the collapse of a railway station awning killed 16 people in November 2024.
Tomorrow, the disparate group of 250 student-backed candidates will have to turn towards ruling, but Sunday evening was a time to party.
At their headquarters, the unknown candidates, many of them lawyers, professors, actors or farmers, hugged and cheered in near disbelief at what they had achieved.
“The people have won! The people defeated a dictator! The people will lead Serbia!” said Nebojsa Cosic while waving a flag on the street.
(Writing by Edward McAllister; Editing by Kirsten Donovan)

Germany investigating ties between the "Gen Z mafia" and Russia - WELT
Kyiv • UNN
German investigators are выясняя whether Russia is recruiting the "Daltons" gang for acts of sabotage in Europe. Two of its suspected members were detained after Starlink was set on fire in Poland.
In Germany, investigators are checking whether Russian intelligence services are using the Turkish-Kurdish group "Daltons," known as the "Generation Z mafia," for acts of sabotage. This is reported by WELT, according to UNN.
Details
It is reported that hundreds of young members of this group flaunt weapons on social media, while two people detained on suspicion of setting fire to a Starlink facility in Poland are considered members of this network. Sources from European intelligence services told the publication that they see signs that Russia is increasingly involving professional criminal networks in acts of sabotage.
An unprecedented number of shootings have occurred in Berlin. Many of the attacks are carried out by a Turkish-Kurdish group that glorifies itself on TikTok. Investigators are now following leads indicating cooperation between the criminals and the Russian regime
It is noted that one of the incidents was the arson attack on a Starlink facility in Wola-Krobowska, Poland, approximately 50 km from Warsaw, which occurred on September 23. The criminals doused a distribution cabinet with a flammable substance and set it on fire. The flames engulfed the power supply and generator.
And on October 12, two Turkish citizens—38-year-old Ümit E. and 34-year-old Müslüm Ta.—were detained in Nürtingen under European warrants. They had been under surveillance for several days. Law enforcement officers believe that they belong to the "Daltons" network.
Previously
According to The Wall Street Journal, a Kremlin representative, after an attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig Airport was exposed, warned the German government that Russia does not intend to stop attacks on European territory. According to U.S. intelligence, Vladimir Putin personally ordered an intensification of the sabotage campaign against NATO countries.

Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Sunday reaffirmed his strong support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, urging Israelis to re-elect him in the upcoming election and calling for Israel to press ahead with its military campaign against Iran until it is completed.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, he referred to an endorsement letter he published on Oct. 18, praising Netanyahu as an “outstanding Warrior Prime Minister” and emphasizing their close relationship in military operations against Iran.
“As everyone is aware, including the enemy, Bibi and I have had a great relationship in winning together,” Trump wrote, citing the US military operation against Iran, dubbed Operation Epic Fury, as an example.
Trump claimed that Iran had lost its navy and air force and that its military and economy were in disarray. He also said Iran's inflation had reached 301% and that a naval blockade had prevented the country from exporting oil. He further claimed that two levels of Iran's leadership, both military and civilian, had been eliminated.
Urging Israeli voters to support Netanyahu, he said: “Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister. We have to finish the job that we started!”
In his Oct. 18 letter to the Israeli public, Trump described Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and an “even greater Partner for Peace” in confronting Iran, referring to what he called Iran's decades-long threats against Israel and the US.
He argued that Iran would eventually have acted on its rhetoric if it had not been confronted, saying the country had been “systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially.” He added that the US would have to take over the effort if Israel elected a different leader.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” he wrote.
Praising Netanyahu's resilience amid domestic and international opposition, Trump said the Israeli leader had grown stronger under pressure and represented the kind of partner Washington expected from Israel.
Trump concluded his letter with an unequivocal endorsement of Netanyahu's re-election bid, declaring: “BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”

Brazil elections: Votes being tallied after polls close
