Brazil elections: Lula wins another term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro
Published October 25, 2026last updated October 26, 2026
What you need to know
- Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro
- It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed
- In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race
- Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win
- Bolsonaro refused to concede, calls for election results to be annulled
Keep reading for the latest updates from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25, with continued coverage into Monday, October 26.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.
Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close
Here's a DW infographic on where the results stand:
France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory
Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."
French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."
"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.
"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.
Big challenges face Lula's fourth term
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is likely to face several difficulties in enacting his agenda in a fourth-term.
Among other things, Brazil has elected its most conservative congress since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.
Flavio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allies could control more than 280 seats in the 513-seat lower house and up to 50 seats in the 81-seat Senate following parliamentary elections three weeks ago.
This could lead to Lula's being forced to cede to congress on decisions about the budget, important legislation and key nominations.
Economic woes
Brazil is also in a period of weak economic growth, with his government forecasting just a 2.3% rise in GDP next year.
This is combined with public debt that surpasses 82% of GDP, the highest rate since the coronavirus pandemic.
Security concerns
Public security also remains a major concern in Brazil, with criminal organizations holding considerable influence in parts of the country.
Lula has said he plans to establish a Ministry of Public Security to combat the problem.
Environmental problems
There are also environmental challenges ahead.
Although deforestation in the Amazon — a major carbon sink and thus vital for the stability of the world climate — fell significantly during Lula's third term, Brazil is still a long way from its goal of ending deforestation by 2030.
EU's von der Leyen hails Lula's win
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has posted an online message of congratulation to "my friend" Lula on his win in Brazil's election runoff.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," she wrote.
"Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," her post continued.
"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."
Could Bolsonaro succeed in annulling the vote?
Some uncertainty still surrounds the final result of Brazil's election, as Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to challenge the outcome over the two-hour extension of polling hours ordered by a Supreme Court judge at the request of Lula da Silva's campaign.
However, legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether such a complaint would meet the legal threshold for the election to be annulled.
Bolsonaro's case would be weakened by at least two factors, analysts said. Firstly, the scale of his loss to Lula and second, the fact that his campaign had also requested an extension in some states.
The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said that the extension of voting hours had not influenced the vote.
The Associated Press cited Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at Brazil's Fluminense Federal University, as saying that Bolsonaro could ask for the elections to be declared null and void by filing a complaint with electoral authorities or the Supreme Court.
"But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said.
"The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact," he said.
Shortly before scheduled voting ended, Supreme Court Judge Christiano had ordered polling stations to remain open for longer after problems with public transport were reported to be affecting voters.
The decision followed a request from Lula's campaign.
Bolsonaro's campaign had also called for an extension of voting hours but only in some conservative-leaning southern states hit by heavy rainfall, flooding and power outages that were said to be disrupting voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazil's leftist president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, according to the country's electoral court.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Sunday's second round vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula's claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
The campaign season was also marred by scandals and mudslinging.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. US President Donald Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."

‘Tonight we celebrate’: Serbia’s students jubilant after poll win
BELGRADE – Celebrations erupted across several Serbian cities late on Oct 25 as people hailed the student-backed movement deposing veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic’s party in a snap election.
Cars flying Serbian flags honked horns in Belgrade as fireworks lit up the skyline and people massed in public squares and near parliament.
“I feel as though I am finally living in a free country,” student Mila Martic told AFP.
The parliamentary election was the culmination of nearly two years of student-led protests after the 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The disaster has been widely blamed on corruption and triggered some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.
Within moments of Vucic conceding defeat, people poured into the streets to join crowds that had already begun gathering shortly after polls closed; within hours, thousands were on the streets in several cities.
Many passersby held three fingers aloft, the student-backed election list’s ballot number and a traditional Serbian greeting, and some lit flares.
Meanwhile, at the Students’ List headquarters, supporters applauded, cried, and hugged each other, chanting “Victory, victory!”
‘So happy’
“I am experiencing emotions I’ve never felt before. I am so happy for my family,” she added, holding back tears.
“Serbia has won as we promised. Never again a tyrant in this country!” Radomir Saicic, a university professor and candidate on the Students’ List, told the supporters in the List’s headquarters.
He urged people to celebrate the victory peacefully and with dignity.
“Tonight we celebrate the best way Serbia knows, with song, dance, hugs and tears of joy.
“Tomorrow the work starts, serious, responsible hard work to build Serbia in which the law applies equally to everyone.”
Meanwhile, groups of hooded men dressed in black hurried out of a pro-government encampment that had occupied a local city park across from parliament for months.
Crowds poured into the park and dismantled the remaining tents; one tent was set on fire, but there were no reports of clashes.
Trucks carrying riot police were seen leaving the city centre as crowds cheered and waved at them.
An AFP journalist saw the students’ supporters starting a folk dance, while Mirjana Nikolic, a candidate on the Students’ List and rector of the University of Arts, paid tribute to “all these young people, without whom none of this would have been possible”.

Thousands protest in Prague against public media funding reforms
Demonstrators allege Prime Minister Andrej Babis and his coalition’s proposed reforms pose a threat to press freedom.
Several thousand people have taken to the streets in Prague to protest against plans to change the funding system for the Czech Republic’s public media, accusing the government of stifling press freedom.
On Sunday, protesters demanded the withdrawal of legislation seeking to abolish household licence fees and replace them with state budget allocations for public radio and television.
The Czech lower house of parliament approved fast-tracking the bill in a rare overnight vote on Saturday after governing coalition lawmakers rushed to open the issue, limiting the opposition’s ability to engage in debate before the vote was held.
The bill, proposed by the governing coalition led by billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, which includes two far-right parties, must still be passed by the upper house before becoming law.
The opposition has pledged to challenge the legislation in the constitutional court. The plan would cut funding for public media by about 15 percent, possibly as early as next year.
At the protest in Prague’s Old Town Square, demonstrators chanted, “We’ve had enough”, “This must not be allowed to pass”, and “4:36”, referencing the early morning hour when the draft was approved by parliament.
Babis has said the plan is not an attack on media independence but a matter of funding transparency.
Critics warn the proposed change would allow the governing coalition to take control of the media. They compare it with the actions of populist governments, such as Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico.
Babis and his coalition, whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine as it fights off a Russian invasion, have a record of attacks against the media.
Public media staffers announced they would go on strike on November 3. They are backed by labour unions, university rectors, churches, international media organisations and many others.
A rally is also planned at Prague’s Letna park on November 15, two days before the anniversary of the 1989 anti-communist Velvet Revolution that ended more than 40 years of totalitarian government.

Vucic Concedes Electoral Defeat, Setting Stage For New Era Of Serbian Politics, Relations With West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:15:42 UTC
08:15:42 KST

BELGRADE -- Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's former president and dominant political figure for more than a decade, conceded defeat to the student-led protest movement in the country's parliamentary elections, potentially ushering in a new era of politics more closely aligned with Europe and away from the Kremlin.
"It is clear that we have lost these elections," he told a news conference late on October 25, after polling stations closed across Serbia.
"The Students' List has won, they will have between 135 and 140 seats and we will have 105. No one else has entered parliament," Vucic said, citing preliminary results as celebrations erupted among student leaders and supporters in Belgrade, Novi Sad, and other cities.
Some observers compared Vucic's loss to the defeat suffered by fellow Russia-friendly authoritarian leader of Hungary, Viktor Orban, in parliamentary elections in April.
A total of 18 electoral lists, with more than 2,400 candidates, participated in the Serbian election, with 250 to enter parliament in the effort to form a new government.
Building 'A New State'
"Tomorrow, we begin working to build a state governed by the rule of law," said Ilija Srdanovic, the leading candidate on the Students' List.
"We showed that change is possible when there is the will to make it happen. Now we must prove ourselves worthy of this moment. The students have won. We want to build a country together where everyone has the right to truth, a voice, and a future," he added.
Radomir Saicic, a professor at Belgrade University and a candidate on the Students' List, said: "Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard. Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future."
European Council President Antonio Costa also hailed the results, saying they would help push Serbia toward potential European Union membership.
"Today, the people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country’s future. Congratulations to the Students' List on its victory in the parliamentary elections," he wrote on X.
"We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to build Serbia’s future in the European Union."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "we stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption, and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union."
Massive Turnout
While the final election results were yet to be announced, independent observers reported that voter turnout could reach its highest level in decades, approaching 70 percent after a day of long lines at polling stations throughout the Balkan nation of some 6.6 million people.
Having served as president since 2017, Vucic resigned in late September. Unable to seek a third term, he was hoping to become prime minister after calling for a snap election.
A large part of the public has been divided between the list led by Vucic's ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and the Students' List, which emerged from months-long protests over the deaths of 16 people in the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024.
The tragedy in the northern Serbian city shocked the public amid reports that corrupt practices had led to shoddy construction work at the railway station, a flagship government project carried out by Chinese companies.
'Dirty Work'
Despite the early concession, Vucic expressed anger at the outcome -- calling it the result of "dirty work" by those in the US who are opposed to the policies of President Donald Trump and by leaders in other European capitals.
"I want people to know that this was the legitimization of a revolution carried out by the people with direct support from various European countries and the American deep state, the one that opposes President Trump."
He added that opponents were "merely carrying out dirty work devised by someone else to bring down a sovereign country. You succeeded for a moment. We’ll see [for how long]."
"By March or April, you will have sanctions imposed on the Russian Federation. You will see. They will do everything they didn’t want to tell you about, everything they lied about, because -- I repeat -- they are merely the ones carrying out someone else’s plans."
Serbia has long-standing ethnic and religious ties with Russia and still has many supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin and opponents of sanctions against the Kremlin.
Vucic has often praised Trump, saying in a UN speech last month that "Serbia supports the actions of the administration of President Donald Trump and sees in his work an opportunity for establishing a more just order in the world and more responsible attitude toward Serbia as a close American ally from both world wars."
However, both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about Serbia’s democratic record. A bipartisan, bicameral group of US lawmakers is pressing for tougher action on what they describe as democratic backsliding, corruption, and growing Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence in Serbia.
Once an ultranationalist, Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for more than 14 years, during which he has consolidated his grip on power by reinventing himself as a reformer balancing Serbia's drive toward EU membership while maintaining close ties with Russia and China.
Praise From US Figures
There was no immediate reaction from the White House, although other figures in the US praised the outcome.
US Republican Congressman Joe Wilson, a longtime critic of Vucic and co-chair of the Helsinki Commission, told RFE/RL that “the Serbian people earned this incredible victory through sheer determination and a commitment to restore the rule of law in their country."
"This will include expelling the pernicious influence of the Chinese Communist Party and diversifying energy away from Russia. This is a new dawn for Serbia as it embraces its place in Western civilization. Dictators are on the run during the Trump administration.”
Ivana Stradner, a research fellow at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL: "Serbia is experiencing the same energy we saw when [late Serbian President Slobodan] Milosevic. as overthrown."
"But history must not repeat itself: Removing Vucic is only the beginning. Serbia now must dismantle the system of corruption, and authoritarian control that sustained his rule and not simply replace the people at the top."
"This is Serbia’s chance to build lasting democratic institutions and put the country firmly on a path toward the West," she added.
Stradner said that Vucic "cultivated close ties with Moscow and Beijing, positioning Serbia as one of their closest partners in Europe. Now Russia and China stand to lose a key ally and a major foothold in Europe.”

Trump claimed that El-Sayed would require a metal detector to enter the chamber, accusing him of wanting to abolish police and federal border enforcement agencies.

Urging supporters to turn out on Nov. 3, Trump warned that voter participation drops when his name is absent from the ballot.
"Please show up and vote, because essentially we are all on the ballot," he said.

Sri Lanka repatriates 40 Iranian sailors treated after being stranded off Galle — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:11:33 UTC
08:11:33 KST

Sri Lanka has repatriated 40 Iranian sailors who were brought ashore from stranded merchant vessels off the southern coast for medical treatment, the Daily Mirror reported.
Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told the newspaper that all 40 crew members received medical attention in the country before departing for Iran on Saturday morning.
The sailors were aboard merchant ships located approximately 24 nautical miles off the port city of Galle when maritime authorities received emergency distress calls regarding their deteriorating medical conditions, according to the Foreign Ministry.
The Iranian Embassy in Colombo organised the repatriation flights, whilst Sri Lankan authorities facilitated their safe transfer through the port of Galle.
"We have coordinated the transfer and carried out our humanitarian obligations," ministry spokesperson Thushara Rodrigo said.
Stranded tankers
Nearly a dozen empty Iranian oil tankers reportedly remain anchored off Galle, unable to make the return voyage to Iran due to an ongoing United States naval blockade.
Sri Lankan officials stated that the vessels are positioned in international waters beyond the country's 12-nautical-mile territorial boundary, confirming that military reconnaissance aircraft and naval patrol vessels remain deployed to monitor the fleet's movements.
The humanitarian evacuation follows an earlier incident in March, when Iran's armed forces reported that 104 crew members of the Iranian warship IRIS Dena were killed and 32 others wounded during a US military strike in waters off Sri Lanka.
According to Iranian state news agency IRNA, the vessel was struck on 4 March while returning from the Milan Peace 2026 naval exercises in India.
Washington subsequently confirmed that an American submarine launched a torpedo attack against the warship.
At the time, Sri Lanka carried out a joint search-and-rescue mission after receiving a distress signal off Galle, transferring the 32 wounded Iranian servicemen to a local hospital.

Belgrade in rapture as Serbian students topple Vucic in historic election
BELGRADE, Oct 25 - Trams and traffic halted by crowds. Tens of thousands of people choking the city's main boulevards; the air thick with smoke; a man on a car waving a flare.
Familiar-sounding scenes after a month of sometimes violent protests across European cities as students take to the streets calling for better education standards and better prospects.
Except, on Sunday night in Serbia's capital Belgrade, students were not protesting but celebrating an election victory after long-time ruler Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-backed list of candidates in parliamentary elections.
It was the culmination of a two-year, peaceful protest movement that called for Vucic to step down and an end to what they said is rampant corruption in the Balkan country - a charge Vucic denies.
The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and shows what power younger generation have when they are able to harness widespread discontent.
"That is the best thing that happened in my life. We will now breathe freely," said Milica, a law student.
Vucic had ruled as prime minister or president since 2014, and oversaw a period of strong economic growth, but he faced growing opposition from student-led protests after the collapse of a railway station awning killed 16 people in November 2024.
Tomorrow, the disparate group of 250 student-backed candidates will have to turn towards ruling, but Sunday evening was a time to party.
At their headquarters, the unknown candidates, many of them lawyers, professors, actors or farmers, hugged and cheered in near disbelief at what they had achieved.
"The people have won! The people defeated a dictator! The people will lead Serbia!" said Nebojsa Cosic while waving a flag on the street. REUTERS

Roundup: Riyadh airport partially reopens as Houthis, Saudi-led coalition continue exchanging attacks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:44 CST
08:00:44 KST

RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh partially reopened on Sunday as Yemen's Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition continued to exchange attacks, and the Houthis warned airlines and travelers against using the airport.
The airport had suspended operations following a series of Houthi attacks that caused multiple deaths and injuries.
On Sunday, the Houthi group said it had launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three attacks against the kingdom, the first of which targeted King Khalid International Airport and "successfully achieved its objective."
Other attacks targeted King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait and a Saudi Border Guard naval base in Jazan.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea renewed a warning to airlines, employees and travelers against using King Khalid International Airport, describing it as "unsafe." He also issued a broader warning against using Saudi airspace while excluding the airspace over Mecca and Medina.
Separately, the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency quoted a military source as warning workers and civilians "not to approach Saudi oil facilities", while cautioning Saudi Aramco shareholders of "losses" if they continued to hold shares in the company.
The Saudi-led coalition on Sunday said it had intercepted and destroyed a total of 12 missiles and two drones launched toward the kingdom, including a ballistic missile and two drones targeting the Riyadh region.
The Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defense said a Saudi citizen and an Asian resident were injured when debris from two intercepted ballistic missiles fell in Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah governorates, while three residential buildings and seven vehicles were damaged.
The Houthi group said Sunday's attacks came in response to what it described as "Saudi aggression" on Sanaa and other Houthi-held areas a day earlier that left "dozens of people killed or wounded, including women and children."
Earlier Sunday, Sarea said Saudi forces had carried out 56 air and missile strikes over the past 24 hours, targeting what he described as "civilian sites" in the provinces of Hajjah, Lahj, Amran, Saada, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Ibb.
A local security official told Xinhua that loud explosions were heard later on Sunday in Yemen's southern port city of Aden, concentrated around the Salah al-Din area of Al-Buraiqa district, a strategically important area that hosts key military bases of government forces and the Saudi-led coalition.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage, nor were there comments from the Houthi group.
The latest exchanges come amid a sharp escalation between the Houthi group and Yemeni government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition, with intensified ground fighting accompanied by Saudi-led airstrikes on Houthi-held areas and Houthi missile and drone attacks on government-held territory.
Also on Sunday, Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy said during a meeting with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in Cairo that the league rejected attacks on Arab countries and reaffirmed its solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its right to defend its security and sovereignty.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. The Saudi-led coalition intervened in the conflict in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

Brazil's Supreme Federal Court extends voting in presidential runoff by 2 hours
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:39 CST
08:00:39 KST

A voter verifies his identity at a polling station during the second round of Brazil's 2026 presidential election in Brasilia, Brazil, on Oct. 25, 2026. Brazil's Supreme Federal Court extends voting in presidential runoff by two hours. (Photo by Lucio Tavora/Xinhua)
BRASILIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (STF) on Sunday ordered a two-hour extension of voting in the country's presidential runoff, with polling stations set to close at 7 p.m. Brasilia time (2200 GMT), local media reported.
STF Justice Cristiano Zanin issued the ruling to address disruptions to voting caused by public transportation problems and heavy rains in several parts of the country.
Earlier on Sunday, the campaigns of incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party and his rival Flavio Bolsonaro, candidate of the Liberal Party and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, separately asked the STF to extend voting hours.
Citing the seriousness and urgency of the reported problems, Zanin ordered the voting deadline to be extended from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. Brasilia time at all polling stations nationwide, tasking the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) with implementing the decision.
Lula's campaign requested the extension after reporting that voters in at least nine states, including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Pernambuco, had encountered difficulties reaching polling stations due to reduced bus services and other public transportation problems.
Bolsonaro's campaign sought an extension in municipalities in Minas Gerais affected by power outages, including the state capital Belo Horizonte, as well as affected parts of Rio Grande do Sul.
At 5:49 p.m., TSE President Kassio Nunes Marques notified all regional electoral courts of the decision so that voting would be extended.
In Rio Grande do Sul, the regional electoral court said it would not reopen polls that had already closed. "In such cases, it is not possible to reopen the voting machines while maintaining the security of the system, and the voting that has already ended will not be resumed," the court said in a statement.
Vote counting was suspended at 5:06 p.m., with 335,743 valid votes counted. By that point, Lula had received 57.66 percent of the votes, or 193,574, while Bolsonaro had garnered 42.34 percent, or 142,169. ■

Bulgaria's incumbent president leads presidential election, but runoff required
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:32 CST
08:00:32 KST

SOFIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Bulgaria's incumbent President Iliana Iotova is leading in the country's presidential election on Sunday, but a runoff will be required to determine the winner, according to exit polls.
According to the exit poll by Alpha Research, Iotova is expected to get 35.3 percent of the valid votes, while the exit poll by Myara Sociology Agency showed that Iotova would get 35.2 percent.
The voter turnout was 22.3 percent and 21.2 percent, according to Alpha Research and Myara, respectively. The two exit polls were announced at the Bulgarian National TV.
To be elected, a candidate for president shall require more than half of the valid ballots, provided that more than half of all eligible voters have cast their ballots in the election. If none of the candidates win an outright majority, a second round vote shall be held within seven days between the two top candidates.
Iotova's opponent in the runoff will be the former Bulgarian caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gurov, who got 32.4 percent according to Alpha Research, and 32.2 percent according to Myara.
The official results will be released no later than Tuesday evening, and the runoff between the two top candidates is to be held next Sunday.
"It is an illusion to think that by not voting, we can change anything in the country," Iotova told reporters after the release of the exit polls.
She expressed concern regarding the low voter turnout and emphasised that citizen's participation in the elections is a necessary condition for achieving real change.
"In the coming years, we must change a great deal so as not to take Bulgaria back to the years of stagnation -- a period during which we missed out on so many opportunities due to division and confrontation," she said.
In a separate statement, Gurov said he would like to call upon Iotova to appear before the Bulgarian citizens in an open and honest debate, to express their positions and views on how they would exercise their powers and how they would act when Bulgaria faces a difficult choice.
"We owe it to all Bulgarian citizens who voted today, but above all, we also owe it to those who stayed home -- those who have yet to decide whether to vote and whom to support," he said.
Bulgarian president is elected for a term of five years. Iotova's term will expire at the end of January 2027. ■

Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout

Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout
Bulgarians will now choose between President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov next week.
Bulgaria’s presidential election is heading to a run-off after polls closed with low voter turnout and no candidate passing the required threshold.
Incumbent President Iliana Iotova received between 35 and 36.5 percent of votes on Sunday, according to exit polls. She will now face former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who scored between 31 and 33.5 percent, in a second round on November 1.
Minister of Interior Ivan Demerdzhiev said the elections “took place peacefully, without the usual practices of vote buying and vote manipulation”, Bulgarian National Television reported.
The NATO and European Union member state saw 27 presidential candidates run in the election.
A run-off was expected, as turnout must reach more than 50 percent of registered voters, and the candidate must secure more than 50 percent of the votes to win in the first round.
Voter turnout was 22.2 percent as of 8pm local time (18:00 GMT), according to the Measure polling agency.
Black Sea attacks
Rising energy costs, inflation, attacks in the Black Sea and Russia’s war in Ukraine were the major issues in the lead-up to the vote.
A series of drone strikes on ships off Bulgaria’s coast, condemned by both candidates, dominated headlines during the campaign period.
Leftist Iotova is backed by Prime Minister Rumen Radev, whose Progressive Bulgaria party enjoyed success in April’s parliamentary elections. Iotova became president in January after serving as vice president.
A former member of the European Parliament and a journalist, she ran as an independent with the backing of both Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party.
Should she win, she is expected to keep Bulgaria in line with Europe, while calling for improved relations with Russia.
After casting her vote, Yotova said she wanted to address “the dire issue of poverty” in Bulgaria, as well as “inequalities and regional disputes”, the AFP news agency reported.
“I believe that there must be peace, stability, and security,” she added.
Gyurov has the support of the country’s pro-Western opposition and signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine as prime minister.
He said on Sunday that he wanted “a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud”.
“Next week, Bulgaria must choose between two personalities, two directions,” he said after the vote, and invited Iotova to a debate before the next round.
Although the role of president is largely ceremonial, the president leads the armed forces, can veto legislation and sign treaties.

His work for foreign countries included projects related to Qatar.

Efe Ozkan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1 at Camp Nou on Sunday, with Kylian Mbappe scoring twice to secure victory in the La Liga El Clasico.
The match began at a relatively slow pace, with Barcelona creating the first notable opportunity through Anthony Gordon.
Real Madrid took the lead four minutes before halftime when Yan Diomande's low cross reached Mbappe in the area. Barcelona defender Gerard Martin's attempted clearance struck the French forward and deflected into the net.
Mbappe then hit the post before Diomande narrowly missed as Real Madrid finished the first half strongly.
Barcelona equalized 16 minutes into the second half when captain Raphinha collected a pass from Pedri and fired through Jude Bellingham's legs into the far corner.
Martin nearly made amends for his role in Madrid's opener shortly afterward, but Real goalkeeper Andriy Lunin produced a superb one-handed save. Lunin started in place of Thibaut Courtois, who was ruled out through illness.
With the match appearing destined for a draw, Bellingham produced a piece of skill in midfield to start Madrid's decisive attack. Substitute Eduardo Camavinga carried the ball forward before squaring for Mbappe, who finished into an unguarded net in the 87th minute.
The result left Barcelona a the top of the table with 25 points, two ahead of Atletico Madrid and three clear of Real Madrid.
Barcelona had been aiming to set a new record for consecutive victories at the start of a Spanish top-flight season, but Hansi Flick's side could not surpass the mark of nine straight wins set by Real Madrid in the 1968-69 campaign.
The victory also edged Real Madrid ahead in the all-time El Clasico record by one, which had been level at 106 wins apiece, with 52 draws before this game. Real Madrid have now scored 446 goals in the fixture, compared with Barcelona's 442.

Massive fire broke out at Shiv Market, opposite Jammu Railway Station
NEW DELHI: Around 35 to 40 shops were completely gutted after a massive fire broke out at Shiv Market, opposite Jammu Railway Station, in the early hours of Monday. No casualties or injuries have been reported so far, while fire and emergency services teams were working to bring the blaze under control. The cause of the fire remains unknown.
BJP MLA Vikram Randhawa said the fire reportedly began due to a short circuit in one shop before spreading rapidly to adjoining establishments. Shiv Market is a major commercial hub with shops selling dry fruits and blankets, as well as eateries and dhabas.“The fire started with a short circuit in one shop and spread rapidly, engulfing surrounding shops. By the time the fire brigade arrived, the entire market had been consumed by the flames. In my estimation, about 35 to 40 shops have been completely gutted,” Randhawa said.Describing the firefighting efforts, the MLA said the blaze had engulfed the entire market by the time the situation could be brought under control. He added that police personnel and senior officers were actively involved in managing the situation.“As it kept growing, by the time the whole system came under control, it had already engulfed the entire market.
Right now, our police are completely alert and actively controlling the situation. You can see that from the SHO to our SP, everyone is personally involved, even holding and dragging pipes all the way to the shops,” Randhawa said.A shopkeeper said at least 25 to 30 shops had suffered total losses and urged the administration to provide compensation to those affected.
“The entire market has been reduced to ashes. At least 25 to 30 shops are a total loss. We pray to God to grant everyone the strength to cope with this — the loss is immense, a total loss. I also urge the administration to step in as quickly as possible and ensure that compensation is provided without delay,” the shopkeeper said.
Randhawa said the full extent of the damage could be assessed only after the situation was completely under control. He said shopkeepers were cooperating with the administration, with the deputy commissioner, SP South, DSP, SHO and their teams present at the site. Members of civil society were also helping with relief efforts.On compensation for affected shopkeepers, Randhawa said the matter would be discussed with the administration later, describing the damage as massive.

Ukraine receives over 230,000 doses of inactivated polio vaccine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:34:00 UTC
07:34:00 KST

Ukraine receives over 230,000 doses of inactivated polio vaccine
According to Ukrinform, the Ministry of Health of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
"Ahead of World Polio Day, 232,500 doses of inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) have arrived in Ukraine for the free vaccination of children in accordance with the National Immunization Schedule," the statement reads.
Ukraine receives these vaccines through cooperation between the Ministry of Health and the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (Gavi). A partnership agreement was signed in late 2024. Under the agreement, Gavi funds part of the vaccine supply in support of Ukraine's national immunization program, in line with the National Strategy for the Development of Immunization through 2030.
Under this partnership, UNICEF is responsible for procuring the vaccines and delivering them to Ukraine, while the Ministry of Health's Public Health Center coordinates their distribution to regional centers for disease control and prevention.
The vaccines are currently being stored at the national warehouse and will be distributed to healthcare facilities across all regions of Ukraine.
The Ministry of Health recalled that World Polio Day was observed worldwide on October 24.
"Thanks to mass vaccination campaigns, the number of polio cases worldwide has fallen by more than 99%, from approximately 350,000 cases in 1988 to 12 in 2023. However, this does not mean we can afford to let our guard down. As long as the virus continues to circulate in even one country, it poses a threat to children worldwide," the statement reads.
The Ministry of Health explained that polio vaccination protects against all three existing types of poliovirus. Immunization is administered using an inactivated polio vaccine. This vaccine contains no live virus and is safe, including for people with compromised immune systems.
To have a child vaccinated, parents should contact their family doctor or pediatrician, or visit the nearest healthcare facility. Vaccination under the National Immunization Schedule is free of charge.
The Ministry of Health also stressed that if a child has missed any routine vaccinations, parents should contact a doctor as soon as possible to arrange an individual catch-up schedule.

Before setting the facilities up in flames, court records showed that Prater spray-painted a Nazi symbol in the parking lot of the Highlander Center. The same symbol was engraved on a rifle used in the terror attack on two Mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, back in 2019.
Prater admitted to committing the arson on the Highlander Center motivated by white-supremacist ideology, and admitted to targeting the non-profit for its faith-based educational priorities and its association with civil rights.

According to the DOJ, Prater obtained documents containing personal information on more than 35,000 individuals allegedly affiliated with Israel's government; however, the DOJ did not specify how Prater obtained them.
Prater took the sensitive information and provided it to an individual he believed was part of Hezbollah and reportedly told the operative to "start the hunt," the DOJ said.
The FBI Nashville field office investigated the case with assistance from the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, according to the DOJ.

Burnham pledges £900m for homelessness amid drive to end rough sleeping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:30:13 UTC
07:30:13 KST

Andy Burnham is to double spending on ending rough sleeping to almost £900m by the end of the current parliament, as he steps up efforts to get people off the streets by Christmas.
The prime minister has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership.
As he prepared for a Downing Street summit on ending rough sleeping on Monday, Burnham said the budget would bring a further £432m commitment to helping to tackle homelessness.
The sum is on top of an initial £442m from Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government budgets that will be allocated to the problem before March 2027.
Speaking ahead of the meeting, which will bring together charities and businesses, Burnham said: “Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life. It’s a thing governments either choose to accept or don’t.
“Well, I don’t accept it. That’s why we’re doubling funding so that people aren’t just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this parliament too.
“But we can’t do it alone. If we’re going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we’re bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts.”
Burnham’s mission to end rough sleeping is already under way with just two months to go before his deadline. There are specialist outreach teams and new accommodation spaces operating in Coventry, and further provision is being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden over the coming weeks.
The additional funding is being provided in an attempt to solve the problem of rough sleeping in the longer term. As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again.
Burnham has previously said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support and, understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.
He has said ending rough sleeping across the country will only be possible “if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve”.
The prime minister’s rough sleeping summit on Monday will bring together businesses, charities, housing providers and local leaders as they attempt to create more lasting changes.
Alongside the government, other organisations are making pledges towards solving the problem, with the National Housing Federation working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.
Virgin Media O2 will provide practical digital support to frontline organisations, while the charities St Mungo’s and Haircuts4Homeless will work with L’Oréal on hair salons and wellbeing provision for those who have been sleeping rough.
Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said it was a “big ambition” and the government would “not back down from making sure everyone has the offer of a route off the streets this Christmas”.
She said: “The first step is giving people a roof over their head and freedom from the nightly struggle to find somewhere safe to sleep. But Christmas is only the beginning and that’s why we will keep working together to tackle the root causes of homelessness and end rough sleeping for good.”
The homelessness charity Shelter welcomed the announcement. Its acting CEO, Mairi MacRae, said the funding showed “the government understands that a safe home is not a privilege, it is a necessity”.
However, the Conservatives dismissed the move, with Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, accusing the government of wanting to spend too much money on ending rough sleeping.
“Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester,” she said. “Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers’ money and more empty promises.”
Referring to the chancellor, Lam said: “[John] Healey must use his budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices. Instead of piling more costs on to hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers’ money.”

Polls open in Brazil for tight presidential runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro
Polls opened across Brazil at 8 am local time Sunday as voters started casting ballots in a closely contested presidential runoff between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and conservative Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Anadolu Agency reported.
The election pits 80-year-old Lula of the Workers' Party against 45-year-old Bolsonaro, the eldest son and political heir of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The runoff follows a competitive first-round vote on Oct. 4, when Bolsonaro led with 47% of valid votes against Lula's 45%. Neither candidate secured an outright majority.
The contest enters election day in a statistical dead heat, with a Datafolha poll showing both candidates tied at 50% of valid votes.
The election has centered on the rising cost of living, public insecurity, and persistent corruption concerns that affect Brazilians' daily lives.
Lula, who governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, returned to power after defeating Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 presidential election by less than two percentage points.
The victory marked the narrowest presidential margin in modern Brazilian history. Lula is now seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term.
Flavio Bolsonaro entered the race after his father was barred from holding public office and sentenced to 27 years in prison following investigations into a planned military coup after his 2022 defeat.
The former president's political base remains strong, with his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, securing a seat in the Federal Senate in the first round.
A victory for Flavio Bolsonaro would mark a return of the right in Brazil and align the country with a broader conservative shift across the region linked to the Trump administration in the US.
More than 150 million registered voters are expected to cast their ballots electronically across Brazil's 26 states and the Federal District.
Preliminary results are expected shortly after polls close at 5 p.m. Brasília time.

Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from Congo
KAMPALA, Oct 25 - Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions.
Uganda says it is Ebola-free after declaring an end to its latest outbreak in July, but there has been concern among health experts after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in Kenya and Nigeria.
Uganda says it is investigating the Nigerian case, which involves the wife of a Swiss diplomat. The woman, 42, returned from Uganda through Addis Ababa to Abuja on Oct. 3, according to Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control, which said she is in isolation and has improved remarkably.
The agency said 53 contacts had been traced.
Ugandan officials are reviewing genomic sequencing, travel information, interactions and movements in coordination with Nigerian authorities and international partners.
Swiss authorities had said the woman is believed to have contracted the virus in Uganda. Baryomunsi pushed back, saying Switzerland was "speaking prematurely". He said the woman's relatives from West Nile visited her in Kansanga, a suburb of Kampala, and that those relatives had visited Congo.
"What evidence do they have that she never travelled there?" he said. "We should speak science, not politics."
Kenya's first Ebola patient had travelled from Congo to Uganda and taken a flight from Entebbe airport to Nairobi on Oct. 3. The patient died two days later.
Both the Kenyan and the Nigerian cases travelled through the same Ugandan airport on the same day but there was no physical interaction between the two, Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, told the press conference, citing a review of the airport's CCTV system.
Baryomunsi said all 60 contacts linked to a Kenyan Ebola case had completed their 21-day monitoring period and been discharged.
"The ministry has intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings. All travellers intending to enter Uganda by air, land or water must complete the passenger locator form," he said.
Genomic analysis of Nigeria's only confirmed Ebola case showed the virus was closely related to the strain detected in Kenya's index case, though Nigerian authorities said there was no evidence that the Kenya case travelled to Nigeria or had a direct connection.
Uganda borders Congo, where the outbreak began, and has previously battled Ebola outbreaks.
Late on Sunday, World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said a nurse was killed and a health worker severely injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the northern Congolese town of Bafwasende.
"Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety," he wrote on X, saying the attack occurred on Saturday. REUTERS

Sri Lanka has repatriated 40 Iranian sailors who were brought ashore from stranded merchant vessels for medical treatment, the Daily Mirror reported Sunday.
Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told the newspaper that all 40 received medical attention before returning to Iran on Saturday morning.
The sailors were aboard merchant vessels approximately 24 nautical miles off Galle when authorities received distress calls concerning their medical conditions, according to the Foreign Ministry.
The Iranian Embassy in Colombo arranged the evacuation while Sri Lankan authorities coordinated their transfer through Galle port.
“We have coordinated the transfer and carried out our humanitarian obligations,” ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo said, according to the report.
Nearly a dozen empty Iranian oil tankers reportedly remain anchored off Galle, unable to return home because of a US blockade.
Sri Lankan authorities say the vessels are in international waters, beyond the country’s 12-nautical-mile territorial limit. Reconnaissance aircraft and naval patrol boats have been deployed to monitor them, the newspaper reported.
In March, Iran’s army said 104 crew members of the Iranian warship IRIS Dena were killed and 32 others injured in a US attack off Sri Lanka.
According to Iran’s state news agency IRNA, the vessel was attacked on March 4 while returning from the Milan Peace 2026 naval drills in India. Washington confirmed that an American submarine carried out a torpedo attack on the ship.
Sri Lanka said it launched a joint rescue operation after receiving a distress call from the vessel off Galle, taking 32 wounded crew members to a local hospital.

Brazil elections: Lula wins another term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro

- In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race

Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory
Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."
French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."
"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.
"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.
Big challenges face Lula's fourth term
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is likely to face several difficulties in enacting his agenda in a fourth-term.
Among other things, Brazil has elected its most conservative congress since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.
Flavio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allies could control more than 280 seats in the 513-seat lower house and up to 50 seats in the 81-seat Senate following parliamentary elections three weeks ago.
This could lead to Lula's being forced to cede to congress on decisions about the budget, important legislation and key nominations.
Economic woes
Brazil is also in a period of weak economic growth, with his government forecasting just a 2.3% rise in GDP next year.
This is combined with public debt that surpasses 82% of GDP, the highest rate since the coronavirus pandemic.
Security concerns
Public security also remains a major concern in Brazil, with criminal organizations holding considerable influence in parts of the country.
Lula has said he plans to establish a Ministry of Public Security to combat the problem.
Environmental problems
There are also environmental challenges ahead.
Although deforestation in the Amazon — a major carbon sink and thus vital for the stability of the world climate — fell significantly during Lula's third term, Brazil is still a long way from its goal of ending deforestation by 2030.
EU's von der Leyen hails Lula's win
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has posted an online message of congratulation to "my friend" Lula on his win in Brazil's election runoff.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," she wrote.
"Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," her post continued.
"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."
Could Bolsonaro succeed in annulling the vote?
Some uncertainty still surrounds the final result of Brazil's election, as Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to challenge the outcome over the two-hour extension of polling hours ordered by a Supreme Court judge at the request of Lula da Silva's campaign.
However, legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether such a complaint would meet the legal threshold for the election to be annulled.
Bolsonaro's case would be weakened by at least two factors, analysts said. Firstly, the scale of his loss to Lula and second, the fact that his campaign had also requested an extension in some states.
The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said that the extension of voting hours had not influenced the vote.
The Associated Press cited Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at Brazil's Fluminense Federal University, as saying that Bolsonaro could ask for the elections to be declared null and void by filing a complaint with electoral authorities or the Supreme Court.
"But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said.
"The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact," he said.
Shortly before scheduled voting ended, Supreme Court Judge Christiano had ordered polling stations to remain open for longer after problems with public transport were reported to be affecting voters.
The decision followed a request from Lula's campaign.
Bolsonaro's campaign had also called for an extension of voting hours but only in some conservative-leaning southern states hit by heavy rainfall, flooding and power outages that were said to be disrupting voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazil's leftist president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, according to the country's electoral court.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Sunday's second round vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula's claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
The campaign season was also marred by scandals and mudslinging.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. US President Donald Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."
