'Missiles from Iran': Facebook, TikTok and Instagram feed us scary news from the past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:43:30 UTC
04:43:30 KST

On Sunday, June 7, late in the evening, Iran attacked Israel. The Israel Defense Forces spokesman quickly released a video: "A short while ago, the Iranian terror regime launched missiles toward the territory of the State of Israel." Across the country, Israelis rushed to tidy up their bomb shelters and braced for another sleepless night.
Two weeks later, Erez was checking his Instagram feed one morning when he came across a video. On screen: the same IDF spokesman, the same posture, the same alarming tone — and the same announcement, word for word. No date appeared on screen; without checking, there was no telling it was the same old video. It looked entirely current.
Another three weeks went by. Avi was scrolling through TikTok and saw it too: the same spokesman, the same message. On September 5, Ayelet saw it as well — 90 days after it was first posted.
In reality, the event happened once. But on social media, the algorithm kept showing users reruns of the emergency announcement, which kept racking up views. As far as the recommendation system was concerned, that's what users wanted.
Recycled war declarations, weeks-old terror attacks raised from the dead, old updates about looming attacks from Home Front Command and other anxiety-inducing posts pulled up from the digital archive are part of a worsening phenomenon on social media, now the main way for people to communicate. One way to put it: Tech companies have erased time, or at least obscured it, pushing old content in the so-called news feed while also hiding the date and hindering the ability to actually check when a post was first posted. And when we lose our grasp of time, a frightening past can come back to haunt us.
A Haaretz digital investigation, based on an analysis of tens of thousands of posts and videos from the Facebook, Instagram and TikTok accounts of six digital personas created for this purpose, points to hundreds of cases in which the algorithm re-served old, anxiety-inducing news, the vast majority on Facebook and TikTok. Many videos carry no visible date, and real users struggled to tell when they were posted. Their comments say as much: "Is this from today???"; "Not again 💔"; "Why cause unnecessary panic"; "Panicked, I thought it was now"; "It would be nice if you put a date on these videos"; "Why. Is. There. No. Date. On. The. Video."
A sample of headlines from the personas' feeds: "Incident has not ended: Shooting attack in Sharon region — cruel murder spree in several locations" (a news site's video, shown 73 days after the attack); "Cleared for publication: Four soldiers killed in Lebanon" (appeared 87 days after the soldiers were killed); "Hezbollah launched rockets toward Nahariya for the first time in weeks" (47 days later); "Initial report: Our forces have begun a wave of strikes in Iran" (64 days later); "Cleared by the censor: Impacts in Karmiel area" (71 days later); "Iranian threat against Israel: 'We will respond decisively and painfully — tonight, look to the skies'" (39 days after the threat). The investigation pins down a phenomenon users noticed but struggled to put their finger on.
The process that led to this point did not happen overnight. Mundane technical changes — part of an economic battle between tech giants worth hundreds of billions of dollars — gradually added up to a phenomenon that is undermining how we perceive reality.
First, the platforms invested heavily in getting people to make and watch videos, and it paid off: Short videos became a cultural phenomenon. Brands and marketers use them to sell products; political campaigners, including in the current election, make content tailored to the format (the prime minister stands out in particular); news outlets worldwide realized that to survive, they had to join the game. Viewing data show a rapid, broad rise in video consumption. No wonder the "clip economy" has become a hallmark of the era.
Second, the same platforms — chiefly Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube — hid or removed timestamps from their videos, branded Reels, Shorts or, in TikTok's case, simply Videos. That lets them serve content untethered from chronology and tailored mainly to users' preferences, raising both the potential for addiction and time spent on the platform. Want to know when the clip you're watching was posted? Often, the date is hidden. On TikTok, researchers have had to build special tools to find it.
It's not just the videos. The platforms have undermined our sense of time in many ways. The feed went from chronological to algorithmic. This is also true for comments which are now by default, sorted by relevance, not date. On Instagram and Facebook, timestamps provide a retrospective perspective that becomes more complex as you scroll back: "13 weeks ago," "a year ago." When exactly was something posted? It's hard to say. But the biggest shift came with short video, which the apps push aggressively. Those are techniques TikTok perfected to deepen users' addiction. Their spread to other platforms is the TikTokification of the information we consume.
This has consequences. This year, for the first time, social media narrowly overtook TV and news websites as a news source globally, according to the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at the University of Oxford. Studies also link greater exposure to security content on social media to higher anxiety. Haaretz's findings add to a growing body of evidence that the way tech giants choose to build social media platforms may harm users' mental health.
Here is another way to think about it. Imagine opening a newspaper with no date anywhere. The stories, it turns out, come from different times — some from today, some from last week, some six months old. And the headline about the war resuming? We won't tell you when it's from. Feel free to guess.
The TikTokification of platforms
Social media has metamorphosed over the years. Facebook arrived early in the millennium as a place to connect with friends and share photos and updates. Twitter, now X, followed as a text-based network; Instagram laid claim to the photo-sharing crown. Then, in 2017, TikTok was born, betting it all on video.
TikTok, owned by China's ByteDance, has gone furthest in erasing time. Its model rests on short videos, many without a visible date: fast, frenetic, filling the screen, each swipe rewarding the user with another. On the surface, it's entertainment. But studies describe a process that erodes the human capacity to make sound decisions and resist harmful impulses. Some parts of the app show a timestamp, but the default For You feed lets users scroll for hours with no sign that they have sunk into the past. Indeed, a European Commission investigation has preliminarily found that TikTok's design encourages addiction in breach of EU law.
"The rise of TikTok since 2017 is perhaps the main social media story of the last decade," the Reuters Institute's Digital News Report says. "It is also the story of a video format that has shaped how people think of online content." Industry leaders have said as much. "People have a lot of choices for how they want to spend their time, and apps like TikTok are growing very quickly," Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told investors in 2022, adding: "This is why our focus on Reels is so important over the long term." Meta owns Facebook and Instagram, used daily by 64 and 58 percent of Israelis, respectively, according to the Israel Internet Association; TikTok, by 34 percent.
This is how everything unfolded: Instagram introduced Reels, its version of TikTok's hit short-video format, as early as 2019; YouTube launched Shorts a year later. In mid-2025, Facebook announced it was moving all its video to Reels, a process it said took a few months. And like TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and YouTube all hid their videos' timestamps — just as more and more users were turning to video for information.
Meanwhile, more people are getting their news from social media: almost 60 percent of Israelis frequently do, according to an Israel Internet Association survey. Yet though the platforms are a central venue for news - which they don't produce, relying on other sources - they don't follow the rules news organizations do. The news stories that the algorithm serves up from the archive into your feed is a striking example of this.
In search of lost time
For the investigation, Haaretz created six fictitious personas modeled on Israeli archetypes; Avi, Erez and Ayelet are three of them. All six got Facebook and TikTok accounts, and four also got Instagram. They scrolled for nearly four months. Haaretz archived every post they were shown and compared each item's original publication date with the date it appeared.
The findings show that resurfacing old content is ongoing and that the platforms recycle it on a large scale, because their algorithmic feeds let them resurface popular posts. The vast majority is innocuous, from stand-up clips to cat videos. But in Israel, where many users click on the security content that regularly fills their feeds, the algorithm also resurfaced alerts about terror attacks, missile fire, assassinations, political announcements and crime — and a report about a person who committed sexual harassment.
The alarming news the algorithm resurfaced came mainly from news outlets, including Kan News, Channel 14, N12, Israel Hayom and Ynet. Recycled posts also came from bodies such as the Israel Police, the IDF and the Home Front Command, and from high-profile figures such as Yoseph Haddad.
By Haaretz's calculation, each digital persona that was created for this investigation was shown an average of two alarming videos a week. Even if this appears to be a low number of recycled scary posts, they have an effect. "It naturally puts us on high alert," says Dr. Almog Simchon, head of the Computational Social Psychology Lab at Ben-Gurion University. "When you get security news, you need to act on it in real time — go to the safe room, check on family. We want an indication, here and now, that if something happened, our loved ones are OK. You need to process the information and figure out whether it's really happening now. If not, you need to cognitively bring down the adrenaline and stress, and you can't switch the system on in an instant and then off as if everything's fine. Recovery takes longer than activation."
Even in doubt, Simchon says, the body needs to treat the signal as something that may have happened. "We don't want to see breaking news about a terrible event and instinctively think, 'This must be old, it probably has nothing to do with me.' If it does concern me, the implications are enormous. So we want to take it into account and pay attention." Resurfacing alarming information, he adds, keeps us close to events and denies us the processing that distance brings.
Users can check when a video was published by stopping on it and clicking. On Facebook, Instagram and YouTube, that reveals the date. On TikTok, it can't be done from the For You feed at the heart of the app; the determined must open the comments and find when the first one was posted.
But this has a side effect. Clicking signals to the algorithm that the content interests users, making it likelier they'll get more of it. In other words, one archived terror attack leads to another. And commenting on an old video, as users sometimes do out of anger or panic, may raise the chances it appears in their friends' feeds.
Researchers at the Israel Internet Association have a clear name for the phenomenon: false information. "One of the common manipulations in spreading disinformation is using authentic documentation of an event detached from its original context, especially the time it occurred," Nitsan Yasur, head of disinformation department at the association, says of the findings. In a study the association conducted during the first Israel-Iran war, he says, the most prominent manipulation was presenting content out of its original time frame. "The truth is only true in its time," he says. Haaretz's investigation shows that social media algorithms naturally behave much like malicious actors.
Maya Ilany, CEO of the Brandeis Institute, which deals with technology, democracy and policy, adds: "We have to remember that ultimately, these are businesses that want to make money. They care about what keeps us on their app the longest. And one of those things is anxiety." The fixes, she says, are at least theoretically simple. "Everything can be reversed. If what they did was put everything into Reels and remove the date, then just reverse it."
Some countries, she notes, have already restricted addictive features. "For example, attorneys general in the U.S. reached an agreement with Meta that includes changing the addictive design for children. In the European Union, there's legislation on what information can be collected and limits on what can be used to target users. But in Israel, there's no law requiring the companies to do this, so why would they do it here?"
More broadly, Ilany says, the preference-based algorithm creates a fragmented reality. She points to the lively debate over whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will order a strike on Iran and whether it would help him in the election — a question, she says, to weigh against the platforms' power to shape how reality is perceived. "If there's a political actor who believes a security emergency would benefit him, he doesn't even need to make it happen in reality. He can create a manipulative feed that leads many in the public to believe we're in the midst of one — and then he has achieved his goal." Meanwhile, the algorithm serving up alarming news from the past seems to be doing that on its own.
TikTok said in response: "Our recommendation system is designed to reflect each user's personal preferences, based on their interactions on the platform. We are committed to protecting election integrity in Israel through dedicated teams, proactive enforcement and advanced safeguards against misleading information, and to keeping our community safe. We do not proactively promote specific political candidates. Drawing conclusions from subjective observation of a handful of accounts, on a platform where millions of videos are posted daily, rests on a fundamentally flawed methodology."
Meta did not respond to a Haaretz's question about our findings in this context, rather responding only to our main investigation's findings.
Haaretz created six digital personas defined by attributes such as place of residence, marital status and gender, but with no political leaning. An AI system logged the posts in their feeds, recording when each was published and when it was shown — 80,000 posts in all. Because the platforms conceal timestamps, the system could date only 13,000 of them. That subset contained dozens of examples of alarming news resurfacing long after publication; a simple calculation of the phenomenon's frequency across the full dataset points to hundreds of cases. A recurring post was defined as one shown at least 14 days after its original publication. Haaretz manually checked the machine's findings. The phenomenon also showed up in real users' private accounts throughout the investigation. Some of the data was collected with the help of Bright Data.

Marine Le Pen has launched her presidential campaign in France amid mass protests
Kyiv • UNN
Marine Le Pen launched her campaign, promising a tougher migration policy and a crackdown on crime. She is supported by 32–33.5% of voters.
The leader of France’s far-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, has officially launched her campaign for the 2027 presidential election. She promised to intensify the fight against crime, restrict immigration, and strengthen France’s sovereignty. Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
Le Pen held her first campaign rally on October 25 in Orléans, amid large-scale protests against the rising cost of living and social inequality.
During her speech, the politician said that France was experiencing an economic, social, and security crisis, and promised to restore order in the country.
We are not living through the end of the world, but the end of their world
Le Pen leads in the polls
According to a poll released on Sunday, Le Pen’s support stands at 32–33.5%. Her closest rival, far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has around 17%.
In her campaign platform, Le Pen promised to restore border controls, automatically deport foreigners convicted of crimes, and intensify the fight against drug trafficking.
In economic policy, she advocates cutting taxes for businesses, reducing bureaucracy, and supporting industry. The politician also promises not to allow any further increase in the retirement age.
At the same time, Le Pen continues to appeal the court verdict in the case involving the embezzlement of European Parliament funds. Due to legal restrictions, her presidential campaign could become more difficult.

Serbia Shows TSMB M-25 203mm Self-Propelled Mortar Firing for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:42:44 UTC
04:42:44 KST

Serbia’s Ministry of Defense has released footage of firing tests of the TSMB M-25 203mm self-propelled mortar for the first time.
The video was published by the Serbian Ministry of Defense.
The October 21 video focuses on the development of Serbia’s domestic defense industry.
However, the ministry did not specify when the firing tests took place or disclose their results.
The TSMB M-25 was developed by Serbia’s Military Technical Institute based on design solutions from the 155mm M-65 howitzer, a Yugoslav version of the American M114.
The system features a 203mm barrel with a length of 24 calibers and an automated loading mechanism.
According to Serbia’s Ministry of Defense, the mortar is designed to engage targets at ranges of 6 to 12 kilometers.
A dedicated range of high-explosive and concrete-piercing ammunition was developed for the system. A standard 203mm mortar bomb weighs approximately 100 kilograms, including about 27 kilograms of explosive material.
The developers also provided for the use of rocket-assisted projectiles to extend firing range and Precision Guidance Kit (PGK) guidance kits.
According to its stated specifications, the mortar can fire up to three rounds per minute. However, there is currently no confirmation that this rate of fire was achieved during testing.
The TSMB M-25 is mounted on a FAP 2026 three-axle wheeled chassis with a 6×6 configuration. The vehicle weighs approximately 19 metric tons and has an armored cab for a crew of four.
The fire control system includes an inertial navigation system, a ballistic computer, communications equipment and a gunner’s computer.
Militarnyi previously reported on the unveiling of the TSMB M-25 203mm heavy mortar at the Partner 2025 defense exhibition in Belgrade. Local residents had spotted the system before its official presentation on September 17.

Roundup: African countries host photo exhibition marking Taiwan's restoration to China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:41:55 CST
04:41:55 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- A photo exhibition marking the 81st anniversary of Taiwan's restoration to China opened in five African countries -- Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania and Mozambique -- from Oct. 23 to 25.
The exhibition features four thematic sections and presents more than 30 photos under the theme "Remembering Taiwan's Restoration, Advancing National Reunification." Chinese ambassadors to the respective countries, local officials, foreign diplomats, scholars, business representatives and media practitioners attended the events.
Guests reaffirmed that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China, and stressed that Africa supports the efforts to safeguard the victorious outcomes of World War II and the post-war international order. They spoke highly of holding such an photo exhibition overseas.
At the opening ceremony of the photo exhibition in Nairobi on Oct. 23, Erastus Mwencha, former deputy chairperson of the African Union Commission, said the restoration of Taiwan in 1945 marked the end of the Treaty of Shimonoseki of 1895 and a monumental moment of restored integrity for the Chinese nation. The historical significance of these developments extends beyond China, and it also resonates profoundly with Africa, he noted.
Mwencha recalled that when the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758 in 1971, restoring the lawful rights of the People's Republic of China, 26 African nations voted in favor.
At the same-day opening ceremony in Abuja, capital of Nigeria, Charles Onunaiju, director at the Center for China Studies, said China's experience of foreign intervention and colonial aggression is closely connected with the issue of national reunification. He said African countries have their own historical experiences and are therefore able to understand China's position on safeguarding national unity and sovereignty.
Sheriff Ibrahim, head of the Center for Contemporary China-Africa Research in Nigeria, said there is a certain similarity between China's efforts to maintain national unity and Nigeria's own experience in maintaining its territorial integrity, expressing confidence that China would eventually achieve national reunification.
On Oct. 24, at the opening ceremony held in Johannesburg, South Africa, Zheng Xingli, president of the All-Africa Association for Peaceful Reunification of China, said that history is the best textbook, noting that the exhibition revisits the history of Taiwan's restoration through a collection of precious historical photos and pays tribute to those who made sacrifices and contributions to national independence and reunification.
At the same-day opening ceremony in Tanzania's commercial capital Dar es Salaam, Joseph Kahama, secretary-general of the Tanzania-China Friendship Promotion Association, said the exhibition demonstrated the importance of preserving historical records for future generations. He said the exhibition offered lessons for Tanzania on documenting history and expressed support for China's position on reunification.
On Oct. 25, at the opening ceremony held in Maputo, capital of Mozambique, former Mozambican President Joaquim Chissano said, in 2025, China officially designated Oct. 25 as the Commemoration Day of Taiwan's Restoration, giving greater institutional significance to this anniversary. The date thus carries a meaning that goes beyond commemorating a historical event, reflecting the importance China attach to preserving national memory.
Luis Canhemba, director of the Information Office of Mozambique, said the exhibition highlights the importance of preserving collective memory, recognizing the events that have shaped a nation's historical journey, and understanding their significance for present and future generations.
Organized by Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau in partnership with several organizations, the photo exhibition will run for at least one week in the five countries. ■

Interview: Maltese bluefin tuna producer sees bigger opportunities in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:41:47 CST
04:41:47 KST

Malta Fish Farming (MFF) chairman Salvu Ellul speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Valletta, Malta, Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Jonathan Borg/Xinhua)
VALLETTA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Nearly three decades after his first trip to China, Malta Fish Farming (MFF) chairman Salvu Ellul expects his company to ship up to 1,000 tonnes of bluefin tuna there this year.
"Opportunity with China will be much stronger for us," Ellul said in a recent interview with Xinhua. MFF is one of Malta's leading producers of farmed Atlantic bluefin tuna.
In 2004, Ellul made his first attempt to export tuna to the Chinese market, on a trip to Beijing. "But it was a bit too early," he recalled, adding that he always believed he would one day sell tuna in China.
That time came in November 2023, when an agreement signed during Maltese Foreign Minister Ian Borg's visit to China gave Maltese farmed bluefin direct access to the Chinese market. The same month, MFF showcased its tuna at the 6th China International Import Expo, where visitors were impressed by the delicacy of the raw meat, Ellul said.
"Now we can sell directly from our factory to China," he said. MFF started delivering to China in 2024 with about 200 tonnes, and this year its factory alone is expected to send 700 to 1,000 tonnes. The company employs over 250 workers and plans to hire more as exports to China grow.
In June 2024, MFF and China's Shandong Ocean Group set up the first China-Malta joint bluefin tuna processing platform, bringing the Chinese ultra-low-temperature processing vessel Ocean Star to Maltese waters.
Ellul said he had long wanted a freezing vessel for his business, while the Chinese side needed a secure supply of fish. "I give that and they give me their security as well. And both together, we have made a great success now," he said.
Ellul described the Ocean Star as the most efficient tuna-freezing vessel in the Mediterranean, processing about 70 tonnes a day. Looking back, he said the hardest part was concluding the deal fast enough to avoid losing a production season. The two sides agreed on the contract in three months and set up the company three months later.
The cooperation is now moving into new areas. MFF has set up a trading company in Shanghai with other partners to develop its fresh tuna business, aiming to deliver fish from Malta to Shanghai daily or weekly, all year round, Ellul said.
Breeding is another area of cooperation. In July, a batch of fertilized bluefin eggs from MFF's farms cleared quarantine in Zhangzhou, in China's Fujian Province, for research purposes.
"That was an ambition from my side," Ellul said. Wild-caught tuna take about seven years to grow, he said, while tuna hatched and raised in China could reach 2 to 5 kg in two years. "And that will be the table fish for the Chinese market," he added, expecting the Fujian project to be on its way to commercial production within five years.
Trade flows both ways. MFF buys bait fish from China, and at the upcoming China Fisheries and Seafood Expo in Qingdao, it hopes to sign agreements to buy more, as well as new sales deals, Ellul said.
On sustainability, Ellul noted that bluefin stocks have recovered and are now healthy under the management of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, and that every fish can be traced from catch to the final client. Next, MFF will work to build its own brand in China, he added.
Business between Europe and China is strong "and it will be stronger," Ellul said. ■
Bluefin tuna are seen being transported to Ocean Star, an ultra-low temperature processing and transportation vessel of China on the Mediterranean sea east of Malta, Oct. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Jing)
Workers harvest Bluefin tuna at a fishing farm on the Mediterranean sea east of Malta, Oct. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Jing)

Serbia closes polls in snap parliamentary elections amid high turnout, reports of irregularities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:39:25 UTC
04:39:25 KST

Talha Ozturk
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Polling stations across Serbia closed at 8 pm local time on Sunday after snap parliamentary elections marked by high voter turnout and reports of voting irregularities.
Voter turnout reached 67.6% by 7 pm, according to estimates published by polling agency Ipsos and the Center for Free Elections and Democracy (CeSID).
The figure was already 8.83 percentage points higher than the final turnout of 58.77% recorded in Serbia’s previous parliamentary elections in December 2023, highlighting a significant increase in voter participation.
The latest figure is not the final turnout, which is expected to be announced after all votes have been counted.
The first preliminary results are expected before midnight.
Some 6.45 million registered voters were eligible to cast ballots in the elections, with 18 electoral lists competing for seats in Serbia’s 250-member National Assembly.
Under Serbian election law, the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) must publish a consolidated report on the election results within 96 hours of receiving all summary reports from polling stations.
Electoral lists must secure at least 3% of the vote to qualify for parliamentary representation, while lists representing national minorities are exempt from the threshold.
Seats are allocated under the D’Hondt proportional representation system, which distributes parliamentary mandates according to the number of votes received by each qualifying electoral list.
The RIK is required to allocate parliamentary seats to candidates within 10 days of publishing the consolidated election results.
The newly elected National Assembly must be constituted within 30 days of the publication of final results, while a new government must be formed within 90 days of the parliament’s constitution.
The elections were monitored by numerous international and domestic observers, including missions from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (OSCE/ODIHR), the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe and the European Parliament.
Observers from the US, Russia’s State Duma and other national parliaments were also registered.
Serbian citizens living abroad were eligible to vote at 93 polling stations across 37 countries, with 102,147 voters registered for overseas voting.
Of the 18 electoral lists contesting the elections, nine represented national minorities.
The snap elections were called on Sept. 9 by then-President Aleksandar Vucic, who signed a decree dissolving the National Assembly following a government proposal submitted Sept. 7.
Sunday’s vote marked Serbia’s 15th parliamentary election since the introduction of multiparty politics in 1990 and its 10th snap parliamentary election.
The last parliamentary elections were held on Dec. 17, 2023.
Ruling party faces student-backed challengers
The elections come amid months of student-led protests and a political crisis that led to President Aleksandar Vucic's resignation in September.
Vucic is seeking to return to government as prime minister through the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
The SNS, which has dominated Serbian politics since 2012, is competing under the electoral list “Aleksandar Vucic - United Serbia.”
Among its challengers is the student-backed “Student List - Students Win,” which emerged from protests following the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.
The student movement has demanded accountability for the disaster, greater transparency, and reforms to strengthen the rule of law and public institutions.
Other contenders include the Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS), led by Ivica Dacic, the pro-European European Serbia coalition, and the nationalist Authentic Right bloc.

Trump rules out Iran strike Sunday as tensions mount across Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:39:24 UTC
04:39:24 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that the United States would not launch an attack on Iran that day, even as tensions between Washington and Tehran continued to simmer, American military forces maintained a heightened presence in the Strait of Hormuz and the State Department ordered some embassy personnel to leave Saudi Arabia.
"There will be no attack on Iran today," Trump told reporters, offering a temporary assurance amid mounting concerns about another round of fighting.
His comments came a day after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his claim that Iran had resumed its nuclear program. Netanyahu also released a simulation Sunday depicting a nuclear bomb striking Tel Aviv.
Trump, however, disputed the suggestion that Iran was rebuilding its nuclear facilities, saying American intelligence indicated little activity at sites previously bombed by U.S. forces.
Asked in an interview with Fox News whether Iran was attempting to restore damaged nuclear installations and what satellite imagery showed, Trump said Washington had extensive surveillance capabilities.
"We can read the badge on somebody's shirt from space," Trump said. "We know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe Mountain. We know the other three [facilities] are obliterated. They're not moving around there very much."
"We're watching them. We have access to every one of the facilities we bombed. They're covered by thousands of tons of rock," he added.
US commander visits Strait of Hormuz
Meanwhile, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, visited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday as American forces continued operations aimed at securing the strategically important waterway.
CENTCOM said Cooper toured the area as U.S. military forces marked what it described as a milestone in helping Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer.
During the visit, Cooper flew aboard a CH-47 Chinook helicopter over the international shipping route to assess the operational environment.
According to CENTCOM, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully passed through the strait with American military support over the past six months.
"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," Cooper said. "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea and is one of the world's most important maritime routes for oil exports.
CENTCOM said commercial shipping through the strait had gained momentum in recent months after U.S. forces cleared naval mines that it said had been deployed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The American military said the mine-clearing operations had allowed vessels to resume using the strait's international shipping lanes.
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," Cooper said.
CENTCOM also claimed that more than 95% of vessels traveling through the strait in recent months had sailed safely despite what it described as unprovoked aggression by the Revolutionary Guard.
The figures, according to the command, demonstrated that the United States and its regional partners maintained control of the international waterway.
US orders embassy staff to leave Saudi Arabia
The State Department confirmed Sunday that it had ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government personnel and their family members from the American Embassy in Riyadh amid fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The confirmation followed reports of diplomatic evacuations from several locations across the Middle East.
"Effective Friday, the Department of State ordered employees to depart Saudi Arabia due to security risks," the department said in a statement.
It cited recent Houthi attacks on Saudi territory, including strikes against civilian airports and other critical infrastructure that had caused civilian casualties and significant travel disruptions.
"The Iran-backed Houthis have carried out acts of aggression against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure," the statement said.
The department warned that the violence could escalate rapidly and spread beyond the areas immediately affected by the fighting.
The evacuation order underscored growing American concerns about the security of diplomatic personnel as hostilities involving Iran and its regional allies threatened to expand.
Sri Lanka evacuates 40 Iranian sailors
In a separate development, Sri Lanka's Foreign Ministry said Sunday that the island nation had coordinated the evacuation of 40 Iranian sailors from 19 commercial vessels operating in international waters near the country.
The operation was conducted at Tehran's request after the sailors experienced unspecified medical problems.
Sri Lankan authorities said Iran had submitted its request through established diplomatic channels and that the sailors had since been returned to the Islamic Republic.
The ministry did not explain why the sailors needed to be evacuated or provide further details about their medical conditions.
Local media outlets, along with India's The Hindu newspaper, reported that the sailors had been aboard oil tankers subject to U.S. sanctions imposed as part of Washington's confrontation with Tehran.
A Sri Lankan government source with direct knowledge of the operation told Reuters that the country's navy and coast guard routinely assist with humanitarian missions.
The latest operation followed Sri Lanka's involvement in rescue and repatriation efforts after a U.S. submarine sank the Iranian warship IRIS Dena with a torpedo off the island's coast on March 4, during the first week of the war involving Israel, the United States and Iran.
Dozens of Iranian sailors were killed in that attack, while Sri Lankan authorities helped rescue survivors.
Sri Lanka subsequently assisted in repatriating the bodies of 87 Iranian sailors, as well as 32 survivors from the Dena and 208 crew members from another Iranian vessel.
Iranians stockpile food and medicine amid fears of renewed war
With Israel's elections two days away and the U.S. midterm elections about a week and a half away, fears of renewed fighting are also growing among ordinary Iranians.
As leaders in Washington, Jerusalem and Tehran exchange warnings and threats, residents of the Iranian capital are preparing for the possibility of another military escalation and further economic disruption.
In interviews with The Associated Press, Tehran residents described stockpiling food, medicine and emergency supplies, while some said they were preparing to leave the city if hostilities resumed.
Fereshteh Hajipour, a 35-year-old mother of a toddler, said she had begun accumulating over-the-counter medications and food in anticipation of a possible war involving more powerful bombs.
The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has contributed to medicine shortages, according to AP, although there have been no indications of widespread shortages of food or other essential goods.
Iran's economic difficulties have intensified as the rial has fallen to record lows and inflation has surged, severely eroding household purchasing power.
A typical monthly salary in Iran is about 400 million rials, equivalent to roughly $150, leaving many families struggling to afford basic necessities.
"Grocery shopping can cost half a month's salary," said Mohammad Mohammadi, 36.
Despite soaring prices, some residents said they felt compelled to purchase additional supplies because of the confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz and the possibility that trade disruptions could worsen.
Mohammad Abdi, 39, said he had stocked up on dried dates, cooking oil and rice for his family.
"I'm worried the situation could get worse," he said.
Others are preparing to leave Tehran altogether.
Hashem Vajdani, a 45-year-old fitness trainer, said he had already packed his belongings and planned to seek refuge in a smaller town in northern Iran if fighting resumed.
"I've already packed my things to go to a safer town in the north of the country," he said. "Today I bought more canned food, crackers and extra blankets."

What Does Trump’s Declining Latino Support Mean for Florida?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:36:07 UTC
04:36:07 KST

William Diaz has a mantra: His only political party is his Venezuelan community.
He doesn’t abide by strict partisan rules, and doesn't believe in only voting for Democrats or Republicans. He supported Republicans Sen. Rick Scott and Secretary of State Marco Rubio when they were running for office in Florida, where Diaz has lived for 37 years.
For these midterm elections, however, the Orlando resident hopes to make a clear statement: He does not support President Donald Trump’s immigration policies and is unhappy with how Republican-backed initiatives have affected his community.
“I voted already, and what I did when I was voting and when I was with my ballot, I was really thinking and praying for all those that has no voice, those that can not vote, those immigrants that are right now victim of actions on the streets,” Diaz tells TIME, referring to Trump’s mass deportation agenda and the expansive influence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). “My people have been suffering that much.”
Diaz is one of more than 2.6 million people who have already cast ballots in Florida, either by mail or through in-person early voting, according to state figures released Sunday. In-person early voting began in some counties Oct. 19 and expanded statewide Oct. 24.
Diaz’s community is one part of a Florida Latino electorate with varied national origins and political loyalties. Taken together, however, Latino voters are a swing vote in several closely watched races statewide. They were key to Trump’s Florida victory in 2024, with 56% supporting him over Kamala Harris, according to the 2024 American Electorate Voter Poll.
But new polls ahead of Election Day suggest that Latino support for the GOP may be on shaky ground—a shift that could put Republicans to the test in Florida and shape the political landscape beyond November.
Why Florida’s Latino voters are frustrated with Trump
Dissatisfaction among Florida’s Latino voters reflects a broader national mood, according to Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of Equis Research, an organization that studies Latino voting behavior.
Concerns about the economy and immigration enforcement tactics are fueling dissatisfaction among Latino voters, who “make up a huge part of the electorate in Florida,” she says, pointing out that both of these issues are “disproportionately impacting” them.
A Univision/YouGov poll, conducted Oct. 2–15, showed that 41% of registered Latino voters in Florida were “very or somewhat worried” that they, a family member, or someone close could be detained or otherwise directly affected by immigration enforcement, compared with 27% of Florida voters overall.
The same poll showed that 4 in 10 Latino voters in the state felt that their finances had worsened over the past year, with 70% disapproving of Trump’s handling of the cost of living in the U.S. That stands in comparison to a 63% disapproval rate from Florida voters overall.
For Johanna Chavez, a Dominican immigrant living in Kissimmee, Florida, the economy is top of mind.
“Many people are concerned about the economy and the price of gasoline … and then there’s the cost of rent, it’s become incredibly, overwhelmingly high,” Chavez, who speaks Spanish, tells TIME through a translator. “All the things they promised would be done—nothing has happened.”
In the past few years, Chavez says it has felt like the United States has started “regressing,” and the opportunities she was looking for when she arrived here have not materialized in the way she had hoped.
“It’s starting to feel just like the situation back in my home country, the Dominican Republic,” she says. “We all came here hoping for change, seeking a better life, but it’s ending up being the same thing all over again. Things just aren’t what they’re supposed to be.”
Jared Nordlund, the Florida State Advocacy Director at UnidosUS, the largest nonprofit Latino rights organization in the U.S., says this is a common refrain among Floridian Latinos; people are upset over how the economy has been affected by tariffs and the war in Iran. Florida was hit particularly hard by rising gas prices after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz squeezed the global energy supply, he says.
“Florida is not a state friendly for public transportation, so people are highly reliant on the cars, and so what they would be paying for food now is having to kind of get broke between … paying to get the gas and then going to get food,” Nordlund says.
The question now is whether that dissatisfaction will translate into votes against Republicans—and whether it will be enough to tip the state’s close races.
Trump’s declining Latino support puts Florida Republicans on notice
Trump’s approval rating has plummeted with Latino voters in Florida, dropping from 58% approval at the start of his term to 36% ahead of midterm elections, according to Equis Research.
According to an AP-NORC poll from October, about 6 in 10 Latino voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency, and more than 7 in 10 disapprove of how he is handling the economy.
A Pew Research Center poll found that Trump’s job approval rating among Latino voters dropped from 38% in February 2025 to 24% in September and October. Of those who backed him in the last election, approval dropped to 57%—down from 93% in early 2025.
The shift may be resonating with Republicans like Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who is seeking re-election in Florida’s 27th District in Miami-Dade—a majority Latino district that Trump carried by some 15 points in 2024. She publicly broke with Trump in her campaign and criticized his immigration policies.
In one ad in September, Salazar said that Trump has “gone too far" with his deportation agenda.
“In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” she notes in the ad.
“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” Salazar continues, addressing Trump. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
Why Latino frustration may not translate into Democratic votes
Guillermo Grenier, a Cuban American professor of sociology at Florida International University (FIU), agrees that many Latino voters are “ticked off” at Trump.
“The population, if you look at the whole Latino conglomerate, is turned off pretty strongly with Trump,” he says.
But South Florida’s Latino electorate is unique; Grenier points out that the state is home to 1.9 million Cuban Americans—the largest concentration in the United States.
As a voting bloc, the community has significant sway. In 2024, FIU’s Cuba poll found that 68% of likely Cuban American voters in Miami-Dade County supported Trump, compared to 23% for Harris—representing his highest-recorded support level in the poll's history.
A shift away from Republicans among Cuban American voters could therefore have significant consequences in South Florida. But disillusionment doesn’t always turn into action, according to Grenier.
“I think a lot of Cubans are pissed off at Trump, but they're still Republicans,” he says.
The Democratic Party’s response to this potential opening may unfold over several election cycles.
“Democrats are going to be in a probationary period with Latinos and with all voters, quite frankly, on whether they can deliver or not,” Valencia says. “One election is not durable support among a particular group.”
Both Valencia and Grenier suggest that it will come down to Democrats proving that they are willing to reinvest in Florida.
What are the key races to watch in Florida?
There are several key races at stake in Florida. Although the state has leaned reliably red for the past three election cycles, Democrats are investing late in the race through campaigning and financing.
Florida Democrats posted a larger monthly net gain in active registered voters than Republicans, according to figures the party highlighted Oct. 1. The Florida Democratic Party touted the gains as a sign of its growing base in the state.
“We’ve spent years rebuilding this party from the ground up. Our organizers are in communities year-round, our volunteers are knocking doors across this state, and Democrats are having real conversations with Floridians about what’s at stake,” Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said in an October statement. “The momentum is real.”
Gov. Ron DeSantis is term-limited and cannot run for re-election, leaving the role open for Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate who has been endorsed by Trump, and David Jolly, who is running as a Democrat after leaving the GOP in 2018.
A poll released Oct. 21 by the Public Opinion Research Lab (PORL) at the University of North Florida (UNF) found that Donalds leads 49% to 47%—within the poll's almost 3-percentage-point margin of error.
Latino voters could be important to Jolly’s chances. The Univision/YouGov poll found that they favored him over Donalds, 48% to 43%, even as Donalds led 50% to 42% among Florida voters overall.
Democrats are taking note. Weeks after Jolly beseeched the Democratic Party to send money to his campaign, the Democratic Governors Association announced Oct. 20 that it will invest $1 million to help close the narrowing gap in the weeks before Election Day.
That trend follows in certain congressional races downballot.
A September poll found Salazar leading Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, a former local news anchor, by just 1 point.
Angie Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is an underdog for Senate, taking on Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody. A recent UNF poll has Moody leading by 49% to 45%, halving the advantage she had in July.
National Democratic leaders and allies have made the trip to Florida to bolster these close races.
Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Democratic ally, rallied in Tampa for Nixon on Oct. 17. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries campaigned with Rodriguez on Oct. 16; they held a campaign event at a Cuban coffee shop and bakery.
The decision received some blowback, with one conservative Cuban influencer taking to Instagram to slam the business for hosting Jeffries. He argued that associating with the Democrats equated to supporting socialism.
For Grenier, the incident shows that Democrats have some serious work to do to gain trust in Florida—and while it might be “too late” to invest in candidates in this election, the party can lay the groundwork for 2028 and beyond.
He said that if Democrats want to build on the momentum after the midterms, they can’t get “gun shy.”
“This new beachhead that [Democrats] are trying to establish is the way to go for the next elections,” Grenier says.
“You know, it was 10 years of investing before Republicans flipped the state in 1996,” he continues. “So, they need to just keep it up, and have national leaders support local leaders.”

Has Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:35:17 UTC
04:35:17 KST

The public has been told repeatedly that John Healey is so concerned about budget leaks that he has set up defence-style “compartmentalisation” to prevent the Treasury’s financial secrets escaping.
The macho military analogies began in mid-August when Healey was said by the Telegraph to be “on a war footing” to stop the drip of information that he believed had beleaguered Rachel Reeves.
The Financial Times added that “military-style protocols” were being deployed, while the Spectator was excited about the use of “classified computer systems” and the i newspaper described a process where officials could sign in to only their parts of the document and could not access the sections they were not working on.
This weekend, the Observer reported that Healey was “flabbergasted” by the lack of security around financial information when he became chancellor and “it was so different to how we did things in the MoD”.
The chancellor is known to have been worried that market-sensitive leaks cost Britain billions in the run-up to the last government’s budgets. But has this time around been so different after all?
Despite the heightened “security” around Wednesday’s budget, many of its announcements have been leaked already from a clear mixture of authorised and unauthorised sources.
It emerged well in advance that there will be a higher tax on banks – a deeply market-sensitive policy – and a package of energy support for the most vulnerable.
There will also be billions of pounds in extra defence spending, directed towards the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, as well as a £1bn crackdown on online VAT sales, with big retailers such as Amazon, eBay and Temu to be responsible for collecting what is due from smaller merchants selling on their platforms.
On top of that, there have been stories indicating the level of headroom the chancellor will be looking at – in the region of £15bn – known in the political trade as “pitch rolling” to avoid alarming the markets or the public.
The Treasury and No 10 have also undertaken their traditional stream of embargoed announcements by press release in the days before the fiscal event, such as a new £1.5bn borrowing facility for local authorities and £1bn for social housing, as they seek to build a sense of action and momentum about what the government is trying to achieve.
Former Treasury advisers believe the rigamarole around budget security is partly designed to deter civil servants and gossiping MPs from thinking they can embark on unauthorised chatter before a policy is ready.
But they also say it is unhelpful for the chancellor to produce a hermetically sealed budget, which could cause a backlash over surprise measures – in the markets, the media, among the government’s own MPs and the wider public.
It is often the less-trailed policies that have tended to go wrong, from George Osborne’s pasty tax in 2012 to Philip Hammond’s surprise national insurance hike for the self-employed in 2017 that had to be abandoned within seven days after a furore among Conservative MPs about breaking their manifesto promise.
Aides say there is a balance to be struck – and it’s not always a good idea to hoard information until budget day. “If everything is kept tight, then you end up surprising people. And that’s called a Liz Truss situation,” says one former strategist from the Tory years.
Healey has been shutting down speculation about various tax rises, from higher capital gains tax on certain assets to lowering the mansion tax on properties worth more than £1.5m – showing he has begun to see the virtue in expectation management and limiting surprises on the big day.
There may still be a few fiscal “rabbits out of the hat” on the day, as Healey seeks to combine a “steady-as-she-goes” budget with some eye-catching measures designed to show the public that the government is on their side.
But if the Treasury really has aimed for military levels of secrecy around its budget, the Ministry of Defence might have something to worry about.

Lib Dems propose six more frigates for Royal Navy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:35:09 GMT
04:35:09 KST

The Liberal Democrats have proposed ordering six additional Royal Navy frigates and expanding British shipbuilding capacity as part of a defence package aimed at responding to the threat from Russia, according to plans published by the party.
Under the proposal, three additional Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates and three additional Type 31 general-purpose frigates would be ordered for delivery by the mid-2030s.
If added to existing government plans, the proposal would increase the planned Type 26 fleet from eight ships to 11 and the Type 31 fleet from five to eight. The government currently intends the two classes to form the core of the Royal Navy’s future frigate force alongside at least six Common Combat Vessels replacing the Type 45 destroyers.
The Liberal Democrats estimate that three additional Type 31 frigates would cost around £1.2 billion, based on an assumed unit cost of approximately £400 million in 2025/26 prices. The party puts the cost of three additional Type 26 frigates at £2.85 billion, using an estimated cost of around £950 million per ship.
A further £370 million would be allocated from the party’s proposed Defence Bonds scheme towards additional shipbuilding infrastructure.
The party describes the policy as providing funding for four new shipyards, although the detailed costing accompanying the announcement says the £370 million figure is based on constructing two further facilities at approximately £185 million each, using BAE Systems’ Janet Harvey Hall on the Clyde as its benchmark.
The frigate orders and shipbuilding allocation amount to approximately £4.42 billion of capital spending under the party’s published assumptions.
The Liberal Democrats also propose increasing the Digital Services Tax from 2 per cent to 10 per cent and using part of the additional revenue to meet personnel and maintenance costs associated with the expanded fleet.
The party says there are no current official estimates available for the through-life operating costs of the Type 26 and Type 31 fleets. Its own calculations assume annual running costs of £20 million for each additional ship by 2034/35, producing an estimated £120 million annual cost for the six vessels.
Liberal Democrat Defence Spokesperson James MacCleary MP said: “We cannot afford to sit on our hands while Putin’s aggression intensifies and our national security weakens. We need a plan which gives confidence to British industry and allows our manufacturers to get on with delivering for Britain’s long-term security.
“By investing now in six new warships and by expanding our ship-building capacity with four new British shipyards, we can regenerate our fleet, protect our vital underwater infrastructure, and ensure Britain has the defence capabilities we need to stand up to the Kremlin.”
The announcement follows a Defence Committee report published on 22 October which warned of serious capability gaps affecting British operations in the High North.
The committee said publicly available evidence of low availability among frigates, destroyers and attack submarines raised questions about the UK’s ability to meet its commitments in the region, while warning that Russian submarine and sabotage activity presents risks to undersea infrastructure and North Atlantic reinforcement routes.
The Liberal Democrats also cited polling conducted by Savanta between 29 May and 1 June 2026 involving 2,234 UK adults. According to the results commissioned by the party, 60 per cent said the government was either probably or definitely not doing enough to protect critical infrastructure from Russian attacks, compared with 26 per cent who believed it was doing enough. Fourteen per cent answered that they did not know.
The party argues that additional orders would also provide a longer and more predictable workload for British shipbuilding, allowing yards and suppliers to invest in workforce and infrastructure with greater confidence.
The government’s existing shipbuilding programme includes eight Type 26 frigates and five Type 31 frigates, while the wider Hybrid Navy plan also envisages new crewed and uncrewed vessels operating together. The 2025 Strategic Defence Review placed particular emphasis on the Type 26 as part of Atlantic Bastion, the Royal Navy’s approach to countering the growing submarine threat in the North Atlantic.
The Liberal Democrat proposal would go beyond those numbers by adding six crewed frigates to the planned force, with the party arguing that the additional hulls should be ordered during the next Parliament and delivered by the mid-2030s.

Ivan Hristanov – Stoyanka Cherkezova: 2.2%
The remaining candidates each received less than 1% of the vote
4.9% of voters selected “None of the above''. Voter turnout stood at 22.3%.
The results available at this stage indicate that a second round of the presidential election will take place on November 1, 2026.
For a president to be elected in the first round, a candidate must receive more than half of all valid votes, and voter turnout must exceed 50% of all eligible voters. Otherwise, a runoff is held within seven days, with the candidate receiving the most votes declared the winner. The president is elected for a five-year term.
A total of 27 presidential and vice-presidential tickets entered the race. Seven were nominated by political parties and coalitions, while the remaining 20 were put forward by initiative committees.

Niki Collier’s photo documentary of Election Day in Dublin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Report
Presidential Election 2026
Niki Collier’s photo documentary of Election Day in Dublin
Sunday 25 October 2026 20:15
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 20:15
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
Six polling stations are available to Bulgarians in Ireland: two in Dublin and one each in Dundalk, Limerick, Cork and Tullamore. Today, Bulgarian-born visual artist and creative professional Dr Niki Collier, who lives and works in Ireland, not only cast her vote but also met, talked to and photographed friends, partners, like-minded people and admirers of her art who had likewise come to the polling station to fulfil their duty to their homeland.
Collier highlights the active role played by young people, the new generation of Bulgarians, some of whom were not even born in Bulgaria but are already helping their parents organise polling stations. Even the youngest, who have not yet turned 18, accompanied their parents to the ballot box to learn an important lesson from them: although all schoolchildren are currently on holiday, civic duty comes first. Exercising one's right as a citizen and casting a vote matter, regardless of how far away from Bulgaria one may be.
PHOTO Niki Collier
Here is a photo documentary of election day in Dublin, sent to us by Niki Collier. It begins with a colourful story that, as she puts it, “sounds a little like a joke, but is true”:
“Two people from the ruling party sit down at a table, and two from the opposition sit opposite them. Two more join them, but they vote for a neutral party. Before long, everyone is talking over one another, each insisting that their position is more right than the others’. A little girl listening to their arguments approaches the oldest parents and asks why they keep telling younger people, who now have children of their own, whom to vote for. The little girl is only two, but she can already see that something is wrong when older people interfere in the choices of the younger generation.”
Niki says similar conversations among relatives take place in many other families, where several generations live under one roof. She introduces us to the people in her photo story.
Alexander Atanasov Chinov
PHOTO Niki Collier
Meet 18-year-old Alexander Atanasov Chinov, who studies international business in Ireland and is the youngest member of an election commission.
“I am glad to be a member of the precinct election commission, and I encourage everyone to vote,” Alexander says, proudly fulfilling this responsibility towards Bulgaria. Before allowing Niki Collier to vote, he carefully checks every digit in her identity documents.
Temenuga Yonkova
PHOTO Niki Collier
This is Temenuga Yonkova, who cast her vote on her 60th birthday. She voted together with her entire family: her husband, Venelin, and her sister Iskra, who had travelled from Varna to celebrate the occasion with her. They are pictured outside the polling station in Santry, Dublin, Ireland.
Temenuga recently served as Ireland's national rapporteur on human trafficking at the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission. As a Bulgarian, she sees these elections as a choice between the past and the future. Her perspective is that of a mother whose children are in their thirties and who hopes for a better future for their generation in Bulgaria.
Simona Sanz
PHOTO Niki Collier
And here is architect Simona Sanz, who is taking the bus to vote because her car is blocked in by a major marathon taking place in Dublin today.
PHOTO Niki Collier
A calm, quiet and sunny day in the Irish capital: unseasonably bright sunshine, but the usual tranquillity. The election commission at the Bulgarian Embassy in Dublin.
Jeylyan
PHOTO Niki Collier
This is Jeylyan, who also lives in Dublin. Today, however, she may not have found a presidential ticket she feels she can trust, and will most likely stay at home.
She is otherwise actively involved in masquerade performances featuring stylised kukeri costumes made from felt by Dr Niki Collier. Here, Jeylyan is wearing the costume of “Freedom”, a fresh interpretation of the traditional kukeri figures.
Polling station in Dundalk, Ireland
PHOTO Niki Collier
And here is the polling station in Dundalk, the place where the group wears Niki's original costumes for Halloween. The group also often hosts lively parties featuring Bulgarian pop music.
Pictured are the polling station commission members: Tanya Panayotova-Harseva, Ivelina Ivanova, Silvana Yordanova, Georgi Dobrev, Aleksandar Shopov, Gergana Pavlova and Diana Pezheva.
Prof. Izabela Naydenova and Dr. Borislav Naydenov
PHOTO Niki Collier
Professor Izabela Naydenova of Dublin University and Dr Borislav Naydenov of Trinity College
Gergana Toromanova Morgan
PHOTO Niki Collier
Dublin-based lawyer Gergana Toromanova Morgan is casting her vote in London, accompanied by her three children. By taking them along, she is setting an example of responsible civic behaviour, demonstrating that one's duty as a citizen remains important even when the family is outside Bulgaria, Niki Collier comments.
This is especially noteworthy given that this is an unusual weekend in Dublin, with a local celebration taking place and the school autumn break beginning, meaning that many people are travelling outside Ireland. Yet the children who have accompanied their Bulgarian parents to vote have already learned an important lesson: civic responsibilities should come before entertainment.
Polling station in Tullamore
PHOTO Niki Collier
And finally, the polling station in the well-known Irish town of Tullamore, whose commission members are Kremena Chinova, Margarita Filipova, Daniela Petkova, Elena Peeva, Dimitar Papukchiev, Dobromir Dobrev and Stoyanka Nikolaeva.

Trump has no designs on taking over Alaska state election, US attorney-general says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:29:49 UTC
04:29:49 KST

Trump has no designs on taking over state elections, says US attorney-general
NEW YORK - The Justice Department’s bid to preemptively block the results of Alaska’s Senate race is not an attempt to give US President Donald Trump control of state elections, US Attorney-General Todd Blanche said on Oct 25.
Blanche’s agency on Oct 23 sued to stop Alaska from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly. But the Justice Department is not setting the stage for overturning an election result if it’s unfavourable to Trump, Blanche said.
“President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape, or form,” Blanche told CNN’s State of the Union programme. “We’re not laying any groundwork for the president to do that.”
Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are preparing for potential federal interference in the Nov 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress, including legal challenges and disputes over voting that could disrupt certification of the results.
In addition to the Alaska lawsuit, the Trump administration has taken other vote-related actions against states, including a lawsuit to stop California from counting certain mail-in ballots and a mostly unsuccessful attempt to force 30 states and the District of Columbia to provide complete voter rolls.
The Alaska action is specific to that state, Blanche said, reiterating the Trump administration’s contention that voters will be “confused” because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names: incumbent US Senator Dan S. Sullivan and challenger Dan J. Sullivan Jr The latter Sullivan is only running “to confuse voters,” Blanche said.
“Never before have opponents gone to such lengths to try to thwart and cheat an election as they’re doing in this case,” Blanche told CNN.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan. His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The lawsuit was filed to give officials “the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law,” Blanche said.
He declined to comment on whether Trump ordered him to file the lawsuit, although the president himself has said he did so. Trump briefly spoke about Alaska again on Oct 25, accusing Democrats of orchestrating Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign.
“They’ve made it very unclear and I think it’s very unfair,” Trump told reporters before boarding a flight to Michigan. “I think it’s illegal because it’s unfair. You want fairness in voting.”
But critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the move as part of a pattern of federal overreach in election oversight.
“The fact that Todd Blanche and the Justice Department are willing to go along with it, they’re willing to put their name on it, is an indication of how far they will go after this election is over to try to challenge the results,” US Senator Adam Schiff, a California Democrat, told NBC’s Meet the Press on Oct 25. Britain will not join Canada’s defence bank, source says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:29:44 CET
04:29:44 KST

Oct 26 (Reuters) - Britain will not join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, in a setback to efforts to create the world’s first global defence bank, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The two countries instead said on Sunday that they would develop a framework for cooperation between their respective defence-funding initiatives, establishing two distinct but complementary institutions to support each other on investment opportunities and strategic challenges.
“We have been working closely to consider how the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) and Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) can best advance our shared objectives. We have agreed to develop a framework of cooperation that works in the interest of both institutions,” the statement said.
The two governments were unable to agree on key issues including the location of the headquarters of a joint institution, the level of joint procurement, lending to members, and the rules around new members joining in the future, a second person said.
The MDM will focus on accelerating defence investment, joint procurement through financing, and bringing together demand across NATO allies to reduce procurement costs, while the DSRB will complement it by supporting investment in defence industries and supply chains, focusing more on single sovereign lending, the person added.
The DSRB has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
There were hopes Britain would reconsider its position under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his team, with the two countries holding talks on the topic recently. Germany had also declined to join.
Britain and Canada said the MDM and DSRB will be designed to work in close partnership, so they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges.
AIMING TO RAISE BILLIONS
The DSRB has been aiming to raise around €100 billion ($112 billion) and use the money to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It will also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers.
So far besides Canada, where the DSRB will be based, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have pledged their support to the bank.
Reuters previously reported that potential member countries had not joined because of concerns including whether the DSRB can offer cheaper financing than highly rated national governments as well as the amount of capital countries would need to commit, the bank’s governance, and overlaps with existing initiatives.
Britain’s Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had recently described the DSRB as a “really interesting and innovative mechanism” and said that he did not see the proposed defence bank and MDM as being in competition.
Britain previously declined to join, citing concerns over value for money. Reuters previously reported that Burnham discussed the DSRB alongside the MDM initiative with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in July and with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden during an August visit to Kyiv.
($1 = 0.8925 euros)

Zelensky undermines Trump more than Iran and Cuba do – Medvedev

Ukraine Retakes Three Villages—Russia Is Already Diverting Marines and Tanks to Stop the Push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:58:17 UTC
20:58:17 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Retakes Three Villages—Russia Is Already Diverting Marines and Tanks to Stop the Push
Ukrainian forces reportedly liberated three settlements near Oleksandrivka and continued pressing Russian positions, prompting Moscow to redirect marine and armored units that had been intended for offensive operations elsewhere, according to an October 25 assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Ukrainian military observer Kostiantyn Mashovets reported that Ukrainian forces retook Perebudova, Komar, and Fedorivka, located east and south of Oleksandrivka.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian troops also advanced from Vesele toward Skudne. Citing Mashovets, ISW assessed that Ukrainian forces likely pushed Russian troops out of a salient northwest of the Fedorivka-Burlatske line.
However, fighting has not ended in the area. Russian forces reportedly still hold positions on the northeastern edge of Perebudova, meaning the situation remains contested despite recent Ukrainian gains.
The counterattacks appear to be forcing Russia to adjust its force deployments.
According to Mashovets, Russian commanders moved elements of the Baltic Fleet’s 120th Naval Infantry Division and the Pacific Fleet’s 40th Separate Naval Infantry Brigade into the Oleksandrivka sector. Those formations are now being used defensively instead of supporting Russian offensive operations toward Huliaipole.
ISW noted that Russian naval infantry units are generally considered among Moscow’s more combat-capable formations and are often deployed to priority sectors.
Elements of both formations had previously fought on the Dobropillia axis before being moved toward Oleksandrivka in March 2026.
Russian commanders have also reportedly transferred elements of the 90th Tank Division into the area. Those units had originally been intended to support Russian operations toward Druzhkivka.
Ukraine has been conducting counterattacks on the Oleksandrivka axis since early February 2026. ISW assesses the effort as part of a broader Ukrainian attempt to disrupt Russian offensive plans rather than simply regain isolated pieces of terrain.
Further Ukrainian advances could threaten the rear of Russian forces pushing west of Huliaipole, potentially complicating Moscow’s broader effort to approach Orikhiv from multiple directions.
Velyka Novosilka also sits near an important road network supporting Russian operations in the area, meaning continued Ukrainian pressure could increasingly disrupt logistics and force Moscow to commit more units simply to hold its existing positions.
ISW described the Ukrainian gains as slow but tactically significant. Their broader impact will depend on whether Ukrainian forces can sustain the advance and how many additional troops Russia is forced to divert from offensive operations elsewhere to contain it.
Earlier, Russian leader Vladimir Putin claimed that Moscow’s forces had captured approximately 6,500 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory and 310 settlements since the beginning of 2026. However, independent battlefield assessments suggest Russia’s actual territorial gains are roughly 45 times smaller than the Kremlin’s claims.

A spokesperson for the London ambulance service said it sent ambulance crews, a clinical team manager, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic practitioner and London’s air ambulance to the scene.
“We treated a child at the scene before taking the patient to a London major trauma centre,” the ambulance spokesperson said.
Anyone with information about the incident has been asked to contact police on 101.

Britain will not join Canada-led defence bank initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
