19:25:45 UTC
04:25:45 KST

Britain will not join Canada-led defence bank initiative
Oct 26 - Britain will not join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, in a setback to efforts to create the world's first global defence bank, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The two countries instead said on Sunday that they would develop a framework for cooperation between their respective defence-funding initiatives, establishing two distinct but complementary institutions to support each other on investment opportunities and strategic challenges.
"We have been working closely to consider how the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) and Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) can best advance our shared objectives. We have agreed to develop a framework of cooperation that works in the interest of both institutions," the statement said.
The two governments were unable to agree on key issues including the location of the headquarters of a joint institution, the level of joint procurement, lending to members, and the rules around new members joining in the future, a second person said.
The MDM will focus on accelerating defence investment, joint procurement through financing, and bringing together demand across NATO allies to reduce procurement costs, while the DSRB will complement it by supporting investment in defence industries and supply chains, focusing more on single sovereign lending, the person added.
The DSRB has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
There were hopes Britain would reconsider its position under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his team, with the two countries holding talks on the topic recently. Germany had also declined to join.
Britain and Canada said the MDM and DSRB will be designed to work in close partnership, so they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges.
AIMING TO RAISE BILLIONS
The DSRB has been aiming to raise around €100 billion ($112 billion) and use the money to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It will also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers.
So far besides Canada, where the DSRB will be based, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have pledged their support to the bank.
Reuters previously reported that potential member countries had not joined because of concerns including whether the DSRB can offer cheaper financing than highly rated national governments as well as the amount of capital countries would need to commit, the bank's governance, and overlaps with existing initiatives.
Britain's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had recently described the DSRB as a "really interesting and innovative mechanism" and said that he did not see the proposed defence bank and MDM as being in competition.
Britain previously declined to join, citing concerns over value for money. Reuters previously reported that Burnham discussed the DSRB alongside the MDM initiative with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in July and with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden during an August visit to Kyiv. Iran has never left the negotiating table, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Sunday, accusing the US of insisting on unilateral demands and attempting to impose them.

Israel must choose national unity over political division - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:23:19 UTC
04:23:19 KST

The latest polls leave little room for doubt: Israel is heading toward a political deadlock more complex than ever before. Current projections suggest that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot can secure a stable coalition with a majority of 61 MKs.
The current political reality suggests that there is no realistic prospect of forming a government without relying on the Arab parties, a scenario that faces mutual boycotts and offers little prospect of governmental stability.
In these circumstances, Israeli society faces two options: another descent into a cycle of recurring political crises, which tore the country apart and deepened internal divisions between 2019 and 2022, or the courageous and pragmatic choice of establishing a broad national unity government.
The advantage of a unity government
Israel’s history demonstrates that in times of national emergency, a unity government is not an undesirable compromise but the most appropriate response to the challenges of the moment. The clearest example is the national unity government formed in 1984 between the Alignment, led by Shimon Peres, and Likud, led by Yitzhak Shamir.
At the time, Israel’s economy was on the verge of total collapse, with inflation soaring into the hundreds of percent. It was precisely this broad political partnership that made it possible to implement the dramatic economic stabilization plan that rescued the economy and steered Israel toward safer waters. The strength of such unity lies in its ability to make difficult and painful decisions while securing broad public legitimacy.
Beyond the urgent economic and security challenges, Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas continue to pose serious security challenges and even existential threats to the Jewish state.
A national unity government formed after the 2026 election would therefore faithfully represent the mainstream of Israeli society. It would comprise the major Zionist parties while keeping extremist elements on both the Right and the Left outside the government, forces whose divisive rhetoric has fueled social fractures in recent years.
Moreover, such a moderate and balanced government, built on broad agreement across most of Israeli society, would be welcomed and highly regarded internationally. It would help restore Israel’s international standing and diplomatic relations at a critical juncture in global affairs.
Israel’s recent experience further reinforces the conclusion that there is no viable alternative. We saw this during the global COVID-19 crisis, when an emergency government was formed, and again in the immediate aftermath of the national catastrophe of the October 7 massacre.
The remarkable resilience of Israeli society and the mobilization of hundreds of thousands of citizens on the front lines and at home demonstrated beyond doubt that the country’s strength lies in its unity.
The difficulties of a unity government
Admittedly, this would be a complex undertaking, likely to generate difficulties and disagreements, as previous national unity governments throughout Israel’s political history clearly demonstrate. History remembers the so-called dirty trick orchestrated by the Labor Party under Peres in 1990 to bring down the national unity government led by Shamir, amid claims that Likud was unwilling to advance the peace process.
Nor must we look far into the past: The collapse of the Netanyahu-Gantz government at the end of 2020 remains a fresh and painful memory. Yet given Israel’s current circumstances, with the country still grappling with a prolonged internal crisis alongside external threats to its very existence, there appears to be no alternative.
In conclusion, the time has come to choose unity over division. Israel’s leaders must rise to the occasion and put personal grievances and narrow political interests aside. This complex task will fall to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, who has repeatedly demonstrated that he is the right person to lead efforts at national reconciliation.
Herzog must use the full weight of his public standing to help establish a stable national unity government. We can only hope and pray that he will do so, and that Israeli democracy will choose partnership, healing, and unity for the sake of future generations. Whatever the election results may be, this is the time for national unity!
The writer is a lecturer and research fellow at the University of South Wales in the United Kingdom. He is the author of Collapse: The Israeli Labor Party, 1992-2024.

Tel Aviv rivals run riot as Maccabi, Hapoel cruise to emphatic Premier League wins

Hapoel Tel Aviv cruised to a 3-0 victory over Hapoel Jerusalem at Teddy Stadium, while Maccabi Tel Aviv overwhelmed Hapoel Haifa 6-2 as the two Tel Aviv sides enjoyed convincing victories in the latest round of Israeli Premier League action.
With 7,000 Hapoel Tel Aviv supporters in attendance at Teddy Stadium, Daniel Dappa opened the scoring just before halftime, collecting a superb through ball from Douglas Owusu before dribbling past a defender inside the box and unleashing a powerful strike into the net.
The visitors doubled their advantage in the 53rd minute when Omri Altman finished off a magnificent backheel from Yannick Leliendal. Less than 10 minutes later, substitute Roie Alkukin tapped home a terrific Leliendal cross to complete the scoring and secure all three points for the Reds.
Hapoel Tel Aviv coach Elyaniv Barda acknowledged that his side had struggled early on before finding its rhythm after the break.
“We weren’t good enough in the first half and didn’t control the tempo enough,” Barda said. “We struggled until we made adjustments at halftime, and bringing on Roie Alkukin also helped us. The second and third goals came from excellent attacking moves involving plenty of passing and movement. They were incredible attacking sequences.”
Hapoel Jerusalem coach laments team's shortcomings
Hapoel Jerusalem coach Lior Zada lamented his team’s defensive shortcomings, particularly the goal conceded just before halftime.
“We had some good spells in the first half and played well, controlling the tempo of the game. But then we conceded a very soft goal at the end of the half,” Zada said. “It was a tough game, but we need to work hard to get results. We’re conceding too many goals, although we’re also playing many of our games against top teams with a lot of quality.”
Maccabi Tel Aviv delivered an even more emphatic performance, defeating Hapoel Haifa 6-2 as Ali Camara scored twice in the second half to help the yellow-and-blue pull away.
Elad Madmon gave Maccabi the lead from inside the box off an assist from Noam Ben Harush, but Arial Mendy equalized for Hapoel Haifa in the 38th minute to send the teams into halftime level at 1-1.
Camara restored Maccabi’s advantage with a header from a corner kick, and Dor Peretz extended the lead to 3-1 in the 58th minute. Sagiv Yehezkel added another shortly afterward, before Alon Turgeman pulled one back for the visitors in the 72nd minute.
However, Camara struck again to complete his brace, and Itamar Noy added a sixth goal from inside the box to cap a dominant performance.
Maccabi Tel Aviv coach Kenny Miller was pleased with the attacking display but insisted his team still had work to do.
“We scored a lot of goals and we had plenty of chances even before we started scoring,” Miller said. “There are a lot of things I’m happy with and a lot of things I’m not. We can’t give the opposition hope at any stage of the game. I’m very pleased with the result. We scored goals, but there’s still plenty of room for improvement.”
Hapoel Haifa coach Haim Silvas said his team struggled to recover after conceding from a set piece in the second half.
“We came into the game determined to show that we’re a good team,” Silvas said. “In the second half, we conceded from a set piece and then there was a kind of collapse. The game opened up and Maccabi Tel Aviv raised the tempo. We were still stunned by the goal and they scored another. From that point on, the hole was too deep to climb out of.”
Elsewhere, Bnei Sakhnin edged Kiryat Shmona 1-0, with Sana Gomes scoring the decisive goal in the 40th minute to secure all three points.
Sakhnin coach satisfied with win
Sakhnin coach Yossi Abukasis was satisfied with the result, even if he felt his team could have won by a greater margin.
“We’ll remain humble. I don’t think this was a great football performance from us, but we created a lot of chances,” Abukasis said. “We had four or five clear-cut opportunities that should have resulted in goals. We could have put the game away much earlier, but we’re happy with the win. It’s very important.”
Kiryat Shmona coach Shai Barda was left frustrated by another disappointing result, with his team having collected just three points from its first eight games.
“We’ve only collected three points from 24, and that’s a fact. This is unequivocally not where we expected to be,” Barda said. “Right now, we’re struggling with a lack of confidence, and the losses are making it difficult to turn things around.”
Ironi Tiberias and Maccabi Netanya shared the points in a dramatic 1-1 draw, as Bar Cohen scored in the 92nd minute to rescue the hosts after Oz Bilu had put the visitors ahead in the first half.
Netanya coach Roni Levy was furious that his side had surrendered its advantage in stoppage time.
“It’s frustrating not to score, but we shouldn’t be conceding in stoppage time,” Levy said. “That’s irresponsible and says a lot about the state of our team. Our mentality probably isn’t good enough, because with the right mentality in a game like this, you win 4-0 comfortably. We didn’t do that and we paid the price.”
Tiberias coach Alon Ziv said his team had overcome a difficult start to earn a valuable point.
“We were about to make a switch in the middle of the match as we started off really poorly,” Ziv said. “We gave up a goal at the end of the half which could have really broken us, but we were able to come back and play well and take a point.”
Maccabi Petah Tikva also picked up a valuable victory, beating Hapoel Ramat Gan 2-1 thanks to a first-half brace from Jose Cortes.
Luan Campos pulled a goal back for the hosts after the break, but Ziv Arie’s side held on to claim all three points and end a five-game losing streak.
Petah Tikva coach Arie welcomed the result after a difficult run of form.
“We’ll take every win we can get. We started well and the first half was very good,” Arie said. “We wanted to win so badly that we weren’t calm enough on the ball. We didn’t play the way we wanted to in the second half, but after five losses, some of them bizarre, we’ll take the win and won’t complain about anything.”
Ramat Gan coach Masai Dego was disappointed with his team’s first-half performance, despite a stronger showing after the interval.
“Ultimately, we can’t perform the way we did in the first half,” Dego said. “We responded well after the break and we shouldn’t have fallen apart. We restored some of our pride and could even have equalized, but it’s a tough defeat.”

Gazans should be sent to emigrate to France or other countries in Europe so that Israel can “conquer the whole territory” of the Gaza Strip, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told The Jerusalem Post in a recent interview, arguing that he supported US President Donald Trump’s plan to relocate Palestinians there.
“If you ask me what should be done in Gaza, we should conquer the entire territory. All of it. It is our land, the Jewish people’s land. And we should encourage emigration,” Ben-Gvir told the Post.
In February 2025, Trump proposed relocating approximately two million Gazans as part of an emigration plan, though the proposal has since stalled.
Amid the current protests in France, Ben-Gvir has recently shared AI-generated videos depicting Gazans being transported to Paris by the far-right minister himself.
“This is a very good plan proposed by Donald Trump: encouraging emigration. Many of them could go to better places,” Ben-Gvir said, arguing they would receive good conditions in Europe.
“There are more attractive places, places looking for workers, and places where they could live more comfortably,” he said.
“Why not send them to France, for example? Give them good conditions in other countries, perhaps Britain, London, or places like that,” the minister added.
Polling projects Ben-Gvir's party to win roughly eight seats in next Knesset
Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit party has been a key member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition.
Recent polling projects Otzma Yehudit to win about eight seats in the next Knesset. Ben-Gvir has announced that he will demand the defense portfolio in the next government.
When asked what he thought about Palestinians who would object to leaving the Gaza Strip, arguing that it was their home and refusing to move even under good conditions, Ben-Gvir referenced the October 7 Hamas massacre in 2023.
“Someone whose home it is does not start a war and massacre children. Someone whose home it is does not rape women. Someone whose home it is does not burn babies. Once they did those things, they lost the legitimacy of making that argument,” the minister said.
“You cannot make that argument and say it was just one, two, or three people, or that it was only a small number. There were many, many, many, many [Palestinians] involved,” he added.
“And there were also people we describe as uninvolved civilians who tortured our male and female hostages.”
“This has to stop. This cannot continue. I believe that someone who says and does these things, someone who inflicts this kind of harm, cannot claim that this is their home. People do not behave like that in their own home,” Ben-Gvir added.
Ben-Gvir advocated for 'bombing Gaza' before October 7 attacks
The far Right minister repeatedly opposed hostage-ceasefire deals throughout the Israel-Hamas War, advocating for continued military action rather than an agreement.
When asked whether he regretted his stance, Ben-Gvir did not answer directly, instead arguing that the cabinet should have listened to him more before October 7. He also said that Netanyahu bore responsibility for the October 7 attacks.
“Before October 7, when I was going to cabinet meetings, I kept saying, ‘Let’s bomb Gaza. Let’s carry out targeted killings,’” he said.
“Imagine if they had listened to me on this ... it’s a great shame,” he added.
Ben-Gvir, whose views are often characterized as extreme, has been criticized for rhetoric that opponents say has contributed to the deterioration of Israel’s international image. He has also faced criticism over rising crime rates, particularly in the Arab sector, during the government’s term.
Regarding the rise in crime in the Arab sector, Ben-Gvir argued that a main factor behind the increase was restrictions imposed on him by Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara.
According to Ben-Gvir, early on, he wanted to introduce spyware into homes in Arab communities to allow police to listen in on conversations.
When asked about criticism that doing so would infringe on the right to privacy, Ben-Gvir claimed that such measures were permissible in some cases.
“There are cases where it is permissible to infringe on privacy, when we’re talking about murderers. In the end, murderers also kill children, including young children, so this is a very good thing.”
Ben-Gvir praises his work as National Security Minister
Ben-Gvir also said he had been unable to secure the budget for certain technological advancements, and that crime rates had lowered after some budgets were approved.
He argued that the police have been doing well, praising officers for their work.
“We have excellent police officers and female officers who are fighting on the front lines. They are entering these communities, exercising force, and establishing governance, and I am very proud of them.”
“Are they lacking intelligence capabilities? Yes, that’s true,” he added.
Ben-Gvir called on the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) to become more involved in police work, arguing that the agency has the technology to enhance the police’s capabilities.
When asked whether he was concerned about the damage to Israel’s international standing that critics say has already occurred and warn could worsen, Ben-Gvir answered that Israel’s image abroad mattered to him, but that he would not “endanger the lives of soldiers” for it.
“I will not endanger the lives of combatants, soldiers, or civilians here just because I want Israel to look good in the eyes of the world,” he said.

Details

Russia’s return to international sport

Serbia voter turnout highest in decades as students oppose longtime leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:19:54 UTC
04:19:54 KST

Serbia’s Vucic concedes election defeat to student-led movement
Vucic says the opposition Student List is projected to win a parliamentary majority after nearly two years of protests.
Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic has conceded defeat to a student-led movement in the country’s snap parliamentary election, saying the opposition group is set to secure a majority of seats.
Vucic said on Sunday that, based on a sample of votes, the Student List was expected to win between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 105 for his electoral list.
While stating that final results were not yet available, the populist leader said, “It is clear that we have lost these elections.”
His announcement was greeted with cheers, euphoria and tears at the Student List headquarters, according to the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency.
“Preliminary results show that students are convincingly leading in almost all polling stations,” Radomir Saicic, a parliamentary candidate for the Students’ List, said in a speech at the movement’s election headquarters.
“Students won, and with them also a hope that Serbia can be a country of justice, freedom and dignity,” he added. “Let this night be the beginning of a new chapter.”
Voting to determine whether Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has governed since 2012, could retain power against a movement born from nationwide anticorruption protests, ended at 8pm local time (19:00 GMT) on Sunday.
The State Election Commission said that by 6pm (17:00 GMT), voter turnout had reached 64.9 percent, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.
University of Belgrade researcher Jelena Vasiljevic told Al Jazeera in an interview published on Friday that the SNS had a reliable voter base, while the students needed to attract people who normally did not vote.
Sunday’s voting was also marred by reports of intimidation and procedural problems.
The Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA), an independent election watchdog, said its observers recorded pressure on voters or election workers at almost a third of the 500 polling stations it monitored.
It also reported failures to protect ballot secrecy.
By 5pm (16:00 GMT), the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy (CeSID), an election-monitoring group, had received about 260 reports of potential irregularities, including ballot photography, group voting and difficulties with identification checks.
Serbians celebrate
Celebrations erupted across Serbia, with fireworks lighting the sky almost immediately after Vucic’s announcement conceding defeat. Tens of thousands crowded Belgrade’s main roads as supporters of the Student List drove around in cars, honking their horns.
Serbians chanted, “Aleksandar is gone”, and sang the student movement’s songs. Crowds dismantled tents set up at a park in central Belgrade, where Vucic’s loyalists had been camping for more than a year.
“It means freedom from a dictatorship that has lasted for 12 years, that I cannot remember a time before,” voter Jana Vasic told Al Jazeera. “I’m not completely sure what our candidates will do first, but I think first for tonight, we’ll celebrate. And then tomorrow, the real hard work starts.”
Belgrade resident Dragana Kovecevic told the Associated Press news agency that she was thrilled that “everyone greets with smiles”. She added: “We are all too happy; finally, we are becoming one normal and free country.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated the Student List on its election victory, writing on X: “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.”
Pressure from student-led movement
In Belgrade, as the election took place, police wearing riot helmets and carrying shields were deployed near the election commission’s headquarters, where roads were closed and barricades erected.
City prosecutors appealed on Sunday for everyone involved in the election to avoid violence.
The election follows nearly two years of student-led protests that began after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people.
Demands for accountability widened into a movement against alleged government corruption and repression. Vucic and the SNS deny the accusations.
The Student List – Students Win, which emerged from demonstrations, fielded candidates drawn from professions including medicine and education, many of whom have no political experience.
The movement campaigned for stronger institutions and an end to corruption.
Some established opposition parties backed the students rather than fielding their own candidates.
Vucic resigned as president in September to run for prime minister, promising higher pensions, public-sector wages and investment.
Supporters credit his leadership with modernising Serbia’s economy.
About 6.5 million people were eligible to vote for 250 parliamentary seats, with 18 electoral lists competing. A majority of 126 seats is needed to form government.

WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump can’t shake the furore over Jeffrey Epstein.
Democrats are preparing to launch congressional investigations into the administration’s handling of files related to the late, disgraced sex offender if they regain power after the Nov 3 midterm elections. They say the administration botched the release of documents and are using the issue to hammer Trump and GOP lawmakers in key races.
“The Epstein investigation is going to be one of our top priorities,” Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said in an interview, alongside probes into the Trump family’s business dealings, allegations of corporate corruption and the president’s immigration crackdown.
“The country wants disclosure, they want release of the files and they want justice for the survivors,” Garcia said.
For Trump, it’s a full-circle moment. The president in 2024 indicated a willingness to release files pertaining to investigations into Epstein. But in office, after releasing several tranches that failed to satisfy lawmakers and many Epstein victims, Trump urged the public and Congress to move on from what he called a “hoax.”
The midterms in 2026 have made clear that many are not ready to move on. With Trump and his party fighting an uphill battle to keep control of Congress, the lingering tumult over Epstein’s crimes has added to the GOP’s electoral woes and underscored how difficult it has been for the president to put the issue to rest.
Polls show Democrats poised to obtain a majority in the House and they have made it clear they intend to open fresh investigations into Epstein’s actions, Trump’s ties to him and the government’s handling of the files.
Any probe would ripple well beyond Washington, with Wall Street and corporate America already bracing for a wave of Democratic investigations. Garcia said major banks that had ties to Epstein’s financial dealings are among those who could be called to testify.
A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the administration was focused on the upcoming midterms and declined to detail any preparations for potential House probes. The administration has nothing to hide on the Epstein case, the official said.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Trump had “been totally exonerated on anything related to Epstein” and through disclosures of files “done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”
Campaign cudgel
Democrats are not waiting until they regain power to put the spotlight back on Epstein.
In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico sought to counter September’s Republican midterm convention by holding an event with an Epstein survivor and demanding that all of the files be released. In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff has criticised how Republicans handled the release of the documents.
And it’s not just the candidates who have kept Epstein hovering over the midterms. At a Trump rally in October, a woman wearing a T-shirt that read “Release the Epstein Files” was physically accosted by supporters of the president and removed from the arena by security. Vice-President J.D. Vance was interrupted by a protester calling for the release of the files at a North Carolina rally on Oct 26.
The Epstein files have long been the centre of speculation over the late financier’s wealthy and powerful contacts and any connections they may have had to his conduct.
“The Epstein issue blows up into a larger narrative of how Republicans were helping their donors, the billionaires, the wealthiest and most well-connected people at the expense of working-class people,” said Neera Tanden, a longtime Democratic operative who leads the Center for American Progress.
Epstein and allegations of child sexual abuse have been a particular lightning rod for elements of Trump’s own base. Some of his supporters helped stoke the so-called Pizzagate conspiracy that sought to link Hillary Clinton to a fictitious cabal of child sex traffickers.
Following his campaign pledge, Trump’s administration released some of the Epstein files a month into his presidency to cheers from right-wing supporters, but many of those documents had been previously released. Subsequent releases were messy, including efforts to redact Trump’s own name from files.
As the controversy dragged on Trump bristled at continued questions from reporters about Epstein.
Trump, who shared a friendship with Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, has repeatedly said he cut ties with him almost two decades ago before his crimes came to attention. Epstein was arrested in 2019 on federal charges that he engaged in sex trafficking of minors. He died in jail by suicide, according to the authorities.
‘Real accountability’
Garcia said Democrats have a two-pronged goal of releasing more files and investigating some of those named in previously disclosed documents.
“There has to be real accountability there. And there has to be real investigation,” he said. “This is one of the most bipartisan issues in the country. People are interested in this topic, people ask about it all the time.”
While current House Oversight Chairman James Comer, a Republican, has investigated the Epstein case to a degree, including through subpoenas and depositions, Democrats say he hasn’t done enough to obtain testimony under oath from key figures.
“People are angry,” Garcia said. “The president made promises, and he went back on them.”
A House Oversight Committee spokeswoman said every witness in the panel’s investigation was required to “verbally acknowledge that they understand their obligation to tell the truth.”
In a statement, the spokeswoman touted the committee’s work, which she said included 19 witness interviews and depositions, releasing approximately 65,000 pages of documents and uncovering allegations of sexual misconduct that were referred to the Department of Justice.
Garcia has called previously for Attorney-General Todd Blanche to testify. When asked about a potential subpoena, Garcia said all options were on the table.
Blanche, who previously served as Trump’s personal attorney, handled the initial release of files and met with Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted for helping Epstein traffic women and girls for sex. Democrats strongly opposed his confirmation, citing among other matters his handling of the Epstein matter.
A Justice Department spokesperson referred inquiries to Blanche’s previous remarks and said the attorney-general will follow the law.
Blanche acknowledged “we made mistakes and I’ve owned up to those mistakes,” such as failing to properly redact documents, in a recent interview with the “Pod Force One” podcast. But he said those actions had been corrected, and defended Trump.
“I can tell you that President Trump, from Day One, said ‘Release as many of the files, I want everything released’,” Blanche said. BLOOMBERG

"Everyone in France agrees with us", Le Pen claimed.
She vowed to preserve France's cultural identity, from its language and traditions to its values and way of life, drawing cheers from supporters waving French flags.
'The rule of law is not the law against the state'
Among her priorities, should she win in May 2027, Le Pen is promising what she calls more security for French citizens. She denounced what she sees as the failings of the justice system under Emmanuel Macron, which she considers far too lax.
"Who can claim there is a rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings, or carry out real raids in front of law-enforcement officers who have been deliberately disarmed, both materially and morally?" she said, referring to the looting and clashes of 17 October on the fringes of protests over the rising cost of living.
"The rule of law is not the law against the state," Marine Le Pen went on, promising "certainty" that cases will be brought and sentences carried out, as well as the expulsion of foreign offenders.
Defending her sovereigntist line, Marine Le Pen also argued for "national priority", saying she wanted to restore "a double border: French and European".
On the international front, without explicitly mentioning Ukraine, she vowed that France "will not send" its young people "to die in reckless or irresponsible military adventures, and even less in wars that are not ours".
Jordan Bardella blames LFI for 'fanning the flames of insurrection'
Leading up to Marine Le Pen's speech, in which she wanted to "rise above the fray", The National Rally's president, Jordan Bardella, introduced her on stage, openly attacking the government and revisiting the week's explosive news.
"The French have seen a power that has fallen, that has given up, that has abdicated even the idea of protecting our compatriots," he said, condemning the violence that broke out on the sidelines of the social movement.
According to the RN president, his party "has appeared as the only option capable of restoring order and bringing back authority". As the crowd gathered at the Orléans convention centre chanted "Macron, resign", he replied: "Don't worry, he won't be long before he is going, it's planned and it's coming soon".
Jordan Bardella also took aim at La France Insoumise (France Unbowed), or LFI, and the party's leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who backs the high school students' movement and the social mobilisation generally, accusing the hard-left party of "fanning the flames of insurrection", which in his view disqualifies LFI "from aspiring to the highest offices of the state".
Start of Jordan Bardella's speech disrupted
His speech was briefly interrupted by members of a Jewish student union who unfurled a banner referencing a French media report alleging he had deleted antisemitic messages from an old Facebook account.

This protest referred to Mediapart revelations concerning antisemitic messages attributed to Jordan Bardella when he was 18. He rejects the accusations.
Le Pen on the campaign trail, Bardella in charge of the party
The Orléans rally took place the day after the National Rally congress, held under heavy police protection, at which Jordan Bardella was confirmed as party leader.

For a time he had been tipped to run for the French presidency himself, if Marine Le Pen's conviction in the case of misuse of funds for European parliamentary assistants had prevented her from standing.
His re-election formalises the division of roles within the duo presented to voters as a "winning ticket": Marine Le Pen will run for office as president of the republic, while Jordan Bardella, strengthened at the helm of the RN, is positioning himself to become her prime minister in the event of victory.
She reiterated this in her speech on Sunday: she wants to form a “national unity” government led by Jordan Bardella.
Another takeaway from the congress: Marine Le Pen has given up chairing the RN group in the National Assembly, in order to focus on the presidential campaign. MP Sébastien Chenu, one of her close allies, is taking over the role.

'Some would have preferred you not to come'
"Some would have preferred you not to come," Marine Le Pen wrote on X, addressing her supporters, while welcoming the atmosphere at the Zénith Centre in Orléans.

Details

I think we are very close to finally reaching an agreement on this issue
The U.S. is removing some tariffs

Trade disputes between the countries intensified after the failure of negotiations in August, when the United States and Canada imposed a number of reciprocal restrictions.

Federal and state security forces remain deployed across the country to oversee voting operations and maintain public order until polls close.

James Tasamba
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Gabonese authorities lifted the ban on social media networks in the central African country after eight months, according to a Saturday statement by the regulator.
The High Authority for Communication (HAC) imposed the ban on major social media platforms, including WhatsApp, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram in February, citing online abuse, a move that sparked widespread condemnation.
The regulator blamed content posted online of undermining national security and social cohesion. It accused internet users of disseminating defamatory, hateful, false and insulting content via social media platforms.
“The HAC has decided to lift the suspension of social media platforms,” spokesman Jean Claude Mendome said in the statement. The suspension aimed to “allow the government to adapt its legal framework to better regulate social media,” he added.
The ban, which was announced amid anti-government protests over the high cost of living, came under criticism from activists who described it as an attack on internet freedom.
To get around the restriction, thousands of citizens are said to have turned to virtual private networks, or VPNs.
Mendome said lifting the ban followed direct discussions with major international technology companies on mechanisms to improve moderation on the platforms.
HAC urged users to be “more responsible and mature in their online exchanges and behaviors, in order to contribute to a healthier, more constructive digital environment that is more respectful of the rights of others.”
A new regulation passed in February requires social media users to provide verified names, addresses and ID numbers.
The Central African country of Gabon is ruled by Gen. Brice Oligui Nguema, who seized power in a 2023 coup that ended 55 years of rule by the Bongo family. He won a presidential election last April, but faced a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election.

The mystery of a skeleton found more than 200 years ago has been solved at Westminster Abbey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:05:57 EET
04:05:57 KST

The mystery of a skeleton found more than 200 years ago has been solved at Westminster Abbey
Kyiv • UNN
Radiocarbon analysis showed that the remains in the Roman sarcophagus date from 987–1052. The likely people buried there are two abbots.
British archaeologists have determined who the human remains found in an ancient Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey in 1820 may have belonged to. Researchers suggest that one of the monastery's abbots, who lived about 1,000 years ago, may have been buried there. Taylor & Francis reports this, citing new archaeological research, writes UNN.
Details
The name Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy resident of Roman Britain who lived in the 4th century, is engraved on the sarcophagus. However, radiocarbon analysis showed that the person whose bones were found inside died much later—in the period between 987 and 1052.
Archaeologist Warwick Rodwell suggests that the remains may belong to Abbot Ælfwig, who died around 1020, or his successor Wulfnoth, who died in 1049.
What else the researchers discovered
Analysis of the bones showed that the person buried was a man aged between 35 and 49, approximately 175 cm tall.
Archaeologists also discovered a Latin cross dating from the 10th–11th centuries on the sarcophagus lid. This supports the hypothesis that the ancient Roman stone coffin was reused for a medieval burial.
In addition, traces of lime and a rectangular structure were found inside the sarcophagus. According to the researchers, these may have been the remains of a wooden coffin that had completely disintegrated over several centuries.
The identity of the person buried has not yet been established conclusively, but scientists have narrowed the list of possible candidates to two historical figures.

NEW DELHI: Even as the Centre moots directly elected mayors with a fixed five-year tenure and a mayor-in-council system, municipal heads from different cities at National Urban Conclave flagged that the move would serve little purpose without giving mayors adequate powers. Rajkot mayor Nehal Shukla also called for time-bound financial audits of civic bodies, saying that “no municipal body can function without financial irregularities”.Participating in a discussion on proposed changes to the Model Municipal Law, Shukla said mayors in municipal governance were like governors, while standing committees wielded financial powers and executive officials remained under the control of state govts.“Wherever we have directly elected mayors, we must have a mayor-in-council. If you don’t give power to the mayor, direct election hardly serves any objective,” he said.Under the mayor-in-Council system, executive powers to run a city on a day-to-day basis are shared between the mayor and a small, cabinet-like group of elected councillors, who are individually accountable for their respective portfolios.Shukla also suggested that municipal elections be conducted by the Election Commission, citing its track record of holding timely general and assembly elections.
He said state govts invariably found one reason or another to delay municipal polls.“The biggest missing thing that needs to be fixed is timely audits to bring financial discipline. Audit reports are delayed by six to eight years, and that’s why irregularities do not come to light. We all know that no municipal body can function without financial irregularities,” he said.Shukla pointed out that rules require tenders to be floated for works or services costing more than Rs 5 lakh, but alleged that this was often not followed. Municipal commissioners, he said, were aware of such violations but approved the transactions because otherwise civic bodies could not function.He suggested that audits be conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). If state auditors continued to conduct them, he said, the law should ensure that the audit backlog did not exceed two years.
Bhubaneswar mayor Sulochana Das, who also participated in the discussion, said municipal laws were robust on paper, but the ground reality was different.“People have more expectations from directly elected mayors. But we have no power. Executive officers such as municipal commissioners are beyond the control of mayors, as we cannot write their annual performance reports or have any say in their appointments. Commissioners change frequently,” she said.

Ukraine war latest: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms

- Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
- Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
- Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
- In less than 24 hours, Russia hits 4 hypermarkets belonging to one of Ukraine's largest retail chains
- Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Starlink and Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, was working at full speed as of the morning of Oct. 24, after it had previously been limited to 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour).
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelensky said. "I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped us. I thank members of Congress, senators, all the media, the State Department, and the President."
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again.
"We record a speed of more than 400 kilometers per hour, the connection is stable," the ministry said.
The ministry continues to monitor and record the work of Starlink and Starshield, according to Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
"This is another example of direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yielding results. And this result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," the ministry added.
Musk later said that Ukraine's military violated the terms of service for Starlink, adding that the "loophole" has now been closed.
Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," he said in a post to X.
"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is not a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk said.
He also claimed that SpaceX has done more than any other company to help Ukraine in its fight against Russia's war.
Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko denied that Ukraine violated Starlink's terms of service.
"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true. In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians," he said in a post to X.
"But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work," Sternenko added.
Using Starlink for drone missions has been "technically impossible" since all drone campaigns that require satellite communications would only work with the military Starshield service, he said.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov also denied Musk's claims, saying that all Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers an hour and do not work on Russian territory.
"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said in a post to Facebook. "It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

Russian attacks killed eight people and injured 51 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 24-25.

Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
The Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day, Russian President Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on Oct. 25.
The statement follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's Oct. 23 remarks that a new round of trilateral talks is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
"The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," Ushakov said.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals, demanding instead that Kyiv cede the only partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Such a concession would give Moscow territory that Russian forces have been unable to capture on the battlefield. Ukraine, in contrast, has agreed to multiple ceasefire proposals put forward by the U.S.
Ushakov said he did not expect the first trilateral meeting after the pause to yield significant results, calling it a "trial run." A peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine "still needs work," he added.
On Oct. 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The following day, Witkoff held a three-hour meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, after which the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks in November.
Witkoff said on Oct. 21 that discussions among Ukrainian, U.S., and Russian representatives would "continue at the technical level."
Putin has long avoided meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief is reportedly seeking a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace deal without Ukraine's participation.
In recent weeks, Trump has also lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that ultimately failed, threatened to cut off intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, and eased sanctions on Russian oil exports.
Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to take part in peace negotiations with Kyiv.

Emirati diplomat who helped deliver aid to Gaza enters UN secretary general race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:00:10 UTC
04:00:10 KST

An Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN helped secure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza has entered the race as a late contender to succeed António Guterres as the world body’s secretary general.
Lana Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, is widely noted for her advocacy of the Palestinian cause and the two-state solution and has won the endorsement of the state of Palestine.
She is however facing criticism over the UAE’s contested role in arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, a group that has been accused of genocide by two successive US administrations.
Nusseibeh, 48, has been one of the leading UAE diplomats denying reports that the UAE supplied weapons to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo in defiance of a UN arms sales ban.
A grouping of Latin American and Caribbean states, CELAC, has also sent a letter of objection to the security council, claiming her late entry came just as a consensus was emerging behind their region holding the UN top job.
Nusseibeh, who was educated at Cambridge University, was born in 1978 in Abu Dhabi, where her father, Zaki, had emigrated after the Arab-Israeli 1967 war made it difficult for him to return to his birthplace, Jerusalem.
She is the niece of Sari Nusseibeh, a distinguished Palestinian intellectual and author of a widely admired book on Palestine, Once Upon a Country.
She has justified her late – but widely predicted – entry into the race on the grounds that the UN security council appears to be close to deadlock on the six remaining candidates in the race, with no one as yet able to establish a clear lead after six rounds of voting, the latest on 16 October.
The latest straw poll – the first in which it was revealed whether any of the five permanent members of the 15-strong UN security council objected to a candidate – ended with Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica holding the lead spot.
But Grynspan faced objections from two unidentified permanent security council members, making it harder for her to claim she is a breakaway consensus candidate. She has support from nine security council members and objections from five. Guterres is due to stand down at the end of the year
Other candidates include: the Argentine diplomat Rafael Grossi; the UN envoy from Guyana, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Olara Otunnu, a distinguished veteran Ugandan diplomat; and Ecuador’s former foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa. Two previously declared candidates have pulled out.
In her vision statement, Nusseibeh said: “At the heart of the UN sits a wager: that states will give up a little today to gain a great deal together over time.
“States have not stopped needing to partner with one another, but they no longer trust that cooperation will yield sufficient returns. Rebuilding that trust, with faster, more certain, and more realistic results, is the work of the UN.”
Brett McGurk, who served in the Biden administration as a top national security adviser, backed Nusseibeh for her work on Gaza.
“How did UAE become the largest global provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to UN data? Because of Lana Nussaibeh – a diplomat who knows everyone and works with them … she would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said.
Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat who heads Donald Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace, said Nusseibeh “has always understood that the UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build”.
He added: “In the Security Council [as UAE representative] she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism. She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN secretariat.”
But there is a fierce backlash from human rights activists who point to the UAE’s domestic human rights record and its alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan, the group responsible for killing thousands, including in the capture of El Fasher in October last year.
A January 2024 report by the UN panel of experts described allegations from sources in Chad and Darfur – including those of arms being smuggled into the RSF from the UAE – as credible.
One of the strongest attacks on Nusseibeh’s candidacy has been mounted by Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, over her denials of UAE provision of any “military, logistical, financial or political support to any faction in Sudan”. The UAE says it supports the formation of a civilian-led government in Sudan.

He noted that when it comes to ending the war, “there is a specific procedure for lifting sanctions.”
The president stressed that restrictions on Russia were imposed precisely because of its aggression—the crossing of Ukrainian borders, the illegal occupation, and the killings—and that lifting sanctions before the war has actually ended is very dangerous.
“I have a feeling—and I’ve lived with it long enough—that when we talk about Russia’s loyalty, we shouldn’t buy it at such a price. In my view, if we remain without sanctions and within the trilateral format, we could end up in a situation where nothing is clear—what happens next? And the sanctions have already been lifted. Who will have the strength—the kind we had at the start of the war—to reimpose all of them, to rally people in such a way that there would be 20 or more sanctions packages around the world? That is why I approach this with great caution,” the Ukrainian president noted.
At the same time, he once again assured that he is ready to participate in a trilateral meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia. Zelensky did not rule out that it could take place in Florida during the G20 summit.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky assured that he would attend the G20 summit in Florida if there were an opportunity to hold talks there with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin to reach peace agreements, but he has not yet received an invitation to the summit.

Russia Develops Tracked Titan UGV Equipped With Roller-Type Mine-Clearing Devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:58:09 UTC
03:58:09 KST

Russia has presented a new tracked unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), the Titan, designed to clear paths through minefields.
The Russian state news agency TASS reported this, citing a representative of the developer.
The vehicle is equipped with two roller-type mine-clearing devices mounted at the front of the hull. They are designed to clear antipersonnel mines across a 2-meter-wide strip. A third mine-clearing device is mounted at the rear of the UGV.
These devices work by applying mechanical pressure to mines. As the vehicle moves, the heavy rollers press against the ground, triggering munitions equipped with pressure-sensitive fuzes. The developer also claims the system can clear mines fitted with tripwire and breakwire fuzes.
The main advantages of roller-type mine-clearing systems are their relatively simple design and ability to clear mines without the direct involvement of combat engineers. However, their effectiveness depends on the characteristics of the mines, the pressure exerted by the rollers and the terrain. Such systems cannot guarantee the neutralization of all mines, particularly those equipped with non-contact fuzes.
The developer says the Titan has an electrically powered tracked chassis and all-around fragmentation protection intended to shield the vehicle from fragments produced by antipersonnel mine explosions. Its low profile and electric drive are also intended to make it harder to detect.
The developer also claims the vehicle has increased resistance to explosions. In the published video, the UGV is shown surviving three detonations of low-powered explosive devices, one beneath each of its three mine-clearing devices.
The vehicle weighs 2.3 metric tons and has a payload capacity of 1 metric ton. Its maximum speed with mine-clearing equipment is 7 km/h, rising to 14 km/h without it. Its stated autonomous operating time is at least 3.5 hours.
The remote-control range depends on the communications link used and is stated as “at least 500 meters.” The platform can also be equipped with electronic warfare systems to protect it against drones.
According to the developer, the vehicle has already undergone testing. Work is continuing to improve its protection, control system and mine-clearing devices. No timeline has been announced for the start of serial production or delivery to Russian troops.
In early October, Russia showed the Shturm heavy assault robotic system, based on the T-72B3M tank, during the Center-2026 strategic command-and-staff exercise.
The system was demonstrated on October 2 at the Chebarkul training ground in the Chelyabinsk region. According to the manufacturer, the military used unmanned vehicles fitted with tank weapon stations and BMPT modules to provide fire support for assault units.

Marine Le Pen delivers a speech at the end of her campaign kickoff rally as part of the party congress in Orléans on October 25, 2026. | Alain Jocard/AFP via Getty Images
ORLEANS, France — Far-right leader Marine Le Pen shed her anti-establishment radicalism on Sunday to portray herself as the guardian of France in her first presidential campaign rally in Orléans, south of Paris.
With polls showing her as the front-runner ahead of the scheduled April 2027 presidential election, Le Pen sought to reassure voters by promising to safeguard France as the country seethes with social unrest and stares down a looming debt crisis.
“Even if today the words that spring to mind are ruin, decline … riots and even chaos … we believe in our people and in France,” she said.
Advertisement
In a speech lasting over an hour, Le Pen told thousands of supporters that she was not aiming for a “revolution” but rather “a real change in power” that would spark a new “Renaissance” in the country.
“We’re not saying: It was better before,” she said. “We say: It was good before and it will be better tomorrow.”
Le Pen also played her usual refrains, promising to restore public order in France, strengthen the country’s borders and expel undocumented migrants if she came to power.
Le Pen and her allies have spent days pushing back against accusations by rivals that the far-right National Rally has helped deepen divisions in France amid the turmoil and disorder sparked by recent student protests. In her address, the four-time presidential candidate refrained from attacking political opponents and pitched her party as the one offering French citizens a brighter future.
“My protective vision will benefit all,” she said.
The eurozone’s second-largest economy is facing a cocktail of crises including cost-of-living protests, difficulties adopting a state budget and a spiraling debt and deficit. The dire situation has spooked the markets, with France’s borrowing costs climbing above 5% last week for the first time since 2002.
Advertisement
According to a senior National Rally official, Le Pen wanted to use her speech to cast herself in a presidential role and to reassure voters hesitant about supporting her. “People mostly agree with our ideas, but some still think it’s a gamble to vote for us,” the official said.
Tensions overflowing
Le Pen’s rally was also a show of force, with over 8,500 supporters gathering in a conference hall in Orléans, many carrying French flags and chanting “Marine, présidente!”
According to POLITICO’s most recent Poll of Polls from mid-October, if the election were held today Le Pen would get 34% of the vote compared to 16% for center-right candidate Edouard Philippe and 15% for Jean-Luc Mélenchon, representing the far left. Most polls have Le Pen winning in a run-off round if no candidate wins a majority in the first round.
Supporters wave French flags during Launch rally for Marine Le Pen’s presidential campaign as part of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National in Orléans on October 25, 2026. | Romain Perrocheau/AFP via Getty Images
Leaders of the far-right party staged a two-day conference in Orléans over the weekend under high security, with heightened police checks and body searches. On Saturday thousands of left-wing demonstrators gathered to oppose the rise of the far right in the center of Paris, while across the country protests attracted hundreds of thousands of people, a week after looting and riots marred rallies across France.
“France is plunging into real violence, which will become out of control if the state doesn’t take control,” said National Rally President Jordan Bardella, addressing the crowd before Le Pen’s speech.
“The National Rally appears to be the only solution to allow the return of order and return of authority.”
Advertisement
France was already reeling after a man randomly opened fire on passers-by in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, killing one person and injuring five, including a girl of 12. French President Emmanuel Macron deplored the incident as “a racist terrorist attack.”
Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure said on Sunday that the National Rally carried “a heavy responsibility” for the Trappes attack because it had created “a mood … suggesting that we are being invaded, that there’s a sort of great replacement.”
The National Rally pushed back on the charges, and instead accused the far left of encouraging the violence.

Venezuela’s opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns from exile
The Nobel laureate’s homecoming follows national protests demanding free elections.
Venezuela’s opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has successfully returned to the country after more than 10 months in exile.
Machado announced her arrival on social media on Sunday, writing, “I am here. With you.”
The current opposition leader, Edmundo Gonzalez, confirmed the news, writing on X that “our leader, my dear Maria Corina, is on Venezuelan soil”.
The Comando Con Venezuela political organisation shared footage of Machado arriving at a church in Lara, where she was greeted by supporters.
Machado first disappeared from public life after being briefly arrested in January 2025. She re-emerged last December in Norway, where she won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to challenge Venezuela President Nicolas Maduro. Maduro was abducted from Caracas by the United States military in January 2026.
Venezuela’s Vice President Delcy Rodriguez has stood in as acting president since then, with the endorsement of US President Donald Trump, and has cooperated with his administration regarding reforms in the country, as well as a deal to grant the US control of over 65 billion barrels’ worth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.
Calls for elections to be held
Rodriguez’s presidency has extended far beyond the 90-day period she was authorised to serve following Maduro’s removal. But she has yet to call an election despite public demand and despite her promise to do so at the United Nations General Assembly in September. The US maintains that the country is not ready yet.
Earlier this week, thousands of Venezuelans took to the streets to call for elections in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years.
Although the opposition is widely believed to have won Venezuela’s disputed 2024 elections, Trump has cast doubt on Machado’s abilities to lead, claiming in January that she “doesn’t have the support within or the respect within the country”.
Machado presented Trump with her Nobel medal when visiting him in the White House weeks later, in what she said was “a recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom”. The US leader has repeatedly voiced his desire to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize himself.
Machado has made previous unsuccessful attempts to enter Venezuela. In September, her team said she had made seven attempts in the space of a few weeks.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on X that “the conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the U.S. supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile.”
Asked to comment about Machado’s return, Trump told reporters on Sunday, “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman.”
“She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe.”

Infamous Nazi-era alpine retreat mostly destroyed in deliberate fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:46:59 UTC
03:46:59 KST

The Eagle’s Nest, a Nazi-era chalet in southeastern Germany, was mostly destroyed in a major fire believed to be the result of arson on Friday night, Berchtesgaden police confirmed.
The historical landmark - in German, Kehlsteinhaus - was engulfed in flames at 9:15 pm local time on October 23. Police and firefighters said access to the fire site, which is located in an exposed position, was difficult, as were the subsequent firefighting operations.
Around 200 emergency personnel from fire brigades in six municipalities, the district fire inspection service, the Bavarian Red Cross, mountain rescue services and the police worked throughout the night, and residual operations are still ongoing.
According to findings so far, no one was injured in the fire, but for safety reasons, investigators have not yet been able to enter the burned building safely.
Shortly after the fire broke out, firefighters noticed a suspicious individual in the vicinity of the scene.
33-year-old man arrested on suspicion of arson
The 33-year-old man was subsequently arrested and is suspected of having deliberately started the fire. At the request of the public prosecutor’s office, he was brought before an investigating judge and, following a diagnosis of mental illness, was provisionally placed in a secure psychiatric hospital.
The public prosecutor’s office and criminal police are continuing to investigate the background to the incident and the suspect’s motive.
The area around the incident remains cordoned off, and a drone no-fly zone is currently in place.
Joachim Hermann, Bavaria’s Interior Minister, suggested the site will be rebuilt; “We’ll hardly be able to leave a ruin standing there,” he said during a press conference in Munich.
He also thanked the firefighters and police officers for their “courageous and determined response,” and praised the “swift arrest of the suspect in the brutal arson attack.”
What is the Eagle's Nest?
The Eagle’s Nest is a historic mountain-top building in the Bavarian Alps near Berchtesgaden, southern Germany.
It was commissioned under senior Nazi official Martin Bormann as a reception house for Nazi leaders and their guests between 1937–1938, and sits about 1,834 meters (6,017 ft) above sea level.
Hitler visited the chalet, although not frequently. It nevertheless symbolizes the Nazi era. Hitler’s residence, the Berghof, was situated not far away.
The Eagle’s Nest survived WWII and opened as a mountain restaurant in 1952 before becoming a major tourist attraction. It usually hosts a historical exhibition.
The TV miniseries ‘War and Remembrance’ (1988) filmed its fictional scenes featuring Hitler inside the actual building.
Normally, access to the building involves a special bus ride up a mountain through five tunnels, then a walk through a 124-meter tunnel and a gold brass elevator ride up to the building.
However, the normal access route was destroyed in the fire.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews (BoD) has passed a motion declaring the UK Green Party a racist party.
This resolution, adopted at the board’s October Plenary Meeting, condemns the Green Party’s decision to adopt a policy branding Zionism as racism, deeming the policy racist and antisemitic. The board will now treat the Greens as it has treated other “racist parties.”
“Today, representatives of Jewish communities across Britain have delivered a clear verdict,” BoD president Phil Rosenberg said.
“By adopting an antisemitic platform, the Green Party of England and Wales has become a racist party. We will treat it accordingly.”
“No political party has the right to tell Jews that a central part of our identity, rooted in thousands of years of history, faith and peoplehood, is racist,” he said.
“The Green Party’s policy brands much of our community, including our synagogues and communal organizations, with that slur. It gives prejudice against Jews a political license.”
Rosenberg said the Green Party’s leadership must now take responsibility for reversing this policy and “confronting the antisemitism it has legitimized.”
He also noted that the BoD recognizes and commends those within the party who opposed the motion, including Jewish members whose warnings were disregarded. Rosenberg said these individuals deserved to be heard and supported.
Motion proposer Ashley Hirst said he was proud that British Jews have “said clearly” that a party which declares that this is racist “is itself a racist party.”
“The board will give effect to the resolution in its dealings with the Green Party of England and Wales and continue to challenge antisemitism wherever it appears in political and public life.”
Green Party became first in Europe to declare itself anti-Zionist
The Green Party became the first mainstream party in Europe to declare itself openly anti-Zionist after voting in the controversial “Zionism is racism” motion at its party conference in Brighton, UK, at the start of the month.
The motion recognizes Zionism as Israel’s foundational ideology that has created and maintains an “apartheid regime” between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.
It further affirms the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and liberation. It supports the establishment of a “single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine, with Jerusalem as its capital.”

France: The sickest man of Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:45:47 UTC
03:45:47 KST

France has become the new sick man of Europe just in time for its next presidential election.
After two weekends that saw hundreds of thousands of protesters hit the streets demanding the government increase teacher salaries, fix run-down schools and help subsidize the rapidly rising cost of living, the European Union’s second-biggest economy is being dragged into a vicious cycle of twin fiscal and social crises that are fueling each other.
“France is on the brink of a financial crisis,” former Prime Minister Michel Barnier told POLITICO. “We need to send a signal to the markets.”
Authorities were able to prevent the type of rioting and looting this past weekend that marked the first round of demonstrations Oct. 17-18, but financial markets are spooked. Even before the demonstrations began, investors were dumping French debt or demanding historically high returns because of the government’s failure to significantly cut a stubbornly high budget deficit, bring down €3.5 trillion of debt, jumpstart growth and reform an unsustainable pension system.
The prospect of a presidential runoff next spring featuring far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen and her far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is in the mix for second place according to most polls, is further scaring investors. Both candidates want to spend billions to lower the retirement age.
The rioting, for now, is estimated to have cost tens of millions of euros, much of which will be covered by insurance. But the chaos is pouring fuel on an already explosive situation by sending worrying signals to investors, especially if the civil unrest continues. The Yellow Vest protests of 2018 to 2020, which came early in President Emmanuel Macron’s tenure, cost the French economy 0.1% of gross domestic product, with shops reporting losses of €2 billion.
“It is clear that protests have an impact on markets,” Eric Lombard, who served as economy and finance minister last year, told POLITICO.
Given that current Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s proposed budget for 2027 already includes €43 billion in savings, leaving little room for more cuts, the government is faced with an impossible choice: Borrow more money and saddle the next generation with billions of euros in interest payments, or hope the protests die out on their own.
“We have a knife to our throats, and we can feel the drops of blood on our jugular,” said a government minister who was granted anonymity to discuss the current situation.
“We need to show that we’ve heard the outrage. But we have little margin for maneuver given the market situation.”
Playing with fire
Mario Monti, who faced a similar situation as Italian prime minister and managed to avert a financial crisis in 2011 with spending cuts and a pension reform, told POLITICO that “things can go very fast.”
Back then, the spread between Italian and German 10-year bonds — an indicator that measures how risky one country’s debt is compared to historically safe Germany — shot up from around 150 basis points to more than 500 within a few months, Monti recalled. The spread between French and German debt was 169 basis points when markets closed on Friday, while the yield on France’s benchmark 10-year bond hit 5.14% the previous day, the highest level since 2002.
France has long been seen as the EU’s “spoiled child,” Monti said, taking advantage of its political and economic weight to bend or break the bloc’s fiscal rules. But few had thought a country that big and powerful would end up on the front line of a European debt crisis.
While the ability of the European Central Bank to buy government bonds on the secondary market under certain conditions gives it a powerful tool to avert a eurozone crisis, Monti says French voters must recognize that a sovereign debt crisis in their country is no longer the stuff of fiction.
“The major problem is that the public is not concerned enough with this risk,” Monti said. “France is not psychologically ready to view itself as the target of a crisis or even as the starting point of a crisis that could spread.”
That malaise isn’t just economic: Many indicators show France has lost confidence in itself.
According to a poll last month, 9 out of 10 French people are pessimistic about the future and believe their children will be worse off than themselves. A pan-European study conducted earlier this year found that only half of French respondents feel pride in the democratic system, compared to two-thirds of Germans and close to 70 percent of Britons.
That pessimism has pushed voters toward more extreme candidates like Le Pen — whose economic platform has been panned by some economists as unrealistic and unserious — and Mélenchon, who wants to set French debt “on fire.” According to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls from earlier this month, Le Pen enjoys the support of 34% of voters while Mélenchon has 15% — meaning nearly 50% of the electorate intends to vote for an anti-establishment figure. Center-right candidate Edouard Philippe, arguably the best-placed mainstream figure to take on Le Pen, has tried to sell himself to voters as a candidate of fiscal discipline who is unafraid to address tough truths. But his campaign has struggled to find its footing.
Doom loop
The officials, lawmakers and diplomats POLITICO spoke with all agreed that France was not at risk of a Greece-like scenario forcing the government to stop paying officials and creditors. But it could very well experience a crisis similar to the one in Italy when Monti replaced Silvio Berlusconi in 2011.
“We are not yet a banana republic which risks filing for bankruptcy,” said veteran centrist lawmaker and budget expert Charles de Courson.
But during rioting earlier this month, in front of the shattered window of an already ransacked supermarket in Paris’ hipster 11th arrondissement, a man with no apparent connection to the shop was encouraging passers-by to go in and steal what they needed. A few meters away, the owner of a Chinese restaurant locked the door behind each client to make sure the rioters couldn’t get in.
These are scenes one would expect in a country on the verge of a sovereign debt crisis, not a member of the G7. Watching from Brussels, Washington or New York, diplomats and economists recognize that Paris will likely fail to bring its budget deficit down to 3% of GDP by 2029 as it previously promised to the EU.
De Courson said France has “lost all credibility” with its European partners when it comes to fiscal issues. Lombard, the former economy minister, said “we failed to honor our commitments,” but held out hope that things could change.
“On behalf of the French people, we made commitments to get the finances back on track, but we didn’t keep them. I was very much in favor of honoring my commitments. But collectively, we didn’t do that,” Lombard said. “So we put ourselves in a position of weakness.”
