The command said the visit coincided with with a "milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer".
The statement added that US CENTCOM had supported more than 3,000 commercial vessels to transit the Strait of Hormuz in the last six months.
"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," Cooper said . "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
The statement added that US forces had successfully cleared international shipping lanes in the strait of naval mines over recent months, alleging that the mines had been laid by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Cooper, it said, “met with service members who supported the mine-clearing mission and thanked them for their commitment and dedication.”
CENTCOM said that the main transit routes through the strait remain free of naval mines and that more than 95% of vessels sailing through it had “passed through safely” in recent months.
Meanwhile, Iran has tied the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to the fulfilment of its seven conditions, which include lifting the US naval blockade of its ports, easing sanctions on its oil exports, and halting hostilities on all fronts.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Washington must implement these conditions before the strait can be reopened, while reports have indicated that negotiations have stalled over disagreements concerning Iran’s demands.

Thousands protest Czech government’s public media overhaul after rushed vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:34:40 CET
03:34:40 KST

PRAGUE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Thousands protested in Prague on Sunday after government lawmakers gave initial backing to public media funding changes in a rare overnight vote despite criticism the overhaul will damage media independence.
The proposal’s first reading was unexpectedly brought to the lower house floor outside the planned order of proceedings on Friday. Opponents and media advocacy groups have objected to fast-tracking the legislation, which will abolish household fees that currently fund Czech public television and radio stations.
The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD party, has frequently clashed with public and private media.
It wants to move funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio to the state budget, which critics say will leave broadcasters vulnerable to political pressure.
GOVERNMENT HAS ‘GONE TOO FAR’, PROTEST LEADER SAYS
Babis says it is a matter of funding transparency and not an attack on independence.
Smaller protests first broke out on Friday at the bill’s unexpected introduction. Speaker Tomio Okamura of the SPD limited debate and scheduled a vote for 4:36 a.m. (0336 GMT) on Saturday.
The bill is now at the committee stage before a later vote.
“Mr Babis … Mr Okamura, nobody in this country believes that your intention was pure,” Mikulas Minar, a protest leader, said on Sunday, criticising the overnight vote.
“(This protest) is a clear message to this government: you have really gone too far this time,” he told protesters who had filled Prague’s historic Old Town Square, amid chants of “Resignation” and “We’ve had enough”.
Organisers plan further protests.
TRUST HIGH IN PUBLIC MEDIA
Czech Television is the country’s most-watched broadcaster across major age groups. Public media are among the most trusted news sources in the country, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey.
The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15%, possibly as early as next year.
Opposition parties have compared the funding changes with reforms in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who oversaw a major expansion of pro-government media.
On Friday, the European Broadcasting Union, along with 15 other groups including other public broadcasters as well as Reporters Without Borders, called for more debate and the removal of any measures threatening the broadcasters’ financial sustainability.
President Petr Pavel also called for more expert scrutiny.
“The Czech Republic is among the few countries in central and eastern Europe where the system of public service and private media works very well,” he said on X on Saturday.

France’s Le Pen launches presidential bid as protests rattle the nation

By Lafken Zepeda and Nicolas Economou
ORLEANS, France, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in next year’s French presidential election, formally launched her campaign on Sunday with a promise to restore order and national confidence.
As France faces one of its most turbulent periods in years, Le Pen cast herself as the best placed to navigate what she described as mounting economic, social and security crises.
“We are not living through the end of the world but the end of a world, their world,” she said of her political opponents.
Le Pen chose to make her first campaign address in Orleans, home to Joan of Arc, the 15th-century warrior heroine revered by nationalists as a symbol of patriotism and sovereignty.
Addressing a crowd of cheering supporters, she promised “zero tolerance” policing and said restoring security was the state’s first duty.
Mass protests over living costs and inequality last weekend descended into looting and vandalism.
OPINION POLL PUTS LE PEN IN THE LEAD
The street turmoil has given Le Pen a boost and an opinion poll published on Sunday put her on 32% to 33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon on 17%, as voters desert mainstream parties for the political extremes.
Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
Seeking to project optimism, Le Pen built her speech around the theme of a national “Renaissance”. She said France was living through a period of upheaval but would emerge stronger if it embraced her vision of security, prosperity and renewal.
“We say: ‘Things were good before, they will be better tomorrow!’,” she said.
Le Pen promised a hard line on immigration, pledging to restore border controls, automatically expel foreign criminals and crack down on gangs and drug traffickers.
Le Pen herself could have to campaign wearing an ankle tag after she was convicted of embezzling European Parliament funds. She is appealing the court verdict.
On the economy, Le Pen pledged spending restraint, lower business taxes, reduced bureaucracy and support for industry, innovation and artificial intelligence. She rejected further increases in the retirement age.
The congress was designed to showcase unity at the top of the National Rally party, with Jordan Bardella re-elected party president and presented as Le Pen’s choice for prime minister.
Bardella’s speech was interrupted by activists from a Jewish student union, drawing attention to recent accusations he made antisemitic comments in his youth, which he denies.
Le Pen has spent more than a decade trying to transform the party she inherited from her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, in 2011, softening its image and broadening its appeal beyond its traditional anti-immigration base.
On Europe, Le Pen stopped short of advocating a French exit from the European Union, but said she would roll back Brussels’ influence, restore national control over borders and laws, and put French interests first, including avoiding foreign wars.
“The future belongs to us,” she said, before leading the flag-waving crowd in singing the national anthem.

I used to spend my weekends on cocaine. Now I spend them running ultramarathons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:34:29 UTC
03:34:29 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Dopamine is a crucial neurotransmitter that helps facilitate reward, motivation, memory and movement within the body. But are its effects always beneficial? Watch Insight episode Chasing Dopamine on SBS On Demand.
Content warning: This article references drug use and addiction
I always had a burning desire to be liked. But my pursuit of 'fitting in' and the subsequent ways I'd seek dopamine came with serious consequences.
Growing up, I felt like a fat little loser and weighed almost 100kg by age 15.
I was bullied for it, not terribly, but it was enough to make me constantly insecure for the next five years.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
I also had one of my testicles removed at this age because doctors believed the tumour that had developed on it was cancerous.
Thankfully, it was benign.
But still, I felt less of a man coming into adulthood.
I was especially desperate to feel accomplished in something after I recovered from surgery and decided I would lose weight.
About eight months after surgery, I had lost 23kg from calorie counting and exercise. And I started feeling confident for the first time in my life.
But this didn't satiate my need to be liked by my peers.
'The guy who said yes to everything'
At 16, I discovered alcohol and found that when I drank, I would become a version of myself that wasn't insecure.
And this is when I started to make more friends.
I became the life of the party in my early twenties — the guy who said yes to everything.
Eventually, if somebody wanted someone to do drugs with, they knew they could call me and I'd do cocaine every weekend.
I'd start with around $1,000 in my account and finish the weekend owing $1,000.
But I felt invincible.
Cocaine weekends and binge drinking
I was also drinking almost 12 standard drinks every night.
I'd often sneak in a few on my shift at work and would often stop in at the bottle shop on my way back because I didn't want to wait until I was home.
This behaviour continued for about six years while I still went to work and had a functional life as a tradesman.
I convinced myself I was just young and having fun — that I was fine.
But my body constantly hurt, my weight had climbed back to around 112kg and I was depressed.
I destroyed friendships, treated my then-partner terribly and put my family through too much.
One night when I was about 20, while absolutely smashed, I crashed my mum's new BMW into a parked car and drove away.
When the owners tracked me down, I was too ashamed and stubborn to face them.
My mum dealt with it for me. I wasn't only an addict; I was also a massive coward.
Although my parents made me do the right thing and call the people to apologise, I still had no remorse at the time.
Not an overnight transformation
Around this period, my best mate at the time and I started talking about trying ice.
We never smoked it, thankfully — although I did try speed on multiple occasions.
I knew by then this wasn't just partying.
There wasn't an overnight transformation.
But between many bad magic mushroom trips (when I would cry thinking about how I'd let everyone down) and the weight of knowing my path was possibly leaning towards jail, I was forced to stop and think about my future properly for the first time ever.
My girlfriend at the time had stuck with me through my absolute worst years because she had seen the good in me before everything went off the rails.
I owed it to her and my family to change my habits and start the road to recovery.
I was still an addict as I then smoked weed daily (only after work) but I had stopped cocaine and alcohol.
And after countless failed attempts, I also managed to string together a few good days of eating better.
I wasn't sure I could lose the weight but as the story goes, a few days became weeks. And I eventually went from around 112 kilograms to about 80 kilograms.
Switching drugs for running
Before then, I had never run 5km continuously in my life.
But something clicked in me when I read a book by an American ultramarathon runner.
That very same day I ran 7.6km. The next day, I ran 10 and then ran 10km every day for a month to train for the Maribyrnong River Run in Melbourne.
I finished in the top 50 out of roughly 500 people. For someone who had never run 5km only a couple of months before, that was absolutely mind-blowing.
I decided I wasn't done yet. I wanted to push my limits on a trail and signed up for a marathon (42km) two weeks later.
I was terrified yet I finished sixth somehow.
That's when this became something much bigger, and I've been running long-distance races ever since.
My proudest physical achievement so far is when I covered roughly 170km in the You Yangs mountain range in Victoria with around 5km of elevation in about 32 hours.
The uncomfortable truth
Looking back, I've realised something uncomfortable about why ultrarunning appealed to me so much.
I still liked feeling like 'the f---ing man', which is what drugs and alcohol used to do for me.
I loved people's reactions when I told them how far I was running. That desire to be accepted never completely disappeared.
In some ways, I had just found another way of getting it. But there's a difference.
Running gives me a measurable way to see how far I've come from the person I used to be.
Chasing dopamine elsewhere
Drugs gave me the reward of dopamine first and made me suffer afterwards.
Ultrarunning works backwards. The longer I suffer, the greater the dopamine reward afterwards.
When everything hurt during my 100-miler (161km), and stopping would have ended the physical pain immediately, I didn't stop.
Because I knew the mental pain of giving up would last much longer than the physical pain of continuing.
Today, I rarely drink but I do smoke weed. I know I'm not at my best because of it, but I still do enjoy it.
I'm not interested in pretending I've become a perfect person. But I'm a completely different son, brother and friend.
My relationship with my family is now so much better, and my mum is my best friend who constantly tells me how proud she is.
'You don't have to return to the insecure person'
I've also started coaching people who want to run trails and ultramarathons.
The fact that somebody would pay the bloke who once couldn't run 5km to teach them how to run further is still wild to me.
Helping people has become the point and I believe it's God's purpose for me — to help others who were where I was.
I regret hurting people, but I don't regret what happened and wouldn't erase those years.
The good I can do with what I've learned can outweigh the bad it took to get here.
I regret hurting people, but I don’t regret what happened and wouldn't erase those years.
Simon Agostinelli
If I could speak to somebody living the life I was living, I'd say that if you can fight your way through this, there's an entirely different life waiting on the other side.
You don't have to return to the insecure person you were trying to escape.
And you have absolutely no idea yet what you're capable of.

Wineries and breweries closing their doors as move away from alcohol bites
In short:
The decline in alcohol sales is accelerating and businesses are starting to close their doors.
It is being blamed on tough economic times, young people drinking less and a rise in popularity of non-alcoholic drinks.
What's next?
Grape growers are calling for government assistance to help with the transition away from solely making wine.
Since opening his Hunter Valley winery about five years ago, Nathan Heuston says his business has plummeted.
"We were averaging, especially on our busy days, up to 220 people," he said.
"This year we've even had days where we've had no-one."
Mr Heuston said his winery went from generating about $20,000 a week to about $2,000 a week.
"We were taking a 10th of what we require to pay our bills. How do you recover from that?"
he said.
This pain is familiar across the industry, with iconic Tasmanian brewer Boag closing its doors last week and trade data in June showing wine exports had dropped to their lowest levels in 22 years as cost-of-living pressures had taken a toll.
Fitch Solutions data shows the amount of wine people are drinking worldwide has been in decline for almost a decade
In Australia, total alcohol consumption fell by about 10 per cent in the three years to 2024.
"And the fall in the 2024 financial year was the sharpest we've seen on record," IBISWorld senior analyst Michael Doyle said.
The reduction stems from younger Australians drinking less, tighter budgets with growing cost-of-living pressures and the rise of non-alcoholic alternatives.
It has forced businesses like Mr Hueston's to make changes such as cuts to staff and production.
"This year we did about 20 tonnes, whereas [previously] we've been doing 60 to 70 tonnes in production," he said.
"All we're going to make is what we've planted in our new vineyard. We haven't bought any barrels for last year and this year coming."
'Most difficult set of circumstances'
This trend has affected all corners of the industry, with the Independent Brewers Association confirming more than 80 breweries had shut down since June 2023.
Seven hotel bars in Hobart entered voluntary administration earlier this year. Liquor sales at Coles dropped 3.3 per cent last financial year, and Endeavour Group, which owns BWS and Dan Murphy's, saw sales at its retail outlets only increase modestly, up 0.7 per cent.
The grape and wine peak body, Australian Grape and Wine, has described this period as "the most difficult set of circumstances" the industry has faced in "generations".
"We're really concerned about what this means for Australian grape growers and wine makers," chief executive Lee McLean said.
Meanwhile, those businesses producing non-alcoholic alternatives are seeing gains.
Non-alcoholic beer sales are projected to almost double in the four years to 2028, from 150 million litres to about 300 million.
It is the fastest-growing beverage across the alcohol sector, accounting for 45 per cent of total non-alcoholic beverage sales in Australia in 2023, and around 10 per cent of all beer sales, according to ANZ.
Co-founder and chief executive of Heaps Normal, Andy Miller, said his non-alcoholic beer sales were growing at about 20 per cent each year.
"[We] saw an opportunity for a product that didn't feel like a compromise to fill that gap," he said.
And consumers have been taking note.
"We're now distributing non-alcoholic beer on tap, which is, I think, another really significant shift in the way that people consume these beers and socialise in on-premise venues," Mr Miller said.
"What we're seeing in some of the more progressive venues around the country is that the non-alcoholic Heaps Normal draft is outselling other alcoholic counterparts."
Adapting to a changing landscape
To remain viable, beer and wine makers must adapt. The peak body, Australian Grape and Wine, anticipates the industry will be "a different shape and size" in the coming years.
"[We are] trying to reclaim a little bit of market share in our existing markets such as the US or the UK," Mr McLean said.
"But also looking to open up new markets like India and those in South-East Asia, which still hold a lot of promise for Australian wine exporters."
Alcohol Beverages Australia executive director Alistair Coe said some businesses were already making changes based on consumer preferences.
"The industry continues to innovate, with greater product diversity … and the growth of low- and no-alcohol products," he said.
But Mr McLean warned not every business would survive.
"The message that we've been giving to government over the last little while is that grape growers and wine makers in many of these regions that are suffering need a hand to make a transition," he said.
"Whether that is a transition out of the industry or a transition to do something else with their property, whether that be growing a different crop or looking at other alternatives for that block of land."
As for where the industry is going and with the pressure of high inflation, Mr Doyle expects more pain.
"People just don't have the money to spend on alcohol like they may have used to," he said.
"I would expect to see a continual slow decline in per capita consumption."
In a statement to the ABC, Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins acknowledged the challenges the industry had faced in recent years.
"The government has delivered over $105 million in funding to support the grape and wine sector," she said.
It included the Wine Equalisation Tax rebate and a new mandatory code of conduct for wine-grape purchases.
"Our government will continue to work closely with industry on future opportunities."

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has returned to the South American nation after nearly a year outside the country, she said on social media on Sunday.

Machado's press team shared images of her in central-western Lara state, in the Plaza del Pueblo de Santa Rosa, where Machado appeared at a church.
The issue of her return has strained her relationship with the US Trump administration, which she has sought to cultivate as an ally since before it removed President Nicolas Maduro from power in January.

"We're being very fair," he said. "But we're taking out millions of barrels of oil a week."

Machado to meet with victims of devastating June earthquake

"She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections," he added.

Machado has said only a "serious, democratic government" can provide the stability needed by investors. In June, she said she would do whatever it took to come home and help the survivors of devastating twin earthquakes that month that killed at least 6,500 people and left thousands missing.
Machado escaped Venezuela in 2025 after living in hiding
Machado was barred by Maduro's government from exiting Venezuela, but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.
Her desire to return had caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, Reuters reported in June.
Machado did not disclose more details about her current location or how she returned.
A faction of the opposition and the interim government held their latest session of talks this month, which aim to remake the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. They do not include Machado's political movement.
Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado's movement who has been living in Spain, confirmed her return in his own post and said he would soon join her.

Security increased as parliament resumes without MP Helen Haines
In short:
The prime minister will pass a motion to suspend normal business in parliament today, allowing MPs to share a message of support for Indi MP Helen Haines.
Ms Haines is in a serious but stable condition in hospital after being hit by a car in what police are treating as a deliberate attack.
What's next?
Security at Parliament House has been increased, as police warn there is a direct correlation between inflammatory political discourse and threats against politicians.
Parliament returns this week without one of its most respected members, Helen Haines, as security measures across public areas of Parliament House are strengthened.
A car struck the independent MP outside her Wangaratta electorate office last week in what police are treating as a deliberate attack.
The 65-year-old mother of three, admired across the political divide for her integrity, suffered severe injuries to her lower body. Both her legs have since been amputated.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is expected to move a motion in the House of Representatives that would set aside much of the day for MPs to offer messages of support.
Members of the crossbench have backed calls for parliamentarians to sign a civility pledge, inspired by the family of British MP Jo Cox, who was murdered in 2016.
Ms Haines was the first MP to sign the pledge earlier this year.
"In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect and compassion," it says.
Ms Haines's seat will be empty at Question Time, with fellow independents pledging to carry forward her leadership example as parliament grapples with ways to approach security in their respective communities.
"The people of Indi will be represented by an empty seat this week, but I hope their voices and the voices of all Australians who want the kind of democracy Helen represents will be heard clearly by the parliament," independent MP Kate Chaney said.
Kooyong MP Monique Ryan said those who loved Ms Haines would try to do justice to the parliament's "most gentle, principled, and kind member".
"I hope that all members will rise to the occasion as Helen would do were she with us," she said.
Independent senator David Pocock said it was hard to articulate the "anguish" felt by his team and the wider community.
"We've been checking in with her family, her team and thinking about how we can best support Helen and everyone most impacted by these events now and over the long term," he said.
"Helen's impact will continue to be felt, however, and should inspire us to keep working to improve our democracy."
Hanson says cartoons here to stay
On Sunday, Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said MPs had a critical role to play in their own safety, warning there was a direct correlation between moments of inflammatory political discourse and increased threats against politicians.
Asked whether One Nation's cartoons depicting politicians being hit by cars were the type of political discourse she was referring to, Commissioner Barrett said they could be.
"We do see examples where there are particular announcements or things like you've just described. There is a reaction amongst the community," she said.
In a post on social media, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson defended the cartoons and said they had "nothing" to do with the attack on Ms Haines.
She said they would "not be going anywhere" and accused the major parties of trying to censor the party because "they don't like scrutiny".
"Free speech, satire, criticism and debate are essential to our democracy," Senator Hanson said.
"When violence touches politicians, the response is immediate: more security, more protection and demands for action. Where is that same urgency when ordinary Australians are attacked?"
Nationals MP and former party leader David Littleproud said politicians had to learn to "play the ball, not the man".
"I think unfortunately we have crept into playing too much of the man, not just in parliament but outside of it as well," he said.
Liberal MP Ted O'Brien said the warning was a "sombre reminder" for all politicians to consider their rhetoric and behaviours.
Asked if politicians needed a code of conduct, Mr O'Brien said he would not pre-empt conversations between colleagues but said everything must be considered.
"What gives me great comfort though is that I think there is a genuine desire on the part of everybody to improve the way things are," he said.
"Parliament can sometimes be a microcosm of our community. There is a lot of anger, a lot of social discontent."
Increased security at parliament
In a letter sent to MPs on Friday, Speaker of the House Milton Dick and Senate President Sue Lines said there would be additional security across certain areas of Parliament House.
"The events of this week involving Dr Helen Haines MP have deeply affected the parliamentary community," they wrote.
"We also recognise that these events may understandably cause parliamentarians, their staff, and families to reflect on their safety and security, including whilst at Australian Parliament House."
MPs met with the AFP for a security briefing last week, with some reporting mixed experiences accessing support.
At the same time, a number of parliamentarians have stressed that safety must be balanced against the need to remain accessible to the communities they serve.
"The very nature of the jobs we do is we're interacting with people all the time as we should be," Labor frontbencher Catherine King said.
Parliament will resume its usual schedule on Tuesday, with the government hoping to pass its Digital Duty of Care, gas reservation and trust tax legislation before the end of the year.

Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:20:26 UTC
03:20:26 KST

Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congo
Kampala says country is Ebola free, but Swiss authorities believe a woman diagnosed in Nigeria was infected in Uganda.
Uganda has ordered citizens returning after travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to quarantine for 21 days, as it steps up precautions against the Ebola virus.
Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi announced the measure on Sunday at a news conference in Kampala, as Ebola cases in Kenya and Nigeria raised fresh questions about travellers passing through Uganda.
The country says it has no active infections after ending its own outbreak in July. Returning Ugandans with a history of travel to DRC will have to pay for their quarantine, the Ministry of Health said.
Officials have also strengthened checks at Entebbe International Airport and land crossings, and require all incoming travellers to complete forms recording how they can be contacted.
Uganda declared its Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak over on July 28. It had recorded 20 infections and two deaths, according to the Health Ministry.
Yet Swiss authorities have said a Ugandan-born woman married to a Swiss diplomat contracted Ebola during a visit to Uganda in September.
Nigeria confirmed her infection on October 20, after she had travelled to Abuja, its capital.
At Sunday’s briefing in Kampala, Baryomunsi challenged that conclusion. He said relatives who had previously visited DRC had met the woman in a Kampala suburb, and questioned whether that possible route of exposure had been ruled out.
“We should speak science, not politics,” he said.
The World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations’ health agency, said on Thursday that the information it had received did not show that the woman herself had travelled to DRC.
Nigerian and Ugandan officials are investigating her movements and possible source of infection.
The inquiry has also turned to a Kenyan man who travelled from DRC through Uganda before flying to Nairobi on October 3. He died two days later, and Kenya has since reported a second Ebola death.
Both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day.
Ugandan officials said on Sunday that security footage showed no physical interaction between them.
Nigerian authorities said genetic testing found closely related viruses in the two cases, but no direct link had been established.
Baryomunsi said 60 people traced in Uganda after possible contact with the Kenyan patient had finished 21 days of monitoring and been discharged.
In neighbouring DRC, where the outbreak began in May, the WHO had recorded 9,704 cases and 4,687 deaths by October 20.
Ebola, which can cause haemorrhagic fever, has reached eight Congolese provinces, making this the country’s largest recorded outbreak of the virus. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.
The strain responsible for the current outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear, according to the WHO. In its October 23 update, the WHO urged stronger monitoring and cooperation across borders, while advising against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries.

More Than 50 Air Defense Turrets Built Around Putin’s Residence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:17:21 UTC
03:17:21 KST

Another 16 towers for air defense systems have been built around Vladimir Putin’s residence in Valdai, Russia.
The findings were reported by Radio Liberty, based on a joint analysis of satellite imagery with OSINT researcher jembob.
The total number of air defense positions in the area has exceeded 50.
According to the investigators, Russia built 16 towers in October within a 50-kilometer radius south of the residence, on the side facing Ukraine.
The new structures form an additional outer ring of air defenses, likely intended to house Pantsir surface-to-air gun-missile systems or Tor surface-to-air missile systems.
Journalists have not yet identified new positions in the northern part of the outer ring. They may be built over the coming months.
The new air defense ring runs through the Khotilovo military airfield and the area around the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
One of the towers at Khotilovo airbase was built as early as March 2026. The airfield is used for Vladimir Putin’s flights, and a dedicated railway line connects its grounds to his residence in Valdai.
Several more positions have been established on the shore of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir, in the middle of which lies Lisiy Island.
Russian military personnel have built a laboratory complex on the island that, according to a Radio Liberty investigation, may be linked to Russia’s biological weapons development program.
Construction of two air defense towers near the facility began in early September, around the same time the investigation into the laboratory was published.
The total number of identified air defense positions around Valdai has therefore exceeded 50. This is roughly half the number of positions established to protect Moscow and the Moscow region since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow and the surrounding region have a combined population of more than 20 million, while fewer than 100,000 people live in Valdai, Valdai District, and the surrounding area within a 50-kilometer radius.
Russia began deploying additional air defense systems near Putin’s residence in early 2023. This included the reported appearance of a Pantsir-S1 system in Yashcherovo, near the residence.
Russia is also strengthening air defenses around Moscow. In July, Militarnyi reported the construction of about 24 new towers for Pantsir systems in the Russian capital region.
In June, following a Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow in May, Russia built at least seven additional towers for Pantsir systems to the north and east of the capital.

America's Wagner Group: Starlink crisis in Ukraine shows dangerous reality for US allies - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:13:16 UTC
03:13:16 KST

On October 14, 2026, Ukraine experienced speed throttling of its connections to Starshield, Starlink’s military counterpart. The imposed strict speed ceilings restricted connections for any terminals or drones exceeding 100 miles per hour.
That grounded or disconnected Ukraine’s faster military strike and interceptor drones, which rely on communication with operators over long distances. Almost as soon as news of the newly imposed limits was disclosed by Ukrainian officials, the game of finger-pointing and shifting the blame between US President Donald Trump and Elon Musk, Starlink’s CEO, began.
Trump announced he had no knowledge of the decision, suggesting the initiative was wholly Musk’s. In turn, Musk claimed to have received orders from the White House. The back-and-forth continued, with both Trump and Musk denying responsibility.
It is not hard to deduce the sequence of events that led to the decision to reduce the coverage: the president and Musk had a conversation, with Trump complaining about Ukraine and how “ungrateful” it was. Musk suggested a way to teach the country a lesson by temporarily reducing Starshield’s services.
The president agreed that it would be a good idea, but suggested the White House should not be directly implicated, given the timing, a few weeks before the midterms, was very sensitive. Yet, no matter how Trump and Musk try to spin the story, the proverbial buck, as put by president Harry Truman, “stops here.”
This avoidance of responsibility is not a new feature of American politics. But the other aspect of the affair has far-reaching consequences, going beyond national borders and carrying worldwide strategic implications.
The US is a superpower possessing one of the most powerful militaries in the world. It is also the major supplier of weapons and military platforms to its allies and countries it deems friendly. Historically, the countries purchasing those weapons understood that their usage and proper maintenance depended on American political goodwill.
The president and Congress could influence or even restrict American-made weapons’ usage and deployment, and many countries have faced those limitations or the threats thereof. Yet it has always been a clear political decision. There was a clear channel of communication to discuss and agree on the matter.
The White House was the responsible party on the American side. Its decisions were politically controlled by internal politics and bilateral relationships. The rules of the game were transparent and well known. That clarity provided the clients of American weaponry a sense of stability and well-placed dependence.
But what if, in the decision to dial down Starshield’s coverage in Ukraine, Musk played a role equal to Trump’s? What if there is a new independent entity in America that can make decisions of a magnitude that, just a few months ago, only the president could?
A slippery slope of who would control Starlink technologies
Elon Musk is not bound by political considerations. His interests are completely independent of those of the president, another country, or bilateral relationships. He is an independent businessman with the power of a sovereign, deciding who wins, who loses, and who dies.
And those decisions are driven not by the art of statecraft, but by his business interests, whims, and caprices. This is not merely the problem of one particular individual, even though, in Musk’s case, that problem is huge.
The wars in Ukraine, Karabakh, and Iran showed how technology has become a decisive force on the battlefield. Those conflicts proved beyond doubt that the huge military conglomerates of yesteryear are no longer capable of providing the technical support a modern military needs to win.
The dinosaurs of old are too slow and cumbersome in a world where a fast pace of development, deployment, and refinement is a must. The American government and the US military have no choice but to rely extensively on start-ups founded by folks with very “interesting” ideas of how the world should be to supply themselves with needed platforms.
Those companies, both private and public, may, as in the case of Starlink, possess dual-use technologies.
Inevitably, the question arises: Who controls the switch? Who controls communication with those devices in the field? The question is of paramount importance because, as Musk has spectacularly displayed, someone in a land far away has the power and ability to stop a war, allow one side to win and another to lose, and effectively play god.
Every American ally in a conflict zone, be it Israel and Ukraine in active wars, Europe awaiting another Russian invasion, Taiwan awaiting China’s channel crossing, or South Korea awaiting another North Korean provocation, is shaken to the core by the Starlink fiasco.
They have all purchased billions of dollars worth of American equipment under the assumption, perhaps no longer true, that its reliability is backed by American political power.
But if that depends on the current state of mind of Musk or another brilliant founder with questionable interests and mental stability, then the US has stopped being an ally, and even a reliable source of weaponry. That means American credibility as a political and military power is lost.
If the American military industry becomes an American version of the Wagner Group, then our power is on a slippery slope to the “dustbin” of history.
The writer lives and works in Silicon Valley, California. He is a founding member of San Francisco Voice for Israel.

Why does Moody’s rate France above Israel? The economic gap deserves scrutiny – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:13:13 UTC
03:13:13 KST

Moody’s decision to keep France’s credit rating well above Israel’s raises a question: How much weight does the agency put on each country’s economic performance?
The US-based credit rating agency affirmed France’s sovereign rating at Aa3 over the weekend. Israel remains at Baa1, four notches lower. Both ratings are investment grade, meaning they fall within the categories generally considered suitable for mainstream institutional investment. The difference nevertheless signals that Moody’s considers lending to France substantially safer.
Sovereign credit ratings assess a government’s ability and willingness to repay its debt. They can influence borrowing costs and determine which investors are permitted to buy a country’s bonds.
Such assessments necessarily extend beyond a comparison of growth and debt figures. War, political stability, institutions, and access to financing all matter. Even so, the contrast between the French and Israeli economies deserves closer scrutiny.
Moody’s first downgraded Israel from A1 to A2 in February 2024, roughly four months after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack triggered the war in Gaza. In September 2024, it cut Israel’s rating another two notches to Baa1, where it has remained.
Israel’s economy has nevertheless demonstrated considerable resilience, acknowledged in assessments by the International Monetary Fund, the international institution that monitors economies and provides financial assistance to member countries.
France, meanwhile, has struggled with weak growth, substantial budget deficits, and political resistance to efforts to repair its public finances. Protests and unrest have added to the pressure on its government.
The question is whether the size of the ratings gap adequately reflects those competing realities.
A substantial gap in growth, debt
Consider economic output per person, a widely used measure of a country’s average prosperity.
According to the IMF figures cited here, Israel’s nominal GDP per capita is expected to reach approximately $72,400 in 2026, compared with about $51,400 in France. These figures measure output in current US dollars and are influenced by exchange rates; they do not directly measure household income or purchasing power.
The growth forecasts also differ sharply. The IMF projects Israeli economic growth of approximately 4.5% this year, while the Bank of Israel, the country’s central bank, forecasts 5.6%.
France’s economy is expected to expand by approximately 0.4%, according to both the IMF and the Banque de France, the French central bank.
Rapid growth after a wartime slowdown requires context. Some of that expansion can reflect the recovery of activity lost during the conflict. Still, growth strengthens a government’s tax base and can make its debt easier to manage. Prolonged stagnation makes those tasks harder.
The debt comparison is particularly striking.
France’s public debt stands at approximately 118.5% of its annual economic output and is approaching 120%. Israel’s debt-to-GDP ratio is approximately 68.6%.
In practical terms, France owes more than the value of everything its economy produces in a year. Israel’s debt amounts to roughly two-thirds of its annual output.
Neither figure alone determines whether a country can repay its creditors. Financing costs, the maturity of outstanding debt, and investor confidence also matter. Nevertheless, the difference is substantial.
France’s budget deficit, the gap between government spending and revenue, exceeds 5% of GDP. Israel’s reported deficit stood at approximately 3.2% as of September.
These figures raise a reasonable question about how Moody’s weighs France’s fiscal vulnerabilities against Israel’s security risks.
How much confidence should promises command?
In affirming France’s rating, Moody’s cited plans for €52 billion in spending cuts.
Delivering those savings requires political support. French governments have faced sustained opposition to pension changes, spending restraint, and other measures intended to stabilize public finances.
France enacted a pension reform in 2023 that provided for a gradual increase in the retirement age from 62 to 64. Subsequent legislation suspended the increases until 2028, illustrating the difficulty of sustaining politically contentious reforms.
A credit assessment must therefore consider the likelihood that promised savings will materialize, as well as the government’s stated intentions.
Labor-market conditions offer another point of comparison. The figures cited here put French unemployment above 8.4%, compared with approximately 2.8% in Israel.
Israel’s low unemployment rate suggests a tight labor market, although wartime labor shortages and military reserve service complicate the picture. Its economy has shown an ability to adapt under extraordinary pressure. That capacity should carry meaningful weight in any assessment of its creditworthiness.
France also benefits from its membership in the eurozone, the group of countries using the euro. Its access to a large common-currency financial market is relevant to its ability to finance debt and helps explain why a simple comparison of national economic indicators cannot tell the whole story.
The issue is how these advantages and vulnerabilities are balanced.
What bond markets can tell us
Government bond yields provide another perspective. They show the return investors demand to lend money to a state.
The figures cited here put the yield on French 10-year government bonds at 5.05%, compared with approximately 4.06%-4.18% for Israeli bonds of the same maturity.
That comparison requires care. French government bonds are generally denominated in euros, while the Israeli domestic benchmark is denominated in shekels. Their yields reflect different interest-rate and inflation expectations, alongside credit risk and other factors.
The yield gap alone therefore cannot establish that investors consider France more likely to default. A stronger comparison would examine borrowing costs on a comparable currency basis or other market measures of sovereign credit risk.
Even with those qualifications, Israel’s economic resilience and France’s fiscal difficulties warrant a fuller explanation of the ratings gap.
Moody’s may reasonably place considerable weight on Israel’s exposure to war and regional instability. It should also explain clearly how it weighs those risks against Israel’s lower debt burden, stronger growth prospects, and demonstrated capacity to withstand disruption.
Credit ratings carry practical consequences for governments, businesses, and taxpayers. A four-notch difference deserves an explanation grounded in evidence that investors and the public can examine.

Jewish Futures 2026 conference to explore how AI could reshape Jewish education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:13:04 UTC
03:13:04 KST

The Jewish Education Project will host its annual conference, Jewish Futures 2026: ‘Becoming Tomorrow’s Educators,’ at Temple Emanu-El in New York City on Monday.
The event will convene Jewish educators and thought leaders to examine how artificial intelligence and emerging technologies are changing how young people learn, connect, and process information, as well as how the role of educators must evolve alongside these shifts.
Participants at the conference will take part in an interactive exercise called “Tzomet Games: Shaping the Jewish Future,” where teams will evaluate potential scenarios for Jewish life in 2050.
The program is designed to help participants identify upcoming challenges, experiment with new methods of learning, and determine which foundational elements of Jewish education remain essential regardless of technological advancement.
The Jewish Education Project stressed that educators must take an active role in responding to modern technological developments.
Jewish education cannot react to changes in technology
“We are living through extraordinary changes in how young people encounter information and make meaning,” said Samantha Vinokor-Meinrath, Senior Director of Knowledge, Ideas and Learning at The Jewish Education Project.
“Jewish education cannot simply react to those changes after they happen. Our responsibility is to help educators understand what is coming, experiment with new possibilities, and also identify the deeply human elements of education that technology can never replace. Jewish Futures is about giving educators the opportunity to help shape that future rather than simply adjust to it.”
The conference will feature a keynote address by technology entrepreneur Sam Glassenberg, called “The Jewish Neuron at Play: What Games and AI Can Teach Us about Learning, Identity, and Our Kids’ Future.” Glassenberg, who leads Emerging Healthtech Initiatives at Sheba Medical Center in Israel and previously served as CEO of FTX Games and founder of Level Ex, will examine what educators can learn from systems built to capture attention.
Drawing on game design, neuroscience, and AI, he will explore how games instruct through challenge, feedback, and reward, and how emerging AI tools offer new ways to examine Jewish history and identity, ranging from analyzing the Cairo Geniza to mapping the Jewish genome.
The event will conclude with an interactive session titled “Educators Assemble!” led by Shoshana Bloom, an ICF PCC-certified coach and speaker who specializes in addressing burnout, overwhelm, imposter syndrome, and procrastination.
Bloom will guide participants in identifying their individual strengths, examining how those traits complement fellow educators, and converting the conference’s discussions about future challenges into actionable steps.

Netanyahu warns of sanctions, opponents warn of collapse: Who's scaring voters? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:12:37 UTC
03:12:37 KST

In the wake of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s comments on Friday about the possibility of using cryptocurrency to bypass economic sanctions, one thing is clear: someone is engaging in fearmongering just a few days before the election.
The question is: Who is trying to frighten whom?
Is it Netanyahu trying to frighten the public? At least that was the instant interpretation of some pundits after he discussed the matter on Friday in an interview with economic journalist Roy Katz on the Channel 10 economic program.
But the full context matters.
Katz asked whether Netanyahu was worried about the day after US President Donald Trump. Netanyahu answered, “Tell me, you’re not worried?”
After saying that the billions of dollars in US military aid would soon come to an end because the US had changed, Netanyahu added that Israel needed to understand that sanctions, including banking sanctions, were possible.
“So you need to organize a bypass economy,” Netanyahu said. “You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that.”
In looking at those comments, it is important to distinguish between what Netanyahu said and what was subsequently attributed to him.
He did not present a crypto economy as his preferred option. He presented it as a contingency plan in the drawer for that rainy day.
Preparing for such contingencies is part of a government’s job. It does not mean that Jerusalem has thrown up its hands, resigned itself to widespread sanctions, and begun planning to disconnect Israel from the global economy.
It means that if the country faces not a rainy day but a deluge of sanctions, the government wants something in the drawer to try to bypass them.
Whether that something would work is a legitimate question. But it is a different question from whether Netanyahu wants to lead Israel into economic isolation.
'Bibicoin' a threat to national security
Because Netanyahu’s campaigns have long warned of the diplomatic and military dangers awaiting the country if voters fail to support Likud, many in the media immediately saw this as the familiar pattern: he was scaring the public again.
But it was not exactly clear how telling voters that Israel could face economic isolation after years under Netanyahu’s leadership was supposed to draw them to his side. What was clear, however, was the frightening picture his opponents painted in response.
Yashar party head Gadi Eisenkot called the “Bibicoin vision” a threat to national security – inflating a remark about a contingency plan into a full-blown vision.
“After he finished dismantling Israeli society and weakening the IDF, Netanyahu has marked the next target: the dismantling of the Israeli economy for generations to come.”
Marked the next target? Netanyahu spoke about preparing for possible sanctions. Eisenkot turned that into an intention to dismantle the economy.
And then came the warning that if Netanyahu’s “vision” were implemented, “Israelis will lose their pensions and all their investments, and many of them will leave the country.”
Talk about trying to scare the voters.
Naftali Bennett, too, got into the act, not to be outdone by his rival in the change bloc.
“In [Netanyahu’s] view, Israel will become a withdrawn and outcast country in the world, disconnected from the economy, academia, and the global technology, so that we will be forced to move to a crypto and isolated economy,” he said.
The problem is that this is not what Netanyahu said. He did not say this was the future he wanted, or even that it would happen. He said Israel needed to prepare in case sanctions were imposed.
Those statements are quite different. The opposition’s responses simply erased what was originally said.
Bank of Israel says cryptocurrencies cannot circumvent sanctions
The Bank of Israel also weighed in, giving the controversy the added authority of the country’s central bank. It said cryptocurrencies could not be used to circumvent sanctions.
That is a substantive objection. If the proposed contingency plan cannot work, the public should know.
But the bank did not stop there.
“The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy,” its statement said. “This is the responsibility of the political leadership, and it should act upon it.”
Of course that is the right course. But who said otherwise?
By setting out that course as a corrective to Netanyahu’s remarks, the bank lent weight to the impression that he had proposed abandoning it: that instead of maintaining Israel’s economic ties and preventing sanctions, the prime minister was preparing to retreat into a crypto economy.
Yet saying that the government is working on a contingency plan does not mean it has raised the white flag on sanctions. Nor does it mean that Israel will stop working diplomatically to prevent them.
Then came a group of 109 senior economists, the Economists’ Forum for Democracy, which emerged from the 2023 protests against the judicial reforms, with a warning that banking sanctions would bring something approaching economic apocalypse.
This, they said, would pertain to soaring unemployment, the disappearance of foreign investment, a collapse in Israel’s global economic standing, unusable credit cards, no access to online retailers such as Amazon, and a mass departure of foreign workers unable to send money home.
And Netanyahu was the one accused of frightening the public.
The consequences of sweeping banking sanctions would plainly be serious. But discussing a fallback plan does not mean Netanyahu is announcing that sanctions are coming, much less choosing to bring them about, and presenting his remarks that way is itself peddling fear.
None of this requires accepting that Netanyahu is above doing the same to win votes. Those looking for examples need not look far.
On Sunday, he shared an AI-generated image on X/Twitter depicting a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, alongside a post by right-wing commentator Yuval Bloomberg warning that failing to elect a leader capable of confronting Iran could risk a “second Holocaust.”
A nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv. A second Holocaust. Days before an election.
That is fearmongering, and it deserves to be called out.
But so does taking a contingency plan, calling it a vision, and warning voters that it will cost them their pensions, their investments, and their access to AliExpress.
The opposition has enough real examples of Netanyahu’s fearmongering without manufacturing another, and then engaging in its own version of spreading fear.

Caretaker oil minister heads to Moscow for GECF meeting

03:09:51 KST

Hamid Bovard will also take part in the group's 28th ministerial meeting, scheduled for Monday, a day before the leaders' summit, oil ministry's news service reported.
Preparatory sessions began Sunday. An extraordinary meeting of the forum's Executive Board, chaired by Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, the Oil Ministry's deputy for international affairs and trade, and a meeting of a high-level ad hoc panel were held to review and finalize key documents, including the summit's final statement.
The forum is an intergovernmental body for dialogue and coordination among natural gas producers and exporters. Its summits and ministerial meetings focus on gas market developments, supply and demand outlooks, energy security and the role of natural gas in the global energy mix. Members also discuss gas market development, trends in liquefied natural gas and the investment needed to meet future demand.
Leaders' summits are held every two years. The first took place in Doha, Qatar, in 2011, followed by Moscow in 2013, Tehran in 2015, Santa Cruz, Bolivia, in 2017, Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, in 2019, Doha in 2022 and Algiers in 2024. The forum has held 27 ministerial meetings since its founding.
It has 12 full members: Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Iran, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Russia, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru and Senegal are observers.
According to figures cited by the forum, members together hold about 70% of the world's proven natural gas reserves, 38% of commercial gas production and 42% of gas exports. Their share of global LNG exports is estimated at about 47%.

Moscow to host 2030 International Weightlifting Championships following lifting of Olympic suspensions
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced on Oct. 25 that the 2030 International Weightlifting Championships will be held in Moscow.
Recognized by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the IWF will be the first Olympic organization to hold a competition in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Concerning the IWF (Senior) World Championships in 2029, it will be staged in Ahmedabad (India), and Moscow (Russia) will host the 2030 edition," the IWF said on its website.
Between its nationwide doping scandal and international outcry over its war with Ukraine, Russia has remained largely sidelined from participating in the Olympics and related competitions since 2017.
On July 7, the IOC provisionally lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC), which had been in place since October 2023. The IOC said on July 7 that the decision followed a legal review that found the ROC "no longer includes as its members any regional sports organizations in territories falling under the jurisdiction of the National Olympic Committee (NOC) of Ukraine."
In response, a group of nine European countries urged the European Commission to halt funding programs for international sports organizations allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete. Ukraine's NOC subsequently appealed the IOC's decision for arbitration.
On Oct 14, Dutch authorities refused to grant visas to three Russian gymnasts, preventing them from taking part in the world gymnastics championships held in Rotterdam later that month.
Previously, Moscow hosted the World Weightlifting Championships in 1983. Since the fall of the Soviet Union, Russia has won a total of 17 medals in Olympic weightlifting competitions. In order to compete internationally, all Russian athletes will have to meet anti-doping requirements set by the IOC.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

Netanyahu lobbying Trump for more election support: report
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked US President Donald Trump to provide additional support for his election campaign ahead of Israel's Knesset vote, Israel's Channel 2 reported on Sunday.
The channel cited a US source familiar with the details and a separate Israeli source who had been briefed on the matter, saying Netanyahu had stepped up his contacts with Trump in recent days in an effort to secure new statements supporting his continued tenure as prime minister.
The US source told the channel that Netanyahu had spoken with Trump twice over the previous three days and asked him to strengthen the endorsement he had expressed the previous week on the Truth Social platform. The source added that Netanyahu had personally proposed wording for additional statements of support that the US president could issue before the election.
The channel also quoted an Israeli source briefed on the communications as saying that Netanyahu had suggested Trump make phone calls to Israeli journalists to express his support for him, in an attempt to amplify the US president’s position during the final days of the election campaign.
According to the US source, White House officials view Netanyahu’s repeated attempts to secure additional support as a “sign of desperation” and an indication that the Israeli prime minister believes he is trailing in the electoral race.
The Likud Party, however, denied the report, insisting that Netanyahu had not asked Trump for any support, either in recent days or before Trump first announced his endorsement. The Israeli prime minister’s office declined to comment, while the White House had not immediately responded to the channel’s request for comment.
Regarding the White House’s calculations, the channel quoted a US official as saying that Trump’s support for Netanyahu could serve the US president’s interests regardless of the election outcome. If Netanyahu wins or remains prime minister in a caretaker government, Trump could claim credit for politically rescuing him and use that leverage to pressure him into making concessions.
If Netanyahu loses and his rivals succeed in forming a new government, its leaders would have an interest in maintaining good relations with Trump, potentially diminishing the significance of his support for their opponent. The channel noted that some of Trump’s advisers see an opportunity to advance his Middle East agenda through an Israeli government led by someone other than Netanyahu, despite the close relationship between the two men, which has also experienced periods of tension.
On October 18, US President Donald Trump announced his full support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Knesset elections, following weeks of hesitation about publicly taking a position. On Truth Social, Trump suggested that electing a different prime minister could affect cooperation between the United States and Israel, particularly on confronting Iran. He described Netanyahu as a key partner for Washington.

Separately, Russia also struck a bulk freighter in the Black Sea that was carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port city of Chernomorsk, the ministry added. The attacks were part of a broader operation that involved strikes on Ukrainian energy and transport infrastructure used to support the military, as well as drone storages and launch sites in a total of 159 locations over the past 24 hours.
Ukrainian officials confirmed strikes on the city of Kharkov, adding that an “industrial facility” was among the targets.
Russia has intensified its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial and logistics facilities in response to Kiev’s continued attacks on the Russian civilian and energy infrastructure. Moscow has repeatedly condemned the Ukrainian attacks as “terrorist acts” aimed at compensating for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the nation’s air defense systems intercepted a total of 532 Ukrainian drones during Sunday night alone. The drones were used in attempted attacks on more than two dozen Russian regions, the ministry stated.
Ukraine’s tactics have led to tension between Kiev and Washington. US President Donald Trump stated recently it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” and find a new person to negotiate peace instead of Vladimir Zelensky, whose presidential term expired more than two years ago. The American president also questioned the Ukrainian leader’s willingness to reach a deal with Moscow and criticized him for continued strikes on Russian oil refineries despite Washington’s repeated requests to stop.
Zelensky has said that Ukraine’s Western backers failed to provide advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches twice in one week in October. He maintained however, that cooperation between Kiev and Washington had not been suspended, echoing Trump’s earlier remarks in which he said the US is “helping [Ukraine], and we are sharing intel.”
In the meantime, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Kiev of abusing his company’s Starlink civilian satellite internet network to launch offensive drone strikes. According to the US-based businessman, a “loophole” allowing the Ukrainian forces to do so was closed.
