Young adults who fear rejection also tend to fear death more, psychology study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:00:32 UTC
03:00:32 KST

Young adults who are especially worried about rejection in their close relationships tend to report a greater fear of death, which in turn is linked to more symptoms of anxiety, depression, and other forms of distress, according to a new study published in Scientific Reports. The findings also suggest that for several types of symptoms, this link depends on whether a person views death as the complete end of their existence or as a transition to another state.
Death anxiety refers to the worry, dread, or apprehension that comes from knowing that human life eventually ends. While it is normal to think about mortality from time to time, many psychologists now view persistent or poorly managed fear of death as a shared factor underlying many different mental health conditions. It can show up as panic or constant worry in anxiety disorders, feelings of hopelessness in depression, repetitive rituals aimed at preventing harm in obsessive-compulsive disorder, or extreme worry about physical sensations in somatic symptom disorders.
These existential concerns often become especially prominent during emerging adulthood, the developmental period spanning the late teens and twenties. As young people build their independent identities and confront major life transitions, they frequently grapple with questions about meaning and mortality, with prior research showing that fear of death tends to peak during a person’s twenties.
How well a young adult copes with the reality of mortality has been linked to their attachment style, which is the characteristic way a person relates to others in close relationships based on their internal sense of self-worth and their trust in other people. Psychologists often categorize adult attachment into four patterns: secure (positive view of both self and others), preoccupied (negative view of self, positive view of others), dismissing (positive view of self, negative view of others), and fearful (negative view of both self and others).
People with a secure attachment style generally manage stress well and turn to loved ones for comfort. In contrast, those with insecure styles rely on less helpful strategies to regulate their emotions, and a 2025 meta-analysis of 18 studies found that adults with higher attachment anxiety or attachment avoidance consistently report a greater fear of death.
Individuals with a preoccupied attachment style tend to experience high attachment anxiety, meaning they are overly sensitive to rejection and abandonment, which can amplify their distress when thinking about death. Those with a dismissing style exhibit high attachment avoidance, meaning they prize extreme independence and suppress their emotional needs, often trying to push thoughts of mortality out of their awareness.
Beyond relationship patterns, how a person fundamentally defines death also shapes how they handle existential fear. In psychology, this belief is called the ontological representation of death, which captures what a person believes happens to their core identity when they die. Some people view death as total annihilation, meaning the absolute and permanent extinction of the self. Others view death as a passage, meaning a transition to another form of existence, whether through a literal afterlife or a symbolic legacy that allows some part of their identity to continue.
The research, led by Alessandro Musetti, an associate professor of dynamic psychology in the Department of Humanities, Social Sciences and Cultural Industries at the University of Parma in Italy, examined how these relational and existential factors work together. Psychologists use the term internalizing symptoms for inward-directed problems such as depression, anxiety, obsessive thoughts, and unexplained physical complaints.
“Death anxiety is increasingly recognized as a factor involved in many forms of psychological distress, including anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and somatic complaints,” Musetti told PsyPost. “However, we still know relatively little about why some people are more vulnerable to death anxiety than others, and why death anxiety seems to affect some individuals more strongly. We wanted to integrate attachment theory with existential psychology by examining whether attachment styles are linked to internalizing symptoms through death anxiety, and whether this process depends on how people fundamentally represent death, either as total annihilation or as a form of passage or continuity.”
To investigate this, the researchers analyzed data from 640 Italian young adults between the ages of 18 and 22, with an average age of about 20.5 years. The sample was predominantly female (83.4 percent) and consisted mostly of students (62.7 percent) or working students (28.8 percent). In terms of religious views, 39.1 percent identified as agnostic, 30.6 percent as atheist, and 30.3 percent as religious believers.
Participants, recruited through social media, completed a series of online questionnaires. To measure attachment styles, the researchers used the Relationship Questionnaire, which asks participants to rate on a 1-to-7 scale how well four short paragraphs describing secure, dismissing, preoccupied, and fearful attachment patterns apply to them. Death anxiety was measured using a 15-item true-or-false questionnaire that included statements like “I am very much afraid to die.”
Participants also completed the Testoni Death Representation Scale, which uses six items rated on a 1-to-5 scale to determine the degree to which a person views death as a passage versus definitive annihilation. Finally, the researchers assessed four types of internalizing mental health symptoms over the prior two weeks: depression, anxiety, somatic symptoms (such as unexplained physical aches and pains), and obsessive-compulsive symptoms (repetitive unpleasant thoughts or urges).
The researchers used a statistical technique called conditional process analysis, which tests whether an indirect pathway between two variables changes depending on a third factor, while controlling for gender. In the initial look at how attachment related to fear of mortality, participants scored an average of 9.31 out of 15 on the death anxiety scale. Higher scores on preoccupied attachment were associated with higher death anxiety, whereas higher scores on dismissing attachment were associated with lower reported death anxiety.
Secure and fearful attachment styles were not linked to death anxiety once all four styles were considered together. The finding for dismissing attachment differs from the 2025 meta-analysis described earlier, which linked attachment avoidance to greater fear of death. The authors suggest that people with a dismissing style may push death-related thoughts out of awareness rather than feel less threatened by mortality.
When looking at how death anxiety connected to mental health, the researchers found that a participant’s view of death played a moderating role for three of the four symptom categories. Death anxiety was linked to worse anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, and somatic symptoms, but only among young adults who strongly viewed death as total annihilation. For participants who viewed death as a passage to another state of existence, higher death anxiety was not linked to higher levels of these three symptom types.
Consequently, the indirect pathways linking attachment styles to these three symptoms operated only among those holding annihilation beliefs. For young adults who believed death is the complete end of existence, having a preoccupied attachment style was indirectly linked to greater anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, and somatic symptoms through heightened death anxiety.
Among those same annihilation-believing participants, by contrast, a dismissing attachment style had a negative indirect association with anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, and somatic symptoms because these individuals reported lower death anxiety. However, the authors caution against interpreting a dismissing attachment style as psychologically healthy. When looking at direct relationships outside of the death anxiety pathway, dismissing attachment was directly linked to higher levels of unexplained somatic symptoms, which the authors suggest may indicate that suppressing emotions and relationship needs can contribute to physical complaints even when conscious fear of death is kept at bay.
Depression followed a different pattern than the other three mental health domains. Whether a participant viewed death as total annihilation or as a passage did not alter the link between death anxiety and depressive symptoms. Instead, preoccupied attachment was indirectly associated with greater depressive symptoms through increased death anxiety across the board, regardless of what the person believed happens after death. Additionally, preoccupied and fearful attachment styles were directly linked to worse symptoms in all four mental health categories, while secure attachment was directly associated with lower depression and anxiety.
“Our findings suggest that psychological distress is influenced not only by how people relate to others, but also by how they make sense of their own mortality,” Musetti explained. “At the same time, the way people understand death appears to matter: when death is experienced as the complete end of personal existence, death anxiety seems more strongly connected to several forms of psychological distress.”
“One finding that surprised us was that the ontological representation of death mattered for anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, and somatic symptoms, but not for depressive symptoms,” Musetti noted. “This suggests that depression may be connected to existential concerns through somewhat different mechanisms than other forms of psychological distress.”
The findings are consistent with research by Musetti and colleagues covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that death anxiety and feelings of relational disconnectedness helped explain the link between attachment anxiety and problematic social media use. Both studies indicate that fear of mortality helps explain how insecure attachment is linked to psychological difficulties, though the earlier study focused on problematic social media habits across a wide adult age range while the new research examined internalizing mental health symptoms in young adults.
The depression results also align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2023, which examined broader existential anxiety and meaning in life among adult mental health professionals rather than death anxiety and attachment styles in emerging adults, and similarly found that existential anxiety helped explain the link between lower meaning in life and more severe depressive symptoms.
Musetti pointed out that the statistical relationships uncovered in the study should be kept in perspective. “The effects were statistically significant but generally modest in magnitude, which is common when studying complex psychological phenomena,” he said. “We are not suggesting that attachment style or death anxiety alone determine mental health outcomes. Rather, our findings indicate that existential concerns may be one piece of a broader psychological puzzle that includes relational experiences, emotional regulation, personality, and social context.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because all the survey data were collected at a single point in time, the study cannot establish cause and effect. While psychological theory suggests that attachment patterns develop early and shape later fears and symptoms, it is also possible that experiencing depression or anxiety makes a young person feel more insecure in their relationships or more frightened of dying.
“A key caveat is that this was a cross-sectional study,” Musetti emphasized. “The findings identify associations that are consistent with a theoretically grounded model, but longitudinal research is needed to clarify causal pathways. Additionally, representing death as a passage should not be interpreted simply as being religious. The construct we studied concerns a person’s fundamental understanding of what happens to the self after death and cannot be reduced to religious affiliation alone.”
There are a few other limitations to keep in mind. Over 83 percent of the participants were young Italian women, and most were students, meaning the results may not generalize equally to men, older adults, or people from different cultural and religious backgrounds where views on death and the afterlife differ. Participants were recruited through social media and word of mouth rather than randomly selected, and the authors note that mediation analyses based on a single time point can overstate indirect pathways. In addition, the researchers relied on brief self-report screening tools rather than clinical interviews, and the two-item measures for depression and somatic symptoms showed only modest internal consistency.
Future studies could track diverse groups of young people over several years to confirm the order in which attachment insecurities, existential beliefs, and mental health symptoms develop. The authors suggest, though this was not tested, that clinicians working with young adults who have a preoccupied attachment style and view death as total annihilation might combine relationship-focused therapy with existential approaches that help build a sense of meaning and continuity, as long as such approaches respect a person’s own worldview.
“One important next step is to examine these relationships longitudinally to better understand how attachment, death anxiety, and psychological symptoms influence one another over time,” Musetti added. “We are also interested in studying whether similar processes operate across different age groups and cultural contexts, since beliefs about death are deeply shaped by culture and life experience.”
The study, “Adult Attachment, Death Anxiety, Representation of Death, and Depression, Anxiety, Obsessive-compulsive, and Somatic Symptoms in Emerging Adulthood: A Moderated Mediation Model,” was authored by Alessandro Musetti, Andrea Zagaria, Vittorio Lenzo, Gianluca Santoro, and Adriano Schimmenti.

Albanese faces stark choice if Trump escalates Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Disquiet among Labor MPs over Trump's Iran war a headache for Albanese
Twenty-three years ago, Anthony Albanese was a newish opposition frontbencher. That year was significant, not for the contribution he made as shadow minister for employment services and training (though he may argue otherwise), but for speaking out against a war he thought was wrong.
Albanese wasn't alone in his opposition; his colleague and longtime leadership rival Tanya Plibersek also said the Iraq war set a dangerous precedent for the world. Together they joined more than 40 senators and Labor MPs who signed an open letter to then US president George W Bush.
Admittedly these Labor MPs were in opposition, but it wasn't just one lone voice breaking ranks. It was 41 MPs. Imagine these same MPs and how they would respond if Donald Trump were around and said we "may do another little Epic Fury", as he did last week, as if it was a trivial game.
Blunting parts of the old brawler
Plibersek said at the time: "We wanted to let him know that there were many people in Australia, including the Labor Party, who didn't support the war in Iraq and we wanted him to know the reasons why."
The letter, which said the pre-emptive military action made the world more dangerous, rather than more secure, was not the only example of Albanese speaking out against the conflict.
In the first month of the conflict, in March 2003, Albanese delivered a speech in parliament that reflected his aggressive, left-wing pugilist style, earning him the nickname "the Marrickville Brawler".
"Our government is about to redefine us in the eyes of the world as willing backers of US militarism. The prime minister took a phone call and immediately said yes to President Bush, because we all know that that decision was made many months ago, before the pre-deployment of troops. We were not even at the meeting where the decision was made."
He went on to say: "We are, with this decision, supporting a pre-emptive strike, which changes forever the way that international politics works."
Albanese did acknowledge the need for regime change; it was the method that Labor opposed, not the sentiment.
Now Albanese is prime minister and a lot has changed. He begins this parliamentary sitting week with Trump saying the US may carry out another military operation against Iran at a time when the war is nearing its eighth month, and rising fuel prices dominate the US midterm elections.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," the president said at a rally in Florida last week as he spoke about the war. He did not elaborate. Operation Epic Fury is the name used by the US military for its war against Iran.
As John Maynard Keynes is often credited with saying: "When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?"
Everyone grows up, grows older and learns in Canberra that the politics of passion give way to the business of governing and pragmatism.
Those around Albanese know the prime ministership is a job he has wanted for a long time, and one he almost never had after Bill Shorten defeated him in Labor's leadership ballot in 2013.
And while Albanese loves being PM, and loves reminding the media, the opposition and his own colleagues of the record 94-seat majority he secured at the last election, running a government has required him to blunt parts of the old brawler.
Now another American president is threatening to escalate a war that is smashing the economy, and this time Albanese has his phone number and doesn't have to sign a letter to get his views across.
The Labor backbench has been muted during the past eight months of this war, but will it remain muted if Trump escalates the war again?
Ongoing war Labor's next pinch point
In the past few weeks, the Labor backbench has become slightly more vocal, although this is coming off a low base. But a new escalation in this ongoing war is likely to be the next pinch point.
When Trump launched a joint offensive with Israel attacking Iran in February, Albanese, supported by Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Defence Minister Richard Marles, issued a statement supporting the action. The statement cited the need to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and a need to protect Australians living in the region.
Back in February, the language was about a short, sharp attack. Like countless conflicts before it, this invasion has dragged on and even senior government figures admit to having no clue when it will end.
As it has dragged on, the cost hasn't just been felt in the Middle East. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent our government into a panic with low domestic fuel supplies and high bowser prices.
Some MPs will want Albanese to condemn Trump over Iran and get some distance from an unpopular president. Labor's strategy at the last election was a veiled signalling that it was the anti-Trump party, that Peter Dutton was a Trump-like figure.
But without stronger language and action, that case will be hard to argue twice. The world is becoming less safe, and Australians are angry about it.
Loading
Every sign we're in uncharted waters
A feeling that the world is spinning out of control is fuelled by a sense of being the recipients of chaos and rarely the decision-makers. A more forceful position on Iran and the US is something Labor MPs have increasingly been hoping for.
In the UK, the fallout from wars in Ukraine and Iran and cyber attacks have led the government to change its language and warn that the uncertainty abroad must be planned for at a household level. This messaging is about control and a sense of agency. People feel they have no control, and some governments are trying to lean into accepting that reality.
A new government "be ready" campaign in the UK is urging the public to prepare for the disruption of everyday services and to stockpile three days of key supplies.
The checklist advises stocking up on bottled water and non-perishable food, a battery or wind-up FM radio to receive updates during outages, and cash in case electronic payments or cash machines are disrupted.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that there was not a "specific thing" in mind when it came to potential emergency incidents, but said the advice might help during power cuts or if a local shop was subject to a cyber attack and was a matter of "everyday national resilience".
Put to him by an audience member that it could be "scaremongering" and push people towards panic buying like during the COVID-19 pandemic, he said: "We want people to be alert but not alarmed, and the truth is we looked around the rest of Europe, what are our friends doing across the continent? They are way ahead of us on some of this stuff."
If Europe is ahead, where are we? We may be geographically isolated but we are not immune to a more unsafe world both economically and strategically.
Our government hasn't told us to start stockpiling yet, but there is every sign that we are in uncharted waters.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly, and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

One in three homicides fuelled by psychosis, as doctors fear growing crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Increase in homicides by people with psychosis due to failings in mental health system, experts warn
In short:
New data suggests 43 out of an estimated 126 homicides in Victoria in 2024 and 2025 (about one in three) were committed by people with psychosis.
Many of the deaths could have been prevented, doctors say, had the perpetrators received proper treatment.
What's next?
Experts have warned this is the result of serious failings in Victoria's mental health system, with some calling for a review of the royal commission's recommendations.
A fourfold increase in the number of homicides committed by people with psychotic disorders in Victoria is the result of catastrophic failings in the mental health system that are exposing the community to dangerous levels of risk, experts have warned.
Frustrated psychiatrists say the alarming uptick in killings by people with psychosis is a triple tragedy for perpetrators, victims and the wider public because many of the recent deaths could have been prevented had the offenders received proper treatment.
Some are also concerned the homicides are just the tip of an iceberg — the most extreme, most visible symptom of a deepening crisis that the mental health royal commission should have addressed but has not, and on some fronts may have exacerbated.
Data compiled by consultant forensic psychiatrist Rajan Darjee suggests 43 out of an estimated 126 homicides in Victoria in 2024 and 2025 — about one in three — were committed by people with psychosis, a significant increase from a decade ago, when one in 10 homicides a year were perpetrated by people with psychotic disorders.
Half of all stranger homicides in Victoria in the same period were committed by people with psychosis, Dr Darjee's research showed, as were two in three intimate partner and family homicides, raising questions about the adequacy of domestic violence prevention policies which emphasise addressing gender inequality and "disrespectful" attitudes.
"I remember looking at the raw number" — 43 homicides in two years, with 45 victims — "going, this is astounding," said Dr Darjee, clinical director of psychiatry at Forensic Behavioural Assessment and Consultation Services and adjunct professor at Swinburne University's Centre for Behavioural Science.
But perhaps the most important finding, he said, was that almost 84 per cent of homicide offenders in the sample had previously received treatment by mental health services, while half were connected with a service at the time of the incident.
'The public should not feel safe'
Psychosis is a set of psychological symptoms that impair a person's sense of reality. A central feature of schizophrenia spectrum disorders, it usually occurs in episodes that last days, months or even years and can include hallucinations, delusions, disordered thinking and disordered behaviour.
Though most people with psychotic disorders are never violent, there is a clear association between psychosis and violence. Australian and international studies also show people with psychotic illness are more likely to perpetrate homicide than people in the general population — a major reason why experts have long stressed the importance of effectively treating psychosis to reduce and prevent violence.
"If you treat people with psychosis early and effectively, you prevent poor outcomes later, including chronic mental ill-health, disengagement from family, not being able to work, homelessness … but also violence and aggression," Dr Darjee said.
Dr Darjee and his colleagues designed the study — which is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal — to understand whether their anecdotal observations were reflected in formal data.
He surveyed nine forensic psychiatrists who write defence reports for courts in Victoria about how many people they assessed in 2024 or 2025 who were charged with murder or manslaughter and diagnosed with psychosis, and whether they were connected with mental health services, among other details.
"It's terrible that 45 people have died, especially when you think the majority of those were probably preventable deaths," Dr Darjee said. "But the homicides are the tip of the iceberg. The bigger [part of the] iceberg underneath means that people with mental illness and their families are living lives that are much worse than they need to be."
Patrick McGorry, a psychiatrist who chaired the expert advisory committee for the Royal Commission into Victoria's Mental Health System, said the homicide data was the result of a "public policy failure" to build a modern system of care to replace the state's old psychiatric hospitals, which were decommissioned in the 1990s.
"What it shows is that people have had ineffective contact with mental health services," Professor McGorry said. "They've either tried to get access but have failed, or they've gained access but haven't been able to get effective treatment, which is what people with serious mental illness need. They get episodes of care rather than sustained, safety net-type treatment."
The royal commission, which ran from 2018 to 2021, was "largely a successful blueprint" to fix the system, he said, but the government "has not really invested properly in implementing its recommendations — every single one has been delayed or poorly implemented".
"I thought for sure the royal commission … would have led to a once-in-a-generation transformational reform — I was wrong," Professor McGorry said. "So I think the only thing … that will actually galvanise the public into demanding something is done is if they themselves don't feel safe. And the public should not feel safe in the context of the current mental health system."
Crucially, he added, most people with psychosis posed no harm when they were well. "It's the acute illness that has made them dangerous and so that's a tragedy — not just for their victims but for them personally — that they've been allowed to harm other people. And it's not a character problem, it's a health problem."
Compulsory treatment can be 'life-saving'
Several experts told ABC News they were particularly concerned about an anecdotal increase in the number of short-term admissions to mental health units when longer stays were generally required to stabilise patients with psychosis.
Many are also worried a royal commission recommendation to reduce the use and duration of compulsory treatment orders has contributed to a system-wide reluctance to use them, including in cases where they ought to be.
"With the best of intentions we've instigated these least restrictive care policies but they've become negligent," Dr Darjee said. "I don't like compelling people [into treatment], I always do it reluctantly, but sometimes it's life saving."
Forensicare chief executive and Swinburne University Adjunct Professor Colmán O'Driscoll agreed people should ideally be compelled to take psychiatric treatment only as a last resort. But he said the mental health system was at risk of "swinging the pendulum too far the other way" if people with psychosis are not being put on compulsory treatment orders when they need to be.
"We always think about these orders as a compulsion on the individual to receive care. In my view, a significant part of their benefit is that they compel the system to provide the care you deserve as a member of our community," Professor O'Driscoll said.
And given psychosis can affect people's ability to make "good decisions", he said, maintaining their engagement with treatment is crucial, and leads to better outcomes.
Australian studies have found people with psychosis are much more likely to be convicted of a violent criminal offence than the general population, but that early and frequent contact with mental health services reduces their risk of reoffending — and those on community treatment orders are less likely to reoffend than those who receive punitive sanctions.
"The starting point is finding a way to conceptualise violence among people with psychosis as a complication of their illness and therefore we should have a health system that sees the prevention of it as core to its work, not separate from it," Professor O'Driscoll said.
He said Victoria should invest more in programs that divert people with psychosis away from the criminal justice system into treatment programs, focus on improving patient engagement with such programs, and upskill the mental health workforce in violence risk assessment and management.
Some doctors also believe there is a trend in Victoria, particularly since the introduction of the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act in 2022, to view a wide spectrum of mental health and "wellbeing" issues as equally important, but that severe mental illness must be prioritised.
"I genuinely think that, even though the royal commission and what came after it hasn't been fully implemented, we need a wholesale review and almost a reversal of some of its recommendations," Dr Darjee said. "And I think in mental health policy and care there needs to be more emphasis on people with severe mental illness."
As long as nothing changed, he added: "We're just going to carry on having lots of people dying unnecessarily."
"I just don't think it's right for a relatively well-off jurisdiction like Victoria to be neglecting people with mental illness as much as we're neglecting them."
Minister for Mental Health Ingrid Stitt did not respond to specific questions but a government spokesperson told ABC News that Victoria's mental health system was focused on ensuring people with serious mental illness could access safe, compassionate treatment.
"Every homicide is a tragedy and while these incidents are rare, it's vital they're not used to stigmatise people living with mental ill-health," they said.
"The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act provides for compulsory assessment and treatment where the legal criteria are met, while recognising that compulsory treatment should only be used as a last resort."

Disquiet among Labor MPs over Trump's Iran war a headache for Albanese
Twenty-three years ago, Anthony Albanese was a newish opposition frontbencher. That year was significant, not for the contribution he made as shadow minister for employment services and training (though he may argue otherwise), but for speaking out against a war he thought was wrong.
Albanese wasn't alone in his opposition; his colleague and longtime leadership rival Tanya Plibersek also said the Iraq war set a dangerous precedent for the world. Together they joined more than 40 senators and Labor MPs who signed an open letter to then US president George W Bush.
Admittedly these Labor MPs were in opposition, but it wasn't just one lone voice breaking ranks. It was 41 MPs. Imagine these same MPs and how they would respond if Donald Trump were around and said we "may do another little Epic Fury", as he did last week, as if it was a trivial game.
Blunting parts of the old brawler
Plibersek said at the time: "We wanted to let him know that there were many people in Australia, including the Labor Party, who didn't support the war in Iraq and we wanted him to know the reasons why."
The letter, which said the pre-emptive military action made the world more dangerous, rather than more secure, was not the only example of Albanese speaking out against the conflict.
In the first month of the conflict, in March 2003, Albanese delivered a speech in parliament that reflected his aggressive, left-wing pugilist style, earning him the nickname "the Marrickville Brawler".
"Our government is about to redefine us in the eyes of the world as willing backers of US militarism. The prime minister took a phone call and immediately said yes to President Bush, because we all know that that decision was made many months ago, before the pre-deployment of troops. We were not even at the meeting where the decision was made."
He went on to say: "We are, with this decision, supporting a pre-emptive strike, which changes forever the way that international politics works."
Albanese did acknowledge the need for regime change; it was the method that Labor opposed, not the sentiment.
Now Albanese is prime minister and a lot has changed. He begins this parliamentary sitting week with Trump saying the US may carry out another military operation against Iran at a time when the war is nearing its eighth month, and rising fuel prices dominate the US midterm elections.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," the president said at a rally in Florida last week as he spoke about the war. He did not elaborate. Operation Epic Fury is the name used by the US military for its war against Iran.
As John Maynard Keynes is often credited with saying: "When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?"
Everyone grows up, grows older and learns in Canberra that the politics of passion give way to the business of governing and pragmatism.
Those around Albanese know the prime ministership is a job he has wanted for a long time, and one he almost never had after Bill Shorten defeated him in Labor's leadership ballot in 2013.
And while Albanese loves being PM, and loves reminding the media, the opposition and his own colleagues of the record 94-seat majority he secured at the last election, running a government has required him to blunt parts of the old brawler.
Now another American president is threatening to escalate a war that is smashing the economy, and this time Albanese has his phone number and doesn't have to sign a letter to get his views across.
The Labor backbench has been muted during the past eight months of this war, but will it remain muted if Trump escalates the war again?
Ongoing war Labor's next pinch point
In the past few weeks, the Labor backbench has become slightly more vocal, although this is coming off a low base. But a new escalation in this ongoing war is likely to be the next pinch point.
When Trump launched a joint offensive with Israel attacking Iran in February, Albanese, supported by Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Defence Minister Richard Marles, issued a statement supporting the action. The statement cited the need to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and a need to protect Australians living in the region.
Back in February, the language was about a short, sharp attack. Like countless conflicts before it, this invasion has dragged on and even senior government figures admit to having no clue when it will end.
As it has dragged on, the cost hasn't just been felt in the Middle East. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent our government into a panic with low domestic fuel supplies and high bowser prices.
Some MPs will want Albanese to condemn Trump over Iran and get some distance from an unpopular president. Labor's strategy at the last election was a veiled signalling that it was the anti-Trump party, that Peter Dutton was a Trump-like figure.
But without stronger language and action, that case will be hard to argue twice. The world is becoming less safe, and Australians are angry about it.
Loading
Every sign we're in uncharted waters
A feeling that the world is spinning out of control is fuelled by a sense of being the recipients of chaos and rarely the decision-makers. A more forceful position on Iran and the US is something Labor MPs have increasingly been hoping for.
In the UK, the fallout from wars in Ukraine and Iran and cyber attacks have led the government to change its language and warn that the uncertainty abroad must be planned for at a household level. This messaging is about control and a sense of agency. People feel they have no control, and some governments are trying to lean into accepting that reality.
A new government "be ready" campaign in the UK is urging the public to prepare for the disruption of everyday services and to stockpile three days of key supplies.
The checklist advises stocking up on bottled water and non-perishable food, a battery or wind-up FM radio to receive updates during outages, and cash in case electronic payments or cash machines are disrupted.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that there was not a "specific thing" in mind when it came to potential emergency incidents, but said the advice might help during power cuts or if a local shop was subject to a cyber attack and was a matter of "everyday national resilience".
Put to him by an audience member that it could be "scaremongering" and push people towards panic buying like during the COVID-19 pandemic, he said: "We want people to be alert but not alarmed, and the truth is we looked around the rest of Europe, what are our friends doing across the continent? They are way ahead of us on some of this stuff."
If Europe is ahead, where are we? We may be geographically isolated but we are not immune to a more unsafe world both economically and strategically.
Our government hasn't told us to start stockpiling yet, but there is every sign that we are in uncharted waters.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly, and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

Israeli bulldozing destroys olive groves in S. Syria
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:56:10 CST
02:56:10 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 25, 2026 shows a view of Jabata al-Khashab in the countryside of Quneitra province, Syria. (Str/Xinhua)
QUNEITRA, Syria, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Israeli forces continued bulldozing agricultural land in Syria's southern province of Quneitra on Sunday, damaging olive groves that local farmers depend on for their livelihoods.
Syria's state news agency SANA reported that the operations were part of construction work on what Israel calls the "Sufa 53" line, involving a military road and a network of fortifications and observation positions along areas adjacent to the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
The route runs through or near several areas of Quneitra and lies within territory covered by the 1974 disengagement arrangements, which established a UN-monitored area of separation between Syrian and Israeli forces following the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, according to the SANA report.
SANA had earlier reported that Israeli forces bulldozed around 13 dunams of olive groves near Saida al-Hanout, a village close to the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights. Residents there have been collecting olives from severed trees piled in their courtyards.
"These olive trees are our livelihood. They support an entire family," Mohammad Ali al-Sawwar, a 60-year-old olive farmer, told Xinhua. "We are not employees who receive salaries every month. We earn our income only once a year."
Al-Sawwar said around 400 olive trees had been damaged or destroyed.
60-year-old farmer Awad al-Sawwar estimated that tanks had bulldozed around 20 dunams of productive olive groves, yet insisted residents would stay.
"We have no intention of leaving it, no matter what happens or how much pressure they put on us," he said.
In Jabata al-Khashab town, Hassan Ahmad, a 50-year-old farmer, said bulldozing operations had destroyed 10 dunams of his olive grove, or more than 400 olive trees, and a livestock shelter, depriving his family of an important source of income during the harvest season.
Ahmad also described continuing insecurity in Quneitra, saying residents still experienced the sounds of shelling, illuminating flares at night, and forest fires.
SANA also reported on Sunday that Israeli military vehicles entered northern Quneitra, setting up a temporary checkpoint and searching passersby before withdrawing.
The bulldozing comes amid continuing Israeli military activity in southern Syria following the collapse of the former Syrian government in December 2024. Syria has repeatedly condemned Israeli incursions on its territory as violations of its sovereignty and the 1974 disengagement agreement. ■

Israel Election 2026: What does Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar stand for?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:55:55 UTC
02:55:55 KST

Yashar, founded in September 2025, is one of many vying for citizens’ votes in the elections for the 26th Knesset, which will be held on October 27.
Led by Gadi Eisenkot, Yashar occupies the political center and currently leads the polls, making the former IDF chief of staff the top contender to lead the next government and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Eisenkot entered politics in August 2022 through Benny Gantz’s National Unity alliance, which brought together Gantz’s Blue and White and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar’s New Hope, taking third place on the list.
Although Eisenkot initially ruled out serving under Netanyahu, he and Gantz joined the emergency government after the October 7 massacre. Gantz became a member of the war cabinet, while Eisenkot served as an observer. Both left the government in June 2024, accusing Netanyahu’s leadership of failing to make the strategic decisions needed to achieve the war’s objectives.
In July 2025, Eisenkot left National Unity and resigned from the Knesset, citing the need for a transparent and democratic process for selecting the party's candidates. He said he wanted to build a broader leadership alternative capable of defeating the government, arguing that National Unity had failed to implement the internal reforms he sought.
Two months later, he founded Yashar alongside former politicians, senior security figures, and other public figures, presenting it as a broad alternative focused on Israel's security, national interests, and democratic character.
Yashar did not exist in the 25th Knesset, but the party has quickly risen through the ranks to become the leading party in the polls, which predict the party to win some 21-23 seats.
Confronting Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah while opposing Palestinian statehood
Yashar places national security at the center of its platform, reflecting Eisenkot’s background as a former IDF chief. The party’s foreign policy focuses on confronting Iran, dismantling Hamas’s rule in Gaza, containing Hezbollah in Lebanon, and determining the future of Palestinian governance and security arrangements.
Yashar presents Iran as a continuing strategic threat. Eisenkot himself has favored a lasting, verifiable resolution of Iran’s nuclear threat.
If diplomacy fails, his proposals include US-enforced restrictions around remaining enriched-uranium sites and wider covert action against Iran’s missile capabilities.
On Gaza, the party’s stated approach combines replacing Hamas with retaining an Israeli security corridor. Eisenkot would also allow reconstruction to advance incrementally alongside partial disarmament. Earlier in October, Eisenkot pledged to destroy Hamas’s military wing and dismantle its leadership within 18 months.
In Lebanon, Eisenkot supports a security zone while seeking stronger American and French involvement in efforts to confront Hezbollah.
Regarding Palestinian statehood, Eisenkot has opposed establishing a Palestinian state, though he told The Jerusalem Post he would consider the Palestinian Authority preferable to continued Hamas rule if those are the alternatives.
On settlements, he told the Post he would return Civil Administration responsibilities to military coordination and restore military coordination of policing in the West Bank.
Eisenkot's goals: Ease cost of living, draft haredim, and reform Israel's economy
Yashar’s domestic platform focuses on reforming military-service obligations, easing the cost of living, and directing economic support toward working Israelis, young people, and those who serve the country.
Yashar’s clearest established position is its opposition to blanket haredi (ultra-Orthodox) exemptions from military service.
Eisenkot has proposed sanctions for evasion and benefits for those who serve, while allowing a limited Torah-study exemption for 3% of each annual haredi cohort. That allowance qualifies his universal-service message and has drawn criticism from opposition rivals demanding no exemptions.
Yashar also proposes expanding service obligations and giving servicemen greater priority in civilian benefits. Its September youth plan proposed raising compulsory-service soldiers’ pay by 15%, with a 50% increase for combat soldiers in their third year.
The party’s proposals place particular emphasis on those who contribute through military service and work.
Economist and Yashar candidate Shaul Meridor placed the “working middle class, young people, and service people” at the center of its economic policy.
Meridor outlined tax changes to reward those bearing the economic and security burden, together with priority in housing assistance and daycare subsidies. The reporting does not specify a full schedule of tax rates.
On living costs and competition, the party has advocated challenging exclusive import arrangements and reducing barriers in concentrated markets such as groceries and cosmetics.
The party’s September youth plan also outlined renter protections, paid internships, and practical financial guidance.
What a vote for this party is likely to produce
A vote for Yashar is most likely a vote to strengthen Eisenkot’s claim to the premiership and help build a coalition with former prime minister Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu, and Yair Golan’s Democrats.
The four parties have agreed to coordinate campaigning and prepare principles for a future government, but have not settled how the bloc’s candidate for prime minister would be selected.
Eisenkot favors the leader of the largest party becoming the candidate for prime minister and has rejected a rotation arrangement. While that position still requires agreement from prospective partners, all four opposition leaders stressed in separate interviews during the election campaign that they would coalesce around an agreed-upon candidate following the election.
In a September interview with the Post, Eisenkot laid out his conditions for coalition eligibility, including accepting Israel’s Jewish and democratic identity, service obligations, and supporting the dismantling of Hamas.
His parameters exclude Arab parties Ra’am and the Joint List, and likely the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties Shas and United Torah Judaism as viable partners.
If the bloc falls short of 61 seats, it would need additional partners or support. Haredi parties accepting service reform represent a conditional opening in Eisenkot’s position, although his allies’ red lines could complicate it.
For voters, Yashar offers a path toward replacing Netanyahu, but the election result will determine how far that path goes.
Eisenkot must turn support for his leadership into a majority whose members agree on who should govern and what they are prepared to concede. The decisive test will be whether he can assemble those 61 seats while preserving the promises that brought voters to him.

CENTCOM chief flies over Strait of Hormuz during Middle East visit, affirms waterway clear of mines

US Central Command (CENTCOM) Adm. Brad Cooper visited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday as part of the US effort to allow shipment movement and crude oil exports through the contentious waterway.
Cooper observed the ongoing operations while flying in a US Army CH-47 Chinook helicopter over the strait.
"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," said Cooper during the visit. "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
Cooper affirmed that the Strait of Hormuz is "free and clear of Iranian sea mines," thanking the US service members who supported and took part in the mission.
"We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry," he said.
US clears mines from Hormuz, Trump accuses Iran of 'fabrications'
In August, US President Donald Trump said the US Navy told him all mines had been cleared from the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump added that "Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed."
A US official confirmed the matter to the The Jerusalem Post at the time, noting that both inbound and outbound shipping lanes in the strait have been cleared of mines by CENTCOM.
On Thursday, however, Trump accused Iran of fabricating recent reports of attacks on oil tankers and naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up oil prices ahead of the November midterm elections.
“Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election,” Trump wrote.
“They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
James Genn, Amichai Stein, and Goldie Katz contributed to this report.

Breadcrumb
Israeli forces advance in Syria’s Quneitra as security officer killed in Daraa
Israeli forces entered Syria’s southwestern Quneitra province on Sunday to resume excavation in the occupied territory, while a Syrian highway security officer was killed and two others wounded in a separate attack in neighbouring Daraa.
An Israeli force accompanied by a bulldozer and an excavator entered the al-Akar area, southwest of Hanout farm near Abu al-Ghaythar hill in rural Quneitra, according to the Horan Free League monitoring group.
The group said Israeli troops were continuing construction of a six-metre-high earth embankment, alongside excavation of a road within it measuring four metres deep and up to five metres wide.
The Golan Media Foundation said the work marked the resumption of the "Sufa 53" project after a pause of about six weeks. It warned that the embankment could extend into farmland and grazing areas, restricting residents’ access and threatening their livelihoods.
The foundation’s director, Fadi al-Asmai, told The New Arab that recent developments on the ground pointed towards an escalation ahead of the Israeli elections.
He linked the movements to two possible developments: an offensive by Suweida’s National Guard militia to retake the province’s western countryside, and Israeli efforts to establish a security belt beyond the Sufa 53 line.
Al-Asmai suggested that a National Guard offensive could seek to win support within the Druze community, which he linked to political calculations surrounding the Israeli elections. He said a wider Israeli security belt would leave local communities more vulnerable to pressure.
The developments come amid tensions in neighbouring Suweida, where Syrian government forces and Druze armed groups have faced off and Damascus has reinforced its positions along the province’s western front.
Israeli forces committed at least 88 violations across Quneitra, Daraa, Damascus and rural Damascus between 8 and 14 October, according to documentation by the Sijil Center.
Security officer killed in Daraa
Separately, a Syrian highway security officer was killed and two others wounded in an attack on a checkpoint in southern Daraa province early on Sunday.
Four gunmen riding two motorcycles attacked the checkpoint at Kharba village, on the road linking Bosra al-Sham and Daraa.
The officer killed was identified as Mohammed al-Miqdad, from Bosra al-Sham, and the wounded men as Omar al-Diyyat and Abdel Mawla al-Diyyat. Both were taken to Daraa National Hospital for treatment.
Checkpoint personnel captured two of the attackers, one of whom was wounded in the exchange of fire, while the other two fled, the network reported.
State news agency SANA said security forces had arrested attackers following a clash, without identifying their affiliations. Al-Miqdad’s funeral took place on Sunday with officials in attendance.

“Everyone is quite positive, and we get the chance to talk to some of them. Some of our compatriots are simply curious to see how election day unfolds at a polling station abroad. I see hope in many of the people who come to vote willingly. I wouldn’t say they feel obliged to vote; at least here, there is genuine interest in the election process. We also see quite a lot of young people. Some are voting for the first time and come motivated and eager to exercise their right to vote, which I think is wonderful. I believe the hope lies with young people, and we simply need to give them the opportunity to realize their full potential. I have great hopes for the younger generation.”
Young Bulgarians in Poland want a president who stands up for Bulgaria’s interests and is not afraid to take a stand, Marinela Koleva told Radio Bulgaria.
PHOTO personal archive
“They want someone who will stand up for their interests, who is educated and well-informed, can speak eloquently at international events, represent the country with dignity and, as I said, is not afraid to express their views clearly and openly.”
As for the campaign and the messages put forward by the 27 presidential tickets, she is certain that not all of them managed to reach Bulgarians in Poland.

“People would have the opportunity to hear directly from the two presidential candidates and see how they think and respond to questions in real time. I believe their answers would be very important and could even be decisive for some voters.”
Marinela expects voter turnout in Kraków to be lower in a potential runoff than it was today.
''People are enthusiastic now and are eager to vote, but I think that momentum will fade by next week and voter turnout will be lower''.

Bulgarians in Geneva: Lack of open debate is missed chance in election campaign

Presidential election 2026
Bulgarians in Geneva: Lack of open debate is missed chance in election campaign
Sunday 25 October 2026 17:54
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 17:54
PHOTO Marin Kachamakov
Font size
There are 11 polling stations in the Swiss Confederation this Sunday. One of them is located at Bulgaria’s Permanent Representation in Geneva. Marin Kachamakov is serving on the precinct election commission there for the ninth consecutive time, his fifth as chair. By noon, just over 50 Bulgarians had cast their ballots at the polling station using a voting machine, although, as is traditionally the case, turnout is expected to be highest towards the end of the day, he says.
“In the previous elections in April, around 85% of voters used the voting machine. Today, the law stipulates that in polling stations where more than 300 people vote, voting must take place exclusively by machine, unless the machine breaks down. So far, we have had two elderly ladies, one aged 85 and the other around 80, who managed to vote by machine without any difficulty.”
As for what motivates people to vote, Marin Kachamakov identifies two main differences, largely along generational lines.
“Our older compatriots come to vote for the sake of their grandchildren or their children. Younger people vote for themselves, primarily for a better life of their own. Their motivation lies in a sense of duty and dignity, and in the desire to help Bulgaria in some way by making their voices heard, however far away from home they may be. And let us not forget perhaps the most important thing: in a democracy, we can always vote for autocracy. In an autocracy, we cannot vote for democracy. People need to reflect on this, understand it and bear it in mind when they cast their ballots,” he stresses.
People want to live better lives, and the president should be a unifying figure for the nation and a check on those in power, Kachamakov believes. Commenting on the campaign and the messages put forward by the presidential tickets, he says:
PHOTO unsplash.com
“People who take an interest in Bulgaria and care deeply about the country are very well informed. However, I am not at all convinced that the major national television channels, without naming them, provide sufficiently high-quality coverage. Important, fundamental issues are being overlooked, while other, more everyday matters receive far too much attention. This indirectly leads our compatriots to rely much more heavily on social media for information.”
In this regard, Kachamakov is unequivocal that the absence of a major televised debate between the leading candidates was a serious shortcoming of the election campaign.
If a runoff takes place next week, such a debate could prove crucial for many Bulgarians, and not only those living abroad. It is difficult to predict today how turnout might differ in that second round. One thing is certain: hope and faith in a brighter future for Bulgaria have not faded.

Another round of heavy showers and thunderstorms were expected to hit the south-west US on Sunday after the region endured days of rain that forced evacuations, water rescues and multimillion-dollar damage.
The National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of the Four Corners – the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah – even as local officials forecast further receding of swollen rivers that surged since rains picked up on Wednesday.
About 4ft (1 meter) of water flooded the home of Shane Ferrari, the sheriff of San Juan county, New Mexico. He said the area’s situation was stable on Sunday, but he and other residents were trying to clean up and deal with damage.
The New Mexico governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, said in a statement on Saturday that law enforcement officials had reported hundreds of water rescues between the cities of Farmington and Bloomfield.
“Families in Bloomfield and Farmington spent the night on rooftops watching the river flood their homes, and our national guard and state police crews have been bringing them to safety,” said Lujan Grisham. “Right now, our focus is saving lives. If you’re told to evacuate, go. Once the water recedes, the state will do everything in its power to help San Juan county families rebuild.
“No deaths have been reported,” she added.
The San Juan River in Farmington on Friday ran 2ft above its previous record set in 1909.
A San Juan county spokesperson, Devin Neeley, said the county did not have official numbers on damage to homes or the number of people evacuated, but he was not aware of any loss of life.
Neeley said the floodwaters were receding but left mud and silt, much of which has been contaminated with sewage because of failures at waste plants. There were still power outages affecting multiple areas, and it would probably be a few days until residents got their power back on.
“It’s a pretty active disaster zone,” he said. “We’re not on the downswing by any means.”
The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and areas of New Mexico.
New Mexico has been hit with back-to-back weather events this weekend. A tornado struck Santa Fe on Saturday, damaging at least eight houses, including roof collapses, according to a statement by the city of Santa Fe. No injuries were reported.

France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen launches presidential bid as protests rattle the nation
ORLEANS, France - Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the 2027 French presidential election, formally launched her campaign on Oct 25 with a promise to restore order and national confidence.
As France faces one of its most turbulent periods in years, Le Pen cast herself as the best placed to navigate what she described as mounting economic, social and security crises.
“We are not living through the end of the world but the end of a world, their world,” she said of her political opponents.
Le Pen chose to make her first campaign address in Orleans, home to Joan of Arc, the 15th-century warrior heroine revered by nationalists as a symbol of patriotism and sovereignty.
Addressing a crowd of cheering supporters, she promised “zero tolerance” policing and said restoring security was the state’s first duty.
Mass protests over living costs and inequality last weekend descended into looting and vandalism.
Opinion poll puts Le Pen in the lead
The street turmoil has given Le Pen a boost and an opinion poll published on Oct 25 put her on 32% to 33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon on 17%, as voters desert mainstream parties for the political extremes.
Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
Seeking to project optimism, Le Pen built her speech around the theme of a national “Renaissance”. She said France was living through a period of upheaval but would emerge stronger if it embraced her vision of security, prosperity and renewal.
“We say: ‘Things were good before, they will be better tomorrow!’,” she said.
Le Pen promised a hard line on immigration, pledging to restore border controls, automatically expel foreign criminals and crack down on gangs and drug traffickers.
Le Pen herself could have to campaign wearing an ankle tag after she was convicted of embezzling European Parliament funds. She is appealing the court verdict.
On the economy, Le Pen pledged spending restraint, lower business taxes, reduced bureaucracy and support for industry, innovation and artificial intelligence. She rejected further increases in the retirement age.
The congress was designed to showcase unity at the top of the National Rally party, with Jordan Bardella re-elected party president and presented as Le Pen’s choice for prime minister.
Bardella’s speech was interrupted by activists from a Jewish student union, drawing attention to recent accusations he made antisemitic comments in his youth, which he denies.
Le Pen has spent more than a decade trying to transform the party she inherited from her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, in 2011, softening its image and broadening its appeal beyond its traditional anti-immigration base.
On Europe, Le Pen stopped short of advocating a French exit from the European Union, but said she would roll back Brussels’ influence, restore national control over borders and laws, and put French interests first, including avoiding foreign wars.
“The future belongs to us,” she said, before leading the flag-waving crowd in singing the national anthem. REUTERS

Thousands protest Czech government’s public media overhaul after rushed vote
PRAGUE - Thousands protested in Prague on Oct 25 after government lawmakers gave initial backing to public media funding changes in a rare overnight vote despite criticism the overhaul will damage media independence.
The proposal’s first reading was unexpectedly brought to the lower house floor outside the planned order of proceedings on Oct 23.
Opponents and media advocacy groups have objected to fast-tracking the legislation, which will abolish household fees that currently fund Czech public television and radio stations.
The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD party, has frequently clashed with public and private media.
It wants to move funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio to the state budget, which critics say will leave broadcasters vulnerable to political pressure.
Government has ‘gone too far’, protest leader says
Babis says it is a matter of funding transparency and not an attack on independence.
Smaller protests first broke out on Oct 23 at the Bill’s unexpected introduction. Speaker Tomio Okamura of the SPD limited debate and scheduled a vote for 4.36am local time on Oct 24.
The Bill is now at the committee stage before a later vote.
“Mr Babis ... Mr Okamura, nobody in this country believes that your intention was pure,” Mikulas Minar, a protest leader, said on Oct 25, criticising the overnight vote.
“(This protest) is a clear message to this government: you have really gone too far this time,” he told protesters who had filled Prague’s historic Old Town Square, amid chants of “Resignation” and “We’ve had enough”.
Organisers plan further protests.
Trust high in public media
Czech Television is the country’s most-watched broadcaster across major age groups. Public media are among the most trusted news sources in the country, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey.
The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15%, possibly as early as 2027.
Opposition parties have compared the funding changes with reforms in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who oversaw a major expansion of pro-government media.
On Oct 23, the European Broadcasting Union, along with 15 other groups including other public broadcasters as well as Reporters Without Borders, called for more debate and the removal of any measures threatening the broadcasters’ financial sustainability.
President Petr Pavel also called for more expert scrutiny.
“The Czech Republic is among the few countries in central and eastern Europe where the system of public service and private media works very well,” he said on X on Oct 24. REUTERS

By Uditha Jayasinghe
COLOMBO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Sri Lanka coordinated the rescue of 40 Iranian sailors from multiple commercial ships in international waters off the coast of the country and supported their return to Iran, a spokesman for the island nation’s foreign ministry said on Sunday.
The ministry received a request from the Iranian embassy via diplomatic channels to rescue the sailors, Thushara Rodrigo, a spokesman for the ministry, said, adding they had been suffering unspecified medical emergencies.
The ministry didn’t give any further details of why they had to be rescued but local media including Indian national newspaper The Hindu reported they were on board vessels which were US-sanctioned oil tankers.
Washington has imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping as part of its war on Iran.
The sailors from 19 ships were brought ashore at Galle Harbour, about 126 km from commercial capital Colombo, and were given medical treatment before returning to Iran early on Sunday morning, the spokesman added.
Sri Lanka’s navy and coastguard typically provide support during humanitarian efforts, a government source with direct knowledge of the rescue told Reuters.
Earlier this year Sri Lanka rescued dozens of Iranian sailors on humanitarian grounds after the Iranian warship IRIS Dena was sunk by a torpedo from a U.S. submarine on March 4.
The bodies of more than 80 sailors who died in the attack were flown back to Iran in mid-March. Thirty-two survivors of the sunken ship, as well as 208 crew members from another vessel, were returned to Iran in April.

By Vivian Sequera, Sarah Kinosian and Keren Torres
CARACAS/BARQUISIMETO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by tens of thousands of cheering supporters as she made her way by car to Caracas on Sunday night, after she arrived home following several failed return attempts which have strained her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration.
“This country is giving lessons to everyone,” she shouted as her convoy entered the capital, leaning out of the sunroof to shake hands and hug raucous supporters
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Machado, who was prevented from challenging deposed leader Nicolas Maduro for the presidency in 2024, has been out of the country for 10 months and spent the previous year in hiding following the disputed election.
On Sunday morning, Machado appeared at a church in western Lara state and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted “liberty!” as she left in an SUV, a Reuters witness said.
She then traveled to the capital in a journey that took eight hours because of crowds. By the time she neared Caracas, festooned in rosaries handed to her by followers, the highway was all but blocked by cheering supporters.
“For the reunion of every family, for freedom of every political prisoner, for the freedom of Venezuela,” she wrote on social media.
Machado’s return was coordinated with the US, Panamanian and Colombian governments, according to a person briefed directly on her movements, who added Trump approved her return and was kept informed about it.
At the White House on Sunday, Trump said he did not know anything about Machado’s return and suggested the US would continue to back Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
“She’s a very nice woman,” he said, referring to Machado. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”
The White House and the State Department did not respond to Reuters questions on the matter.
RETURN PREVIOUSLY DELAYED
Machado’s efforts to return have tested her relationship with the Trump administration, which she sought to cultivate as an ally even before it captured Maduro in January and took him to New York for trial.
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Trump said in September it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela.
US officials have asked Machado at least once to delay her return, Reuters reported in June, and she has made several failed attempts to enter the country. Her team did not disclose details of how she returned.
Machado traveled in a private plane from Panama to Colombia and crossed overland on Sunday to Venezuela, four people familiar with her trip told Reuters.
One person briefed on her movements said the flight took place late last week and US security contractors guarded her during the journey. Rodriguez and the country’s authorities were warned by the US not to interfere or threaten her safety, the person said.
“The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado to Venezuela are the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which have already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement on Sunday.
“We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”
A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado’s political movement.
The Venezuelan Communications Ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Machado’s return.
SUPPORTERS CHEER MACHADO ON ROUTE
“Maria Corina Machado will achieve liberty and democracy in Venezuela,” said Hernan Adames, 69, as he celebrated with other supporters in Barquisimeto.
Zuleima Granadillo, 61, an employee at the Ministry of Education, waited for Machado at a point on the highway in Aragua state, closer to Caracas.
“What does Machado’s arrival mean? All paths are opening up for us, the future is opening up, we have a light, and we are going all the way to the end,” she said.
“This dictatorship is already over with the arrival of our leader.”
Machado plans to meet victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, told Reuters.
“She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections,” he added.
International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
Machado has said that only a “serious, democratic government” can provide the stability needed by investors.
She had been barred by Maduro’s government from exiting Venezuela but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.
Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement released an app on Saturday to collect voter registration information from Venezuelans abroad. The group hopes eventually to share data from the app, which was built by 15 staff over the last 18 months, with a reformed electoral council so users can be officially added to voter rolls.
Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado’s movement who has been living in Spain, said on X he would soon join her in Venezuela.

The Central Election Commission of Bulgaria must announce the official results within 48 hours after voting ends.

Based in Paris, CRASH conducts and directs studies and analysis of MSF actions. They participate in internal training sessions and assessment missions in the field.
Based in Geneva, UREPH (or Research Unit) aims to improve the way MSF projects are implemented in the field and to participate in critical thinking on humanitarian and medical action.
Based in Brussels, MSF Analysis intends to stimulate reflection and debate on humanitarian topics organised around the themes of migration, refugees, aid access, health policy and the environment in which aid operates.
This logistical and supply centre in Brussels provides storage of and delivers medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions.
This supply and logistics centre in Bordeaux, France, provides warehousing and delivery of medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions.
This logistical centre in Amsterdam purchases, tests, and stores equipment including vehicles, communications material, power supplies, water-processing facilities and nutritional supplements.
BRAMU specialises in neglected tropical diseases, such as dengue and Chagas, and other infectious diseases. This medical unit is based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Our medical guidelines are based on scientific data collected from MSF’s experiences, the World Health Organization (WHO), other renowned international medical institutions, and medical and scientific journals.
Providing epidemiological expertise to underpin our operations, conducting research and training to support our goal of providing medical aid in areas where people are affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or excluded from health care.
Evaluation Units have been established in Vienna, Stockholm, and Paris, assessing the potential and limitations of medical humanitarian action, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of our medical humanitarian work.
MSF works with LGBTQI+ populations in many settings over the last 25-30 years. LGBTQI+ people face healthcare disparities with limited access to care and higher disease rates than the general population.
The Luxembourg Operational Research (LuxOR) unit coordinates field research projects and operational research training, and provides support for documentation activities and routine data collection.
The MSF Paediatric Days is an event for paediatric field staff, policy makers and academia to exchange ideas, align efforts, inspire and share frontline research to advance urgent paediatric issues of direct concern for the humanitarian field.
The MSF Foundation aims to create a fertile arena for logistics and medical knowledge-sharing to meet the needs of MSF and the humanitarian sector as a whole.
A collaborative, patients’ needs-driven, non-profit drug research and development organisation that is developing new treatments for neglected diseases, founded in 2003 by seven organisations from around the world.
Noma is a preventable and treatable neglected disease, but 90 per cent of people will die within the first two weeks of infection if they do not receive treatment.
The GeoMSF platform is a dynamic one-stop-shop website for all of MSF's GIS related services and products. Access maps and applications through the catalogue, request geographical support, or produce a map on GeoMSF.
Another senseless Russian attack kills and wounds several people in Dnipropetrovsk
Share
Crisis Update25 October 2026
On 24 October, at around 6 pm, a Russian drone struck civilian infrastructure in Synelnykove, Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine, some 80 kilometres from the frontline.
The strike occurred in an area with homes, cafés, and shops, less than one kilometre from a hospital supported by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). Four people were killed and more than 13 injured in the attack, according to the Ukrainian authorities. The hospital responded to a mass-casualty incident.
One patient told me he had just stepped out for a coffee, but ended up in hospital with serious injuries.Karina Ivanova, MSF anaesthetist
“We heard the sound of a drone, and moments later there was a loud explosion,” says Karina Ivanova, an MSF anaesthetist. “Patients began arriving one after another with blast injuries to their limbs, abdomen, chest, and head. Some also had burns.”
“Several patients had severe bleeding and needed emergency surgery,” says Ivanova. “One patient told me he had just stepped out for a coffee, but ended up in hospital with serious injuries.”
Local medical staff, working alongside an MSF anaesthetist and paramedics, treated 15 people, including four with severe injuries.
An MSF ambulance transferred two patients – a 50-year-old woman and a 20-year-old woman – to a hospital in Dnipro for specialised surgery.
Some patients, including an 11-year-old child, experienced acute stress reactions and received mental health support from local psychologists.
Repeated attacks by Russian forces are killing and wounding civilians in the capital, Kyiv, in regions next to the frontlines, and even in towns and cities hundreds of kilometres away in central and western Ukraine. MSF condemns attacks on civilian infrastructure. This is a war against people — against civilians trying to live their everyday lives.
