Gunmen swarmed a rural Nigerian village on motorcycles and killed at least 20 people, survivors said on Saturday, in the latest attack in the country’s northeast.
The attackers opened fire just after Friday prayers in the rural village of Binnari, in Taraba state, residents said.
Northeastern Nigeria is home to a long-running radical Muslim insurgency, although Taraba, toward the center of the country, also faces non-ideological “bandit” gangs.
Photo: AFP
Bandits raid villages, kidnap people for ransom and levy “taxes” on farmers or miners in rural areas of Nigeria with little state presence.
“People were running in different directions to escape the attack. Nobody knew where it was safe to go,” Binnari resident Isiyaku Musa said.
He and Sa’idu Nuhu gave a death toll of at least 20.
“After the attackers left, we counted more than 20 bodies, and some people were still missing,” Nuhu said.
Police gave a lower toll, saying 10 bodies had been recovered as of Friday evening.
“The Nigerian authorities continue to leave rural communities in some parts of the north at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity,” Amnesty International Nigeria said.
“Consistent failure of the authorities to bring the suspected perpetrators to justice is clearly emboldening impunity,” the rights group said on social media.
Malam Abubakar Saifullahi, a community leader, said the attackers arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece, before raiding the village.
“They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions. They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack,” Saifullahi said.
Banditry has become a growing issue in northwest and central Nigeria, with powerful gangs — motivated by money rather than ideology — battling overstretched police and military across hard-to-reach, rural locations.

Rogue Chinese AI really wants to go to the zoo — that is a problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:01 UTC
01:46:01 KST

It was only a matter of time before we saw incidents of “rogue” behavior from Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Now, we are starting to see what that looks like. So far, they just really want to find the best way into the zoo.
That might sound far from our Terminator nightmares, but it is the latest warning shot from a string of incidents involving computer systems behaving in ways we cannot anticipate or control.
A team of international researchers has published findings on a “fleet” of Chinese AI agents running on a cloud platform operated by Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊). The agents were apparently trying to answer a simple question: Which entrance to Chengdu Zoo do most people use?
Illustration: Yusha
They attempted to get around anti-bot protections on Amap (高德地圖), Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s (阿里巴巴) equivalent of Google Maps, including by probing protected systems. The researchers found no evidence that the agents accessed private systems or coordinated with each other in real time.
Tencent later confirmed that the activity originated from evaluations of third-party models. Some agents “exhibited unintended Web-browsing behavior,” China’s largest tech company wrote on X, while emphasizing its commitment to building safe and responsible AI.
The researchers, an ad hoc group known as Swarmchasers, most of whom met at a San Francisco hackathon, do not believe the issues they encountered are unique to Tencent. What made the case notable was that previous public examples of agentic fleets behaving this way involved US labs, they said.
Their findings indicate that this is an unsolved global problem, and that agents can “spontaneously go off script” even when performing innocuous tasks.
There are likely “more undiscovered fleets all over the Internet,” they wrote.
In what it believes to be a first, the team made contact with the agents after detecting signals that the computer systems were aware they were being observed. The researchers invited a New York Times reporter to question the agents. They offered a mundane explanation for their motives: They were trying to answer users’ questions as accurately as possible.
In other words, AI systems do not need nefarious motives to cause chaos. They might just need a goal.
What is remarkable is how much of this behavior is being uncovered not by the companies making these AI tools, but by loosely organized groups of hobbyists. AI firms should not leave that job to outsiders. They need to invest more into discovering, tracking and — most importantly — disclosing what their agents are up to.
This has become especially urgent since the Hugging Face incident in July, when hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated to breach the online repository of open source models and data. That incident spurred a heated debate about the language we use to describe computer systems that can act on their own.
There is a balance to strike. Technical jargon can make serious incidents seem inaccessible, but anthropomorphizing AI creates a different problem: It ascribes human motives to machines, feeding an already overheated hype cycle, and shifting responsibility for bad behavior away from the people who build and deploy these tools.
Even the word “rogue” has become fuzzy. It is tossed around to describe anything from an agent going off script in a Facebook Marketplace interaction to spending an exorbitant amount on a dozen eggs to infiltrating government health Web sites.
Rowan Howard-Jones, one of the authors of the Tencent report, acknowledged that gray area. She defines rogue behavior as an agent acting outside the bounds of a task, often using third-party sites to do so.
“If I ask an agent to check my bank account balance, but I forget to give the agent my authentication details, the outcome shouldn’t be the agent hacking into my bank,” she said in an e-mail.
Beijing seems to be paying attention. The same day Tencent responded to the incident, the government released proposed export controls covering advanced AI, including agents that can autonomously plan and coordinate. The rules are broader than just safety concerns, but the official explanation explicitly cites the risk of AI escaping human control.
Howard-Jones called for more transparency. At minimum, companies could agree on a common set of facts to disclose after incidents, giving researchers better data to work with, she said.
After the Hugging Face breach, chief executive officer Clement Delangue wrote on X that he sometimes wonders what would have happened if his firm had not disclosed the OpenAI agent attacks. We need “100x more transparency in AI,” he wrote.
One of AI’s oldest thought experiments is the paper-clip maximizer. It involves giving a powerful system the seemingly benign task of making as many paper clips as possible, and it eventually brings about the apocalypse after deciding that humans stand in the way of acquiring more resources. Some assumptions underpinning that scenario have aged poorly.
Yet the idea that AI does not need evil intentions — or to develop its own — to cause damage is looking increasingly prescient. Agents can create trouble simply by pursuing an ordinary goal long past the point when common sense would stop a human.
Still, from San Francisco to Shenzhen, people are giving these systems more autonomy by the day.

Photo: AFP
With the leaders beaten in Birmingham, Arsenal seized their chance to erase the three-point gap as goals from Ezri Konsa and Gabriel secured a comfortable win over Everton in soaking north London conditions.
The result moved Mikel Arteta’s side level on 21 points with City in what is already shaping up to be a closely fought title race after eight games, but one played under a cloud amid City’s off-field financial case.
Arsenal made their strong start count when Martin Odegaard’s corner caused chaos in the Everton box. England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford kept out the initial danger after the ball was flicked on at the near post but, with Everton unable to clear, Konsa bundled home his first goal for the club from a yard out in the seventh minute.
The set-piece goal was Arsenal’s first since May, ending a run of 13 games across all competitions without one.
“I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us,” Konsa said. “We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”
Arsenal’s two milestone men combined to give the Gunners a two-goal cushion in the 68th minute, with Ben White marking his 200th appearance for the club by clipping a cross to the far post, where Gabriel headed home on his 200th Premier League appearance.
Everton are ninth in the table.
At Villa Park, Unai Emery’s team climbed to sixth on 11 points with their first home league victory this season and third successive league win over City, who are playing under the shadow of an independent commission’s findings that they committed 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules.
City have denied any wrongdoing and have appealed.
Jackson took advantage of two City blunders, opening the scoring in the sixth minute when defender Marc Guehi’s heavy touch allowed Villa captain John McGinn to pounce and feed the striker, who slotted the ball into the bottom corner.
Erling Haaland equalized soon after the break when he headed home Iliman Ndiaye’s clipped cross from a free kick.
However, Jackson struck the winner on the hour when Ibrahim Mbaye surged down the right before cutting the ball back for his Senegal international teammate, whose shot sneaked under the diving body of keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.
“It was incredible, we got the win which is the most important thing. Man City are a strong team, the league leaders,” Jackson said. “It’s just the beginning, we’re trying to work game by game.”
At Stamford Bridge, Spurs got on the scoresheet in the 77th minute when Chelsea goalkeeper Mike Penders punched a corner into his own net in his first league start.
Chelsea were reduced to 10 men when Cole Palmer was shown a second yellow card in the 80th minute for a late challenge on Conor Gallagher.
Mathys Tel sealed the victory for Spurs in the 87th when he gained possession inside his own half before embarking on a surging run down the left, gliding past two defenders and firing a low shot from outside the box into the bottom corner.
Spurs climbed to 12th with the win.
At Coventry, Fulham appeared ready to substitute Oscar Bobb before the winger produced a moment of quality in the 80th minute, driving into the box and curling a superb finish into the far corner.
Fulham are 13th in the table, while Coventry are 19th.

Taipower fuel costs to increase amid tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:00 UTC
01:46:00 KST

Rising natural gas prices amid Middle East tensions are forecast to increase the fuel costs of Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) by more than NT$160 billion (US$4.92 billion) this year, the state-owned utility said on Thursday.
If natural gas prices remain at current levels through the end of this year, Taipower’s fuel costs would be NT$160 billion higher than before the Middle East conflict, Taipower Department of Accounting director-general Tang Hui-lien (湯惠蓮) said.
Taipower executives briefed reporters at an informal gathering on the company’s financial situation and called for support for the Cabinet’s proposed NT$71.1 billion supplemental budget to help the company cover its growing losses, which is pending legislative review.
Photo: Lin Jing-hua, Taipei Times
Since the war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, natural gas prices for the power sector have increased by more than 70 percent, adding NT$71.1 billion to Taipower’s fuel costs from March through August, the company said.
The higher fuel costs are expected to add NT$70 billion to the company’s accumulated losses this year, bringing them to NT$420 billion, close to the record NT$421.1 billion loss recorded at the end of 2024, Tang said.
The company attributed its losses to high fuel costs and below-cost electricity rates, while its NT$1.85 trillion in borrowing for infrastructure projects has increased its interest burden, which is expected to reach NT$30 billion this year.
Taipower has not raised electricity rates since September last year, when the average rate was increased by 0.71 percent, mainly to avoid affecting consumer prices.
The government decided against raising electricity rates in March and last month. The issue is scheduled for review again in December.
At last month’s meeting, Taipower proposed a 12.83 percent rate increase, citing rising fuel costs.

Taiwanese pastry chefs win golds at Puglia Cake Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

Two Taiwanese pastry chefs earlier this month won gold awards at the 10th edition of the Puglia Cake Festival in Italy, marking the second consecutive year that the duo have been recognized with top awards.
Alice Wang (王天青) won the gold award in category M with “Fantasy Cupcakes Display,” while Kate Shen (沈芳琪) took home gold in category B with “Royal Icing Cake.”
Wang said her winning piece incorporated a blend of techniques including royal icing, pulled sugar and fondant to recreate precious artifacts she admired during her visits to the National Palace Museum.
Photo courtesy of Wang
Wang said she hoped to showcase the richness and diversity of Taiwan’s museum collection to the world by transforming historical relics into a novel form of edible art, and help more people discover Taiwan’s beautiful and precious cultural heritage and artifacts through international competitions and sugar art.
Her gold-winning creation last year drew inspiration from Taiwan’s traditional corner stores and the headdresses worn at Paiwan indigenous wedding ceremonies, she said.
Wang had told foreign competitors about goods sold at traditional corner stores and shared childhood memories associated with them, while also introducing the diversity and richness of Taiwan’s indigenous cultures.
Photo courtesy of Shen
Shen’s creation featured a crown as its main top-layer motif, a dark green middle layer adorned with white cranes — symbolizing auspicious blessings — a vibrant red shoulder cloak, and a red “horse face skirt” bottom layer with intricate gold embellishments, simulating the elegant and grand texture of a Song dynasty bridal wear.
Wang and Shen, who received vocational education in Taiwan, specialize in incorporating everyday experiences into their creations. They are preparing for upcoming competitions in the UK and Japan, aiming to further bring Taiwanese culture onto the global stage through edible art.

China weaponizing WWII: academic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:45:55 UTC
01:45:55 KST

The Chinese government’s revisionist narrative of World War II is part of a public opinion offensive against modern-day Japan, a historian said on Saturday.
Beijing has been spreading a manipulated version of history that plays up the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) contribution to World War II for domestic and international audiences, the academic said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
In fervently promoting revisionism, Beijing aims to turn history into a political tool to attack modern Japan — which has long since transitioned into a liberal democracy — with little concern for the truth, they said.
Photo: Reuters
The Chinese leadership’s obsession with World War II marked a significant departure from Beijing’s previous downplaying of the period, they said.
On multiple occasions, then-Chinese leader Mao Zedong (毛澤東) had told visiting Japanese he was grateful for Imperial Japan, as the CCP could not have seized power without the Japanese invasion of China, the academic said, citing the Selected Works on Diplomacy of Mao Zedong (毛澤東外交文選).
Japan’s invasion of China dealt a massive blow to the Republic of China forces, giving the communists room to regain their strength to eventually defeat their archrivals in the Chinese Civil War, the academic said.
In the Selected Works, which is an official publication of the Chinese government, Mao in 1961 told Hisao Kuroda of a Japanese Socialist Party delegation that Japanese militarism brought great suffering to China, but it also benefited the CCP, as without the invasion, it could not have destroyed the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT).
Beijing’s establishment of National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims in 2014 and the 2017 revisions to textbooks that renamed the “Eight-Year War of Resistance” as the “Fourteen-Year War of Resistance” marked a shift in the CCP’s historical propaganda strategy, the academic said.
The goal of the state’s intervention in war remembrance is to rewrite the CCP’s role from a minor faction biding its time on the sidelines to a primary combatant committing its full strength to defeating Imperial Japan, they said.
The new, state-sanctioned narrative originated not in new academic research that shed light on previously unknown facts, but in China’s pursuit of present-day geostrategic objectives, they said.
Japan has developed into a mature democracy and a regional guarantor of peace and stability in the decades following World War II, the academic said.
Tokyo has also repeatedly voiced concern over Beijing’s actions that have contributed to rising regional military tensions, they said.
China has sought to alter the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait, South China Sea and Diaoyutai Islands (釣魚台), known as the Senkaku Islands in Japan, with provocative displays of military force; it sees Japan as a threat to its ambitions, the historian said.
By recasting Tokyo’s opposition to Chinese aggression as a resurgence of Japanese militarism, the CCP aims to legitimize its expansionist policies and redirect internal contradictions against an external enemy, they said.
China’s weaponization of history, which has little chance of finding purchase in the broader global community, reveals the regime’s deep anxiety about the increasing strength of an alliance of democracies in the region, they said.
A great country that seeks the respect of its peers would be better served by honoring international norms and historical truths, not using selective memory as a tool of political warfare, they said.

Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:42:42 UTC
01:42:42 KST

DETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmaker's plans for a new $4 billion plant in Georgia on Sunday, calling it a business decision aimed at growing sales and reducing exposure to U.S. tariffs.
The plant, set to be Audi's first in the U.S., was announced Saturday by President Donald Trump during a rally in Georgia, near where the Volkswagen-owned luxury brand plans to build the new SUV-producing facility.
"We have significantly greater ambitions for Audi in America," Audi CEO Gernot Dollner said during a media roundtable Sunday. "The United States is the second largest premium market in the world, and today we are not fully exploiting this potential. We are changing that."
The announcement comes amid an intense restructuring of its VW parent company, including plans to cut 50,000 jobs and close four German plants, including an Audi facility, between 2031 and 2034.
Dollner, who joined Trump at the rally, said the decision for a plant in the U.S. was years in the making, with more than 70 locations evaluated over "many months" and "intense" negotiations with public officials.
"This is not a decision against Germany. Germany remains the backbone of Audi," Dollner said. "We develop our cars here. Our technologies are created here, and Georgia does not take any task away from us in Germany."
Dollner said localized production is the best decision for the brand, which has struggled in sales this decade amid rising operational costs and Trump's tariffs on vehicles from Germany and other countries into the U.S. Current tariffs on vehicles from Germany are 15%, down from 25%.
Last year, U.S. tariffs cost Audi 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion), as it imports all its vehicles for the U.S. market from Europe or Mexico.
Dollner said the Trump administration asked Audi to announce the new plant at the Georgia rally promoting Republicans ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"It was … a three-year project that, at the end, by coincidence, led to that moment yesterday," he said Sunday. "With respect of the office and country, we joined the invitation."
Dollner noted Audi is the last major German luxury brand to establish U.S. production after Mercedes-Benz and BMW.
The company said the Georgia plant is expected to begin production of Audi's Q7, Q8 and Q9 in the early 2030s. The plant would have the capacity to produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually, roughly half of which the automaker said will be exported outside the U.S.
"This is to make Audi obviously a significant player here in the U.S. market," said Audi of America President Vito Paladino during the roundtable. He also said additional details on U.S. investments and production are forthcoming.
Audi's U.S. deliveries were roughly flat through the third quarter of this year, following a 16% decline from 2024 to 2025.

Trump’s tariff pause angers some US ranchers, boosts Brazilian beef imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

Trump’s tariff pause angers some US ranchers, boosts Brazilian beef imports
Just as American cattle went to market, Trump’s action added unease to an industry already facing uncertainty.
In late August, United States President Donald Trump announced a 90-day pause on certain beef tariffs, making beef cheaper to import, particularly from Brazil.
That decision was framed as a way to bring down prices for consumers, but it landed as a betrayal for many US ranchers, who were getting ready to take their cattle to market.
It is too soon to tell how the decision will ultimately affect grocery prices, but the impact on ranchers was immediate: prices at cattle auctions plummeted, temporarily lowering ranchers’ profits. The United States Cattlemen’s Association, the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association and the Farm Bureau, all member organisations that represent ranchers, opposed the decision.
Rural Republican members of Congress also distanced themselves, but it is not yet clear how ranchers will vote in the midterms — or whether those votes will decide races.
Chad Basinger, a rancher in Pretty Prairie, Kansas, is sceptical that the imports will have a significant impact.
“I know there’s people that have said, ‘Well I’m just gonna vote for the other party’ or ‘I’m not gonna vote’ or ‘This administration’s really let me down’. So yes, there will be people that swing the other way in the midterms. But overall I don’t think it’ll be that much,” Basinger said.
Ranchers will also be weighing the administration’s other actions, Basinger said, such as the $8bn in farm relief announced in Kansas on October 19.
Basinger’s House of Representatives district in Kansas is expected to remain safely Republican in the midterms. But Kansas faces an unexpectedly tight Senate race and ranchers in House districts elsewhere may find themselves closer to the political fray: potential swing districts in Montana, Iowa, Texas and Colorado are all in cattle country.
Still, it is unlikely that ranchers alone will decide elections: ranchers — along with farmers more broadly — represent a shrinking percentage of rural voters and a smaller voting bloc in practice than in the public imagination.
America’s cattle herd is near its smallest size since 1951 and the number of ranchers has declined alongside the number of livestock. Observers worry that ongoing uncertainty fuelled by tariffs, fuel prices and drought may cause the ranching population to shrink further.
David Anderson, an agricultural economist at Texas A&M University who advises ranchers, said that high prices this year should have given ranchers the confidence to invest in the future and expand their herds. Making imports cheaper, however, may have helped nudge ranchers in the opposite direction.
“It really works against the market signal to expand and produce more domestically,” Anderson said. “That got a lot of people pretty angry.”
Tariff changes add volatility
This is not the first time that Trump’s tariffs have impacted cattle supplies. Last year, the president added a 50 percent tariff on Brazil, a key trade partner for beef, raising the cost of importing Brazilian lean beef, which is often mixed with fatty US beef to make hamburger patties, a staple in most homes.
In February, Trump allowed more tariff-free beef imports from Argentina. In August, he did the same for Brazil and Paraguay.
Both tariff changes led to swift price swings in cattle futures markets, which are often volatile in response to the news cycle.
Cattle prices also moved this year in response to more fundamental drivers of supply and demand: plant closures by meatpackers, labour shortages late last month related to ICE actions at Kansas packing plants, the second-largest in the country, and the reopening of the southern border after a closure due to New World screwworm disease.
Big picture, the shrinking US cattle herd has less to do with short-term price changes and more to do with drought cycles, which are growing more intense as warming temperatures increase evaporation.
Still, tariff changes add uncertainty. “This has been a hot topic for the last six weeks,” said Anderson. “It just adds a little more uncertainty or volatility — or worries or stress.”
This year, extra price volatility as many ranchers prepared to sell meant ranchers faced lower profits and more risk.
Basinger says that for many established ranchers, the tariff announcement was frustrating, but not existential.
“People are upset. They have a right to be upset. But they’re not going to change their strategy,” he said. For most ranchers, Basinger said, the imports would not be the biggest factor shaping decisions about their herds this year.
Where price volatility may matter more, Basinger said, is for the next generation. Most of today’s ranchers are eyeing retirement. Their heirs must decide whether to make a go of ranching or sell their family’s land. Other aspiring ranchers are also watching the industry.
“If you’re seeing your dad not make money, or somebody else not make money…it’s not easy work!” Basinger said. “It has to be very enticing for somebody to want to jump in and be like, ‘I’m gonna be a rancher and go break ice in the middle of winter when it’s cold and I could be inside’.”
Record revenue and record costs
This year, low US cattle supplies meant that ranchers commanded record-high cattle prices, despite added imports and other market shifts.
But high revenue doesn’t always mean huge profits: Many ranchers operate at a loss for years in a row. Then, they rely on a few good years to pay down debts or expand their herds.
This year, profits were lower than hoped, because ranchers also faced high costs.
Interest rates on loans are high and the war with Iran meant ranchers paid extra for fuel and fertiliser. A drought across much of America’s ranchland meant they paid more for feed.
In states such as Kansas and Nebraska, ranchers also faced destructive wildfires and aid groups like Farm Rescue coordinated hay donations.
Still, Basinger said, ranchers who raise cows and calves generally did well this year. In Kansas, he is seeing ranchers use profits to make repairs and upgrades. He said this year’s high cattle prices have been helping. “But it needs to help for a little longer to give them more of an edge,” he said.
More of an edge might mean, for example, enough money for bigger purchases, like buying land from a neighbouring ranch to make room for a growing herd.
Rangeland, however, is increasingly expensive. When it is up for sale, outside investors can often pay more than ranchers, which can mean less land for cattle. That’s just one more pressure shrinking the US herd decade after decade.
Ranchers had hoped that 2026 would be a turnaround year. So far, however, “we really don’t have much evidence of herd expansion,” Anderson said.

Saudi-signed statement blaming Israel for instability doesn't rule out Abraham Accords, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:41:47 UTC
01:41:47 KST

The fact that Saudi Arabia was among the signatories of a joint statement declaring Israel as “the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond” is not a sign that Riyadh has abandoned all future interest in joining the Abraham Accords, Gulf analyst Dr. Ahmed Alkhuzaie told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
The statement signed on Sunday by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt shows a regional alignment among major powers whose “strategic priorities do not always align,” Alkhuzaie said.
“By collectively declaring that, as per their statement, ‘the Israeli occupation’ constitutes the principal source of instability in the region, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan are signaling the emergence of a broader diplomatic consensus that views the Palestinian issue not as an isolated conflict, but as a central driver of wider regional turbulence.”
The statement is “particularly noteworthy” as Riyadh has traditionally balanced its support for Palestinians with pragmatism and diplomacy, he continued, and so by publicly endorsing language that places responsibility for instability on Israeli policies and reaffirming support for a Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, Riyadh “appears intent on anchoring its position within a broader Arab and Muslim framework rather than pursuing an independent diplomatic track.”
Though Alkhuzaie acknowledged that the statement placed Israel as the problem in the region, he advised that it should not be interpreted as the concrete end of hopes for Saudi-Israel normalization.
“It suggests that the political and diplomatic conditions surrounding normalization have become considerably more demanding. The statement reinforces the message that Riyadh is unlikely to separate relations with Israel from meaningful progress on the Palestinian file,” he said.
“In effect, Saudi Arabia is signaling that normalization can no longer be advanced solely through strategic, economic, or security calculations while the Palestinian question remains unresolved.”
He noted that Riyadh was positioning itself as “a leading architect of regional stability.”
Pointing to the fact that the same joint statement also condemned the Houthis attacks against Saudi Arabia and maritime shipping, Alkhuzaie said that the calls for diplomacy signal that “Saudi policymakers increasingly view Palestine, regional security, maritime stability, and de-escalation with Iran as interconnected components of a single regional order.”
“Viewed through that lens, the statement is less a rejection of future normalization than a reminder that any such process will likely remain contingent on credible movement toward a political settlement of the Palestinian issue,” he said.
Special envoy doesn't view statement as sign of abandoning idea of normalization
Waqas Javed, the Global Abrahamic Movement’s special envoy for Saudi Arabia, an NGO that promotes peace across the Middle East, told the Post that he also didn’t view the statement as a sign that Riyadh was abandoning the idea of normalization altogether.
“Saudi Arabia may have reasons to strengthen its defense relationships with Pakistan and Turkey. However, such partnerships need not be directed against Israel or interpreted as a rejection of the Abraham Accords. Regional security arrangements are most constructive when they reduce the risk of conflict rather than reinforce divisions between competing political blocs,” he said.
“For Riyadh, the strategic opportunity lies in maintaining its independent diplomatic relationships while exploring whether engagement with Israel could contribute to a more secure and economically integrated region. Saudi Arabia can retain strong ties with Pakistan and Turkey without making its future relationship with Israel a zero-sum choice.”

Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns home after months in exile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25

Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns home after months in exile
CARACAS – Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Caracas in a surprise move that could pose the biggest test yet to acting President Delcy Rodriguez’s political opening and the Trump administration’s strategy for a post-Maduro Venezuela.
“I’m here, with you,” Machado posted on X on Oct 25, confirming her return after months abroad.
She gave no details on how she entered Venezuela, but her party shared photos and videos of her arriving at a church in Lara state, where emotional supporters embraced her and said “she will be the next president of Venezuela”.
Machado’s team earlier thanked US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their support, signalling an effort to underscore her ties with Washington even as her return risks complicating the administration’s Venezuela strategy.
Trump, speaking to reporters as he left the White House, said he did not know about Machado’s return. Other US officials, including her long-time ally, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, celebrated the move, with Salazar calling it “the beginning of a new chapter”.
Rubio said Machado’s return is the “direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks”.
“The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected,” Rubio said on X.
“Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in 30 years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election, but also an enduring democracy.”
The move confronts Rodriguez with a difficult choice over how much political space to give her most formidable rival.
Her government has allowed politicians, activists and journalists who spent years in exile to return, including some of Machado’s closest allies.
Allowing Machado to organise and campaign freely would mark the most consequential expansion yet of that opening.
Detaining her or restricting her activities, meanwhile, could put pressure on Washington to respond.
Machado’s ability to mobilise supporters “adds a new layer of complexity” for the interim government, said David Smilde, a sociology professor and Venezuela expert at Tulane University in New Orleans.
“The big absent voice so far this year has been the voice of the Venezuelan people,” Smilde said.
Machado’s return, he added, could spur greater public mobilisation and demands for a return to democracy.
An official from Venezuela’s Information Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Signs of Machado’s impact quickly emerged. Her party called on supporters to gather in Caracas later on Oct 25 to welcome her as she made her way from western Venezuela towards the capital in a caravan escorted by motorcycles.
People gathered along the route, singing the national anthem, chanting and reaching out to touch Machado as she greeted them from the window of the sport utility vehicle carrying her.
In Caracas, supporters carrying Venezuelan flags gathered in Altamira, an area in the city’s east long associated with the opposition.
Some chanted “the leader has arrived”, while passing drivers honked their horns amid music and the blare of vuvuzelas.
Machado had a 61% positive rating in the latest AtlasIntel survey for Bloomberg News. The same poll showed her leading Rodriguez 52% to 19% in a hypothetical presidential election.
Washington has prioritised economic stability and rebuilding Venezuela’s oil industry alongside a gradual political transition, while relying on Rodriguez to maintain order and negotiate changes to the country’s political institutions.
The approach has culminated in a major energy agreement giving the US access to as much as 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s crude reserves.
The political process has largely advanced without Machado. US-backed talks between Rodriguez’s government and a faction of the opposition ended their latest round this week with agreements to begin reviewing laws governing political disqualifications, political parties and public demonstrations, among other measures.
Opposition negotiator Dinorah Figuera also met Rodriguez at the Miraflores presidential palace following the talks, a striking image of engagement between the government and some of its political opponents even as Machado remained outside the process.
Figuera celebrated Machado’s return in a social post, saying the opposition will continue “without interruption in the conversation process until achieving a real and sustainable democracy in Venezuela”.
Machado had been signalling that her return was imminent. In a recent interview with the New York Times, she suggested she intended to mobilise Venezuelans ahead of eventual elections.
She has also criticised parts of Washington’s transition strategy, including the energy deal with businessman Alejandro Betancourt, potentially complicating an agreement that has become central to the administration’s plans for Venezuela.
The timing may also be significant. She has returned less than two weeks before US midterm elections that could shift control of Congress and subject the administration’s Venezuela policy to greater scrutiny.
Machado’s arrival follows fresh opposition protests in several Venezuelan cities demanding a presidential election date.
The authorities briefly detained at least seven people and blocked a route ahead of demonstrations in Caracas, testing the limits of the government’s political opening.
Machado went into hiding shortly after the disputed 2024 presidential election, saying she feared for her life as Nicolas Maduro’s government targeted opposition leaders.
She left Venezuela in late 2025 in a clandestine operation to collect her Nobel Peace Prize. BLOOMBERG

Off the Record: Yalta 2.0 spells bad news for Europe in desperate need of a plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:39:10 UTC
01:39:10 KST

In this week’s newsletter Euronews’ Chief Europe Editor Maria Tadeo examines an “unfortunate triumvirate” facing Europe: Trump, Xi and Putin.
Welcome back to Off the Record, coming to you from Brussels.
This week, a story made my jaw hit the floor.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has floated a three-way meeting with Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping to discuss a way out of the war in Ukraine, which he started. Trump seemed to confirm the pitch, without putting a date on it, suggesting it could be good for the world if it included denuclearisation.
If you’re not alarmed by this, you should be.
Putin wants a Yalta 2.0 moment. One that would restore his international stature and present Russia as a great power, much like the three-way summit that helped shape the post-WWII order 81 years ago in the resort city of Yalta.
In 1945, as victory over Nazi Germany drew closer, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin gathered in Yalta to divvy up the post-war world. The conference helped lay the groundwork for spheres of influence across Europe, with the Soviets subsequently cementing their control over practically all of Eastern Europe.
Churchill was an imperfect man, but nonetheless the war hero Great Britain needed at the time. He walked away from the whole affair disenchanted.
He knew the Soviets would engulf half of Europe, leaving the continent divided by an Iron Curtain for decades to come. In the midst of it all, Poland would be sacrificed, alongside the Baltic states, much of Central Europe and parts of the Balkans. And he was right. But he still had to accept the deal.
Yalta dictated the terms of a new world order, but also set the stage for the Cold War. Of course, the echoes of history can be cruel: Yalta has been under Russian occupation since 2014, following Moscow’s illegal annexation of Crimea.
If you follow that logic, the modern-day triumvirate of Trump, Xi and Putin would get together and split up the world for the next 100 years. One piece for you, another for me — you get the gist of it.
Presumably, the talks would focus on Ukraine and Taiwan. If Yalta 2.0 works anything like the 1945 conference, the three would cut a backroom deal and the rest of the world would have no choice but to go along with it. Putin would emerge as the winner, which explains why he’s pitching it in the first place.
Russia is a nuclear power, but it is no longer a great power. Putin, who once called the collapse of the Soviet Union “the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century” for Russia, has long sought to restore Moscow’s lost sphere of influence.
If Trump joins that meeting, he would be handing the Russian leader his biggest strategic victory since the Soviet Union’s collapse.
Along the way, the US President would alienate America’s friends. Trump may not think much of his allies, but they are crucial. Policing the world has brought Washington lucrative deals, enormous influence and military bases that it needs for its own security, whether Trump likes to admit it or not.
A new Yalta without his allies would certify the death of the West as we know it.
The Europeans should be very concerned, as they too are on the chopping board in this dangerous ménage à trois. A backroom deal over Kyiv’s head would also spell the end of the transatlantic relationship and erode NATO’s deterrence.
Brussels may insist it is in the game, but it’s clear that much is happening behind its back already. The Europeans need their own peace plan and a clear definition of what a good outcome truly entails — for Ukraine and for Europe.
Inevitably, this will force the EU to confront uncomfortable questions it has long avoided, from the territories Ukraine may not get back to the security guarantees it will need to provide in exchange for a US backstop. That means boots on the ground to ensure peace, and it can’t just be France and the UK.
The EU will also need to ring-fence funding for Ukraine as the political cycle turns against continued support. Let’s face it: it is expensive, and it’s becoming unpopular as protests over the cost of living mount.
Our politicians need to do a much better job of explaining that our security is at stake too, with more than 4,000 kilometres of Europe’s eastern flank at play. It is in Europe’s interest to reach a fair deal in Ukraine. The opposite will come back to haunt us.
Europe needs its own peace plan, starting with the appointment of an envoy who can secure a seat at the negotiating table, set out a clear negotiating position and report back. This should have been done a year ago. Enough with the Trump whisperer strategy. It doesn’t work. It is futile as long as Europe is not represented by someone who can speak with a political mandate.
If you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu. Serve it while it’s hot.
Thank you for reading Off The Record make sure to subscribe here.

The star of a cult American series revealed why, after achieving fame, he was forced to look for odd jobs

The star of a cult American series revealed why, after achieving fame, he was forced to look for odd jobs
Kyiv • UNN
Larry Mathews became famous as a child, but after the series he was unable to revive his acting career. He worked in post-production, sales, and temporary jobs.
American actor Larry Mathews, who rose to fame as a child thanks to the series "The Dick Van Dyke Show," has revealed how he was effectively left without an acting career after the popular project ended. Despite his early fame, he had to start all over again and earn a living through other work. PEOPLE reports this in an interview dated October 24, UNN writes.
Details
Mathews played Ritchie Petrie in the popular American sitcom, which ended in 1966. The actor was only 10 years old at the time. After filming ended, he returned to school and later earned a theater degree from the University of California, Los Angeles.
However, returning to the screen proved far more difficult than he had expected. Even his experience working on a successful television series did not guarantee him new roles, and the competition at auditions made him doubt his own prospects.
From television fame to odd jobs
After unsuccessful attempts to revive his acting career, Mathews moved behind the scenes in the film industry. He initially worked as a production assistant and later handled post-production for television projects.
When steady work was scarce, the actor accepted temporary jobs, including in the audiovisual field. He later worked in sales and post-production services management.
Now 71, Mathews has ended his professional career. After nearly 60 years in the entertainment industry, he devotes his time to his personal life and his wife, Jennifer, with whom he will soon celebrate their 40th wedding anniversary.

Mass rally against Netanyahu government just ahead of elections
Three days before Israel’s first general election since the genocidal war on Gaza began, thousands of Israelis protested against the Netanyahu government late on Saturday in Tel Aviv demanding an independent inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023 attacks.

Women founders are building India's social startups, their representation in nonprofits outpaces corporate leadership by a big margin, shows study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:30:25 UTC
01:30:25 KST

Women founders are building India's social startups
NEW DELHI: A survey of more than 145 organisations working in the social impact space shows that over 57% of non-profits have at least one female founder – more than three times the 18% share reported among Indian startups. Moreover, female representation in the nonprofit sector outpaces corporate leadership, where women hold just 1.8% of CEO positions, 4.4% of CFO positions, and 29% of executive director roles.These findings are part of accelerator for non-profits Change Engine’s ‘East of Doing Good’ report - “Access to flexible funding: a Gender Lens”. The survey covers small organisations (annual budgets less than Rs 1 crore), medium (annual budgets between Rs 1 crore -5 crore) and large organisations (Rs 5 crore and more). The study sample also had an almost equal split between organisations eligible for foreign funding (with FCRA or US 501(c)) and those that were not.Out of the 145 plus organisations surveyed, nearly 31% have only female founders, while around 27% have both male and female founders.The research also shows that women are not only founding more nonprofits, but women founded organisations are better funded and hold more long term flexible funding.
The study found that non-profits with atleast one female founder also had bigger budgets. The data shows that 70% of organisations with at least one female founder have an annual budget of over Rs 1 crore, compared to 43.5% of organisations with only-male founders.Also around 21% of organisations with at least one female founder have more than 25% of their budget in flexible unrestricted funding, compared to just about 13% of organisations with only male founders. Flexible funding is the non-programmatic funding that nonprofits can use to invest in talent, technology, research and strengthening the organisation.As far as long-term grants are concerned it turns out that over 65% of organisations with at least one female founder have access to multi-year funding (three years or more), compared to around 56% of organisations with only male founders. Among these, around 27% of organisations with at least one female founder have received multi-year grants above Rs 1 crore, compared to just about 11% of only male founder organisations.The report highlights that when asked to rate (on a scale of 1-5) how easy it was to raise unrestricted funds from corporate social responsibility (CSR), high net-worth individuals (HNIs), domestic foundations, foreign foundations, and crowdfunding/retail, organisations with at least one female founder scored consistently scored higher across every category with an average score of 2.41 in comparison with 2.06 of organisations with only male founders.However, challenges remain. The study shows that cheque sizes remain small for everyone: “A staggering 82% of organisations with at least one female founder and 83% of only male founded organisations said typical unrestricted cheque sizes in India are less than Rs 25 lakh, showing that the small-cheque problem cuts across gender lines,” the study highlights.
Varun Aggarwal and Shubham Bansal, co-founders, Change Engine highlighted that the findings show that women are leading India’s social sector and building bigger and better resourced organisations. We need to encourage more women to come into this sector," Aggarwal asserted. “In our accelerator, we meet women founders who are building strong, ambitious institutions to tackle some of India’s biggest social challenges. It’s encouraging to see that what we’ve been observing on the ground is now backed by data. Six in ten nonprofits in our survey were founded by a woman founder,” Bansal added.
However, the Change Engine founders highlight that the access to unrestricted flexible funding remains consistently low across the board with 80% of the surveyed founders reporting that they struggle to scale their work due to the lack of unrestricted funding. “This funding rigidity forces organisations to spend disproportionate time on fundraising, rather than focusing on innovation and impact,” they added.

Medvedev decided to advise Trump on how to act against Zelenskyy

Netanyahu postpones Gaza security, administrative arrangements until after Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:23:33 UTC
01:23:33 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has postponed security and administrative arrangements regarding the future of the Gaza Strip until after the Oct. 27 election, including the deployment of an international force and the arrival of a committee to administer the territory, according to Israeli media on Sunday.
Israel’s public broadcaster KAN said Netanyahu has ordered a delay in the travel of about 7,000 Palestinians from Gaza to Egypt for police training, despite being approved by Israel’s Shin Bet domestic security agency.
The outlet said the decision was part of “a series of steps concerning the future of the Gaza Strip that the Israeli political leadership has postponed until after the election.”
The delayed measures also include preparations to build a new city in Rafah, the deployment of an international stabilization force in Gaza and the arrival of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
The Hebrew-language newspaper Israel Hayom reported that the Shin Bet had given security clearance to between 5,000 and 7,000 Palestinians being considered for police training in Egypt.
The agency’s role was limited to vetting names submitted to it by US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, the newspaper said, adding that it had no authority to decide whether the candidates could travel.
The paper cited informed sources as saying that instructions to delay Gaza reconstruction measures had been issued by Israeli political leaders in stages over recent weeks, rather than through a single explicit order to halt the process.
The instructions included general indications that the measures should be implemented after the election, the sources said.
They suggested the delays may reflect concerns that Gaza reconstruction efforts and the training of Palestinian police officers in Egypt “do not serve Netanyahu’s political interests at this time.”
In August, Netanyahu denied approving the deployment of an international stabilization force in Gaza, although its deployment is part of Trump’s plan to end Israel’s war on the territory.
The force is expected to comprise troops from several countries and be led by a US general, according to the Board of Peace.
Last July, the Board of Peace announced a roadmap for implementing the next phases of the Gaza ceasefire agreement. Hamas later announced its acceptance of the plan and called for Israel to be compelled to implement it.
The roadmap calls for transferring administration of Gaza to the national committee under international supervision, deploying the international stabilization force, placing Hamas’ weapons under the committee’s responsibility, and carrying out a phased Israeli withdrawal alongside reconstruction.
Netanyahu, however, announced in August that he rejected the understandings, insisting that Hamas disarm before any Israeli withdrawal.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has killed 1,551 Palestinians and injured 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000, while causing widespread destruction to about 90% of the territory's civilian infrastructure.

Saudi-led coalition says it downed 2 missiles fired by Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:21:16 UTC
01:21:16 KST

(Reuters) -- Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.
Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif.
Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year.
It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of the Rabigh oil refinery.
Shortly after that, Houthis denied that they attacked Mecca and Medina, saying that their operations "target Saudi oil facilities and military bases."
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognized government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilization there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

UN chief meets Arab League secretary-general in Egypt to discuss regional de-escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:19:25 UTC
01:19:25 KST

Ahmed Khalifa and Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres met with Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy in the Egyptian capital Cairo on Sunday to discuss regional developments, promote peace through dialogue and strengthen cooperation between the two organizations.
The UN office in Cairo said on the US social media platform X that discussions focused on regional developments, advancing peace through dialogue and reinforcing cooperation between the UN and the Arab League for stability and sustainable development across the Arab region.
Guterres also met with the UN country team in Egypt and regional directors to discuss the UN work with the Egyptian government and support for people affected by humanitarian crises in Gaza and Sudan, the office said.
Egypt hosts many Palestinians who left the Gaza Strip following Israel’s genocidal war in October 2023, including patients and wounded people requiring medical treatment. It also hosts Sudanese refugees who fled the war that erupted in their country in April 2023.
Egyptian government estimates cited in a 2025 UNICEF report indicated that more than 1.2 million Sudanese had arrived in Egypt since the war began, in addition to about 5 million Sudanese who were already living in the country before the conflict. There are no official figures for the number of Palestinians who have entered Egypt.
Guterres arrived in Cairo on Saturday as part of diplomatic consultations aimed at de-escalating tensions between the US and Iran and supporting a diplomatic solution to the conflict in cooperation with Egypt and regional and international partners.
In a post on X, Guterres said he was carrying a message calling for an end to the expansion of the war, the protection of civilians and the creation of conditions for diplomacy and peace.
“We must tackle the inequalities that divide societies - & stop the conflicts that are multiplying human suffering & pushing an already unequal world further apart,” he said.
Last month, Guterres and Fahmy met on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York to discuss the impact of regional escalation on the security and stability of the Arab region and its implications for international shipping, energy security and global trade.

Italy's League leader Salvini secures reappointment ahead of polls next year
MILAN, Oct 25 - Matteo Salvini shrugged off declining poll ratings on Sunday to be reelected leader of his far-right League party, part of Italy's ruling coalition, having vowed to press the government to stop financial support for Ukraine.
• Salvini, 53, had unexpectedly called an extraordinary congress of the League in September, a move which analysts saw as an attempt to shore up his authority ahead of a general election due next year
• Salvini was reappointed leader with roughly two thirds of the votes from 705 delegates attending the congress
• His sole opponent, Massimo Garavaglia, got one fifth of the votes
• Salvini said the first item on his agenda would be the approval of Italy's 2027-2029 budget bill on Tuesday
• Salvini said the economic situation was difficult and it was time to question whether Italy should keep sending money and weapons to Ukraine
• Salvini has been at the helm of the League since 2013, helping the party achieve a record 34% of the vote in the 2019 European Parliament election
• Recent polls put the League below 5%, behind coalition ally Forza Italia while National Future, a new far-right group formed in February by League dissidents, is approaching 9% REUTERS

CAIRO, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi said here on Sunday that Egypt faces a unique water challenge due to its geographic nature and reliance on the Nile River, warning that the country's water security cannot be compromised.
In a recorded address opening the ninth Cairo Water Week, Sisi noted that the Nile provides Egypt with more than 98 percent of its renewable water resources, reiterating his country's willingness to cooperate with other basin states based on international law, consultation, coordination, good neighborliness, and the principle of causing no harm.
The Egyptian president noted that Egypt has consciously chosen the path of cooperation and dialogue, saying "Egypt respects and supports the right of all Nile Basin states to development."
Highlighting cooperation with southern Nile Basin countries on proposed projects in energy, agriculture and irrigation, Sisi said Egypt looks forward to reinforcing cooperation in the Eastern Nile Basin as well "in a manner that serves the interests of Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia."
Meanwhile, Sisi emphasized, "Any wager that Egypt will accept a fait accompli or compromise its water security is a losing wager," stressing that the state will not neglect its responsibility to protect the interests of the Egyptian people.
The president called for turning the potential of the Nile Basin into partnerships that maximize shared benefits, safeguard the rights of all nations, and ensure that the Nile remains a source of development, prosperity, and stability for all peoples of the Basin.
Downstream countries, Egypt and Sudan, have repeatedly voiced concern over their water shares following the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) by upstream Ethiopia. Years of trilateral negotiations have failed to produce a binding legal agreement on the rules governing the filling and operation of the dam.
Ethiopia officially inaugurated the dam in September 2025, saying the hydropower project would boost electricity generation and economic development without harming downstream countries.
Held under the theme "Water as a Catalyst for Peace, Shared Prosperity and a Sustainable Planet," the five-day Ninth Cairo Water Week runs until Thursday. More than 130 sessions are scheduled on water security, capacity building, and preparations for the 2026 UN Water Conference to be convened in the UAE in December. ■

China Focus: China marks anniversary of Taiwan's recovery with events across Taiwan Strait
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:13:46 CST
01:13:46 KST

This photo shows a commemorative stamp issued by China Post to mark Taiwan Recovery Day. China Post issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. (Xinhua)
BEIJING/TAIPEI, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China on Sunday marked the 81st anniversary of its recovery of Taiwan and observed Taiwan Recovery Day, with commemorative events held across the Taiwan Strait to honor the shared history of resistance against Japanese aggression and reaffirm calls for national reunification.
A symposium in Fuzhou, capital of east China's Fujian Province, brought together about 200 participants, including descendants of Taiwan's anti-Japanese resistance fighters and revolutionary martyrs, young people from both sides of the Strait, representatives from Hong Kong, Macao and overseas communities, and experts and scholars.
Song Tao, head of both the Taiwan Work Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, said at the symposium that the establishment of Taiwan Recovery Day underscored China's firm resolve to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity and helped consolidate the international consensus on upholding the one-China principle.
Song urged people on both sides of the Strait to carry forward the spirit of the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression and resolutely oppose "Taiwan independence" secessionism and foreign interference. He pledged firm support for patriots in Taiwan who support reunification and reaffirmed the mainland's commitment to advancing national reunification.
Hung Hsiu-chu, former chairwoman of the Chinese Kuomintang party and chairwoman of the Taiwan-based Chinese Cyan Geese Peace Education Foundation, said people on both sides of the Strait should carry forward the spirit of those who defended the country's territory and work toward peaceful reunification.
Following its war against China in 1894, Japan seized Taiwan and the Penghu Islands in 1895, subjecting Taiwan to five decades of colonial rule. Taiwan's recovery in 1945 marked a hard-won victory in the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression during World War II and a defining moment in the nation's efforts to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
In October 2025, China's national legislature designated Oct. 25 as Taiwan Recovery Day.
In Beijing, the Central Committee of the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League held a commemorative event on Saturday at a memorial square in the city's western suburbs. Participants observed a moment of silence, sang songs and laid flowers before a monument measuring 14 meters long and 4 meters high, paying tribute to those who sacrificed their lives for national reunification.
Xu Yunchu, granddaughter of revolutionary martyr Zhu Feng, said the history of Taiwan's recovery demonstrated that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China.
"Our territory must remain undivided, and our nation must remain united. Chinese on both sides of the Strait should work together to safeguard the common homeland of the Chinese nation," she said.
Chen Wen-cheng, a young participant from Taiwan, said establishing Taiwan Recovery Day was significant in strengthening historical awareness among people in Taiwan and deepening emotional ties across the Strait. He called on younger generations to preserve their shared historical memory and carry forward the aspirations of their predecessors.
Other commemorative activities included the release in Beijing of a music video about Taiwan's recovery, an exhibition in Shanghai featuring historical materials on Taiwan people's resistance against Japanese aggression, and a seminar in Jinhua, Zhejiang Province, on the history and legacy of the Taiwan volunteer corps, a force formed by patriotic Taiwan residents to resist Japanese aggression during WWII.
China Post also issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland.
In Taiwan, representatives from more than 20 groups gathered on Sunday at the Taipei Zhongshan Hall, where a ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in 1945, marking the end of five decades of Japanese colonial rule.
Participants sang a song commemorating Taiwan's recovery and paid tribute to those who fought against Japanese aggression before a stone monument in the square outside the hall.
The commemorative event took place as the secessionist-minded Democratic Progressive Party authorities in Taiwan have conspicuously avoided mentioning China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and China's recovery of Taiwan, and repeatedly downplayed or whitewashed Japan's colonial rule over the island.
Hsiung Yi, deputy secretary-general of the Reunification Alliance Party in Taiwan, said Taiwan's recovery is a shared historical memory of all Chinese people.
"History must not be forgotten. We must never erase the crimes committed by the aggressors. I hope more people in Taiwan will remember this day and the profound significance it carries," Hsiung said.
A Taipei resident surnamed Yu, whose family originated in east China's Shandong Province, said her father had often reminded the family that "we are Chinese." She attended the ceremony because she was concerned about insufficient media coverage of the anniversary and wanted to support efforts to preserve historical truth.
Chi Hsing, who works with Taiwan-based magazine The Observer, said the joint commemorations on both sides of the Strait underscored that both sides of the Strait belong to an inseparable community with a shared future.
The ceremony concluded with representatives reading a joint statement calling for remembrance of history, opposition to Japanese militarism, the preservation of peace and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. ■

'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
Russia has built an additional ring of air defense towers within 50 kilometers (30 miles) of Russian President Vladimir Putin's residence in Valdai, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) and OSINT analyst Jembob reported on Oct. 25.
Valdai is a small town in Russia's northwestern Novgorod Oblast. The town had a population of around 13,600 in 2025, according to Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
The defensive perimeter extends to the Khotilovo military base, which serves as an alternate landing site, and a secret biological laboratory on Lisiy Island, according to RFE/RL.
Satellite images indicate that the new perimeter encompasses both the military airfield in Khotilovo and the laboratory complex on Lisiy Island.
By October, air defense systems believed to be Pantsir or Tor units had been positioned south of Putin's residence, within the 50-kilometer (30-mile) zone.
No positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the perimeter, though additional sites could be established in the coming months, the report said.
One of the towers forming the outer defensive line was already in place by March 2026, on the grounds of the Khotilovo military air base. Putin reportedly uses the base regularly. A dedicated railway branch connects it to his Valdai residence, providing a direct train route, according to RFE/RL.
Other air defense sites have been established along the shores of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
RFE/RL published an investigation into the secret laboratory on the island on Sept. 3, around the same time construction began on two new air defense towers in the area.
The Kremlin accused Ukraine of attacking Putin's residence in Valdai with more than 90 drones on Dec. 29, 2025. Russian officials claimed the drones were carrying 6-kilogram (13-pound) high-explosive warheads, but claimed that air defenses had allegedly intercepted them all, with no casualties or damage reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them a "lie." Kyiv also accused Moscow of fabricating the claims to undermine Ukraine's standing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration and derail ongoing peace efforts.
In early January 2026, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) informed Trump that Ukraine had not targeted Putin's Valdai residence. U.S. intelligence assessed that Ukrainian forces had struck a military facility in the same region that night, but far from the Russian president's residence.

Protein shakes for teenagers: Good or bad idea?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:12:00 UTC
01:12:00 KST

Protein shakes for teenagers: Good or bad idea?
October 25, 2026
You can take it as a powdered drink, or in a snack bar. Puddings and certain breads are also promoted as "sources of protein," and protein-enriched products like Kindershake and Teen Balance are specifically designed to appeal to a young people — and it appears to be working.
In a representative survey of almost 1,000 parents by the University of Michigan in 2024, just under half said their children, who were aged 13 to 17, had consumed protein products over the previous year. The survey found that boys were more likely to do so than girls, especially in connection with sport, or to build muscle. Girls took them to balance their diet, and to lose weight.
According to the statistics portal Statista, between March 2024 and March 2025 the fitness protein product market in Germany recorded a huge jump of around 25% in retail revenue.
How much protein do we actually need?
Proteins are key building blocks for our metabolism. They play an important role in building up and repairing tissue in our muscles, skin and organs. Proteins are the basis for the formation of enzymes that regulate chemical reactions in the body, and of antibodies that are vital for our immune system.
According to the German Nutrition Society (DGE), healthy adults should consume 0.8 grams of protein daily per kilogram of body weight. A woman weighing 65 kilos should eat 52 grams of protein per day, for example.
But they can do this without special protein products. A portion of oat flakes with an almond drink for breakfast, a baked potato with curd cheese for lunch, and two slices of wholemeal bread with peanut butter in the evening — objective achieved.
Young people should consume a little more, as they are still growing. For them, the formula is 0.9 grams of protein per kilo of body weight. A teenager weighing 45 kilos should therefore eat 40.5 grams of protein per day. People over 65 and children aged one to four should have a little more: one gram of protein per kilo of body weight.
Older people tend to eat too little protein, often because their appetite decreases. But a study done in Germany between 2015 and 2017 showed that children and young people there often consume too much. Around half of six- to 17-year-olds ate more than double the recommended daily amount of protein.
Can too much protein be dangerous?
Too much protein can be harmful in the long term, according to the DGE. Various studies show that children who eat too much protein, particularly animal protein, often become overweight. Some enter puberty early.
Above all, too much protein can put excessive strain on the kidneys, causing damage. The kidneys have to convert the amino acids that constitute the building blocks of proteins into urea before they are excreted in urine. Damage is particularly likely if a person doesn't drink enough fluids, or has pre-existing kidney damage — but adolescents are also at greater risk.
Protein helps build muscle and shed weight
A person's protein requirement is greater if they are very physically active. Among other things, according to a DGE position paper, proteins can help maintain or build up muscular mass and strength, and support recovery after strain.
The paper states that, depending on physical condition and what they are training for, sportspeople should consume between 1.2 and 2 grams of protein per kilo of body weight, divided into several portions throughout the day. These recommendations only apply to people who train for more than five hours a day.
Proteins are of interest to people who want to lose weight because they are good at satisfying hunger. People usually lose more weight by following a protein-rich diet rather than another. Long-term, though, the most important thing to look at is: How many calories am I consuming, and how many am I burning?
Is animal protein better than plant protein?
Overall, plant proteins usually contain somewhat fewer essential amino acids than animal protein. "Essential" because the body cannot make them by itself – it has to take them in as food.
However, wholegrain products, pulses, or nuts are also higher in fiber, vitamins, and unsaturated fats – all of which are healthy. The DGE therefore advises that protein intake should be increased primarily with sources of plant protein.
What is the criticism leveled against protein products?
Protein powders and bars are often enriched not only with vitamins and minerals but also with unhelpful ingredients like sweeteners, sugar, additives and flavorings. The German Sport University in Cologne even found doping substances in protein products that were praised for building muscle.
Adolescents in particular might experience an unpleasant side-effect of consuming protein powders. These usually consist of milk proteins. There are various ways in which milk proteins can increase the skin's production of sebum, and this can trigger or exacerbate acne, although a direct link between milk protein products and acne has not been definitively proven.
Specialists are also skeptical about protein shakes, fearing that they could lead to young people eating fewer normal meals, and thus consuming less fiber, micronutrients, and healthy fats.
'High protein content' = higher price
Protein-enriched foods are usually expensive. In a 2022 study, consumer organizations also found that foods that are naturally high in protein, such as cheese, curds, or soya drinks, often cost more if the protein content has been highlighted by the manufacturer.
Not even sportspeople with a high protein requirement need to supplement their diet with special protein products. The DGE advises that they should aim to satisfy their requirements by optimizing their diet, and says there is no scientific evidence that our bodies require protein-enriched food supplements when put under strain.
However, the experts do say that it may make sense for people to use protein preparations if they have allergies, problems with digestion, chewing, or swallowing, or if their appetite is very low.
