Why is the Middle East waiting out the Trump presidency?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:08:54 UTC
01:08:54 KST

There appears to be little prospect of lasting peace between Iran and the United States while Donald Trump remains in the White House. This is a view that an increasing number of serious actors across the region now seem to share. Eight months into Iran war, Washington has neither broken Tehran’s resolve nor found a clear path out. The president’s own remarks point to a narrowing set of options. Trump told TIME he does not believe peace with Iran is ever possible, a striking admission from the leader still expected to negotiate one.
Tehran, for its part, has set conditions it knows this administration cannot meet, insisting that sanctions and threats be lifted before talks resume and that not a single gram of enriched uranium leaves the country. Neither side is bargaining towards a settlement. Each is waiting for the political ground beneath the other to shift.
Trump’s problem is that the ground is shifting under him first, as the 3rd November midterms approach with his approval rating near 39 per cent and crude trading above 110 dollars a barrel. The House has voted three times to restrict his war powers in Iran, with Republican candidates in competitive seats now campaigning openly on ending the war to lower petrol prices. Facing a likely defeat, the president has promised no strikes before polling day while Central Command has reportedly been told to prepare for resuming major combat operations. Therefore, it is quite likely that Trump may order striking Iran even before the mid-term day.
Analysts have noted that a Republican defeat could strengthen this incentive, as a president with little left to lose at the ballot box faces fewer costs for escalation. Yet such strikes would do little damage control, since a Politico survey found 46 per cent of voters said ending the war before the election would not change their vote at all. Iran has meanwhile fortified its nuclear sites and warned that regional energy infrastructure would be targeted, so any parting blow risks sending oil prices even higher.
The president’s own inner circle appears to have read the same numbers and is quietly positioning itself for the aftermath. Vice President JD Vance, reportedly sceptical from the outset, has kept his distance and this week declined to endorse Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, his chief rival for 2028, spent the same week in India on a trip devoted largely to trade rather than Iran.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, by contrast, made an unannounced visit to Israel a day after Trump endorsed Netanyahu, keeping himself firmly in the frame. Commentators suggested as early as April that Hegseth was being set up as the fall guy should the war end badly. His visibility since has only reinforced that impression.
The Gulf states have reached the same conclusion. They are hedging accordingly against an American policy they no longer trust to last. The UAE joined the campaign against Iran in February, yet they opened a backchannel with Iranians lately after the realization that it is better to deal directly instead of relying on the US. Moreover, the UAE, by the virtue of being in support of the Saudis vis-à-vis Yemen, is trying to find a diplomatic way to lower tensions. It signals a striking reversal in barely eight months. Having absorbed thousands of Iranian missiles and drones, Abu Dhabi appears to be securing its own understandings before Washington’s next round begins.
Yemen shows how the burden is being shifted, since the United States has twice rebuffed Saudi requests for airstrikes against the Houthis and says it will not take kinetic action for now. Instead, the UAE has reportedly agreed to resume funding anti-Houthi forces in southern Yemen. This is an arrangement that lets Washington stay out while a partner carries the fight on its behalf.
Iran’s strategy rests on patience and its leaders appear confident they can absorb another year or so of American pressure before the political weather in Washington changes. Its posture towards Saudi Arabia fits this reading more closely than the images of burning airports suggest. Houthi strikes have killed at least 19 people at Saudi airports, and the Wall Street Journal has reported Revolutionary Guard officers helping to direct them. Yet within days of the deadliest attack, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called Riyadh to offer mediation with the Houthis and insist the crisis had no military solution.
The aim is not to destroy Saudi infrastructure but to convince the kingdom that American protection is unreliable and that any opening to Israel will carry a heavy price. Riyadh has begun to absorb that lesson, but the pressure is unlikely to ease while Trump remains in office and Tehran sees no reason to settle.
The real question is how Israel reacts to all this, both during the remainder of Netanyahu’s tenure and after it. Trump has endorsed Netanyahu so he can help “finish the job” against Iran, and Israel has reportedly asked that any renewed strikes wait until after its 27 October vote. Polls give Netanyahu’s coalition fewer than 50 of the 61 seats needed to govern, raising the prospect of a weakened caretaker with every reason to keep the Iran file burning.
A successor led by Gadi Eisenkot would hardly soften Israel’s line on the Iranian nuclear programme, but it might be less willing to tie national strategy to American president’s fortunes. Should Israel strike alone after an American exit, Gulf hedging would only accelerate and normalisation with Riyadh would recede further from view.
Tehran and the Gulf have made their calculations. Both now wait for a different figure in the Oval Office.

The health and wellbeing of around 1200 Palestinian civilians in the West Bank is being put at risk by the forced displacement being carried out in response to a terror attack carried out by two terrorists last week, multiple Israeli human rights organizations told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
The IDF announced that its operation in the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighborhoods near the military checkpoint at the entrance to Hebron was aimed at locating terrorists and weapons and would include demolitions.
The Palestinian Authority condemned the operation as “collective punishment,” while Palestinian officials warned that it would have a significant impact on civilian life. Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, head of Hebron’s municipality, told Reuters that around 1,300 additional people faced losing their homes, on top of the 1,200 already displaced.
Al-Jabari alleged that the military had demolished shops, factories, homes, and roads in Hebron.
Milena Ansari, director of Physicians for Human Rights Israel’s Palestinian Territory Department, told the Post that the effects of the latest operation were already being felt by sick and vulnerable residents.
Palestinians fear displacement could be more long-term
Citing the testimony of Osama Abu Sbeih, a Palestinian ambulance driver with the private Al-Salam Ambulance service in Hebron, PHRI reported multiple incidents in which patients were unable to reach critical medical care promptly, including a six-month-old baby suffering from a lung infection who had to wait two days to be transferred from a hospital in Ramallah to Hebron.
“Crews are relying on passing patients from one ambulance to another at checkpoints. Even our mobile clinic that usually goes across the West Bank to provide medical treatment couldn’t reach Msafaryatta for a scheduled medical day,” Ansari said. “But it’s the long-term damage, which is a bit less visible but is as serious as what we’re seeing right now on the ground.”
Ansari shared her fears that the temporary displacement would become more long-term, and warned that the Palestinians housed in temporary shelters or in the crowded homes of relatives would be at risk. Noting that many of the shelters lack proper heating, entering the winter months without proper housing could drive respiratory infections.
For those with chronic conditions, she continued, the disruption to routine can create emergencies. Patients with hypertension, diabetes and on dialysis might particularly struggle should these disruptions become long-term, she warned.
“The psychological toll of being forced out of your home in the middle of the night, especially for the children…These psychological hardships last longer even after an operation ends,” Ansari shared.
Israeli rights group tells IDF there's no link between demolitions and terror attack
The Association for Civil Rights in Israel, in a letter addressed to senior officials in the IDF, including IDF Central Command chief Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, seen by the Post, complained that there was no evidence of links between the houses being destroyed and the terrorists who carried out last week’s attacks.
ACRI also shared concern in response to the Palestinian claim that some of the displaced were removed from their home at night and left without shelter, that worshipers had been cut off from accessing the Ibrahimi mosque and that thousands were cut off from reaching work and school.
“No attack, however grave, gives the military license to punish an entire city. Families who had nothing to do with the attack are being driven out and their homes demolished, while ministers present this to voters, a few days before the election, as the price Palestinians must pay. That is collective punishment. The military must stop it and let these families return home now, and ACRI will use every legal means available to make sure it does,” said Noa Sattath, Executive Director of ACRI.

Enforce the draft, but don't punish haredi kids for their fathers refusal to serve - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:07:35 UTC
01:07:35 KST

“If they don’t serve, they shouldn’t get a shekel.” This line has become a staple of the High Court of Justice rulings, attorney-general opinions, Knesset speeches, and WhatsApp groups. It is no longer rhetoric. Since the High Court ruled in June 2024 that there is no legal basis for exempting yeshiva students from the draft, the sanctions have only grown.
Yeshivas lose funding for draft-age students, and the Labor Ministry’s daycare criteria now deny the subsidy to any family whose father is classified as a draft evader, even if he is employed. Draft bills go further: National Insurance benefits, housing programs, property tax discounts, driver’s licenses, and travel abroad.
For a kollel family of six, “benefits” is a bureaucrat’s word for groceries. Stripped of euphemism, the proposal is that the state will help feed a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) father’s children if he serves, and not if he doesn’t.
Whether haredim must serve (many already do, in the Hashmonaim Brigade) is a hard argument between citizens. Settling it by controlling who eats is not an argument at all. It is a tactic, and it has a history.
Lenin made “He who does not work, neither shall he eat” a principle of state in May 1918, calling it the “root principle of socialism” in a letter about seizing grain. Within months, Petrograd (now Saint Petersburg) was rationing bread by class.
Stalin wrote the slogan into his 1936 constitution; Mao’s 1975 constitution adopted it too. Each makes the same move: the state decides what counts as work, then feeds those who comply. Trotsky saw where that leads: where the state is the sole employer, the principle becomes, “Who does not obey shall not eat.”
The slogan has been used on Jews before. The 1918 Soviet constitution disenfranchised clergy, creating the lishentsy. Rabbis, kosher slaughterers, and cantors were counted as non-laborers; from 1929 they were denied ration cards, evicted from state housing, and their children barred from universities.
The Yevsektsiya shut cheders (schoolrooms) and yeshivas on precisely the grounds now heard in Jerusalem: that men who sit and learn produce nothing.
The Nazis followed the same path, stripping Jews of their professions, their children’s schooling, and public welfare before reaching for anything worse. Every clause of the argument is now being said, in Hebrew, by people who would be horrified to hear its Russian original.
A democracy enforces its laws on individuals; it does not ration bread to communities. If the Knesset passes a draft law, the state may summon, try, fine, or jail each man who refuses, as it would any secular evader. Sanctions on the evader himself – a fine, his license, his passport – are ordinary tools of law. But the state may not make children answer for their fathers.
A three-year-old in Bnei Brak did not dodge the draft. Cutting her daycare subsidy enlists no one; it punishes her. A sanction that falls on a child is a child’s lunch withheld until her father complies.
Israel should reconsider its tactics with the Haredi draft
Jewish law refuses to condition food. The Talmud (Bava Batra 9a) and Shulchan Aruch (Yoreh De’ah 251:10) rule that one who asks for food is fed at once, without investigation.
The Torah’s model of the citizen who does not fight is not the parasite but the Levi, whom the Rambam (Hilchot Shmita v’Yovel 13:12-13) described as set apart for God’s service and fed by the nation, a “standing open” to anyone whose spirit moves him. The vocabulary of “parasites” is not Jewish. We borrowed it.
Welfare states condition benefits on need and income; the Soviet way was conditioning them on obedience, and on a father’s obedience for his child’s food. The daycare rule, applied even when the father works, shows what Israel is doing.
Israel should also consider who it is pulling the lever on.
There are about 1.4 million haredim, with a birth rate near six and a half, and a quarter of Jewish first-graders – on CBS projections, a third of Israel’s Jews within a generation. Squeezing a 10th of the country’s consumers is not a policy but a recession. And they are the keepers of what held the Jewish people to this land through two thousand years of exile.
Nor are they unwilling to fight: Hashmonaim soldiers have fought and fallen in Gaza, not because their children’s daycare was threatened, but because the state built a framework that kept their kashrut, prayer, and rabbis intact. Israel can have the Hashmonaim or the ration book. It cannot have both.
Coercion does not integrate; it disintegrates. Stalin’s Gulag, where rations were graded by output, should have produced perfect compliance. Solzhenitsyn records the opposite: the special camps forged a solidarity that erupted in strikes and revolts, culminating in the 40 Days of Kengir uprising. A sanction felt at the kitchen table binds families to their community.
Every lost daycare place becomes evidence for those who call the state an enemy of Torah, and the young man who might have enlisted must now do so as a defection from his besieged neighbors. The Talmud (Sotah 47a) teaches that the left hand pushes away while the right draws near.
Integration succeeds by making membership worth having: units like Hashmonaim whose soldiers leave as observant as they entered; respect for those diligently learning; career tracks that honor the beit midrash; and a public language that treats Torah as a shared treasure rather than a debt.
The High Court has never affirmed the haredim’s right to serve in such a unit. If it will not, its call for integration is not sincere; it is an attempt to uproot haredi values. Alienation produces radicals; belonging produces citizens.
“Her ways are ways of pleasantness.” A Jewish state that wants its most devout citizens beside it should try those ways first.
The writer is an attorney in Jerusalem and principal of David Page Law, a full-service law firm with an emphasis on real estate, wills, trusts, and estates. He has taught law at the Hebrew University at the Faculty of Law and made aliyah after a judicial clerkship and a year in Washington DC’s largest law firm. He is also a member of R’ Daniel Belsky’s Kollel and the author of Rav Gustman, on the Rosh Yeshiva who was the last Dayan of Vilna, and the creator of the podcast The Kings of Israel.

====================================================================================================

Israel must confront double standards in Hebron security, accountability - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:07:29 UTC
01:07:29 KST

I reject all armed attacks, and I believe that security for Israelis and dignity for Palestinians must form the foundation of any shared future. That position also compels me to ask: Why does an entire Palestinian city become the target of sweeping military measures after a single attack, while we see no equally determined response to protect Palestinians from repeated settler attacks?
Events in Hebron following the October 23 attack make this question urgent. Reports of closures, families forced to leave their homes, raids and demolitions describe measures whose impact extends beyond the perpetrators, affecting large sections of the population and their daily lives.
In my assessment, the speed and scale of this response reveal a political template ready for implementation, activated after Friday’s attack: expanding responsibility from the perpetrator to those around him, then to the neighborhood and the city, and turning civilian life into an instrument of pressure.
This is a political interpretation of the pattern of response, rather than a claim to possess a document proving that the operation’s details were prepared in advance. The question this pattern raises is whether the objective is to pursue those responsible for the attack or to subjugate an entire community by making it bear the consequences.
A double standard in responding to attacks on Palestinian civilians
That question becomes even more pressing when we compare this response with the treatment of settler violence.
When Palestinian civilians are killed in attacks, their property is burned, or their communities are assaulted, where is the mobilization to ensure their protection? Where are the effective, sustained measures to prevent further attacks and bring those responsible to trial?
I reject collective punishment, whether directed at Hebron’s residents or at the residents of settlements from which attackers targeting Palestinians emerge. I demand one standard: Pursue the perpetrator, protect the victim, and do not hold civilians responsible for crimes they did not commit.
The fact that some settlers have been arrested does not, by itself, answer this question. The measure of a law enforcement system is its ability to prevent attacks, investigate them, and hold perpetrators accountable. The problem lies in the persistent gap between the scale of the violence and the effectiveness of deterrence and accountability.
In its reports, the Israeli organization Yesh Din has linked settler violence against Palestinians to the settlement expansion project and described the support this violence receives from state institutions. These findings deserve serious scrutiny and accountability.
In my view, this disparity reflects a deliberate political approach that has become entrenched in practice: tolerance of settler violence that pressures Palestinians to leave, alongside the use of extensive force and measures affecting entire communities when violence comes from the Palestinian side.
The political consequence of this tolerance is clear: Remaining on their land becomes more difficult for Palestinians, while the settlement presence expands. When this pattern repeats itself, it becomes difficult to treat it as a series of security failures disconnected from politics.
The result is two systems of protection and accountability operating on the same land, with their effectiveness varying according to the identity of the perpetrator and the victim.
Protecting lives in the West Bank
Another aspect of this contradiction appears in the way the West Bank is presented within Israel’s statistical framework. Israeli tables covering the population of Israeli localities there count settlers, who number roughly half a million, while the millions of Palestinians living on the same land fall outside that population category.
This statistical distinction reflects the scope of those tables. It does not mean that Palestinians are not counted by other bodies, nor does it establish, on its own, the existence of a discriminatory security policy.
But it raises a deeper question about the exercise of authority: Do the Israeli military and security institutions regard Palestinians as residents whose rights and needs require protection, or primarily as subjects of surveillance and control?
Palestinians exist, and they have a clear legal status and rights. Under the law of occupation, Israel has obligations toward them, such as protecting them from violence, including settler violence, and maintaining public order and civilian life. Those obligations do not disappear because Palestinians lack Israeli citizenship.
The issue, therefore, is the responsibility of an authority legally obliged to provide protection, and the need to hold it accountable when it fails to fulfill that duty or applies it selectively.
Any system that exercises military control over land, roads, and people’s movement, while providing effective protection to one population and leaving another exposed to attack, creates a crisis that goes beyond an isolated security failure. It makes identity a decisive factor in determining who enjoys safety and whose life is restricted in the name of someone else’s security.
As a Palestinian who advocates dialogue and a democratic, demilitarized Palestinian state alongside Israel, I see this reality as a danger to the future of both peoples. We ask young Palestinians to believe in peaceful political action. That choice needs tangible results and confidence that the rights, lives, and property of those who embrace it will be protected.
When a peaceful Palestinian cannot protect his home from an attack or reach his workplace because of a measure imposed on him despite his having no connection to any attack, the credibility of the path we urge him to follow is weakened.
In Masar Jadid – New Path – our guiding message is “From confrontation to dialogue.” We work for politics that improve people’s lives, institutions that protect them, and accountability for perpetrators, whoever they may be.
The people of Hebron deserve protection, freedom of movement, and a life of dignity. So do Palestinians exposed to settler attacks throughout the West Bank.
The true test of any policy claiming to deliver security is its ability to protect civilians and hold those responsible for violence accountable under one standard. Security for Israelis will not be sustainable as long as Palestinians living under Israeli control are denied effective and equal protection.

Fresh protests in Tirana, despite new measures to curb unrest

Fresh protests in Tirana, despite new measures to curb unrest
TIRANA, Oct 25 - Protesters poured onto the streets of Tirana on Sunday hours after Prime Minister Edi Rama announced new measures to stem a wave of anti-government demonstrations.
On a rainy afternoon, protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry and then walked to Rama's office, setting on fire chairs he had placed in front of it as an invitation to a dialogue with the government.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities this month.
Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings and banks, smashed shop windows and pulled up paving stones to throw at police.
"I believe that those who demand my resignation are mistaken if they think they can impose it through violence or any other means, but I do not believe that everything they say or demand is wrong," Rama said in a video address.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful summer protests against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and won a fourth term in office last year.
Earlier on Sunday, Rama introduced new measures to curb violence including fines of 500,000 lek ($6,188) for everyone who participates in a protest that turns violent even if he or she does not commit acts of violence. REUTERS

Musk urged people to pity the “poor Russian conscripts” fighting against Ukraine

American billionaire Elon Musk called for sympathy for Russian conscripts taking part in the war against Ukraine. He called them "children" who allegedly have no choice but to fight and die in drone strikes, UNN reports.
Details
We should sympathize with the poor Russian conscripts. These children have no choice but to fight and die in drone strikes
Notably, in his call for sympathy, the billionaire focused specifically on Russian troops. At the same time, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and its army continues to conduct combat operations on Ukrainian territory.
Sympathy for the troops of an army that invaded Ukraine
Musk's words create a revealing contrast: in his statement, Russian troops who are on the territory of another state as part of an invading army are presented primarily as victims of the war.
At the same time, Musk's statement did not raise the issue of the responsibility of the Russian leadership for starting the full-scale invasion.
Thus, the billionaire's call to sympathize with Russian conscripts overlooks a key circumstance: they are not fighting to defend Russia against an invasion, but on the territory of Ukraine, which is defending itself against Russian aggression.

Dutch Army Plans to Replace Kodiak Engineer Vehicles After Just 12 Years in Service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:02:32 UTC
01:02:32 KST

The Dutch Ministry of Defense plans to replace its Kodiak engineer vehicles and, in cooperation with Germany, acquire additional Leguan tank-launched bridges.
The Dutch Ministry of Defense outlined the plans in an official letter to parliament dated October 22, 2026.
The Dutch Army has operated Kodiak engineer vehicles since 2014. They are designed for engineering tasks, mine clearance, breaching obstacles, and creating passages for military vehicles.
However, the Ministry of Defense considers the vehicles outdated because their protection no longer meets today’s battlefield threats. The vehicles also have low operational availability because individual systems and components malfunction.
The military initially considered upgrading the Kodiaks under a Midlife Update (MLU) program but abandoned the option because of its technical complexity and lengthy implementation timeline.
The ministry emphasized that the war in Ukraine has shown the need for modern capabilities to overcome engineering obstacles directly in combat.
The replacement and expansion program has been allocated a budget range of €250 million to €1 billion in 2026 prices, including a risk reserve.
The Ministry of Defense plans to complete the study and procurement preparation phase in the first half of 2028, after which it will present further plans to parliament. The type of replacement engineer vehicle has not yet been determined.
In October, Militarnyi reported the start of trials of two Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiak engineer vehicles in Germany. German troops received them without the Natter remotely operated weapon stations originally planned for installation.
The AEV 3 Kodiak is an armored engineer vehicle developed by Germany’s Rheinmetall in cooperation with Switzerland’s RUAG, based on the Leopard 2 tank chassis.
It is designed to clear paths through minefields, breach engineering obstacles, prepare defensive positions, and perform earthmoving tasks. In 2014, the Netherlands received 10 vehicles for its engineer units.
The Kodiak weighs about 62 tons and is equipped with a front-mounted excavator arm, a bulldozer blade, and two winches.
The blade can be replaced with a specialized mine plow to clear paths through minefields.
The Dutch Ministry of Defense also plans to procure additional Leguan tank-launched bridges to strengthen its engineer units.
To do so, the Netherlands intends to join Germany’s contract for modernized Leguan bridge-layers. Germany is expected to sign the relevant agreement with a German supplier in the first quarter of 2027.
The additional bridge-layers have been allocated a budget range of €50 million to €250 million in 2026 prices, including a risk reserve. The exact number of vehicles has not been disclosed.
The Leguan, manufactured by KNDS, is designed to rapidly deploy bridges across water obstacles and dry gaps. The system, mounted on a Leopard 2 chassis, can deploy either a single 26-meter bridge or two 14-meter bridges.
In January, Belgium signed a contract with KNDS to order eight wheeled Leguan bridge-layers worth approximately €80 million.
In February, it was also reported that the Netherlands planned to acquire WiSENT 2 armored recovery vehicles to equip new units.

Polls close in Serbia as strongman Vučić faces challenge to 12-year rule – Europe live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25

Updated projection: Student List wins with 52.9% vote, 141 seats in new parliament
The latest version of the Ipsos/CeSID poll, updated with the partial results, gives the Student List 141 out of 250 seats in the new parliament with 52.9% of the vote share.
That’s well clear of the 126 required for majority.
Vučić’s list will have 103 seats in the new parliament, with 38.8% of the vote share.
Four minority parties will take the remaining six seats in the new assembly.
Student opposition movement ends strongman Vučić's rule in Serbia - summary
Jakub Krupa
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for tonight as the clocks strike half past midnight in Belgrade.
The opposition grassroots movement Student List has won a landslide in the Serbian parliamentary election, ousting the country’s authoritarian leader Aleksandar Vučić.
The leaderless student movement, which started less than a year ago in protest against alleged widespread state corruption (17:42), is projected to have a clear majority in the new parliament (21:43, 22:22, 00:37).
The result appears to have been driven primarily by unprecedented mobilisation across the country, with the final turnout projected to be just below 70%, the highest since the first election in 1990.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” Vučić conceded (21:35), prompting wild scenes of celebrations in Belgrade and other Serbian cities (21:45, 22:01, 22:08, 22:19, 22:38, 22:42, 22:45, 23:21).
Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, and has been the country’s leading government figure for more than a decade (17:14).
A prominent Student List candidateRadomir Saičić hailed the result as “a victory of courage over fear, of hope over indifference,” as he stressed “the great responsibility” facing the movement. “Tonight, we celebrate … Tomorrow, the work begins,” he said (22:34).
The result was warmly welcomed by EU leaders,Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa, as they expressed their hopes for a new start in the bloc’s relationship with Serbia (23:39, 23:54), despite the movement’s ambiguous positioning on the EU (16:48).
Hungary’s prime minister Péter Magyar was the first national EU leader to offer congratulations, drawing parallels with his victory over Viktor Orbán earlier this year (22:48, 23:09).
In a likely further embarrassment to the ousted strongman Vučić, Serbia will have to hold presidential elections in the coming months to choose his successoras the head of state (23:34).
Thousands of diaspora voters joined in lengthy queues to cast their votes around the world (20:41), with up to three hours wait in London (18:58, 19:09).
For now, that’s all from me, Jakub Krupa, with contributions from Ana Milosavljevic on the ground in Belgrade. Thank you for joining us tonight.
Updated projection: Student List wins with 52.9% vote, 141 seats in new parliament
The latest version of the Ipsos/CeSID poll, updated with the partial results, gives the Student List 141 out of 250 seats in the new parliament with 52.9% of the vote share.
That’s well clear of the 126 required for majority.
Vučić’s list will have 103 seats in the new parliament, with 38.8% of the vote share.
Four minority parties will take the remaining six seats in the new assembly.
'The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together,' EU enlargement commissioner says
EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos is clearly hoping for more engagement from the new government in Belgrade.
In her congratulatory message on X, she said:
“Dear Serbia, you have made your voice heard! After nearly two years of protests for democracy, the rule of law and the fight against corruption, Serbians turned out in historic numbers. Congratulations to the Student List on your victory!
These are the very values at the heart of our European Union. A new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together.”
“Today in Serbia is a vivid reminder that the will of the citizens and their right to freely decide on their future are the foundation of every democratic change.
I congratulate the representatives of the Student List and firmly believe that a new chapter lies ahead for Montenegro and Serbia, based on respect and open dialogue, without unnecessary escalation of tensions.
The citizens of both countries deserve relations that will be measured by concrete results of cooperation, and not by the depth of diplomatic misunderstandings.”
Montenegrin president Jakov Milatovic also joined in:
“I congratulate the Student List on their electoral victory, and the citizens of the Republic of Serbia on their clearly expressed democratic will. I am convinced that this electoral result will open a new chapter in the relations between Montenegro and the Republic of Serbia, based on friendship, sincere dialogue, and commitment to a shared European future.”
The change of government in Serbia could indeed significantly shift the dynamic in the western Balkans, although again we should not necessarily expect an immediate move against Russia (17:54).
Council of Europe’s secretary general Alain Berset has also offered his congratulations.
He says:
“Congratulations to the Student List of Serbia on your electoral result.
Serbian citizens have made their democratic choice. We welcome former President Vučić’s acceptance of the result and commitment to a peaceful democratic transition.
Council of Europe stands ready to work with Serbia’s democratically elected leadership to strengthen human rights, democracy and the rule of law.
Your perseverance, energy and commitment to European principles and Serbia’s future have brought you this far. You can count on our support.”
'We stand ready to support reforms ... and work to advance Serbia's future in the EU,' von der Leyen and Costa say
European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen and European Council president António Costa have congratulated the Student List on their victory in tonight’s election in Serbia.
“Today, the people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country’s future. Congratulations to the Student List on its victory in the parliamentary elections.
We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.”
As explained earlier, it may not be quite that straightforward when it comes to the EU… (16:48).
Vučić’s gambit backfires as Serbia will need to host second elections to choose his presidential successor
Jakub Krupa
By the way, Vučić’s decision to step down as president to contest this election now puts him in a very awkward position.
Because, erm,the Serbian people will now have to choose his successor as the head of state, and looking at the results tonight, he may not like the outcome of that process either.
After his resignation, a close Vučić ally – the outgoing speaker of the parliament and former prime minister Ana Brnabić – has temporarily stepped into the role as acting president.
But once the new parliament forms, the new speaker will have to decide the next steps for recruiting the full-time replacement.
The process is complicated and CRTA has a good explanation on all possible dates here, but essentially the vote needs to take place before the end of the year.
Despite some similarities, Student List's win in Serbia is slightly different than Tisza's in Hungary – snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
When thinking about today’s opposition win in Serbia, there is an understandable temptation to compare it to Hungary and the fall of Viktor Orbán in April – and Magyar clearly plays on that in his reaction, too (22:48).
And there are some undeniable similarities in how the two countries visibly grew tired of their increasingly authoritarian leaders.
The opposition forces in both countries – Tisza in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia – have some things in common, for example their sort of catch-all character as they formulate their demands in the broadest possible terms to attract all sorts of voters, while relentlessly focusing on corruption and demands of accountability for political leaders.
On a technical level, they both focused on a door to door campaign, making a point of covering thousands of kilometres across the country, and reaching out to voters directly, instead of being a sort of talking shop with ideas. They also both adopted elements of national folks and symbolism for their campaigns.
But there are also very substantial differences.
The Serbian Student List does not have a single strong leader figure in sharp contrast to Péter Magyar’s strong position in Tisza. It is based on a grassroots group of people with little prior experience of frontline politics, and not on a former insider who switched sides, with all sorts of upsides and downsides that come with that. For one, we do not even know who could be their PM.
The Student List’s path to a parliamentary majority was also technically more complicated or, put it simply, required a larger win. That is largely down to the mechanics of the Serbian electoral system, which – unlike the setup Viktor Orbán had tailored in Hungary with the intention of helping his own party, not the opposition – does not offer the same disproportionate winner’s bonus.
Finally, the underlying issues demanding immediate attention are possibly much bigger and more complicated to resolve in Serbia than in Hungary, particularly without the option of getting some EU funds flowing quickly after the vote to buy you some good will and time. Hungary’s Tisza is much more openly pro-European than the Student List.
But Magyar clearly and, at least to an extent, rightly sees the two movements and their victories as linked: earlier this morning, he even posted a slightly cheesy post reminiscing the times he and his parents spent at an unnamed Serbian restaurant in Budapest, “which has since closed down.”
“Fortunately, you can still find great ćevapi in plenty of places, whether Sarajevo-style or Serbian-style,” he added, posting a picture of himself with the said ćevapi.
(There are some sensational Serbian places in London, too. Just saying.)
Hungary's Magyar congratulates the Student List on election win
Hungary’s prime minister Péter Magyar – who came to power ousting Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power – is among the very first European leaders to offer his congratulations to the Student List.
In a post on X, he says:
“I have just spoken by phone with the leaders of the Students’ List @studentblokade, who won the elections in Serbia, to congratulate them on their victory. I assured them of Hungary’s support.
I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle.”
Earlier tonight, he cheekily said:
“In Serbia, @avucic has conceded defeat. The Students’ List has won an absolute majority in the elections. Celebrations have begun in the streets across Serbia. Sound familiar?”
'We will remember this moment for the rest of our lives'
Ana Milosavljevic
in Belgrade
“I think this is a moment we will remember for the rest of our lives,” Sara, 24, says as she smiles with her friends.
“It’s simply the realisation of our dream. And it’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors.”
She continues:
“I think this is a victory for everything we stood for, for all the values we promoted through the student movement. And I’m very glad that we’ve proven that Serbia only wins when the students win.”
"After 14 years, we finally feel freedom again,” Nemanja, 29, says when we start chatting amid celebrations in Belgrade.
“We feel that justice will come and that this will become a beautiful and good country, where people can get ahead through their own knowledge and abilities.”
'A victory of courage over fear, of hope over indifference,' Student List's Saičić says, but adds 'tomorrow, the work begins'
Speaking at the Student List’s election night party, chemist Radomir Saičić had one of the strongest speeches as he thanked all who cast their votes in today’s election.
But he said “tonight is about more than just the results: it is about the people who kept believing when things where at their hardest, who refused to give up, to believe that nothing could ever change.”
He calls it “a victory of courage over fear;of hope over indifference; and of conviction that Serbia can, and must, be different.”
He says the victory “is not a personal trophy; does not belong to any of us,” and brings about “great responsibility” for all those in the new parliamentary majority.
“Tonight we have shown that change is not only possible, but that there is a will for it. Now we must prove ourselves worthy of the trust we have been given. …
Tonight, we celebrate in the way Serbia knows to do best: with song, dance, embraces, and tears of joy. And tomorrow? Tomorrow, the work begins.”
In pretty moving scenes, some people offer handshakes, high fives and even bear hugs to police officers as they stand aside from blocking the streets, despite earlier concerns about a potential mobilisation of security forces.
The crowd is now moving towards Slavija square, where they held their final pre-election on Thursday.
Crta’s projection is very similar to that of Ipsos/CeSIR (21:43):it puts the Student List at 51.2% with 134 seats in the new parliament, well clear of the 126 required for the majority.
Vučić’s list is in the second place with 40.4% of the vote and 106 seats.
10 seats are expected to go to minority groups, including three seats each for Hungarians and Albanians.

Ships in Black Sea switch off transponders to avoid drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:00:57 UTC
01:00:57 KST

Sunday 25 October 2026 17:24
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 17:24
PHOTO .maritime.bg
Font size
A Sierra Leone-flagged vessel carrying grain from the Ukrainian port of Reni to Egypt was sailing off the Bulgarian coast on 24 October with its tracking transponder switched off. The vessel’s name has not been disclosed for security reasons, Maritime.bg reports.
During radio contact, Bulgaria’s Vessel Traffic Services (VTS) centre advised the officer on watch to activate the ship’s Automatic Identification System (AIS) to ensure safe navigation in Bulgaria’s territorial waters.
The vessel replied that the system had been switched off at the explicit request of its insurer to reduce risks during the voyage to the Bosphorus.
Commercial vessels in the western Black Sea are increasingly switching off their AIS systems at the request of insurance companies. Others are also using equipment to jam GPS signals, the publication notes, creating safety risks for ships and their crews.

Returnee from Czechia: Apathy on election day is surprising
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

Author
Gergana Mancheva
News
Returnee from Czechia: Apathy on election day is surprising
Sasho Vakashinski: The first thing i did today was vote
Sunday 25 October 2026 17:06
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 17:06
PHOTO Reuters
Font size
One of the few Bulgarian compatriots who voted early this morning was Sasho Vakashinski, who recently returned to Bulgaria. He is from the village of Pokrovnik, near the town of Blagoevgrad (Southwestern Bulgaria).
“The first thing my family and I did today was go and vote. This is an obligation of every Bulgarian citizen, a right guaranteed by our Constitution. However, I see that many people do not exercise this right, both in Bulgaria and abroad”, Sasho Vakashinski said in an interview with Radio Bulgaria.
In previous elections, he voted in the Czech Republic. He says that the problem with polling stations abroad is logistical: people have to travel long distances because polling stations are located only in Prague, at the Bulgarian Embassy. Meanwhile, more than 50,000 Bulgarians live in the Czech Republic, spread across various cities throughout the country.
Sasho Vakashinski has been living in Bulgaria for over a year now and today he is surprised to see such apathy among his fellow Bulgarians on election day, even in their own homeland.
PHOTO BGNES
“I don’t know why people in Bulgaria make excuses and don’t go out to vote. Even if they were undecided in the first round and didn’t know whom to vote for, I don’t think voter turnout would be particularly high even in a runoff election. I’ve been back in Bulgaria for a little over a year now, and I can see people’s attitude toward elections. There is a complete indifference here. People no longer care about what will happen to Bulgaria. Everyone is clinging to some job that pays very little, with no concern for the country’s future. And the country’s future is the future of our children and grandchildren. What are we going to leave these children? A country that has fallen apart?”
“Unfortunately, Bulgarians living abroad are much more active in elections and think more about Bulgaria than those who live here”, our compatriot adds sadly.
PHOTO mfa.bg
“Many people are returning to Bulgaria, not only from the Czech Republic, but also from the UK, Italy and Germany. Quite a few of them are young people who were not even born in Bulgaria. I hope that these people, who did not grow up in the country but hold Bulgarian citizenship, will be the ones to bring about change. You simply cannot have a minimum wage of just EUR 620 in Bulgaria! In the Czech Republic, for example, the minimum wage in Czech koruna is equivalent to EUR 800. But hardly anyone there actually works for the minimum wage, it is just a formal baseline. Starting salaries are higher. Recently, some friends of mine from the Czech Republic came to visit, and they were surprised to find that many products in Bulgarian shops were more expensive. And I am not even talking about restaurant prices. Everything that was priced in leva last year is now priced in euros, while wages here are half what they are in other countries. That is the reality. If someone had told me years ago that I would return to Bulgaria, I would have laughed at them. But here I am today, living in Bulgaria with my whole family. We now live in a village near Blagoevgrad. But even here in the city, there are no jobs. Most people work in Sofia, and to avoid paying rent there, they commute every day. The tragic thing about Bulgaria is the lack of employment opportunities. There are a few shops and perhaps a small workshop employing 10 to 20 people. For a regional city, that is practically nothing.”
After spending more than 15 years in the Czech Republic, Sasho Vakashinski has returned to Bulgaria only to find that, in his homeland, little seems to have changed.
“If you have no money here, you simply end up dying on the street. A minimum wage of just EUR 620 would be enough to bring people out onto the streets in protest in a country like France, for example. But we are a nation that has fallen asleep, despite our glorious past. Still, I hope we will have a glorious future, too! We Bulgarians may be slow to wake up, but once we do, nothing can stop us. That is what I’m hoping for”, said Sasho Vakashinski.

How the menstrual cycle might alter ADHD symptoms in women taking stimulant medication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

The menstrual cycle appears to modulate the severity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) traits in women taking common stimulant medications. A new small study suggests that these traits peak in severity during menstruation and ease soon after, pointing toward a need for hormone-aware treatment plans. The research was published in the Journal of Attention Disorders.
ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by distraction, impulsivity, and hyperactive behavior. Medical professionals historically viewed the condition as something that primarily affected young boys. That diagnostic gap is rapidly closing, and women now make up nearly half of the adult ADHD population in the United States. Women often present with different behavioral patterns than men, leaning toward severe inattention and internalizing behaviors rather than disruptive hyperactivity.
Despite facing daily impairments in their careers and social lives, women remain largely underrepresented in ADHD research. One distinct biological variable separating women from men is the constant fluctuation of ovarian hormones. During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, estrogen levels rise and peak near ovulation. The subsequent luteal phase features elevated estrogen and progesterone, which then drop rapidly shortly before menstruation begins.
Researchers suspect these hormones play a direct role in brain chemistry. Low estrogen levels are thought to decrease dopamine signaling in the brain. Because dopamine is the primary neurotransmitter involved in focus and attention, these natural hormonal drops could theoretically worsen ADHD symptoms.
Researchers Rebecca Zaritsky, Stephanie C. Reed, and Suzette M. Evans wanted to understand how these hormonal variations interact with ADHD treatments. Prior laboratory work demonstrated that amphetamines, the most commonly prescribed class of ADHD medications, can be less effective during the luteal phase of the cycle. Case reports from clinical settings also hinted that some women experience worsening moods and fading concentration right before their periods.
The research team designed a study to track these daily changes prospectively. The investigators recruited participants through online advertisements to monitor their daily experiences. They screened for individuals between the ages of 18 and 40 who experienced regular menstrual cycles lasting between 21 and 35 days.
To join the study, participants had to report an ADHD diagnosis and currently use amphetamine salts (commonly known by brand names like Adderall) for treatment on at least five days of the week. The team excluded anyone taking hormonal birth control, as well as individuals using other psychiatric medications. After exclusions and dropouts, the researchers ended up with a small study of 30 participants who completed the required long-term tracking.
Each individual filled out an initial survey detailing their medical history, baseline mood, and general impulsive behaviors. Following this baseline assessment, participants completed a daily online survey for 35 consecutive days. This extended timeline ensured the researchers could capture data from one full menstrual cycle for every participant.
The daily questionnaires asked participants to rate their current ADHD symptoms on a standardized four-point scale. They evaluated 18 distinct symptoms, splitting them equally between inattentive traits and hyperactive-impulsive traits. Participants also rated their daily mood variations on a six-point scale measuring 17 distinct emotional states, and reported their exact medication dosage for the day. Finally, they noted whether they were actively menstruating or spotting.
The researchers averaged the daily survey responses and grouped them into three specific biological windows. These windows included the first five days of menstruation, the mid-follicular phase shortly after bleeding ends, and the late luteal phase just before the next period begins. Participants reported their most severe ADHD symptoms during the active menstruation phase. In contrast, they experienced comparatively milder symptoms during the mid-follicular phase.
When researchers separated the specific types of ADHD traits, hyperactive and impulsive behaviors showed variation across the cycle phases, but after adjusting for multiple comparisons this amounted only to a trend rather than a statistically significant difference. Inattentive symptoms also fluctuated, but the differences were not statistically significant. Participants did not report any differences in how much their symptoms generally impaired their daily lives across the different phases.
Mood tracking revealed a correlation between negative emotions and ADHD symptoms. Participants reported elevated negative moods during both the late luteal and menstruation phases compared to the mid-follicular phase. The individuals who experienced the largest drops in mood during menstruation also reported the greatest increases in ADHD symptoms. This correlation held true for both inattentive and hyperactive traits.
Daily amphetamine doses remained remarkably steady across the entire cycle. Participants did not instinctively take more medication to compensate for feeling more distracted or hyperactive during their periods. The research team had hypothesized that some participants using flexible dosing regimens might attempt to counteract their worsening symptoms with higher doses. This lack of adjustment might reflect strict prescribing practices, as many doctors do not encourage patients to alter their daily stimulant intake based on their menstrual cycles.
This research relied entirely on self-reported surveys. The investigators did not measure hormone levels in a laboratory to perfectly confirm each biological phase, opting instead to estimate phases based on reported bleeding days. The small sample size also limited the statistical power of the analysis, meaning the results require verification in larger populations. Because participants taking other psychiatric medications were excluded, the results might not represent individuals managing ADHD alongside conditions such as mood disorders or premenstrual dysphoric disorder.
The study design carried a few distinct demographic and methodological limitations. The researchers did not explicitly gather information on gender identity, meaning the relationship between gender identity, hormone cycles, and ADHD remains untested in this specific context. The standardized survey tool used to track daily symptoms was also based on older diagnostic criteria. This older framework lacks recent diagnostic updates designed to capture how ADHD presents in adults.
The research team also looked at baseline mental health using standardized questionnaires for depression and anxiety. They found a trend suggesting that individuals with higher baseline depression and anxiety scores might experience slightly smaller shifts in ADHD symptoms across their cycles. However, having a higher overall symptom count on average consistently predicted a lower ADHD-related quality of life.
Future studies will need to incorporate direct hormone sampling to precisely map biological changes to behavioral shifts. Researchers might also explore how oral contraceptives or specific antidepressants impact this hormonal cycle in neurodivergent populations. Some clinics have already begun testing symptom-based dosing regimens, where patients take slightly more medication during the specific weeks when their natural hormones work against them. Tracking these targeted interventions could eventually help doctors provide highly individualized care for women navigating adult ADHD.
The study, “Changes in ADHD Symptoms and Mood Across the Menstrual Cycle in Females Treated With Stimulants: A Pilot Study,” was authored by Rebecca Zaritsky, Stephanie C. Reed, and Suzette M. Evans.

Glaciers are melting and revealing millennia-old secrets: what archaeologists find beneath the ice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:00:01 EET
01:00:01 KST

Glaciers are melting and revealing millennia-old secrets: what archaeologists find beneath the ice
Kyiv • UNN
The melting of glaciers is revealing mummies, weapons and clothing to archaeologists, including the 5,300-year-old body of Ötzi. Moisture and air threaten the finds.
Due to global warming, glaciers around the world are rapidly melting, revealing unique finds to archaeologists that had remained hidden beneath the ice for millennia. Among them are mummified human remains, ancient weapons, clothing, and other household items. BBC reports, UNN writes.
Details
One of the most famous finds was Ötzi the “Iceman,” whose body was accidentally discovered by German tourists in the Alps in 1991 at an altitude of about 3,200 meters. At first, they thought they had come across a victim of a recent accident.
However, radiocarbon analysis showed that the man lived approximately 5,300 years ago, before the construction of the Egyptian pyramids. His body was so well preserved that researchers were able to make out tattoos, determine the composition of his last meal, and discover an arrowhead lodged in his shoulder, indicating a violent death.
Thousands of ancient artifacts are emerging from beneath the ice
According to a 2025 study, from 2000 to 2023, the world's glaciers, excluding the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, lost an average of about 270 billion tonnes of ice each year. The fastest melting occurred during the last decade.
Norwegian archaeologist Espen Finstad said that over the past 20 years alone, researchers had found thousands of items that had previously been concealed by the ice.
It is a huge historical freezer that no longer works. That is why these artifacts are reappearing in the world, and many of them have been preserved just as well as they were thousands of years ago
Archaeologist Andreas Putzer emphasizes that such discoveries are particularly valuable because they make it possible to study the daily lives of ancient people. Unlike burials, where objects were often placed deliberately, finds such as Ötzi preserve the items a person used directly before their death.
At the same time, melting glaciers are creating a new problem for archaeologists: once ancient objects emerge from beneath the ice, they are exposed to moisture, air, and temperature fluctuations, which can cause them to deteriorate rapidly.

Billionaire Trump backer says Ben-Gvir, Smotrich should not serve in next Israeli government
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:59:19 CET
00:59:19 KST

By Steven Scheer and Alexander Cornwell
JERUSALEM, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Billionaire American investor Bill Ackman on Sunday said that Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich should not serve in Israel’s next government, saying the two far-right politicians had caused enormous damage to the country’s reputation.
The public intervention by the prominent hedge fund manager, who is Jewish, comes just two days before Israel’s general election, in which polls show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition and the opposition.
Ackman wrote on X that from the perspective of someone who had an understanding of how Israel was perceived in the United States, “Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions.”
BOTH MINISTERS HAVE FACED SANCTIONS
The founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, who praised Netanyahu last week, said a government without the two ministers would send a message that Israel was “turning a new page.”
“This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large,” he said.
The Abraham Accords are the 2020 agreement, mediated by President Donald Trump’s first administration, that saw Israel establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. It later reestablished official ties with Morocco.
Representatives for Ben-Gvir and Smotrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
As ministers in Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have overseen policies widely perceived as discriminatory against Israel’s minority Arab population and Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank.
Several countries, including Britain, Canada and Australia, have imposed sanctions on the two ministers over accusations that they have incited violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party is projected to win around 10 parliamentary seats at Tuesday’s election, up from 6, while Smotrich’s Religious Zionism is projected to win 8, up from 7.
Ackman, who was visiting Israel last week, and who along with his wife Neri Oxman owns 5% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, supported Donald Trump’s candidacy for president in 2024. Trump last week publicly endorsed Netanyahu for prime minister.
Nimrod Goren, the president of Israeli think tank Mitvim, said Ackman’s statement appeared to reflect a desire among Trump’s circles for Netanyahu to drop his far-right allies after the vote to form a ‘unity government’ with opposition parties.
However, Gadi Eisenkot, the leading challenger to Netanyahu, and other opposition party leaders have ruled out forming a government with Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
Speaking at a Tel Aviv conference on Thursday, Ackman praised Netanyahu, who he said had done a good job in protecting and defending Israel since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
Thousands of Israelis rallied in Tel Aviv on Saturday calling for an independent inquiry into the attack that killed around 1,200 people.
(Reporting by Steven Scheer, Alexander Cornwell; writing by Alexander Cornwell; editing by Andrew Heavens)

The riots left 14 officers injured, four of them seriously, while a municipal police officer was also injured.

128 arrested in Barcelona riots as Italy detains activist who praised Hamas' October 7 massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:51:08 UTC
00:51:08 KST

Spanish police arrested 128 people during a night of looting, vandalism and violent unrest in Barcelona, authorities announced Sunday, as a wave of youth-led protests continued to sweep across European cities. Meanwhile, Italian police detained a 30-year-old pro-Palestinian activist suspected of encouraging further unrest through social media, with local reports revealing his history of praising Hamas' October 7 attack on Israel.
The disturbances in Barcelona began Saturday evening, when hundreds of young people gathered around Plaça de Catalunya, one of the city's busiest central squares, following calls circulated on social media. The gathering had not been authorized by local authorities and quickly descended into violence.
Video footage shared online showed groups of young people, many dressed entirely in black and wearing masks, running through the streets, smashing store windows and carrying away stolen merchandise. Clothing, footwear and electronics stores were among the businesses targeted.
According to the Catalan regional police, known as the Mossos d'Esquadra, 23 businesses were vandalized or looted, while firefighters responded to 33 fires involving street furniture, garbage containers and other property.
More than half of those arrested were minors, according to authorities. Catalan police chief Sílvia Catà said 73 detainees were under 18, while other police summaries put the figure at 72. Only two of those arrested had previous records for public disorder offenses. Fifteen police officers were injured during the disturbances, four of them seriously.
Some of the most alarming scenes unfolded inside shopping establishments. Videos showed customers trapped inside stores, including the El Corte Inglés department store, after security shutters were lowered to prevent looters from entering.
Other footage showed masked rioters kicking through shop windows before fleeing with merchandise. In several cases, participants broadcast their actions live on social media, where viewers could be seen encouraging them.
Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni condemned the violence and warned that those responsible would face legal consequences, including potential action against the guardians of minors involved.
Catà described the disturbances as violence for its own sake, saying investigators were working to establish the backgrounds of those detained and determine how the unrest had been organized.
Although the participants did not appear to belong to a single organization, police said they had coordinated their activities through social media. Online posts encouraged young people to join an anti-establishment movement, sometimes using the slogan Instituts Indignats, a reference to the French Lycéens Indignés, or "Angry High School Students," movement that has mobilized demonstrators in France in recent weeks.
The incidents come amid a broader wave of demonstrations across Europe, although the protests have varied significantly in their demands and levels of violence.
Soldiers deployed in Milan, protesters enter Rome's Colosseum
Italy has become another focal point of the unrest, particularly Milan, where violent clashes and looting the previous weekend involved approximately 2,000 young demonstrators, according to police. Many were teenagers from working-class suburbs, including children of immigrant families.
Italian authorities responded to fears of renewed violence Saturday by deploying large numbers of police officers and soldiers to major cities.
In Milan, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government sent an additional 500 soldiers to reinforce the security presence, alongside thousands of police and other law enforcement personnel. Authorities also conducted preventive checks and tightened security around transport hubs and shopping districts.
Businesses prepared for the worst. Luxury retailers in Milan's famous fashion district, including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, covered their windows with wooden boards to protect them from potential attacks.
Thousands of demonstrators nevertheless gathered in the city, chanting slogans against Meloni and displaying banners reading "No to the lies of the state." One group dumped waste outside the offices of Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic oversized electricity bill in protest against rising costs.
Despite fears of another violent outbreak, the main demonstration in Milan ended largely peacefully, in contrast to the previous weekend's destruction. A separate group of about 30 far-right activists, described as soccer hooligans associated with Inter Milan, appeared briefly and shouted anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans before being isolated by police.
Rome also saw heightened security, with authorities restricting access to luxury shopping streets and major landmarks. A small group of protesters attempted to force its way into the Colosseum, and some entered the ancient amphitheater before being escorted out by security personnel.
Elsewhere in the capital, an anti-war march turned tense despite organizers' efforts to prevent violence. Participants had been urged to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible to demonstrate that they had no intention of attacking police.
Nevertheless, brief confrontations broke out near Piazza della Repubblica, where officers used batons, tear gas and water cannons to disperse demonstrators. Similar tensions were reported in other Italian cities, including Turin, as protests continued over economic hardship, government policies and international conflicts.
The Moroccan-origin activist suspected of inciting unrest
As Italian authorities investigated the violence in Milan, attention turned to Youssef Siher, a 30-year-old Italian citizen of Moroccan descent who had become prominent in pro-Palestinian activist circles.
Police detained Siher on Saturday following an investigation into a social media movement called Movimento 17 ottobre, or "October 17 Movement," which promoted demonstrations across several Italian cities.
According to Italian reports, Siher created an Instagram page and Telegram group after the initial outbreak of violence in Milan, using the platforms to encourage further demonstrations and urge followers to take control of public squares.
Investigators suspect that the online campaign sought to capitalize on anger among young Italians, particularly those from immigrant backgrounds, toward the authorities.
Following searches of properties associated with Siher, investigators reportedly recovered electronic files containing proposed gathering points and organizational details for demonstrations planned for Saturday. At least one of those locations was subsequently used by pro-Palestinian protesters.
Siher was detained on orders from Milan prosecutors and is under investigation for alleged criminal incitement, organized violence at public demonstrations and terrorism-related offenses. He has not been convicted. Italian authorities also placed his wife under investigation in connection with the same alleged offenses, although she remained free.
There is an important distinction between the allegations against Siher and his possible responsibility for the earlier unrest. His online movement emerged after the initial disturbances in Milan, and Italian reporting has cautioned that investigators have not established whether he exercised actual command over the original rioters.
The investigation has nevertheless brought renewed scrutiny to Siher's background and his previous activities.
Siher, who grew up in the Brescia area in northern Italy, pursued higher education in communications and political science at the University of Milan. He also studied political Islam, Middle Eastern politics and geopolitical affairs.
His academic background included research experience at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, known as ISPI. He also worked as a freelance journalist, contributing to Italian publications including Il Fatto Quotidiano and Il Foglio. Although he had no previous criminal record, Siher had become increasingly active in pro-Palestinian organizations and demonstrations in Italy.
According to Corriere della Sera, Italian intelligence agencies had taken an interest in him in 2024 after he established an organization called Alba Nascente, or "Rising Dawn." The group reportedly promoted demonstrations against Israel and disseminated material sympathetic to Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.
Italian media also reported that Siher had collaborated with a satellite television channel described as close to Hezbollah. The nature and extent of that alleged relationship have not been independently established.
His past statements about the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel have attracted particular attention. On the day of the attack, Siher responded to a social media message by Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini expressing solidarity with Israel by writing "Allahu Akbar," meaning "God is greatest."
In a subsequent article published by the online magazine Miccia, Siher argued that few people in the West had understood the true meaning of Hamas' October 7 operation, known by the organization as Al-Aqsa Flood.
He described it as "a revolutionary act of decolonization," portraying the assault through an ideological framework of resistance to colonialism. The statement has since resurfaced in Italian media coverage of his detention.
Siher continued publishing criticism of Israel and the Italian government in recent months. In some writings, he sought to connect separate incidents involving the deaths of young men from immigrant backgrounds during encounters with law enforcement, presenting them as examples of wider institutional discrimination.
Investigators are now examining whether his online activity went beyond political advocacy and crossed the legal threshold into criminal incitement or the organization of violence.
The case comes as European authorities confront the growing role of social media in mobilizing demonstrations, including gatherings that begin with political demands but escalate into coordinated attacks on property and confrontations with police.

The dollar has hit an all-time record in Ukraine: what is happening with the exchange rate
Kyiv • UNN
The NBU set the dollar exchange rate for October 26 at UAH 45.2021 — a new all-time record. Cash exchange rates may differ.
The National Bank of Ukraine set the official exchange rate of the dollar for Monday, October 26, at UAH 45.2021. The U.S. currency reached a new all-time high against the hryvnia. UNN reports this, citing NBU data.
Details
The previous record was recorded on October 14, when the official dollar exchange rate stood at UAH 45.0802. Thus, the new figure exceeded the previous high by approximately 12 kopecks.
At the same time, the euro also remains near record levels. However, the exact exchange rate of the European currency for October 26 is not provided in the data cited.
What the new dollar record means
The NBU’s official exchange rate is used for accounting and other calculations stipulated by law. At the same time, cash exchange rates at banks and exchange offices may differ from the rate set by the regulator.
The new dollar high indicates a further nominal weakening of the hryvnia against the U.S. currency. At the same time, the official exchange-rate record alone does not mean a sharp jump in the dollar’s value on the cash market.

The U.S. program had already restricted certain U.S. investments involving China in semiconductors, quantum technologies and artificial intelligence.

"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."

Russia failed to create its own strategic silicon: the multimillion-ruble contract was terminated
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:41:05 EET
00:41:05 KST

Russia failed to create its own strategic silicon: the multimillion-ruble contract was terminated
Kyiv • UNN
Russia terminated a 400 million ruble contract due to the failure to carry out work on producing silicon for power electronics. The launch may be postponed until 2028.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade of the Russian Federation terminated a RUB 400 million contract with a Rosatom enterprise that was supposed to develop technology for producing special silicon for power electronics. UNN reports this, citing the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine.
Details
Due to the failure to fulfill its obligations, the launch of domestic production of the strategically important material in Russia may be postponed until at least 2028.
The contract was with JSC Research Institute of Instruments, which is part of the Rosatom structure. The enterprise was supposed to develop technology for manufacturing 150 mm-diameter silicon wafers needed to produce high-power electronic components.
The agreement was concluded in December 2024, and the work was scheduled to be completed by the end of 2026. However, the contractor was unable to fulfill its obligations even under the first stage of the project, which involved manufacturing pilot batches of the material and conducting preliminary tests. The deadline for completing the first stage expired on May 15, 2026. At the same time, the institute failed to provide the required reporting documentation and documents for accepting the work. Due to the breach of the contract terms, the Russian ministry imposed a fine of RUB 1.5 million on the enterprise, which remained unpaid at the time the agreement was terminated.
The project envisaged mastering the production of ingots and polished wafers of neutron-transmutation-doped single-crystal silicon. This material is used to manufacture power thyristors, IGBT transistors, and high-speed diodes, which are used in electric transport, power equipment, as well as the defense and space industries. However, Russia currently has no domestic production of this type of silicon, while the procurement of foreign counterparts is complicated by the material's strategic purpose. That is why the development was supposed to become one of the elements of Russia's import-substitution program in the field of high-tech electronics.
The enterprise was expected to prepare the technological foundation for creating production with a capacity of at least 100,000 silicon wafers per year. The transition to mass production was planned for 2027. However, following the termination of the contract, these deadlines have been called into question. According to Oleksandr Tymoshenko, head of Troichni Technologies, the development of production of the strategic material in Russia may now be postponed until 2028 or later.
Recall
In March 2026, the Armed Forces of Ukraine attacked the Kremniy El Group plant in the Russian Federation, which manufactures chips for missile systems and unmanned aerial vehicles. The plant produces components for Iskanders and S-400s.

The public intervention by the prominent hedge fund manager, who is Jewish, comes just two days before Israel's general election, in which polls show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition.
Ackman wrote on X that from the perspective of someone who had an understanding of how Israel was perceived in the United States, "Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions."
BOTH MINISTERS HAVE FACED SANCTIONS
The founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, who praised Netanyahu last week, said a government without the two ministers would send a message that Israel was "turning a new page."
"This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large," he said.
The Abraham Accords are the 2020 agreement, mediated by President Donald Trump's first administration, that saw Israel establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. It later reestablished official ties with Morocco.
Representatives for Ben-Gvir and Smotrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
As ministers in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have overseen policies widely perceived as discriminatory against Israel's minority Arab population and Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank.

Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party is projected to win around 10 parliamentary seats at Tuesday's election, up from 6, while Smotrich's Religious Zionism is projected to win 8, up from 7.
Ackman, who was visiting Israel last week, and who along with his wife Neri Oxman owns 5% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, supported Donald Trump's candidacy for president in 2024. Trump last week publicly endorsed Netanyahu for prime minister.
