Economic Watch: European firms put Chinese technology to work
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:32:36 CST
23:32:36 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 22, 2026 shows the opening ceremony of the 19th Europe-China Business and Technology Cooperation Fair in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province. (Xinhua)
CHENGDU, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- At a machinery factory in Vicenza, Italy, Chinese-made robots weld components and move materials. The machines come from Chengdu CRP Robot Technology Co., Ltd., which now has more than 20 partners across 13 European countries.
Thirty years ago, German entrepreneur Harald Kumpfert relied largely on European technology for his energy-saving projects in China. Today, he buys Chinese heat pumps, thermal storage equipment and heat exchangers, and is trying to introduce Chinese technology to Europe.
"Now most technology is actually from China," Kumpfert said at a business fair in Chengdu, capital of southwest China's Sichuan Province.
The 19th Europe-China Business and Technology Cooperation Fair, which concluded Friday, brought together about 200 Chinese and European companies for nearly 400 one-on-one business meetings.
Kumpfert's experience shows the importance European businesses place on Chinese suppliers.
In a 2026 survey by the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, 94 percent of respondents said sourcing from China was important or very important to their supply chains and business success, while 75 percent said that their production lines in China were more efficient than those elsewhere.
The automotive industry shows how competition and cooperation can develop side by side.
China's rapid advances in new energy vehicles have intensified competition for established European automakers. Yet European carmakers remain interested in investing in China and are working with Chinese companies to explore opportunities in European markets, according to Adam Dunnett, secretary-general of the chamber.
Dunnett described China's electric vehicle development as "nothing short of amazing" and said there was considerable scope for further cooperation.
"I think there is a much bigger upside to what can happen in the future than perhaps the focus on all the challenges that we are facing right now," he said.
Some European businesses are also expanding their research and development operations in China.
Swiss specialty chemicals maker Sika Group has 33 factories and four of its nine global R&D centers in China. Zhang Yejiong, President of Sika China, said the company was expanding local R&D while incorporating low-carbon requirements into product development.
Chinese components are also attracting European researchers. Juha Röning, a professor at Finland's University of Oulu and euRobotics' Vice President of Research, said the availability of Chinese-made sensors, motors and gears allowed researchers to concentrate on developing new applications rather than building every component themselves.
For equipment manufacturers, selling to Europe increasingly involves more than shipping machines.
CRP Robot is working with European local partners to improve technical support and after-sales services, its deputy general manager Deng Shihai said. Luigi Gambardella, president of the international digital association ChinaEU, said Chinese robots entering European factories could also generate business for local engineers, software developers and service providers.
European producers, meanwhile, are pursuing opportunities in China's consumer market.
Hervé Grangeon, founder of Ergaster Distillery in France, came to Chengdu seeking distributors for his gin and whisky, while Spanish ham producer Garcia Lizana is preparing the documents needed to enter China.
Smaller European businesses, however, often struggle to find local partners and navigate market-entry requirements, Zhang said. He suggested that local governments and business associations could help them identify opportunities by providing policy guidance and connecting them with potential Chinese partners.
Among the technologies on display was a Chinese elevator energy-saving system that caught Kumpfert's attention. Having spent much of his career bringing European technology to China, he now plans to explore cooperation with its Chinese developer. ■

World Investment Forum 2026 opens in Qatar amid global economic uncertainty
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:32:35 CST
23:32:35 KST

DOHA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- The World Investment Forum 2026 opened here on Sunday, bringing together more than 5,000 participants to discuss global investment challenges and ways to increase capital flows to developing economies amid geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty.
Organized by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and hosted by Qatar, the three-day forum, themed "Investing in the Future," is attended by the prime ministers of Qatar, Lesotho, Libya and Madagascar, four deputy prime ministers and nearly 50 government ministers.
More than 80 sessions featuring over 400 speakers will cover investment policies, artificial intelligence, entrepreneurship, sustainable finance, climate change, tourism and emerging industries.
The forum opened as new UNCTAD data showed continued weakness in global investment activity.
Its latest Global Investment Trends Monitor, released Sunday, said the value of international investment rose in the first half of 2026, supported by major transactions in strategic sectors, while new investment projects and cross-border transactions continued to decline worldwide.
Investment in sectors critical to development, including infrastructure, energy, healthcare and food systems, fell by more than 25 percent in developing countries, the report showed.
UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2026 also found that more than 80 percent of global foreign direct investment was concentrated in just 20 economies in 2025, highlighting persistent disparities in international capital flows.
The forum's agenda includes two ministerial meetings on investment and entrepreneurship, as well as discussions on investment opportunities in the Gulf region and other emerging markets.
For the first time, the event features a dedicated track on artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on investment in AI infrastructure and opportunities for developing economies.
Other new topics include investment in post-conflict reconstruction and recovery, the space industry and cultural sectors.
Launched in 2008, the World Investment Forum is held every two years to discuss international investment policies and promote investment in sustainable development. ■

China Focus: Health work, emergency facilities back post-quake resettlement in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:32:30 CST
23:32:30 KST

BAQEN, Xizang, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Rescue and relief efforts continue after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, with public health and epidemic prevention work underway in affected areas, according to local authorities.
The earthquake, which struck Baqen County in the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, has left 16 people dead and 76 others injured so far. More than 12,000 residents were evacuated after the quake.
To prevent public health risks after the quake, disease control teams in Baqen County have carried out comprehensive epidemic prevention work. The work includes infectious disease monitoring of more than 3,600 residents across 35 resettlement sites, disinfection of public areas and high-risk contamination spots, and drinking water safety testing, the earthquake relief headquarters of Nagqu said on Sunday.
In the immediate aftermath of the earthquake, hospitals near the disaster zone swiftly dispatched medical workers for rescue efforts.
On Saturday, a female villager from an affected area with an abrasion on her left ankle told Xinhua, "The doctor arrived before dawn on Friday and promptly applied ointment and bandaged it for me." A 23-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, also received basic health checks, including vital-sign measurements.
Multiple resettlement sites have set up mobile medical stations, each staffed with health workers ready to treat common illnesses and minor injuries, with regular checkups, medicine supplies, disinfection, and basic psychological counseling.
The epicenter in Baqen County sits at an average altitude of nearly 4,800 meters, where temperatures are already low in late October. Yet inside the tents set up for displaced residents, stoves keep the shelters warm.
On Saturday, the first batch of new-generation emergency relief facilities, including a mobile food vehicle, a water purification station, and an eco-friendly toilet, was put into use in the affected area in Baqen County.
The mobile food vehicle allows four people to work inside the truck-sized box and eight outside at the same time. Meals for 300 to 500 people can be fully prepared in just two hours.
At 6:30 p.m., the first meal off the stove was braised beef with potatoes and stir-fried greens, drawing many residents over to try it.
"The truck is really cool, and the food tastes great too," said Norbu Tsering, a villager from Maru Township.
"The truck is equipped with a high-pressure rice steamer which can cook 18 trays of rice at once. The stainless steel tableware is washed after use, then sterilized in a disinfection cabinet for the next round," said Ma Hua, deputy director of the 999 emergency rescue center in Xizang.
Access to clean water is crucial but challenging in the quake-hit plateau, especially in winter.
In Maru Township, a mobile water purification station can purify two tonnes of well water per hour. Equipped with solar power generation, insulation materials and an energy storage system, it is designed to operate in temperatures as low as minus 30 degrees Celsius, said Ji Tao, head of the Baqen branch of the company that provided the purification facilities.
Five administrative villages in Maru Township had already received the water purification facilities, Ji said, adding that coverage would be expanded.
Near the purification station, an eco-friendly toilet with rooftop solar panels and a waterless, flush-free system has been put up. Solar power provides lighting and drives fermentation, while enzymes break down waste in a sealed tank, which can be used as fertilizer, according to Tsewang Ngodrup, an official with the Nagqu municipal science and technology bureau.
More than 5,000 rescue personnel have been deployed at all levels. Relief supplies from central and local governments are arriving in the disaster zone in succession. ■

Providing humanitarian assistance to Iranian crew members brought ashore after falling ill on vessels outside the country's territorial waters is in accordance with international maritime law and recognised humanitarian principles, Deputy Health Minister Hansaka Wijemuni said. ■

China

23:32:17 KST

ALMATY, Kazakhstan, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's growing investment in tennis infrastructure, expanding tournament calendar and emerging junior talent are laying the foundations for sustained success, Asian Tennis Federation President Yuri Polsky said.
Speaking to Xinhua on the sidelines of the 2026 Almaty Open, Polsky praised the rapid development of tennis in China, highlighting the country's achievements at the elite level and efforts to cultivate the next generation of players.
"Tennis in China is growing pretty fast," Polsky said, pointing to the impact of Zheng Qinwen's historic women's singles gold medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
Zheng's triumph, which made her the first Asian player to win an Olympic singles gold medal in tennis, represented a significant milestone for the sport in China and helped raise its profile among the wider public.
"The Olympic gold was a big improvement, and it showed the Chinese population that tennis is a priority sport," Polsky said.
China has established itself as an increasingly important destination on the international tennis calendar, hosting major events including the Shanghai Masters, China Open in Beijing and Wuhan Open, as well as Billie Jean King Cup competitions in Shenzhen.
Beyond professional tournaments, Polsky highlighted the construction of new tennis facilities and the expansion of junior competitions as important elements of China's long-term development.
"At the regional level, a lot of new tennis centres are being built," he said. "New tournaments are happening."
Polsky said he had seen plans for the new Beijing facility, which would feature tennis courts on two levels, including both clay and hard courts.
"It's an amazing project," he said.
He added that such investments would help China develop a stronger pathway for young players seeking to progress from grassroots competition to the international stage.
"We can not only build high-level tournaments for the professionals, but also ensure that the next generation of players will be coming and participating in events which eventually lead up to the Grand Slams," he said.
Polsky also expressed confidence in the quality of China's emerging players, citing the country's recent performances in international under-12 team competition.
"I've just seen the Chinese team of 12-and-under players participating in the Intercontinental Cup," he said. "I saw how good they are, how they're winning. Actually, the boys won."
For Polsky, the combination of elite-level success, improved facilities and a growing pool of young talent suggests that China's tennis development extends well beyond its current generation of leading players.
"That shows that the next generation of Chinese players is very good, so I believe there is a big future," he said. ■

Home search

"Another fearmongering video from Netanyahu," Eisenkot wrote. "You are hysterical. As in every election campaign, once again the same method of lies and fearmongering."
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of threatening Israelis with mass destruction after, he claimed, failing to achieve the objectives of the war against Iran.
"You have failed. In two days, the people of Israel will show you that at the ballot box," Eisenkot wrote.

Undecided voters should take a closer look at Bennett’s B’Yachad - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:21:55 UTC
23:21:55 KST

Undecided about whom to vote for on October 27? You’re not alone. Until recently, my family was also.
But forget what the confusing and contradictory polls are telling you about the division of Knesset seats, if elections were to be held today (which they are not). So much can still change due to the almost unprecedented number of undecided voters, which is higher than any election in recent memory.
According to a recent column by Israel Hayom’s political analyst Moshe Klughaft, 26 seats worth of voters – or an astounding one-fifth of the voting public – have yet to make up their minds about which slip to place in the ballot box on Election Day.
B’Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett, has a lot of undecided supporters, which is to say that many people tell pollsters they are leaning toward voting B’Yachad. That makes sense, since Bennett was the clear frontrunner before other parties entered the race, and he was probably those voters’ original preference.
What this large leaning voter reserve also means, however, is that on Election Day, B’Yachad has a greater potential to outperform all expectations.
As for my family, we’ve come off the fence and come back home to Bennett, and we’ve pointedly done so while there’s still time to encourage others to join us. Here are the three reasons that sealed our vote:
1. Only B’Yachad has effective plans to fix Israel’s problems and the experience to implement them: Since leaving office in 2022, Bennett invested enormous time and resources studying problems most affecting Israelis and developing working plans over how to solve them.
The slate they are presenting to voters was recruited on the basis of experience and competence, not petty politics. Bennett’s list is primed to hit the ground running and bring crucial fixes to everything from the cost of living to education, healthcare, and more.
2. B’Yachad’s Service Law is a national imperative: Bennett’s principles regarding the untenable and unsustainable situation of the country’s current social and economic contract with haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens have been consistent since he entered the campaign. More importantly, they represent the only realistic path moving forward.
While every other party is either ducking the issue or vowing to dictate outcomes to the haredi parties as a fait accompli, Bennett has been talking directly to the haredi public, engaging with them as fellow Jews and opening frank conversations on hard truths about why things can’t continue the way they are, economically or societally.
“For anyone who doesn’t work and doesn’t serve [in the IDF] – they will not get a single shekel,” Bennett said plainly and openly. He holds this sacred position not out of malice but simply because the taxpayer, wage-earner, and reservist will not carry them on their backs.
As former prime minister, Bennett knows intimately that Israel’s continued prosperity as a nation depends on taking decisive action now. Only Bennett’s plan will incentivize service and reward those who serve without widening internal societal divisions in the process.
3. Rather than sharpen our divisions, only B’Yachad focuses on what unites us: Sometimes you can judge a book by its cover, and here, B’Yachad’s name is what it’s all about. Certainly, Bennett is a man of the political Right, but his brand of leadership is inclusive, not exclusionary.
B'Yachad transcends ideological labels
Rather than being pigeonholed by ideological labels, this is a party that transcends them, grounding itself in the Israeli consensus on settlements and security and drawing support from Zionists of all backgrounds and persuasions who are willing to work together to fix what’s broken.
In our family, my voting history is on the Right, while my wife’s is on the Left. After looking at all the choices in this election, we’ve both come to the conclusion that Bennett’s leadership and B’Yachad’s broad-based policy agenda is what the country needs most right now.
In the aftermath of October 7, ordinary Israelis came together to support one another and unite for a greater good. Bennett and B’Yachad have elevated that positive energy into a political movement that has the power to repair and revitalize our government agencies from the inside out.
Each vote for B’Yachad on Election Day will help them help us – all of us – build a brighter and better future for every citizen of Israel.

Druze experts condemn Tom Barrack's accusations against Syrian Druze, warn of sectarian violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:21:54 UTC
23:21:54 KST

US envoy Tom Barrack’s claims that the area between Sweida and Daraa was “the captagon manufacturing operation of the world” and that a Druze sheikh was using perceived American and Israeli backing to “persecute other Druze” have drawn criticism from the Druze community, with some Israeli experts telling The Jerusalem Post on Sunday that the remarks had led them to question his suitability for the role.
Speaking in an interview with Lebanese-Australian podcaster Mario Nawfal on Friday, Barrack alleged that Druze in the area were living off the manufacture and sale of illicit drugs.
“It’s not Israel that worries me. It’s a particular Druze sheikh who utilizes the perception of Israeli backing of some alignment with America to persecute other Druze,” Barrack said.
Although Barrack did not name the sheikh, his comments have been widely interpreted in Arab media as referring to Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, a spiritual leader of the Druze community who has called for Israeli support and independence from Syria.
Growing calls for Syrian Druze independence
Calls for independence and Israeli support among Syria’s Druze community have grown more frequent since Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power in late 2024.
Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, the formerly designated terrorist organization led by Sharaa, has a documented history of persecuting Druze, while the sectarian massacres in July 2025 and sporadic violence since have further fueled fears of Damascus’s Islamist government.
Against this backdrop, Israeli Druze diplomat and historian Dr. Reda Mansour criticized Barrack’s remarks in a post on X/Twitter, describing his attribution of the global Captagon trade to the Druze region and his criticism of its local leadership as “highly irresponsible” and untruthful.
“By baselessly criminalizing an entire ethnic minority, these statements put the vulnerable Druze community in southern Syria at direct risk of sectarian violence and targeted jihadi attacks. Painting a minority enclave as an illicit hub paints a dangerous target on their back for extremist networks,” Mansour wrote.
“Diplomacy demands accuracy, not reckless generalizations that compromise human lives. We stand in solidarity with the Druze community in Syria.”
Concerns rise amid ongoing violence against Druze community
Mansour’s concerns come amid continued violence against the community. More than 1,300 Druze were killed in the July 2025 massacres in Sweida and surrounding villages, according to UN figures, while subsequent outbreaks of sectarian violence have continued to see civilians abducted and killed.
Civilians have also been killed in Jordanian military strikes on facilities Amman alleges are used for weapons storage and drug manufacturing. In a strike on January 18, 2024, for example, Jordan killed sisters Farah and Dima, aged three and five, along with their parents and other members of their extended family.
Dr. Mordechai Kedar, a research fellow at the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, told the Post that Barrack’s comments and “lack of understanding” of the region have “brought a lot of damage to the whole Middle East.”
Doubting Barrack’s knowledge of the issue of Sweida or the sectarian violence, Kedar said that he thought Barrack was relying on information provided to him and not the information on the ground or from the people affected by the violence.
Jonathan Hessen, a senior fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, added that Barrack’s remarks were not just “dismaying” because they showed a disregard for the safety and security of a community that has already been subjected to multiple massacres but because his statements were factually unfounded.
“Even when the Jordanians launched airstrikes in southern Syria, the majority of the targeted warehouses were actually in Daraa, the province south of Sweida, where the Bedouins reside,” he said.
“One warehouse was also targeted in Sweida, although I am not aware of its contents. However, those targets were provided to the Jordanians by Damascus, so there are certain aspects that need to be taken into account.”
He noted that Barrack has a pattern of minimizing the suffering of those across the Middle East where the impact would disrupt his broader plans, referencing both Barrack’s comments last week, where he insisted that the Islamic regime was “not evil,” and past commentary on Syrian violence.

Israel cannot promote democracy while sidelining Arab voters - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:21:50 UTC
23:21:50 KST

Distance can be a benefit on occasion, even though you are open to the accusation of being too distant and detached to understand or have any credible insight. Observing Israel’s election campaign from a distance and having no allegiance to any specific political party can, however, be advantageous.
Of course, the absence of allegiance does not mean that, if you are concerned about Israel’s future and the well-being of all its people, you lack opinions and hopes for the election’s outcome, but this article is not about that. It is about Israeli democracy.
In the midst of adversity and international criticism, Israeli governments and politicians have, for many years, emphasized that Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East. So have Israel’s supporters when publicly battling on the international stage, broadcast and social media those dedicated to Israel’s destruction.
Regular elections in Israel are contrasted with the absence of Palestinian elections since 2006 for the Palestinian Authority and for the presidency since 2005.
Canceled PA elections illustrate need for Palestinian institutional reforms
Two weeks ago, PA President Mahmoud Abbas yet again canceled elections scheduled for November 28, pushing them off to next September. His four-year term, now extended to 22 years, is one of the issues that illustrate Palestinian institutional reforms that need to be implemented.
The response to Israel’s adversaries falsely depicting Israel as an apartheid state is to assert that 21% of Israelis are Arabs and to correctly detail the extent to which Israel’s Arab citizens are integrated into Israeli society and the many important positions they hold.
The fact that members of Israel’s Arab community and their political parties participate in Israeli elections and are members of the Knesset is a clear example to contrast the Israeli state with the despotic monarchies and dictatorships that govern other states in the region.
Twenty-one percent of voters in a hotly contested election campaign whose outcome is uncertain can play a pivotal role in the formation of Israel’s next government. Yet most of Israel’s main political parties do nothing to court their vote. The rhetoric of many simply alienates Arab voters.
In past elections, some Israeli political parties have chosen to demonize Israel’s Arab electorate to sow fear and generate political support. For most of that electorate, the Arab parties have been the only real choice and, save for Naftali Bennett’s short-lived government, have been excluded from any role in Israeli governance.
As a consequence of the barbaric murders and atrocities of October 7 and everything that followed, political polls have shown that a majority of Jewish Israelis oppose any Arab party participating in Israel’s next government or the next Israeli government being dependent on any Arab party support.
They include Ra’am (United Arab List), which, for the first time, has included a prominent Jewish Israeli on its list, Yoav Segalovitz, a former Yesh Atid Knesset member.
He was deputy national security minister in the Bennett government and a former major-general in Israel’s police, where he headed Lahav 433, the elite national crime anti-corruption investigation unit, and was chief of the police’s intelligence and investigation department.
Voters' verdict may force a change in perspective
The primary parties whose leaders have a credible chance of becoming prime minister, forming the next government, and electing the largest number of Knesset party members all say they will not include an Arab party in government or form a government dependent on an Arab party.
There is a fear that should there be any doubt on this issue, electorate support will plummet.
The fear factor, readily exploited by various government ministers and party candidates in the current election, both undermines Israeli democracy and the value of votes cast by Israel’s Arab community. It is also setting the scene for a tied election and further political instability should all who have adopted that stance adhere to it post-election.
The perspective promoted by some Israeli politicians is that Israel’s Arab community is a potentially subversive terrorist minority within the state, a minority whose polling stations need to be more carefully observed than others on polling day. Why? Because that creates fear, and they hope it increases support for those who promote it.
They also hope for a prevalence of unnecessarily intimidating oversight that discourages Arab voters from supporting Arab parties. The same politicians in between elections use Arab Knesset members as props when acclaiming Israeli democracy.
You cannot have it both ways. Embrace the existence of Arab Knesset members as illustrative of Israeli democracy and also marginalize Israel’s Arab voters and do everything possible to discourage them from voting.
Israel’s Arab community is not a 21% subversive minority within Israel’s midst. They have not taken to the streets since October 7 and acted out like the thugs, rioters, ideologues, and antisemites in France and Italy.
Their misrepresentation as such by those in government or by some aspiring to government, together with the deprecating rhetoric to which they are subjected, is a stain on Israeli democracy and is used by Israel’s adversaries as proof of their caricature, hostile depiction of Israel.
The final days of campaigning are likely to be contaminated by such rhetoric, as well as polling day. In addition to the damage it does to Israeli society and the sense of alienation it creates within the Arab community, regard should be had to the additional damage it will inflict on Israel’s already tarnished international reputation.
Parties and party leaders have already detailed which parties they perceive as acceptable partners with which to form the next Israeli government. Both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition bloc may discover that when the votes are counted, a stable government cannot form without the support of an Arab party.
If Israeli Arabs vote in higher numbers than in recent elections, that may be a certainty.
After the elections, the voters’ verdict may force a change in perspective.
Ministers from an Arab party as part of the next Israeli government would not merely further undermine the apartheid lie and enhance Israeli democratic representation in government but might also bring badly needed new perspectives and insights to government that benefit all Israelis of every background.

He is also a former Irish minister for Justice, Equality & Defense, a former member of the Irish Parliament, and former chair of its Foreign Affairs Committee, as well as of the EU Council of Justice & Home Affairs ministers & Council of Defense Ministers. ====================================================================================================

Swiss-born Jerusalem artist Ariane Littman spreads her wares across the nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:21:43 UTC
23:21:43 KST

Life proffers numerous opportunities for a change of direction at various junctures along our meandering, undulating pathway on terra firma.
Some may be more obvious than others. But the question is whether we (a) discern them and (b) reach out and grab them by the horns and see how they play out.
Ariane Littman appears to be particularly adept at both.
The Swiss-born sixtysomething multidisciplinary artist from Beit Zayit maintains a strong presence in the national arts arena, with solo exhibitions and spots in several group shows currently dotted around the country.
Her latest run-out is on display at the former National Library of Israel building on the Givat Ram campus of the Hebrew University, within the framework of the Jerusalem Biennale.
It is a dramatic work which goes by the evocative title of Sanguine Fields, and forms part of the Reflected Light: An Active Vision set that feeds off the monumental stained-glass window triptych, Isaiah’s Vision of Eternal Peace, created over 40 years ago by Mordechai Ardon.
The biblical prophecy of beating swords into plowshares and finally dispensing with the need for military action is both emotive and thought-provoking. Sadly, it remains pertinent today, as politically festered violence continues to claim lives and cause anguish at all sorts of flash points across the globe.
On the domestic front, Littman’s work references Oct. 7 and its convoluted aftermath, including the long, drawn-out hostage situation.
If that wasn’t clear from the clutch of red-tipped elongated white gauze drapes suspended from butcher’s hooks, the enamel bowl placed near the amorphous medical fabrics spells it all out. The vessel alludes to incantation bowls used by Jews, Christians, and other cultures such as the Mandaean to ward off evil spirits.
Littman’s piece has that fateful date – 7.10.23 – inscribed on both the interior and exterior surfaces, dozens of times, in very small, compactly spaced numerals.
Bandaging the wounds
“I took hundreds of bandages and opened them up,” Littman explains. “I get them from a hospital supplier.”
That fits the wounded collective and personal bill. The white clusters hang airily, yet densely and somehow concretely, in a manner that seems to defy gravity.
The ethereally leaning posture also suggests a flame-like entity reaching for higher domains.
“It is not a static work,” she adds, a mite needlessly.
That creative and curative endeavor followed in the emotional and immediate temporal wake of the Hamas attack.
“I was paralyzed for six weeks. I was simply incapable of doing anything [artistic],” she recalls. “The only thing I managed to do was to mark that date.” It was to become a lengthy process. “I did that for a year,” Littman continues.
That was an instinctive move, mostly the result of a desperate need to assuage some of her pent-up distress at the doomsday scenario that was playing out down South, and the pain of the families of the dead and those taken into captivity in Gaza. “I didn’t know about the Babylonian origin [of incantation bowls], so I went to take a look at some [in a museum].
The work began to take corporeal and impassioned shape. The bowl at Givat Ram contains a telling blood-red dried residue.
“What you have here is gauze bandages soaked in red, which dripped all night into the bowl,” Littman says.
She had originally meant to place a receptacle beneath each gauze assemblage, but wisely ultimately opted not to subject the public to sensory overload.
Gauze bandages have been a leitmotif of her oeuvre since 2009, when she and her family went through a trying episode. Her then nine-year-old daughter, Kalia, was on a fourth-grade field trip and sustained third-degree burns when a large pan of boiling water and oil spilled all over her.
That was, naturally, an emotional game changer for Littman, but it also provoked some new aesthetic thinking, as the bandages she helped apply to her daughter’s mutilated limbs became an integral tool of her craft.
I got evidence of that change of substance tack at Littman’s studio in deepest Talpiot. It is a capacious workspace with plenty of light. The large, high-ceilinged main room, and entrance corridor, are jam-packed with past creations and images thereof.
Gauze upper strata partly mask Israeli flags and roughly delineated excerpts of our national map. Some incorporate yellow thread, suggesting surgical repairs, while one has yellow thread spots dotted around Gaza. “That marks the locations, roughly, where the hostages were being held. The color of the twine references the yellow ribbons used as a symbol of solidarity with the Israelis incarcerated in Gaza,” Littman enlightens.
She studiously followed post-Oct. 7 events.
“I was glued to the TV set for some time,” she says. “I didn’t fight in the war, and I didn’t go to the South to volunteer. But the least I could do was listen to what the relatives of the victims and the hostages were saying. It was like listening to Holocaust testimony.”
That eventually found its way into her creative continuum, allowing her to distill some of her sentiments through her hands-on pursuit and, hopefully, set her emotional house a little in order.
Littman did not initially set her sights on art as an all-consuming occupation.
After making aliyah from her home in Switzerland, in the French-speaking region near Geneva, in the 1980s, she took a degree in Middle Eastern studies and international relations at the Hebrew University.
Perhaps that was something of a throwback to her English-born father’s – David’s – clandestine participation in a Mossad operation, in 1961, to get Jewish children out of Morocco to Switzerland and thence to Israel. He was an archaeologist who spent time here on excavations.
Her mother is a now 93-year-old writer who goes by the nom de plume of Bat Yeor, deftly alluding to her birthplace of Egypt. Yeor is the biblical name for the Nile.
Culture abounded in the Littman household, and the artist recalls being taken to museums around Europe, which sowed the seeds for her eventual choice of profession.
Death leads to a new life
There is plenty of quotidian drama to Littman’s bio, which naturally informs her art. It was, in fact, a seismic family event that shuffled the emotional pack and set her on her artistic path.
Her world turned upside down when her brother, Daniel, committed suicide at the age of just 23.
“After that, I said to myself: ‘Life is short. I have to do what is really important.’ I applied to Bezalel [Academy of Arts and Design] and was accepted. That changed my life.”
That new – and ongoing – lease of life was sparked, tragically, by a life cut far too short.
The decision to try a different line of study and, thereafter, professional interest had, it seems, been percolating for some time. It was also part of Littman’s heartfelt desire to find an alternative means of getting her ideas and feelings out there.
“I always thought that, despite everything, art is a different means of communication compared with communicating through war or fighting.”
There’s no argument there.
“There are all sorts of artists and art forms. But at the end of the day, it is about communicating. People may connect with one work or another, and that’s fine. For me, it is a better form of communication.”
Littman has a point, and we would do well to bear that in mind if we ever come across, say, a piece of avant-garde music or conceptual art that may appear nightmarish or simply rubbish to more conservative minds.
As far as we know, relatively few people have been killed because of their artistic output. Yes, the Nazis banned what they called Entartete Kunst – degenerate art – which was generally modern forms of art, or works created by non-Aryans. Similarly, various other totalitarian regimes have persecuted artists who did not toe the party line. But if we add up all the millions killed in wars over the centuries, the number of the former pale almost into insignificance.
If it is true, as the clichéd wisdom has it, that artists need to go through some emotional mill in order to create, sadly Littman qualifies there, big time.
“There is my brother, and my daughter’s terrible accident, and I have a sister, just one year older than me, with special needs. It hasn’t been easy.”
Her determination to follow her heart and stick to what is really meaningful for her, in the wake of Daniel’s suicide, had knock-on effects in other areas of her life, too.
“I also decided to get married,” she says.
Many years later, she got divorced, but she has three charming daughters, as she maternally and proudly puts it. There was more than a whiff of naches in there.
Going out on a limb
Littman’s CV is a multilayered affair, but if one thread runs through it all, it is her drive to jump in at the deep end and see things through.
She served as a photojournalist during the dangerous Second Intifada times, learning to take pictures as she went along. This was before digital cameras were readily available, and she says she milked her fellow snappers for professional tips on the fly.
She also got some help from someone close to home, literally. “Rina Castelnuovo, the great New York Times photographer, was a neighbor of mine. She took me to all sorts of places. I used my dad’s old Leica,” she chortles.
You could put Littman’s dynamic artistic trajectory down to the great reserves of energy and joie de vivre she exudes. That certainly helps. But she also imparts a robust desire to meet life head-on and see what she can possibly make of it.
“At the end of the day, as an artist, I can decide that I only create within the confines of my studio, or I can decide that my studio is also out there, in the field. It is there that you can understand more.”
That entails ingesting the myriad stimulants that everyday life proffers, rather than holing up in cloistered surroundings and focusing on one’s inner world.
There are arguments to be made for both approaches, but Littman is clearly the outgoing type. She, presumably, would go along with celebrated exiled Chinese artist Ai Weiwei’s succinct observation: “Life is art. Art is life. I never separate it.”
“I have always chosen not to be in the Kantian place of disinterestedness. I chose to be in the place of the emotion and exploration,” she declares.
“I think my approach [to art] also came from my lack of understanding and the desire to understand – even if, in the end, I realize I don’t understand anything. One has to try to touch on something and understand it.”
As a keen cyclist, Littman also appreciates the value of the journey, and not just the satisfaction of achieving one’s goal, of arriving at the planned or sought-after destination.
Taking the mother’s healing perspective
Oct. 7, 2023, continues to reverberate across Littman’s daily life and her work. She seeks solace through her art, and also strives to generate some comfort to others.
That line of thought and feeling spawned In the Eye of the Storm, an audiovisual installation with Lake Kinneret (the Sea of Galilee) and its healing powers at its core.
Motherhood is also a central element of the work, in which Littman encounters two bereaved mothers, Liat Friedman and Layla Abbas, whose sons, Shahar Friedman and his commander, Jamal Abbas, were killed in Gaza in an attempt to save their comrades in arms.
It is a suitably moving piece, which also features gauze bandages, which the mothers wrap around Chana Orloff’s iconic Mother and Child sculpture at Kibbutz Ein Gev.
In the Eye of the Storm is currently on show at the Yigal Alon Centre at Ginosar, on the northwestern corner of the Kinneret.
The installation is part of Littman’s ongoing series Wounded Land.
The act of bandaging works of art, monuments, and trees is a powerful gesture of healing.
She even once bravely allowed herself to be completely swathed in bandages, to the point of not being able to move any part of her body, and pushed out onto the gently lapping waters of the Dead Sea.
“That was scary,” she recalls. “I had to make sure I didn’t tilt too much; otherwise, I would have capsized.”
They say that, to be a true artist, you have to go out on a limb or two. Littman certainly makes the grade on that score.
As an olah keen to feel at home here, Littman quickly gained fluency in Hebrew and developed a preoccupation with maps and geographic spots, relating to their human and political characteristics.
That, as we all keenly and corporeally know in this part of the world, can be a highly contentious issue. But Littman appears to be made of sterner stuff, a prerequisite for making headway through the minefield of insecurity that is the lot of many an artist, particularly in the state support-starved cultural field.
She maintains a more-than-steady working pace, and also has several works on show at the Haifa Museum of Art at the moment. And there is a new book in the offing, called “Art in A Time of War After Oct. 7, Wounded Land 2023-2026.”
Notwithstanding her ever-expanding portfolio, and her almost ubiquitous presence at art repositories across the country, including as a member of the Agripas 12 collective now based at Givat Ram, Littman continues to grapple with the whys and wherefores of her craft.
“I wondered whether there was any value in creating art,” she confesses. “With all this violence, and people being killed, how could art help? Do we need art at all?”
The answer came from without, from foreign climes.
“I went to Paris, to the Picasso museum, and I saw artworks that were made in times of war by all sorts of French and Italian artists, in addition to Picasso. I realized that they moved me, that they meant something to me, all these years later.”
Judging by her exhibition success to date, Littman’s own creations appear to be having an effect in real time, but she is still hopeful that several years down the road they will continue to convey her healing, stimulating message.
And who knows? Perhaps they – and art in general – will make a difference for the better.

Ahead of next month's UK-EU summit, Burnham said he favours an 'honest discussion' about the divisive issue of re-adapting free movement between the UK and the EU. But in an interview in London Sunday Times, he ruled out ever joining the Schengen zone or adopting the Euro.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated he was open to readopting the European Union's free movement rules as part of Britain's future relationship with the bloc, said a report published Sunday.
The Labour prime minister has promised to lay out different options for closer relations with Europe around the time of a long-awaited UK-EU summit in Brussels next month.
Burnham, who has even touted the possibility of Britain applying to rejoin the EU one day, said the country should have an "honest discussion" about how immigration to the UK has changed since Brexit.
Immigration was one of the main reasons for Britons voting narrowly to leave the EU during the divisive 2016 referendum that was triggered by the right-wing Conservatives.
Immigration 'is different' since Brexit
Burnham said immigration into Britain had been "different" since the country left the EU in early 2020.
"It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn't as difficult (as now)," he told the Sunday Times newspaper.
"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."
Burnham, in office since July, has committed to predecessor Keir Starmer's 2024 election-winning manifesto which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union. But the question of reciprocal youth mobility has pushed free movement to the top of the agenda.
The project faces strong opposition and legal hurdles
That means he may seek to win a mandate for any major change in Britain's relationship with the EU at the next general election, which is currently not expected until 2029.
Burnham told the Sunday Times, "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining" the euro or the Schengen borderless area, which the UK was not a part of pre-Brexit.
Nigel Farage, leader of the far-right and anti-immigrant Reform UK party, called Burnham's comments on free movement a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
Burnham and EU leaders are hopeful of striking deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions tradings when they meet on 20 November.

Migrants in EU see how authorities treat Middle East, do not accept it — Putin

23:17:48 KST

MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. The stance of European countries toward issues in the Middle East inevitably influences the mindset of migrants who have arrived in EU countries from that region, Russian President Vladimir Putin told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin.
"Look at what is happening in the Middle East. People who arrived in European countries a few years ago via migration channels, their children who have since grown up, perceive an injustice being committed against their compatriots and their brothers in faith," he said.
"And this, too, shapes their mindset regarding how they should respond to the actions of the authorities in the country where they currently reside," Putin added.

Russia Launches Steregushchiy-Class Corvette Grozny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:17:04 UTC
23:17:04 KST

The Amur Shipbuilding Plant (ASZ) has launched the Project 20380 (Steregushchiy-Class) multipurpose corvette Grozny.
INTERFAX.RU reported this, citing the Russian Pacific Fleet’s press service.
The ship is the fifth serial-production corvette of this project being built at the Pacific Fleet’s plant and the ninth Project 20380 vessel overall.
The corvette was laid down at the shipyard on August 23, 2021. The Pacific Fleet currently operates the corvettes Sovershenny, Gromkiy, Hero of the Russian Federation Aldar Tsydenzhapov, and Rezkiy.
According to the press service, the Grozny crew has already been formed. On October 5, it began training, after which it will arrive at the shipyard to take part in the vessel’s completion and commission it into the fleet “in the coming years.”
Project 20380 vessels are multipurpose guided-missile corvettes. They can operate in distant maritime zones and are designed to engage enemy surface ships and submarines, as well as provide artillery support for amphibious landings.
Steregushchiy, the project’s first vessel, was laid down in late 2001 and delivered to the Baltic Fleet in early 2008.
Key specifications of Project 20380 corvettes:
In late July, it was reported that Russia had begun fitting ships of this class with additional machine-gun mounts to protect them against Ukrainian drones.
Several positions along the sides of the Russian Baltic Fleet corvette Stoikiy, based in Baltiysk in the Kaliningrad region, were observed to be equipped with 12.7 mm Kord machine guns and 7.62 mm PKM machine guns.
Stoikiy primarily performs escort duties. It has reportedly provided a corridor for a Russian cargo ship that docked at the Syrian port of Tartus to replenish supplies at Khmeimim air base.
One corvette of this project, Boikiy, sustained serious damage in a Ukrainian strike drone attack on June 3, 2026. At the time, the ship was in dry dock in Kronstadt for scheduled repairs. After at least two drones struck the vessel, a large fire broke out aboard and, according to satellite imagery, engulfed a substantial part of the superstructure.

LONDON, October 25. /TASS/. Qatari mediators visited Tehran on October 25, Reuters reported, citing sources.

From lawyer's office to kitchen: dad of American soldier killed in Ukraine volunteers in Kharkiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:15:00 EET
23:15:00 KST

From lawyer's office to kitchen: dad of American soldier killed in Ukraine volunteers in Kharkiv
Edward Wilton's son was killed serving in Ukraine's International Legion. Now Edward has moved to Kharkiv to help civilians. Every day he helps prepare hot meals for local residents, including hospital patients.
Source: Independence Avenue Media
Details: For most of his adult life, Edward Wilton practised law in Florida. But after the death of his son, who served as a volunteer in the International Legion, Edward came to help Ukraine too.
In January 2026, Edward retired and moved to Kharkiv for good. Now he works at the Pekelna Kuhnya (Hell's Kitchen) charity alongside many other volunteers from around the world – the United Kingdom, Poland, Japan, Sweden and other countries.
Every day they prepare more than 1,200 meals for local residents, most of which are delivered to the city's hospitals.
Quote from Edward: "I returned to help Ukraine and to help out what I think is my country too."
Details: Edward said he does his best to be useful, adding that he adores Kharkiv and loves Ukraine and its people. He thinks it is an incredible place to live – a place he now calls home.
In an earlier report, Edward told Suspilne Ivano-Frankivsk that he has Ukrainian roots. He said his mother had always told him that she was Ukrainian, Polish or Austrian, and that this uncertainty prompted him to research his family history.
Eventually Edward discovered that his great-grandfather came from Kosmach, a Hutsul village in the Prykarpattia region, and emigrated to the US in 1912 or 1913. Edward raised his son, Edward III, with an awareness of his Ukrainian heritage and in the spirit of Ukrainian traditions.
Edward said his family had preserved some traditions that were passed down through his mother's family, particularly around celebrating Christmas and Easter, and had talked a lot about their ancestors' heritage.
Edward III had always wanted to become a soldier. He was unable to complete his military training in the US, but spent several months training to become an emergency medical technician.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Edward III travelled to Ukraine and joined the International Legion. He served in the Bravo Company under the alias "Hans" and took part in complex combat operations, for which he was awarded the Order of Courage.
Edward said his son had trained with various weapons, studied tactics with his unit and was very proficient with a grenade launcher. He added that Edward III was one of the youngest in his unit and that his brothers-in-arms perhaps had more combat experience than he did.
Edward said his son had not said anything about returning home before the war was over: everything was connected to the war. His son had had several opportunities to return home but had refused, saying he had not yet earned that right; he believed he needed to do more than he was doing.
Edward said his son was fascinated by Ukraine and did not want to return to the US.
Edward III died in April 2023 from a shrapnel wound, aged 22. He and his brothers-in-arms had come under artillery fire while moving out to positions in Luhansk Oblast.
Edward said his son really wanted to be in control of his own life. He recalled reading the Iliad with him when his son was a child, including the passage about Achilles, who had to choose between a long, uneventful life and a short, heroic one. Edward said his son had told him even then that he wanted a short, heroic life rather than a long, boring one, and added that that is exactly what happened.
A memorial in honour of the fighter now stands in Kosmach – the village that his father now regards as his home. Since losing his son, Edward has treasured the certificate presented to him for his service.
"My son said he didn't mind dying, but he wanted to be remembered," he said.

Decline in industrial production in Europe since 2021 has been dramatic — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:13:48 UTC
23:13:48 KST

MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. The decline in industrial production in many leading economies in Europe since 2021 has been "simply dramatic," Russian President Vladimir Putin said.
"Compared to 2021, the decline in industrial production across many of Europe’s leading economies is simply dramatic. In Germany, the continent’s primary economy, often described as its locomotive, the drop ranges from 1.5% to 5.2%, triggering a whole chain of negative consequences for the entire eurozone economy," he told Vesti reporter Pavel Zarubin.
Industrial production in Russia has grown by 10% since 2021, and the manufacturing sector has climbed by 21%, Putin added.
"By the way, industrial production in Russia has grown by 10% compared to 2021. The manufacturing sector added 21%. There is, after all, a significant difference between minus 5.2% and plus 10% or, in the case of manufacturing, plus 21%," he added.

Brazil election: Lula, Bolsonaro cast votes in final bout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:13:00 UTC
23:13:00 KST

Brazil elections: Lula wins another term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro
Published October 25, 2026last updated October 26, 2026
What you need to know
- Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro
- It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed
- In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race
- Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win
- Bolsonaro refused to concede, calls for election results to be annulled
Keep reading for the latest updates from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25, with continued coverage into Monday, October 26.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.
Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close
Here's a DW infographic on where the results stand:
France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory
Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."
French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."
"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.
"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.
Big challenges face Lula's fourth term
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is likely to face several difficulties in enacting his agenda in a fourth-term.
Among other things, Brazil has elected its most conservative congress since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.
Flavio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allies could control more than 280 seats in the 513-seat lower house and up to 50 seats in the 81-seat Senate following parliamentary elections three weeks ago.
This could lead to Lula's being forced to cede to congress on decisions about the budget, important legislation and key nominations.
Economic woes
Brazil is also in a period of weak economic growth, with his government forecasting just a 2.3% rise in GDP next year.
This is combined with public debt that surpasses 82% of GDP, the highest rate since the coronavirus pandemic.
Security concerns
Public security also remains a major concern in Brazil, with criminal organizations holding considerable influence in parts of the country.
Lula has said he plans to establish a Ministry of Public Security to combat the problem.
Environmental problems
There are also environmental challenges ahead.
Although deforestation in the Amazon — a major carbon sink and thus vital for the stability of the world climate — fell significantly during Lula's third term, Brazil is still a long way from its goal of ending deforestation by 2030.
EU's von der Leyen hails Lula's win
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has posted an online message of congratulation to "my friend" Lula on his win in Brazil's election runoff.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," she wrote.
"Europe's partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come," her post continued.
"Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate."
Could Bolsonaro succeed in annulling the vote?
Some uncertainty still surrounds the final result of Brazil's election, as Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to challenge the outcome over the two-hour extension of polling hours ordered by a Supreme Court judge at the request of Lula da Silva's campaign.
However, legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether such a complaint would meet the legal threshold for the election to be annulled.
Bolsonaro's case would be weakened by at least two factors, analysts said. Firstly, the scale of his loss to Lula and second, the fact that his campaign had also requested an extension in some states.
The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said that the extension of voting hours had not influenced the vote.
The Associated Press cited Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at Brazil's Fluminense Federal University, as saying that Bolsonaro could ask for the elections to be declared null and void by filing a complaint with electoral authorities or the Supreme Court.
"But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said.
"The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact," he said.
Shortly before scheduled voting ended, Supreme Court Judge Christiano had ordered polling stations to remain open for longer after problems with public transport were reported to be affecting voters.
The decision followed a request from Lula's campaign.
Bolsonaro's campaign had also called for an extension of voting hours but only in some conservative-leaning southern states hit by heavy rainfall, flooding and power outages that were said to be disrupting voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazil's leftist president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, according to the country's electoral court.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Sunday's second round vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula's claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
The campaign season was also marred by scandals and mudslinging.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. US President Donald Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."

"The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact," he said.
Shortly before scheduled voting ended, Supreme Court Judge Christiano had ordered polling stations to remain open for longer after problems with public transport were reported to be affecting voters.
The decision followed a request from Lula's campaign.
Bolsonaro's campaign had also called for an extension of voting hours but only in some conservative-leaning southern states hit by heavy rainfall, flooding and power outages that were said to be disrupting voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazil's leftist president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, according to the country's electoral court.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Sunday's second round vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula's claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
The campaign season was also marred by scandals and mudslinging.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Lula will have to manage relations with Washington as the Trump administration in the US increasingly asserts its influence across Latin America. US President Donald Trump is a close political ally of the Bolsonaro family, and Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."
