What is spina bifida, and are there ways to prevent it? A doctor explains
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:46:42 EET
22:46:42 KST

What is spina bifida, and are there ways to prevent it? A doctor explains
Kyiv • UNN
Every year, up to 300,000 children are born with spina bifida. Doctors advise starting to take folic acid even before conception.
October 25 is World Spina Bifida and Hydrocephalus Awareness Day. Obstetrician-gynecologist, Candidate of Medical Sciences, and head of the postpartum department at the capital’s Perinatal Center Vladyslav Yavir told UNN in a comment about what these developmental defects are and what prevention of their occurrence exists.
Every year, up to 300,000 children worldwide are born with a diagnosis of spina bifida. In fact, this figure may be higher, as not all countries record information about this fetal developmental defect as a separate item in medical statistics.
Spina bifida — what it is and how this developmental defect is linked to hydrocephalus
Spina bifida (split spine) is a congenital neural tube defect (an embryonic structure from which the child’s central nervous system develops), in which the formation and closure of the structures of the spinal canal are disrupted. In severe forms, particularly myelomeningocele, the membranes and neural structures of the spinal cord may protrude through the spinal defect.
As Vladyslav Yavir explains, severe forms of spina bifida are associated with impaired normal circulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
"As a result, CSF may accumulate in the ventricles of the brain, causing hydrocephalus to develop. At the same time, hydrocephalus does not occur in all children with spina bifida," the doctor says.
Prevention with folic acid
Taking folic acid can help prevent the development of spina bifida.
"Timely intake of folic acid can significantly reduce the risk of neural tube defects. According to research, a substantial proportion of such defects can be prevented by ensuring an adequate supply of folates to the body even before pregnancy begins. However, even proper prevention does not guarantee the complete elimination of the risk," Yavir explains.
According to the doctor, the neural tube forms and closes very early — approximately by the 28th day after fertilization.
"That is why folic acid supplementation should begin before pregnancy, preferably 1–3 months before conception," the doctor says.
According to him, there is a standard preventive dose of folic acid. However, there are high-risk groups for whom significantly higher doses may be recommended.
"First of all, these include women with a previous pregnancy complicated by a neural tube defect, patients with pregestational diabetes mellitus, and women taking certain medications (antiepileptic drugs)," Yavir explains.
High-dose supplementation is usually started before conception and continued until the end of the 12th week of pregnancy.
"It is important to emphasize that a high dose of folic acid should not be prescribed independently. It must be determined by a doctor after assessing individual risk factors.
That is why I always emphasize the importance of preconception care: the best time to prevent many congenital developmental defects is before pregnancy begins," the doctor says.
Folates can be obtained from foods such as green leafy vegetables, legumes, and citrus fruits. However, as the obstetrician-gynecologist explains, even a balanced diet does not always provide a sufficient amount of folates to prevent neural tube defects. Natural folates have lower bioavailability compared with synthetic folic acid, and some of them are destroyed during heat treatment.
"That is why the WHO and CDC recommend that women planning a pregnancy or capable of becoming pregnant take 400 mcg (0.4 mg) of folic acid daily in the absence of indications for a higher dose. Proper nutrition is important, but it does not replace the recommended prevention with folic acid," the doctor says.
Detecting developmental defects during pregnancy
Modern prenatal diagnostics makes it possible to detect spina bifida during the child’s intrauterine development. The primary diagnostic method is an ultrasound examination (ultrasound scan).
-  First-trimester ultrasound (11–13 weeks + 6 days): an experienced specialist may already suspect open spina bifida based on characteristic ultrasound signs, including changes in the fetal intracranial structures. 
-  Second-trimester ultrasound (18–22 weeks): the main stage for a detailed assessment of fetal anatomy. It makes it possible to detect a spinal defect, possible protrusion of the spinal cord membranes and neural structures, as well as characteristic changes in the brain.  
-  Biochemical screening: an elevated level of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in the mother’s blood during the second trimester may indicate an open neural tube defect, but in itself does not confirm the diagnosis. 
Timely detection of the defect makes it possible to conduct an in-depth examination, assess the prognosis, and determine the further management plan for the pregnancy.
"Today, a diagnosis of spina bifida does not mean that treatment options are unavailable. In specialized centers, fetal surgical closure of myelomeningocele may be possible when clearly indicated. Studies have shown that, in carefully selected cases, such an intervention may reduce the need for cerebrospinal fluid shunting and improve the child’s motor function. Surgical treatment after birth is also available. In such cases, the defect is usually closed during the first days of the child’s life. If hydrocephalus is present, additional neurosurgical treatment may be required," explains Vladyslav Yavir.
At the same time, the doctor emphasizes that none of these methods guarantees the complete elimination of neurological impairments. In addition, surgery carries serious risks, so the decision is made by a multidisciplinary team after detailed counseling of the parents.
That is why preventive folic acid supplementation before pregnancy remains the most optimal approach. It should be started at least one month before planned conception, and, as the doctor clarifies, preferably three months beforehand.
"This is a simple, accessible, and scientifically proven way to significantly reduce the risk of severe congenital neural tube defects. As an obstetrician-gynecologist, I always emphasize: a healthy pregnancy begins not with two lines on a test, but with a conscious attitude toward one’s own health even at the stage of planning it!
After all, the best treatment is the one whose need we were able to prevent through timely prevention," Yavir concluded.
Attention!
This material is for informational purposes only and is not medical advice or a treatment recommendation. It does not replace consultation, diagnosis, or treatment by a specialist and may not serve as a basis for self-prescribing medications. If you are planning a pregnancy or are already pregnant, consult an obstetrician-gynecologist or family doctor.

Israel needs unity: Why Herzog must bring Netanyahu, Eisenkot together - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:44:53 UTC
22:44:53 KST

I am a right-wing religious Zionist, an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American, and a father raising four children in Jerusalem, and I am frightened.
Not because Israelis disagree, disagreement is part of democracy, but because our politics increasingly teaches us to hate one another more passionately than we love the country we share, while our enemies watch, our international standing collapses, and the wounds of October 7 remain open.
I know where I stand politically. I believe in secure borders, Jewish sovereignty, and Israel’s unquestionable right to defend its citizens. Hamas must never again govern Gaza. Iran and its terrorist proxies must be deterred. The Jewish people cannot subcontract their survival.
Right-wing and left-wing are equal owners of the same country
But being right-wing does not require me to treat left-wing Israelis as enemies. Their children serve beside ours. They run into shelters when the sirens sound. They bury loved ones, pay taxes, and worry about the future of the same country. They are equal owners of it. The same is true in reverse.
Supporting a change in government does not justify dismissing millions of traditional, religious, or conservative Israelis as primitive, dangerous, or morally inferior. Netanyahu’s voters will not disappear if he loses an election, just as his opponents will not disappear if he wins. Israel belongs to all of us.
That truth should guide President Isaac Herzog after the election. Current polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party competing for leadership, while neither bloc appears certain to command the 61 Knesset seats needed to govern. Israel may awaken to another divided parliament and another invitation to paralysis. We cannot afford it.
October 7 was not only a military and intelligence catastrophe. It was a warning about what happens when leaders become distracted by internal warfare, institutions lose public trust, and citizens begin viewing one another as threats. Hamas crossed a physical border after we had already allowed hatred to cross every political and social border within Israel.
Our enemies study us. They hear our leaders call one another traitors, fascists, and enemies of democracy. They see clashes among secular, religious, right-wing, left-wing, Jewish and Arab citizens.
They do not interpret our division as healthy democratic debate. They interpret it as weakness and wait for the next fracture.
Israel’s diplomatic position is also in danger. The Jewish state is increasingly portrayed not as a democracy defending itself, but as the source of every regional crisis. Antisemitism and propaganda drive much of this campaign, but our poisonous politics makes it easier. A country that cannot speak respectfully to itself will struggle to speak persuasively to the world.
This is why Herzog must become more than a ceremonial observer after the election. He cannot dictate a coalition, overturn the voters’ decision, or force rivals to trust one another. But he possesses something rare in Israeli public life: an office intended to represent the entire nation.
Herzog should invite Netanyahu and Eisenkot to the president’s residence and keep bringing them back until they seriously consider a broad Zionist unity government.
Not a government without disagreement. Not a government designed to rescue political careers. A government of limited national repair.
Such a coalition should begin with a clear program: restore security and border readiness; establish an independent state commission to investigate the failures surrounding October 7; confront Iran and its proxies; rebuild Israel’s international diplomacy; reduce the cost of living; require meaningful military or national service across society while respecting genuine Torah scholarship; and protect every law-abiding citizen from terrorism, organized crime and political violence.
It must also address Israel’s excluded communities. Ethiopian Israelis should not be remembered only during elections or cultural ceremonies. Arab citizens who reject terrorism and accept the laws of the state should not be treated as a permanent fifth column. Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens should not be spoken about as if they are strangers to the Jewish future.
Rights bring responsibilities, but responsibilities must also bring belonging. Unity does not mean moral confusion. Israel must distinguish democratic disagreement from support for its destruction.
Leaders who excuse terrorism cannot be trusted with national security. But disagreement over courts, settlements, religion, or Gaza does not make an Israeli disloyal.
Becoming protectors
Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, of blessed memory, taught that society is the home we build together. A home cannot survive when family members would rather burn it down than allow a rival to sit at the head of the table.
Netanyahu has devoted much of his life to Israel’s security and international standing. Eisenkot served the country as a soldier, commander, and chief of staff, and he paid the unbearable price of losing family members in war.
Each man represents citizens who love Israel. Each also carries responsibilities greater than his personal grievances. They do not have to admire one another. They do not have to erase their disagreements. They must decide whether their hatred and mistrust are more important than the country they both claim to serve.
I made aliyah with my wife and four children shortly before October 7 because I believe in Israel, not merely as a refuge, but as the shared moral project of the Jewish people. I did not bring my children home so they could inherit a nation divided into tribes that no longer recognize one another.
The next October 7 must never happen. Preventing it will require weapons, intelligence, and secure borders. It will also require Israelis to become protectors of one another again.
Herzog, bring Netanyahu and Eisenkot to the same table. Ask them to place Israel above ego, party, and personal history. The election will determine who wins seats. Leadership will be measured by whether they can save the house we all share.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh receives more support in bid to become next UN secretary-general
Unknown

2026-10-25
13:44:44 UTC
22:44:44 KST

Cypriot Foreign Affairs Minister Constantinos Kombos said on Friday that he supports UAE Ambassador Lana Nusseibeh as the next United Nations secretary-general.
Kombos wrote on X/Twitter that he has known Nusseibeh for years, noting that she "is an experienced, highly effective and well-respected diplomat, with an approach focusing on dialogue, compromise and tangible outcomes, while also having a strong track record in supporting multilateralism and the United Nations."
He also noted that it was time for a woman to become the next secretary-general, saying, "it is becoming time-sensitive to ensure that the selection process proceeds."
On Thursday, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said member states unanimously endorsed the United Arab Emirates' nomination of the ambassador for the position, according to the Saudi Gazette.
This is important as support for Nusseibeh grows, with Albudaiwi attributing the unanimous support to the GCC countries' commitment to strengthening multilateral cooperation and reinforcing the UN's role in maintaining international peace and security in accordance with the principles and objectives of its Charter, the Saudi Gazette reported.
The Maldives, BoP's Nikolay Mladenov support Nusseibeh's nomination
The Maldives said on Sunday that it welcomed Nusseibeh's nomination. In addition, Nikolay Mladenov, who is a key official with the Gaza Board of Peace and formerly served as Bulgaria's defense minister and Foreign affairs minister, wrote on X that "Lana Nusseibeh has always understood that the #UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build."
"In the Security Council she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism," said Mladenov. "She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN Secretariat. Wishing you courage and strength for the journey ahead and much success!"
Nusseibeh has served as the UAE’s foreign affairs minister and as the UAE’s permanent representative to the UN in New York from 2013 to 2024. She also served for four years as foreign affairs assistant minister for political affairs.
Since the organization was founded in 1945, the UN has had ten secretaries-general, including an acting leader from 1945 to 1946, though some have been more memorable than others. Sweden’s Dag Hammarskjöld, who served from 1953 to 1961, was an energetic leader who sought to achieve a ceasefire in the Congo. He died in a plane crash while on his way to Zambia.
U Thant, who served in the 1960s, was the first non-Western secretary-general. He was followed by Kurt Waldheim in the 1970s. Waldheim was an intelligence officer under Nazi Germany, which made his appointment strange, considering the UN was founded after the defeat of the Nazis. In the 1990s, former Egyptian diplomat Boutros Boutros-Ghali became the head of the UN. He was largely seen to have failed at key moments, such as during the Rwandan genocide.
In the last decades, the UN has seen secretaries-general who appeared relatively ineffectual, such as Kofi Annan, Ban Ki-moon, and current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
As part of a complex election process, an informal straw poll of officials in the deciding UN Security Council last week gave [former Costa Rican vice president Rebeca] Grynspan a narrow lead over her closest competitors: Guyana’s former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina’s International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi, Euro News reported.
The report notes that the winner needs at least nine votes from the 15-member UN Security Council without a veto from any of the five permanent members - the US, the UK, France, China and Russia - and they have until the end of December to choose the successor to Gutteres, before the UN General Assembly confirms the appointment.
Euro News also noted other candidates, including former Ecuadorian foreign minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese president Macky Sall, former UN under-secretary-general Olara Otunnu of Uganda, and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.
Nusseibeh currently serving as UN Women Executive Board president
According to a UN biography of Nusseibeh, the ambassador currently serves as UN Women Executive Board president and was recently appointed co-facilitator of the Ad Hoc Working Group on the Revitalization of the UN General Assembly by the General Assembly president.
A website that appears to have been created for her candidacy notes that Nusseibeh is currently on leave from government responsibilities to focus on her UN secretary-general candidacy.
The website also includes a statement attributed to Nusseibeh, in which the ambassador says she is "stubbornly optimistic about the future of our world and the important role multilateralism will play in it."
"I am offering active, hands-on leadership on peace and security: acting earlier, bridging divides and pursuing practical first agreements that save lives now and create space for broader peace," she said, adding that she "will bring that same urgency and focus on results to development and human rights – building a more focused, responsive UN that delivers for the people it serves."
Nusseibeh was born in 1978, is married, and has two children. She has a BA and MA from Queens’ College at the University of Cambridge. She also has an MA in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London.
Prior to her UN role, she established the UAE Foreign Affairs Ministry's Policy Planning Department in 2009 and served as its first director for three years. She also served as the UAE’s Co-Special Envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan. She also headed the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) task force at the ministry.
French-language media platform and digital news outlet IsraJ noted Nusseibeh’s important family background, saying her family originally lived in Jerusalem and that her Emirati citizenship came from her father, Emirati President Cultural Advisor Zaki Nusseibeh.
It added details about the family's rich academic and intellectual background and its long roots in Jerusalem and the region, with relative Anwar Nusseibeh having been a prominent figure in Palestinian and Jordanian politics.
Wounded in 1948, Anwar Nusseibeh served as Jordanian Defense Minister and later as Jerusalem Governor under Jordanian rule. After 1967, he conducted discreet contacts between Israel and Jordan regarding the future of the West Bank.
IsraJ further noted that the ambassador's uncle, Sari Nusseibeh, is a former president of Al-Quds University in the West Bank. He wrote several important books, including Once Upon a Country about his family and Palestinian issues.

Why Netanyahu's supporters remain loyal to him despite his failures - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:44:33 UTC
22:44:33 KST

For over a decade, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to retain the loyalty of his supporters despite profound failures under his leadership. He has been described as Israel’s most successful politician, the greatest political survivor, and the leader of a personality cult.
Millions of Israelis vote for Netanyahu because they genuinely share his political worldview that Israel must be exceptionally strong, distrust the Palestinians, fear Iran, oppose territorial concessions, and regard the Israeli Left as naïve, all legitimate political positions.
The more puzzling question is why personal loyalty to Netanyahu remains so resilient even when events appear to contradict the image of him as Israel’s indispensable protector.
What does Netanyahu offer his followers beyond policy? Perhaps the answer lies in something deeper than politics. He offers psychological security through powerful rewards: security, identity, certainty, conviction, and collective struggle. To reinforce these bonds, he has also used the divisions within Israeli society with remarkable effectiveness, creating a powerful distinction between “us” and “them.”
Understanding these psychological dynamics may help explain Netanyahu’s extraordinary political resilience, and why his most devoted followers remain loyal even when the facts appear increasingly difficult to reconcile with his image.
Netanyahu’s most powerful political appeal
Netanyahu’s most powerful political appeal has long been security, not merely security as policy but as an emotional promise. Israelis live with a profound awareness of vulnerability shaped by the Holocaust, wars, terrorism, Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah.
Netanyahu has built his political persona around the image of an experienced leader who recognizes dangers and can protect Israelis. During Operation Protective Edge in 2014, he said, “The ultimate responsibility for your security and peace is mine, as prime minister.”
The message is not only about trusting his security policies but more about trusting him with their security. Security is identified not with a government or policy but with Netanyahu himself. The question is no longer whether Netanyahu made mistakes, but who can protect us if not Bibi.
Netanyahu also offers identity. His rhetoric often blurs the distinction between himself, his supporters, and the nation. In October 2025, he told the Knesset: “We are Jews, we are Israelis, we are strong.”
This framing makes opposition to Netanyahu appear to some supporters not just as political disagreement but as opposition to the country and its security. It also taps into longstanding resentment toward Israel’s traditional elites.
Netanyahu has been remarkably effective at turning that resentment into solidarity with himself. Politics shifts from a contest between competing ideas toward an “us versus them” struggle. Once politics becomes an identity conflict, evidence is less powerful.
Another characteristic is Netanyahu’s projection of certainty. In July 2026, describing a change in Israel’s security doctrine following October 7, he said: “I am taking the reins, and I am changing it.” Netanyahu consistently presents himself as someone who sees what others cannot see and possesses the experience to provide the solution. His implicit message is reassuring.
Since people dislike uncertainty, particularly when it feels existential, they want someone who appears to understand what’s happening, knows what must be done, and is confident to act.
Another mechanism sustaining Netanyahu’s following is his ability to turn criticism into conviction. In 2021, he said: “The test of leadership requires that the right decisions be made even when they are not understood at any given moment and their justification becomes clear later on.”
Netanyahu has created a protective shield around him. If events prove him right, he was right. If they prove him wrong, it means history has not caught up with him. Therefore, he is never wrong, as it may simply be too early to know. This creates a remarkably resilient form of loyalty.
The fifth element is the sense of permanent external collective threat. Iran has occupied a central place in Netanyahu’s political narrative for decades, while Hamas, Hezbollah, and other enemies reinforce the perception that Israel is surrounded by hostile forces. The threats are real and Netanyahu’s uncompromising strength is presented as the only reliable means of protection.
In January 2024, Netanyahu declared: “No one will stop us, not The Hague, not the axis of evil, and not anyone else.” Such language positions him as the leader standing between his people and a hostile world. And his followers feel they cannot afford to weaken the person protecting them. As long as the threat remains, the protector is indispensable.
The phenomenon of cognitive dissonance
Netanyahu’s political success cannot be separated from his ability to turn political disagreement into questions of identity and belonging. Israeli society has long contained profound ideological, religious, ethnic, and social divisions. The crucial question is what political leaders do with those divisions.
When opponents are portrayed as dangerous rather than simply mistaken, compromise becomes harder. Disagreement can become disloyalty, and defending the leader can become a way of defending one’s own side.
This helps explain the phenomenon of cognitive dissonance. When reality conflicts with a deeply held belief, people may reinterpret reality, so the belief can survive. Political attachment can become intertwined with identity, fear, and belonging. After years of defending a leader, acknowledging that he failed can mean reconsidering one’s own judgment.
That may be the deepest source of Netanyahu’s resilience. For some devoted supporters, letting go of Netanyahu may feel like letting go of a part of their identity, security, and certainty that he has come to represent.
The writer is an Israeli Canadian, formerly an economist and senior policy adviser in the Ontario Public Service, Canada. She is active in Jewish community life in Toronto and Miami, and writes about Israel, Zionism, and the relationship between Israel and the Diaspora.

Settler violence is a political blind spot in Israel’s election campaign - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:44:25 UTC
22:44:25 KST

Even as settler violence grows increasingly prominent abroad, Israelis seem somewhat ambivalent. According to a recent survey, 78% of the public call Judea and Samaria and a Palestinian state important or very important. But asked to prioritize, they rank it dead last: cost of living at 35%, haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription at 18%, the Iran war at 17%, judicial reform at 16%, and the future of Judea and Samaria at just 7%.
Before accusing Israelis of monstrous disregard, remember that in the Israeli political system they have only one vote to decide the prime minister, judicial reform, and security policy all at once. If you had only one dollar to invest, where would you place it?
Israelis will faithfully recite the cost of living – but as Naftali Bennett has discovered, to his dismay, they are not being honest. His comprehensive economic plan, released in early July, landed somewhere between negligible and nil. By contrast, the cost of living barely features in Gadi Eisenkot’s campaign, yet that hasn’t stopped the exodus from the one party to the other. The real number-one concern for Israeli voters has always been, and continues to be, security.
To an outsider, the correlation between settler violence and security looks weak, if not negative. The vigilantism rampant in the West Bank doesn’t make Israelis safer – but for a certain sector, cracking down on it represents the opposite. That is why the opposition hasn’t capitalized on the seeming "wild west" created, largely by government incompetence, 20 minutes from the capital. They will mention the issue when a particularly egregious event occurs, but don’t expect a poster reading “If he can’t secure Judea and Samaria, can he secure Tel Aviv.”
Such an ad would collide with two associations of settler violence, both of which the movement itself reinforces. In the Israeli political dictionary, the antonym of the settlements is the Palestinian state: Speak harshly of the movement’s excesses, and you are heard as lending a hand to the people trying to bring one about.
Settler violence tied to claims to Palestinian statehood
Meir Deutsch, director-general of the prominent settlement NGO Regavim, drew that connection explicitly not long ago, arguing that the “settler violence” narrative is a foreign-funded campaign engineered “to create the tool that will force the State of Israel to establish a Palestinian state.”
The second association is folded into that same charge: foreign. Regavim’s report casts the campaign as EU-financed and amplified by hostile voices abroad, and Deutsch points to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s own acknowledgment that settler violence helped justify a partial American arms embargo in the middle of the war. To make settler violence a headline issue, then, is to risk sounding at once obtuse about the real threat and faintly foreign in one’s preoccupations.
All of this is built on a fundamental truth: Israeli elections run in only one direction – rightward.
That’s why the self-styled “right-wing defense minister,” Israel Katz, fired the head of IDF Central Command on live TV for continuing to hold a violent settler, Tal Yinon Dardik, in custody and why even now he flatly rejects reinstating administrative detention for what he insists are a “handful of Jewish rioters.” The stunt ended in a swift and humiliating walk-back, but it captures a broader perception on the Right: Taking on the campaign against settler violence is a winning cause.
If there is internal polling on the issue, it has not been leaked. The truth is no one knows how many votes such actions secure, but it certainly secures a flank.
Right-wing politicians rarely hesitate when red lines are clearly crossed: A direct assault on IDF troops, like the violence seen last April, triggers immediate outrage across the political spectrum, while an indefensible action against Palestinian civilians, such as the Jit rampage, forces even figures like Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich to disavow perpetrators as rogue “criminals” divorced from mainstream Zionism.
But when the focus turns to the daily friction, political calculus changes. Leaders find it far safer to dance around the problem than to risk getting launched leftward for stepping on a partisan landmine.
Settler violence won’t be the wedge issue of the election. It won’t even be a widely discussed one – it’ll feature in attacks on the government as second fiddle at best. Not because people think settlers are right, but because attacking them makes one sound left-wing.
The writer serves as the English director of the Ribo Center and the editor of Amit Segal’s newsletter, It’s Noon in Israel.

Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home

Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.
The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.
The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.
Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.
Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.
It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.
Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.
The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.
Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.
However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.

Bosnia Deserves Better Than Permanent Probation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:43:00 UTC
22:43:00 KST

When the war in Bosnia ended in 1996, the Dayton Peace Agreement provided for a high representative, an international figure appointed by the 55 member Peace Implementation Council. The high representative has powers to impose or annul laws and to remove elected officials. The position was intended to be temporary and critics say that it has become an obstacle to the development of democracy in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The fight over who should replace Bosnia and Herzegovina’s High Representative has exposed a deeper divide between Washington and Brussels: what to do with an international protectorate that was meant to have evaporated decades ago. The United States is right that Bosnia needs to move beyond open-ended foreign supervision. But if Washington wants a Bosnia that welcomes American investment and commercial engagement, simply weakening the machinery that has governed the country for three decades will not get it there.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The impasse proves the point. Europeans remain reluctant to dismantle the Office of the High Representative (OHR), empowered to impose laws and remove officials under its “Bonn Powers”; Washington has grown impatient with what it sees as an unaccountable brake on sovereignty. Europeans suspect an American bid to muscle into institutions that Brussels has spent years building; Americans suspect a European bid to preserve a protectorate past its purpose. Both suspicions contain some truth, and neither side gains from paralysis.
The immediate dispute
The immediate dispute concerns a person; the deeper problem is a system with no clear end in sight. Christian Schmidt resigned as high representative on July 1, charging the Peace Implementation Council (PIC) – the 55-odd states and organizations overseeing the 1995 Dayton settlement – with urgently finding a successor. His deputy, the American diplomat Louis Crishock, became acting high representative: for now, an American is running the apparatus his own government wants scaled back.
The July 14 deadline for a new high representative passed without agreement – not because of Bosnian obstruction, but because PIC ambassadors failed to reach a compromise. That should matter to Washington. If the objective is a Bosnia more sovereign and commercially open, the question is not whether the OHR should last forever – plainly it should not – but how to leave behind a state capable of standing without it.
A managed exit offers more leverage than passive disengagement; the alternative is a vacuum in which entrenched interests exploit ethnic divisions while outside powers less aligned with Bosnia’s sovereignty compete for influence. Washington’s instinct, articulated in its broader Western Balkans policy, is to empower local actors over open-ended supervision; European officials say much the same, even if distrust of American intentions has kept them from acting on it.
Thirty years ago, the Dayton Peace Accords stopped a war by dividing power among Bosniak, Serb and Croat blocs rather than building a fully functioning unified state – an achievement in itself, but a peace agreement drafted at speed to stop the killing, not a constitution designed to elaborate a functioning state. Bosnia remains suspended between that emergency architecture and the normal life of a sovereign nation.
It is tempting, particularly in Washington, to conclude that Bosnia’s institutions are themselves the obstacle and that the PIC and OHR are simply failed mechanisms best left to wither. But the deeper problem is horizonless oversight, which neither drives reform nor pushes politicians to take responsibility when they can hide behind an administrator’s extraordinary powers instead.
That drift has been compounded by neglect – as one senior European diplomat put it wearily, few in Brussels know much about Bosnia any more, and fewer really care – and by dysfunction: the PIC has not met at ministerial level for nearly 20 years, and the OHR has become entrenched to the point of paralysis.
Russia’s presence in the PIC, too, is a particular absurdity: a state waging war on one European neighbor sitting in judgment on the peace of another. Its 2021 bid to force the issue through the UN Security Council failed, and it has since largely boycotted the Council’s work on Bosnia.
None of this excuses Bosnia’s own political class, too many of whom remain trapped in the past and act provocatively precisely because the high representative’s powers shield them from consequences. But the protectorate has entrenched a culture in which responsibility is always someone else’s: Bosnia’s divisions have been curated, in part, by the very structures meant to heal them.
Office of the High Representative
The OHR was meant to close in 2007, then 2008. Instead that deadline morphed into the “5+2” agenda: five objectives and two conditions with no date attached, several still unmet two decades later. A benchmark with no timetable is not a transition plan but a permanent probation system, and the cost is economic and generational: investment that might come to Sarajevo goes instead to Zagreb or Belgrade, and young Bosnians leave for Vienna or Munich rather than build careers at home.
Tellingly, even Europeans who helped build the system now recognize this. In a recent Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung essay, former High Representatives Carl Bildt and Wolfgang Petritsch argued the OHR should be abolished without delay – proof that the case for ending supervision is no longer dismissed as a peculiarly American view. But their proposed route, tying closure closely to EU accession, has a problem of its own.
Whether Bosnia’s problems are better resolved inside the EU than left to accumulate outside it is for Brussels and its member states to determine – that is not Washington’s fight. But relying on accession – a moving target, and not Bosnia’s to move – makes for an unstable peg on which to hang the OHR’s closure. A better answer is to give the exit its own timetable, set ahead of that hard-to-predict point.
The answer is neither to walk away tomorrow nor to preserve the OHR indefinitely, but to use the machinery one final time to make itself obsolete: reconvene the PIC at ministerial level, narrow its purpose to a single task, and invest one individual of sufficient standing – palatable to both Washington and the Europeans – to negotiate the shape of a post-OHR Bosnia and direct the Bonn Powers toward that terminal purpose. That High Representative could then set a realistic timetable against the existing 5+2 benchmarks, publicize progress as each is met, and wind the office down accordingly, without prejudice to EU accession but not held up by it either.
There is a useful principle elsewhere in the Western Balkans. The Berlin Process, a decade-old initiative backed by Berlin and Brussels, has focused on regional economic integration rather than indefinite political oversight. Washington need not embrace the European project behind it to recognize the underlying logic: countries become more stable partners when they trade, invest and build institutions as sovereign actors, not when economic engagement entrenches the very powerbrokers whom reform should be displacing.
This is the basis of a genuine US-European bargain – Washington presses for less intrusive supervision and more commercial opening, Europe insists the transition leave behind functioning institutions rather than a vacuum, and the levers each side controls are aligned behind one timetable. The pay-off, if it holds, is striking: the day may usefully come when nationalist rhetoric in Bosnia is relegated to football chants and graffiti – the ordinary background noise of an imperfect European democracy, rather than an existential threat requiring a foreign administrator’s powers of censure. That day should arrive by design, through the PIC’s one final ministerial act – convening to invest a high representative with that terminal mandate – and a Bosnian settlement finally trusted, and required, to stand on its own.
Bosnia has spent 30 years suspended between international supervision and sovereign responsibility. The objective now should not be another 30 years managing that suspension but ending it – deliberately and credibly – in a way that serves Bosnia’s sovereignty and American and European interests alike. Bosnia could then do what it has long been ready to do: build, rather than merely endure, its own future.

Two Pilots From Russia’s Elite “Russian Knights” Aerobatic Team Killed in Fighter Jet Crash

13:41:55 UTC

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Two Pilots From Russia’s Elite “Russian Knights” Aerobatic Team Killed in Fighter Jet Crash
Two experienced Russian military pilots assigned to the “Russian Knights” aerobatic demonstration team have reportedly been killed in a training flight accident, raising questions about whether their deaths are connected to the loss of two Russian Su-30SM fighter jets earlier this week.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi on October 24, citing Russian news website amic.ru, the pilots were identified as Colonel Oleg Yerofeyev, a decorated military pilot, and Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Kochetov. Preliminary reports indicate that the accident occurred on October 22, although the exact date and circumstances remain unclear.
Both officers served at Russia’s Aviation Equipment Demonstration Center, which operates the Russian Knights aerobatic team from Kubinka airfield near Moscow.
Yerofeyev was deputy head of the center and had accumulated approximately 3,300 flight hours. Kochetov worked as a flight safety inspector and had logged around 1,500 hours. Both were qualified to operate several Russian fighter aircraft, including the MiG-29, Su-27, Su-30SM, and Su-35S.
The reported deaths may be connected to two separate Su-30SM losses recorded on October 21, when Russian military aviation reportedly lost two fighters in a single day. Both crew members were confirmed dead in one of those incidents.
Militarnyi noted that the October 22 date reported by Russian media could be incorrect, potentially linking the pilots’ deaths to the earlier crashes. However, the possibility of an additional, previously unreported aviation accident has not been ruled out.
The Russian Knights aerobatic team was established on April 5, 1991, as part of Russia’s 237th Guards Aviation Equipment Demonstration Center. Based at Kubinka airfield in the Moscow region, the unit operates advanced fighter aircraft, primarily Su-35S jets, and performs at military ceremonies and international aviation events.
According to Militarnyi, pilots from the team are regularly assigned combat missions, generally flying operational military aircraft rather than the jets reserved for aerobatic demonstrations. However, aircraft belonging directly to the Russian Knights fleet have also been documented performing military missions.
Earlier, on October 15, Ukraine’s Navy reported destroying six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers in a Neptune missile strike on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region.

Death toll rises in Nigeria’s Taraba massacre as residents flee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:41:54 UTC
22:41:54 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
The death toll from a gunmen attack on a rural community in northeastern Nigeria’s Taraba State is disputed, with the state government reporting 25 fatalities while Amnesty International puts the number at 40.
The attack occurred between Friday evening and Saturday morning in the Binnari community, Karim-Lamido Local Government Area, where armed men stormed the area and opened fire on residents.
Amnesty International said Saturday evening that at least 40 people were killed in the assault, while the Taraba State government on Sunday put the death toll at 25. The discrepancy could not immediately be independently reconciled.
Witnesses told Anadolu that the assailants arrived on motorcycles, attacked residents and looted property, including food supplies, cash and motorcycles. Homes and shops were also set ablaze, forcing survivors to flee to neighboring communities.
The attack has triggered renewed concerns over the protection of rural communities in Taraba, where residents have faced repeated threats from armed groups.
State Governor Agbu Kefas on Sunday condemned the killings and called on security agencies to intensify efforts to protect residents and apprehend those responsible.
The governor’s reelection campaign council separately warned politicians against politicizing the tragedy following criticism of the state government’s handling of insecurity.
Amnesty International called for an impartial investigation into the killings, justice for the victims and stronger protection for communities at risk of further attacks.
The incident adds to Nigeria’s persistent security challenges, with rural communities in several regions facing attacks by armed groups, kidnappings and killings. The violence has displaced residents and intensified calls for stronger protection of vulnerable communities.

Vucic’s mother attacked during Serbian election – SNS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Vucic’s mother attacked during Serbian election – SNS
The mother of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic was attacked by his political opponents in Belgrade on Sunday, his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) has alleged.
Serbia is voting for its next government and Vucic is running for prime minister. His ruling coalition has been polling strongly against a student-backed opposition movement, attempting to remove SNS from government after 14 years in power.
“A group of young men... shoved Angelina Vucic, screamed at her, and tore open the bags of groceries she was carrying from the market,” SNS said in a statement on its official website. The statement alleged that the attackers were aligned with anti-government protesters who have occupied universities and blocked roads across the country.
The party denounced the alleged assault as an “unacceptable act of aggression, humiliation, and intimidation.”
“No one’s mother, no one’s grandmother – no woman at all – should ever be a target of violence due to political differences!” it added, demanding that police take decisive action against the attackers.
Vucic resigned on September 27 following two years of protests, saying he wanted to participate in the election as an ordinary citizen. His ruling coalition led the student-backed opposition by 47% to 40%, according to an Ipsos poll published on Thursday.
Anti-government protests followed the deadly collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in 2024, which killed 16 people and sparked allegations of corruption and safety oversight failures.
Vucic has accused foreign organizations of funding the ongoing demonstrations, alleging on Thursday that actors abroad wanted to remove him from Serbia’s political landscape.
The politician has also pledged to keep Serbia out of any future war with Russia if elected, warning that Europe is preparing for a military confrontation with Moscow.

Charity begins at home: Ireland must get its priorities straight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:40:38 UTC
22:40:38 KST

Charity begins at home: Ireland must get its priorities straight
The Irish political week has once again been marked by bitter exchanges, this time over the Triple Lock Agreement, our long-standing tradition of military neutrality, and whether a referendum should be held before any fundamental change is made to it.
Taoiseach (Ireland’s prime minister) Micheal Martin has accused the country’s largest opposition party Sinn Fein, which fiercely opposes the idea of dismantling Triple Lock, of not giving a “continental” about Irish neutrality. The word is his own, and it is worth reflecting on its meaning.
But I have a question of my own for Mr. Martin: does he give a continental about the health and well-being of the Irish people?
What does neutrality mean to a parent whose three-year-old child is suffering in agony while waiting nine hours in Galway Regional Hospital? What comfort does it offer families struggling to access essential medical care, or parents and students caught up in this week’s education strikes? And what of the many other problems that continue to weigh upon ordinary Irish households?
The latest figures, obtained from the HSE by Padraig Rice, Social Democrats TD and Chair of the Oireachtas Committee on Health, make the situation even more difficult to ignore. Between January and July of this year, more than 70,100 people in Ireland either left emergency departments before completing their treatment or did not wait to be seen. A further 31,821 patients waited longer than 24 hours to be admitted or discharged. The average waiting time in emergency departments was 9.3 hours.
These matters concern real people, their children, their dignity, and their daily lives. Before our leaders lecture us about international responsibilities, should they not first explain why such basic needs remain unmet at home?
Ireland is not a wealthy country merely because figures on a government spreadsheet say so. A country’s true wealth lies in the quality of its health service, the education of its children, the reliability of its transport, and the infrastructure that allows people to live and work with confidence. By that measure, we still have much to do.
Yet Irish taxpayers are repeatedly asked to support ever greater expenditure connected with the conflict in Ukraine. At what point do we pause and ask whether our priorities are in the right order?
Mr. Martin, charity begins at home. Have you forgotten the recession of 2008 and the painful years that followed? Irish families know what it means to endure financial insecurity, lost opportunities, and the consequences of decisions made far above their heads. We should remember, too, the countries that stood by Ireland during difficult times, and consider carefully where our obligations lie today.
This week, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, has again been pressing for further support for Ukraine while criticizing US President Donald Trump. Ordinary European citizens are expected to accept the bill.
But surely there comes a moment when the people who pay must be entitled to ask questions.
I believe European citizens should stand up for themselves, examine the priorities of their leaders, and refuse to treat every pronouncement from Brussels as unquestionable wisdom. Supporting a country in distress is one thing; allowing an open-ended political commitment to overshadow pressing needs at home is quite another.
Imagine what could be achieved if public money were spent with greater care and accountability. Imagine health services where children did not have to wait hours in pain, schools where disputes did not repeatedly interrupt education, and transport and infrastructure that served communities as they deserve to be served. These are not some extravagant dreams – just the reasonable expectations of a modern society.
Meanwhile, EU leaders continue to speak as though the destruction of Russia were a realistic or desirable political objective. I believe this approach is dangerously misguided. Russia is a major power, and European security requires clear thinking, diplomacy, and an honest assessment of the risks of prolonged confrontation. Declaring ever more money and resources necessary does not, by itself, bring peace any closer.
Nor does constant hostility offer a convincing vision for Europe’s future. António Costa, Kaja Kallas, Ursula von der Leyen, and other senior figures in the European hierarchy should be judged by the consequences of their decisions, not by the strength of their rhetoric. The EU was supposed to offer cooperation, stability, and prosperity. It should not become an institution in which confrontation abroad takes precedence over the needs of its own citizens.
And what of Ukraine itself? If European leaders genuinely care about the Ukrainian people, surely their first concern should be the preservation of human life and the search for a sustainable peace. Endless conflict brings suffering, displacement, destruction, and the loss of generations who might otherwise have built a future for themselves. The human cost deserves at least as much attention as the political ambitions of those directing the response.
I do not believe that the future of Europe should be built upon the assumption that Russia must be destroyed. I believe it should be built upon realism, diplomacy, accountability, and the recognition that war always extracts its price from ordinary people first.
Ireland has its own history of hardship, resilience, and recovery. We know what it means to struggle, to rebuild, and to depend upon the solidarity of others. That history should make us thoughtful about the suffering of people elsewhere, but it should also remind us of our responsibility to our own citizens.
Before asking Irish taxpayers to shoulder yet another burden, our government should explain what it is doing to ensure that a sick child receives timely treatment, that pupils receive the education they need, and that public services function as they should.
Mr. Martin, the question is not whether Ireland should care about the wider world. Of course it should. The question is whether caring about the wider world has become an excuse for neglecting the people who elected you.
Charity begins at home. So does responsibility. And so, ultimately, should political accountability.
It is time for Ireland, and for the EU, to put ordinary people back at the center of public life. Our taxes should serve the public good, our leaders should be answerable for their choices, and diplomacy should seek to preserve lives rather than prolong their destruction.
The people of Europe deserve nothing less.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Overnight Ukrainian drone attacks killed four people in southwestern Russia’s Belgorod region, one in the Lipetsk region and damaged an industrial site in the Perm region of the Ural Mountains, officials said Sunday.
In the city of Belgorod near the Russian border with Ukraine, an attack killed three people and injured 13, said Belgorod regional governor Alexander Shuvayev.
The overnight attack on Belgorod damaged 30 apartment buildings, 35 cars, four houses, three administrative buildings, eight commercial premises and three social facilities, Shuvayev said.
In a separate incident on Sunday morning, one person was killed and another injured when a Ukrainian drone struck a car in the village of Voznesenovka near the town of Shebekino, local authorities said.
A drone attack on Russia's Perm region damaged an industrial facility, injuring five of its workers, regional governor Dmitry Makhonin said on Sunday.
Emergency services were at the scene and the injured people received the necessary medical help, he said on the state-backed MAX messaging app without providing further detail on the nature of the damage.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk during an overnight attack.
The ministry said the vessel was being used to supply the Ukrainian army.
Russian forces also hit a logistics center, a distribution center and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv. The ministry said the facilities had been used for storage and distribution of dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian military.
Reuters could not independently verify the Defense Ministry's information.
Later on Sunday, southwestern Russia's Lipetsk region Governor Igor Artamonov said a Ukrainian missile strike on an industrial zone in the city of Yelets killed a security guard and injured a paramedic.
Artamonov said the security guard worked at one of the industrial facilities located on the site. The paramedic at the medical center was taken to hospital, where she was receiving the necessary treatment, the governor said.
The governor did not identify the facility that was hit in the strike.
Reuters could not independently verify the report. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

BRASILIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Voting in the second round of Brazil's 2026 presidential election officially began at 8 a.m. local time (1100 GMT) on Sunday, with polling stations across the nation set to close at 5 p.m. local time.
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the ruling Workers' Party faces Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party candidate and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in the runoff after the two topped the first-round vote.
In the first round held on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro led with about 47 percent of valid votes, while Lula came second, trailing by roughly two percentage points. Several recent opinion polls have shown a tight race between the two candidates.
Under Brazil's electoral rules, a presidential candidate who secures more than half of the valid votes in the first round wins outright. Otherwise, the two candidates with the most votes advance to a runoff to determine the winner. ■

ALMATY, Kazakhstan, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Daniil Medvedev successfully defended an ATP Tour title for the first time in his career on Sunday, recovering from a set down to beat Georgian qualifier Nikoloz Basilashvili 6-7 (6), 6-1, 6-3 in the 2026 Almaty Open final.
The top-seeded Russian overcame a strong start from Basilashvili, who matched Medvedev from the baseline in a closely contested opening set before fading as the match wore on.
Medvedev, who remained unbroken throughout the contest, gradually asserted his authority to secure his fourth title of the season and the 25th of his career after one hour and 53 minutes.
Basilashvili began confidently, using his powerful groundstrokes to put Medvedev under pressure and force a first-set tiebreak. The Russian held a set point but was unable to convert as the Georgian edged ahead.
However, Basilashvili struggled to maintain his early intensity, with Medvedev's consistency and defensive skills increasingly frustrating the 34-year-old.
The defending champion dominated the second set 6-1 before carrying that momentum into the decider, where he continued to dictate play and landed 78% of his first serves to complete the comeback.
"It was not easy but I had my chances in the first set. I got a bit unlucky," Medvedev said. "I knew I would probably have my chances to turn the match around. But I am happy to win."
Despite having won titles at several tournaments on multiple occasions, Medvedev had never previously managed to defend an ATP Tour crown.
"It is just a matter of time, luck, a moment," he said. "I was feeling fresh, physically good. Sascha [Bublik] being injured in the semis gave me an extra push in the final and I am happy to finally do it."
Medvedev reached Sunday's final after home favorite Alexander Bublik retired injured during their semifinal on Saturday, having lost the opening set 6-3. The Russian had earlier beaten Japan's Sho Shimabukuro and France's Terence Atmane.
The victory adds to Medvedev's titles in Brisbane, Dubai and Chengdu this season, with only Italy's Jannik Sinner, who has won six tournaments, claiming more ATP Tour titles in 2026.
The triumph also strengthened Medvedev's hopes of qualifying for November's season-ending ATP Finals in Turin.
The former world No. 1, who won the event in 2020, sits fifth in the live qualification race with 2,670 points, 790 clear of 10th-placed Alex de Minaur, the first player outside the qualification places.
Medvedev, who competed at the ATP Finals for six consecutive years from 2019 to 2024 before missing out last season, will next compete at the ATP 500 tournament in Vienna.
Despite the defeat, Basilashvili enjoyed an encouraging week in Almaty, reaching his first tour-level final since losing to Roberto Bautista Agut in Doha in 2022.
The five-time ATP Tour champion is set to climb 30 places to world No. 98 when the rankings are updated Monday, returning to the top 100 for the first time since February 2023. ■

Police: Signs of radicalization visible among younger teens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:38:00 UTC
22:38:00 KST

Police: Signs of radicalization visible among younger teens
Signs of radicalization are appearing in increasingly younger people and are already evident among 12- and 13-year-olds, said Pärtel Preinvalts, head of the radicalization prevention group at the Police and Border Guard Board's Northern Prefecture.
Preinvalts said the change in Estonia is not happening in isolation and can also be seen in other Western countries, including the United States.
"The age threshold is moving steadily downward in terms of young people's development. Whereas previously it was 15- and 16-year-olds, today it is 12- and 13-year-olds or even younger," Preinvalts said.
The number of violent crimes carried out by juveniles has risen over the last decade. There are fewer incidents such as shoplifting or vandalism and significantly more cases involving violence.
The proportion of juvenile crimes carried out against another person rose significantly from 2016 (27.5 percent) to 2022 (48.8 percent) Last year, the rate was recorded at 44.7 percent.
"Although the overall numbers may be falling, the proportion of crimes that have a much greater impact on victims and the community is increasing," Preinvalts said.
A sense of belonging
The head of the radicalization prevention group said young people often develop a sense of belonging through shared activities that may not initially appear to have anything to do with radicalization.
Many teenagers who join a group may not even realize what kind of gang they have joined until an adult explains it to them.
"Unfortunately, a recurring motive is so-called patriotism, which quite quickly turns into hatred," Preinvalts said. He added that, under the guise of patriotism and love of one's country, what often actually takes place is hostility toward minority groups and the seeking of conflict. This happens both in the media and in public spaces.
"It all starts online and quite soon moves into public spaces, for example through the distribution of stickers and other propaganda materials," Preinvalts said.
Democracies encourage civic activism regardless of age, he said, adding that a radical worldview and strongly defined views of the surrounding world are often part of a young person's development.
"Many grow out of it and pose no threat," Preinvalts added.
Glorification of violence
Radicalization becomes a problem when it is accompanied by the glorification of violence or, in the worst-case scenario, its use. Preinvalts said ideological influence has never been as accessible to young people as it is today.
"Content is often determined by algorithms, and after stumbling upon something a few times, a person may unknowingly become a consumer of material that gradually normalizes unlawful behavior," he explained.
"However, it is important to understand that thoughts and beliefs play an important role in maintaining democracy. We have a free society," the official continued.
Preinvalts added that the state cannot and does not want to interfere with people's beliefs, but it has a responsibility is to ensure the safety and security of all residents.
Ministry wants to stop repeat offenders
The Ministry of Justice is now looking for a service provider to help young people with extremist views avoid further offenses and return to education or the labor market. The ministry has announced a small-scale procurement with an estimated value of €40,000.
The service is aimed at young people aged 14 to 29 whose offenses are linked to extremist views or an interest in them. The goal is to reduce the risk of further similar offenses and support young people in distancing themselves from extremist views, developing social skills and reintegrating into society.
The counselor providing the service must have at least two years of experience working with young people or young people exhibiting risky behavior. They must also have knowledge of how extremist views and radicalization develop, including young people's need for belonging, identity crises and the spread of extremist ideologies online.

Hellenic Basketball Federation president resigns amid match-fixing investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:37:24 UTC
22:37:24 KST

Liolios has denied the charges against him, and his defence team has argued that there is no solid evidence linking him to match fixing, describing the case as a conspiracy.
Vangelis Liolios, the president of the Hellenic Basketball Federation (EOK), announced on Sunday that he was stepping down from his role, as he appeared before an investigating magistrate in connection with an ongoing investigation into allegations of match fixing in Greek basketball.
The inquiry focuses on claims that games linked to betting markets were manipulated, with authorities examining the possible involvement of referees and other figures within the sport.
The case has hit a crucial phase, with suspects being questioned and judicial authorities reviewing the evidence gathered so far.
Liolios has denied the charges against him, and his defence team has argued that there is no solid evidence linking him to match fixing, describing the case as a conspiracy.
Allegations
According to information made public so far, the investigation concerns allegations of bribery and the offering of benefits to referees, players and club officials in order to influence the course or outcome of basketball games.
Authorities are examining 49 matches played between 2016 and 2026, ranging from professional and lower national divisions to youth and school championships.
Prosecutors say that the alleged offences were aimed partly at manipulating matches that could feature in betting markets in Greece and abroad.
The acts under examination are said to have been committed on a repeated basis, either by individuals acting alone or in cooperation with others.
Liolios and his close associate, Giorgos Mavraganis, have been giving evidence before the investigating magistrate.
Liolios' defence has disputed the evidence presented in the case file, arguing that allegations against him are not backed up by evidence showing that he was involved in match fixing.
His lawyer, Panagiotis Papaioannou, has also questioned the way in which messages related to the case were made public, arguing that publishing select excerpts was not enough evidence to draw reliable conclusions.
Former referee remanded in custody
One of the most significant developments in the case was the decision to remand in custody former referee Petros Papapetrou following his deposition on Friday.
According to reports, police found €820,000 in cash at his home. He is said to have claimed that the money came from income he accumulated over 25 years, from his work as a referee, his job at the forestry service, family earnings and property sales.
He reportedly said that his combined income with his family from 2001 to 2026 amounted to €1.5 million and that he gradually withdrew and saved the money from bank accounts because his living expenses were limited.
Papapetrou's lawyer, Orestis Georgiadis, disputed the allegations and announced that the defence would appeal against the decision to remand him in custody.
He said that documents have been submitted which, according to the defence, prove the lawful origin of the cash.
More depositions scheduled for Monday
The judicial process is expected to continue on Monday, with international referee Vasso Tsaroucha, EOK refereeing adviser Ilias Koromilas and former referee and member of the Central Refereeing Committee, Tasos Piloidis, scheduled to give statements.
These depositions form part of a broader effort by authorities to clarify the role of all those named in the case file and to consider whether more people may be involved.
Following the latest developments, the EOK board held an emergency meeting and stressed that it was closely monitoring the situation.
The Federation underlined that its priority was to ensure its smooth operation and the orderly running of all leagues and competitions. It announced that the board was also meeting on a continuous basis, twice a day, in order to assess developments in the case.

US updates travel warnings for 13 Middle Eastern countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:33:53 UTC
22:33:53 KST

Breadcrumb
US updates travel warnings for 13 Middle Eastern countries
The United States has updated travel advisories for 13 countries across the Middle East, citing the risk of further attacks by Yemen’s Houthis and alleged Iranian efforts to target American officials in the region. The revisions come alongside reductions in staffing at several US embassies amid concerns over a wider escalation.
The advisories, dated 23 October, cover Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. The updates revise the security warnings rather than raise the countries’ existing advisory levels.
"The possibility of regional effects, including the potential for flight disruptions, makes a region-wide advisory update important and prudent," a State Department official said in comments shared by PBS correspondent Nick Schifrin.
The department said the revisions reflected increased potential for armed attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials. Those claims come amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition, including missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory.
Advisories by country, and what they mean:
Eight countries are listed at Level 3, meaning Americans should reconsider travel, while five remain at Level 4 — "do not travel", the State Department’s highest warning. The country-specific warnings are:
- Bahrain: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Iran: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism, wrongful detention and other risks.
- Iraq: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- Israel: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and unrest.
- Jordan: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Kuwait: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. Washington cites crime and other risks.
- Lebanon: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- Oman: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Qatar: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists “other” risks, rather than a separate terrorism, crime or unrest indicator.
- Saudi Arabia: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks. The update follows Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, including the 10 October strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
- Syria: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- United Arab Emirates: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Yemen: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
US authorities have urged Americans to monitor embassy alerts and airline operations, prepare for possible flight cancellations or airspace closures, and maintain emergency departure plans that do not depend on US government assistance. They also recommend enrolling in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program to receive security updates.
The warnings follow Friday’s reports that Washington was reducing staffing at its embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE. Axios first reported an intelligence memo alleging that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached "advanced stages"; the Associated Press subsequently obtained the memo and confirmed the staffing reductions with US officials.
Those four embassies remain open under restricted operations, and personnel are not subject to the same compulsory departure order issued on Wednesday for non-essential US staff and their families in Saudi Arabia.
US officials have denied that the staffing changes are linked to prospective new US or Israeli strikes on Iran. The advisory updates themselves do not establish that another military operation is imminent, although the move comes amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, with US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warning that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran before the upcoming US midterm elections.
