Burnham call for debate on free movement with EU draws mixed Labour response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:31:05 UTC
22:31:05 KST

Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers but risked a rift with “red wall” Labour MPs, who say it could jeopardise Brexit-voting seats.
The prime minister made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.
Burnham also revealed his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in their manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.
The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].
“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
His remarks were supported by Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, as well as Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe. However, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among those Labour MPs who have previously been more cautious about closer ties with Europe, while a number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.
Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she would “like to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be, and then put that to the people at a general election”, and Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means”.
A number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion include Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary.
At a New Statesman event during the Labour party conference in September, however, Mahmood said rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”.
One senior minister under Keir Starmer said the reopening of the debate on free movement was “brave” given how divisive it had been in the Brexit years. “It’s a question of timing. Public opinion is of a place where you can start to have this debate,” he said. “Theresa May, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer: what they were all trying to do was get as close as possible without freedom of movement. There is now the a possibility of being brave and making the case on single market and free movement without going for rejoin.”
Labour MPs with pro-Brexit seats have expressed scepticism about rejoining the bloc, including Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement.
One red wall MP said they thought debating free movement was the right thing to do but many colleagues in the north-east, especially in coastal areas, had begun to raise serious concerns. “These MPs are definitely raising the alarm,” they said. “Andy may have to work out if he can win without them, which is brutal but true.” Another Labour MP from a Brexit-voting area said it would “undoubtedly put seats at risk to Reform” but that Burnham was making an argument from a position of strength, having taken the party to higher poll ratings in recent weeks.
Worries were brought up publicly on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “1 million young people that are out of work”.
In his party conference speech last month, Burnham fired the starting gun on the argument about rejoining the EU as one potential route, but his latest comments suggest he appears to be favouring the option that would avoid a referendum.
Although Labour’s manifesto pledges no return to free movement and the single market, Burnham signalled it could still be up for discussion at next month’s EU summit.
Burnham’s comments at the weekend drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”.
“He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added.
Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move more freely for jobs within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services.
Luke Tryl, a polling and focus groups expert at the More in Common thinktank, said on Sunday that people tended to be less concerned about free movement given years of high non-EU migration but would be more exercised about EU budget contributions or joining the euro.
During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023 under a new points-based system, up from 330,000 before the Brexit vote.
Burnham’s decision to open the debate on free movement was welcomed by some businesses, which have grown frustrated at the lack of progress on the issue, and on reducing the extra paperwork required to do business with EU customers since Brexit – both seen as obstacles to faster economic growth.
The British Chambers of Commerce lobby group called for the Treasury to analyse the various economic options for different forms of EU-UK relationships. Most economic studies have concluded that a closer EU relationship would benefit the UK economy.
William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said the common understanding strategy agreed by Keir Starmer in May 2025 was “approaching the ceiling of what can be achieved”.
This week’s budget is expected to underscore the damage to the economy from Brexit, including from a drop in net migration. The Resolution Foundation, a thinktank, said that if migration falls by 300,000 over the next five years it would translate to a hit to government tax revenues of £4.7bn in 2029-30, reducing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies, another thinktank, estimated that lower net migration estimates would reduce the chancellor’s “headroom” by between £1bn and £5bn by 2031-32, depending on how the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) chooses to model the expected reductions in population.
The OBR has previously estimated that Brexit barriers to trade and free movement have caused a long-term hit of about 4% of UK output.

Cruise missiles struck the “Energiya” defense-industrial enterprise in the city of Yelets in Russia’s Lipetsk region on Sunday, Oct. 25, targeting one of Russia’s foremost manufacturers of specialized power sources for guided missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, Radio Liberty and open-source intelligence monitors reported.
Lipetsk Region Governor Igor Artamonov confirmed an attack on the municipal industrial zone on Sunday, stating that municipal emergency services and defense specialists deployed to the impact zone, while refraining from identifying the enterprise in his initial dispatches.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to independent Russian monitoring outlet Astra and military open-source intelligence channels, incoming cruise missiles struck the production complex of the Energiya research and production enterprise.
Local monitoring channels and defense analysts suggested that the precision interdiction was executed using air-launched cruise missiles, potentially British-supplied Storm Shadow systems.
The facility functions as Russia’s largest scientific and industrial developer in the specialized field of autonomous chemical power sources, high-capacity accumulator batteries, and electrochemical energy units.
Specialized batteries for air defense, aviation, and drones
The Yelets plant occupies a critical, specialized niche within the Russia’s military-industrial complex, manufacturing electrochemical power components across military, aerospace, and civil aviation sectors.
Drones Strike Russian Titanium Producer Avisma in Urals
The enterprise develops and serially manufactures autonomous power supplies, specialized primary battery arrays, and compact lithium cells integrated directly into Russian strike drones, loitering munitions, and electronic control systems.
Energiya’s power units are essential components installed within surface-to-air missile systems, airborne avionics suites, naval combat vessels, and specialized guidance complexes for ballistic and cruise platforms.
Due to its strategic integration into the Kremlin’s defense-industrial supply chain, the Energiya enterprise is subjected to comprehensive international sanctions imposed by the US, the EU, the UK, Canada, Switzerland, Japan, Australia, and Ukraine.
The facility has previously been targeted in long-range interdiction strikes. In May 2025, an aerial strike ignited a major blaze across one of the primary production workshops, followed by a separate strike reported in January 2026.
Campaign against Russian military suppliers
The missile strike on Energiya in Lipetsk region coincides with an expanding Ukrainian precision campaign systematically targeting critical suppliers of specialized components, chemical precursors, and metallurgy across Russia’s rear defense sector.
Overnight into Sunday, long-range Ukrainian strike drones hit the “Avisma” chemical-metallurgical complex in Berezniki in the Perm region – located 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) away in the Ural Mountains – damaging a core facility of the world’s largest titanium producer vital for Russian combat aircraft, jet turbines, and missile fuselages.
Concurrently on Saturday, Ukrainian precision munitions struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical facility in Samara region and the Omsky Kauchuk chemical enterprise in Siberia, both of which manufacture synthetic rubbers and chemical binders essential for solid rocket propellant used in Iskander-M ballistic missiles and intercontinental systems.
Those operations followed confirmed precision Storm Shadow missile strikes on the Proton defense microelectronics complex in Oryol, which destroyed key production facilities supplying optoelectronics and power semiconductors for missile and air defense platforms.

Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arrest 25

Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arrest 25
Officers baton-charge demonstrators in overnight operation as activists demand government action on soaring rents and home shortages.
Police in Portugal have cleared a camp in central Lisbon set up to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators and making 25 arrests.
Dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square shortly after 2am (02:00 GMT) on Sunday.
They had warned protesters that their tents would be dismantled if they were not removed, threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted.
Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday’s protest march by thousands along one of Lisbon’s main avenues.
A smaller camp of about 50 tents was also dismantled in Porto’s Praca D Joao I public square, where police made six arrests.
Police said the operation was “proportionate” and that the 25 people arrested in Lisbon were later released and are due in court on Monday.
While police reported seven minor injuries among officers and protesters in the two operations, the activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 people were hurt and called for a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday.
“Choosing the early hours of the morning to unleash dogs and baton-charge peaceful protesters is a political decision. It shows this government would rather repress those denouncing the housing crisis than address it,” the group said.
Home affordability crises
Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017 while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit.
Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent.
The Bank of Portugal estimates a shortfall of 300,000 homes nationwide, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.
The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a bill to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained.
The protests in Portugal echo recent demonstrations in Spain over home shortages and surging rents.
There have also been protests in cities including Paris, where small student demonstrations over school conditions broadened into wider protests against government economic policies.

This repeated disrespect toward our national president is happening at the direct behest of Modi and Shah. The nation will not forgive this. The nation is watching," he added.

Black Sea Becomes More Dangerous Than Persian Gulf, With Over 570 Ships Attacked Since January
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:28:33 UTC
22:28:33 KST

Since the start of 2026, more than 570 ships have been attacked in the Black Sea, and at least 40 sailors have been killed, making the route more dangerous for commercial shipping than routes in the Persian Gulf.
The Financial Times reported this.
The intensity of the attacks increased significantly over the summer. Between July and September, 387 ships were attacked — more than five times the number in the previous quarter.
According to maritime security company Ambrey, Russia was responsible for about 90% of attacks on shipping over the past 45 days.
One of the latest incidents was an attack on the cargo vessel Khoryv off the Romanian coast on October 23. The vessel caught fire and sank following the strike. One sailor was killed, and three others went missing.
The increase in attacks is also affecting shipping companies’ operations. Over the previous month, fewer than 10 vessels passed through the ports of Greater Odesa, compared with about 400 in July.
Attacks on ships in the Black Sea were more than six times higher than in the Persian Gulf. In the Strait of Hormuz area, 24 sailors were confirmed killed over the same period.
Additional factors include threats to shipping and a sharp rise in insurance costs. According to insurers, war-risk insurance can reach 15% of a vessel’s hull value — almost twice the rate for ships in the Persian Gulf.
High costs and security risks are forcing some companies to abandon Black Sea voyages. Others are instead using older, cheaper-to-insure vessels. According to the FT, some are up to 50 years old and in poor technical condition.
Militarnyi previously reported that on October 6, Russian aerial and naval drones attacked two merchant vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, one of which sank.
On October 23, the civilian vessel KHORYV capsized off the Romanian coast following a drone attack.
In response to the new threats, NATO announced it would send additional patrol aircraft, radars, and drones to the Black Sea.

Ethnic minorities in England less likely to get breast cancer diagnosis from routine screening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:28:23 UTC
22:28:23 KST

People from minority ethnic backgrounds in England are up to a third less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via routine screening, and are more likely to be diagnosed in an emergency setting, analysis has found.
The research, carried out by academics at the University of Surrey and funded by the charity Breast Cancer Now, involved analysis of 86,564 adults diagnosed with the disease between 2009 and 2019, from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink and the Cancer Registration Tumour and Treatment datasets.
The analysis found that people from Black, Asian and mixed backgrounds, alongside people from deprived backgrounds, were up to 33% less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, while these groups were also up to 31% more likely to be diagnosed via urgent suspected cancer referral, and up to 37% more likely to be diagnosed via emergency presentation.
Manveet Basra, the associate director of public health, inclusion and awareness at Breast Cancer Now, said the analysis revealed that people from marginalised groups “face inequalities at every stage of their breast cancer experience, and tragically this impacts their survival rates”.
Basra added: “This research helps us understand who is less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, [who] might wait longer to get diagnosed or experience delays in treatment, and knowing what barriers they face enables us to work towards eliminating them.
“Determined to improve breast cancer care and survival rates outcomes, we’re funding world-class research that actively identifies and addresses inequities, working with policymakers to improve equal access to screening, and ensuring our information, campaigns and life-changing support services reflect the diverse needs of everyone affected by this devastating disease.”
Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide among women. It accounts for about one in four cases of cancer and is one of the leading causes of death in women under 50. Identifying women at higher risk early can pave the way for additional screening or preventive treatment.
The research also revealed that people living with a learning disability faced poorer cancer outcomes: their time to diagnosis was 18% longer than people without a learning disability, and they faced a 10% longer wait time for treatment.
This research adds to existing evidence of the unequal outcomes people from marginalised backgrounds face in regards to cancer.
A previous study showed that ethnic minorities required more visits to GPs than other people before being diagnosed with cancer. On average, one in five people across England require three or more GP interactions before being diagnosed with cancer. But for people from ethnic minority backgrounds, the figure rises to one in three, according to analysis of the NHS cancer patient experience 2022 survey by QualityWatch, a joint programme from the Nuffield Trust and the Health Foundation.
Research from the UK Health Security Agency has also suggested that young black women are more likely to have aggressive breast cancer tumours, experience poorer care and have higher mortality rates, but are significantly under-represented in clinical research.
Dr Rob Kerrison, an associate professor of cancer care and co-lead of the cancer care expert group at the University of Surrey and the lead investigator of this study, said: “We know that some groups of women in the UK have poorer breast cancer survival than others, but until now we have had only a limited understanding of why. Our findings suggest that inequalities in access to screening and timely treatment may be part of the explanation.
“Women from a range of disadvantaged and under-served groups were less likely to have their cancer detected through screening and often waited longer to start treatment. If we are serious about improving breast cancer outcomes, we need to ensure that everyone can access screening and receive prompt treatment, regardless of their background or circumstances.”

No reports of problems at polling stations abroad, voting proceeds normal
Sunday 25 October 2026 13:59
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 13:59
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Voting in Bulgaria’s presidential and vice-presidential elections abroad is proceeding normally, with no reports of problems at polling stations so far. This was announced by Radi Naydenov, head of the Elections Working Group at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
According to him, just under 100 people voted in New Zealand, where the process went smoothly.
Asked about the organisation of the vote in the United Kingdom and Türkiye, where the number of polling stations is higher than at previous elections, Naydenov assured reporters that there had been no reports of irregularities so far. He urged Bulgarians living abroad to exercise their right to vote.
Boryana Stoynova, deputy head of the Elections Working Group, stressed that Bulgarian voters should carefully check polling station addresses before setting out to vote.
“Unlike in Bulgaria, where polling station addresses generally remain unchanged, abroad they often vary from one election to the next. This applies in particular to polling stations located outside diplomatic missions,” Stoynova explained.
She added that a dedicated section for the presidential election had been created on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website, listing the addresses of all polling stations abroad, BTA and BGNES reported.

Israeli election to test Netanyahu's ability to hold power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:27:06 UTC
22:27:06 KST

Israeli election to test Benjamin Netanyahu's ability to hold power
Tens of thousands marched in Tel Aviv last night demanding Benjamin Netanyahu's government answer for the failures that led to the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks. "We cannot be a dictatorship!" said one woman. "And we cannot have these criminals running our country."
Tuesday will be the first parliamentary elections since the attacks. Thirty-nine parties are running, but essentially one man is on the ballot: Netanyahu. Over three decades, Netanyahu — known here as Bibi — has dominated Israeli politics.
And in a market outside Tel Aviv, opinions about the prime minister are as varied as the offerings here.
Asked whom he will vote for, restaurant owner Benny Abraham replied, "Likud and Bibi Netanyahu."
"Bibi can handle the whole world," Abraham said. "Bibi is charismatic. He has a strong voice. The world loves him." He added affectionately, "He's the king of Israel."
Many others, like Liat and her husband Sharon, could be lumped into the "Anyone but Bibi" camp. "I don't hate him, OK, I think he did the good things to Israel, but no more," said Liat.
Sharon described Netanyahu as "more or less, very good politician, but not a [good manager]."
The divide on Netanyhu stems from controversial changes sidelining the country's judiciary; an ongoing trial on corruption charges; and allegations he failed to heed prior warnings about Oct. 7.
While some people say they feel Netanyahu protects Israel, 80-year-old Margalit Moses told us she does not feel the prime minister protects her. Moses was kidnapped by Hamas in the Oct. 7 attack. Nearly a third of the residents of her kibbutz, Nir Oz, were killed or captured. Oct. 7 moved many Israelis further to the right — but not Moses.
"I hope people will understand that we have to change the government so the new government will be more middle, or a little bit left," she said. "We'll change the mind in Israel about the Arabs. If we can make peace with them and live in peace with them, it's, for me, very important."
Netanyahu's campaign has framed these elections as existential for Israelis. In an intersection less than a mile from the Gaza Strip, political posters read "Right or Palestine," with members of the opposition parties depicted on the left.
Leading the opposition challenge is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff. His son was killed fighting Hamas shortly after the Gaza War began. Eisenkot left Netanyahu's government in 2024, accusing him of prolonging the war and delaying a hostage deal to appease his right-wing coalition partners.
"For Israelis, [Eisenkot] represents the anti-Bibi, something more pragmatic," said political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin. She says that while President Trump endorsed Netanyahu, Eisenkot is unlikely to dramatically change course on the issues of most concern to Mr. Trump and the U.S.: the wars in Gaza and Iran.
Asked if Eisenkot represents a substantive change in terms of policy, Scheindlin replied, "I think for Israelis, the biggest change he represents is that they expect him to form a government that does not have religious extremists and right-wing ultra-nationalist populists, and doesn't have Jewish supremacists. The biggest things that he would do differently is that he wants to establish a state commission of inquiry into Oct. 7 and draft the ultra-Orthodox. And those are two overpowering issues in Israeli life, particularly for the opposition."
Polls show Eisenkot's party with a clear lead, but to form a government he'd likely have to build a coalition with at least four other parties.
Despite what the polls say, Scheindlin says there is still a chance that, a year from now, Netanyahu could still be prime minister: "Absolutely. He is the master of engineering politicians, coalition bargaining. He has more experience than anybody else at masterminding the political system within legal means. And so, we certainly could be in a situation where Netanyahu is prime minister a year from now."

He had been due to attend that event, but cancelled his visit on the advice of doctors to aid his recovery, the Vatican said on Oct 23.
The Pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on Oct 13 after being diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

Kremlin reacts to reports of possible EU negotiator on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:24:18 UTC
22:24:18 KST

Kremlin comments on EU’s Ukraine negotiator quandary
The EU stance on the diplomatic process to settle the Ukraine conflict has not been constructive, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Berliner Zeitung reported earlier this week that Finnish President Alexander Stubb is being seen as the most likely candidate to represent Brussels in possible peace talks with Moscow, Washington, and Kiev. Finland’s proximity to Russia – the two countries share a 1,340 km border – and Stubb’s good relations with US President Donald Trump make him the best fit for the job, according to the paper.
When asked to comment by TASS on Sunday, Peskov said that “the EU has been willing to [appoint a negotiator] for a very long time, but it either cannot do so or lacks the resolve to do so.”
The bloc’s stance “can hardly be called constructive” because its leaders “are only talking and not taking any action,” he stressed.
However, the Kremlin spokesman noted that “if there was to be a negotiator – that would be good. And if that negotiator was someone genuinely committed to facilitating a peaceful settlement – that would be even better.”
Peskov did not say how Moscow would react if Stubb is actually given the job. The Finnish president has been one of the staunchest supporters of Ukraine in the EU. In an interview with German tabloid Bild in August, he claimed that Ukraine was “the best security guarantee” that the bloc had against Russia, arguing that “If Ukraine loses, we lose.”
Following a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, Moscow announced that it was ready to restart trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev to settle the Ukraine conflict. The next such meeting could take place in Abu Dhabi in mid-November, according to the Kremlin.
The Telegraph reported on Thursday that there has been “a growing sense of urgency” in Europe to find a representative to join the peace negotiations, despite refusing to talk to Russia for years and insisting on a military solution to the Ukraine conflict.
The paper also placed Stubb on its list of candidates being considered by the EU, which also included Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Czech President Petr Pavel, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and the head of the Norwegian government, Jonas Gahr Store.
Speaking about peace negotiations on Friday, European Commission deputy chief spokesperson Arianna Podesta stressed that “there is an expectation that there will be a multilateral-level discussion with representatives at a senior official level, and the EU will be present at these talks.”
On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that the EU leaders “constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. But I hope that it will pass.”
Putin reiterated that Moscow is not seeking a truce but “definitive, long-term agreements” as a result of the Ukraine peace talks, adding that the discussions should also address a wider all-European security architecture.

A Bar-Ilan University mathematics professor accused of planning mass terrorist attacks against Arabs insisted Sunday that he was mentally sound and did not need psychiatric treatment, as a district court in central Israel declined to order a psychiatric evaluation against his wishes.
"I was normal and I am normal. I'm certain I don't need a psychiatrist," Professor Shahar Nevo told the Central District Court in Lod. Nevo faces charges of preparation to commit an act of terrorism, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice over an alleged plot to carry out coordinated attacks against Arab civilians.
According to the indictment, Nevo devised a plan involving 72 attackers divided into 12 cells, with the aim of killing hundreds of Arab Israelis and Palestinians. Prosecutors allege that he intended to recruit participants and secure support from elements within the military. Nevo has not been convicted of the charges.
During Sunday's hearing, Nevo asked to address the court and complained that the public had been given an incomplete picture of his plan. He said only the first page of a 20-page document had been published, creating what he described as a misleading impression of his intentions.
"At the previous hearing, I was told that the public nature of the proceedings was important. I understand that only the first page of my plan, out of 20 pages, was published," he said. "The first page makes me appear to be someone unleashing a war on the people of Israel all at once. In fact, the main part is on pages two through 20, and I would ask that those pages be published."
Nevo also named two public figures whom he claimed should face prosecution before him: Moshe Feiglin, chairman of the right-wing Zehut party, and podcast host Ori Melamed.
"I don't really see myself as sitting in the defendant's seat. I understand that I'm in legal proceedings," Nevo said. "There are two people who should be here before me: Moshe Feiglin and Ori Melamed. These two people are among the most extreme on the right."
Feiglin was mentioned in Nevo's alleged plan as a political figure he hoped to enlist, but he did not comply with any of Nevo's demands. Melamed's name has not otherwise appeared in the case. Neither was accused of involvement in the alleged plot.
Nevo also complained about his detention conditions at Ayalon Prison, asking to be transferred to the religious wing. "The conditions in the transit facility at Ayalon are very bad for me," he told the court. "I was told this wasn't the time, but I'm asking to move to the religious wing of Ayalon Prison. It would help me greatly."
A central issue during the hearing was whether Nevo should undergo psychiatric evaluation. He strongly opposed the possibility, saying he had never previously received such an assessment and saw no reason to undergo one now.
"I've never been examined psychiatrically. I've never gone anywhere near those areas, and I don't want to," he said. "I think I'm perfectly fine."
Nevo pointed to his academic career as evidence that he had been functioning normally throughout the period in which he allegedly developed the plan. "I held a position as a university professor while preparing the plan and working on it," he said. "I ask the court not to push in that direction. I was normal and I am normal. I'm certain I don't need a psychiatrist."
His attorneys, Hadar Sharir and Alon Porat of the Public Defender's Office, told the court that after reviewing the investigative materials, they accepted the existence of prima facie evidence against their client. However, they argued that the evidence presented a more complicated legal picture than the indictment suggested.
"We will reserve our arguments for the main proceedings," the defense attorneys said. "A considerably more moderate picture emerges than the one reflected in the facts of the indictment." Their position did not amount to an admission of guilt.
At the conclusion of the hearing, Judge Eliana Danieli accepted the parties' positions and ruled that there was no justification for ordering a psychiatric evaluation against Nevo's wishes. She noted that neither the prosecution nor the defense had requested such an assessment and that Nevo had expressly opposed one at both the previous hearing and Sunday's proceedings.
The judge emphasized that compelling someone to undergo psychiatric evaluation, particularly under hospitalization conditions, was a serious and intrusive measure. She also noted the prosecution's position that Nevo had behaved rationally and logically during questioning.
"Considering the positions of the parties' attorneys and the respondent himself, and the prosecution's argument that the respondent behaved logically and rationally during his interrogation, I do not find grounds to order an examination against his will," Danieli ruled.

Factbox-What are Brazilian voters’ main concerns?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:17:23 CET
22:17:23 KST

By Isabel Teles
SAO PAULO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Brazilians headed to the ballot box on Sunday, in a runoff vote that pits right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, against leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Here are the main themes that have driven the campaign:
INFLATION
Cost-of-living concerns are widespread. More than two-thirds of respondents told a Quaest poll in August their purchasing power had declined versus the previous year.
• Annual inflation stood at 4.58% in the 12 months through September, above the central bank’s 3% target, pushing prices — including for food — higher
• Lula has pledged to implement measures to allow for steady cuts in borrowing costs and keep inflation under control
• Bolsonaro wants to reduce and stabilize public debt to bring interest rates closer to international levels and steer inflation toward the central bank’s target
CRIME
Crime is another major concern for Brazilians. While Brazil’s homicide rate fell by 40% over the last decade, improvements in fighting crime have been uneven, according to the Brazilian Public Security Forum, a think tank.
• Bolsonaro has pledged a heavy-handed approach to criminals, promising maximum-security prisons and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses
• Lula wants to increase the federal prison system’s capacity to hold gang leaders, while still investing in poor areas to reduce the influence of organized crime
CORRUPTION
Corruption is also at the top of voters’ minds, with both Lula’s circle and Bolsonaro facing scrutiny in high-profile cases.
• A major scandal that led to the collapse of mid-size lender Banco Master has sparked multiple probes, including into Bolsonaro over alleged corruption and money laundering, accusations he denies
• Bolsonaro has pledged to fight corruption by shielding state-run companies and pension funds from political appointments and expanding transparency in public spending
• Lula has vowed to deepen anti-corruption and transparency policies even as his son - who has denied the allegations - is being investigated in probes involving alleged influence peddling, corruption and fraud
PUBLIC FINANCES
Brazil’s public finances are under pressure, especially due to pensions and social benefits. The difficult fiscal outlook has sparked fears of welfare cuts, while many Brazilians are struggling with debt arrears due to years of double-digit interest rates.
• Public debt has risen by more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term, reaching 82.9% of gross domestic product
• Brazil’s benchmark interest rate of 13.75% remains among the highest in the world
• Long-term interest rates fell sharply after Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected first-round performance
• He has promised to ramp up fiscal adjustment, targeting 1.5% of GDP improvement in the primary balance within 18 months to lower borrowing costs
• Lula has reiterated commitments to improve Brazil’s primary balance targeting an effective surplus near 1.3% of GDP by 2030, versus a projected 0.4% deficit this year
FOREIGN POLICY
After US President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a swathe of Brazilian goods in 2025, foreign policy became a more prominent issue for many Brazilians.
• Bolsonaro has courted Trump and other right-wing allies globally
• He wants to rebuild ties with Argentina, the US and Israel, arguing relations with each are close to breaking point
• Lula has campaigned for a foreign policy based on multilateralism and stronger ties with the Mercosur bloc of South American states and the BRICS nations
• ($1 = 5.0086 reais)
(Reporting by Isabel Teles; Addtional reporting by Marcela Ayres, Luciana Magalhaes; Editing by Oliver Griffin and Aurora Ellis)

Tragedy at funeral in Brazil: Man sits on father's grave, falls inside and dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:17:10 UTC
22:17:10 KST

A funeral in Brazil ended in a second tragedy when a 48-year-old man visiting his father's grave fell into the tomb and died after the concrete slab covering it collapsed beneath him.
Adilson Marsaro had arrived at São José Municipal Cemetery in Linhares, in the southeastern Brazilian state of Espírito Santo, to attend the funeral of a friend who had been killed in a road accident. During the ceremony, he decided to visit his father's grave nearby.
According to Brazilian newspaper O Globo, witnesses said Marsaro arrived at the cemetery on a motorcycle and greeted the mourners. He then left his motorcycle and helmet behind and walked toward his father's grave, where he sat down on the concrete covering.
Suddenly, the structure gave way beneath him, sending him falling into the burial chamber. Mourners nearby heard the noise of the collapse and called emergency services. However, by the time rescue teams arrived, Marsaro was already dead. The following day, he was buried in the same cemetery.
Following the tragedy, the municipality of Linhares issued a warning urging visitors to exercise extreme caution when visiting the cemetery, where nearly 18,000 people are buried.
City officials stressed that while the municipality is responsible for cleaning and maintaining the cemetery's public areas, the upkeep and structural maintenance of individual graves remain the responsibility of the families.
The warning comes ahead of All Souls' Day, known in Brazil as Dia de Finados, which falls on Monday, November 2.
Observed annually on the day after All Saints' Day, the holiday has its roots in the Catholic tradition of praying for the dead. In Brazil, it is a national holiday during which millions of people visit cemeteries to honor deceased relatives, clean graves, lay flowers and light candles.
With large crowds expected at cemeteries across the country, local authorities frequently issue safety guidelines and warnings ahead of the holiday, reminding visitors to take precautions around aging graves and burial structures.

Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said a foreign representative was allowed to physically visit Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.
The visit by Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, Pope Leo XIV’s special envoy, marks a potential step toward greater access to Ukrainian captives, whom Russia has largely kept inaccessible to international humanitarian organizations.
Cardinal Zuppi visits Ukrainian POWs
Lubinets said he had been informed that Zuppi was allowed to meet Ukrainian servicemembers held in Russian captivity. The prisoners also confirmed that representatives of Russia’s human rights ombudsman had begun visiting them.
Lubinets said he regularly meets with Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova. At their latest meeting, the two discussed further steps toward returning Ukrainian citizens held by Russia.
“Every exchange is negotiations,” Lubinets said, adding that each one offers a chance to make progress on returning both prisoners of war and civilians.
During his three-day Moscow visit in September, Zuppi also met with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, Russia’s human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, and children’s rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova, according to Vatican News.
The discussions covered missing persons, family reunification, and the return of Ukrainian children, with Zuppi calling for faster checks to help families reunite.
Lubinets said he hoped the new access would continue and pledged to keep working toward the return of all Ukrainian citizens held in Russian places of detention.
Russia blocks access to Ukrainian captives
Russia has kept the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) from accessing Ukrainian prisoners of war since 2024. The ICRC is mandated under the Geneva Conventions to visit prisoners of war and monitor their treatment.
Around 1,500 Ukrainians held by Russia have never had their status as prisoners confirmed by the ICRC and face prosecution, according to Ukraine. Without confirmation of their captivity, their families may lack official acknowledgment of their whereabouts and status.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution
On 23 October, Ukraine returned 270 people from Russian captivity, including 261 military personnel and nine civilians. The released captives included five survivors of Russia’s July 2022 attack on the Olenivka prison barracks, as well as Ukrainian defenders held since 2018.

Trump’s Big Lie About Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Donald Trump has just claimed that the United States had done “a lot” for Ukraine, but that Ukraine has done “nothing” for the United States.
This is unjust in the highest degree. And not just untrue in the normal sense – it is a big lie designed to bring about horror and chaos.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the moment, the United States has agreed to purchase Russian diesel, which breaks its own laws as well as international sanctions agreements, and in effect places America on the Russian side of the war. It is also denying Ukraine access to Starlink services (which have been paid for), thereby making it much harder for Ukraine to defend its people against Russian attacks.
The United States provides almost no military aid to Ukraine, and it has been the policy of the Trump administration to deny such aid.
Europeans purchase American arms and deliver them to Ukraine, but even these contractual agreements are not being met by the American side. The most important weapons in question are Patriot interceptors, which Ukrainians need to defend themselves from Russian ballistic missiles.
In other words, the Trump administration has acted to make Ukrainians more vulnerable to Russian attacks. In case there was any doubt about the general drift of this: The president of the United States has now repeatedly called for the president of Ukraine to leave office. And so the question is not how much the United States is doing for Ukraine. The question is why the United States is working to help the Russian aggressor right now.
‘Trump Is Cooked’: Republicans Clash Over Ukraine as Midterms Loom
But that might not even be the greatest injustice in Trump’s statement that “You know what, we’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us.” Ukrainians have fought the largest war since 1945 for almost five years now. The war is longer than the First World War and longer than the American engagement in the Second World War. They suffer military and civilian casualties every day.
Proportional to population, they have suffered losses on a scale Americans have never experienced, with the exception of the Civil War. They live through the equivalent of a 9/11 in Russian terror attacks every few weeks.
And yet Ukrainians are defending themselves, and very effectively. In so doing they are also giving a great deal to us. Because they have been doing so for so long and so well, it is – sadly – all too easy to take for granted Ukrainian contributions to American and world security. So I will just enumerate a few of them here.
Ukraine is defending the basic principle of international law, which is that states are sovereign and that one state should not seize territory from another by way of aggression.
Ukraine is fulfilling the entire NATO mission, which is to defend Europe from Russian aggression. It is doing the job that NATO assigns to its thirty-two members, which include the United States and Canada. Ukraine is doing this job itself.
Ukraine is making a world war less likely. Russia has already brought to life the most worrying security concern on the scale of Europe, which is a Russian invasion of a European country. On the scale of the world, the greatest risk is Chinese aggression in Taiwan. By defending itself, Ukraine has demonstrated the difficulties in offensive operations and made such a war more likely.
Ukraine is making a nuclear war less likely. Russia is a nuclear power. Ukraine is not. If Russia is allowed to defeat Ukraine, other middle powers will likely draw the conclusion that they need to build nuclear weapons in order to defend themselves. By holding back Russia, Ukraine is also holding back nuclear proliferation.
Ukraine is defending us all from oligarchy, from the rule of the very wealthy. Putin’s idea that Ukraine is not a real country is the example of an oligarchic fantasy, the kind of centibillionaire nonsense that can take lives and destroy the planet. By resisting Russian aggression, Ukraine is showing that democracy can defend itself.
Ukraine is providing an example of freedom. In Ukraine, even during conditions of war, civil society functions, and people speak their minds. Under Russian occupation, an entirely different mode of life prevails: Women are raped; children are deported to Russia to be assimilated; local activists are murdered; young men are forced into the Russian army to die; total uniformity is imposed.
And so what Trump says is wrong in the very broadest of senses. Ukraine is doing work for our security and for our liberty. Ukrainians have held off the worst and bought the rest of us time.
And Trump’s claim is also wrong in the narrow sense. Ukraine has been providing battlefield intelligence to the United States from the beginning of the war. It has shared its experience of modern warfare with American institutions. It even sent – in these most trying of times inside Ukraine – hundreds of its own experienced air defense troops to the Near East to help protect Americans and their allies from Iranian drones.
Imagine what those Ukrainian crews, separated from their embattled country to defend Americans, are thinking right now, as their contributions are denied, and as their own families are put in greater danger by US policy.
Trump’s statement is not only unjust. It is not only a lie. It is a big lie, whose purpose is not to describe the world but to change it, to blame the victim and assist the aggressor, to betray the ally and destroy the alliances, to create a world in which everyone must feel unsafe except the wealthy and powerful, a world in which all that matters are the personal feelings and personal dealings of a handful of oligarchs and dictators.

EU members’ mistakes behind mass protests – Putin
The recent wave of protests that swept across Western Europe were the result of the EU’s own mistakes, Russian President Vladimir Putin said. European countries, he added, are struggling to manage the migration crisis.
“Europeans are dismantling their own traditions, so they are even less able to convey them to migrants,” Putin told journalist Pavel Zarubin.
Mass protests took place again over the weekend. Demonstrators, reportedly angry over soaring living costs and inept government policies clashed with riot police in several cities.
The anti-givernment unrest has largely been inspired by the protests in France, which began in September and then spread to other countries.
Putin said some European leaders are unable to take responsibility for unrest. Instead of analyzing the situation and identifying its causes they tend to blame other countries – first the US and now Russia, he said.
“But they quickly came to their senses and reverted to their traditional accusations against Russia. My first reaction when I saw this was surprise, because to claim that we are provoking mass protests in major European cities is really going too far,” the president said, adding that it reflects the leaders’ weakness in being unable to tackle the situation.
Putin believes Europe lacks the resources to integrate all migrants, and that has led to a crisis.
France remains a focal point of the protests, with at least 410,000 people taking to the streets nationwide on Saturday, including around 110,000 in Paris, according to French Interior Ministry figures.
Protests have also taken place across Italy, following a wave of violence last weekend in cities including Rome, Naples and Bologna. Police deployed water cannons and tear gas to disperse unruly demonstrators.
Major anti-government demonstrations have also been held in Brussels, Belgium and Lisbon, Portugal with thousands marching against soaring rents and unaffordable housing. Spain has joined the weekend of protests too, with a massive pensioners’ demonstration held in Madrid. On Friday night, protests erupted in the center of Barcelona with over 100 people arrested overnight.

Not sure who to vote for? Here are Israel’s main political parties and what they stand for ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:10:12 UTC
22:10:12 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Not sure who to vote for? Here are the main political parties ahead of Israeli elections
Not sure who to vote for? Here are the main political parties ahead of Israeli elections
From Netanyahu’s Likud to Eisenkot’s Yashar and Winter’s Amcha Israel, the contenders differ on security, military service, religion and the courts
Israel’s election on Tuesday brings together longstanding political rivals and new challengers competing over the country’s direction after three years of war.
Security dominates the campaign, alongside disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service, judicial independence and accountability for October 7.
Likud: Netanyahu campaigns on security and experience
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu presents himself as the leader best equipped to confront Israel’s enemies and manage its international relationships. Likud’s campaign highlights military achievements against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran, while critics point to the October 7 attack occurring on his watch.
The right-wing party favors a strong military presence along Israel’s fronts and changes to the judiciary. Netanyahu’s dependence on ultra-Orthodox coalition partners complicates efforts to expand military recruitment, making the draft a central political challenge.
Yashar: Eisenkot offers security credentials and institutional reform
Former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot has emerged as a leading challenger to Netanyahu. His new party combines a security-focused approach with promises to rebuild public trust and strengthen democratic institutions.
Its priorities include a state commission of inquiry into October 7, rebuilding affected communities, military or national service for all, stronger public education and greater economic competition. Eisenkot also advocates a constitution and safeguards for an independent judiciary.
Beyachad: Bennett and Lapid seek a comeback
Former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid have joined forces in an alliance combining right-wing and centrist constituencies. Their platform emphasizes security, ultra-Orthodox integration into military service and employment, support for reservists and constitutional reform.
After losing ground earlier in the campaign, Beyachad has seen a modest recovery in recent weeks. Kan’s final poll gave it 14 seats, up two from the previous survey, while Channel 12 projected 15. The improvement strengthens its position in the opposition camp, although Bennett has not committed to backing Eisenkot for prime minister.
Yisrael Beiteinu: Hawkish security and secular government
Avigdor Lieberman’s party combines hard-line security policies with a strong secular agenda. Once associated primarily with immigrants from the former Soviet Union, it now seeks broader support among voters demanding universal service and reduced religious influence over public life.
Its priorities include military or national service for ultra-Orthodox and Arab citizens, greater separation between religion and state, and a tougher approach to Israel’s enemies. Lieberman’s opposition to cooperation with ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties could complicate coalition negotiations.
Otzma Yehudit: Ben-Gvir’s far-right security agenda
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s party advocates expanded Israeli sovereignty, settlement growth and a tougher approach to policing and terrorism.
Its proposals include Israeli resettlement of Gaza, encouraging Palestinian emigration, wider civilian access to firearms and the death penalty for terrorists. Supporters portray these policies as necessary for security; opponents regard them as extremist and damaging to Israel’s international standing.
Religious Zionism–Zehut: Settlements, Jewish identity and smaller government
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party is running with Moshe Feiglin’s Zehut. The alliance supports expanding settlements, extending Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank and opposing Palestinian statehood.
Religious Zionism emphasizes the state’s Jewish character and limiting judicial authority. Zehut brings a libertarian economic agenda centered on smaller government, reduced bureaucracy and greater private initiative.
The Democrats: Golan champions the Zionist left
Yair Golan leads the party formed through the merger of Labor and Meretz. It opposes annexation, favors a diplomatic resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and supports cooperation with moderate regional partners.
Domestically, it advocates stronger democratic safeguards, universal service, civil marriage, recognition of non-Orthodox conversions and greater investment in public services. Its willingness to cooperate with Arab parties distinguishes it from much of the Zionist opposition.
Shas and United Torah Judaism: Protecting ultra-Orthodox interests
Both parties prioritize Torah study, religious institutions and opposition to compulsory military service for yeshiva students.
Shas primarily represents Sephardi and Mizrahi ultra-Orthodox communities and also emphasizes assistance for lower-income households. United Torah Judaism represents Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox communities, with a strong focus on religious education and communal autonomy. Their resistance to draft legislation is a major dividing line with opposition parties demanding a broader sharing of military service.
Ra’am: Abbas prioritizes practical gains for Arab citizens
Mansour Abbas’s Islamic-rooted, socially conservative party focuses on tackling crime, improving housing and securing investment in Arab communities.
Ra’am joined the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021 and argues that participation in government delivers more than remaining in opposition. This election, it has placed former senior police officer and Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz second on its slate, reinforcing its focus on fighting organized crime and cooperation across communal lines.
Amcha Israel: Winter faces pressure from Netanyahu
Retired brigadier general Ofer Winter’s new right-wing party emphasizes decisive military action, opposition to Palestinian statehood and universal service. Its slate includes Arab Israeli activist Yoseph Haddad as Winter’s deputy, while its demands for sharing the service burden could create friction with ultra-Orthodox parties.
Despite Winter’s early endorsement of Netanyahu, Likud has intensified its campaign against Amcha Israel, arguing that votes could be lost if it fails to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold.
Candidate Davidi Ben Zion quit the slate amid pressure and concerns about wasting right-wing votes. Netanyahu welcomed his departure and urged others to follow.
Winter subsequently acknowledged that committing so early to recommending only Netanyahu might have been a mistake, while maintaining that he would remain in the right-wing camp. The dispute has become a prominent fight within the right as Amcha Israel battles to enter the Knesset.

Israel to close all West Bank land crossings on election day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:09:00 UTC

Israel to close all West Bank land crossings on election day
October 25, 2026
The Israeli military said on Sunday that all land crossings between Israel and the West Bank will be closed during Tuesday's parliamentary election.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that, from Sunday, Palestinians would "not be permitted to enter Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley for work" — using terms used by many in Israel to refer to the occupied territories in the West Bank.
The army added that it would enforce "a ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers … as well as the closure of all land crossings throughout Election Day" on October 27.
The announcement came amid an ongoing Israeli military operation in the West Bank following a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen near the city of Hebron on Friday.
Two Israeli soldiers were killed and three others injured in the attack, according to the IDF, which said the two suspected attackers were also killed.
The Palestinian militant group Hamas hailed the attack but did not claim credit for carrying it out.
What have Israeli politicians said?
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to exact a heavy price for the attack which came just days before the poll in which he is facing a tough battle to secure a new term.
The Israeli army said it had been operating in 40 areas throughout the West Bank on Friday and Saturday, with locals reporting that soldiers had announced evacuations over loudspeakers late at night.
Israeli forces said they had "apprehended approximately 40 suspects, including terrorists affiliated with the Hamas and Islamic Jihad terrorist organizations."
The mayor of Hebron, Yousef al-Jabari, told broadcaster Al Jazeera that some 2,200 people had been forced from their homes since Israeli raids began on Friday.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz confirmed that figure, telling Israeli broadcaster Kan that "selected army units are currently operating there" and that Palestinians "will not be allowed to return … until we've finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron."
Israel's far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a Defense Ministry position overseeing civilian affairs in the West Bank, said he personally ordered "the immediate demolition of a row of illegal structures" in the territory following Friday's shooting.
"Anyone who messes with us will quickly understand that he will pay a painful price," he wrote on social media.
What have Palestinians in Hebron said?
In the Hebron neighborhood of Ein Deir Baha, vacated buildings were marked by X's and the streets were deserted, except for a handful of Israeli military vehicles, reported the AFP news agency, which added that Israeli flags had been draped on a house apparently taken over by troops.
Higazi Shawer al-Tamimi, 70, a shopkeeper with a senior role in the neighborhood, told AFP he was awakened at 1 a.m. by soldiers who said he had to leave and gave him only a short time to pack.
He added that, for other residents, leaving the neighborhood was much more difficult. "My wife's mother, who is 90 years old and lives in the area, had to be carried out because she is ill," he said.
In Al-Tamimi's opinion, the West Bank operation is taking place because Netanyahu wants to win the election with "the blood of the Palestinian people."
Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister but his security-first reputation was shattered by the deadly attack by Hamas fighters on October 7, 2023, in which more than 1,200 Israelis were killed. The attack sparked an Israeli invasion of Gaza which has left over 73,000 Palestinians dead, many of them civilians.
Following Friday's attack, Netanyahu vowed the response so far would be followed by an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967.

Lone soldiers, b'not sherut find a true home at the Michael Levin Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:08:05 UTC
22:08:05 KST

"That’s where I find family. That’s where I find community. That’s where I feel at home.”
This was a female lone soldier’s response to the question of whether she knew of the Michael Levin Base. The soldier, who had made aliyah from Atlanta a year earlier, met the base’s co-founder Richard Corman by chance in synagogue. Corman had approached her, as he often does when he sees soldiers, simply to thank her for her service.
Corman recounted the conversation earlier this month during his speech at the annual MLB gala, the title of which was “Three Years Since Oct. 7: Where Are We Today?” When Corman told the soldier that he had helped establish the base, she became emotional and thanked him. His response reversed the gratitude: “It’s an honor to meet you.”
About the base
The Michael Levin Base is a nonprofit supporting lone soldiers and lone b’nei sherut before, during, and after their service.
Founded in 2020, it was named in memory of lone soldier Michael Levin, who made aliyah from the Philadelphia area and volunteered to serve in the Paratroopers Brigade. Levin experienced firsthand the challenges of being a lone soldier and spoke about creating stronger support for others serving far from home. He was killed aged 22 in the Second Lebanon War in 2006.
The base provides meals, practical assistance, mental-health and emotional support, laundry facilities, community programming, guidance and post-service resources for young adults serving Israel without immediate family support nearby.
That mission has taken on added weight since Oct. 7. At the gala, the organization’s leadership said demand for its services had grown exponentially, with more young people seeking advice, Shabbat and holiday meals, supplies, laundry facilities, and, increasingly, trauma counseling.
What began with $100,000 in seed funding and the hope that soldiers would simply show up now serves approximately 3,600 young men and women. The base runs more than 70 programs and events each month and has expanded its support across English-, Hebrew-, Russian-, French-, and Spanish-speaking communities.
As such, the vision of Levin has now become a critical, lifesaving reality for thousands of soldiers and National Service volunteers.
As President Isaac Herzog put it in a prerecorded address opening the gala, “Michael Levin knew what it means to be a young person living alone in Israel while serving with every ounce of his being in the IDF.... There is something so beautiful about the fact that his memory has become a calling for so many to give his vision meaning in the present.”
Herzog said Levin had wanted others facing the same challenge to have “the support, the resources, the warmth, and the security” that come from community and belonging.
The Michael Levin Base seeks to provide that support system, serving as a home away from home and providing a loving family for those serving without nearby support systems in Israel.
New, larger Jerusalem center
In June, growing demand led the organization to open a Tel Aviv branch, bringing its services closer to soldiers living in central Israel.
In September, it also opened Habayit, a partnership serving religious lone b’not sherut and female lone soldiers. Forty young women attended its first Shabbat meal. The Jerusalem base will be moving to a permanent, expanded center on Jaffa Road in January 2027.
The larger center is expected to more than double the number of lone soldiers and b’not sherut the organization can host for Shabbat meals and other events.
The gala also brought into focus what the term “lone soldier” can obscure. Choosing to serve is not simply a decision to put on a uniform. It can mean leaving behind parents, friends, language, and an entire support system before confronting the pressures of military service itself.
Showing up for those in need
Panamanian Ambassador Ezra Cohen described that transition in personal terms. Panama currently has seven lone soldiers serving in Israel, he said, and at one point had 16.
For Cohen, the need for a support network became particularly tangible during Sukkot.
He recounted receiving a call during the recent holiday from “a very worried father from Panama, whose son is a brave soldier who was on the front lines and then got depression.
“The father said: ‘Ezra, please see what you can do.’ So I immediately contacted Michael Levin, and within hours they spoke to him, his superiors, and they are taking care of him.”
For Cohen, this anecdote demonstrated the way in which the base shows up for those in need; how it makes sure a soldier thousands of miles from his family does not have to navigate a crisis alone.
“After Oct. 7, we as a Jewish society, Israel as a country, is much stronger. But our soldiers need their support, need their comfort zone, need to be in a family. So when we host many of our lone soldiers at our home on Shabbat and we talk about their experience, they express we are not alone. And this is the core of the Michael Levin Base Foundation.”
Lt.-Col. Jonathan Conricus, former IDF international spokesperson, echoed that message while placing lone soldiers within the wider story of the war.
Conricus recalled joining IDF forces during the early ground operation at Shifa Hospital in Gaza (at the start of the war). There, he met a reservist who had previously been a lone soldier and who had returned to Israel from the US on one of the first flights after Oct. 7 to rejoin his unit.
At a point when Israel had yet to gain control over much of Gaza, and the trajectory of the war remained undetermined, Conricus said meeting that soldier and his comrades gave him confidence that Israel would endure. He called that spirit Israel’s “X factor.”
Because of this, he said the work of the base in helping “our brave soldiers, specifically our lone soldiers, have a home away from home” is so “crucial.”
Thousands strong
Nearly seven years after the organization began, Corman returned to the encounter with the young soldier from Atlanta. Her answer had simplified the base’s expanding programs, new branches, and thousands of participants to the three most important things: family, community, and home.
For Corman, this is the whole point. “We started from scratch, hoping that people would come,” he told the audience. Today, the base serves approximately 3,600 young men and women.
“I pray and hope that the Michael Levin Base continues to be strong and grows to respond to the modern-day heroes of Israel.”

Ukrainian Company F-Drones Develops Low-Cost F-Jet 80 Interceptor to Counter Shaheds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:07:52 UTC
22:07:52 KST

Ukrainian company F-Drones is developing the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor drone designed to counter Russian jet-powered strike drones.
The New York Times reported this.
The new drone is being positioned as a low-cost interception system, with a target price of around $7,000.
To improve accuracy, engineers plan to equip the interceptor with artificial intelligence to help detect and pursue aerial targets.
In comments to Militarnyi, the developers said the project aims to create an interceptor powered by a compact jet engine producing 8-10 kgf of thrust.
One of the main development challenges is keeping the drone’s cost low. The developers aim to keep the price between $5,000 and $7,000 to enable simple, mass production.
Thanks to its jet engine, the F-Jet 80 is intended to counter Russian Geran-type jet-powered drones.
According to Ihor, an engineer-designer at the company, the drone has already intercepted and destroyed several targets.
Russia is expanding its use of jet-powered strike drones in its war against Ukraine. Traditional kamikaze drones powered by internal combustion engines fly relatively slowly, making them easy targets for Ukrainian interceptor drones.
Jet engines allow drones to fly faster and pass through areas covered by air defense systems more quickly.
Militarnyi previously reported that Russia had increased production of Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered strike drones to 4,000 units per month. This is twice the production volume of piston-powered Geran-2 drones.
Meanwhile, intelligence data indicate that Russia produces around 2,000 piston-powered Geran-2 drones each month.

Netanyahu trial defense presses Mandelblit over Eshel wiretap he ordered halted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:07:43 UTC
22:07:43 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s defense pressed former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit on Sunday over whether investigators exceeded his authorization, as Judge Moshe Bar-Am questioned how police were supposed to distinguish between steps they could have taken independently and those requiring further approval.
The sixth day of Mandelblit’s testimony at the Jerusalem District Court focused on a wiretap of Netanyahu confidant Natan Eshel that Mandelblit ordered stopped, and on the early inquiries that developed into the criminal cases against the prime minister.
Defense lawyer Amit Hadad argued that investigators gathered evidence through unauthorized actions and then used it to secure permission to investigate further. Mandelblit maintained that he had approved examining defined subjects, while acknowledging that the Eshel wiretap should have been brought to him beforehand.
Under Basic Law: The Government, opening a criminal investigation into a sitting prime minister requires the attorney-general’s consent. Hadad’s questioning has sought to establish exactly what Mandelblit approved, when he approved it, and whether investigators stayed within those limits.
Mandelblit, who authorized the investigations and later approved the indictment, was called as a defense witness. Netanyahu’s trial began in May 2020 and concerns three cases involving alleged gifts and dealings with media owners. He denies wrongdoing in all three.
Mandelblit angry about Eshel wiretap
On Sunday, Mandelblit said he had been angered to discover that police were tapping Eshel, a close Netanyahu associate involved in his personal and political affairs. Investigators had obtained a court warrant, but Mandelblit said they had not sought his approval.
“When I discovered it had been done, I ordered it stopped immediately,” he said.
Hadad argued that Netanyahu was the operation’s real target, pointing to references in the warrant to Eshel’s contact with the principal suspect, described as “a senior elected official.”
Prosecutor Keren Tzviran disputed that interpretation. She said the warrant concerned suspicions against Eshel himself, and that references to Netanyahu did not make every suspected offense listed in it an allegation against the prime minister.
Mandelblit said he had not been specifically told that numerous conversations between Eshel and Netanyahu had been intercepted. He said his concern was the sensitivity of listening so closely to someone so involved in the prime minister’s affairs.
Investigations into alleged gifts may have gone beyond A-G orders
The questioning then returned to the development of Case 1000, which concerns expensive gifts Netanyahu allegedly received from businessmen Arnon Milchan and James Packer, and actions he allegedly took to benefit Milchan. Netanyahu faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in that case.
Hadad challenged whether permission to examine accommodation associated with Packer at the Royal Beach Hotel extended to questioning Milchan’s assistant, Hadas Klein, and driver Yonatan Hasson about gifts to Netanyahu and his wife.
Mandelblit said he had not known the details of that questioning. He maintained, however, that he had not stopped the broader examination of suspicions that Netanyahu received substantial benefits from business people.
Bar-Am pressed him on how investigators were meant to understand those boundaries, asking whether the permission amounted to blanket approval to examine Netanyahu’s affairs.
Mandelblit rejected that characterization. The subject itself set the limits, he said, and investigators were expected to return to him as significant suspicions developed. They did not need approval for every individual action.
Bar-Am questioned whether investigators needed more concrete instructions to prevent them from mistakenly doing something they were not permitted to do. Mandelblit said regular meetings were intended to provide that oversight.
He also distinguished the early information about cigars and champagne from the evidence that later persuaded him to authorize a full investigation. What changed his assessment, he said, was information suggesting a regular supply of gifts and the use of code names, which he viewed as indicating concealment.
Mandelblit said the wording police proposed for Netanyahu’s first questioning had angered him because he believed it pushed Case 1000 toward bribery, while he viewed the suspicions as closer to breach-of-trust issues.
The distinction is critical to the charges ultimately filed. Netanyahu faces fraud and breach-of-trust allegations in both Case 1000 and Case 2000, which concerns discussions with Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon Mozes about favorable coverage in exchange for steps against rival newspaper Israel Hayom.
The bribery charge is in Case 4000, alongside fraud and breach of trust. Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu advanced regulatory measures benefiting telecommunications company Bezeq in exchange for intervention in the Walla news website’s coverage.

High Court strikes down petition to end sperm donor anonymity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:07:35 UTC
22:07:35 KST

The High Court of Justice has struck down a petition seeking to allow children conceived through sperm donation to learn the identity of their biological father, leaving in place the rule that keeps donors anonymous.
The issue was raised in a High Court petition by the organizations Choosing Family and B’Tzalmo, which oppose anonymous donation, and the court asked to hear the ministry’s position. The panel can either leave the current anonymous-only system in place or allow two parallel tracks, anonymous and non-anonymous; adopting its recommendations would require changes to existing legislation.
The petitioners argued that the provision guaranteeing donor anonymity violates children’s right to know who their biological parents are.
Israel currently permits only anonymous sperm donation. Under the Public Health Regulations, disclosing identifying donor details is prohibited.
A woman who wants to conceive with a man she knows must present a parenting agreement between them that overrides any other arrangement, meaning there is no route to an identified donation without a commitment to fatherhood behind it.
Who regulates sperm donation in Israel?
Sperm donation in Israel is not regulated by primary legislation; every donor signs a form confirming the donation is anonymous and that no identifying detail will be passed to the woman purchasing the sample.
Last year, the Justice Ministry published regulations for a database registering egg donations that will also record whether the mother was fertilized with a sperm donation, in which case the donor’s code will be registered.
The move followed a petition filed five years earlier by Choosing Family and B’Tzalmo demanding a registry to prevent marriages between relatives, given that a man can donate at several sperm banks and there was no orderly registration of donors.
