The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine published information on 30 units of foreign-made technological equipment used by Russian enterprises to manufacture ballistic missiles and their components. This was reported by UNN with reference to data from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
Despite sanctions restrictions, Russia’s military-industrial complex continues to depend on foreign technologies.
Details
On the War&Sanctions portal, Ukrainian intelligence published data on equipment manufactured in China, Germany, Taiwan, the United States, Turkey, Switzerland, and Italy, which is used by Russian enterprises to manufacture missiles, altimeters, aerodynamic control surfaces, gyroscopes, and other weapons components. The Main Directorate of Intelligence notes that Russia is still unable to fully replace the industrial equipment of the world’s leading manufacturers with domestic analogues.
At the same time, the number of Chinese machine tools and machining centers, including five-axis ones, is increasing at Russian defense enterprises. Chinese equipment also depends on foreign components, including European, Japanese, and Taiwanese numerical control systems, servomotors, high-precision spindles, bearings, and measurement systems.
Among the equipment identified by intelligence:
-  the GX-650 five-axis universal machining center manufactured by the Chinese company Hyper Machine Tool, which is used by the Votkinsk Plant. The enterprise manufactures 9M723 "Iskander-M" ballistic missiles and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 "Kinzhal" air-launched ballistic missile; 
-  turning and milling machining centers manufactured by the Chinese company Shtral, which are used by the "PEMZ \"Molot\"" enterprise to produce electronic equipment units for "Iskander-M" missiles; 
-  measurement equipment manufactured by the German company Rohde & Schwarz, installed at the "UPKB \"Detal\"" enterprise, which manufactures altimeters for "Zircon" missiles. 
The Main Directorate of Intelligence emphasizes that, in order to limit Russia’s ability to continue producing weapons, it is necessary to strengthen international control over the supply of industrial equipment and components. In particular, intelligence calls for checking the end users of products and the actual locations where they are used, controlling the supply of spare parts, software, and consumables, and regularly auditing distributors and intermediaries.
They propose paying particular attention to investigating cases in which foreign products reach Russia’s military-industrial complex and identifying their supply chains.
In addition, Ukrainian intelligence calls for restricting the supply of numerical control systems, tools, and other components to Chinese manufacturers whose equipment is delivered to Russian defense industry enterprises.

This, as noted, reduces the enemy’s capabilities to attack Ukraine and civilian infrastructure with drones of various modifications.
-  "the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the city of Tolyatti, Samara region, rf, struck on October 24. A process pipeline, two butyl rubber production units, and one rectification unit were damaged". 
This, as reported, strikes at the production chain for solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.
"The Defense Forces of Ukraine are striking the enemy’s military facilities within the framework of the right to self-defense guaranteed by Article 51 of the UN Charter," the General Staff emphasized.

Following the extension of martial law, the Verkhovna Rada extended mobilization
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada, by a vote of 281, extended general mobilization for another 90 days starting October 31, 2026. Earlier, Parliament extended martial law.
On October 26, the Verkhovna Rada supported extending the period of the general mobilization for 90 days from October 31, 2026, UNN reports.
Details
"Parliament extended the period of the general mobilization in Ukraine (No. 16183). A total of 281 members of parliament voted in favor. The document provides for extending the period of the general mobilization in Ukraine from October 31, 2026, for 90 days," the parliament said.
According to MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak in a social media post, "also for 90 days, that is, from October 31, 2026, to January 29, 2027."
Prior to this, martial law in Ukraine was extended for 90 days.
Parliament supported the extension of martial law in Ukraine26.10.26, 12:50 • 692 views

Earlier, on October 26, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy submitted to the Verkhovna Rada draft laws proposing to extend martial law in Ukraine (No. 16182) and the general mobilization (No. 16183) for another 90 days.
According to the explanatory note, the first proposes "extending the period of martial law in Ukraine from 5:30 a.m. on October 31, 2026, for 90 days."
According to the explanatory note, the second provides that "the period of the general mobilization is extended from October 31, 2026, for 90 days."

Vice speaker of Slovak Parliament opposes funding Ukraine with frozen Russian assets
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Vice speaker of Slovak Parliament opposes funding Ukraine with frozen Russian assets
Vice Speaker of the Slovak Parliament Tibor Gašpar has called the confiscation of frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine's military needs unacceptable.
Source: European Pravda, citing Gašpar in an interview with the Russian agency TASS
Details: Gašpar said that regarding the issue of frozen Russian assets, Slovakia emphasises the need for a thorough legal assessment, caution and consideration of the long-term consequences of any decisions made.
Quote from Gašpar: "In November 2025, Prime Minister of the Slovak Republic Robert Fico expressed disagreement with the proposal to confiscate frozen Russian assets and use them to fund Ukraine's military needs. Such an approach towards confrontation and confiscation is unacceptable."
Details: As Gašpar recalled, Fico drew particular attention to possible litigation, the risk of retaliatory measures and the consequences of such a move for future peace negotiations.
Quote from Gašpar: "At the same time, he stressed that using these assets for the post-war reconstruction of Ukraine could be more appropriate than directing them towards the further funding of military operations. The Slovak Republic is interested in ensuring that any decision in this sphere has a clear legal basis, complies with international obligations and minimises the risk of further deterioration in international relations."
Details: Furthermore, according to Gašpar, it is necessary to seek sustainable solutions for financing Ukraine's reconstruction that will promote regional stability and create conditions for establishing long-term peace.
Background:
- Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever recently expressed confidence that the European Commission will not reopen discussions on using frozen Russian assets held in Euroclear to finance Ukraine.
- During the EU leaders' summit on 16 October, De Wever firmly opposed discussions on the idea of using frozen assets belonging to Russia's Central Bank.
- Meanwhile, Vsevolod Chentsov, Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration, proposed using Russian funds frozen in Europe for Ukraine's needs in phases – an idea that, in his view, could help shift Belgium's position.

Royal Navy frigate crisis deepens as old warships wear out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:03:21 UTC
21:03:21 KST

- Two of the Royal Navy’s five remaining Type 23 frigates are expected to be declared unseaworthy, Navy Lookout reported, citing industry insiders.
- That could leave three frigates in service in 2027, with only one available for operations at a time.
Britain’s Royal Navy could be left with just one frigate available for operations at any given time next year, as two more of its five remaining Type 23 frigates are expected to be declared unseaworthy within months, leaving three ships in service in 2027 with one at sea, one in training and one in maintenance, British tabloid The Sun reported, citing a report by naval news site Navy Lookout.
Navy Lookout said industry insiders had told it that two of the five Type 23s will almost certainly have to be declared unseaworthy in the next few months, without naming the ships. The fleet now consists of HMS Kent, which has been in refit for more than two years, along with HMS Portland, Somerset, St Albans and Sutherland, which cover the navy’s main anti-submarine tasks. The youngest of the four was commissioned in 2002, in a class designed for an 18-year service life, and the ships are being retired because their light steel hulls are corroding beyond economic repair.
The frigates hunt Russian submarines in the North Atlantic, protect the Royal Navy’s nuclear-armed ballistic missile submarines as they leave and return to port, and guard undersea communications cables around the British Isles. Former frigate captain Cmdr. Tom Sharpe told The Sun that two tasks cannot be dropped, the towed array patrol ship that tracks Russian submarines in the North Atlantic and the Fleet Ready Escort that responds to threats in British waters, and that keeping even one ship available from a fleet of three becomes harder as the hulls age.
“If we are down to three frigates there will be times when none are available. We are wide open,” said Cmdr. Tom Sharpe.
The warning followed a House of Commons Defence Committee report on defense in the High North, published last week, which found that the navy’s readiness and ship numbers fall far short of the government’s own requirements. The committee cited an internal NATO assessment that reportedly ranks Britain 31st of 32 allies on the speed of rearmament, ahead only of Iceland, and recommended that no further towed-array Type 23 leave service until a new Type 26 frigate replaces it on a one-for-one basis.
“The current reality could hardly be bleaker,” the committee said.
The Royal Navy has had a minimum requirement for 19 frigates and destroyers since 2010, but now operates 11: six Type 45 destroyers and five Type 23 frigates. HMS Richmond and HMS Iron Duke were retired in July, Iron Duke less than three years after a £103 million (about $138 million) life-extension refit, and The Sun reported that around half of the remaining escorts have not sailed for two years.
Replacements are running late. The first Type 26 anti-submarine frigate, HMS Glasgow, is now expected to start contractor sea trials in the first half of 2027, almost a decade after construction began, with initial operating capability planned for October 2028, while the Ministry of Defence says only that the first Type 31 general-purpose frigates will arrive “by the end of the decade.” According to Navy Lookout’s reading of the committee report, the combined frigate force could fall to two ships in 2031 and not recover to eight until 2037.
The warnings come as Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said Russia could be ready to attack by 2030 and that Britain must prepare accordingly.
“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
The Ministry of Defence said the Royal Navy continues to meet its operational commitments around the world while bringing new maritime capabilities into service, and that it is spending £8 billion (about $10.7 billion) on new ships. The government has two months to respond to the committee’s call for a plan to raise frigate, destroyer and submarine availability before 2030.
